A short and sweet adventure through some crazy computer world where everything (and everyone?) is a computational function. There is an interesting, albeit terse and not very upfront story told in a sort of Dark Souls-esque manner through the new abilities you pick up.
I really like the extensibility and customizability of the weapon and ability choices you get in the game as well. Much like Diablo 3 or Path of Exile, you can mix and match abilities to form new ones depending on the situation. The game's difficulty can be easy or hard, depending on your skill with designing your functions. If it's still not hard enough, there are extra bits you can turn on to make the enemies hit harder, but gain more experience from as a result.
I wish I could play more of it without venturing through the story again. Bastion was great because you could leap in to a sort of arena/arcade mode and play there, but in Transistor you sort of have to gain access to those throughout the story.
All in all, a solid game with great visuals, great flexibility in combat, and an interesting story.

most who review bl2 emphasise on the unique art style, witty humor and freedom of the game. while i can see that many would enjoy the game, i personally just... didn't... maybe it's just me.
the art is great! i think it looks pretty cool, nothing wrong with that.
the "witty humor" i feel comes off as just immature and stupid. it's the same kind of humor that's emphasized heavily in those cheap soap operas that use laugh tracks too much. 'funny' is determined by how stupid the characters act, how ridiculous they look and how unexpected their actions are and personally i just found it annoying.
the game itself was okay. the beginning felt pretty slow, although as the game went on i kind of got into it. after playing for 10+ hours the game just felt so one-dimensional. even with dlcs, the game is simply running through a level and shooting stuff. it's not satisfying shooting like many other run and gun games, it's not creative with it's humor and it doesn't require you to think with any puzzles or other challenges. the game slows down too much imo and it's just retrieving an object for someone or killing an enemy to complete a quest so you can complete the next one... and the next one and the next one.
as for dlc, i enjoyed what they did with several of them, revamping what the shop looks like, while still bringing in characters from the previous quests. again, apart from this, it didn't feel that different from the other quests and got boring pretty quickly.
the class system is pretty one-dimensional, some classes are much more basic that others and though you can allocate skill points into different trees to customize the way you play your character, it still just feels a little lacking.
multiplayer aspect is pretty good, i enjoyed it for the most part. sometimes we had trouble joining each other's games but eh, every game is like that.
borderlands 2 is far from a bad game, but i personally just didn't enjoy it that much. i'd still give it a solid 5/10 because i can see how many others would enjoy this.

Ignore my playtime, I've played decades offline before I decided to honour the company and purchase the game.
This game is really amazing and incredibly addictive. There is always something more to do just before you log out, until suddenly its been 3 hours more. You create a factory starting from scratch and the more you advance the more you can automate everything.
The layout and how you design and build your production circuits, distribution networks, power systems, transportation etc is all very innovative and everyone will have a different idea, opinion, there are so many forum posts etc discussing the optimum setup for blablabla with lots of mathematical calculations proving that in some way it is 0.0003 percent more efficient.
Also it is a very satisfying feeling to lay back and look at your fully automated, symettrically arranged, nicely lit, walled, protected and LARGE factory with its network of automated trains and flying robots and just feel happy about how amazing your masterpiece is. Aaaand then you notice that if you just changed this or added that it could be better, aaand bye bye another 6 hours...
Oh I forgot to add that while building etc you constantly create a sort of smog/pollution which as it grows begins to attract the attention of the alien nests near by, and they start attacking you. This happens quite early on and it can be challenging at times, a full array of laser turrets along the entire exterior of your factory, protected by double walls, powered by far away non-polluting oasis 'solar-panel farms' and 'accumulator-farms' is quite effective in dealing with them automatically.
*Also as far as I'm aware this game does get frequent updates and mods - it has a very active community.

The campaign is extemely iffy sometimes.
I'm playing as Macedonia and was allied, strongly (+300 Happiness), with Athens.
They asked be to join the war effort against the seleucid empire, and doing this would improve my relations with Egypt - it was nothing but profitable and efficient.
After Athens gets rammed for 5 turns straight, i finally muster a indestructible force, one that slaughtered it's way through all of the Athenian's enemies and I finally reached the seleucid Empire, I gathered my fleet and established a foot -hold in settlements in Southern Syria (Seleucid Territory) so i could distract their forces whilst i took their provice capital in Northern Syria with the bulk of my fleets and Army.
I decided to wait a turn for winter to pass and for replenishments for my units to arrive. Knowing the souther conflict would displace their units for atleast 3-4 turns.
But behold, Athens decides to sign a peace treaty and form a military alliance with the Seleucid empire in that SINGLE turn. After about 15 turns of them getting hammered.
I had to attack their Province capital, assuming i could repair my alliance afterwards as a superior force to Athens. This mean't that i wouldn't have to retreat and be sandwhiched by two enemies, rather than one. (Athens and Seleucid)
Now, I have -500 happiness and am being relentlessly assaulted by Athens - Not only has this soured MY alliances of Sparta, Rome and Athens (My Greek-roman allies) which have been earning a TON of profit off of me (Now they cancel their trade and Alliances) it has left me weakened in my home state and in the middle of an unwinnable conflict in the middle east.
Like WTF - So stupid.
I declared war on ALL their enemies to bring peace between our nations, and now i can't repair our relationship because they keep throwing cannon fodder at me. (Even on Hard, they can't push me out of small townships)
It has come to the point where i have to abandon 8 hours of work and commit to the northern conflicts to protect Rome.
And i'll probably have to annihilate Sparta, as it is a powerful State with one single city and about 2 fleets and 4 armies surrounding it.
A near impossible feat.
It is fun, but completely illogical and senseless.
I broke one non-aggression treaty that Seleucid empire brokered with me, and now i'm an international criminal. Even though they have been slaughtering thousands of greek soldiers.

Where to start with this...
I originally played this on a Powermac G5 when it first came out around the end of 2008, I remember that I originally got it sometime around the 2008 election. My attention was focused on this game the whole time.
It's one of those games where it seems extremely simple at first, but then the complexities and depth of it gradually shine through. The puzzles are neat, and I never had to use any skips until the last part (and I normally sucka t puzzles) but they don't feel easy, they feel satisfying regardless.
The visuals are nice, and they're crisp and good looking, and most importantly they do NOT resort to trying to look like pixel art. However, the game does run at a low resolution and there is no way to change it.
The soundtrack... Well, let's just say it's one of the best soundtracks in an Indie game ever produced. It is well performed, it is entirely originally composed, and it doesn't resort to sounding like chiptune or 16-bit stuff to try and manipulate nostalgic nerves. One of the best parts of the game for certain, and even better is that all of the soundtrack (the full versions, not the shortened versions in the game) can be found right on Youtube. Very memorable soundtrack, I can say that about very very few games.
Buy it? YES! It's on sale frequently anyways.

Just Cause 3 adds some new things while taking away some of the older ones. No longer can you dodge roll, run and stunt positions are more limited. However you get explosive rocket boosters, better teather and rather convenient wingsuit.
JC3’s World looks prettier but it has less variety than JC2.Gone are large urban cities, christmas like mountain villages and desert dunes. However we get better game play feel. While that might sound like poor substitute for the lost world diversity, it actually makes the end result far more enjoyable - at least for good while.
There are hints of somewhat unfinished aspects of a game here - mainly how the story ends very poorly and abruptly. Some kind of polish is also lacking from various smaller things (like clouds are not as good up close as JC2, max flight height is less, upgrades seem to become pointless at some point…). It is also worth to mention how few cars there are in the game.
Overall a very enjoyable game that might not stand the test of time like JC2 did.

This is one incredible little game and it all (well mostly) takes place in a tiny little border control booth. It's up to you to let people in to the country and of course they have to have the right papers, a good reason, ID, a visit visa or sometimes even unique documents. The rules of the games change for every work shift that passes you by and you have to make sure that you take a real good look at EVERYTHING to see if the documents are real. If they are you send them on their way in to the country, and if they're not, you send them packing (or call the security on them).
When I started playing I really enjoyed making sure that all the papers are correct and it feelt simple enough to keep a good flow. But... the further I came in to the story everything started to get harder and harder. Checking the papers became a timed puzzle that you have to solve as fast as possible, you have a family that you have to feed and get medecine for, you have events and secret organisations that you have to make sure to keep track of. And once in awhile... you have to reach for a gun... and shoot intruders.
Everything is creating a horrible and very... realistic story which really ends up touching you. I was surprised by how much you could feel for this game. Definatly worth a try if you enjoy story and puzzle gaming.

Despite what people say, this game is a pretty decent one. While you can pay with real money for licenses, there is in game currency that you can acquire for doing missions, playing in tournaments, etc. This money can be used on certain weapons, and all licenses. With a guest membership (the one that you get upon downloading the game), you get a license to hunt whitetail deer, rabbits, and pheasants. You also get a rifle, a shotgun, and ammo. This is plenty to have fun with as I mostly only hunt whitetail and pheasants and I have a membership.
Getting away from the guest side of things, (where most negative comments come from), I played with a guest membership for a little over a year. At first I could agree with some of the comments, however when I figured out how to play, I had a great time. I ended up paying for a membership bundle that came with a year long membership, a year's worth of all licenses, and a load of weapons, stands, and equipment. Alongside all of that I can host private servers and have a great time hunting with friends.
In close, I would personally give this game a 8.5/10. I would wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes hunting or games related to it.

The Room is a fun game about a series of puzzle boxes. You must examine the boxes from all angles to find hidden bits and clever doodads that you can manipulate to unlock more of the like. The boxes are, for starters, gorgeous if you're into that kind of thing. There are ornate bits, there are clockwork bits, there are twisty bits, slidey bits, and some supernatural bits.
Honestly, I found that last one to be kind of disappointing early on. The best part about these boxes is that they really seem like they could be built in real life... up until you get to the impossible magic parts. This isn't game ruining, and by the end I didn't mind so much. It does help with the mysterious nature of things. But part of me would have liked to just work my way deeper and deeper into one big, realistic puzzle box to find some unknowable treasure within.
At the risk of repeating myself, I honestly found that last one to be kind of disappointing. Without revealing the actual plot any, I'll say that the ending kind of isn't really an ending. You unlock all of the boxes and then you're told hey great there are more of these to come. Not really any big revelation at the end or anything satisfying, just "buy the sequel" in so many words.
This isn't really a big deal either, though. The puzzle boxes are truly their own reward, and they're what you're actually here for. Although that does bring me back to my second paragraph in a way, since if the plot doesn't really matter and doesn't really lead up to much, then we probably didn't need to go supernatural after all.
The game controls well. It's clearly an enhanced tablet port, and the controls are held over from the touchscreen days. But for once that's not a bad thing. The controls work. You click and drag to rotate the things in front of you or interact with various things. Click to look at things and interact in other ways, and double-click to get a closer look at specific parts of the puzzle boxes. Right-click to zoom back out. Simple, yet effective.
The puzzles aren't going to break you. Worst comes to worst, the hint system question mark will appear in the upper-left corner if you go like two seconds without making progress. I'm just going by how it felt, on that one. Many puzzles are of the find an item, figure out where to use the item variety. There are plenty where you must align your view to line up the parts of an image a la those Riddler puzzles in the Batman: Arkham series. Most all of the puzzles are pretty simple, though. A few maybe disappointingly so (especially those ones where you slide a thing from one end to the other by rotating the tracks in the center with it on them).

Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs is the long-awaited sequel to commercial, critical, and youtube success Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The original Amnesia was lauded for daring to put you in the shoes of a defenseless wimp in a legitimately threatening environment in an age where every top-selling protagonist was a linebacker with a machine gun for a di.ck. But that was the gaming environment of yesteryear, and now you can't swing your machine gun around the steam store without co.ck-slapping five or six pretenders to Amnesia's throne. The question must be asked, then, if a sequel to Amnesia can hold up in an age where it's not the sole poop-inducer of the day.
To complicate matters more, this isn't a true sequel but rather a spin-off of sorts made by The Chinese Room, who were not yet most famous for making Everybody's Gone To The Rapture because they were too busy being most famous for making Dear Esther. This definitely qualifies them to take up the Amnesia's mantle, as Dear Esther was a slow, psychological thriller in which the player slowly discovers that they've spent ten dollars on a bad poem and also Steam refunds aren't a thing yet.
So then, does A Machine For Pigs succeed in being a worthy follow-up to Dark Descent? The answer would appear to be something approaching a yes, but that's entirely dependent on what that first entry was.
From a
perspective, there shouldn't be too many surprises here. There are a host of environments the character must navigate, hiding and running from monsters and solving the odd puzzle in order to progress. The main difference here is that the inventory has been done away with, stripping away many of the puzzle elements that were so prevalent in the original. Puzzles are not completely absent, but the ones that survived the culling of item storage tend to be of the pick up object and put it in a place variety, as well as a few wheels and switches that need cranking. This difference may well be what draws a few people away from AMFP but in my opinion it cuts away the least fun element from the original, namely collecting a menagerie of sh.it that boiled down to a host of different shaped keys. “Ooh, a crowbar! I wonder wha- oh, it unjammed this door.” “Ooh, a bunch of different chemicals, this coul- oh, it dissolved the pink god-jam that was really just a door in a costume.” Those bits always felt too gamey and out-of-place in a game about surviving against the supernatural and uncovering the story behind your predicament, besides the fact that they seem to imply some divine level of prescience on the part of protagonist Daniel over what exact piece of bullsh.ittery will open the door. The keys are understandable, the monsters in Dark Descent are clearly anal about locking doors behind them, but how Daniel knows to grab the specific vials of deus ex formula before seeing the door they're meant to melt is beyond me. I know to do it because they glow in a very video-game like fashion, but if Daniel is really seeing the right items glow an off-blue we may need to acknowledge that Daniel himself was the pink jam-god all along.
So yeah, A Machine For Pigs doesn't have those. And I like that about it.
The other major difference is the loss of the sanity mechanic, which honestly I find a much larger loss than the inventory. The mechanic did very little in the original, and besides some sound effects and a bit of a blur to Daniel's vision I don't think there was any meaningful impact on gameplay (some say that monsters find you more easily at low sanity, but I never found this to be the case). However, I found it endearing in a sort of Lovecraft-ish way, very reminiscent of those old protagonists who would go loopy at the first suggestion of anything supernatural. The little details that would change at low sanity was great, especially the paintings of Alexander that would go all after-effects ghost face. The refill of sanity upon completing a puzzle was a fun, cheap way to reward the player for progressing, and as a gamer in the 21st century I need pointless little rewards to give me that next fix. I can see why they would get rid of the mechanic, this is fundamentally a different kind of story than Dark Descent, but it's still missed.

-wise, this game is at least on the same level as Dark Descent. This is still the story of a man forced to come to grips with a past he no longer remembers, but where the first game focused more on a blur of general bad things Daniel had done, newcomer Oswalt is dogged by very specific crimes that work very well in the context of the Industrial Revolution. The game makes no attempt to say anything about the time period that wasn't done to death by the turn of the 20th century, but it's still a very fascinating, well-paced story that felt much more like an unfolding narrative than the original. Dark Descent had a lot of cool rooms and moments, but I never felt like anything important was happening and a feeling of progression towards a goal was sort of absent. Oswalt at least has a goal he's after, and the game is structured in such a way that not all of the narrative occurs before the actual start of the game. It's still about Oswalt learning about and coping with his past, but The Chinese Room seems to have realized that this does not exclude things from happening as you are playing as well. One level in particular stands out in my mind as the biggest point when the story pivots.

, this game is exactly what you'd expect from an Amnesia title. Many of the models look directly taken from the first game, but there are enough new things to escape the common spin-off trapping of resembling a high-quality mod more than a standalone title. The monsters, completely unique to AMFP, are actually really terrifying given their concept and are unlike most I've seen in any media. Anyone familiar with the words directly proceeding Amnesia in the title should have some clue as to the identity of these beasts. Overall this game is of the same general graphical style and fidelity as the original, which is admittedly not great but often excusable given the game's strategic use of darkness in the player's surroundings.
The
design may be one of the greatest strengths of the title, as the soundtrack enhances the ambiance through effective use of period-appropriate music that succeeds at being both mournful and haunting. Most of the game is still devoid of music, allowing you to hear the thump of the monsters moving around, the hiss of the machinery, and the glut of other fantastically off-putting sounds that the game throws at you. My one complaint is that a few too many of the sounds can be construed as monsters walking about, which I do realize was intentional on their part. It's just that, intentional or not, I feel like a dumbass crouching along the walls and travelling ten feet per minute because I'm not entirely sure that the game and I are vibing on what exactly a hoofbeat should sound like. I'm phrasing it as a complaint, but it's entirely possible that this ambiguity of noise enhances the experience for some people.
Overall, this is a different sort of beast than Dark Descent. If you were a fan of the less gamey elements of the original title, this will sate the same thirst. It's definitely not for everyone, but this is one of the stronger entries in the spooky walk around genre.

Just 2 things I want to say first, 1) This is my first review so please dont expect anything amazing and 2) although I only have 33 hours on record, I played this on console when it first came out. Let's get started then.
Just Cause 3 is a very fun but frustating game that could be brilliant but falls short. There is so much enjoyment in just sticking a rocket propelled explosive on the back of a military jeep, tethering a couple of enemies to it, grappling out of the way and watch the ensuing fireball that, hopefully, kicks off a massive chain reaction featuring many more explosions. The graphics are great, the audio crisp and the UI easy to use.
However, the story isn't that good (but who plays JC for story anyway...), the MOD upgrade system completely linear, choas points now serve no other purpose than to show how much you've destroyed and some weapons become redudant very early on, such as the RPG.
In order to unlock these MODs, you are required to take part in a variety of challenges, whether that's wingsuiting down a mountain, racing an F1 round a busatling capital or oblitaring a military base. Most of these are quire fun, other's... not so much. Bike races, for example or borderline impossible to achieve 5 gears(stars) on due to the terrible controls - at first the bike is unrepsonsive and lazy, once you get up to speed it will randomly perfrom a 180 and quite possibly fly into the air. The plane controls are also as bad,  a touch on the "A" or analogue stick will send it barrel rolling into a nearby cliff.
The combat is a bit lacking, with any dodging or sprinting replaced with just a grapple. You are just hammered with bullets constantly. Although saying that, gunfights are very easy - aim at head, shoot at max 3 bullets, done, repeat for any nearby enemy.  Enemies seem to spawn anywhere you aren't looking as well.
Attack helicopters are,most of the time, absolutely devastating, just spamming rockets and infinitely spraying minigun bullets at anything or anyone. Watch out for SAM batteries though, as they will hunt you down mercilessly, and 9 out of 10 times the missile will hit you, crippling your helicopter to a smoldering wreck.
In conclusion, JC3 is a fun game with jam packed with explosions and spectacular cinematic pieces, but is consistently let down by obnoxious glitches, bugs  and lack of quality controls that will remove any immersion you once had.
Honestly, wait until it goes on sale before buying, and even then do so with caution.

I've been wanting to review Distraint for a year now, but for some reason I kept putting it off. Now with the release of the Deluxe Edition I have a good excuse to finally do it.
Distraint is a creepy psychological horror game centered around a man named Price. Price's job is to seize properties, and he'll have to seize them no matter what if he wants his promotion into the big company.  It's a straightforward premise that carries a simplistic yet powerful message.
The horror itself won't terrify you, but it is very well done for a 2D puzzler. The lighting, sounds, and pacing is spot on.  The atmosphere itself can carry the game alone. The story keeps you on your toes throughout because you are invested in these characters and situations.
Now that I've talked about Distraint, I think it's  fair to talk about the new upgrade that just got released.
For those of you who have played the original Distraint, the Deluxe Edition is a great improvement.  At first I was weary of the dynamic coloring being added. I thought taking away the grey shading would make it less eerie. Luckily, adding color enhanced the art style and brings the game to life in a new way. The audio is much clearer and the lantern has been ditched for improved lighting. There is an option to launch the original Distraint or the Enhanced Edition in the launcher. I'm enjoying the Enhanced Edition more but it was worth playing both just to see the improvements that went in.
Distraint is a simple short horror game that does it's job well.  It pulls off a chilling atmosphere with simplistic gameplay and puzzles while establishing it's own unique style. It's very weird, and it embraces that.
The game manages to throw you into this moral dilemma without presenting you with any choices.
Right now it's $1 on sale, so if you are interested, it's worth the price and more. It'll last you about 2 hours on average for one playthrough

Recommended, as a peculiar shade of Zen gaming.
I am really impressed by the depth and involvement that such minimal game can punch.
Mind, though: in Arstotzska, the game plays you. You may start off cool and grand, but by the end of the day you will have been whacked hard enough, and at the threshold of the (in-game) month you will be all shivers and totalitarian paranoia.
Whenever you try and invest in humanitarianism or just plain friendliness, nastiness and practical losses will hit you harsh, eventually, steadily contriving to scoop your soul away.
All you will strive for is to reach the end of the shift with the least damage to your frayed dignity and salary. Whatever it takes to get there.
Slowly, but eventually, you stop sympathizing with those pesky freedom fighters and thinkers and you will be most annoyed with those popping up with problems and stories to unroll. Like, "FFS, don't come and waste my working time, you incompetent sub-citizen!"
Whoever is not part of the System becomes Persona non Grata, to you personally, and mighty so. The System feeds you, you are its dog. Love the System. Swerve from your cold detachment and there you go, down down the ditch, Persona non Grata yourself.
This game made me understand better my real, East European country: I never realized how easy it is to betray the lofty values of civilization when bread is your only aim, and the aim itself stretches not farther than tomorrow.
Great, might say infinite, replay value: you against the Evils and the dull Average Joe. The game ticks hypnotic and crunches the hours. In fact you only can get better trough total immersion in the geography and psychopathy of the fictional world of Astotzska: spot the anomaly is, then, your profession and your bread. Great satisfaction to crack a tricky counterfeit in a fraction of second and a burning humiliation when you fail to spot the elephantine one)

So, to recap:
Pros:
-Colorful and Amazing Visuals
-Amazing Soundtrack
-Polished and fun combat
-Overall great experience
Cons:
-A bit too short
-Wanted a more in-depth explanation of the story
Despite the few things I wish were done better, this game is incredible. I reccommend it to everyone who liked Bastion, or even if you didnt like it. Despite its key similarities, this game is a suprisingly fresh take on what made Bastion great. You may find something you like.

Distraint is a short, indie psychological horror game which relies heavily on its dark atmosphere and story. The plot revolves around a young man whos job is to evict people. It speaks about the guilt he goes through, and his struggle to control his greed and not let it control him. What I liked about this game the most is how much it speaks out to the real world as these events are becoming more and more common.
The art style is polished and simple. The same applies to the gameplay. It's just you moving around with the WASD keys, picking things up, and interacting with them to progress the story. It requires a bit of thinking, but is very easy and not much of a challenge. The music fits the atmosphere almost perfectly and makes the happy parts of the game much cuter and heartwarming.
The ending of the story provides a rather nice twist which, in my opinion, was the best way to end it. The game itself is only a 2 hour play, and its price is suitable for that. I do think that if it were more than 2 hours it would've gotten boring due to the repetitive gameplay.
One thing that irritated me, however, was a small bug which didn't allow you to interact with objects/people unless you approached them from a certain side. But it wasn't that big of an inconvience.
I'd give this game a 75/100 and I think that it's very much a must-buy when it's on sale (despite the fact that it already is very cheap).

FF XIV realm reborn is a great MMORPG. The story is good and intriguing with lots of lore, the scenes are pretty, graphics are superb, the soundtrack is consistent. The races and classes are various. There are two tank classes, two healers, and lots of DPS classes. There are so many things to do while you are leveling. You can do the main quests, side quests, or you can do specific duties( instanced quests which you complete by yourself), levequests (instanced short party missions), tradeleves (where you deliver a specific item to a receiver party), FATES (dynamic events like in GW2) dungeons etc. The combat is a solid tab targeting. The thing I like most about this game is the pace of combat. The pace is not rushed like some other MMORPGS (I am looking at you RIFT) where you die or kill in 3-4 seconds. You can actually think and react. The game has a very good crafting system and a solid marketplace where you can sell/buy goods to/from other players. Also you can try multiple classes with one character. Bored of being a monk? You can switch to archer by going to the archers guild and getting new equipment and putting on your new gear. You do not have to create a new character. IF you joined the guild for the class changing class is very easy. Just change your weapon your class changes too. Of course you start from level 1 with your new class. But it is better than creating a new character as you get a constant experience boost if your character has already achieved lvl 50 in any other class which makes leveling up faster.
Well for the negatives I can point 3. The first is the slight leveling grind. If you want to try a compltely different class and you make a new character you notice the grind. The other negative thing is the absense of a pure support class like a paragon in Guilds Wars or Bard in RIFT. The bard class in FF XIV has some support skills but it is mostly DPS and bards queue as DPS for dungeons. Scholars (the other healing class) has a support type pet but the class is healer. The 3rd is the insufficent level of soundacting for such a quality game. The mainquests mostly lack soundacting. You just read the text while the lips of the NPC are in motion which makes a funny scene. Strangely there is soundacting in some quests especially if you are being introduced to someone important.
It is a great MMORPG (could be the best out there) which totally deserves its montly fee. The servers are crowded with people and the community is generally very polite. If you are a MMORPG fan it is impossible not to like this game.

The subsciption system is a bit of a pain for a broke college kid, BUT the game itself is fantastic. It's what you would expect from a FF game, beautful scenery and characer design, smooth combat system, AND you can make hot anime boob girls. 10/10.

I received this game as part of a bundle deal...without it, I would have never purchased it.  That's not to say I don't like it, I do.  It's just that I've played it before.
This is the first game in The Room series by Fireproof.  Originally on IOS (Apple) devices and then Android, this is a nice tactile puzzle game with a bit of nebulous plot behind it, some nicely rendered objects, and some perfect mood-setting music.  The first time I played this was on an Android device, and it took me a little while.  This time I played through the whole game very quickly, because like most puzzle games without randomized values it suffers from a flaw, that of players' lack of desire to replay something they already know all the answers to.
However, as this is a port, let's address how good the port is.  All the content in the original mobile release plus the "epilogue" chapter are included.  The graphics are scaled appropriately, but it feels more stretched than remade.  some textures are blurry.  I played on 1920x1080 on the game's "Amazing" graphic setting.  On my nVidia graphics card, I did get the occasional texture flicker.  The sound is as perfect as in the mobile version.  There were a couple changes/additions to some of the puzzles in order to make up for the lack of mobile hardware (motion sensing).
If you have never played this, it's worth it.  If you've already played it on your phone or tablet, it's probably not worth it.

Transistor is very much Art and Atmosphere first, game second. Art through the hand-painted backgrounds, the absorbing soundtrack, and the excellent voice acting by the ever-present narrator. Atmosphere through a strongly original setting in a cyberpunk-meets-computer code world, original protagonists, great character backgrounds and just the right spark of humor. All of this makes sure you are sucked into the world of Cloudbank.
Even though the gaming elements come second, they are well worked out and are sufficiently deep to tickle the puzzler and optimizer inside of you. Since you can set your own level of difficulty through in-game mechanics, Transistor is able to easily offer the right level of challenge.
Overall: strongly recommended and easily one of the most original and absoring games I've played in the past 5 years.

The demo for this game was so good it made me get a steam account just so I could play the full version. I get twinkly-eyed when talking about this game, and I talk about it to anyone who will listen. Such an aware and astute political comment. The game some how manages in that little cube checkpoint to be all about human relationships, and how compassion and revolution relate, and a million other themes. Even if you don't play compassionately, I think it's still true that it's about compassion. So there's a lot of heavy material, a lot that I still think about after months. But also it's funny and light? I think it goes back to the charm of relationships and interactions. There are so many potential stories in this game, you see so many people come by the checkout, and you are also confronted with whole states, but somehow the story stays small and personal too, in a way that replicates real politics. I could go on. Just play the game, you'll think a lot about states and morals and rebellion and empathy and power in the process.

This game is really amazing and incredibly addictive. There is always something more to do just before you log out, until suddenly its been 3 hours more. You create a factory starting from scratch and the more you advance the more you can automate everything.
The layout and how you design and build your production circuits, distribution networks, power systems, transportation etc is all very innovative and everyone will have a different idea, opinion, there are so many forum posts etc discussing the optimum setup for blablabla with lots of mathematical calculations proving that in some way it is 0.0003 percent more efficient.
Also it is a very satisfying feeling to lay back and look at your fully automated, symettrically arranged, nicely lit, walled, protected and LARGE factory with its network of automated trains and flying robots and just feel happy about how amazing your masterpiece is. Aaaand then you notice that if you just changed this or added that it could be better, aaand bye bye another 6 hours...
Oh I forgot to add that while building etc you constantly create a sort of smog/pollution which as it grows begins to attract the attention of the alien nests near by, and they start attacking you. This happens quite early on and it can be challenging at times, a full array of laser turrets along the entire exterior of your factory, protected by double walls, powered by far away non-polluting oasis 'solar-panel farms' and 'accumulator-farms' is quite effective in dealing with them automatically.
*Also as far as I'm aware this game does get frequent updates and mods - it has a very active community.

Yes. Would recommend/10.
It's not a perfect game by any stretch of the imagination and the main gripes that people may have with the game include how character progression via quests is 'one-time'. Normally this would be perfectly normal but in FF14, one character can achieve max level in every single class. Quests are not non-exhaustive which leads to an inevitable dungeon and FATE (world event) grind. Also, the global cooldown is also 2.5 seconds which may feel extremely slow paced to people more used to 1 second GCDs or 'reactive' games such as Guild Wars 2. Also, subscriptions.
I also think it is worth mentioning that if you live in non-NA/EU/JP regions (e.g. Oceania) you will have to play with a moderate-high amount of latency (150~400ms) which may frustrate you in certain dungeon/raid instances.
With all that said, all classes, jobs and crafting professions play very differently to each other which adds a lot of variety in the game. The plot is actually cohesive and builds up to quite a climax over time if you're into storyline. Dungeons and raids can be extremely challenging (RIP SCoB Savage Mode) And heck, it's Final Fantasy.
If you have the time, money and friends to play the game with, it will be a pleasant experience. Just remember to join a Free Company (guilds) as soon as you can - buffs, new friends and always someone to talk to (freebies may be included).
P.S. Pitiful 4 hours because I don't launch the game via Steam.

After slowly creeping, sneaking and otherwise holding my breath through the first Amnesia it was no surprise I was eager to jump straight into its sequel for another dose of bowel loosening terror.
Where the first game relied heavily on item management to persevere through the rigours of mental torture and keep your lantern filled, the sequel only uses the journal for guidance as did its predecessor the rest of the game is spent traversing a mess of industrial era buildings filled with cacophonous machines, dark passageways and hideously filthy experimental rooms. The puzzles laid out are nothing fiendish however when you have something lurking nearby that could rip you apart mistakes are easily made.
The atmosphere isn't much different from the first although in actuality the creatures chasing you (yes I said creatures as in more than one) are far more horrifying the locales are even more twisted and the ambient sounds really mess with your mind, armed only with a lantern with a focussing lens which adapts it to work further but on a narrow beam I spent more time beneath the cities streets than I care to remember, slowly working my way forward I cringed every time the monster squealed nearby it was all I could do to pray the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s didn't find me, this is another solid game for the Amnesia series,  one that doesn't disappoint... "Arstotzka so great, passport not required." If only, Jorji, if only.
The demo for this game was so good it made me get a steam account just so I could play the full version. I get twinkly-eyed when talking about this game, and I talk about it to anyone who will listen. Such an aware and astute political comment. The game some how manages in that little cube checkpoint to be all about human relationships, and how compassion and revolution relate, and a million other themes. Even if you don't play compassionately, I think it's still true that it's about compassion. So there's a lot of heavy material, a lot that I still think about after months. But also it's funny and light? I think it goes back to the charm of relationships and interactions. There are so many potential stories in this game, you see so many people come by the checkout, and you are also confronted with whole states, but somehow the story stays small and personal too, in a way that replicates real politics. I could go on. Just play the game, you'll think a lot about states and morals and rebellion and empathy and power in the process.

I put a few hours into this game on early access.
I'm going to make this short and address two main questions:
1. The claim the developers made in that this is the successor to Ragnarok, is that true?
2. Does this game retain value in how fun it is, in other words does the price in time/money show in fun you may have?
1. Yes this is essentially what I recall Ragnarok Online being like, community aside you will always meet bad and nice people in mmos and the elitists are always going to be there but this game has everything RO suffered from with none of the things that really kept people with RO. It has bots and spammers but no amazing spells or abilities, nothing that makes your character feel unique/deadly/amazing it just feels like a horrible shadow of what RO was with regards to the few things that RO did right.
The Music and Art are without a doubt RO in quality, the map design and exploration of each map is great... it just that your character wont feel like you are making any progress. You have so many classes fine but everyone of them are seeded with abilities that feel gimmicky as heck. I guess they wanted to add more player usage of controls in combat but this simply wasn't the right way to do it: it simply adds the attributes monotonous and cumbersome to what is a core part of the game... combat.
2.
I would say no to this, if this was a buy to play build then yes it retains its value since you can get about 60 hours through the game before you are no longer interested in getting 100% completion on a map. Then yes this may even be a buy on steam sale type of game. However it's a cash shop kind of game which makes it harder to describe... so I'll split this into two parts.
One - if you do use the cash shop then yes you essentially speed up your experience of what the game has to offer, it's nice to get you to the above mentioned 60 hours, at which point you've probably found yourself considering the value of the game and decided to shelf it for a while only to find you never return amid memories of noted bots, spammers, and most importantly gimmicky skills that didn't make you feel like a badass and made combat a chore. So yes the cash shop can be worth it if you want to experience more of the game before reaching the 60-80 hour range.
You also get to look nice but again you may look unique but your abilities are sad perverted reflections of the ones RO offered.
Two - I haven't spoken to anyone who kept playing past the 1st month, and I think like most of them I really wanted this game to be great, I didn't care if it was the next RO just that it was a great game. You do at the begining get a pretty nice thematic area of learn the game in. It in my opinion really pulls you in. It's later on things become bland and a grind fest. I was litterally only grinding to progress the story. I didn't care to make my character stronger, I didn't care about what abilities I got because they were all gimmicks. I knew how to play but you get level blocked by both which npcs are willing to talk to you based on your level and enemies that will 1 shot you if you aren't on their level.
You start to notice how gimmicky your abilities are at higher levels more clearly when creatures become hp walls. You spend so much time doing ridiculous things to get your spells to do the most they can do before they fade away that it just gets old. I'm not sure what they were thinking of when they made some of these abilities. So no this isn't something worth my time at least is what I decided later on.
In conclusion I can't recommend this game no matter how much I want to, maybe I can check it out in a few more months but there are some deep problems with the design choices on abilities anyway if you do get it enjoy.

Well this will definitely be a hard one. After finishing this and the first game back to back i'm having really mixed feelings about it. If you're looking for a good interactive story with a fairly well thought out plot you'll probably have a blast with A Machine for Pigs. If you're, however, looking for a successor to The Dark Descent with a similar atmosphere, gameplay and terrifying setpieces you probably will be sorely disappointed.
+ The story told is by all means good.
+ While different, the atmosphere AMFP creates is unique and foreboding on it's own right.
+ Late 1890's London is an amazing locale for a game and in my opinion much more interesting than the castle in the first title.
Aand that's pretty much where the positives end. The rest of this "review" will probably sound like a rant, so i'd just like to point out at this point that if you can get the game for 5 bucks or so i'd definitely recommend it as i enjoyed the things the game did good a lot. There are however some pretty glaring issues i just can't overlook and that really hamper the game from being really good.
- They removed most of the gameplay mechanics from the first game, like, literally most of them.
- No sanity meter.
- No oil to refill your lantern, it now has it for an infinite quantity.
- No tinderboxes to light candles.
- No inventory system to collect items in, instead all the puzzles are done a la Half-Life 2 item dragging. (It sucks by the way.)
- Since you basically don't have to deal with the darkness anymore, nearly all of the games spooks are handled via jumpscares. Gone is the near traumatizing atmosphere of the first game in which you really were ♥♥♥♥ed beyond imagination if you ran out of tinderboxes and oil.
- About 4 hours long, which is about half the length of TDD. This could also be a positive because if it was any longer i swear to god i would have dropped it halfway through for the sake of padding out the game.
- No puzzles. Yes, you read that right. Sure, there are valves to turn and buttons to press but they require absolutely NO effort whatsoever. I was kinda sceptical about the whole "Walking simulator" thing people have been throwing this game at but to be entirely honest it isn't all that far away from the truth.
- The main antagonists of the game are not scary, like, at all.
So yeah, i really can't give this a positive review no matter how hard i try. If you can get it for cheap it's definitely worth it for the story and some cheap thrills but that's about it. Even the modding scene is worse than in TDD because there are literally almost no mechanics to play with in the game.

This isn't a bad game, except for it's mechanics. (YOU CAN'T PICK UP ANYTHING). The story is not terrible, but is poorly understood throughout most of the game, and personally I expected the sequal to be about either Daniel returning to the ruins of Castle Brennenburg or playing as Daniel's son left alone after Daniel suffered from (Amnesia maybe?) some type of disease, but this was truly dissapointing.

It's not a perfect game by any stretch of the imagination and the main gripes that people may have with the game include how character progression via quests is 'one-time'. Normally this would be perfectly normal but in FF14, one character can achieve max level in every single class. Quests are not non-exhaustive which leads to an inevitable dungeon and FATE (world event) grind. Also, the global cooldown is also 2.5 seconds which may feel extremely slow paced to people more used to 1 second GCDs or 'reactive' games such as Guild Wars 2. Also, subscriptions.
I also think it is worth mentioning that if you live in non-NA/EU/JP regions (e.g. Oceania) you will have to play with a moderate-high amount of latency (150~400ms) which may frustrate you in certain dungeon/raid instances.
With all that said, all classes, jobs and crafting professions play very differently to each other which adds a lot of variety in the game. The plot is actually cohesive and builds up to quite a climax over time if you're into storyline. Dungeons and raids can be extremely challenging (RIP SCoB Savage Mode) And heck, it's Final Fantasy.
If you have the time, money and friends to play the game with, it will be a pleasant experience. Just remember to join a Free Company (guilds) as soon as you can - buffs, new friends and always someone to talk to (freebies may be included).

Honestly my favorite modern MMO. I've put countless hours into it and still find it endlessly enjoyable. The classes are all fun and unique, the crafting is active and interesting, and thanks to the job system you can experience everything the game has to offer with a single character.
I took a break after finishing end game and getting all best in slot gear for my main class, but when I came back I found out that there was almost double the endgame content as when I left. This game is ever changing and ever expanding, new content is being added quite regularly, and it's not just new raids or dungeons. Whole new story quests, expanding on the lore, are added extremely often.
I'm going to sum up my feelings in a list of good and bad from my perspective,
******************************************************************************
What's the good:
The combat: It's slower then most other MMOs but that is a benefit, giving you more time to make a choice on what to do next and how it will be effective. It flows naturally and feels satisfying with just the right amount of power. Later in the game a boss fight stops being just a harder monster you need to work through, but instead becomes a kind of dance, each member of your party having their own role on the stage.
The Quests: Yes, they are a lot of fetch quests and breadcrumbs, it's nothing special in the MMO world... But it somehow is. With all the dialog, lore, and the streamlined loot system, the quests in this game somehow transcend the "Go here and do this" standard. The first major thing you might notice? The quest givers know damned well what you're there for, the world has a long history of adventurers and questors, everyone knows you're there to help them with anything and damned if they are not going to take advantage of it. This makes for quite a fun experience as you do the most basic tasks for someone too lazy to pick up vegetables that are literally 5 feet away, and they acknowledge it. If you play and get to level 50, I HIGHLY recommend the "Hildibrand" Quest series started in Ul'dah, it will have you laughing till the end.
The Dungeons: The dungeons in this game are basic, but awesome. Each able to be run in about 20-30 minutes and comprising of 3-4 bosses and trash. But they have a ton of atmosphere and charm, each one clearly was carefully crafted to be both visually appealing and challenging. And don't be fooled when you see the labels of "Hard mode" when you get to end game, Hard mode dungeons are not in fact just more difficult versions like in other MMOs, the game designers in fact go back and remake a dungeon from scratch, using the same location but a different path, with different trash and different bosses. Every Hard Mode is a whole new dungeon with a whole new story to it, causally taking place after the events you caused in the normal mode.
Community: Other then a few bad eggs and elitists the community is extremely helpful and kind, you should never lack any help if you need it just by asking around. The game actually incentivizes high levels to help low levels with the Syncing system where a high level in specific situations can scale his/her level down to match a dungeon/quest/fate.
*****************************************************************************
What is Bad:
Global Clock: All actions by players and mobs are on a global clock. This gives the game a somewhat turn based feel to it where everything is in time and synced together. Why is this bad? Because for more then a few classes in order to get the most out of your abilities you need to time them PERFECTLY based on this clock, and the fact that you can't see or interact with it means that you'll be guessing based on the countdown on your abilities. Best example of this being a problem is on the summoner Job, where timing your dots right makes the difference of 100% of your damage or 80% of your damage if you get it wrong.
Insanely difficult dice roll quests: At end game, there is a series of quests to get your "best" weapon. This is... the most bull♥♥♥♥♥♥you will ever have to face in a game. You have to win 12 random dice rolls, and failing one means having to try again... Did I mention that each dice roll happens AFTER you finish one of the many random events around the world? That you have to wait up to 15 minutes for? Even with higher drop chance it is still Bull. (My best time for completing this quest.. 6 days, friend took more then 2 weeks) Lucky that this is optional.
Character creation limitations: What's that? Wanna play with a friend who already plays the game? What's that? They are on the Levi Server? Well FK YOU! Servers every now and then (some more then others, to the point of being closed more often then open) will close their gate to new players, this is done to keep the servers from being over loaded, but this has the nasty side effect of keeping players from playing together on the servers they want, specially the more populated ones where you have more people to interact with and more options for guilds/fcs. Why is this done? Well that brings me to my last problem.
Gold Spammers: Yup, the ever present MMO issue is here but 1000x worse. These pesky parasites will spam all chats, all areas, all the time. They even personally PM you with their virus ridden web links, promising massive amounts of gil for your hard earned money. This is done through the in game player search, where they just have to go alphabetically to find every single one of us and spam us one at a time. Of course they get banned, only to instantly make a new random name account and get right back into the game. they come in the thousands and they want all of your money, and in my opinion is the sole reason that servers are rotated the way they are. It's annoying, it's frustrating, and no mater how many of them you block there are always 5 more to take their place. Every now and then Square does a mass Hardware ban and that quiets them for a week or so wile they buy new computers/servers but it's only a temporary fix to a permanent problem.
**********************************************************
All in all, in my opinion, the good outweighs the bad. This game is an experience, an amazing experience. I've never had more fun with an MMO in my life and I'm not sure I ever will. No one would have thought that after the disaster that was the original FFXIV that this would be what comes out of it. I ask any of you reading, at LEAST give the 2 week free trial a chance.

I guess I'm really late to the party. For a long time, I've been hearing this game take a lot of praise -Yahtzee even loved it! So why am I so late to play Papers Please? Well, I kept thinking that it's a morality-driven game, that seeks to soften your heart with emotional shortcuts about NPC strangers and darkside vs lightside choices like we see in so many games (cough...Bioware...cough). Boy, I'm sure glad I was wrong.
Make no mistake, this game has a lot of empathy potential. It paints a dystopian picture of a soviet country in a world region with poor living standards. Lots of people are seeking to enter the borders from other countries around you, be it to flee conflict, to seek work or to have surgery in your country's better-equipped hospitals. You have to manage helping strangers with their implied problems who sometimes don't have their paperwork in order, with not slipping up at work to keep you and your family fed and sheltered. Bonus points if you come from an ex-communist country like me and you know from your parents what it means to live with rationed food and heat in a government-assigned apartment.
However, the game also gives you incentive to play the villain once in a while, and it's sort of fun be be a prick. You're stuck at a clerk's desk doing a monotonous job, and then a guy comes in and insults your son's pencil drawing he lovingly made for you? I'll be sure to comb that jerk's passport for ANY small irregularity. The game likes to play with you quite a bit, small spoiler examples include
Some immigrants can be really lousy people up to no good. It's very satisfying to catch smugglers, abusers or even smug little NPCs like the aforementioned who like to come in your office and give you lip.
If it were only about the morality, though, I wouldn't have played Papers Please so obsessively. The gameplay though is more than satisfying:  in late stages, very intricate paperwork requires you to sweat while checking each paper carefully, praying you don't ♥♥♥♥ up a mini quest, then clenching your teeth for a few seconds after you process someone waiting to see if you're getting that dreaded citation for messing up. Most of the narrative is implied instead of spoon-fed and depends on you making mental connections; it's really fun when you catch some little typo in the name of some bloke's hometown that tips you off they forged their passport and are up to no good; or when you notice a lady has 2 extra pounds than it says on her entry permit - you search her and she has drugs strapped beneath her skirt.
Papers Please has a wonderful playful tone very appropriate to a cartoonish satire. Precisely nailing the style of humour of Russian jokes, where people poke fun at heavy themes in a light-hearted stoic manner, the game's dark humour and catoonish estethic (from its delightfully sovietic music to its laconic, stilted English) suit this soviet dystopia masterfully.  The game has very little exposition. The longer you play, the more you'll become familiar with the various nations and their particularities, gleaning the geopolitical situation of this fictional area from newspaper articles (that react to your perfomarnce guarding the border) and from dozens of personal stories.
I'm really glad that I bought this game on a whim and I hope I'll get the chance to see more creative gems like Papers Pleaser and to support more devs like Lucas Pope who enrich our experience.

I delayed my purchase of this game for quite a while after release for a few reasons.
1. My old computer did not meet the requirements, though I was in the market for a new one.
2. The game had so many issues at release.
I waited until the reviews started to take a turn towards the positive as issues were resolved.
While I didn't run into too many technical issues (a few crashes and 1 bug interfering with completion of a challenge) some design choices detracted from the enjoyment far too much.
Story:  (4/10)
The story was forgettable.  You are aiding the rebellion of Medici to overthrow a evil military dictator.  You are given little to make you care about more than that.  Two of the NPCs stick out in my mind.  Your childhood friend, Mario.  He provides moments  of backstory about your character that are entertaining.  The writing never fleshed out your back story enough to my liking.  Another member of  the rebellion, Dimah, has a fantastic backstory that I felt was only told sufficiently through collectible audio logs. This was reallly a missed opportunity to engage the player.
Lastly, the ending.

Sound: (8/10)
Explosions!!!  If you've played any of the other Just Cause games they are a big part of the draw.  The weapons/explosions/vehicles all sound powerful.  They make you feel strong when you attack.  The rush of air as you freefall or fly with your wingsuit at fast speeds sounds fantastic as well.  The music wasn't very memorable, but sound effects were great.
Graphics: (6/10)
Graphics are a mixed bag here.  The game looks FANTASTIC! Finding a machine to  run it efficently at high graphic options is the problem.  My new  computer suffered from many FPS issues, as many others have experiences.
Gameplay: (4/10)
I was  hoping for a game that I could play casually and use as stress relief after tough days at work.  Just Cause 2 had been that wonderful blend for me and I had hoped for more of that.  What I got was far different.  New skills are unlocked via challenges.  These challenges are a big part of the game, but they seem like they were not given enough consideration.  These are all timed or score based.  The margin of error for the top rating on each challenge varies wildly.  In some you could make many mistakes and still come out with a top rating.  Others require a near perfect run.  This seems like a huge design oversight.  Many of these became an exercise in frustration for me, a far cry from  the relaxation I was looking for.  The open world exploration aspect of the game is fun, a lot of fun.  The challenges are in some cases god awful.  Failing and reloading over and over hoping for a perfect run, and micromanaging every little movement you make. Along  the same lines, the game has the worst load times I have ever seen.  FPS drop during a challenge can cause you to fail which is very frustrating. One challenge in fact suffers from an invisible wall problem, causing it to be near impossible.  For a completionist, this was a nightmare.  Nearly 40 runs of the same 2 minute content, with a 1 minute load time to get around a problem in design.  A friend of mine took nearly 70 runs for the same issue.
On the positive side, this  game has the best depiction of wingsuit flight I have played.
Overall: (4/10)
I wanted to like this game, I really did.  I can't recommend this game.  Completionists should avoid unless really intent on playing.

For the longest time I refused to play this game because it didn't seem like something I would enjoy. I took one look at it and, despite loving the art I just scratched it off. Even now I can't recall what made me buy and play this game, but boy I am glad I did.
The art is simply stunning, it was really immersive and I enjoyed the parts where it were clearly visible. The soundtrack was incredible, and I will definitely listen to it in my own time, without playing the game, it was that good. I'm not usually one much for soundtracks in games, unless they are close to my heart and mean something to me, but this game has impeccable music. The combat system was interesting and I admit, I sucked at it for a good portion of the game, but I got the hang of it halfway through, making it a lot more pleasant to play through the game.
The story, oh boy. I did not expect to get attached to Red's partner (does he have a name? somewhere?) I grew extremely fond of him, I felt a connection with him. That was really strange because this doesn't happen to me in games, never. So, I found myself being drawn close to him and enjoying his company and just caring for him dearly, even when, hell, I barely knew the guy. I liked that the game left a lot of things to your interpretation, for you to draw your own conclusion. The ending also had me tearing up, not gonna lie.
All in all, it was a brilliant adventure, one I did not expect when I was picking up this game at all. I will be playing it again, if not for the additional flavour text then for the art, music, Red and him (and for the achievements, but shh).
I strongly recommend this game, even if you think it's not going to be your cup of tea. You might be surprised.

This game is like a computer, A graceful system of components working perfectly in harmony with eachother.
The combat system is mindblowingly well crafted. Every Function() aligns perfectly with one another, Creating a massive number of different combinations and builds.
This makes Transistor a very flexible game, you can -very much so- tailor the combat after your own playstyle. Whether you want to be quick and stealthy or damage dealing and tanky, Whether you want to play it in real-time or in turn-based, this game will allow you to do so, every playstyle is viable.
The story is well paced and presented in an intruiging mysterious manner, leaving you to connect the dots yourself. Reading the various logs is important if you want a grasp of what is really going on. Yet the story would be just as enjoyable if you didn't read them, although you would probably be a bit confused as to why some events occured.
The narrative is also carefully woven into the experience as a whole. There's no ludonarrative dissonance here, at least not that i noticed. The combat and things you do all makes sense within the narrative, for example; every Function() acquired is actually a digital "trace" of a (often deceased) person. and the Function()'s nature reflects who they are (or were in life).
The protagonist's trace for instance, is a disruptive stun ability, which reflects her personality as a rebellious musician who often sparks controversy with her lyrics.
This game is simply beautiful, the sound design, the art direction, the graceful combat system, the story, the acting, and all so well put together into what seems to be perfection. Every aspect of Transistor is strong. Much like a supercomputer.
Of course there will be people disagreeing with me. But mostly over things that are subjective. Mechanically and technically the game is near perfection. Most problems people would have with transistor i'd think would be subjective and down to one's individual taste.

text:
World of Goo is an addictive and challenging physics-based puzzle game that forces you to think. A powerful message is sent, opening your eyes to the fact that we pollute so much of our Earth just to make useless items because we think they look nice.
In this game, you use your mouse to build structures out of these cute little orbs of muck, called “gooballs”. You have a set goal of gooballs to collect, but it is better if you collect more. For those of you that strive to get high scores in games, the amount of gooballs you got, the time it took to get those gooballs, and the amount of moves you made in order to get said gooballs are shown at the end of the level. There is also a sandbox mode where you can compete with others all around the world in order to try to build the tallest goo towers. I, personally, find this mode to be sort of boring, but there are others out there who I know love it and have a lot of fun with it.
The graphics in this game are very good, and unless you have an extremely old computer or video accelerator, it doesn’t lag at all. The art style is very attractive, and each level has a different look to it. There are also many different “species” of gooballs to discover as you play the game. Both of these things provide for a spectrum of colours and designs to keep the game exciting and new.
To accompany all of these things, Kyle Gabler created a stellar soundtrack for the game. Every track on the soundtrack is beautiful, and the artist even included notes for his inspirations and ideas for many of the tracks, found on this website:
.
Overall:
Pros:
-Addictive
-Challenging
-Has a message
-Good graphics
-Doesn’t lag
-Cute character/stage art
-Gorgeous soundtrack
Cons:
-Sandbox mode can be boring

I have many thousands of hours across multiple TW titles, so it's fair to say that I am a huge fan of these games. However, CA has been taking the series downhill, fast, and I absolutely hate the direction they're headed.
Although I think the Warhammer spin-offs are fine as games in their own right, I don't support them as TW titles. Part of the huge draw I've had to TW games over the past 10+ years has been the complete immersion in historical worlds. While there were always elements of the games that may have not had full historical accuracy, the focus was still in making the player an armchair general or emperor from an actual time period, and letting them control world history from there. Whenever you wanted to take a break from war or diplomacy, you could right-click to a world of essays about anything and everything from the time period, or just relax listening to the stellar music. I can't count how many nights I played late into the early morning saying 'just one more turn' because I just couldn't get enough. Sometimes I would keep a running log of tasks I needed to complete for my empire on my phone, while out and about in my actual life. There was no detail small enough to skip. Games like Rome 1, Medieval 2, Empire, Napoleon, and Shogun 2 were truly special to me for this reason.
Then all of a sudden they decided to venture off into the Warhammer universe, throwing out all history completely, and applying the same familiar mechanics. These mechanics are great to be sure, but the whole experience feels empty to me now. At least before I was able to somehow rationalize the insane amount of hours I put into the games as a thorough lesson in history, politics, and geography, that made me feel like I was being less wasteful with my time. It's just not as easy to justify putting countless hours into a fantasy title in the same way, for me at least.
Recent titles starting with Rome 2 seem to have this absurd manufactured difficulty that just doesn't feel right, almost like you swear the game is cheating sometimes. The math just doesn't add up when there is a 1% chance of something happening, and it happens every 4-5 turns. Low-level enemy agents with no skills will land 100% of their attacks. A rival nation will virtually never bend to accept a trade agreement or come to peace terms in an entire campaign. You need to create a general unit to have any force at all, because apparently in all of human history there have never been small detachments or raiding parties that operated without a commander in immediate proximity. It's like you just get penalized for doing well now, and it completely defeats the purpose of creating a sprawling empire which is the whole point of the game in the first place. In most cases you're better off just staying still, and even then you just rot from the inside out because of the game's building system. None of it feels accurate at all. There is simply no winning in the traditional sense, only losing, and it's completely by design to be that way.
Now let's talk about this epidemic of gouging people to death for DLC that CA has become so fond of lately. There used to be a time where you could buy a video game and it would be complete -- at launch -- for better or worse. Slowly, major developers started to incorporate little DLCs here and there like a skin you could buy for a dollar, a new costume, etc. Now it seems like it's practically impossible to find a AAA title that doesn't cost 200 dollars when all is said and done, and so much of the time you're buying stuff just to fix the game, or return it to what it should have been when the game came out! You need to pay for a 'blood pack', while during the entire game people are being trampled by elephants and fighting with swords? What?
All in all, Rome 2 is good, but it was the beginning of the end for me. I've watched my playtime hours in TW games steadily decline since this title, pretty much like reverse Moore's law over the past few years, and for the first time ever I haven't even bought the most recent title. They just don't do it for me in the same way anymore, and it's disappointing because they were always my go-to games. I really hope that they return the focus of these titles back to what made them so popular in the first place. I'm recommending this primarily out of unconditional love for the originals.

(Keyboard and mouse review)
*********************************
Good game, better and more distinctive than most of its genre, not as fun as Bastion (previous, similar game by the developer).
LIKE BASTION:
They're both WASD+mouse action RPGs, not Diablo-type point-and-click action RPGs, so that's a huge plus (Transistor allows for point-and-click or a gamepad, but I don't recommend using either).  They both have highly-customizable difficulty settings (though Bastion did this better), and they're both quite breakable with the right build.
Neither one allows much going back, but there's a new-game-plus system in both.  Everybody raves about the music, but it's above-average at best, karaoke cheesy at worst (same as Bastion).  The voice acting and dialog punch is top-notch, same as Bastion.  It is far more of a time-suck than Bastion (not better or worse, depends on how empty a person you are).
LESS FUN THAN BASTION:
There's less incentive to explore your environment, there's little in the way of a collection system, the story feels samey and less effective than Bastion's, the drama is significantly cheesier in its delivery.  There's less diversity of enemy art (lots of evil robots designed by Apple).  The roll ability isn't present, so real-time combat is weaker (this is a surprisingly big one).
MORE FUN THAN BASTION:
The strategy element is flawed but fun.  You can pause the game at a moment's notice and automate your character (which is useful and entertaining but locks you into real-time for a few seconds), or you can plan a real-time attack and test damage, range, etc. with no penalty.  On the downside, automation sometimes won't register moves that it seems like it should, or it'll miss or miscalculate or something else frustrating.  Bastion doesn't have anything but real-time, so it's good, and it's the main thing that makes Transistor not just Bastion with different art.
Attacks/abilities are more diverse than in Bastion, and far more of them are useful.  Every ability triples as a passive upgrade and an upgrade to another ability, and if you ever earn duplicates they do modify each other.  I've had a buttload of builds and most worked, where in Bastion I couldn't tear myself away from the wide musket/fast cannon combo.  Theorycrafters will have a mathgasm.
The environment art is beautiful and the character art isn't weeaboo.  I mean we all like weeaboo sometimes.  It's okay.  I won't tell.
MORAL:
If you think you'd like it, haven't played Bastion, and you're not set on the pause/automation component, get Bastion and play it with a mouse and keyboard.  If you have Bastion and liked it, get this, you'll like it.

Rating a game like Ironclads 2: Caroline Islands War 1885 is somewhat harder than some would think. Totem Games tends to cringe when people call the game a wargame. Developers likes to think of this game as more of a simulation title rather than a wargame. In some respects they is right.
As a game though this is a very good one, one that anyone interested in naval warfare should look at. In fact, this game would make an excellent follow on for that title.
The game is not a fast paced game. Yes, you can speed up the time in the game, in fact, you will have to if you want to play the game at all, but even so this is a slow paced game and the action fulfils itself over time. If you want a quick bang bang style game then this isn’t it. The ships of the time were notoriously inaccurate in their firing and in this game it is evident. You will fire dozens of shots at an enemy ship before you will finally sink it. Yes, there may be a lucky shot but don’t count on it.
If you are even remotely interested in naval warfare from the age of steam then this is a very good game to check out. The game isn’t perfect, the interface can be frustrating to newbies but the game is fun, and engrossing.
In the end I recommend the game.

This is a hard review to write as Total War Rome (the first one) is one of the most interesting entries in the series.  This game has both techinical faults and strategics.  This game is a crash and a half every hour or so.  There seems to be major memory leaks and overflow errors that really detract from whoever did the QA for this game.  This is about as bad as Shogun II when it came out and still is very unstable with the first expansion pack out.  The strategic problem in this game is that all the building statistics without playing with mods so heavily favors low taxes and food production that it becomes a solved game very quickly.  There is very little in the way of useful tradeoffs, you basically have to keep a major food surplus first, then think about building on a very low secondary basis, while minimizing taxes.  There should be more tradeoffs like in Medieval II between different winning strategies.

Papers, Please, is a spectacularly clever game. Consequences greatly effect what is already the far-from-content life of which you spend stamping passports at a border checkpoint. But this task alters beyond promise, and presentation in ways that I cant help but call bold. New mechanics are added as the game progresses, as well as characters to sacrifice for. This game made me feel for the poor 8-bit immigrates being denied access back into their country, it also made me choose who to betray and how to go about situational hardship. Managing finance and family was an interesting take on putting a face or a name to your character. 30 different endings, spanning 30+ days will keep you playing more than you probaby should, and unique gameplay only further insures this.
Games like this make me think, and not many games do that, even fewer that are 16-bit, and fewer more at this price point.
Do whatever it takes to give this game a place in your Steam Library!
