Transistor is a game that deserves more attention; charming in both gameplay and aesthetic, it should be pleasing to many.
Gameplay integrates strategy into the action, allowing the player to flash through and take out enemies in how they see fit. Skills are also customizable, allowing for creative combinations that will suit the player's style. And for those who wish for more of a challenge, Limiters are eventually made available, increasing the threat the enemy poses in exchange for extra experience.
The game has a wonderful atmosphere, with its beautifully crafted backgrounds, dynamic yet lonely colors, somber soundtrack (made even better with Red's humming), and the Transistor's dialogue adding to the futuristic setting and story of mystery, loneliness, and dread. The skills you obtain and use also have interesting biographies of their own; unlock and read them if interested.
While it is short, Transistor is quite linear and exploration will reward the player with supplementary dialogue, information, or pointless surveys. Gameplay-wise, movement can be cumbersome due to its point-and-click format and the player will have to rely on the strategy mode a lot during combat, which may deter action gamers.
As such, Transistor will most likely appeal to audiences who like strategy, aesthetic, and atmosphere. But as mentioned in the beginning, the game's charm is pleasing and should at least be tried out.

By far the most beautiful game I have ever played...
A majestic tale steeped in cells, digitalisation and politics, with even a quip of romance backed with an amazing soundtrack that compliments the ambience of the game, giving it a forlorn yet yearning quality. Add a responsive narrator to the mix in the spirit of Bastion's Rucks, and we have absolute narration and immersion..
Combat is primarily turn-based with some real-time ARPG and variety of specialisations involved, conferring a old yet new feel to the gameplay. It skillfully balances the dreadful tempo plaguing turn-based strategy and the mindlessness of real-time action to create an equilibrium between the depth of and interactivity of combat. There is even an option to strengthen the difficulty of your opponents allowing for some replayability and a sense of challenge.
Its only weaknesses lies in the linear storyline and dearth of reasons to play this game again save for the aforementioned option. That said, this game is wonderfully executed and will marvel you on your first playthrough.
Overall, a must play for those seeking a fantastic mix of strategy and customisation.

This follow up to the Dark Descent is very different, but still touches on some similar themes and elements.
Mandus awakens in his mansion with no memories of what has happened in the recent past. It's December 31st, 1899, and he explores, eventually coming across someone on the other end of a phone line that instructs him to awaken differen parts of a massive machine.
To say much more would be to spoil a lot of the elements that become clear in the story. But this is a game that mixes the abstract with the concrete, lending it an otherworldly quality despite being about something as steadfast as industry. It's a good story told well, although I have to say that the seling point on the Steam page of "the darkest tale ever told in a video game" is highly exagerrated, although it's still pretty damn gruesome and dark. It's a bit confusing in some ways, but by the end the overall picture of what's going on is more or less clear.
This game does away with the inventory and sanity system of the previous game and places pretty much all of its focus on moving the story forward. If the dark Descent was a more traditional survival horror game, with invetory and health management, as well as a sanitys ystem, this is a much more story and atmosphere driven game, with little in the way of puzzles (any puzzles you encounter are basically just bringing object A to a certain spot or turning a valve, so they feel more like busy work than anything). In fact, this whole game is streamlined from the first. It's far easier, with enemy encounters being simple to get through.
So while the Dark Descent might be a better pure horror game, this game is much more narrative driven, with a focus on moving the story forward. I guess this difference explains the mixed user reviews on Steam, but the story is wellexecuted and the atmosphere top notch, which makes this a solid play for horror fans.

I must admit, I had the highest expectations for this game. Since it was labelled as the sequel to the brilliant (and bloody scary) Amnesia TDD. However, this was anything but a sequel to me.
With the dark descent, the sanity mechanic was a key factor in maintaining fear, as it would put you under more and more pressure, forcing you to be resourceful and managing the use of the lantern to avoid the inevitable. However, in machine for pigs, the lantern is still there but sanity is gone, and the lantern never even runs out. This causes you to feel secure as you don't have to think about the lantern ever running out, let alone even needing to use it (most areas were adequately lit). The dark descent also had a brilliant way of making you scared of nothing. Creepy sounds, unnerving ambience and groaning monsters made you believe that you were under attack, even though you weren't. Machine for pigs didn't have nearly as much of this as TDD, and at times I barely felt scared, let alone unnerved or tensioned.
The dark descent was critiscised for it's linear maps and somewhat weak storyline, which was understandable and a good story does help in a game like this. Even though this is fixed with machine for pigs, I never took the time to notice since the game wants you to focus on it's supposedly "disturbing" and "interesting" dialogue. For christ's sake, if I was at least unnerved by the atmosphere then I might have wanted to realise what was going on. No wonder this game has been said to be a "walking simulator". I mean, if you want one of those then get a treadmill.
The story was alright at best, since the vast amount of text and pitiful amount of gameplay was distracting. It's ironic that the previous little issues in the dark descent that distracted you from the horror are the ones that have been fixed, and make it worse. Yes, the story is better than the dark descent, but I was expecting a horror game. Something branded with the title "Amnesia" suggests that it will be scary. The addition of this game has done nothing but ruin the name.
I completed this game in roughly 4 hours, which was not long by any means. The odd part is that it felt as if I was flying by. The dark descent was scary, and this would often make you stop and take a break (and a poo). I was trying to progress into the game and trying to find some scares, and before I could it was over.
Then I realised, why is this game so utterly underwhelming? I read up and found out that it wasn't made by frictional games, it was made by the chinese room. There's the problem. They only know how to make these walking simulators (dear esther), so it would be obvious that they would have incorporated some aspects into machine for pigs. This does show however, that it was the worst idea ever and they should have actually tried making it scary, instead of being like glue and not adapting to the given task.
My final words are, just buy the dark descent if you haven't already and play some custom stories. Tenebris lake, The great work and Subconscious trials are all better than this game, and are all made by a couple of guys with no budget.

The game really failed to bring me in. I thoroughly enjoyed the first one, but this one just seemed to lack the right atmosphere to snag my interest. The general lack of direction on what I'm supposed to do and why also contributed to that failure. This game not only fails against similar competitors like "Alien: Isolation", but it also fails to stack up against its predecessor.

In my opinion, the Dark Descent may have been the more terrifying of the two games, but Machine for Pigs told the better story. The community following for this series seems to overlook the story of either game and instead compares the levels of how "scary" the overall experience is, which I think is a poor way to judge this game. Sure it has the name "Amnesia" in the title and we may attribute that title to a "scary game", but I think this is overlooking greater factors in what makes this series unique.
I liked the Dark Descent as the scary, immersive, and atmospheric game that it was, but I do believe it fell short on the story. A Machine for Pigs was not, as disappointing as it was for some people, not nearly as scary as it's predecessor. However, in my time with it I found the game to be just as immersive as the first and it told a much better story than Dark Descent did. This game is not flawless, keep in mind. It is made by a different team than the one behind Dark Descent, and as a result it's more likely than not they did not use the game engine to it's full potential. A Machine for Pigs is not the most well optimized game, suffering from frequent frame drops and screen tearing issues despite having Vsync enabled. I run a GTX 970 and an FX8350 and I was unable to get a stable 60FPS unless I played on the preset "medium" graphics setting.
To sum up what I liked and disliked about the game, though:
PROS:
1) Monsters patrol areas instead of teleporting in and out of the map. Sure, a majority of the encounters ARE scripted, but unlike in Dark Descent if you do happen to die the monster WILL still be there when you load back in.
2) This game has phenomenal and immersive sound design. Best played alone and with headphones.
3) The game doesn't hold your hand through the last hour of the game like the Dark Descent did with Agrippa.
4) There were no plot holes in this story that I was able to pick up on.
5) Removal of the inventory screen, Part 1. Throughout my playthrough of the first Amnesia I must have collected atleast thirty tinderboxes that I never felt the need to use.
CONS:
1) Poorly optimized, screen tearing, frame drops, and I did encounter a glitch where an object I needed for a puzzle got stuck halfway through a wall.
2) Lack of interaction with the world. There are so many locked doors that you can interact with that serve no purpose, but meanwhile the only objects that Mandus CAN interact with are chairs and items needed to solve a puzzle.
3) Removal of the inventory screen, Part 2: Mandus's lantern never shuts off and he regenerates health. Along with this, in the Dark Descent there were items you would acquire from earlier parts in the game you find uses for later on. In Machine for Pigs, there's no need for an inventory screen because any item you need for a puzzle will be in the general vicinity.
4) Removal of the sanity meter. I can understand Mandus possibly not being afraid of the dark like Daniel was, but if I saw a deformed man pig hybrid patrolling an area I would get spooked by it.
5) The game is short. Even shorter than Dark Descent. Like 4-5 hours tops.
Overall, I did like the game for it's story but was slightly put off by the lack of puzzles and the poor optimization. I would give it a 7/10, and I would only recommend buying it during a sale.

This game is not Ragnarok Online version 2. The core gameplay is fun and interesting, but its design/technical problems are noticeable and might affect your experience. I recommend you try it out with some decent Korean MMO expectations.
Take note that this is coming from a F2P, ex-RO player whose played up to Rank 4 Level 100 (that's still early game, current cap is Rank 8 Level 330). To make things easier, here's some dot points going from pro to neutral to cons:
+ Gorgeous aesthetics, player sprites are well-done and nice map BGMs.
+ Fairly satisfying to grind huge clusters of enemy mobs, especially when using a controller.
+ EXP Card system allows you to use your EXP gained from questing at any point in your game, which allows you to skip grinding early-mid game by using them on the highest parts of the level EXP curve. EXP curve resets also exist. However, grinding is unavoidable in late-game.
+ Silver (in-game money) and equipment isn't going to be an issue until 170+, allowing you to focus on leveling up more.
+ Tokens (gives you premium benefits on entire account) can be bought from other players in the in-game Auction House with silvers, instead of TP (real cash).
+ Decent KB+M and controller support. Mouse support is currently a bit iffy.
* Somewhat complex class circle system. There's 8 ranks to progress to, 4 base classes with their own class progressions, and total amount of classes in the game is close to 60+. But it's very unforgiving, you can't reset class progression, creating class builds wily-nily can possibly screw you for late-game, and meta builds exist. So don't screw it up.
* Game is fairly linear with its story questlines, up to you if that's a pro or con.
* Game is soloable, depending on where you're currently at and your character build. Again, can be a pro or con.
* I can't comment on the publishers due to my short time with the game, but take some of the extremely negative opinions in the net with a grain of salt.
- Game optimisation right now is absolute crap. My rig with a GTX1080 and i7-7700 still dips down to 25-30 FPS when strolling around busy town maps. Can't comment on netcode since I'm an Aussie player that plays on a NA server, lag is pretty much something I've coped with.
- The game discourages you from doing leveling dungeons with friends due to the insane 600% party EXP bonus that you get from auto-queueing with strangers.
- The dungeon/mission queue system forces you to stay on the entrance map until the system works out your 5-man party. Queue times are also long (15-30 minutes average) due to currently low population numbers.
- Non-existent end-game stuff to do, aside from your typical Korean grinding for gear and Solmiki (think Endless Tower from Ragnarok Online).
- Some ridiculous F2P account restrictions, especially on the trading and AH front.
- Some annoying bugs exist like broken quests or missing treasure chests. Nothing game-breaking though (yet).
- Lack of better customisation options for your characters. Mostly restricted to hats, hairstyles and costumes (most bought with TP).
In it's current state, Tree of Savior can be a fun game but it is plagued with some problems that can potentially affect your experience. So proceed with caution.
PS. This is not the "true" Ragnarok Online 2. It never will be.

This is a great purchase if you are a Magic fan or would like to learn the game, without making ridiculous annual investments to keeping up with new cards every year. A significant improvement over the original DotP available on Steam, now including text chat, toggle voice chat, and multiple new decks. Decks are now customizable in this game, with the exception of land cards (i.e. the game will automatically add or remove land cards to your deck, but you can switch out any other cards, whether unlocked or default in that deck). This game also includes online Two Headed Giant (differing from the original, which was only local co-op), which lets you play 2v2 online against the AI or other players.
The game also includes some interesting Magic lore, a new interface, new music (takes on a more ambient tone), and new sound effects. Computer AI has also significantly improved.

Ignore the bad reviews, this game is so much fun provided you recognise it for what it is: a B-Grade Indie game. Come with no expectations of awesomeness or perfection and you will be thoroughly entertained.
You also need to know what you're doing, here's a few tips:
1. Choose a community server labelled "Rules, RP". The admins are quick to ban hackers and also deal with griefing
2. You will be griefed. Expect to do a lot of harvesting only to have someone attack you and take your stuff. It happens. Do it to someone else to vent rage, or take a days break from the game.
3. Hold "C" to pan the camera while harvesting to watch out for potential griefers. Trust no one when alone
4. Join a big guild straight away to get used to combat etc. before you venture out on your own
5. Only build with cobblestone and Iron doors or higher when they're available. Anything less can be chopped through or lockpicked. Also make sure your smelter is enclosed or really high.
6. You need a roof. Players can jump on top of each other to boost over high walls, so always have a cobblestone or higher roof.
7. Have a small 3 block high "Safe Room" that you store your chests and sleep in. preferably up high with plenty of iron doors from entrance of base to within room
8. Double doors (no space in between two doors) can glitch and kill you
9. If a hacker comes in and destroys your base (a rare occurance on a well-administered community server), rather than rage quit, take it as your chance to try a new themed based you've been thinking of doing. Egyptian pyramid? Hobbit hole? Tree house? maybe just a better designed castle from the last
10. Server wipes are good, not bad. Get in there quick for that mountain you wanted to crest but was claimed by someone else last time.
11. Regularly practice fighting, even if you don't want to. Because it will be forced on you at some point. Also aim high when fighting, head shots are the key
12. When just harvesting, leave all gear except tools and some food/water at your base. Regularly drop off harvested materials. If you get robbed no point losing everything.
13. Have 2 doors, spaced apart, as your entrance. This prevents people sneaking in.
14. Use a bandit trap. This is a tall open topped cobblestone tower next to your base that can be jumped into but not out of. If someone is chasing you, they might chase you down into this tower and kill you. They cant get out though. Wait until they starve or log off, then simply remove blocks to get in and kill their sleeper to get yours and their stuff. Must be high though. A lobby room at the entrance to your base also works, if you close the first door behind them. Must be 3 blocks high to prevent them log spawning to the beach.
There's more, but I hope the above helps. Again, don't listen to the spoilt brats giving negative reviews. Just take my advice, learn from your mistakes, and enjoy this glitchy yet addictive Indie game :)

Divide Et Impera.

If you are a fan of this time period (or also Europa Baraborum) and are on the fence of Rome2 go check out DEI first.
So thanks to this and only this would I recommend Rome2. Which in a way is very unsetteling when you consider that in order to make a game enjoyable you need to have the community lift it up and pick up where the developers cut short. Transistor is a game that deserves more attention; charming in both gameplay and aesthetic, it should be pleasing to many.
Gameplay integrates strategy into the action, allowing the player to flash through and take out enemies in how they see fit. Skills are also customizable, allowing for creative combinations that will suit the player's style. And for those who wish for more of a challenge, Limiters are eventually made available, increasing the threat the enemy poses in exchange for extra experience.
The game has a wonderful atmosphere, with its beautifully crafted backgrounds, dynamic yet lonely colors, somber soundtrack (made even better with Red's humming), and the Transistor's dialogue adding to the futuristic setting and story of mystery, loneliness, and dread. The skills you obtain and use also have interesting biographies of their own; unlock and read them if interested.
While it is short, Transistor is quite linear and exploration will reward the player with supplementary dialogue, information, or pointless surveys. Gameplay-wise, movement can be cumbersome due to its point-and-click format and the player will have to rely on the strategy mode a lot during combat, which may deter action gamers.
As such, Transistor will most likely appeal to audiences who like strategy, aesthetic, and atmosphere. But as mentioned in the beginning, the game's charm is pleasing and should at least be tried out.

Overall, a must play for those seeking a fantastic mix of strategy and customisation.

In Papers, Please, you play as the newly-installed border agent for the fictional dystopian country of Arstotzka. Reviewing passports, forms, tickets, permits, scans, fingerprints, ID cards, and vaccination records against an increasingly complex and daily-changing set of rules, you are the judge of whether each newcomer is granted entry, turned away, detained, or even shot.
Sandwiched among the ordinary visitors, travelers, immigrants, asylum seekers, and diplomats, you encounter characters whose future rely on your discretion. These encounters range from the humorous to the heartwrenching, and you have to decide whether to adhere to your guidelines or your sense of right and wrong, whether you're better off taking a bribe or accepting your piecework pay. Some of these decisions have gameplay consequences, while others are merely matters of conscience. Meanwhile, your ability to pay for your family's basic needs rests upon your ability to quickly and accurately process the line of faces waiting in front of you each day. To me, these encounters and decisions were the most compelling part of the game. The player is able to make interesting and consequential choices and either advance or hinder an underground rebellion movement, as well as the lives of individual people.
Most of the time, though, you're just processing paperwork, and that's about as interesting as you would expect. The game does a good job of simulating the inanity and tedium of comparing item after item against rule after rule, checking for discrepancies; of pulling out the "DENIED" stamp, aligning the passport under it, pressing down upon the stamp, putting the stamp away again, and handing each piece of paper back to its owner. If you like details a lot, are a bit OCD, or enjoy spot-the-difference games, this might become curiously addictive for you, but even as I compulsively continued to stamp paperwork, I experienced a nagging sense that what I was doing felt more like work than fun. I played through the story mode twice for the achievements, and although I was much better at processing the paperwork the second time around, I also found myself thinking about how many game days were still coming with an odd sense of dread. The first time around, there was at least the tension of whether I'd be able to make it through the full month and get to the end of the story (on my very first try, I reached the ending where you run out of money very early on), but on my repeat playthrough, I felt like I had to go through a great deal of tedium to reach the few meaningful encounters that I was interested in experiencing again, differently.
The game does feature several different "endless" modes, complete with leaderboards, but I see very little incentive to play them, since for me they remove the best parts of the game and keep the most dull. But if processing an infinite line of passports holds appeal for you, that option is available.
One final note: the save system in Papers, Please is excellent. It uses a branching system that allows you to start from the beginning of any game day in any of your previous playthroughs and continue from there, making going back for achievements or to see alternate endings much easier than it might otherwise have been.
Overall, I'd recommend this game for its unique concept, quirky humor, evocative decision-making, and immersive ambience. The story is worth seeing through to a few of its 20 possible endings -- but probably not all of them. Keep in mind, however compelling this game is, it's still a simulation about paperwork.

This game is a true exploration of what a video game can achieve. Video games aren't all about fantasy, war, dragons, magic and monsters. Papers, Please proves that this medium is limitless. In Papers, Please, you are put in the shoes of a border control agent in the fictional soviet country of Arstotzka, where you are charged with either allowing or denying access of your great country to foreigners and citizens alike, based on an ever-shifting policy handed down to you each morning. You must check backgrounds, passoports, work visas, and make sure everything matches up. But be quick, because you only have so many hours a day and you get paid per customer, and if you try to rush it, you might mess up and cause the poor woman who came through before to be murdered by the man you should have just denied access...
You get the point. This game is an amazing study of the human condition and a harrowing insight to one poor man's life in Arstotzka.

Papers, Please will definitely suprise you. Whatever you might think about a game in which your main goal is to stamp virtual papers, you're probably wrong. The premise of Papers, Please honestly doesn't sound like it would be very engaging. It sounds like work, and work just as boring as what most of us play games in order to escape and try to forget until the next morning when we have to go do it all over again. It doesn't seem like a game I'd be happy to have spent 11 hours playing so far. But. It is an excellent game.
There is more to this game than the mindless repetition of a dead end job. It takes attention to detail and quick thinking. You have to make decisions that will affect your and your family's survival in the long run. Choose to live in a better, more expensive apartment, and whether or not to buy food or heat for your household. Work with or against the rebels, or with or against the tightly run government of Arstotzka, or neither. Detain or simply deny entry to people with incorrect papers. Decide if your son deserves that gift he asked for on his birthday. And these decisions all lead to one of several different endings.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's great in its simplicity, and an interesting concept that I'm very glad someone decided to turn into an incredibly odd-sounding game. Go ahead and give it a shot. You'll like it. And if you don't, you're probably a Kolechian terrorist anyway.

After the disaster that was Call of Juarez: The Cartel that brought the franchise to a modern-day setting, Techland have returned with Call of Juarez: Gunslinger, a return to the series' Wild West theme. And it works spectacularly.
Story: The game takes place at the late days of the Old West and centers around the bounty hunter Silas Greaves, who stops off at a saloon and regales them with questionable stories of his encounters with infamous Wild West figures such as Billy the Kid and Sheriff Pat Garrett. The story can be surprisingly deep if you think about it, especially when you uncover the reason for Silas' journey, which will not be spoiled here.
Gameplay: Gameplay is similar to normal first-person shooters but with noticeable differences. For example, there is the Concentration mechanic which, when activated, slows down time and highlights enemies, allowing for quick and easy kills. Another good example is the "Sense of Death". When charged and an enemy is about to deal the final blow, Sense of Death activates, slowing down time and giving you the opportunity to lean left or right out of the bullet's way. If you lean in the right direction, you are restored to full health and are allowed to continue the bandit slaughter. The game also changes depending on Silas' narration. Enemies appear at random, structures rise out of and sink into the ground and it generally makes the levels more interesting. As you kill enemies and discover "Nuggets of Truth" in Silas' stories, you gain experience points to follow down each of the three paths of Gunslinger, Rifleman and Trapper, each with preferred playstyles and weapons. When not playing through the main campaign, there is also an Arcade mode where you travel through different levels and attempt to beat your score for completing the level and demolishing every enemy in your path.
Downsides: Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a pretty fun game, but there are a couple of downsides with it. For one, the game lacks any multiplayer component. Even though it's probably for the best considering the Concentration and Sense of Death mechanics, it's still a pretty big disappointment.
+Surprisingly deep storyline
+Spectacular western gunplay
+Level up and increase skills
-No multiplayer component
Final Verdict: Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is definetly worth the purchase, especially if you enjoy games like Call of Duty and Red Dead Redemption.

Before starting the second installment of the Amnesia series, it is important to note that the property has been handed off from Frictional Games to The Chinese Room. The new developer's slant on the series takes everything that made Amnesia:The Dark Descent what it was and pushes it in a more narrative direction.
This is still clearly an Amnesia game - all the physical representations of the character's increasing fear are still present: the blurred screen, the panicked breathing, the random hallucinations. It just has slightly different priorities. There is a story to tell and anything that would get in the way of that has been dealt with. Death results in a respawn to the closest safe space and possibly even the removal of the threat that killed you. Puzzles are made obvious by journal entries and the solutions are never far away. The levels are designed to offer only a few directions at a time, so as easy as it is to get turned around in the dark, it's never hard to get back on track. The old oil lantern has been converted to a more modern electric model and has a near infinite charge. It only needs to be put away to rest every once in a while; there's no fuel or power to watch slowly drain out. The character is in less jeopardy than in the first game, so A Machine For Pigs ends up being less frightening most of the time. The horror now comes from the slow revelation of how appalling the state of affairs has become. This is not a game that wants to scare its players with threats or challenges; its sole focus is on the macabre tale at hand. It's a good thing then that the tale is so compelling.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a psychological thriller created as the sequel to the first game, Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Although the game plays somewhat like the first installment, it is actually a very different game in terms of storytelling and jump scares. Let me just say, if you are going into this game expecting the same experience as the first, you will be disappointed.
A Machine for Pigs takes place in the late 1800’s after the industrial revolution, and the world has been modernized. Gone is the need for lantern oil, and tinderboxes, as your new lantern never runs out of battery power. Sanity is also apparently not an issue any longer and you won’t have to deal with any inventory screens either. The story itself is a long twisting tale of a tortured man who has done some pretty awful things. His journey to reclaim his troubled memories is a journey through the mind of a man driven to the brink of insanity from the overbearing weight of emotional loss. Determined to correct his mistakes and set everything right, he finds himself on the precipice of his own destruction.
As for gameplay, the traditional Amnesia style of solving puzzles shines through as the player will need to solve many throughout the game by interacting with the environment around them. The sound is, of course, another compliment to the Amnesia series, and gives the player that same sense that they are being followed continuously by something… or someone.
There are a couple chase sequences and moments where the player will be required to hide in the darkness to avoid detection, but the monsters themselves seem to be rather linear and will appear and run off in a preplanned route many times throughout the game. Most people were disappointed with the monsters as they don’t actually bust down doors and search for you like they did in the original Amnesia. Basically, if you avoid them then they will avoid you. But that does not mean it isn’t scary, the atmosphere of the game is incredibly creepy and there is barely any warning as to when a monster is in the area.
This game is worth playing for the story alone. Go into this game as ‘A Machine for Pigs’ and not ‘Amnesia.’ As a game of its own, it is great and worth checking out. But if you are looking for the same horror experience as the original Amnesia, skip this one and try out Soma.

I feel as though I would like this game more if "Amnesia" wasn't in the title. It's a sequel that tries to take a more cinematic approach to its story but forgets to be scary as it goes along.

Even the first few scares are effective and the creatures seem like they'll be a step up from the previous ones. But once you begin to head into the factory, that's when the game starts falling apart for me...
Over time, gameplay simplifies from exploring your surroundings to a linear cinematic walk-simulator where you're literally walking forward just to progress the game. The story gets vastly confusing and far too complicated for its own good (still believing itself to be shocking by the time its over). The environments inside the factory become very one note and not interesting. Enemies rarely appear and are easy to evade. Collectables fail to add world-building/character development and become useless/tedious to read after a while. And this game constantly shoves its title in your face by literally making everything about "machines" and "pigs" with no subtlety at all.....By the end, I found myself just pushing through to get to the end, unlike the first game where I was extremely excited to witness the ending...
And the sad thing is, I still found a lot of good in the game. All the above ground scenes and areas are pretty cool and exciting to explore. The creatures are scary in these parts and there are small moments throughout where it manages to be creepy. But ultimately, it fails to keep its momentum going as the game progresses

Transistor has much of the same charm as Bastion: excellent presentation, touching story, and a soundtrack you'll listen to long after finishing the game. But where Bastion is a pure action RPG, Transistor takes inspiration from more tactical games in the form of its Turn() feature.
At your behest, time ceases to pass, and you may choose a series of actions that will be executed in swift succession. You will almost certainly need to use this technique; your enemies are numerous, and their attacks are more powerful than yours, but careful use of Turn swings the odds in your favor. For this reason, I would mainly recommend Transistor to players who enjoy tactical games. If you try to play it as an action game in the style of Bastion, you will most likely be annoyed by Red's slow and cumbersome moves.
While the story is very good, it's rather confusing during your first playthrough. This is a game that demands much; you will need to scour the lore to find out what is going on. But if you take the time to research, you are rewarded with a beautiful tale of a singer and her journey through a flawed utopia.

While the soundtrack sometimes seems like an ode to elevator music, it definitely is very good at building the atmosphere.
I think that an explanation of some of the mechanics in game could help improve the experience, however the lack of a serious tutorial makes the game feel more immersive which I am all for.
The customisations to your moveset are a curse and a blessing, some combos work amazingly and others are mediocre.
8/10

A beautiful RPG, with deep combat, and an engaging story.
I had played bastion before, so had high hopes coming into transistor, yet was surprised at how much I enjoyed this game. There are obvious similarities: a smooth voiced narrator, tight combat mechanics, smart difficulty (where 10 variables are provided for you to adjust the difficulty in transparent, specific ways), isometric view, charming aesthetic, and a great soundtrack. Among the similarities though, there are significant differences that make this very much its own game, rather than bastion 2.0.
The most significant difference, is perhaps the combat. Rather than weapons, you collect powers, which can be equipped as skills, skill upgrades, or passive abilities. This provides a lot of complexity for building your character, with scope for many viable strategies. The combat is pseudo-turn based, in which you can alternate between hacking and slashing your way through in real time, and carefully queuing up your attacks and movements in frozen time. Such combat did a good job of maintaining the pacing of the game, while also providing the opportunity to experiment with new combat strategies without being restricted by mechanical competence (although mechanical competence is still required to dodge during the time that the ability to freeze time is on cooldown).
The aesthetic is also very much it's own, with a jazz soundtrack against a cyberpunk landscape. Both are excellent, and I have listened to the soundtrack several times since finishing the game. The setting was was well chosen, providing a good framework to pose questions relating to freewill, democracy, change vs permanency, and responsibility. However, although the setting was rich, and there were many details to embellish the main story, I often found myself somewhat confused as to what the bigger picture was. This didn't prevent me from enjoying the story, but did bother at me at parts. I'll link to a video and an article at the end of this review I found helpful in regards to the story/meaning (spoilers obviously).
The most subtle difference is probably that of the narration. Although the narrator is omnipresent in both bastion and transistor, unlike in bastion, in transistor the narration is happening in real time, as the plot unfolds. This means the narrator is not omniscient, effectively furthering the tones of chaos and survival.
The game is a good length (about 7 hours for one play through), not over staying it's welcome, and with challenges to enable deeper probing of game mechanics. However, it takes a little while for the combat to get rolling, as only after some time are an expansive arsenal of powers unlocked. Fortunately, a game plus mode extends the length of the game, and randomly generated assortments of enemies provides a forum to fully explore the combat.
5/5

Dark Souls II is a taxing but rewarding journey through a bleak land devoid of hope. The game perfectly intertwines gameplay mechanics and story in ways I had not previously thought possible. The more you delve into this franchise the more you will be amazed. If you couldn't already tell I think this game should be in the library of anyone who enjoys both challenging gameplay and engaging story. However, I want to clear up a misconception regarding this game and its siblings. It IS challenging, it DOES require your attention, but it IS NOT what I would call hard. There is no point in the game where you do not control the difficulty (save for those PVP invaders who have been playing since launch). You can always grind more souls and become an overpowered beast to brute force your way through a segment, its what I did my first playthrough. This game is very much possible and very fair to its players. The difficulty stems from your own mistakes.

In Papers, Please you are the head of an eastern European-esque household, and you have been selected by the Labor Lottery to do your part as an immigration inspector at a border checkpoint. Got all that? Your job is to sit in your booth on the Arstotzka/Grestin border and check everybody's paperwork for incorrect info and falsified documentation. You will be checking for anything and everything across the board. From incorrect genders to slight differences in weight, to wrong photos, to mismatched birthdates, to missing copies of newly required identification, to forged stamps, to possible aliases. On top of it all, the rules are constantly changing. You may be asked not to admit anybody from a certain country. And then the next day you're asked not to, anymore. It keeps you on your toes, and keeps you paying attention so you don't become complacent and bored.
It seems daunting, at first. It truly does. But as you go, you get the hang of things. Your first playthrough might not be great, but that second one will undoubtedly be much, much better.
Now, this is not all that you'll have to worry about. Your family needs food, heat, and of course a place to live (among other things). These things cost money. You receive $5 for every properly processed traveller, $0 for your first two mistakes of the day, and an increasing penalty for each mistake after that. In a typical day, I can usually manage about 10-12 correct assessments, although not all days are exactly typical, and you may find yourself going home early on occasion for this reason or that.
Then comes the real decisions. You hold the cards, here. You could let somebody pass with incorrect credentials, but you will receive a citation. Rack up enough citations, and you can expect a chewing out down the line. Plus the aforementioned lack of pay/penalty. On the other hand, some people give you good reasons to let them through. A story of love or revenge. Bribery. Or perhaps you just like the person and figure you don't need $5
badly at the moment. You will need to weigh the pros and cons, and maybe take a few chances as you just try to do your job and keep your head down... or maybe a little more.
There are 20 endings in all, but that's a little misleading. Several groups of those are just variations on a single ending. Only a handful of endings will grant achievements. And only one will unlock Endless Mode.
It really probably doesn't sound amazing just having it described to you. But trust me when I say that the fun gameplay and unique personality and atmosphere of Papers, Please will thoroughly draw you in if you just play it a little bit for yourself. For that, it's worth the buy.
Glory to Arstotzka!

DISTRAINT is pretty solid artistic-wise and by the end of the story it manages to make you understand what was into Jesse's head and communicate its messages. But video-games have their technical aspect, too, and said aspect wasn't exactly on point.
The reason I avoid playing adventures is because I get lost trying to figure how to proceed rather than enjoying the storytelling - and this game is no exception. It started pretty well and I would probably not even mention this as a problem if it wasn't for the last hour or so, when it had me going back and forth searching for things or the right door to open since it was linear and I couldn't proceed otherwise. I caught myself anticipating the end of the game after a certain part, although the end softened my frustration.
With these being said, I still reccomend playing the game. Firstly because I value the creator's time to make it a lot more than the player's time to play it (although one could argue that's a wrong way of thinking) and secondly because of the really low price. Just keep in mind that if you don't like adventures, like myself, you might have a bit of a hard time making it to the end without feeling bored.

I feel it is important to open this review by saying that by no stretch of the mind did

I also feel like this is one of those reasonably good, short, often discounted — and therefore cheap — titles that, for those reasons alone, attract a barrage of people that find no imminent reason to give it a thumbs down but instead find easy means of writing a two line review giving it a thumbs up.
It is a ridiculously easy task to recommend
by means of a single paragraph review praising Jesse for his one-man handiwork, artistic skills and creativity. It is, however, much more taxing to look past that mask of success and into the misery that must be the life of a badly scripted businessman who can't decide between good, wrong, insanity and sanity and, for the love of me, seems to live in world where every evicted place reeks of a profound degradation, much like his own home.

The disharmony in Price's personality does not translate to the player by means of conflicted writing, but instead by writing conflicts. The final straw of that is Price's final decision, which is as predictable as it is final towards completely snuffing out what could have been a brilliant character progression or, perhaps, a light of hope.

Sometimes it was gore-related — cannibalism is one example and a Fargo-inspired scene another —, sometimes it took the form of something that moved in the corner of your eye, sometimes it was just a random explosion of sound. During all those instances, my blank expression persisted and my nostalgia of atmospheric games grew ever stronger.

This game is like the "escape the room" flash games you play on Armor Games but 100 million times better. Let me just categorize what I feel about this game and give ratings that fit accordingly:
Comparing this to the iOS version, the graphics are like night and day. This game's art style and performance is well worth what you pay for and makes other games of its price pale in comparison. You get what you pay for and more.
The music is very ominous and surreal, but not memorable. It gets the job done alright, but it lacks a certain charm that other games of its genre provide. It may be up to personal taste on this one, but it didn't wow me like in other games of this genre (E.G. Machinarium, Sam and Max, or even Superbrothers: Sword and Sworcery). This won't detract you from the game in the slightest, though.
I like the challenge and difficulty curb this game provides quite a lot. It doesn't baffle you to a point of frustration, but at the same time doesn't hold your hand. I also like that hints are optional and are given in subtle bursts rather than shoving the solution in your face. The puzzles were quite varied for the most part and really made me think and use the tools that were in front of me. I will say, though, that there is a certain puzzle in this game that is way overused and not spiced up enough to be considered fresh. You'll know what I'm talking about once you play the game. It isn't a chore but really doesn't engage you or bring much pleasure after being used so many times. Another thing I find problematic is the range in which some areas give for clicking. While not a problem towards the beginning, one or two puzzles later on frustrated me because I knew where a certain item needed to go but couldn't access the spot that I needed to put it in. But there is one puzzle
that was just plain cheap. It requires too much trial and error and lacks any rhyme or reason. I just looked up the solution for that one online. Nitpicks aside, it's a solid game.
While some might expect a bit more out of the story and say that the plot given is just fluff, I found the plot to be an added bonus that gave more headway to the imagination and let the player fill in the gaps as he or she goes. It didn't expect you to get what was going on because the issue of solving the puzzles was more important. It's more up to intepretation with the optional writings and a small array of cutscenes played out intermittently. In that sense it feels likes a story similar to The Polar Express (the book) or Where the Wild Things Are, just more adjusted to an adult style of storytelling. It fits the game and gets the job done. My only problem with it would be that the proverbial glue holding it all together seemed kind of weak at times.
Trust me when I say that I am not a length snob. For the price I paid, I had plenty to enjoy out of a very good quality game that didn't overstay its welcome. I feel that if it were longer, it would have gotten stale and contrived very quickly. People now are just so spoiled with their bajillion hours of game-time like Skyrim or The Witcher 3. Not to say that games like that are bad. All I'm saying is that people need to chill when a game decides to end after a few hours in as opposed to a hundred. No problems here.
Considering what this game provides you and the frequency this game goes on sale, I don't think you'll regret your purchase.
tl;dr It's fun, not perfect, but a worthwhile experience. Overall I rate this an

Where do I begin? Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2. It's been a long time since the glory days of CoD. 2009 seems like a lifetime ago, yet again like yesterday. A whole FPS generation has grown up since this game came out. Hard to believe it's been 8 years. I was 12 when it released and I remember begging my mom to let me buy it for my Xbox 360. One week after launch, I got it. Playing Call of Duty online seemed like the most amazing thing ever. I remember getting up at 6am one summer morning just to play because I was so excited. UMP Silenced ready to go on Skid-row. In 2012, I moved to PSN and played it there. In fact, I played this CoD for many years. When a new CoD came out, I always came back to this. The DLCs came out along with the new Stimulus playlists I remember. Then there was the care package glitch, where you could climb and double tap right on the d-pad to get double care packages. Remember 3rd person cage match? Remember boosting in FFA with a tactical insertion with a buddy? Remember trying to find your way into a 10th prestige lobby from TTG? Remember holding down X to lock the FFA lobby? Remember having buttons in your name? Remember FAL rapid fire mod? Remember the shotgun attachment on hardcore? Remember the Rust pipe glitch? Remember Michael Myers? Cops n' Robbers? Remember clan battles and 1v1 quickscopes? Remember trickshotting and trying to go big on YouTube? Remember calling that guy bad for hardscoping? Remember being amazed that someone had fall camo a week after launch? Remember getting online on a Friday night just to have fun? MW2 gave us that. Memories you can't replace. I made many friends on this game and I can tell you I have well over 1500 hours in game across my years of playing on the different platforms. I hope one day they remaster this gem of a shooter for the next generation of young FPS gamers to enjoy. Call of Duty may be a thing of the past for most of us and some may just say it's another video game, but Modern Warfare 2 holds a special place in my childhood and brings home the title of the greatest FPS of all time.

Of course you should feel entitled that they conform their payment model to other games, that bare very little simularity to what they have created. /sarcasm  This isn't an arcade game like a Cabellas special, it actually makes you have patience and some skill. Tree of savior was a free to play MMO that I came across while looking for multiplayer games on steam. After a week of playing, this is summary that I've come up for this game. Below are the pros, cons, evaluation and conclusion that I came up with during my playtime. Feel free to scroll down all the way to the conclusions as the evaluation might get long.
Overall rating: 3/10
Pros:
1. Very nice music and map design.
2. You don't need to change equipment frequently.
3. Interesting method of combat, you have to move around to get striking/evade advantage.
4. Many interesting classes to choose from.
5. Finishing main quests will lead you towards another story, which I find it great considering that some other MMO main quests are pretty much way too long.
Cons:
1. One week restriction for auction houses and trade for new players.
2. Absurd prices for DLC and in-game purchace.
3. Skill stutter. <-- My character gets stuck and does nothing if this happens.
4. Serveral mob unbalancing at higher levels.
5. Bots getting in the way of farming and/or missions.
Evaluation: After a week, I find that I gradually lost interest in the game as I hit level 155. I'm going to write out some of those reason starting with the first: the game or the levelling isn't bad but the monsters around my level such as the orange lizardman or the pink horn mole has an absurd amount of hp that makes questing boring af.
Secondly, this is addressed by many others: bots. Now bots are generally low level afk characters designed to travel around and kill monsters around the said area to grind up money illegally etc, but over time they aren't even a big problem. I see more afk bot classes that are the necromancer using the skeleton archers to "legally" bot on various high level maps, especially mini-dungeons. This makes it painfully hard to get mobs that you need to kill for your quest or farming item. Although I highly doubt the GMs would do anything about it since there were so many complaints from the beginning.
Thirdly, account 1 week limitations. According to others, that feature was to stop bot from taking advantage of various features, but I would ask: What does that accomplish? For the bots to do sales, they probably do shiz like buy overpriced items or even sell off their accounts since currency itself is untradable. During this period, what does the 1 week limitation do? If anything, I would say this only hinders legit player by making the item trading feature even more disappointing than it already is.
Conclusion: I won't really recommend this game to new players as over time with the things going on, it'd just ultimately feel like a waste of time.

Papers, Please is the best desk space management simulator I have ever played.
To be truthful, I never would have bought this if I hadn't tried it for free, first. Trying to figure out why people loved the game so much, all I came away with was that you worked at a thing and you looked at papers and you had to make tough decisions that could affect you, your family, or the people you meet. Which, you know, doesn't sound bad or anything, it just doesn't hype me up to the level of the people who understood it better.
So if you get the chance to play it, do it. That's what I'm telling you before we get into this. If you know somebody who has it, ask them to let you play to, say, Day 5 or something on their computer. It will be on your Steam wishlist that evening, sure enough.
In Papers, Please you are the head of an eastern European-esque household, and you have been selected by the Labor Lottery to do your part as an immigration inspector at a border checkpoint. Got all that? Your job is to sit in your booth on the Arstotzka/Grestin border and check everybody's paperwork for incorrect info and falsified documentation. You will be checking for anything and everything across the board. From incorrect genders to slight differences in weight, to wrong photos, to mismatched birthdates, to missing copies of newly required identification, to forged stamps, to possible aliases. On top of it all, the rules are constantly changing. You may be asked not to admit anybody from a certain country. And then the next day you're asked not to, anymore. It keeps you on your toes, and keeps you paying attention so you don't become complacent and bored.
It seems daunting, at first. It truly does. But as you go, you get the hang of things. Your first playthrough might not be great, but that second one will undoubtedly be much, much better.
Now, this is not all that you'll have to worry about. Your family needs food, heat, and of course a place to live (among other things). These things cost money. You receive $5 for every properly processed traveller, $0 for your first two mistakes of the day, and an increasing penalty for each mistake after that. In a typical day, I can usually manage about 10-12 correct assessments, although not all days are exactly typical, and you may find yourself going home early on occasion for this reason or that.
Then comes the real decisions. You hold the cards, here. You could let somebody pass with incorrect credentials, but you will receive a citation. Rack up enough citations, and you can expect a chewing out down the line. Plus the aforementioned lack of pay/penalty. On the other hand, some people give you good reasons to let them through. A story of love or revenge. Bribery. Or perhaps you just like the person and figure you don't need $5
badly at the moment. You will need to weigh the pros and cons, and maybe take a few chances as you just try to do your job and keep your head down... or maybe a little more.
There are 20 endings in all, but that's a little misleading. Several groups of those are just variations on a single ending. Only a handful of endings will grant achievements. And only one will unlock Endless Mode.
It really probably doesn't sound amazing just having it described to you. But trust me when I say that the fun gameplay and unique personality and atmosphere of Papers, Please will thoroughly draw you in if you just play it a little bit for yourself. For that, it's worth the buy.

Bastion is an easy and accurate point of comparison for Transistor; if you like one, you'll probably like the other. But the gameplay here is a lot deeper and richer, so it's worth a look even if you didn't care for Supergiant's previous effort.
Similar to Bastion, the story is simple but beautifully presented. The futuristic/maybe-computerized city of Cloudbank is a visually lush setting for monster bashing, and the snippets you find and decipher throughout the game paint a unique portrait of the city's history and the villain's motivations. It's easy to get drawn in, even if, from a player's perspective, you're just running around murdering everything in your path.
It probably helps that your rampaging is so enjoyable. Combat is real-time, but you can periodically freeze time to cue up a string of commands as if it were turn-based. That combined with the incredibly flexible system of combining your power-ups into increasingly elaborate attacks opens up a tremendous number of options, both on-the-fly and in terms of your overall playstyle. Want to kite around and chip away at range? You can spec for that. Want to play fully real-time as a bruiser? Sure. Want to mind control everyone into killing each other? Go for it. Run around unleashing monster turn-based combos whenever you can? Yessir.
If anything, the biggest problem is that the mechanics are SO flexible that it gets daunting. Thankfully, there are a handful of mechanics that guide you towards new combinations (avoiding the Diablo 3 "here is a new option that you have no reason to care about" issue) and, like Bastion, the game's difficulty is rather forgiving but has options for you to increase it on the fly.
But bottom line, this is beautiful, enjoyable, and distinct experience that doesn't overstay its welcome. Highly recommended.

So, going into this game I was expecting something just as great, if not greater than The Dark Descent, however going into it I ended up feeling it to be not just not quite as scary as The dark descent, but also a huge lot easier.. In this game, unlike the dark descent, you don't have to be sparesome with fuel for the lantern, nor do what you can to keep sane, there's no such thing really as picking items up and keeping them in your inventory, such as keys you'd find, pick up and with them unlock doors to progress, in this game, where you need to go is already open... not to mention, you can't really sidetrack because if you try, you'll find that all the doors you're not supposed to go through, will be locked.. I was expecting greatness from this game, being the sequel to the dark descent if I'm not entirely mistaken, but after playing through it, I must say it fell short... the game felt short, was not quite as scary, even if sometimes very eerie in a way, but that's more around me not being a huge fan of steaming-engine sounds basically :) To sum it up, this game feels like a reply to people who have played The Dark Descent, complaining about it being "too hard" or "too obscure".. it feels like the game is made as a very much easier version than it's prequel.. Things I felt whilst playing the game, which kept coming back for several reasons is mainly disappointment, honestly... the game could've been so much more if it only kept some of the core elements of the dark descent, such as an inventory, keys/other "ulocking" items, fuel for the light source, whichever kind you'd like, and a health+sanity tracker etc. Unlike the dark descent this game felt very linear, never really branched off where you could pick where to go, what to get first of the x number of items you needed to progress etc.. If you're looking for a good horror game, or have played the dark descent, and are thinking about getting this one aswell, I'd say you'd be better off getting/sticking to Amnesia: The Dark Descent and leave this one be, since it's more a dissapointment in comparison to TDD, than it is enjoyable in and off of itself.. Sadly that's how I'm going to have to lable this game.

There'll be a handy list of all the pros and cons below if you're into that sort of thing, although it is a bit concise. If you're a patient reader who can handle a crap-ton of text (or an in-depth review, you could say) I wholeheartedly recommend you to tag along.
Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this game was not developed by Frictional Games, the developers behind the Penumbra games and The Dark Descent.
Frictional merely published this game.
this game got on release was that "it wasn't as scary as The Dark Descent". Heck, most even said that "it wasn't scary at all".
I completely disagree.
most definitely so. I don't know how this came to be, but this is definitely how I felt while playing the game. You might already be thinking that I'm a colossal wuss, which I humbly deny, as this is definitely not the first horror game I've played. I went into the game with the same expectations as everyone else, thinking that it's the weakest of Frictional's titles and all that.
I surely did.
Complaint number two was directed at the lack of resource management, which has been a core feature of all Frictional's past titles.
People flipped their sh*t when they heard of this, let me tell you. I spent a good thirty minutes looking at the Metacritic user reviews for this game, and they all basically roasted the game for having "dumbed down the gameplay to oblivion" and "taken away the fear of losing light".
I can see the logic behind both of these arguments, especially the latter. The former just seems silly. I actually didn't like the resource management in The Dark Descent that much, as tinderboxes were way too common and oil was really hard to find. I felt restricted because I didn't want to waste any oil. Infinite fuel seemed like a godsend if anything. Despite this, the game wasn't too bright at all, I'd say it was the opposite.
and I actually kind of agree on this one. I'm not saying they weren't scary, because they were (they're monsters for a reason, duh). They just weren't "as scary". One of the major cons I would personally give this game is the
. Perhaps one of the most iconic pieces of audio in Frictional's games are the terror meters, which are basically the monsters' chase themes. Not only do they indicate that the monster has begun its hunt and that you should haul a**, they are a critical factor in maintaining the suspense of the chase. I'm sure everyone remembers the
in The Dark Descent, as it was easily distinguishable and altogether terrifying. SOMA had multiple, one for each monster type, all of which were f*cking terrifying as well.
It's basically machine noises. And when you take into consideration that you will be near machinery for a big part of the game, the mistake becomes clear. One time I had literally no idea that I was being hunted, just because the chase theme was so quiet and indistinguishable from the ambience. The chases were still pretty scary, but definitely lost some of the terror that the other games had.
Let's now look at some things that people actually liked, for once.
The Chinese Room as a developer has their focus set on story-driven games, and it shows. The story is such an improvement from The Dark Descent's, which I found to be quite dull and it didn't catch my interest.
The writing is stellar, and the notes were a blast to read. I wouldn't say that the story reaches SOMA's level of excellence, but it's great nonetheless.
The overall audio is great, especially the voice acting. The composer isn't our beloved Mikko Tarmia this time, but Jessica Curry still managed to make an epic score suitable for a horror game like this.
I haven't seen many people talking about the environments, actually. I thought that the overall milieu was certainly more interesting than in The Dark Descent. I didn't really like TDD's trite castle setting, so I eagerly awaited what this game had to offer. After my first hour with the game I was already very happy with the choice they made. As a big fan of steampunk, I found the environments quite pleasing.
I guess I've covered it all now, so here's the promised list for the impatient.
I still don't understand why people are so mad about this game. The things that they took away from this sequel aren't really that significant, and I found the changes to be quite good. The story is a huge improvement over the last game's. And yes, the game can still be scary, especially if you play it in a proper environment (at night, in the dark and with headphones. This is how every horror game should be played, for goodness' sake!).
I honestly thought this was a worthy sequel. Such a shame that everyone seemed to dislike it.

At first, I really liked the game and ideas behind it.  Hackers were and still are a major problem on the official servers, but a decently sized commuity server with active staff is a suitable replacement.  Becoming king was a thing I never really did, but it was fun to help others overthrow a bad one.  It's fun to build up resources, meet people, PvP a bit, create bases, things like that, but it gets boring after a while.  Often my friend and I have to come up with some crazy scheme to make the game fun, like the unrealistic goal of setting up ten trebuchets on some poor man's house or something.  Unlike most people, I don't find a problem in the PvP as long as you have a decent ping and so does the person you're fighting (under 70 or so, I've found).  The Chivalry fighting mechanics are great, and I was pleased to find that I was able to perform well in combat due to my hours playing Chivalry before.  That's all fun and games, but, now I'm not so sure if, at this moment, I would reccomend buying it.  Sure, it's a great game for the price, but it's riddled with a few hiccups, and the performance is not great even if you have a beefy gaming rig, but definitely not unplayable.  What I'm really worried about is the developers abandoning the game, which they appear to hold a reputation for doing, like they did with their last early access game.  I didn't buy into the rumors in the beginning but now that the game's been released and there's still plenty of, albiet small issues, and CodeHatch hasn't released much in the past few months other than "exploit and bug fixes" that don't do much, I'm getting concerned.  Hopefully I'm wrong.  Hopefully they'll release some awesome updates and fixes.  But I honestly don't know at this point.  Basically, buy the game if you want to have some fun, but I wouldn't expect many updates in the future.

Thanks to the most recent update I unfortunately have to give this a negative review - the update completely broke the food system. Literally just yesterday I had a food surplus of almost 200 in my Grand Campaign - loaded up today after the update and now have a shortage of over 250!! Now virtually every single building takes up a ridiculous amount of food. Military buildings (barracks and training buildings) and even temples now take up as much food as your province capital/settlement (eg tier 4 capital takes 8 food, tier 4 barracks takes 8 food, and so on), meaning you now need a ludicrous number of farms to keep your food in the postitive. Now almost every single city in my campaign, including the AI ones, have a food shortage.
The change may be acceptable when starting a brand new campaign, as you would be able to build accordingly, but this completely screws over anyone who is midway through one as they will have to dismantle countless structures and replace them with farms all while watching their armies dwindle from attrition.
This really needs to be fixed. Either go back to the old system or rebalance it and reduce the amount of food taken by all these structures.

I bought JC3 during the recent Autumn Sale, and at first I was having a literal and figurative blast.
I have a beefy gaming rig, and the game played like a breeze for the first eight or ten hours at G-Synced 120+ FPS constant. It really was a smooth experience. Then the troubles began... but I'll get to the technical troubles in a minute.
I'll start with the actual game. JC3 is quite fun on the surface of it, and there are even more ways to get around and blow stuff up now, thanks to the wingsuit and retractable tethers. There's nothing quite like tethering two enemy soldiers and an explosive barrel to an attack chopper, reeling in, and watching as the unfortunate soldiers' flaming bodies blast off from the burning wreckage, which then hopefully crashes into some fuel tanks for even more destruction.
Those glorious moments are marred by steps backward from JC2, though. One thing to note is that Chaos points do absolutely nothing now except show huge numbers, even though they still appear every time you blow up a Chaos object. Upgrades are obtained by earning Gears for completing challenges. In my opinion, challenges should have been a separate reward track, and Chaos points still used for character progression.
In general, combat is now even more "cinematic" than in JC2, and often not in a good way. You can no longer sprint or dodge in JC3. With sprinting gone, the grapple basically must be used for absolutely everything mobility-related; otherwise, Rico is waddling around like a lame donkey. Dodging is gone, because every last semblance of tactics or strategy have been removed from combat. You're showered with bullets at all times (Rico is much more durable in JC3), and enemies simply respawn around you constantly.
Seriously, they'll respawn anywhere your camera isn't looking. If you for example clear all the enemies from a table of land that's sheer cliff on three sides, grapple away down the only path to that table of land, and then grapple back a few moments later, there'll be enemies there again. How did they get there? Did they turn invisible like the Predator and sprint past you? It's a mystery!
It's the same if you're flying an attack chopper. Have you taken out all the SAM sites, flak turrets, enemy choppers, and boats at a base without even scratching your paint? Doesn't matter, helicopters and boats will spawn nearby constantly until they manage to take you down when your attention is elsewhere.
Yet, at the same time, fights are very easy.
Now, onto the vehicle controls that also helped usher in my technical difficulties. The vehicle controls are bad, but motorcycles take the cake. Even riding at moderate speeds (or low speeds, or high speeds), motorcycles either barely turn at all, or they whip around 90-180 degrees in the blink of an eye.
To try to improve the experience, I plugged in a standard Xbox One controller (which takes an eternity to be recognized by Just Cause 3, causes weird lag on every load, and can also crash the game). With a controller, the motorcycle was very slightly easier to control, but not by much. It still either barely turned or whipped around frenetically, whether I was tilting the stick a little or a lot. This isn't realistic, as some fans of the game claim. I've ridden motorcycles and dirt bikes in real life, and I play proper racing simulators too. Funny, the real thing and the simulated things don't control like hot garbage.
The automobile controls are much better, especially if you've got an agile sports or race car. The helicopter controls are easy; the plane controls are terrible. If they were going for a realistic feeling, they failed and ended up with garbage controls instead. In general, expect to be frustrated by the vehicle controls.
Now, after I started using the controller for vehicles, the frequency of crashes and hanging on load increased tremendously, and that's what eventually caused me to quit the game before finishing it. Seriously, this is a console port that can't even support a standard Microsoft gamepad properly! It would be funny if it weren't so obnoxious. This is a well-known issue and, no, it still hasn't been fixed.
Speaking of things that haven't been fixed, there are longstanding issues in JC3 that Avalanche never bothered to fix, For example, in the town of Surpicco, once you've destroyed all the Chaos objects and have done everything but capture the police station and fill the "Wreak Havoc" meter, enemies stop spawning prematurely. You have to leave the police station, go to a different town, get heat, go back to Surpicco, and then lure the enemies near/into the station before killing them in order to fill the Havoc meter. Yep, it's as annoying as it sounds, well-known issue, they never bothered to fix it.
So in summary, it's a real shame, but avoid this game. It tries hard to be good, and it almost is good, but there are so many backsteps and frustrations that it's just not worth it.

The mandatory "escort and protect" missions were truly designed just to be annoying, not fun. They had a great villain, and it was just... wasted.
I'll just cover the control issue. The other flaws will just have to fend for themselves.
Cars: if you have a controller, it might (MIGHT) work better. But the physics off-road were just, ugh. Horrible. No, driving off-road doesn't mean you're on ice, and having me be able to crash through a thick-trunked tree, then slam to a stop on a BUSH, is just too much to ignore.
Boats: HA! totally useless without a crew. When on a boat you're basically moving at a slow crawl, and the guns are invariably 3 hits away from the totally overpowered opponents, who DO have crew, and CAN fire and manoevre! So you can either drive, or fire, but not both. The opponents will get behind you, are faster than you, and never miss. Good luck with that.
Planes: never have I seen such a hash of controls. Remapping kind of works, but really the only way to get it working right is with a joystick, assuming the game supported it. Instead of, you know, doing it right using MOUSE and keyboard on a PC.
Motorcycles: yeah, go ahead and do a 90 degree turn without any input from the operator, then refuse to turn when I try to do so. This happened often enough to make motorcycles completely useless off-road, and only barely better on roads.
I guess other players have much higher annoyance threshholds, that or they don't want to downvote a game they paid so much for and was so well hyped in the propaganda. That or it plays very differently on consoles, which is my guess.
[edit] forgot to add: they can't even stay consistent in their own game. In one sequence, you're flying a military jet, trying to catch up to a twin-engine puddle jumper. Can you catch up? Like hell you can, because hey, physics don't matter when whoever writes the game says it doesn't matter, no matter how much it takes you out of the immersion! Oh, and the precision aiming gear mod breaks target locking on missiles. HOW MANY YEARS has this game been out, and they still haven't fixed that bug?  So many more issues I haven't covered here, hence the "do not recommend".
