I would like to start the review by saying that this game is awesome!
I know the developers have copped alot of flak from the micro transactions, BUT, it is a really good idea in my opinion. The game would not have progressed so far without it, and in real life, you DO need to purchase weapons and ammunition and venture out into the wild to hunt animals.
With that said, I dont have the oppotunity to hunt deer, moose coyote etc as I live in Australia. I commend the devs highly on the realism of hunting(not sure if some Aussies are on the team as they have the roo behaviour and toughness fairly accurate to rl)
If you have patience, the game really pays off ( if you dont, then the game will teach you patience) I found it to be really immersive, even with the free license. It covers a wide variety of animals if you purchase a subscription.
People complain about the subscriptions etc, but this is what fund the devs to create new content and I am more than happy to pay for the conent available now.
Its not just the huge range of animals, the amount of weaponry, ammo and hunting equipment available that has me hooked on this game. You can use tents to create a fast track spawn location (usually have animals spawn near you too) or you can sit it out and call the animals to you with callers, scents or animal baits.
I believe most of the negative feedback comes from fps fans or people are bored with music playing in the background. I highly recommend playing with headphones if you are in a noisey environment (I have sound cancelling ones that are really effective) as sound plays a key role in the game. Fair enough the animal calls register on the huntermate, but not the footsteps of the animals.
I'm giving this a thumbs up as it is by far the best hunting game I have played. Feel free to ask any questions about the game, Ill answer them the best I can but  am by no means an expert. I have only played 12 hours at the time I wrote this.
I do think it is a game you will love or hate though. If you love hunting and have the patience and no time to get out there in real life, this is your game of all games. This is not Cabela's "arcade" hunting!
Time for an update :)
After playing for over 700 hours (I also use the stand alone launcher but still have around 550 hours logged through steam)
I still think the game is awesome, and youi dont even really need the micro transactions to fully enjoy the game. That said, it is recommended to grab some weapons and licences from the store to fully enjoy the game and this helps the devs to create awesome new content such as the latest addition of Timbergold Trails reserve.
This is by far the largest map, and EW have done a fantastic job.
I would fully recommend the game to anyone, whether you are a casual gamer or spend most of your day gaming.
There is so much fun to be had with the multiplayer or with the competitions/missions that are running. Plus EW release one off comps and missions that keep things interesting. A few comps that have been released require you to complete missions as a qualifier. Gotta say I love this concept, but not for everyone as some of the missions can be challenging.
Overall, this game is not for everyone. If you like hunting, have some patience, then this game is worth a shot. It is free to play afterall, and have an option to upgrade. I have spent around 100000em$ (one of the game currencies that you can get good deals on) I have almost every weapon in the game plus a massive collection of equipment ranging from camo clothing, tents, bait sites, blinds, tree stands/tripods, deployable towers, decoys and more. *5000em$ costs around US$43 but worth it when they have bonus days such as the deployable hunting tower offers included.
The licence packages are also great value, giving free run on all species for the licence period plus bonus equipment/weapons based on the package purchase.
Once again, this is a free to play game and not a trap at all. The format is designed to allow players to try it out (and free to play players have their own class of comps where they can win em$ too) All the additional gear that is purchased helps the devs develope new content and further expands the great content.
Keep up the good work EW, looking forward to more :D
Edit again:Regular game updates/addititions keeps me active within thr game with more stuff to hunt. All the updates are a big bonus to the game that I already love. I am quite happy to keep playing without an udate as the regular competitions keep the game interesting enough as it is. Great work from the team at EW. Looking forward to the new reserve :) (they seem to be adding them almost every year) LOVE IT!

Where do I begin? Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2. It's been a long time since the glory days of CoD. 2009 seems like a lifetime ago, yet again like yesterday. A whole FPS generation has grown up since this game came out. Hard to believe it's been 8 years. I was 12 when it released and I remember begging my mom to let me buy it for my Xbox 360. One week after launch, I got it. Playing Call of Duty online seemed like the most amazing thing ever. I remember getting up at 6am one summer morning just to play because I was so excited. UMP Silenced ready to go on Skid-row. In 2012, I moved to PSN and played it there. In fact, I played this CoD for many years. When a new CoD came out, I always came back to this. The DLCs came out along with the new Stimulus playlists I remember. Then there was the care package glitch, where you could climb and double tap right on the d-pad to get double care packages. Remember 3rd person cage match? Remember boosting in FFA with a tactical insertion with a buddy? Remember trying to find your way into a 10th prestige lobby from TTG? Remember holding down X to lock the FFA lobby? Remember having buttons in your name? Remember FAL rapid fire mod? Remember the shotgun attachment on hardcore? Remember the Rust pipe glitch? Remember Michael Myers? Cops n' Robbers? Remember clan battles and 1v1 quickscopes? Remember trickshotting and trying to go big on YouTube? Remember calling that guy bad for hardscoping? Remember being amazed that someone had fall camo a week after launch? Remember getting online on a Friday night just to have fun? MW2 gave us that. Memories you can't replace. I made many friends on this game and I can tell you I have well over 1500 hours in game across my years of playing on the different platforms. I hope one day they remaster this gem of a shooter for the next generation of young FPS gamers to enjoy. Call of Duty may be a thing of the past for most of us and some may just say it's another video game, but Modern Warfare 2 holds a special place in my childhood and brings home the title of the greatest FPS of all time.

To me, it feels way more luck based than skill based, bottom line. Not a good recipe for a puzzle game.
Simple game with great visuals, a fun soundtrack, and a solid premise. However, I do not recommend this game because of the physics. It is a physics puzzle game, but with zero control over what the free gooballs do and with unpredictable goo placement, it is needlessly difficult to build a cohesive tower without it toppling over. The puzzle should be in deciphering how to build a structure to get to the end pipe, not endlessly working the goos over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over because you can't get them to drop where you need them. Example: the Tower of Goo level should be a fun introduction on how to build tall towers; the solution is extremely obvious. Instead, you need to spend all your time retrying because the goos all run up one side of the tower and pull it down, or you can't get the goo to span the right previously placed gooballs. If I know where to put it to add integrity, and I simply can't because the game won't let me, I'm not solving a puzzle I'm rolling the dice. Even following a freaking youtube tutorial where someone beat the level, I couldn't replicate the solution. Does that sound like a puzzle to anyone else?
I'm no stranger to difficult games, but at least with many of those you know what you're doing wrong. This isn't intellectually stimulating or challenging, it's just tedious.

Great game at its core and conception. Lots of small issues and bugs that keep it from being true AAA quality. However, the game still manage to feel polished when things go right.
IMC is a dedicated, but small, developer so the game is constantly getting tweaked and improved; albeit too slowly for some.
Good for those who:
- feel nostalgic for the MMOs of the early '00s.
- enjoy 2D overhead action RPGs.
- play long sessions and don't mind grinding. OR play short sessions daily (daily quests).
- enjoy having a very wide and varied pallet for character progression.
Bad for those who:
- will not settle for less than a final production product. (ToS is on a development journey)
- dislike grind, but are looking for long play sessions.
ToS is a unique experience in the modern gaming scene, both in its production and content. The game does have many flaws, which are constantly (and slowly) being addressed by IMCs small development team. The experience, as a whole, is very positive. While not perfect, ToS deserves more than "mixed" ratings.

Bastion is an easy and accurate point of comparison for Transistor; if you like one, you'll probably like the other. But the gameplay here is a lot deeper and richer, so it's worth a look even if you didn't care for Supergiant's previous effort.
Similar to Bastion, the story is simple but beautifully presented. The futuristic/maybe-computerized city of Cloudbank is a visually lush setting for monster bashing, and the snippets you find and decipher throughout the game paint a unique portrait of the city's history and the villain's motivations. It's easy to get drawn in, even if, from a player's perspective, you're just running around murdering everything in your path.
It probably helps that your rampaging is so enjoyable. Combat is real-time, but you can periodically freeze time to cue up a string of commands as if it were turn-based. That combined with the incredibly flexible system of combining your power-ups into increasingly elaborate attacks opens up a tremendous number of options, both on-the-fly and in terms of your overall playstyle. Want to kite around and chip away at range? You can spec for that. Want to play fully real-time as a bruiser? Sure. Want to mind control everyone into killing each other? Go for it. Run around unleashing monster turn-based combos whenever you can? Yessir.
If anything, the biggest problem is that the mechanics are SO flexible that it gets daunting. Thankfully, there are a handful of mechanics that guide you towards new combinations (avoiding the Diablo 3 "here is a new option that you have no reason to care about" issue) and, like Bastion, the game's difficulty is rather forgiving but has options for you to increase it on the fly.
But bottom line, this is beautiful, enjoyable, and distinct experience that doesn't overstay its welcome. Highly recommended.

Story-driven action game where you can periodically pause the action and plan out a "turn()" of lightning-fast movements and attacks.
The gameplay is linear but offers a ton of customization, since every equipable ability can also be used to upgrade any other ability or to provide a passive bonus. The game's difficulty can also be customized between fights by activating or deactivating various "limiters". Combat in real-time can unfortunately feel unfair or sluggish, since at higher difficulty levels you're expected to make good use of "turn()". Nonetheless, the gameplay is innovative and interesting.
The graphics are extremely pretty, and the game's dark plot is provided through some very clever indirect storytelling. Nothing is fully explained, but there are hints and details hidden everywhere.

I would like to start the review by saying that this game is awesome!
I know the developers have copped alot of flak from the micro transactions, BUT, it is a really good idea in my opinion. The game would not have progressed so far without it, and in real life, you DO need to purchase weapons and ammunition and venture out into the wild to hunt animals.
With that said, I dont have the oppotunity to hunt deer, moose coyote etc as I live in Australia. I commend the devs highly on the realism of hunting(not sure if some Aussies are on the team as they have the roo behaviour and toughness fairly accurate to rl)
If you have patience, the game really pays off ( if you dont, then the game will teach you patience) I found it to be really immersive, even with the free license. It covers a wide variety of animals if you purchase a subscription.
People complain about the subscriptions etc, but this is what fund the devs to create new content and I am more than happy to pay for the conent available now.
Its not just the huge range of animals, the amount of weaponry, ammo and hunting equipment available that has me hooked on this game. You can use tents to create a fast track spawn location (usually have animals spawn near you too) or you can sit it out and call the animals to you with callers, scents or animal baits.
I believe most of the negative feedback comes from fps fans or people are bored with music playing in the background. I highly recommend playing with headphones if you are in a noisey environment (I have sound cancelling ones that are really effective) as sound plays a key role in the game. Fair enough the animal calls register on the huntermate, but not the footsteps of the animals.
I'm giving this a thumbs up as it is by far the best hunting game I have played. Feel free to ask any questions about the game, Ill answer them the best I can but  am by no means an expert. I have only played 12 hours at the time I wrote this.
I do think it is a game you will love or hate though. If you love hunting and have the patience and no time to get out there in real life, this is your game of all games. This is not Cabela's "arcade" hunting!
Time for an update :)
After playing for over 700 hours (I also use the stand alone launcher but still have around 550 hours logged through steam)
I still think the game is awesome, and youi dont even really need the micro transactions to fully enjoy the game. That said, it is recommended to grab some weapons and licences from the store to fully enjoy the game and this helps the devs to create awesome new content such as the latest addition of Timbergold Trails reserve.
This is by far the largest map, and EW have done a fantastic job.
I would fully recommend the game to anyone, whether you are a casual gamer or spend most of your day gaming.
There is so much fun to be had with the multiplayer or with the competitions/missions that are running. Plus EW release one off comps and missions that keep things interesting. A few comps that have been released require you to complete missions as a qualifier. Gotta say I love this concept, but not for everyone as some of the missions can be challenging.
Overall, this game is not for everyone. If you like hunting, have some patience, then this game is worth a shot. It is free to play afterall, and have an option to upgrade. I have spent around 100000em$ (one of the game currencies that you can get good deals on) I have almost every weapon in the game plus a massive collection of equipment ranging from camo clothing, tents, bait sites, blinds, tree stands/tripods, deployable towers, decoys and more. *5000em$ costs around US$43 but worth it when they have bonus days such as the deployable hunting tower offers included.
The licence packages are also great value, giving free run on all species for the licence period plus bonus equipment/weapons based on the package purchase.
Once again, this is a free to play game and not a trap at all. The format is designed to allow players to try it out (and free to play players have their own class of comps where they can win em$ too) All the additional gear that is purchased helps the devs develope new content and further expands the great content.
Keep up the good work EW, looking forward to more :D
Edit again:Regular game updates/addititions keeps me active within thr game with more stuff to hunt. All the updates are a big bonus to the game that I already love. I am quite happy to keep playing without an udate as the regular competitions keep the game interesting enough as it is. Great work from the team at EW. Looking forward to the new reserve :) (they seem to be adding them almost every year) LOVE IT!

First off, I wanna say, props to Jesse for putting this together in 3 months.  It's obvious a lot of work went into the game, and it's awesome that he was able to get it completed.
This game is, artistically, beautiful.  I absolutely HATE retro graphic, 2D side scrollers, but this one really changed my mind.  The music and sound effects were amazing, the characters were well drawn and had neat swaying motions.  The game looks nice.
But it does not play nice.  No, no.  This game is slow and a snooze-fest.  The 'puzzles' aren't puzzles.  You walk from point A to point B to point C, back to point B, and then maybe over to point D.  There isn't really a whole lot of logic involved in these puzzles.  The hitboxes for selection can also be wonky at times, so you can easily skip over certain action items.  Act 3, I had to actually use a guide, since there is no map/point of reference to where you've been.  You just wander aimlessly and go down a memory checklist, hoping you are going in the correct direction.
Price also moves at a snail's pace.  It's fine at first, because you get to see the art, but during segments like I have described above, it makes the game about twice as long as it needs to be (my playtime was idle, I spent an hour 15 actually playing).  It just gets dull, and the story needs to move along.
The writing is absolutely horrendous.  The other negative reviewers hit the nail on the head.  The story reads like an edgy highschooler's emo diary.  It's trying to make some deep statement against 'the man' and how debt collection is somehow inherently evil (???).  Isn't it just as evil to NOT pay your debts?  Yea, moral relativism is a pain, I know.
Also, it seems that Jesse couldn't decide on a tone for the game.  Price goes from "I'm so sorry madam..." and "I'm an evil whippersnapper" to "[Expletive]!" "[Expletive]!" "[Expletive]!" at random times.  It is just all over the place.  There are weird drug-induced mushroom castles one moment and blood covered walls the next.  I did like the creepy ambiance that the game provided though, I am not a big horror buff, so I did jump a few times.
All this said, the game was 99 cents, and it WAS an experience.  I do not believe that it is a good game, by any definition of the word, and the Overwhelmingly Positive review is mind boggling to me.  If you wanna blow an hour and play a poorly written, yet pretty game, then DISTRAINT is for you.
I do not regret purchasing it.  However, I do not feel like I would recommend it.
Edit:  Removed unnecessary vitriol towards people who did enjoy the game.
This is the game for those looking for a short horror that unnerves and leaves you unsettled after the ending credits roll.

This game is an example of very interesting concepts and very fascinating (and disturbing) art and story.  Unfortunately, it suffers from a difficulty curve based only on how time consuming and frustrating certain levels are.  Most of the challenges rely on either counter-intuitive presentation (e.g. requiring the player to fling goo balls into an area that claims to be dangerous but isn't) or making the player guess what the physics will decide to do next.  The interface is mostly just dragging goo balls where you want them, but many of the levels require dragging specific goo balls quickly, which is often impossible to do because of the game not selecting the right one if there's any overlap.  This issue is then made worse by only certain goo balls being removable after placing them (which the player has to figure out themselves) as well as by the only way of reversing a move being to click on the little bugs that pop up for no explained or intuitive reason twice.  Not once, twice.  If you only click on one reversal bug, the game almost always reverts back to the most inconvenient possible situation.
The two biggest things I took away from this game was a deep sense of boredom and the feeling that the makers don't understand how an object's center of gravity works.  Even the constantly moving goo balls do not explain those bizarre weight mechanics work

Okay, so this is my first time doing a review of something, so hopefully I do well. Overall, I thought this was a great game, albeit short, and was a wonderful purchase for such a low price.
Visuals: 10/10
The visuals were a nice upgrade from the original iOS graphics, and many little details and touches really helped the immersion factor of the game.
Sound & Music: 10/10
The music and noises in the background definitely help to set the eerie tone that the devs were going for. While not necessarily memorable, the music and sounds are a must-have in this game, otherwise the atmosphere wouldn't quite work.
Puzzles: 8/10
Many puzzles were a bit too simple, and others were a serious downgrade from the iOS version. In places where you had to use two fingers on the mobile game, you instead just do the switches one after the other with the mouse. In the future, it would be nice if these types of puzzles were altered to suit the PC platform instead of showing leftover better ideas from the mobile version. I also found many puzzles a bit simple, but that could be just me.
Story: 8/10
The conveying of story fragments through sequential letters sprinkled throughout the playthrough was very interesting and worked quite well for the game. However, I would like for the next game (which I have not been able to play, due to my Android phone being incompatible) to have more story-driven elements to it, as I found that by the time of the next letter, I had nearly forgotten the last letter. On my second playthrough, however, I noticed a lot of symbolism sprinkled throughout the game referring to the main story, so perhaps they do a better job of reminding you than I give them credit for.
Enjoyment: 9/10
I enjoyed myself immensely while playing The Room (both the Steam and Android versions) and would reccommend it to most people I know, save those who throw puzzles out the window for Call of Duty or TF2. Regardless, if you like to solve puzzles and like a good atmospheric game, perhaps a little psychologically thrilling story here and there, this is definitely for you.

Pros:
Looks like a good class system, lots of options to build you character.
The skills are fun, combat is fun. I actually found myself running around killing stuff because I enjoyed it, not just to move a bar (or two in this case).
Geat art, the artstyle is a bit funky but the art quality is excellent.
Mixed feelings:
The armor you equip does NOT show up on your character. Instead, you equip a Costume item and that's what you look like.
With the only character customization being hair style and hair color, you will see a lot of same-y anime people running around. You get a new costume when you unlock a new class, so there's that.
The upside to this is that getting a new piece of gear doesn't make you look like a hobo until you get it matched with a set.
The downsides include:
Being a gingerbread wizard from the wizard factory.
Not ever being able to look like an adventurer. (or a hobo)
Missing out on what looks to be some nice looking armor pieces.
You're locked into whatever the devs decide you can look like. This is the case for almost every game, but usually you get to mix-n-match armor from different "sets" to create something that JUST might be unique for 10min until someone sees you and copies it.
Cons:
Need to be level 40 to use the Marketplace to buy people's horribly overpriced crap. (probably 3 days of quests and grinding)
Need to subscribe to use your inter-character storage.
Those things are understandable, they need to make money or the game fails.
But the game needs to work or it fails anyway, so these are deal-breakers:
The netcode is a bit janky, the game tells me I'm getting consistent ping under 40ms, yet I will still see enemies teleport across the screen because their location is desynced.
Afte playing for 2 days, the game no longer works. It brings up the launcher window, loads it to 100%, then disappears and does nothing.
I have a lot of other games I'm looking to play right now so I'm not going to waste much time getting this working. If this is your jam then I assume there's a fix out there somewhere.
I wish I could rate this "Yes, but..." but I can't, so it gets a brutally honest no from me.
I'm just glad I only wasted 2 days instead of a lot longer.

Possible Fix - Crashing or Unable to Load Game
If your game is crashing or not loading up, disabling Windows' Data Execution Prevention (DEP) may help avoid this issue.
Run Command Prompt (cmd) as Administrator, and then type the following line:
bcdedit.exe /set {current} nx AlwaysOff
Afterwards, restart your computer, and the game will crash less or not at all/start working again.
(If you ever wish to revert this change, simply change "AlwaysOff" to "AlwaysOn".)
Note: If you are not the Administrator of your computer, you will not be able to change this setting. Also, since this changes your system's settings, use the command at your own risk.

The plot is intentionally obscure - in the beginning the player has exactly no idea who's who, where is the plot happening and what are the rules of the world. You're probably aware that this is a beautiful game (nobody reads reviews before watching the trailer, right?), and it is BEAUTIFUL, the art and the songs. I see that most reviewers mention that and that the story is cool, but not so many people emphasize this enough:
During combat you use your skills (therein called "functions"), run around and etc... but you also have a "turn bar" that when fills up, allows you to "pause" the fight; it sort of allows you to "script" what you're going to do next. You have a certain number of "turn points" to spend on using skills and moving around. Once you're done, you "unpause" and your character will "run the script".
That idea in itself is worth the game, really.
The skills are AWESOME. There are 16 "only", but they are VERY DIFFERENT. "Bounce" hits the target and ricochets around; "Breach" has a long range and pierces the target and walls. "Crash" causes little damage, but stuns the target, which increases the next damage; "Void" does not cause any damage, but increase the damage for the next few seconds. Now, these are their Active function; skills can be used in Passive mode as well - which give you some bonus or protection - or be Combined (in the game its called "upgrade") e.g. Breach + (Bounce + Crash) will pierce through targets in a straight line, but also ricochet and stun. Mind you, Bounce + (Breach + Crash) is not the same thing, nor is Crash + (Breach +  Bounce).
The combinations and possibilities for combos are so overhelming that I've finished the game twice and never settled down for one single combo line, always changing. The combat system is just plain amazing.
Finally, another reason to buy this game: it is a Supergiant Game. These guys are one of the best small studio I've seen around, professional products released in mature state, also customer support was great when I needed. Back these guys as much as you can, they deserve it.

Probably my GotY 2014 - intense turn based combat coupled with beautful neon-art-deco themed levels with an absolutely killer soundtrack.
First the (very few, and pretty minor IMO) negatives;
1. Perhaps a little more enemy variety? The different foes are introduced at a reasonably pace but once you find an ability combo that works for you there's very little need to tailor your powers to the bad guys which is a bit of a shame as the combat system is at its best when you're tinkering with potential combos.
2. For such a vibrant looking world, there's only really a cast of 6 characters - people are mentioned plenty in the excellent little lore entries, but otherwise it feels a bit lonely in there. You could easily argue that's a design decision, as the whole place definitely does have a "the world is ending" kind of vibe, but given the richness of the sound and art direction it feels like a missed oppertunity.
3. The time between turns is mostly spent dodging (unless you upgrade a function to be useable while you wait for your turn) - fun when you narrowly avoid death, a bit frustrating when you are narrowly killed.
The positives;
1. INCREDIBLE art and sound direction. The soundtrack is excellent - I'm not a music critic, but I loved the tracks - real care and effort went into the music which comes out sounding like some kind of cyber-blues, a melancholy electric buzz. When not in combat you can push a button to have Red hum a harmony with whatever track is playing, which manages to be simultaneously awe inspiring and  little unnerving. The city looks stunning - highly stylised in neon-art-deco it really feels unique, like a city at the height of its glory. The colour palette is bright, engaging and serves to make each level a treat to look at. Best digitised city 2015.
2. Great turn based combat - the game encourages you to try your powers and skills in different and new ways by unlocking little lore entries and story accompaniment which serves to really push you to try different combinations. This makes pretty much every fight on your 1st playthrough feel fresh and interesting as you juggle about an increasing range of abilities. However, once you've unlocked a lot of the powers and upgrades and found your preferred combo you settle into a rhythem in the last 30mins- still very enjoyble but not quite the same as that wonderful experimentation phase.
3. The "Limiter" system - finding the game too easy? There are up to 10 additional options you can enable to make the game harder, including the obvious like increased enemy numbers, to taking more damage to more subtle ones like reducing the numbers of skils you can use or making it necessary to finish off downed foes or cause a downed enemy to potentially split into two copies of itself. I much prefer this style of difficulty modulator - you can craft your challenge and do it in a mchanically interesting way as opposed to just dieing easier and quicker.
Honourable mentions;
1. The ghostly shadows of other players occasionally walk around in the background, which is pretty cool. There's no utility to it, but it's done in such a way that makes me feel like there's a million iterations of Red fighting their way through a million different Cloudbanks.
2. Voiceacting and singing - the voiceacting is pretty great, especially from the Transistor itself. The singing is sadly very rare in the game, but is equally beautiful as the harmonised humming.
3. Recurse mode- basically a new game + mode, which I always appreciate. It shakes up enemy placement and generally ramps up the dificulty to compete with your full suite of skills.
4. A boss battle that's acually pretty cool and well done. Personally, I find that to be a rarity in modern games.
TL;DR An excellent turn-based combat game, with art, sound and music to fall in love with. Play for neon-cyber-art-deco-blues, don't play if all you care about is shooting things.

Transistor is the second game of Supergiant Games, a small independent developer known for Bastion. Transistor follows in its footsteps with its gorgeous visuals and beautiful music, which is again matched to the story of the game. The story is based around Red, a singer who lost her voice, and the Transistor, some sort of high-tech cyberpunk sword which also can talk. Its used as primary weapon and can also “absorb” the essence of deceased persons, which unlocks new abilities, here called functions. They can be used in four active slots, as modifiers or in up to four passive slots. Every function can be used in any type of slot with varying effects, using them in different slots unlocks new lore to read about the persons symbolized by the function.
Experimentation is key, as the game does not hold your hand but encourages to change the skill set around to find effect combinations. Combat can be done in real-time and with a pause mode, called turn(). In turn(), skills can be chained together and are then executed in super speed. But the game does progress, even slightly, which sometimes can the damage predictions shown in turn() render moot. The system takes some getting used to, but ones mastered is very effective and unique, although some say it is similar to the combat used in the Fallout series, which I haven't played (yet).
The story is again a part of the game. It takes place in the city of Cloudbank, which has a very unique art deco cyberpunk setting, where an AI only know as “the process” has gotten out of control. The Transistor is a key component in battling it, but I'm not giving away anything more. Logan Cunningham is back, this time as the voice of the Transistor with is signature cowboy-style voice. But this time more characters speak (except for the Protagonist) which have equally unique, but very skilled and fitting voice actors.
The game is a very unique experience, the visuals and music alone make it a masterpiece, not even considering the well crafted story. Compared to Bastion, it adds a combat system that needs some getting used to, but is very rewarding.
Also: If you got friends/family/etc. that don't think games can be art, show them Transistor. If this game does not convince them, probably nothing will.

I got this game a month ago.... My life has been taken over.
But in all seriousness, this game is fantastic. I've played a lot of mmo's during my years of computer gaming and I have never once had the real patience to grind through them to reach the end game. This game however has held my attention from start to finish, the cutscenes and dialog are all very well done for the story and this game is just very engaging to me.
Clearly since this game is an MMORPG it does take a bit of grinding here and there to get the the end game stuff, but let me tell you once you get to endgame it all starts there. There is so much to do at the end game its rediculous. I still havent gotten anywhere close to finishing it. I've only just scratched the surface of my Relic weapon not to mention only just beating the First Coil of Bahamut....damn T9. And the primal fights are just a fun way to pass time when you feel like making a farm party for them. Tbh just about everything in the endgame is incredibly fun, to me anyway, and will keep you busy for quite a long time. Not too mention this game is very friendly to Casual players as well as Hardcore ones. The combat itself in the game pretty much easy straight through the whole game till the end game. Casual players can find themselves just hanging around talking with people in the community or just maybe running some dungeons for loot or fun, While Hardcore players can find themselves getting engrosed in the endgame constantly trying to get that Primal or Turn clear, as well as farming several endgame raids and bosses all to get that one piece of gear they want.
Additionally you don't even need to level a combat class specifically. I know quite a few people who were so engrossed in crafting and gathering that they maxed a few of those classes before even hitting level 50 with a combat class.
Speaking of combat, in this game personally I feel that they did the combat right. Everything feels very easy about the combat and the moves and combos flow together very nicely, it doesnt feel clunky.
This is all I have to say for now, and I very highly reccommend this game to anyone who loves MMORPG's and is a fan of Final Fantasy.

Reached about the 190 hour make, and that's about when my "reset-itis" really kicked in, constantly wanted to start one a perfect seed. I'll admit the game itself causes you to fully restart.. in all the good ways. I don't want to spoil too many thing if you go in knowing nothing, but i'll say this: You start playing and you think "This is such a clever, good and effecient design", but the game progresses, new technologies are unlcoked and you then say, OH MAN, the game mechanics just got SO much deeper. That leap, the first time around, and for the several times it happens is SO much fun, andbe forewarned if you have slight bit of OCD. You will [gladly] stopa nd reset a new map.
In all, I feel like I hit the gold mine with an early access game; I wouldnt ever expect another to be this good. It is a near perfect game. tldr: If you've settled for the garme Triple A games dish out at full price, you, as a gamer, deserve so much better, and at the current price of $20, it's a damn steal!

I'm an old school gamer (think Atari 2600 and Pong), so I admit that retro graphics appeal to me.
Still, there are retro games which are ridiculously difficult, and sometimes it's a cheap gimmick: suck in the old school gamers, and give them something so difficult, they can brag and say "See?  The graphics are bad, but this is too difficult to be a BAD game!"
That is not what Droid Assault is.
First off, I *like* graphic simplicity, but this feels "slick", as if the developers cared to make a game that doesn't look cheap.  Secondly, it IS difficult.  You'll win a bunch of levels, but if you start from the beginning every time, you'll find yourself stuck; getting past the upper levels requires starting the game at the later levels - which itself is difficult.
Gameplay: you have different bot models, and you have a limited resource with which you can take over new ones.  It's almost impossible to use pickups to buff up one 'droid to INVINCIBLE POWAH.  Healing is minimal (but it does exist), which means you have to strategize which 'bots to play, and which bots to leave to an AI death.
The more you play, the more you'll find that the strategy is all-important - and THAT is what I most often like about retro gaming.  This game has replayability, but not because you've built up an unstoppable 'bot; that's impossible.  Instead, Droid Assault rewards smart game play.  Honestly, for the price I'd say you can NOT lose, and you may just find yourself sucked into a game the way you used to when you were younger.
I hope this review is useful...
EDIT: as a follow-up, I reviewed this game a while ago - and I'm STILL playing it, even though I've got almost a dozen newer games since then.  Replayability is definitely one of this game's strong suits

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Who'd have thought checking paperwork could be so fun?
Labelled as a dystopian document thriller, 'Papers, Please' sees you trying to support your family as you check and punch paperwork on the border to the fictional country of Arstotzka. Checking date-of-birth and ID numbers match, asking for tickets and work permits, checking thumbprints and keeping an eye out for reported criminals, your list of tasks grows day by day and the opportunities for deceit begin to pile up. Just as you get used to the system, someone throws a molotov across the border and new, tighter regulations get introduced.
The game is fantastic in how it presents itself, the story and gameplay are seamlessly integrated, and you face tough moral decisions and questionable actions. Do you let a man's wife pass into the country with her clearly forged passport? Do you detain someone smuggling in medicine for her own family? When you're struggling to pay the bills and your wife and son are sick, do you take the bribe pushed your way? The game is generally bleak, although offset with a quirky charm, and it is always interesting.
New twists to your expected procedures are frequent, and the citizens you deal with range from terse to vibrant. There are multiple endings, most of them grim, but there's the opportunity to replay the start of any day with a fantastic branching save system.
Thoroughly recommended. Glory to Arstotzka.
(P.S., I've played the iOS version for about 6 hours, hence my low playtime)

PROS:
-Pretty graphics, better than TDD imo
-Very interesting backstory (that you probably won't be able to completely piece together by playing the game normally, and will have to look up on the wiki)
-Some pretty creepy design choices, such as
, the children and the toys at the beginning, and the opening cutscene with the pig when you start a new game
-Good sound design
-Solid voice acting
CONS:
-Not very many enemies throughout, which severely hurts the horror/tension aspect
-No management of resources is required. This added a LOT of stress to TDD. It made it so that you could be your own enemy if you used too many tinderboxes, or used the lantern too much
-Virtually no real puzzle solving
-EXTREMELY PREDICTABLE plot twist
-There are a few instances where the game tries too hard to be creepy, but isn't
-Shorter than I expected
CONCLUSION:
I don't recommend this game, but just barely. Good external/aesthetic design choices, but the overall horror aspect is done very poorly (which is ultimately the biggest reason I can't recommend it. It has its moments, however), and the story progression within the game isn't marvelous either.
SHOULD YOU BUY IT?:
Discounted, if you really want it. It's not the worst horror game out there, but I wouldn't invest $20 in it.

This is barely even a game. There is no health or sanity system, there are no hard puzzles, no lantern oil, no platforming, no skill required, no real difficulty. It's not a game, if anything it's a walking simulator as the critiques say, and they are right.
However. Once you get over that fact, Amnesia Pigs is another kind of experience. Forget the tight grip you have over your controls, your expectations of difficulty, and just immerse yourself. Much like the first Amnesia, this episode is magnificently written, chilling dark, gorgeously atmospheric and the story is marvelous... But this time it's on a whole new level. What it lacks in the gameplay aspects, it moved all of it to the depth of the story, the design and aesthetics of the scenes and details, the music, the sound design and the astounding, practically perfect voice-acting. The game seems uninterested in providing any sort of gaming entertainment, just a few thrills and scares to give it the spice and have you feel the tension, and requires an appropriate mindset to be enjoyed. It's a design choice, apparently a signature of a Chinese Room, and it's not bad. I just wish they had given at least a few clues to everyone who bought this game and expected an episode 2 of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, as to what the game was. It was not their best choice, as it left a lot of fans extremely disappointed and drove them away from what the game actually tried to convey.
If you're unsure whether to buy this or not, just be aware that it is not really a game, but it's not a movie either. There are indeed parts when you'll be chased by a disturbing nightmarish creature, and there are parts when you'll be wondering what to do to progress. They're just not the core of the game, which would rather be its incredible story, dialogue and, most of all for me, atmosphere. As long as you're aware of this and you're still interested then yes, it's worth your money.
Personnally it's been years since I've played it and I've kept a truly great memory of it. I still listen to parts of the soundtrack, some of which are even coupled with lines of in-game dialogue - that's how amazing the voices are. They remind me everytime of what the story had to say and I'll never forget the melancholy of its themes and its brilliant atmosphere.

Just like most of these survival type games, Reign of Kings (RoK) is... alright.  There's nothing innately wrong with the gameplay or the style, and the character creation is downright hilarious, which is a plus.   But there is something to be said about the fact that this is just another survive and build game, very similar to rust, but with the twist of a "King" that resides in a castle (on the original map) and is able to tax the people of the server.  This is interesting, and gives some forced role play which can be somewhat interesting even if you aren't usually into RPing.  The main problem with this game is it's optimization, which can and hopefully will be fixed, I have a reasonably strong computer that's able to deal with many games that are much nicer than this, but just like DayZ and to a certain extent rust, this game has some optimization issues.  Survival Building games like this truly cannot be played well without a team of friends to play with.  If you are alone you'll probably survive one to three nights before getting raided and essentially losing all reason to play.  Survival Building games like this also call for some insane amount of time to be spent playing them, so if you are interested.  Strap in as it will take a long time to get just about anything done.
I'll break it down easy peasy below so you don't have to read all that if you don't want to.
Pros:
Hilarious Character Creation
Easy Learning Curve
Simple Mechanics
Fun if you like to build and survive (in video games)
Interesting Forced Role Play
Cons:
It's just another builder survival game
Optimization is horrible
Rust is probably better overall...
You basically need a group of at least three people to strive.
I wouldn't recommend it to be honest, but it's really not horrible if you think you'd like to pick it up and have some friends to play with.

For an older game the graphics still hold up pretty well and have great charm.  They really nailed that frontier feel of Wild West while perfectly capturing the spaghetti western tone.  I can easily give this game a solid recommendation.  I sincerely hope it gets a sequel some day.

But the main thing that makes the combat rad, are the powers. More like, you have these different powers, and you can make them your 'active' powers, use them as an upgrade to another power, or set them as a passive ability. So what I'm getting at is:
Except they're not endless, but still, I mean. If you get bored with what you're working with, switch it up. If you're just not hacking away at the enemies as good as you want to, switch it up. Tired of being god-like 'cause you found the perfect combinations? Switch it up.

Developed by a single guy in the timespan of 3 months, Distraint is an impressive little package that tells the tragic story of a man who finds himself, as part of his job, expropriating people from their homes.  A big theme explored here is guilt and the story unfolds itself by way of showing the player how the main character deals with this guilt as a result of his job.
This 2D indie is a unique experience with an art style I haven't quite seen before.  It has a charm to it that you can easily appreciate.  For me personally, it reminded me of Silent Hill because of the many doors you open during the game and the symbolism all throughout, for example, guilt has a manifestation which you will see playing. There is also a bit of gore in Distraint but it's not excessive by any means.
If you don't mind a sad narrative that explores meaningful themes and is thought-provoking, then Distraint is definitely worth your time.  I should note that at certain points in the game you may find yourself lost or have no idea how to progress; it happened to me a few times because the game does not hold your hand.  You need to pick up the pieces as you go and pay close attention in some areas.  If you get stuck though, there are guides that can help so it's no problem.
Right now as of 6/25/17 Distraint is $1 and for that price you cannot go wrong.

This small indie game was very fun to play at the end of a long school day before going to bed (;
The story is about a young man working for a legal firm who finds himself being made evict people out of their homes who otherwise have nothing. Over time he begins to question himself over the morality of this activity and this dilemma is what the progression of the game centres around.
The game's strong points reside in the aesthetically pleasing pixellated artstyle and colours that tie inwith the main tone of the story, leading to the next point; story. Distraint tells an interesting story that makes the listener want more and concludes very well. As well as this, the game's soundtrack is very well done.
Listed as horror, Distraint puts the player on edge at points but never overdoes it, which I appreciate.
Although not for players who enjoy a faster paced AAA experience, I highly advise you pick up this game for under 1$ as it goes on sale frequently.

I'm not entirely sure why The Room is called 'The Room'. It's more like a series of puzzle boxes, and so while playing it I began mentally referring to it as 'Myst-in-a-Box'. Like Myst, The Room is a game where you solve puzzles to advance through the story.
Of course, The Room is a much more modern game than Myst, and playing on PC, you'll quickly notice its touch-controls roots. Overall, it wasn't tough to control via mouse, except for when you look closer at an item in your inventory, which required a click-drag-drag-drag-drag movement. This was mostly a useless action on my part anyway, since viewing objects in your inventory rarely advances the game, but the 3D objects in The Room are pretty, and thus want to be looked at.
That's probably The Room's greatest strength, its graphics. Updated from its original 2012 debut on iOS to take advantage of the extra horsepower allowed with a PC, The Room is simply beautiful. Often, things looks so pretty, you kind of just get caught up looking at all of it, ignoring the impossibility of the way the series of puzzle boxes unlock and unfold. The story is also somwhat interesting, though without spoiling the game, I have to say that I was pretty disappointed with the ending.
As of this review, The Room is going for $5 on Steam, and that seems like a great bargain. Maybe it is - I spent nearly 4 hours to finish it, without using any hints, and I generally had a good time doing it. But then, the game is also currently selling for $0.99 on mobile devices, and aside from the lesser graphics, I imagine the experience is pretty similar.
And then there's that ending. It's just really not good. Not that I didn't get a certain satisfaction from merely finishing the game, and not that I wouldn't recommend it to puzzle game fans anyway, but I have a hard time thinking that even mobile users got any fulfillment from the ending. I'm not sure if Fireproof Games was thinking about eventually adding more content (or more likely, a sequel), but despite their name, I still felt a little burned upon finishing.
Like I said though, I did enjoy the time I spent actually playing the game, and for anyone looking for a decent, relatively short puzzle game, I'd still recommend The Room. Just don't expect much from the ending, or to see much of any actual rooms.

To be honest, I didn't know what to expect when I started playing "Papers, Please". Some friends of mine recommended the game highly and as it was on sale, I bought it. Though the concept behind the game is simple, you're a border cop who is to grant or deny access to your country to people based on the papers and other evidence they provide, it can get quite complex.
The first days of the game introduce new concepts at a fast but manageable pace, steadily adding to the complexity of your task. Though the concept may sound boring, it's actually quite entertaining due to the colourful characters that appear at your booth (some are humorous, some address real-life issues like human trafficking), the puzzle work involved, the cheesy coldwar era communist state setting and the "reward" overview at the end of every day.
I've only played a couple of hours yet, but am really enjoying the game. Only drawback I have identified is that sometimes people with ok documents and motives blow themselves up after I've granted them access to the country. I've "retried" these people several times and can find nothing wrong. Maybe these are scripted events to increase difficulty? If so, I would have gladly known about it, as I'm currently unsure what I'm doing wrong. Otherwise a very enjoyable experience.

TL;DR (take away message):
I can not recommend this game. I would truly love to... but I simply can not. I had high hopes for the game and was looking forward to a spiritual successor to Ragnarok Online (during its prime). Sadly, the game has gone downhill since initial release and is showing no sign of recovery. Despite a lot of potential, nostalgia, and an actually good game at its core... the overall experience is a poor and frustrating one.
The biggest culprit, I feel, is the dev team itself at IMC games. A persistent disregard for the community has lead to their rare attempts to fix issues being so idiotic and heavy handed that they hurt the general player base more than the offending parties. More often than not, serious issues are unresolved or even just not acknowledged... while the in game premium/cash shop seems to never be neglected. I have played on and off since launch day, and many bugs and other problems (ranging from annoying to gamebreaking) present at launch have yet to be fixed. Add to that simply terrible optimization resulting in even good machines being slowed down by the overly simple graphics, and very few people have stuck around.
This has lead to a decline in the player base to the point where you will very often be the only one in a zone, with most towns populated by fewer than a dozen AFK shops.
Unfortunately, this is one more case of a good opportunity lost due to a bad company. It looks like this game is the real one that needed a "Savior."

An addictive game where we strive for efficiency and success.
Having spent over 48 hours on this game in 2 multiplayer sessions I can certainly say this is an addictive game as its centered mostly on base building with survival becoming more important later in the game.
Base building: 5/5
Survival: 3/5
Multiplayer: 5/5
Base building quickly becomes a fun challenge of figuring out the most efficient way of bringing raw materials to various factory buildings.
Factories build faster than you can but they don't automatically build sub-parts so to build these subparts you have to build infastructure which explains very quickly where my time disappeared to, yet I still felt interested in the game as demand increased in production all new problems around my base started to form.  New problems, new player solutions.. its the most addictive part of the game and probably part of its success.
Survival is one of the more lacking parts of the game in my opinion.
Factories produce pollution forcing enemy bases to spawn and attack;  these attacks are fast and typically end in seconds and the outcome usually comes down to the tech you have.
At the end of the day the enemy is there to harass you and remind you that the game's fail condition is when you forget your resources are running out before clearing out enemies.
Multiplayer is the same as singleplayer and can easily save you time building or defending your base and I've often found the fun in attempting to work on solutions for what my coop friends have been working on.

Graphics are a bit toonish but grow on you quickly, and the combat is a blast with the usual choices between a variety of guns, shields, and grenades to suit your playstyle. Replay is a lot like diablo and such games, same story but tougher monsters. If you do no side quests and no DLC, the main story line can be relatively short. You get rewarded for completing challenges (like kill 100 bugs, or set 50 enemies on fire) in the form of "badass" points that apply to all your characters and give you miniscule bonuses in areas such as shields or gun damage that eventually stack up.
Casual gamers can solo the basic game, and after that, you'll need to pay careful attention to skills and gear or group up. While I'm not a huge fan of replaying the same story over and over, when I need a shot-em-up fix, this one does the trick.

I understand why Frictional Games did not want to do a follow up to Amnesia the Dark Descent, i mean there first game was already perfect so why bother. It's also an interesting gamble that they hired The Chinese Room to make a Sequel considering that they have never done a horror game.

Unfortunately it's a walking simulator and the focus on sneak gameplay and horror encounters has been strip down to a bare minimum. So the only thing that is there is a level design about clicking a few switches and a audio narrative story about a tale of love, death and pigs. Thankfully The Chinese Room now's how to Tell a story since they have done that in the past with Dear Esther and with Everyone goes to the Rapture (which would release on the ps4 a few year later).

Emily is Away is a short 30-ish minute game that sticks around for just long enough to get you attached. This is a game where your choices DO matter.

The game shines when you play it as truthfully as possible (i went as far as typing out the actual sentences instead of spam-typing) and has a very realistic, relatable ending. However, on subsequent playthroughs the charm starts to fade away as you start to see Emily as less of a person, and more of a program. Eventually the experience becomes less personal and more gamey, which is why I recommend playing through it only once, and then letting Emily go.
I felt so many emotions in those 30 minutes, from being caught in a lie to feeling vulnerable as I exposed my feelings. I tip my hat to Emily is Away for nailing it where larger games have often faltered (telltale).

Look, I've played my fair share of retro 2D style, pixel graphics-esque indie horror games like Lone Survivor, The Final Station, Claire, Uncanny Valley, Home, Reveal the Deep, Settled, The Last Door, etc.
Distraint… doesn’t live up to the “Overwhelmingly Positive” review. I have no qualms about the graphics, sound, atmosphere, or puzzles—they were decent.
My issue with this game was THE PLOT. The plot was laughably cliché, the characters were one-dimensional caricatures with no emotional depth, and the symbolism was heavyfisted.
Stories that focus on the protagonist’s guilt and horrific manifestations of said guilt actually require the protagonist to have actually DONE something guilt-worthy. Like killing their wife. Stealing from an elderly couple in order to survive only to find that they have died of starvation the next day.
… Working for the IRS doesn’t constitute as a soul-crushingly guilty action. It’s a JOB.
If my landlord kicks me out because I can’t pay the rent, is he a morally-deprived landlord? Hell no, it’s just business.
Same logic applies in this game. Just because Price is the harbinger of bad news doesn’t mean he has to shoulder the personal burden of evicting the residents out of their apartments to the point where blood-smeared elephants are chasing him through endless hallways.
The moral of this game is that GREED = BAD. Yet Price wasn’t greedy—he was trying to make a decent living. He’s clearly very poor, judging from the decrepit state of his apartment from the ruined kitchen to the leaks in his ceiling. His parents are dead, despite the fact Price is in his 20-30’s. He’s an underdog, trying to survive in a tough world—and he immediately gets lambasted for pursuing the most unpopular career known to mankind. Sorry, but someone has to do it.

It's not the greatest game of all time by any means, but it's certainly better than many. It's entirely possible that because of my limited experience with arcade shooters that I had a hard time getting into it; I expected greater similarity to a standard FPS experience of ducking behind cover and shooting when you can. That's not the case, you have to be aggressive.
Visually speaking, this game is an absolute masterpiece. The game's several years old and it looks like it's coming out next year. With the rare exception of the animals (which don't feature too prominently anyway), the animation, models, and textures are pretty much peerless. I wish I could have spent more time gawking at the scenery.
Gameplay-wise, it's pretty fun once you get the hang of the weapons and get a few skills under your belt. There are a couple levels where the game becomes frustrating. There are a several night/cave chapters that required adjusting gamma levels, which was difficult since I consistently went between washed-out and pitch-black. There's another swamp map that slows your movement drastically at the same time the difficulty spikes. It may be realistic, but it sure as hell is annoying.
Despite getting frustrated and putting it down often, I couldn't stop picking it back up. The narrative is delivered excellently, through the main character recounting his tale to a bunch of folks at a bar. Silas' voice acting, and theirs, is PHENOMENAL. I'm rather fond of all the characters despite having spent less than ten hours with them. His inconsistencies, pointed out by their commentary, result in the story changing after you already played through it, which is always entertaining. The voice acting is flawless as well, and I definitely recommend staying until the end of the game, as the story catches up dramatically right at the end. Arcade mode seems fun, but isn't really my thing.
I spent three or four afternoon on this and had a good time. It's not a genre that particularly gets me going, and it's a bit slower of an FPS than most. But even someone who knows they could have enjoyed it more recognizes that this game has INCREDIBLE polish and was a great a labor of love from all those who worked on it.
A must-have if you like arcade shooters, and an experience you'll look upon fondly if you don't.

This game, during the first days, looked like it was going to be easy, but as the game progressed I had no idea it was going to be so stressful! First, you always have to keep an eye out for forgeries, mistakes and other discrepancies. Second is the pay which is at an all-time low, so it makes it quite hard to feed your family. Third is all these offers from other people claiming that they will give you money, but sometimes, you can't accept because then your job would be at stake. But hey, that's what makes the game so fun! The part that stands out to me most though, is that at every ending, it says "Glory to Arstotzka.", which I've found can have different meanings depending on how the game ends. If ended in criminalization, "Glory to Arstotzka." can mean, "You don't deserve to be a part of Arstotzka. Glory to the rest of us.". If ended in doing your job well, it can mean, "You are accepted as one of us. Glory to all of us, including you." Three words that say the same thing, but mean different things. This game is definitely worth playing.

Amazing building game.
If you just watched the trailer video and were put off by how complicated this game looks, stop right there.
Factorio is incredibly deep and complex, and a new player loading my factory I've worked on for 50 hours will indeed be lost - but the game doesn't start that way. You start with a dude standing in a field, and a few supplies to build 2 basic items. From that, you'll gradually add new machines and technologies to your toolkit.
If you've tried this game and couldn't get into it, watch a short YouTube tutorial of someone going through the first 10 minutes of the game. There's a certain way you interact with *everything*, and once you understand that, the game opens up.
The developers are great about supporting the game, too, with constant, significant updates. I encourage you to play the experimental betas instead of the mainline one - the "beta" releases are surprisingly stable.
Great mod community, too - you'll find lots of "essential" mods to tweak your gameplay experience.
I can't say enough good things about Factorio. I think the worst thing about it is the price - gamers see a game that's a too-cheap indie title, when the depth and sophistication of Factorio is so much better than that.
Oh, and the graphics suck, but they have a certain kind of charm that just works.

This game is simply amazing. It brings back the good top down feeling from starcraft, and truly proves that good game mechanics trumps gimmics and graphics.
You will go through so many stages while playing game; assuming no FAQ or tutorials. The campaing is definetly a good tutorial, but i found a healthy balance between freeplay and campaign is a must; it can get frustrating other wise. In all, i havent looked back much to the campaing.
Reached about the 190 hour make, and that's about when my "reset-itis" really kicked in, constantly wanted to start one a perfect seed. I'll admit the game itself causes you to fully restart.. in all the good ways. I don't want to spoil too many thing if you go in knowing nothing, but i'll say this: You start playing and you think "This is such a clever, good and effecient design", but the game progresses, new technologies are unlcoked and you then say, OH MAN, the game mechanics just got SO much deeper. That leap, the first time around, and for the several times it happens is SO much fun, andbe forewarned if you have slight bit of OCD. You will [gladly] stopa nd reset a new map.
In all, I feel like I hit the gold mine with an early access game; I wouldnt ever expect another to be this good. It is a near perfect game. And I say "Near perfect" because the game developers read my mind. "Man, would be nice if i could do this, and the GUI had that. People post on the forums and they deliever.
tldr: If you've settled for the garme Triple A games dish out at full price, you, as a gamer, deserve so much better, and at the current price of $20, it's a damn steal!

ESO is a feature-rich MMO that allows you to have different focuses according to your available playing time and interests. However, to get the full benefits of character development, you need to strike a balance of experience in crafting, PVE, PVP, exploring and questing. The subscription offering benefits everyone because it ensures Zenimax will continually come out with events, features and contests to keep the subscribers interested. I purchased the products rather than subscribed because in Asia (on the NA server), maintenence downtime means 4-8 hrs lost every Monday during the peak Asia and Australasia gaming window. Subs get a 10% experience bonus though over purchase-users. Different servers for geo (NA and EU) and platform (PC, PS2, XBox) so if you plan to play with friends you need to be on a common platform and server.
Zenimax has changed game mechanics and features over time according to exploits that can bias gameplay or level the playing field where necessary. This proactive managment should improve the game's life which is a benefit to the user wrt  the $$ and time invested in the game.
At about 1500 hrs invested so far, I have still only achieved just over half of the total achievements of the game. I think users in NA or Europe will get achievments faster because there is a larger on-line presence during peak game hours in those locations and teamwork is required for many of the achievements. In AustralAsia, it can be a challenge to get a group of 4 or 12 together to tackle some of the pledges or trials.

I have to give the creator credit for making this in the short timeframe he did. Visually, it's just as professional as bigger studio efforts. It really looks good, and clearly a lot of effort went into the creation of the whole package. Quality looks, quality sound... But something's missing. I'm having trouble understanding why this is rated as overwhelmingly positive. Not to say that I couldn't be wrong, but I felt Distraint missed the mark, and suffers from a bit of an identity problem, trying to be too many things at once.
My biggest issue is that is markets itself as a horror game in the vein of something like Lone Survivor. The problem is that, aside from very few disturbing moments, you're never really in danger. The storyline almost completely avoids the horror aspect and instead deals with feelings of guilt, humanity, and inability to cope with the demands of the main character's job. Unfortunately, instead of taking a dramatic tack, that inability manifests itself in horrific hallucinations that are just jarring in transition.
I don't know, it could just be me, but I can't recommend Distraint, not when there are more focussed horror and dramatic games out there. That being said, this was also rated as overwhelmingly positive, so maybe other people are getting something out of it that I didn't.

Definitely a nice game, 8/10 overall:
-The graphics are quite basic, to be honest. It's not the best part, of course, but it definitely does its job. Really dark and unsettling in many parts of the game, with fair contrast between many zones, especially "safe" ones.
-Sound: Doesn't have much sound engineering, to be honest. It doesn't need it much, anyways. -History: Now, this is where it shines brilliantly. Quick Summary: First person shooter in the old American west. This means six-shooters, cowboys/Indians, and fast draw dueling. The game’s narration is very well done, coloring the story and mixing in a bunch of famous names that you may be familiar with, like Billy the Kid and Jesse James. The game’s campaign is rather short, but has replayability so you should get your money’s worth. By the way, the game’s graphics remind me a lot of Borderlands, though that might be unintentional.
The game’s story is told by the narrator Silas Greaves, an old grizzled bounty hunter who’s telling his tale to a few people in a saloon. It’s important to note that Silas is an “unreliable narrator” which means for all we know, his story is mostly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. In fact, the people listening to him call him out a few times, and as you play, things change (trees sprout out of the ground, or people appear out of nowhere, reminiscent of the Animus in Assassin’s Creed).  Basically, by the end of the story you’ll know that old Silas is making a lot of things up.
As for gameplay, Gunslinger is basic first person shooter with regenerating health. If you’ve taken damage, you just need to hide for a few seconds and you’ll recover. There are only a few weapons, but as you progress you level up and buy passive skills, and unlock upgrades to the weapons. For example if you invest in long range skills you’ll unlock an upgraded version (gold) of the rifle. You also have 2 gamechanging tools at your disposal other than weapons: Concentration, and Sense of Death. The biggest advantage over your enemies comes from concentration. You build up a power meter as you kill enemies and you can activate it with a push of a button. This slows down time and highlights all your enemies for you, also allowing you to kill them with a single shot in most cases. Sense of Death is the ability to do a little quick time event to dodge a gunshot that would kill you (and come out with full health). You can only do this every couple of minutes but it will save your♥♥♥♥♥a lot, while concentration allows you to clear mobs of enemies.
The highlight of the game though is the one-on-one, fast-draw dueling that happens when you encounter a boss. It takes some getting used to since you need to control 2 elements at the same time, hand speed and focus. The game’s little tips during loading screens make it sound like focus and hand speed give you an edge, but they are 100% necessary, because the duels last less than a second once guns are drawn.
In addition to the game’s campaign, there is a Duel mode and an Arcade mode. In Duel mode, you can take on all the bosses again one by one. It can get pretty frustrating especially when you’re dueling more than one person at a time (you only get 6 lives in Duel mode), but is quite a bit of fun. In Arcade mode you run through the game’s levels as fast as possible, trying to chain your kills into combos to get a high score.
Pros:
+Fun story, told in an interesting manner
+Duels are awesome, and stressful in a good way
Cons:
-If you speed run the campaign, you could probably finish in about 4 hours. It’s short but, the game’s cheap so it’s not a big deal.
-There isn’t much variety in the kinds of weapons you can use. Pistol, rifle, shotgun, and dynamite stick is basically it. There are a few variations of the pistol, but the differences aren’t especially noticeable. I went through the game with the rifle almost exclusively since it has the best zoom when aiming down the sights. None of the weapons have a scope.
-The enemies are basically all the same, other than bosses. They just dress differently. A rifle headshot will kill any normal enemy once you have the golden gun.
Overall, the game is a nice little gem and worth playing through if you have it. It was in the $1 tier of a Humble bundle so you may actually own it already.

Do not confuse this game with the other Call of Juarez titles, they have poor reviews for a good reason.
This game is a historical fiction western, as if someone took a rail shooter off the rails.  Narrator heavy, but otherwise felt like it belonged in an arcade next to Big Buck Hunter... where only veteran carnies win and the nerdy braggards fail to impress their dates.
This is not your "charge in with a rocket launcher" FPS.  The controls and levels are set up as shooting galleries, not as strafing arenas.  It's linear and has regenerative unquantified health.  Falling damage will kill you pretty much every time, swimming works but you can drown by surprise.  For a game as unforgiving about taking hits, the lack of a cling-to-cover mechanism is incomprehensible.  It has upgrade trees, but not all disciplines are equal (stick with the revolver path to start) and they play more like unlockables than RPG builds anyway.  There are collectibles you can miss, but can always get them in later play throughs (though it's ideal to get them all on the first run through with easiest difficulty for the experience boost).
Your first play-through might suck.  The narrator is his own worst enemy AND the unique levels just aren't intuitive (causing me to have to frequently look up an explanation after being stuck in a repetitive death grinder).  The checkpoints aren't necessarily in bad spots, but I hope you like your ammo levels and upgrades that just got saved.  Half way through the first play through, when I gave up on the shotgun and learned to love the revolver, it became a LOT easier.  Of course, if I learned how to use the concentration power sooner (it actually works more like click on/off sprint stamina than "an ultimate") I might have found it easier to start.
There are ten arcade missions separate from the story.  They are worth a play through at least once (after the story), but someone obsessed could end up spending more game time replaying them dozens of times rivaling the story itself.  You get to choose an arcade-mode primary class (six shooter/ shotgun/ rifle) and each class gains experience (by completing other levels with that class) towards preset skills.  I did six shooter until the last arcade, when I had to level up rifleman (in earlier missions) to beat the last one.  To get three stars, you have to combo chain almost all the enemies in the level, and will probably need to have unlocked most skills for that class to do it.  Watch a youtuber play one of these to understand the gameplay if you aren't sure you want to buy the game.
The game encourages you to play again (New Game Plus) at a harder difficulty (keeping your upgrades); from that standpoint it shines because now you know what you are supposed to do.  That's also the only realistic way to get all the skills.  But as a once-through-and-move-on-to-the-next game, it's not a polished / balanced story with smooth flow.  The best thing I can say for this game is that in working through my backlog and trying to constantly switch up genres, this game genuinely does break molds and try new things from what I'm used to.  I had a lot more fun playing on Hard after mudding through the first time on Normal.  Then "True West" is Hard without the aiming reticle (hint use gun sights or a bit of sticky note).
Value $9, or much higher if you love spaghetti westerns.  It'll be fairly short (6 hours) if you keep a guide handy and don't replay... but you really should slog through and try a replay.

I've not played many subscription based MMORPGs before, I used to play World of Warcraft before the cataclysm expansion, but I've played more than my fair share of free to play ones, and I can say without a doubt, that this game is amazing.  While the graphics aren't as nice as some of the more modern MMOs out there, it's by no means ugly to look at.  Between the scenery, the effects of differen't spells and weapon skills, you'll be enthralled the first time you play it.
I'd say if anyone is wanting to give this game a try, that they do so knowing it's not like other Final Fantasy titels, with the exception of Final Fantasy 11, so please don't think it'll be a singleplayer games you can just buy and play.  The upside of going through Steam is you can use your steam wallet to pay for your subscription, and you can use other methods as well if you like, so it can be pretty convenient if you happen to get a lot of steam gift cards or just find using steam to purchase stuff easier.
If you do give the game a chance, please put it a bit more time than you would with other games, the first 5-10 hours is pretty much just introductory stuff, teaching you the basics of the game.  Also for those of you who prefer to play solo, pretty much all the content, apart from dungeons and end game raids, can be done by yourself.
I'd give this game an 8/10, while the graphics are a bit dated, and the fact that you can solo most of the content and not all the cinamatics are voice acted, it's a very good MMORPG, and should keep your attention for a while.  I know I can see myself playing this game for a long time.
