EDIT (3/5/17):
I have decided that I have put enough time into the game to give a real review now.
This initial part is just my personal story regarding this game, the TL:DR review info is below.
To begin, I believe this game is very well put together. Following that, I also find the game incredibly boring. It follows the MMORPG trope of being an incredible end-game grind with no signs of relenting until you've wasted countless days of your life trying to get a single horse (or bird) to complete your irrelevant collection. Beyond the optional grinding, there are weekly locks on a dozen or more progression items, making sure that the player does not progress beyond their peers. This in a way, rewards players for being 'first' to do something. Though personally I find it incredibly frustrating to have to follow theses standards, and return every week, every day, to progress a fraction of a percent.
So I find myself asking, "why do I do it?"
Why would I torture myself with such miniscule changes, so little reward for hours of work. My answer, it turns out, is incredibly silly.
I first came to this world, with prior experience in the Final Fantasy Franchise, and this game was everything I had hoped it would be from a Final Fantasy MMO, post Playstation 2 era, I played every single day of my 30-day free trial, and when it ran out, I immediately bought more. I continued to play it every day. This trend has continued to this day, though I'm a bit busier now and I do occasionally have to skip days. I had so much fun exploring this new world, meeting new friends who I would still call friend to this day, mastering the mechanics of the game, and following the beautifully crafted story of this game, that even now, I yearn to feel that feeling again.
I play, in the hope that I will feel that again, I miss being new to Eorzea, I miss meeting the new NPCs, I miss learning new skills. This was my first MMO that I truly have dived into, and I feel as if it will be the last one I will enjoy.
For reference, other MMORPG titles I have played :
WoW Cataclysm (Private Server)
Tera
The Division
Tree of Savior
Neverwinter
Now as for an actual review-
: 8/10
FFXIV: A Realm Reborn successfully captures the feel of what a Final Fantasy world is supposed to be, combining the fantasy world of dragons and magic, with the future technology of the Allagan, but fails to hold through to the end. With lack of ingenuity in an already stagnant genre, the gameplay closes the curtains on an otherwise magical experience.
: 9/10
Nobuo Uematsu does it again ladies and gentlemen. Uematsu once again creates a captivating array of orchestrated pieces for every and any situation. From calm seas, to the strongest of storms he has written a piece for the occasion. This music becomes a driving force behind the story, and the major encounters, setting up these incredible landscapes of sound for the player.
: 5/10
If you have played another MMORPG, you know exactly what you are getting into. With the exception of the armoury chest system, which allows you to play every class on a single character. If you are new to the genre, you may find yourself intrigued by the active battles, need for positional attacks and use of cast timers and group buffs. These are all things that will inevitably tire the average player, they stay the same the whole way through with slight changes to the animation and numbers they produce. The gameplay is basic to put it bluntly. That being said there are quirks to it, there are of course ways to min/max everything you do. So if you take pleasure in that, you might enjoy it more.
: 7/10
Final Fantasy games have always tried to create a story driven experience for the player, and A Realm Reborn is no different. This has by far the deepest, most thought out story from any MMORPG that I have played. The characters have unique traits, they laugh, they love, they cry. Throughout the game you will meet new heros, villians, and the occasional idiot. You may hate some, love others, or even completely ignore the story all together. That is why I think this story deserves praise, without getting into the actual content. This game is completely enjoyable with no knowledge of the story, and they even offer to show you the cutscenes at a later time if you wish to view them. This allows players to play at their own pace, if they are tired of watching hours of cutscenes after every quest line, they are free to skip it and come back later.

Really fun action/strategy hybrid. You start with a crap droid and capture others, which in turn act as allies that you can switch to, but act autonomously. Droids themselves can move around and shoot in any direction, with various speeds, weapons and properties. It's really easy to get in to, really hard to master. The checkpoint system is more than fair, though, so you can always head back to a previous checkpoint level to use the squad you had when you last made it to that level, so if you really screw up a run, or are aiming for an achievement ("Flush" is a nightmare), you can slowly push the odds in your favor, as sometimes your AI buddies can march to their deaths when they have multicore brains.
It plays very well, has local coop and offers gradual challenge jumps to ease you into the more chaotic battles that can occur. Just keep in mind how the checkpoint system works, and you won't end up with a fist through your monitor.

You can become qualified to work in the immigration department after only a few hours of gameplay.

In this game, you are an inspector working at the immigration office, controlling who comes in and who not. While Papers, Please has simple graphics and looks easy to play, it actually isn't. As an inspector, you need to follow strict regulations such as checking the person at the counter if he or she has all the right documents. And whether those documents could have been forged; information are correct etc. You flag them out if they are not who the documents specified, or they are suspected smugglers etc.
In the story mode, the checks get harder by the days following the daily news that is happening, and there are cases whereby the immigrant has special reasons to want to get through, but does not have all the necessary documents; or a bribe to get entry when you need the money for your family etc. It all boils down to choices as an inspector, whether it is morally right to allow entry at the expense of breaking the rules, which would mean there will be penalty, or go strictly by the book in a heartless, unwavering fashion.
Overall, the game is well-made and is fairly addictive, and there is an endless game mode which can be unlocked when you meet certain requirements in the story mode.

You play as a man named Mr. Price who is burdened over the things he've done where he then pays the "price" of the consequences created by his actions following the orders of his bosses. (*coughs* Pay the price. You get it,right?)
By actions,I mean "Distraint" which means the seizure of someone’s property in order to obtain payment of rent or other money owed by that someone. (Yay! I'm learning new words and their meani- No.)

Borderlands 2 is the RPG shooter game of my dreams, with amazing replayability and a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of raid bosses to do with your friends/other members of the community.
(not to say it doesn't have its own flaws and bugs)
Borderlands 2 is the "continuation" of borderlands (1) which you don't have to play in order to understand this game. The tutorial of the game pretty much explains every basic function within the first minutes of the game. Although the story will reference the first game, its still not necessary to have played it. If you, on the other hand already played the first one and have STILL not played this game theres a lot of stuff in this for you too.
Characters:
The first thing you might notice about this game might be the 4 playable characters (6 if you bought GOTY edition which i highly recommend). These characters are called "Vault hunters" and just as the name suggest, they hunt vaults. They were called to Pandora by the CEO of "Hyperion" and probably my favorite villan ever "Handsome Jack". An ironic self obsessed ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who i would consider as the REAL comic relief (Except for Claptrap... ♥♥♥♥ CLAPTRAP). So the first vault hunter introduced is Axton: The commando, Axton uses sentries and grenades to his advantage. Next up is Maya as the siren who uses magical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t... ahem i ment siren powers to control the battlefield. Salvador the gunzerker = Dubble pow pow and Zero the edgy kid
Gameplay:
The game pretty much works as any other RPG shooter, you collect guns (there are over 1 BAZILLION) which u can find in containers, dead bodies and in quest rewards. the core gameplay alone is enough to keep a player that enjoys collecting stuff and grinding at least 30-40 hours. But if you do buy the GOTY edition (which i highly recommend) you will get 4 additional campaigns with their own special weapons and shields. You also get 2 amazing characters Krieg the psycho and Gaige the Mechromancer. That might last you another 40 hours ish if u don't feel like doing raid bosses or all the side quests.
PROS AND CONS
Pros:
- Long content full game with enjoyable characters (both playable and npc's).
- story with a lot of bad puns and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jokes that are somewhat entertaining.
- a ♥♥♥♥ load of raid bosses and side quests to do after (or during) the story missions.
- True (Ultimate dlc) vault hunter mode, which scales the enemies up to higher levels although you have to start from the beginning of the story mode.
- almost every enemy is unique
Cons:
- a lot of the "OP" weapons are dlc's and a lot of the fun story lines and characters.
- The game can get repetitive if you're farming a certain item.
- It might not appeal to the casual player that doesn’t like the ”farming” concept.
- jokes and voice lines might be considered ”controversial” or ”offensive”.

I enjoy nearly every minute of this game and I don't regret my purchase at all. The graphics are beautiful, the world really does look like Tamriel, and the traditional Elder Scrolls mechanics like sneaking, lockpicking, bounty, books, dialogue options, and combat were implemented very well for a MMORPG. However, there are some strange design choices that really bother me.
First, the level scaling sucks. I know you want players to explore freely, but exploring just isn't as fun when the challenge is taken out of it. What is even the point of leveling when the only levels of enemies are "solo" and "group"?
Second, I was shocked to have discovered that I already maxed out 4 of my best spells at level 32.  I'm not into crafting so what the hell am I supposed to level for 18 more levels? You only get two hotbars with 5 slots each and can only have one active hotbar at a time, so I guess I'll be reusing the same handful of spells for the rest of the game. Coupled with the fact that you can count the classes to choose from on one hand, the skill system just seems really limited and constrained. I currently have six unused skill points and I have no idea what to use them on. There are three main spells left to unlock for my class, one in each spell tree, but by the time I unlock them I will have at least ten unused skill points.
Lastly, the fairly empty cities and lack of social activity make this game feel a bit lonely, at least until I travel to a random solo area where I find a bunch of other players doing the same solo quest without paying any attention to each other. Everyone seems to just go about their business and there is little player interaction. It is like thousands of people are all playing a singleplayer game even though they share the same world.
I know this seems like a negative review, but I actually really like this game and will keep playing in the hope that it only gets better. While this game does not suffer from many of the traditional MMO problems, it does suffer from the modern trend of being too streamlined and overly simplified. I have not tried the PvP yet so hopefully I won't be disappointed by it.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is an MMORPG. The rebooted/revamped version of the atrocious Final Fantasy XIV, and the 100th billionth game in the Final Fantasy franchise.
FFXIV:ARR is much like what WoW used to be when WoW was good. They took much of what made WoW great back in vanilla/The Burning Crusade and used it to shape FFXIV:ARR, adding a modern touch on top.
After the failure of Final Fantasy XIV, Square Enix got rid of most of the development team and learnt from their mistakes. What they've ended up with is an amazing MMO with tons of content and fine details to keep you playing for months.
The game offers a unique class system much like FFXI, where you're free to change your class at any time you wish, by simply changing your weapon to that of the class you wish to equip. There's 9 classes to choose from, with each playing a different role: tanks, healers, and DPS's. Each of these classes later turn into jobs, offering more abilities for you to gain and unlock. There's also 8 crafting classes, and 3 gathering classes available.
The game is filled with various dungeons, raids, and trials which are essentially boss fights.
Many MMOs lack true end game content, however FFXIV:ARR is mostly focused on end game content. Many consider the game to not start until you reach level 50 (which takes anywhere from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how you play and how often you play). The game offers many dungeons for leveling, and even more for late game. Many of which are harder versions of leveling dungeons. On top of this, there's multiple raids ranging from your traditional raids with many players (24 in this case), or smaller 8 player raids. Finally, for those who love boss fights there's plenty of trials to keep you entertained. These are mostly primal fights with varying levels of difficulty.
There's tons of gear in the game each offering unique looks, allowing for huge amounts of customisation. In terms of character customisation, there’s quite a few options for you to choose from. There’s 5 different races, with each offering two sub-races of sorts. For example, your traditional “human” race has both midlanders and highlanders. The game does not offer sliders for things such as eye shape, nose shape, etc., but instead has four different types for you to select, with each sub-race having a different selection. As well as this, there’s plenty of hairstyles for you to choose from, with a wide range of colours to select as well as a highlight colour.
The game’s OST is absolutely amazing, and possibly one of the best I’ve ever heard in a game. There’s tons of tracks with unique songs for each field location, dungeon, trial, raid, and everything else.

The game is updated every couple of months adding more items, dungeons, primal fights, new music, and much more. So there’s always plenty to do.
FFXIV:ARR is subscription based. You can pay $12/month for 1 character per world, with a maximum of 8 characters. Or you can pay $15/month for 8 characters per world, with a maximum of 42 characters. Though with the way classes work, you won’t be needing more than a single character usually, so the limit is hardly an issue. Some people are turned off by subscription fees, however $12/month is a small price to pay for such a great game, which constantly gets more content. The lack of F2P or B2P also prevents P2W aspects, and usually means the community is better in general.
Overall, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn has to be the best MMORPG I’ve ever played. The sheer amount of content has kept me hooked for over 400 hours, and will continue to do so as the months go on. If you’re looking for a great MMORPG to play, and have the money to invest, I could not recommend this more.

Gunslinger is a great single player FPS with light RPG elements.  All the guns feel good to use and feel distinct from one another. Every time you get enough points to level up you can invest in one of three different areas of skill: pistols, rifles, and shotguns. Now there's nothing wrong with a linear game if it's done well and Gunslinger is, but it's important to keep that length in mind because that means that on your first playthrough you can't unlock all the skills, so you have to choose carefully. Call of Juarez Gunslinger is an arcade style western shooter with excellent voice acting and great gun play. The story takes place in a saloon in Kansas where the hero, Silas Greaves, recalls his adventures in the wild west. The part of the game that you play are the stories being told around the table at the saloon. This means sometimes someone makes a comment or a claim that contradicts what is happening which leads to some very interesting story moments. For example, in the first level when you get to a certain point another character starts narrating what he thinks happened and you play it out...only to find out from Silas that things went a different way. This narrative device helps elevate what could have been a simple revenge story into something that is something along the lines of a mystery with some humor thrown in.
As far as game play goes, gun play doesn't get much better than this. You have three gun types but given this is a relatively short and often cheap game (price wise) it doesn't really ever become a problem. There are variants for each of the three guns (rifle, shotgun, pistol) but I honestly never noticed a difference. In addition you can dual wield pistols which is great in certain situations but not most. This is by no means a criticism as all guns are extremely satisfying to use. The action is quick and can be challenging, but is always reasonable. In addition to the relatively linear shooting sections of the games are duels (or essentially showdowns). These stand offs can start out frustrating as you have to keep both hands steady (on a controller it's manipulating both sticks, on keyboard and mouse it's A and D and the mouse). Fortunately you have infinite tries in the story mode as you'll sometimes find yourself facing off against more than one person, which can take awhile to get the hang of.
Visually and aurally the game shines. Gun sounds sound accurate and when the bullets start really flying and richocheting it really shines. The visual style is hard to describe. If you look at it from one way it looks like the game is lightly cel-shaded even though the majority of the 3D objects aren't outlined. It's a subtle effect that contributes to the over the top story being told. No western would be complete without great blood splatter and this game delivers in that area as well. Seeing that huge, spaghetti western style blood splat never really gets old.
In addition to the story mode there is an Arcade mode and a Duels mode. The arcade mode is a series of levels where you go for the highest score possible. Getting three starts requires keeping a combo up for most of the time which isn't too hard considering the volume of enemies but there are parts that do require some practice if you want those achievements. The duels mode is a set of 14, back to back duels in which you have six lives to make it to the end. This was initially quite challenging as you get an achievement for completing all duels "honorably" (meaning you don't draw before the enemy). The duels are taken straight from the story mode and some weren't even in the story mode to begin with which leads to some new encounters.
From an achievements point of view this game is overall very easy to 100%. The only areas where I had trouble were the arcade mode and duels mode but once you get the controls down it'll be a cake walk. There are of course difficulty based achievements, story achievements, and some special action achievements as well that are pretty fun to get (all but one but I won't spoil it).
Overall, Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a great deal. It's usually pretty cheap on Steam or other retailers and packs a great amount of content for what you pay for. I had a great time with it and highly recommend.

Something I loved was the set up of you having a wife, son, mother in law, and uncle to support. At the end of each day nearly all your money goes to their food and heat, so if you ever want to move up to the upper-class apartments, you've pretty much got no choice but to kill off family members.
This says a lot about who your particular character is. You've got the option to abandon them all and leave the country. You could stick by them and suffer in poverty. What kind of man are you? Who are you?

I am met by an eerie room filled with mystery, suspense and confusion. The Room is dark and the only source of light is a faint glow from a window and a spotlight on a stand. My gaze moves to the middle of the room and I can't help but notice the massive safe. On top of the safe I notice a letter which I proceed to open merely to find a key enclosed with a very peculiar note. After reading the note I'm left completely perplexed. I look at the key I was given but I quickly begin to feel helpless when I search for a keyhole somewhere on the magnificent safe.
The key doesn't seem to fit into any of the strange openings or contraptions I spot on the safe. I start thinking less of the key and more of the safe. I begin to study the safe closely and analyze every tiny nook and cranny I can find. Suddenly, success! I found something! A tiny panel the size of a matchbox slides open...
The Room really shines in my world. I love a good puzzle game and this title certainly gets the job done. As you start the game, you notice the soundtrack playing right away. The soundtrack doesn't feel repetive and still manages to support the atmosphere it wants to create very nicely. Besides the sounds, the puzzles are fun. When you face a seemingly impossible lock with nothing but mystery, The Room challenges you to think outside the box and solve it's many riddles. The Room gives  you a nice feeling when you solve a puzzle and coupled with very neat and detailed graphics, it feels genuinely satisfactory to solve a puzzle.
When playing The Room, it's important to savor every bit of the atmosphere as it's a semi-short game but surely worth playing and spending time with.

In my layman's opinion, I would defenitely recommend this game for anyone fond of the genre. I played both games in the Amnesy series ("A dark descent" (AdD) and "A machine for pigs" (AmfP)) and I completely enjoyed the ride in each one of them.
Both games are similar in their mechanics, but not exactly the same. In AdD there are more puzzles to solve and things to interact with such as light sources or flasks, or to look after, namely health and sanity. Most of these elements are not present in AmfP which, all in all, made me feel it somewhat closer to a walking simulator than its predecesor. At least, for a good number of chapters in the plot from the beginning. However, I think Jessica Curry's score is, hands down, a huge bonus in this second game in the series. Both games really hit the spot in terms of ambiance, spooky effects and a plot that keeps you glued to the screen to the end. Besides, the fact that all you can do against wandering monsters is to avoid them (or run for your life when they actually detect you) really gave me the creeps every time I run into one of them. From this point of view, AdD is more effective in giving you gooseflesh. However, if you immerse yourself in the plot (especially by reading all the notes and/or diary entrances) and especially in the ambiance both games proved me to be a very rewarding experience.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is thematically fascinating. It's more of an interactive story than a game. The only issues I had with A Machine for Pigs were the bluish haze/fog that many people complaint about, and the high temperature this game caused my GPU to reach. In spite of those issues, this is still worth playing through at least once for fans of Amnesia: The Dark Descent.

A couple of downsides. Firstly, as I previously mentioned, the game starts very slowly. Secondly, in my opinion, the puzzles in the game are not even remotely as challenging as in The Dark Descent. A solid arcade top-down shooter by puppy games, a company whose games i usually enjoy.
But there is one big problem that makes me not want to recommend it.
In the game, you are playing as a network of sorts, you start out with one robot body, and as your score racks up you are given "transfer points" that you can use in order to hack and transfer your network to any hostile robot (the stronger the robot, the more transfer points are required), turning them into you, the robot body that you just left behind still continues to function, and acts as an AI partner instead, you can switch back to being your previous robot body without cost, so if your AI partner is in a sticky situation, you can assume control over them and try to fight your way through said sticky situation.
Ideally you want to hack as many robots as possible (not the ones that require 1-3 transfer points though, as they die very easily) since you can swap between robot bodies whenever you want.
Having an army of them spread out across the map effectivly gives you the ability to jump from body to body to whichever on the map you please, so that you can be virtually everywhere at once.
Now for the problem, since the robot bodies that you currently aren't inhibiting runs on autopilot, they are dependent on the game's AI, which is functional, but at later levels the AI simply cannot keep up and gets absolutely steam-rolled by the tougher enemies, they can even wipe out your entire army with ease, leaving you with only one body left to inhabit.
What i think you're supposed to do in that scenario is to switch between the bodies as fast as humanly possible and try to save them all. but it seems close to impossible. So i tried a different strategy: not creating an army at all, and instead focus on transfering to a single robot with more survivability, and then collect as many powerups as possible to increase said survivability.
And what i found was that the game doesn't drop enough powerups in order to make this possible. So i gave up.
Now there seems to be people who have beaten this game, so something must work. and it may just be i who suck. But in the end i still cannot recommend Droid Assault, because it's too dependent on its AI, creating artificial difficulty as a result. Something simply ain't right when one has to avoid using the main mechanic of the game.
EDIT: I did manage to beat it, but only by exploiting the "sharp bullet" power-up that allows you to shoot through walls. I picked a robot with high survivability and upgraded it fully. and then i just hid in ventilation shafts etc. and shot blindly towards that which the radar pointed me to. (the radar points you to the closest enemy)
I have a feeling that the developers didn't intend me to beat the game that way

Ingredients
2 large eggs
Salt and pepper
2 to 3 tablespoons shredded cheese (optional)
1/4 to 1/2 cup filling, pre-cooked if necessary (optional)
2 teaspoons unsalted butter
Minced parsley, to garnish (optional)
Equipment
Mixing bowl
Whisk
8-inch nonstick skillet
Spatula
Dinner plate
Instructions
1. Whisk the eggs: Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper. If you\'re adding cheese or other fillings, make sure they are prepped and nearby.
2. Warm the skillet and melt the butter: Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.
3. Pour the eggs into the skillet: Pour the whisked eggs into the skillet. Immediately tilt the pan so the eggs coat the entire bottom. The eggs should sizzle on contact; if not, continue cooking, but remember to heat the pan a little longer next time.
4. Drag and push the eggs to form waves: Use a spatula to gently drag and push the cooked eggs from the edges toward the center of the pan, making space for the uncooked eggs and forming waves in the omelette. Tilt the skillet so that the uncooked eggs flow into the open spaces.
5. Cook the omelette for 1 to 2 minutes: The omelette will finish cooking in 1 to 2 minutes. When done, the bottom will be set and the edges will look crisp. The top of the omelette should still look fairly wet and uncooked, but there will no longer be any loose, easily flowing liquid egg — the omelette will continue cooking off the heat, so finish when you think the top still seems a bit underdone.
6. Top with cheese and fillings: If using, sprinkle the cheese and fillings down the center of the omelette.
7. Fold the omelette: Fold the bottom third of the omelette over the center, and then fold the top third down. Alternatively, fold the omelette in half.
8. Slide the omelette onto a plate: Gently slide the omelette onto a plate and garnish with parsley. Eat right away while still hot.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is an arcade style western shooter with excellent voice acting and great gun play. The story takes place in a saloon in Kansas where the hero, Silas Greaves, recalls his adventures in the wild west. The part of the game that you play are the stories being told around the table at the saloon. This means sometimes someone makes a comment or a claim that contradicts what is happening which leads to some very interesting story moments. For example, in the first level when you get to a certain point another character starts narrating what he thinks happened and you play it out...only to find out from Silas that things went a different way. This narrative device helps elevate what could have been a simple revenge story into something that is something along the lines of a mystery with some humor thrown in.
As far as game play goes, gun play doesn't get much better than this. You have three gun types but given this is a relatively short and often cheap game (price wise) it doesn't really ever become a problem. There are variants for each of the three guns (rifle, shotgun, pistol) but I honestly never noticed a difference. In addition you can dual wield pistols which is great in certain situations but not most. This is by no means a criticism as all guns are extremely satisfying to use. The action is quick and can be challenging, but is always reasonable. In addition to the relatively linear shooting sections of the games are duels (or essentially showdowns). These stand offs can start out frustrating as you have to keep both hands steady (on a controller it's manipulating both sticks, on keyboard and mouse it's A and D and the mouse). Fortunately you have infinite tries in the story mode as you'll sometimes find yourself facing off against more than one person, which can take awhile to get the hang of.
Visually and aurally the game shines. Gun sounds sound accurate and when the bullets start really flying and richocheting it really shines. The visual style is hard to describe. If you look at it from one way it looks like the game is lightly cel-shaded even though the majority of the 3D objects aren't outlined. It's a subtle effect that contributes to the over the top story being told. No western would be complete without great blood splatter and this game delivers in that area as well. Seeing that huge, spaghetti western style blood splat never really gets old.
In addition to the story mode there is an Arcade mode and a Duels mode. The arcade mode is a series of levels where you go for the highest score possible. Getting three starts requires keeping a combo up for most of the time which isn't too hard considering the volume of enemies but there are parts that do require some practice if you want those achievements. The duels mode is a set of 14, back to back duels in which you have six lives to make it to the end. This was initially quite challenging as you get an achievement for completing all duels "honorably" (meaning you don't draw before the enemy). The duels are taken straight from the story mode and some weren't even in the story mode to begin with which leads to some new encounters.
From an achievements point of view this game is overall very easy to 100%. The only areas where I had trouble were the arcade mode and duels mode but once you get the controls down it'll be a cake walk. There are of course difficulty based achievements, story achievements, and some special action achievements as well that are pretty fun to get (all but one but I won't spoil it).
Overall, Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a great deal. It's usually pretty cheap on Steam or other retailers and packs a great amount of content for what you pay for. I had a great time with it and highly recommend.

The Room is beautiful, inventive, and dull as a door-knob. Which is to say not entirely dull, not without charm and interesting little bits and bobs inside that make it tick yet ultimately simple and unmysterious. This is not a puzzle game; not really. It doesn't ask you to invent clever solutions or solve difficult mysteries. I began the game taking notes, hardened by years of advanture games, room escape games, and so forth. It turns out the game never asked me to do anything unexpected. There were a few genuinely clever puzzles but only a few in a game that is entirely built around this sort of thing. That's a real shame---I find it's a bit odd to approach difficulty in these sorts of games because what is obvious to one is not obvious to another; suffice to say what challenge this game does have is primarily observational--it rarely tests your memory or your problem solving or your abilitiy to make hypotheses or logical leaps. Merely your ability to notice. For my part I found it easy and a bit boring. I kept hoping it would surprise me and prove fiendish but the only difficulties I ran into were moments when I knew I just hadn't clicked the right one of about ten things I knew I could click yet.
It's a shame because games like this really shine when there are multi-lateral puzzles; multiple paths you can start moving down at once that feed back into each other, sure, and coallesce to a single point but that nonetheless allow you to move back and forth in a slightly less linear fashion.The trouble of course is that one designers leap of logic is another player's bloody-stupid-"who-the-heck-would-have-thought-of-that-nonsense?-that-doens't-make-any-sense!" But that acknowledged, I think The Room should have pushed much further into that territory.
The movements and animations certainly were nice ... but there were so many points when it could have used expansiveness to make even it's simpler solutions more challenging or cool--but once you leave the large safe you leave it for good, progressing ever forward and never looking back to do intersting things with old, familiar objects. Our guide assured us our intelligence would see us through but all that saw us through was explicit codes written on the box in UV ink (close enough). No clues, no riddles no references as promised by the tutorial sequence. Even taking this game as a breezy secret-box sort of thing rather than a true puzzle, I feel it wasn't inventive enough in the right way to meet it's own mini-fiction square-on.
It's a lovely object, but not a fascinating one. I was disappointed.
WHERE THE ♥♥♥♥ IS THE ROOM TWO?!

What I wanted from The Room was a virtual representation of physical puzzle boxes akin to Pinball Arcade; devices too complex and expensive to construct and maintain to exist anywhere other than the private collection of an ecentric hobbyist.
What I got was magic.
Nearly every puzzle in The Room involves tapping or pushing or twisting something until it won't go any further, then putting on the magic eyepiece that causes magic to happen so that magic can solve your problem for you. I'm aware my complaint is incredibly specific, but if you're looking for what I was looking for you won't find much of it.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is an MMORPG. The rebooted/revamped version of the atrocious Final Fantasy XIV, and the 100th billionth game in the Final Fantasy franchise.
FFXIV:ARR is much like what WoW used to be when WoW was good. They took much of what made WoW great back in vanilla/The Burning Crusade and used it to shape FFXIV:ARR, adding a modern touch on top.
After the failure of Final Fantasy XIV, Square Enix got rid of most of the development team and learnt from their mistakes. What they've ended up with is an amazing MMO with tons of content and fine details to keep you playing for months.
The game offers a unique class system much like FFXI, where you're free to change your class at any time you wish, by simply changing your weapon to that of the class you wish to equip. There's 9 classes to choose from, with each playing a different role: tanks, healers, and DPS's. Each of these classes later turn into jobs, offering more abilities for you to gain and unlock. There's also 8 crafting classes, and 3 gathering classes available.
The game is filled with various dungeons, raids, and trials which are essentially boss fights.
Many MMOs lack true end game content, however FFXIV:ARR is mostly focused on end game content. Many consider the game to not start until you reach level 50 (which takes anywhere from a few days to a few weeks, depending on how you play and how often you play). The game offers many dungeons for leveling, and even more for late game. Many of which are harder versions of leveling dungeons. On top of this, there's multiple raids ranging from your traditional raids with many players (24 in this case), or smaller 8 player raids. Finally, for those who love boss fights there's plenty of trials to keep you entertained. These are mostly primal fights with varying levels of difficulty.
There's tons of gear in the game each offering unique looks, allowing for huge amounts of customisation. In terms of character customisation, there’s quite a few options for you to choose from. There’s 5 different races, with each offering two sub-races of sorts. For example, your traditional “human” race has both midlanders and highlanders. The game does not offer sliders for things such as eye shape, nose shape, etc., but instead has four different types for you to select, with each sub-race having a different selection. As well as this, there’s plenty of hairstyles for you to choose from, with a wide range of colours to select as well as a highlight colour.
The game’s OST is absolutely amazing, and possibly one of the best I’ve ever heard in a game. There’s tons of tracks with unique songs for each field location, dungeon, trial, raid, and everything else.

The game is updated every couple of months adding more items, dungeons, primal fights, new music, and much more. So there’s always plenty to do.
FFXIV:ARR is subscription based. You can pay $12/month for 1 character per world, with a maximum of 8 characters. Or you can pay $15/month for 8 characters per world, with a maximum of 42 characters. Though with the way classes work, you won’t be needing more than a single character usually, so the limit is hardly an issue. Some people are turned off by subscription fees, however $12/month is a small price to pay for such a great game, which constantly gets more content. The lack of F2P or B2P also prevents P2W aspects, and usually means the community is better in general.
Overall, Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn has to be the best MMORPG I’ve ever played. The sheer amount of content has kept me hooked for over 400 hours, and will continue to do so as the months go on. If you’re looking for a great MMORPG to play, and have the money to invest, I could not recommend this more.

Heard this game mentioned in a podcast by CCP Grey.  Thought I would check it out, saw a few YouTube videos, but had no real inkling of WTF it was about.  Downloaded the demo, and I was hooked.
This game feeds my Obsessive Compulsive Disorder.  This is like all the fun bits of Tekkit/Minecraft without the tedious parts of minecraft.  It's a resource management game with infinite scope for advancement.
Building your first belt assembler, then your first Assembler Assembler, trying to find enough red circuits to build Speed Modules, then there is Speed 2 modules, and then Speed 3 modules which are insane gobblers-of-resources.
Launched my first rocket in a multiplayer game with a friend, we hadn't seen what was involved beforehand, and it took everything we had to make it happen (and we thought our resources were overstocked prior to making a rocket).
Now we're making a huge map, with trains everywhere, completly solar power, with armies of bots, using blueprints to copy and stamp out factories, using Power Armor Mk 2 with five personal roboports and a robot army to clear out trees and help build stuff (from blueprints).  It's amazing, everything moves in an orderly fashion, and you have to deal with problems before they arise because dealing with them afterwards can suck if you're all bound up with the innate Spaghetti of belts weaving around and under other belts, pipes, assemblers, tanks and train lines.
Best $US20 I've spent all year.  After the steep disappointing slope of No Man's Sky, this game was refreshingly amazing, and I can't recommend this highly enough.  Get the demo, watch the youtubes, join Reddit and the Official Forums, and climb on board for unlimited fun.
I bought this game in mid September 2016.  It's now less than a month, and I've sunk 240 hours into playing the game, and umpteen dozens of hours watching youtube playthroughs and strategy guides.  Value for money is high, replayability is high, this is not a fad game, it's ... cracktorio!

A great mini game with retrocute graphics from Puppygames. Your task is to start out with a small robot and clear enemy ship's levels one by one at same time upgrading yourself by capturing and taking over enemy robots.
The robots vary with speed, armor and armaments and once you have captured an enemy unit, it then follows you assisting you with clearing the rest of the level. You can then easily switch between your robots while AI controls the rest of your group.
Game is very entertaining, easy to hop in and out, while the difficulty level between levels slowly increases. It gives me nice flashbacks from the old Paradroid game in C64, though Droid Assault is much more action oriented and doesn't require careful planning.
It's made by Puppygames - of course I recommend it to everyone.

The game features a main story,10 arcade levels and a dueling mode.It has cartoony graphics with comic-book like cinematics.While playing the main story you will level up and unlock new abilities or special guns.You can also find collectibles hidden throughout the levels.
The main story is rather short.The game has 7 levels that would take around 6 hours to complete.Even if the story is short,it's well worth it to buy the game just for that.You get right into it,shooting tons of enemies in the wild west with a Bastion style narrative experience.Silas Greaves the main character of the game relates his adventures to a group of people in a bar.Sometimes he gets stuff wrong or toys with his audience which leads to you playing that part of the story all over again or starting it over another way.The voice acting is top quality and the dialogue is comedic at times.
Your equipment will consist of a few guns.Shotguns,rifles and pistols.Later in the game you can unlock Akimbo from the skill tree and be able to hold two pistols at the same time.A few types of different rifles,shotguns,dynamite and that's about it.Even if the gun diversity is low,the guns feel great.The game has a bullet time feature.You can dodge upcoming bullets that would be fatal to you.Also you can slow down time.During the main story you encounter a few boss battles which offer unique gameplay.For most of the game you will shoot seemingly endless waves of enemies in a arcade style setting.The dueling feature of the game is very well done.

I love Skyrim. And the Elder Scrolls series, for that matter. This game isn't (and doesn't try to be) Skyrim; if Skyrim was a popular movie franchise, this would be the spinoff TV series. Not as high budget in story or combat mechanics, but having a certain something that is its own.
All that being said, the developers are constantly refreshing features and if you have an MMO itch and love elder scrolls lore, this might be the one to give a go. It fit the right combination for me: voice scripted quests (yep, that same carousel of voice actors from Skyrim), the ability to play in first person, and it being both familiar and unique and not pushing the MMO features if you aren't as interested.
It's definitely best played with a friend (either existing or ones you seek out in game) where you can explore and progress together. Alone, you should probably look to Skyrim. But if you want to have a game in your pocket that you can play with friends in Tamriel when you are in that non-commital kind of mood (you know what I mean), give it a whirl!

World of Goo (Originally developed in 2008 for the Nintendo Wii) came out in 2009  for the PC by small indie developer 2D Boy, and it's one of the games that started the indie game craze of the 2010s.
Great music, it's catchy and always fits the mood of the puzzle you're on.
Wack story, I honestly can't tell if this game is trying to send me a message about how evil corporations are, or that finding any source of energy won't matter if big business is still around. Either way telling the story through painted signs is kind of dumb. I think a narrator would have fit the game better.
The art design is lame to me, but some people might enjoy its jaggedness because it fits the story.
The game physics were very well developed for such a small development team.
The majority of the puzzles were challenging and manageable, but there were a few puzzles that were so hard that I honestly couldn't see anyone getting through them without using a YouTube guide.
No replay value whatsoever unless you're an achievement hunter.
The World of Goo corporation tower game isn't very enjoyable, it's really just a boring mini-game.
I would recommend getting this game if it's on sale for $5 or less.
The game automatically adjusts to a 800 X 600 screen resolution. If you decide to run it full screen , you have to manually override the config.txt file (There's a guide on the World of Goo steam page).
Overall it's a 7.5/10

God I haven't played this game in close to a year, now, but I finally decided to get my♥♥♥♥♥♥together and post a review.
I meant to do this a year ago, in case you hadn't realized.
Anyways, this game really isn't new anymore, but it's still an amazing horror experience. We all know that this chapter in Amnesia really had a LOT to live up to- It was the sequel to one of the greatest horror games that had ever come out in, like, the history of horror ever. Hell, this series started up the most popular channel on Youtube, and got a lot of people into this genre who would have never thought twice about it.
I am ashamed to say this, though, this game was too scary for me.
I haven't finished this game simply because I got too freaked up, logged out, never picked the game back up again. I LOVE horror games- And I love Amnesia, but not when I'm actually playing it myself, I soon realized.
The AI for the Manpigs is the same used for the Grunts in the original Amnesia, and they act almost identical in every way shape or form.
The main characters are also very simliar- Daniel, a guy who was innocent, gets ♥♥♥♥ed up and used by another dude. Madnus, who was innocent, gets ♥♥♥♥ed up because of the orb and is used by the orb and is twisted into thinking differently and doing things he would have never done before. I won't spoil much, but he basically creates this machine that he tells everyone is going to "provide food for London," but was really built to turn people into Manpigs.
I'm not really sure why people have such a problem with the storyline of this game, though. I think it's FAR better than the original Amnesia, to be blunt. I got into this one faster and was captivated by the fatherly relationship between Madnus and his sons, yet the obvious deterioration of Madnus' mind, especially as he was having vivid flashbacks where he was saying very questionable things.
THE ENDING. WAS AMAZING.
To this day I use some of the lines in the ending scenes in poetry and writing. It's crazy how well scripted this videogame was and just how beautiful the story was altogether.
If you're looking for a good horror game that's going to scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you, but also a really great storyline that you can get into and really appreciate, than this is your game. There are a few jumpscares, although they aren't *that* bad, comparatively. The ending can get a bit frustrating working through, but it's worth it eventually.
If you're hell-bent on comparing this one to the original Amnesia, don't. They're very different games with different feels but at the same time have the same mechanics. Don't let this idea of what you want it to be like cloud your judgement for what it actually is.

For what it is, it's okay. But as an Amnesia game, AMFP fails to supply a worthy sequel to the original game and provides nothing engaging for new players.
This sequel focuses on story much more than gameplay. Which in theory is fine, but the problem lies in how the story is told. Almost all exposition is conveyed through notes that you have to read and frankly, it's tedious. Not that the first game didn't have this feature, but in TDD, it didn't take up a lot of your game time. I feel like this note mechanic is a bit problematic considering it's completely optional. If the player doesn't want to read the notes, then they don't have to.
Other than some dialogue sprinkled in here and there, the lore is very exclusive to these notes. And while it's unlikely that a player would actively avoid every single note, it's very easy to miss pages and therefore miss vital information. I certainly missed some in my playthrough. There's also a journal that you write in every so often, but most of the time it explains things that literally occurred moments beforehand. So unless you have the attention span of an infant, it isn't extremely helpful.
With so much focus on story, I have to admit that I wasn't exactly engrossed. There were moments that peaked my interest (for example, the final ten-ish minutes are pretty engaging) but when the majority is mostly exposition, it becomes a bit of a chore to get through. It seems that it could have been better suited for a different medium, because video-games offer a lot of options in providing narrative other than text. Why not utilize mechanics that explain important exposition through gameplay?
The environments are fairly linear and therefore aren't super explorable, which is unfortunate considering the half of this game that isn't reading is exploring. Since I wasn't really digging the story and characters, I just wanted to continue progressing so I could comeplete the game. Even then, that wasn't very difficult to do. I beat AMFP in about four and a half hours. And again, that alone is totally fine. Brief games aren't coherently bad. But within that four and a half hours, I didn't feel like anything really happened until the third act. As aforementioned, the ending was good, but not enough to redeem the game as a whole. A nice payoff requires build-up which wasn't present here.
But of course the obvious issue with the game is that it barely resembles Amnesia at all. It just sort of carries the title and, other than a few nods, doesn't really acknowledge TDD. There is no sanity mechanic. There is no inventory. There is no health or lantern maintanence. It's easy to nitpick how different it is, but the issue is less because it isn't the same and more that what it attempts to accomplish isn't as effective. All of the gameplay in TDD helped flesh out the survival horror aspect of the game. It made you feel helpless. AMFP, on the other hand, just feels like a really long hallway that you have to get to the end to. But you're also reading a novel at the same time. What gameplay it has is too barebones and simple to hold up on its own.
It's painfully easy. There aren't really many puzzles, and the ones that are present could barely be considered puzzles. Find this item, place it here, repeat. The monsters aren't difficult to avoid. And that's when they're even around; there are very few confrontations with enemies in this game. Since their appearances are so sporadic, it makes them less impactful. Which I suppose the fact that they don't have much presence could be argued as a good thing, since some games do the exact opposite with worse results.
However, looking back at TDD, you never knew if the area you were in was safe or if there'd be a monster around the corner. The player is constantly on edge and it's because of a very meticulous pacing and well-placed enemies. In AMFP, you don't care if there's a monster around the corner. I think I died maybe twice. Also, and this might just be from personal experience, but I had to deal with more glitches than I usually do with other games. I fell through the floor within the first half hour.
The monsters aren't scary or memorable like the ones from TDD. The idea of being hunted is frightening, but that alone won't carry the fear. Most likely for the reasons I've already explained. Not only that, but the jumpscares in this game are pretty 'cheap.' And I actually like jumpscares in games. They tend to get a lot of hate most of the time, but when done well, it can be very effective. This is not the case for AMFP. I'm not sure if this is related, but the soundtrack at times is obnoxiously loud and I have a suspicion that it is done simply to snatch some easy scares. But instead it's just annoying. All in all, if a horror game fails to make the player scared, unsettled, or disturbed, then something's probably wrong.
I'm sure there are other things I could complain about, but all of the critiques of AMFP come back to the same reasoning. It's not because it isn't an Amnesia game. It's because it's genuinely boring.

First and foremost Machine for Pigs is nothing like Amensia: the Dark Descent, so much so that I refuse to even it call it an Amnesia title.  Don't expect this to even marginally resemble Amensia: the Dark Descent because you will be sorely disappointed.
Everything that made the original what it is known as today, a well designed and terrifying horror experience start to finish, is non-existant in Machine for Pigs.  There is no more health, sanity, lantern fluid and tinderbox necessities and there isn't even a means to examine what condition you're in after you suffer physical damage from enemies.  There is also no inventory to store the very few items you come across.  Granted, the only items you ever need to pick up are obviously only to solve puzzles, if you can even call them that because all they really involve is picking up an item and inserting it into whatever contraption.  There isn't anything puzzling whatsoever.
One final thought on items is that you must literally carry them in your hands to where they need to go, again, because there is no inventory.  Not a huge deal, however it is  bothersome nonetheless especially if you accidentally drop something and have to go look for it.  All of this  has been removed and I would love to know what the developers were thinking when they made these decisions.
I do wish Frictional Games, Amnesia: the Dark Descent's developers would have gone through and created Machine for Pigs; the Chinese Room evidently had no idea what they got themselves into.  Ultimately Machine for Pigs does not live up the hype its predecessor proved and is an astounding failure in comparison and if it were a standalone title too.  It is no more than a dumbed-down, unbearably linear walking simulator with the occasional half-arsed jumpscare thrown in to laughably try and capture an ounce of horror. I'd suggest avoiding this altogether unless you just need to say that you finished both Amnesia titles.

My first Call of Juarez games, a FPS set in the old west of America. You play Silas Greaves, a bounty hunter, entertaining some bar patrons with stories of his past dealings. But are they tall tales, as Greaves has survived overwhelming odds while chasing down some of the most infamous killers in history.
The game play isn't complex. You have limited loadout options: rifle or shotgun, side arm, dynamite.  You only a few variations of weapons at your disposal. There is a leveling up system of 3 skill trees and you have 2 skills: A bullet time and  last breath, which gives you a chance to dodge a kill shot. This has an arcade feel to it. There is no stealth or tactics per say, just shoot-kill and move on. There is also dueling which is a bit tricky. You hover a slow responding reticle over a shifting for while inching your hand towards your holster.
There are 3 modes of play: story, arcade, dueling. Story mode is playing through the story of Silas and also have access to collectibles which gives you real history of many of the characters and places in the game. One of the highlights is the narration which will alter levels to be more like the truth and some nice touches were enemies comment in disbelief as when you don't die or seemingly never miss a shot. Arcade has 10 modified areas from story mode, where you try to maximize score through head shots, multipliers, and other bonuses. In dueling, you play through 15 duels, some are repeats from story mode.
The style is faded colors with forced letter boxing so it took me a little bit to get used to seeing enemies and the some what limited POV. The textures aren't great and assets are used multiple times. There is a new game plus and, as I said, 3 modes, so there is a good chunk of content with replay ability if you want better scores. It's not a must game to own, but for $15 it's a solid purchase.

Somewhere between Minecraft. Ark: Survival evolved and Chivalry is this game, and it sits really well for being in such an awkward place. The general feel of the game is very Ark, you wake up on a beach and start gathering your resources, build tools from scratch to start harvesting nodes at fixed points in the game of higher quality materials etc. But with a slightly more minecraft building block system, which is not a bad thing,
I never really got the feeling that ARk's Paper thin walls could stop a dinosaur, I would've much preferred to be building in nice solid blocks, also looks better aesthetically for double thick walls, but both systems are good and that's my personal preference. The game also uses a similar active crafting stystem to Ark, where you can craft items from your inventory and then return to gameplay while the crafting process completes, and where stations will autocraft what you have told them to and store the output even if you are not present. For me this is a fantastic system.
The maps could be bigger but will house 40 players comfortably if they form a few factions and don't all live alone. They can become quite crowded though. Gameplay is great, combat system works almsot exactly like CHivalry's with a wide rang eof weapons craftable both ranged and melee. You can also craft training weapons with which to train your recruits etc. and of course whips and beating rods for any slaves you pick up along the way.
That's right, slaves. Not so useful on a normal server unless you're a sadist but if you're on an rp server, wishing you had a bigger house and see a lowly peasant running through the flax field then it may just be an idea to make yourself a cage/cell for him to sleep in and rope him up. if the rules allow it and you can beat/trick him into compliance.
I found it very hard to get slaves to co-operate at first but then I did a little thinking and looked back to real life history and I realised that this is because Chattel slavery is stupid (slavery where you just outright own the person and their kids).
In america, before an african practice was set as the norm by an ex-slave, slavery was legal, but it wasnt forever and wasnt really for nothing. You could make a man work for 7 years, and in return give him a sizeable chunk of land etc. as payment. Using the crest system this is exactly what I did, for 1 days work i gave them a leather crest, and for a second day's work I upgraded that to iron, on the third day's work I sent them home with all their tools etc. and had great success. Much like in real life, people came to ME to become slaves.
Now where the game gets really good is its political system, on a normal server if you take the throne you get a crown, a sword, and the opportunity to tax people, but since everyone on that server will want you dead you may as well tax high and get what you can while you can if you don't have a good guild backing  you, it's on rp servers where the politics really shine where war can't be declared for reason like "just because" and a king needs to die before he can be replaced. These servers encourage the king to be fair and give people few reasons to want him dead, the fairer the better because more would come to your aid if you were attacked by the evil invaders of an enemy guild.  On a good rp server I find myself doing a social dance with each new guild I meet, weighing each other up and trying to decipher the motives of the other guild. You will often find yourself in a warroom as if you were in a low fantasy film discussing the enmy factions' movements and stocks, changes in behaviour and military development, border growth etc. It is VERY cool to have a game that puts you in this position.
Even if you are, like me, not inclined to strict rp you become immersed and begin to enjoy adopting the role of ambassador for your mini-nation.
Downsides now, the community, don't expect to keep a house long on most servers, if a raidoff mod on the server doesnt kick people off for raiding you when youre offline then regardless of if that server had a rule against it you will be raided. Many of the offiicial EU servers are flooded with chinese people who like to, in the morning for EU, treb all the bases and kidnap sleepers (offline characters) to cage them and when they log in tell them all about how "china no. 1" etc. People generally dont follow community server rules and most servers arent equipped to deal with these people. Some, like a server I'm not sure if I'll name yet, have admins who will fly into your fully secure courtyard at night to steal everything you have and kill you. On an rp server.
Worse than this is the hacker problem. I rarely find a server that hasnt been plagued by hackers and to be honest I'm starting to give up and just say "Hey,I'll host my own server as soon as I get some friends together from this game and buil my own from there, take regular backups and make sure to keep everyone sorted out" but the truth is there's few friendlty people in this game, it's all griefers and hackers for the most part.
There's a few glitches that have left me dead too, this game isn't really fit to be called a finished product, werid physics make odd death spots in your base where for no reason you'll take damage just standing in places that can range from 1 tile to whole rooms. If an animal dies on a rocky hill next to you then it will probably glitch through the floor, leaving you with nothing which is crap, but worse is that as it does so it can fling you far enough into the air to kill you upon impact with the floor. Loot bags also have a habit of falling through floors and landing inside walls etc.
It's really unpolished, and the community is terrible. It doesn't protect itself from hackers in any way, and though I recommend the gameplay, because there's no real servers I can recommend and no other way to play it, I can't recommend THE GAME.

I think its about time I wrote a review for SMITE, my really first ever review too. Now SMITE is a game I have been playing it since more or less the BETA so ages before it was even added into the Steam database and have had a lot of experience with this game. Pros -
- Smite has good graphics for a MOBA game alongside quite a few options to help fully optimise your overall experience so everyone more or less has access and can play the game.

Cons -
- Now even though there are quite a few pros there are also a few cons about the game. One con of the game is the learning curve, I mean most MOBAS require quite a lot of playtime before you realise what you are actually doing and its not different for SMITE either, the learning curve can be quite steep at times.
- Because of the fanbase of SMITE has grown over the years it has been out, it also means there can be toxic players around that try and make you feel worse about yourself and they are quite strict when it comes to actually playing the game.
- Because of the massive amount of gods, its quite hard to learn about every single god and depending on your personal opinion, some gods may not suit your playstyle and might not have as much fun.
Thats my very first review of SMITE and of any game ever, I hope you found this useful and thank you for reading my review and remember, just Have Fun!

Let's get a few things out of the way here before I get into any depth regarding Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs.
- I loved Amnesia: The Dark Descent, despite not being nearly as spooped by it as many others have been.
- I've been a fan of a lot of Frictional's other work beyond The Dark Descent, especially the Penumbra games.
- I genuinely enjoyed The Chinese Room's Dear Esther, albeit its tediousness. It wasn't great, but it was kind of neat.
- Given that The Chinese Room worked on this instead of Frictional, I expected something different.
And there's the key, really. This is -not-, by any means, a successor to The Dark Descent. At best, I'd call A Machine For Pigs a reinterpretation of the thematics presented in The Dark Descent, but entirely its own beast. If anything, Machine For Pigs may have been better off without an Amnesia name on it at all, though there are enough nods to The Dark Descent that it works, kind of.
Whereas The Dark Descent dealt a lot with ever-present threats, a growing sense of dread, and to some extent, the consequences of your actions, A Machine For Pigs feels a lot more passive in nature. You're solving puzzles the entire time, but it's rare that you're trying to elude any pursuers or otherwise keep yourself alive. The pull in A Machine For Pigs is the very slowly building mystery around the facilities you explore; a nagging question in the back of your head as to what the hell is going on and why you're any part of it. If nothing else, it nails the Amnesia legacy in terms of atmosphere, which is present in scads. It's also nice to see that atmosphere is fairly consistent; there are plenty of visual shifts, but most of them segue together and are explained when they occur, thus keeping them from being too jarring.
The gameplay itself is alright at best, and has several points where it drags. Puzzle complexity rarely advances beyond "You need a thing. Oh, the thing's in the next room. Thanks for the thing. Now go here where you need some new thing." This is somewhat disappointing, but it also keeps things moving quickly enough and makes it that much easier for a wider audience to finish. If anything, A Machine for Pigs warrants a playthrough just to tickle your brainmeats for a bit.
Oh, and you can stack chairs. Almost any chair. I recommend it.

This game helped me through severe depression after my wife left me. I was a mess, binging on coke and strippers to try and forget the pain she brought to me. Next thing I knew I was shooting Heroin in a Vietnamese rice farmer's hut. Don't ask me how I got there and why I decided to stay for 7 months amongst his family of 12, but I thought this was the end of my miserable life. As I lay naked in a pile of my own and what was mostly the vietnamese family's vomit and excrement... there I saw it. The light glistening on the screen. It seemed MW2 had swept the world by its feet and even in the remote jungles of Vietnam it managed to find itself. It was clear to me, this was a sign. God himself intended for me to see it. The little vietnamese child obviously didn't know what he was doing, as the little noob camped in the corner with his ACR with dual attachments of a heat sensor and a silencer, I marvelled at the beauty of this game. At once I got up, and I ran. Did I know which way to run? No. But I didn't let that stop me. Sooner or later I was back in the humble streets of my hometown. I picked up MW2 for PS3 at tescos and went on to play the game for 4 days straight without food or water. My mother and father were a little worries considering they presumed me dead and I hadn't bathed since I was back. But if there's anything I learned it's that In those 4 days I was born again, although I soiled myself several times and passed out once, I knew what it meant in life to experience pure joy and happiness. As a married man with 2 beautiful children now I really hope MW2 is brought on to next gen consoles; it will bring the utmost joy to me, and my children will be able to relive the pure ecstacy I felt. Of course they're not old enough to play yet and not even nearly mentally developed to even comprehend what would be going on as they are still babies. But the bright and vivid images of their father getting that 30th kill streak with his ump-45 silencer will fill their small hearts with pride. As they watch their father roar in triumph as the screen goes white and the battle ceases. There I will stand proud a man. A man with a 5.2 K/D ratio. A true champion. A figure to look up to. A figure to learn from. And you better believe that once they are of legal age I'll teach them and guide them to achieve the successes I have. But alas as my imagination delves deep into a utopian world it hits me that in fact this is not the case. Instead I lay here in bed next to my Russian mail-ordered wife. where only these fantasies numb the cruel pain of life. Although I am happy to have a wife and children, my profession as MW2 montage specialist has failed to provide for me in recent years; in fact my primary source of income is the allowance my mother gives me weekly. I forgot to mention that my job situation has resulted in me living at my parent's home... But I digress. Thus I cannot even begin to explain the importance of bringing MW2 to next gen consoles. It has become a joke that not a single person will pay for a copy of my ps3 MW2 360 no-scope montages. The dedication and time I put into these videos cannot be overstated. I hope that this petition succeeds. For the sake of my wife Vladimir, and my children Terminal and Highrise I pray this comes true. Nothing will bring me more joy. Nothing.

I have my doubts about the devs allowing this negative review to remain, but I'll post it just in case they get off their high horse and develop the courage to face criticism.
A developer flat-out told me that they've given up on working on Linux controller support. He then said it was supported, but not when it doesn't work.
He also said that steam was 32-bit only, and couldn't launch 32-bit games. Neither of those things is true.
Their response to me pointing that out was basically "well, I guess maybe _now_, but we don't have time, so it doesn't matter". If you don't have time, that's fine, but why are you selling abandonware at any price?
It's a Java program. It doesn't even need to care about bit depth. For some reason they're shipping the entire Java runtime with their games. WHY?
Basically, they're lazy and incompetant. If you call them out on their BS, they patronise you, insult you and ban you.
I can't criticise the game itself, because I can't play it. No joystick support. No QWERTY keyboard. No remapping. The joystick config file ("doesn't work? you fix it!") is virtually undocumented, and doesn't behave in a way that makes sense. Can't map a joystick axis to movement? o_O

ESO (The Elder Scrolls Online) is an immersive, lore-riddled, choose your own fate, extended experience of the elder scrolls series, with millions of different ways to go about how you want to play the game. pro's:

-There is always something to do, with a(n) nearly limitless means of gaining leveled loot, general gear, and boosting items.
- unlimited arrows should you choose to use a bow and go the way of an archer (no carrying them around seperately weighing you down).
- Hacker/Cheaters are nearly non-existent to the point that you'd have to literally go looking for them in the Cyrodiil pvp to find one, let alone a team. (this game leaves nothing to be desired, so there is nearly no incentive for people to cheat in any form, for any reason)

The game is good, not because of a good developing team, but because of the concept itself and the community.
Since the game is actually pretty buggy, laggy and in a certain extent, incomplete, one may ask me why i decided to positively review this game, wich means that i actually suggest to buy it;
To answer that question, we have to make a premise about the game genre and the ambientation:
First of all, there are not many Rust-like games wich are as realistic and good as it and, as icing on the cake, most of these are based on a futuristic\post-apocalyptic era, wich means that, if you are, like myself, interested in medieval or fantasy-medieval roleplay or simple survival, you will be forced to make hard choiches.
RoK is one of the few medieval RPG games wich actually had, and still has, a possibility to emerge and become a living legend:
It has plenty of building blocks, wich allow the player to make an actually very realistic building, if necessary;
It has a decent graphic and a good style, and the combact mechanics look good, even if a bit clunky;
It has all that is necessary for an actual medieval roleplay and... It fails.
It fails because the developers stopped adding more stuff, it fails because the community seems pretty divided on what to do to improve the game, and it fails because people slowly abandon it.
Still, the idea, the concept, is good, and the game, with all the flaws (many) and the merits (few) is certainly one of the best of its genre:
It is more populated than Gloria Victis, and faster and less expensive than Life is Feudal, wich makes it a good competitor.
So, answering to the initial question:
The game sucks, really; but it is funny to play it and, tragicomically, worth it.
Dear community of RP enthusiasts, please consider giving it a try, maybe with a friend, in order to show to the developers support for an idea wich, again, has a potential that they seem to not see anymore.
Thank you for reading.

This is not a sequel to Amnesia: Dark Descent. It is just another game in the same style made by the same team.
A Machine For Pigs is not what I would call a game. It is a first-person visual novel.
A Machine for Pigs is extremely well-written, just like Dark Descent was. The story is deep, intense, horrifying, grim, and gruesome. It tells a tale of a wealthy industrialist in the waning days of the 19th century who, wracked by madness and illness, does some pretty terrifying things. Through the game you discover the tale in bits and pieces as you play this man who has, of course, awakened from a fever-induced amnesia.
You travel through the streets of London 1899 and through the halls and corridors of your estate and eventually, the titular Machine. You walk around with a lantern, solve very simple puzzles (put this thing here, pull this switch, pull this thing, open this door... that sort of thing), and avoid monstrosities called Manpigs. There is very little of the latter and a great deal of the former (that is to say, this game is basically a ton of walking through corridors).
Just like with Dark Descent, I found myself thoroughly bored and just hoping for the next bit of story. I think I'd rather just read this thing as a short story.
However, the game does serve up a phenomenal atmosphere, which is something a written novel could never do. The sound effects, the glimpses of the machine and its dark, dark work through bars, windows, and catwalks, the background screams and squishing of viscera, blood, fluids pumping through pipes, lots of breathing and flashes of electricity and steam venting all serve as a perfect backdrop for a tale that wonderfully captures Victorian horror; the steam, the feeling of Progress! Science! Wonders! Mystery!, the primitive but promising technology, and the supreme evils of Empire, God, and Man all set the stage for a deliciously darkthought exercise in what it would be like for this man as he descends into pure insanity. You really feel for him as he desperately seeks redemption for what he has done.
I can't say I liked the game, but I did like the story. The pace, just like with its predecessor, was glacial, and that turned me off for months. Coming back to it felt like a chore, but I'm sure lots of people love games like this. It just ain't me.
The graphics were good but not as good as Dark Descent. Almost the whole game takes place in endless dark metal corridors with lots of brass, pipes, steam, and dark wood accents. It gets really boring after a while.
It's super easy to avoid the manpigs... even easier than the Dark Descent. In addition they got rid of the dumb "insanity" mechanic as well as stupid inventory management of oil and crap for your light. Now your lantern just works and all you have to do is walk through about five hours of this game to get to the end and get the whole story.
Just no

I really like this game.   It uses a top-down perspective with WASD controls and mouse aiming, which is a control scheme/persepctive combination that I really like and I think is underused.  The droid designs are surprisingly diverse considering how simple the models are.  There is also a deeper level of strategy than one might expect.  You need to balance the number of droids in your squad against the strength of each of them, since you only get so many "transfer points."  More powerful droids take more points, so it's hard to fill up on really strong ones.  You also room for a range of playstyles; you can play it like a bullet hell with a really fast droid and evade shots left and right, you can stay back with a long-range weapon and try not to die, you can switch between a few really strong droids and balance upgrades between them, you can power up a single droid and have a bunch of low-level minions swarming around, et cetera.
This game surprised me in a very good way.  Look for it on one of the giant steam sales.  It's only $10 without special pricing.  If you see it at 75% off or better, buy it immediately.
