This is a game from the creators of Revenge Of The Titans, a top-down shooter at it's core and so much more once you get into the depths. Each bot you can control has a generally unique description and use, some are good at tanking, others good at firing missles from a distance. This game encourages exploration and essentially is a score attacker's wet dream.
Breaking down the mechanics, you can control up to 8 different units at a time, although doing so is risky. Once you release control of a certain droid, you've handed it over to the AI which isn't entirely tantamount to suicide for the bot, but damn near close. Either way, you'll be doing most of the work unless you simply don't want to. There's a variety of playstyles that Droid Assault caters to, from the sniper to the tank, and better yet.
There's upgrades. Not all upgrades apply to all bots, but the vast majority do. Speed, defense, attack damage, armor. Powerups litter the field and the game pushes you do pop open every single crate for that either special overleveled bot, or a weaker variant that might just drop that piece of salvation you've been looking for. Crates themselves serve as holding containers for random bots geared towards the level you're playing on. So you won't be getting a massive boss-esque bot out of one in your first level or two.
Moving onto Bosses, there are a slew of them in the game that all follow the same archetype. Two to four guns on each side which are destroyable for further powerups, and a primary weapon. Tactics mean everything or nothing depending on how well you've progressed. There's a defenite rougelite element to the game and it's worth replaying over and over if only to get that final ending.
Basically, buy it. It's good, fun, and a new update just included local co-op which supports the gamepad wonderfully. You wont regret it unless you've forgotten there's a demo out as well:

When I first started this game, I was impressed.  I began using computers with a very old version of Windows not unlike the version mimicked with sounds and graphics here.  The old startup sound is enough to send a shockwave of nostalgia throughout me.
Nostalgia for the older Windows aside, the gameplay didn't make that much sense.  At first, I had a lot of trouble entering my first name and username and moving forwards, as well as selecting an icon.  The problem I had was that the game wasn't aligned properly.  I had to place my cursor a few centimetres to the left to click on the buttons.
Then, there was the story.  Each chapter is divided into a year, starting in 2002.  It's basically a text-based story, with several elements of both storytelling and progression that just fell flat.
First,
While gender shouldn't really matter, it kind of does.
Second,
it feels really weird when I'm trying to type in the answer I selected and I'm pressing different buttons.
Third, Emily is soooo talkative.
Finally,
Verisimilitude is heavily lacking in this game, and the background noises can drive you
.  Dorm rooms aren't supposed to sound like that anyways.
In conclusion, while this game may seem cute and while it may awaken nostalgia and feelings for AIM messaging back in the day, this game doesn't really pander to much else.  If you want a visual novel, this isn't it.  If you want a text-heavy, slow paced, story-based game to waste time, then this is it.  Unless you really hated the older versions of Windows.
The verdict?  Don't play it.  It's not really worth it.

DISCLAIMER: The lack of recommendation has nothing to do with the game being bad. There's very little I can say about it that's bad, mostly just that I didn't really personally enjoy it.
That being said, the one negative aspect this game does have is that there is a good degree of tedium involved. Some levels are painfully slow or repetitive, but not too many in the end. The level design is diverse, almost to the degree of being too much so as some ideas don't feel fully developed before the game ends. The graphics and music are wonderful and the story and humor present are pretty good too. This game mostly just fails for me on a gameplay level, as there's a bit of a luck factor involved in the harder levels, and no real difficulty curve to speak of. The level I found to be the most challenging (and one that put me off from playing for several days) was about at the halfway point of the game. There's also one World 1 level severely out of place, as well. And since you're required to beat every level to finish the game (well, you *could* skip them but where's the fun in that?) I could see that level being a real roadblock to many first-time players. There's also some metagame about bulding the tallest tower you can but there's not really any point to it. Like I said though, I can't say this is a bad game, just one I don't personally enjoy very much.

Distraint is a very solid Horror Adventure game that one can complete in about 2 hours. I'll list some positives and negatives.
Pros -
Great atmosphere.
Good choice of music and sound effects.
A pretty well realised story.
Cons -
A few grammar mistakes I noticed. Nothing too drastic but I saw at least 3 that made me pause and go... did I read that wrong, or... no it just is wrong.
It's a lil on the short side but then again I think it doesn't overstay its welcome.
Maybe it's just me but the anti-capitalist theme felt a bit heavy-handed. It was very clearly the point of the story but to have the main character be named Price, the lovely lady be called Goodwin and one of your bosses be named Moore. Like we get it, it's about greed! Some dialogue gave me that same impression too. But hey, I guess it really cared to get its point across.
Besides, I imagine the dev speaks English as a second language as he's Finnish, so I can definitely excuse a bit of heavy-handedness. It just made me laugh a bit when I feel like it was meant to be tense or impactful.
Anyway, very high quality game especially considering it's a one-man team. Props to Jesse Makkonen, I see him respond to the community and he seems like a great dude. Keep making games!
I give Distraint a 7.5/10

Tree of Savior is a fun game, but not the "spiritual successor to Ragnarok Online" that it claims to be, other than its beautiful asthetics.  It's definitely worth checking the game out for the artwork and music alone if you enjoyed RO, but the gameplay may be different than what you expect.

Item/equipment variety is still a bit lacking, many items of the same tier or star level have nearly identical stats, making your choice pointless.  Overall the game is in a much better place than it was a year ago when it launched, hopefully it continues to improve even more in the future.

Honestly, I think people are too hard on this game.
Is it as scary as Amnesia: Dark Descent? Not necessarily, but then Dark Descent was such an unexpectedly delirious and exhilerating experience. It was a surprise. The difference with its sequel is that people have been expecting A Machine For Pigs for a while; based on those expectations, some were disappointed.
I was not. A Machine For Pigs doesn't need to be as scary as Dark Descent. Of course there are plenty of moments in that game which made my blood run cold, such as the infamous chase through the flooded Archives with a monster snapping at your heels, the damned Prison area which gave me plenty of mini heartattacks, and just the growl of those disgusting monsters. Yet I remember only a few moments from that game, which to me are not as important as the overall experience. What was the most scary for me was actually the story, and learning about Daniel. At the beginning, he's a man that drank the Amnesia potion to make himself forget the horrors the Baron had inflicted. But of course, as we descend deeper into Brennenberg, we realize the truth. Near the end, I wasn't even sure Daniel deserved to be saved (which is why the three different endings pleased me so much).
A Machine For Pigs has a story that is just as good, and in some respects, better than Dark Descent. It has its moments too, but A Machine For Pigs is all about how it leaves you feeling than the individual moments you can remember. The core element of discovering the story through notes, and the journal entries of Oswald, is still there. We learn he's a drunkard (wine is, after all, its own form of Amnesia). We learn he's a butcher. We learn he wants to be more effective at butchering through the use of technology. We learn his wife died in childbirth, which clearly has a bad affect on his sanity (like a true madman, he wants mmotality, and creates a machine to that effect). He apparently wants to save his children, and is guided by a vaguely familiar and sinister voice over the scattered telephones. His journal entries are distrubing enough, littered with contempt, hatred, anger, dispair, and revolting descriptions, all which offer a glimpse into his deranged mind.
You really need to appreciate the briliance of this, along with the other core elements that made Dark Descent amazing, which A Machine For Pigs definitely has: the sound, the constant oppressive and immersive atmosphere, the music, the voice acting, and the mystery. Despite the tension which keeps you constantly on edge, you want to keep exploring the machine. You feel compelled to descend further down, past the scraping metal, the wails of steam, the screams and groans of the machinery, the flickering lights, the thick, putrid smell as its often described, the pulsing of the engines-A Machine For Pigs does a fantastic job of creating the setting. The fact that I felt no relief when I was briefly outside is also a testament to that accomplishment. The rain slicked and gloomy London streets offered no breath of fresh air.
A Machine For Pigs is memorable for its hauntingly beautiful settings. Now, one of my complaints is that there is not really a sense of urgency. That's practically a requirement given the premise, but unlike the constant fear of having the Shadow chase you in Dark Descent, A Machine For Pigs takes its time delivering on the scares. To be sure, there are scares to be had, and there are a few jumpscares right from the very beginning. The urgency comes in bursts, mostly from being chased by the grotesque pig-men. The puzzles are mostly unnecessary (like the Sanity meter in Dark Descent, which did little more than blur the screen) and mostly frustrating.
Interestingly, while I was playing, I couldn't stop thinking of Pink Floyd's video for Another Brick In The Wall. That's totally a good thing! I also couldn't shake the eeriness, the dread. The disgust, eventually, because just as I felt ultimately repulsed by Daniel, Oswald proved to surpass even Daniel's selfishness and brutality. That's why A Machine For Pigs is so good, in my opinion: the sum of its parts is an experience worth your time and careful attention.
The blood splattered walls of the factory where the pigs are slaughtered take on an even more vile nature when you read Oswald's diary because his descriptions of people, often as "swine," sends chills down your spine. Pigs are closest to humans, biologically speaking. And Oswald's pursuit of fortune, and of leaving a legacy which survives flesh and bone is accomplished without scruples and through ruthlessness which makes Daniel seem like a saint. His creation is the machine, and the setting of Industrial Revolution era London, with all of its distinct British cruelty, child labour, capitalism, and new technology is simply perfect to tell a story that is fundamentally about greed. And the bloody path we carve to sate it.
And there are scares. Some require a bit more thinking and putting the pieces together, some require running away and hiding, some can make you yell and flinch away from the screen. It's good we don't have to gather oil for the lantern (it runs on electricity now, anyway) or that we need to gather an inventory because I think in this context, it would become tedious. Instead, we can focus on the atmosphere, story, and the scares. We can get lost in the growls and squeals, the heavy, incessant labours of the machine, and simply unravel the insanity within.
So is A Machine For Pigs scary, all in all? That depends on your definition of scary; it will scare you when and where it's supposed to, in a heart pounding, sweaty hands sort of way. Think of it as a rush, a wave of fear that crashes into you, whereas Dark Descent was a constant flood.
Yet instead of comparison, we should enjoy A Machine For Pigs rather as its own unique, interesting, and dark vision of human nature. So I think the real question should be: is A Machine For Pigs horrifying? And the answer is absolutely. That is the point, after all.
Truly, I am not a fan of horror. I was intrigued by Dark Descent because my friends wouldn't shut up about it, with good reason. I've found that the genre is deeply rooted in all the sorts of sad, brutal, sick and twisted ways humans strip away their humanity (usually by trying to become more than what we are; most of the time, the sacrifices aren't worth it). This game is no exception.
A Machine For Pigs is certainly deserving of sharing the same panicked breath with Dark Descent.

Droid Assault might be the first game of its kind that I've played. It's your standard top-down twin stick shooter, but with the fascinating ability to completely hijack and become your enemies.
I particularly enjoyed the discovery of different powers of various droids. They range from being able to hover, to shooting lasers. Outside of that gimmick, though, I'm not sure what else there is to say.
I would have liked a way to scan the droids I am about to take over. As it is now, you have to remember what droids have what powers based on their appearance, which is kind of hard to tell since they all look vaguely alike. Also, the AI for your allied drones is just awful. I have no idea how to keep an army alive for any sort of boss.
There's a rudimentary upgrade system that is based entirely on random things dropped by the levels. I would have liked a way to upgrade things between levels as well.
Curiously there tends to be little reward for blowing up enemies. I guess survival is its own reward, but would it have been too much to ask for experience or cash? Something that makes me stronger.
I feel that the game suffers from its sheer lack of story or ending. At least Ultratron and Titan Attacks had a final stage before it loops to the beginning again. This game just goes on and on. It harkens a little too far back to the Atari days where we do nothing but play for points. I'm sure that style of gameplay appeals to some people, but definitely not me.
Overall, fun at first, but becomes completely and utterly pointless.

Lyman Raymond Lamb (March 17, 1895 – October 5, 1955) was a Major League Baseball player for the 1920 and 1921 St. Louis Browns.
Lamb made it to the big leagues at the end of 1920. In nine games, he hit .375. He was a utility player for the entire season after that, but his batting average slipped to just .254.[1] The Western League's Tulsa Oilers acquired his contract in January, and he never played in the majors again.
However, Lamb thrived down in the high minors. His 68 doubles in 1922 helped lead Tulsa to the pennant. He hit 71 doubles the year after that and then 100 in 1924. The 100 doubles (over 168 games) set an organized baseball record.[2] That season, Lamb also led the league in hits, with 261.[3] Lamb stood at just 5 ft 7 in (1.70 m) and weighed 150 lbs.

Reviewing this game without spoiling too much is difficult. I suppose that already spoils some things about the game, namely the fact that the overall "feeling" is always changing. There is no status quo. No settling into things. Enemies get harder with time, everything keeps changing, and it all works within the game's atmosphere.
Many keep mentioning that "if you liked Bastion, you'll like this game". Now, that is true, but don't go thinking that this is just "sci-fi Bastion". Yes you once again find yourself as a nameless protagonist in an isometric world that's suffering through a highly unusual catastrophe. Logan Cunningham returns as the narrator with a voice so enjoyable you could listen to it read the phonebook. And of course, the soundtrack is amazing yet again and you should buy it.
But what's different from Bastion? Well its no longer a hack-n-slash, I'm honestly not sure what to call its combat system aside from an odd mix of turn based strategy and real time strategy. The new combat system also forces you to constantly improve. Its a rare time when you feel like you have things totally under control, there is always a feeling of needing to improve, of needing to improve your own skills to keep up with the evolving enemies. I don't mean this as a feeling of being constantly overwhelmed, but more a feeling of always being just on the edge. The RPG elements are also greater, as opposed to Bastion's "pick two weapons and a drink for your loadout", there is now a large amount of variance to what you walk into battle with.
Supergiant games as also improved on storytelling, at least in regards to including more speaking characters, and you will feel things about all of them. Be it hatred or sorrow or whatever else, the writing is very well done. Without spoiling anything, I think I liked Bastion more based on tone. I still greatly enjoyed Transistor and I highly reccommend you buy it and buy the soundtrack too.

Transistor, aesthetic wise, think Blade Runner meets Cowboy BeBop.  But that really isn't a fair description at all.   First of all I want to say I am not a big RTS fan at all.  So I was very much on the fence about Transistor.  I got it in the Winter Sale of 2014 and just got around to playing it and boy was it a treat.  Gameplay aside this game is ART.  The visuals are stunning and the soundtrack is stellar as we have come to expect with composer Darren Korb of the previous SuperGiant game Bastion acclaim.  Ashely Barrett (also from Bastion fame) has some outstanding vocals as well.  I am not going to compare this game to Bastion they are both good in thier own right.  I enjoyed the Real time/Planning kind of gameplay Transistor brought to the table.  Really unique.  It's a great game albeit short.  I didn't do any extras or training missions and the story took me about 4 hours.  The story (to me) was kinda ambigous and convoluted, but I think that was the point to get people discussing theories and what they interpreted it as.
All in all it's a great game, pick it up if you want to see some gorgeous visuals, hear some great music, and have a unique experience only SuperGiant can deliver :)

If you enjoy logic puzzles, don't buy this game.  You may forget to continue eating and sleeping if you do.
Factorio is an amazing logic puzzle that naturally grows more complex and difficult as you move along.  The campaign is short and sweet (basically an extended tutorial) but the real fun is in the free runs.  I think the reason this game resonates with so many people is because the difficulty curve is PERFECT.  I never felt frustrated playing this game because whenever there was a problem, it was always incredibly easy to diagnose, and it was always a problem with my design, not with the game.  That's not to say these problems are easily fixed though;  As you learn, you'll probably want to start from scratch before reaching the endgame just because you know you can build it better with everything you've learned.
Basically, this title is an absolute gem.  I would say they should charge more, but these user reviews are really the only way to advertise such an odd and brilliant game, and more people NEED to play it.

In Distraint, you play as Price, an ambitious young man who works as some sort of tax executive for a prestigious company, seizing people's properties, in hopes of proving himself and getting a partnership. However, along the way, Price realises the impact his job has on the lives of the people whose property he seized, forcing him to re-evaluate his career choice. As guilt settles in, Price begins to lose his mind...
The main focus of Distraint is its interesting story, told well through text and visuals, as there is no voice acting. Although a horror game, Distraint isn't scary per se, but it manages to be unsettling and get the message of its story across.
The writing is good,  although it can get naive at times and there are a few typos. Thankfully, nothing major that ruins the experience. The visuals are simple, well done and they serve their purpose. Paired with the good sound design, they can sometimes create an eerie and immersive atmosphere. The best example of this is when you're at Price's apartment.
The gameplay could be best described as a side scrolling point & click, without the pointing and clicking. Price has an inventory and can store up to three items which you get by interacting with the environment. You then use these items to solve puzzles in order to progress the story. The puzzles are simple, but engaging enough to keep the game fun and the story going.
Overall, I believe Distraint to be a good game. Its only two hours long, but those two hours are well spent. It definitely delivers for its asking price; You get good bang for your buck, as some would say. And considering it goes on sale often and that there are plenty of giveaways for it (One of which I got my copy from), it's worth a try.

Initially, it seems like a great idea but unfortunately, it's pretty poorly executed, mainly due to how loose the team management is but otherwise due to how poorly the allied AI perform.
There's many ways this game could be improved, giving the player more control over their team would be a given, making the stats of each robot a little clearer so it's possible to identify the advantages and disadvantages of having them as part of your team as opposed to just hopping system to system blindly hoping for the best would be another, it's also possible to upgrade robots via pickups however they're incredibly vague too, perhaps if it was possible to equip each system individually and change their upgrades?
I'd suggest giving this game a miss and checking out another of Puppygames works, they're definitely great developers and Droid Assault is simply not on par with their other three games.

It isn't scary.
This is the biggest problem with this game. Yet interestingly enough, you don't realize it at first. I loved playing the first Amnesia game, and so I went into this game with the same mindset. Hide from the monsters, solve the puzzles, answer the mystery at the center of the plot. The game certainly starts like its predecessor. The atmosphere is spooky, and the game doesn't throw any overt scares in your direction at first, just hinting at the horrors that might await. Overall, this works really well. But here's the problem: almost none of the scares are real.
What do I mean by that? Well, in the first Amnesia game, most of the time when you heard or saw something that could threaten you, that threat was real. There really was something to hide from. Your fear was justified. In MFP that's really just not the case. I can count on one hand the number of times I was truly in any danger. Most of the time the game plays some scary sound effects suggesting that a monster is nearby, but in reality it's just nothing. You can just safely walk your way through 90% of this game without a care in the world. It does take a while to realize it, because often you'll jump into some hiding place and wait for the monster (which isn't really there) to walk by, so you'll assume that you didn't see it because you hid, and not because there is nothing there in the first place.
Really, "just walking" is unfortunately way too good a way of describing this game. I really feel that The Chinese Room were the wrong people for an Amnesia sequel. They just don't do interactivity very well, and in really weird ways too. For some reason there is almost not a single object in the game that you can pick up, unless it's a crucial part of some puzzle. I really just don't get this, given that in Dark Descent you could pick up and move most objects you found lying around. This change immediately just reminds you that you're in a game, which messes with the immersion needed to pull off a good horror game. Aside from the house at the start, the big sprawling levels are gone, and instead you just follow along a narrow path. The player just isn't allowed to interact with the world that they're in. There are almost no monsters for them to fear, there are objects that they can move without express permission, and there are no places to explore. In the end, this just reminds you that you're in a game, and lets you know that you're walking down a hallway with scary noises.
It's been said many times before, this game isn't very scary. However the story is solid and if you take it for what it is, it's an enjoyable game.

However, only play this game if you are willing to sacrifice the scare factor for other qualities.  It may not be particularly scary, but this game has rightfully earned its place as my favorite survival-horror title.

I loved Just Cause 2, and if you did too, you'll enjoy this one immensely as well. If you're new to the franchise, Just Cause is basically better described as Just 'Cause, because you're spending 99% of the game blowing up stuff just because you can. It's an absolute blast and a pleasure. If you're a fan of vast open world sandbox games, this one's for you.
As a sequel, I'll address some changes:
- Greater emphasis on sandbox aspects; destroyed structures will respawn upon reload regardless of the situation, allowing you to blow them up again - can be a con if you're a stickler, but for me this was a huge plus as one of the downsides of the prior games was the feeling of not wanting to save since you wouldn't be able to destroy the same stuff again.
- Wingsuit; a whole new way to explore the world that's in my opinion vastly superior to the usual parachuting (which is also available here), so you're constantly getting air time which is a blast. I would also highly recommend grabbing the Sky Fortress DLC if you're into flying around since it grants you access to a wingsuit-booster early on that you can use to get infinite flight time.
- Quality of life changes; they've done away with the bloated economy system which took you out of the sandbox every now and then - now, Fast Traveling and item drops simply cost a one-time consumable called Beacons which can be refilled at any allied settlement. Vehicles and items come in comically packaged storage containers that pop open with flair when they hit the ground so you don't have to worry too much about careful positioning when you select drop points.
- Remote cabling; you can now have up to two additional cables to simply connect between any two objects that can then be retracted remotely under any circumstance. This allows you to create some fun scenarios and really feel like Spiderman. This can be done simultaneously with your own cabling for movement and hooking onto things so you don't sacrifice one for the other.
- No QTE's; they got rid of the pesky quicktime events that made acrobating between airborne and moving vehicles a major hassle. HUGE bonus that goes unnoticed but is greatly felt.
:
- Cars are clunky; the driving in JC3 is far inferior to the previous entries in my opinion. You constantly will find yourself performing random drifts from the slightest turns and precision turns are practically impossible. You don't spend much time driving thankfully, but I'll get to that later.
- Story; it's cliche at best. You'll notice a copious amount of copy-pastes from other popular franchises such as GTA and Assassin's Creed with the way the characters interact. There's the unique Just Cause premise of Rico Rodriguez (the titular character) being a "Dictator Removal Specialist" which is a title that's always made me chuckle, but a uniqueness in name alone.
- Too many ways to get around; this is tough to put under negatives because in many ways I absolutely love the abundance (wingsuit, parachute, grappling hook, e.t.c.), but as a result of all of the gadgets at your disposal, vehicles such as planes and helicopters become relatively unexciting. As stated earlier, cars are downright useless and the only time I'll bother getting in them is for the utility of a tank or to rescue a friendly during a randomly-occurring mission that requires you to do so. Overall, I prefer the game the way it is, but whenever I'm forced to use a vehicle for any reason it feels out of place and sometimes more inconvenient than it should.
- Crashes and poor optimization; there is always a lot happening on the screen at once and the game doesn't really know how to handle it. Usually the game can deal with a heavy load, but every now and then it'll just completely give up and stop responding, forcing you to restart the program. I have a beast of a computer and this isn't a problem with any other game so I have to attribute it to the optimization - plus, others seem to have this problem as well. It doesn't happen very often for me, but your mileage may vary.
- Questionable port quality; availability of keybinds are relatively awkward in distribution and you often feel like this would be played better with a controller despite the fact that ironically, I don't prefer playing this game with a controller. Additionally, getting the resolution and fullscreen to stay steady is way more difficult than it needs to be. It'll sometimes minimize when I change completely different options and alt-tabbing out of the game for any reason can lead to some wonky results when you tab back in.
All in all, I would highly recommend this game if you can snag it for $10 or less on sale, which happens pretty often. You'll get your money's worth for sure as long as your computer matches the specs. It's a great mindless sandbox game for when you just wanna have fun and not think too much. I would not personally pay the full $50 price, however.

Not that I ever doubted that videogames do qualify as art, but Transistor should make it obvious to anyone.
The game's artwork is done in a gorgeous, colourful style of cyber-Art Nouveau with maybe a touch of Noir (oh, that does sound really pretentious, doesn't it... what about the nods to certain paintings I imagine seeing in for example the posters? even worse? ok.)
As probably expected, it has an amazing soundtrack, and you can even (sort of) interact with it in the game (Transistor has a hum button, and you won't know how great that is until you played.)
The story is tragic and delivered spot-on. between terminals and the great narrator you're left to fill in the blanks about the place you're in, but the picture practically paints itself. Ha... The narrator is also the same voice as in Bastion, yet somehow the role he plays manages to be entirely different this time around.
Very importantly, the game isn't lacking in its set of mechanics either. The combat system is deep and highly customisable, with not only the options of building attacks and defenses but real-time and turn-based mode as well. The limiters available can raise the difficulty if so desired. The game is just a little short, but definitely replayable in NG+.
Overall, Transistor is just awesome. Get it.

Now i have a question for you- do you think it was funny? Answer for this is more important than you think. Let me explain. Entirity of Borderlands 2 it's written by that guy with beard- Anthony Burch (fun fact- Ashley- second character in sketch and Anthony sister is voice actor of one the most well known characters from B2- Tiny Tina) . And it goes without saying that Borderlands will have similar style of comedy- random, sarcasstic and somewhat childish. And that can be huge problem if you don't like it, especially considering that this game is long and uses it's style of comedy quite frequently. But if you do you are in for a wild ride. Same rule goes for insane characters- you love them or you absolutely hate them.
But now for the most important part- gameplay. It's fast, it's brutal, it's disgustingly addicting. B2 it's propably the best RPG/FPS game right now, even 5 years after it's release. There are multiple reasons for this.
There are 6 different classes, all of them have their own unique interesting character, skills and playstyle. Tons of content. And i'm dead serius about that- they expand the lore, they have huge variety and most of them are even more random and funny then main campaign.
As i said- DLC is great. There are 4 different mini-campaings all set in new locations with own theme, they add enough content to justify buying them and some even add new mechanics- like Pirate's Booty adding new class of weapons
Let's get to negatives now, and let's start with darker side of DLC- mini-campaings are great and all, but if you play them at too high level they might turn absolutely useless to you, not giving you any good weapons or EXP. This game should be the face of everything I hate- blind production in the name of "research" so that you can produce more things at a faster rate. And exterminating the aliens of the planet you're invading because they have an issue with your♥♥♥♥♥♥of their  landscape. That being said, it is extremely compelling. The game forever shows you that you can always do better. You can always build more efficient routes. You can be more elegant, faster, more productive. Suppose you wanted to make an inserter- a crane-like arm that can move an object from an adjacent belt and move it to either another belt, or a chest, or an "assembly machine"- a factory. To make an inserter, you need one iron plate, one iron gear and one electric circuit. The plate is the product of a forge, where raw iron is cooked into workable plates. Gears cost one plate to make. A circuit is a plate, and three pieces of copper wire, themselves made from copper plate. So to make an inserter you need one gear assembly machine, one copper wire assembly machine, one circuit assembly machine and one inserter assembly machine, plus the forges and coal to make the metal plates in the first place, and some sort of electrical power so that the inserters and assembly machines run. If this itself sounds dull, it is. What is fascinating is how to make it perfectly efficient and maximally productive. Playing this game is how I imagine how and engineer or someone who feels compelled to build pac-man in minecraft feels on a daily basis, seeing everything as abstraction, attempting to make everything perfect. It's a hellish feeling. I hate this game. But you should buy it if only for the experience and joy of doing it right.
The game does have a substiantial issue with pacing. In a campaign mission, there's usually at least half an hour of just plain waiting. The music is bad. Some of the recipes are unnecessarily obscure. The game isn't extremely keen on hand-holding, and likes a lot to trick you and point and laugh at your errors. Like failing to kill all the aliens before you start Big Industry. I would have appreciated a slightly more close focus to chemistry. Additionally, like in Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, I'd have loved to be able to befriend the aliens.
In short, Factorio is a big playbox just perfect for someone who looked at Minecraft and thought, "This game needs to have all its charisma sucked out of it, and replaced by AUTOMATION. BLEEP BLOOP I HAVE NO SOUL."

At its heart the game is about change, as you go year by year, chapter by chapter, you see Emily holding on to the the past, whilst she talks about everyone else changing. Although this game is extremely short, with only about 30 minutes of real gameplay and not much replayabilty, it is sweet, thought-provoking and emotional. Combine this with, what I like to call, the fake typing mechanic, it becomes an interactive experience. The only improvement I could ask for is for your choices to have more of an impact on the ending, but that is one short-coming that can be completely ignored. All in all, this is a short, sweet and powerful game, that definitely has become a must play.

Distraint is a lovely little quirky game.   The game plays through as a combination of 2d walking and talking simulator, with a little bit of Use-X-on-Y puzzle logic problems.   The puzzles are nice and simple, and mostly involve walking back and forth a lot, trying things on things.  For the most part, the puzzles are solved in a few seconds, and don't get in the way of the narrative.
The background story is that you're a repo agent, climbing the ladder in an organisation.  The trouble is... you keep being given the nasty jobs, and your conscience is starting to get the better of you. Soon, it becomes a struggle against your rebelling conscience... Or... are you really just starting to see the truth about yourself?
The environment is built from interconnected 2d side-on areas,  lovingly drawn  and split between apartment blocks, woods, a cemetary, a hospital and the offices of your employer.  Each 'episode' (i.e. day) involves the same overall goal (serve a Distraint on someone), with the same "Before you can do it, you must do me a favour" quest which has kept Bethesda in cookie money for all these years...  However, each day takes place in a different location, and the quests become more and more unusual as the game goes on.
At the end of the game, if you've been paying attention, you'll pretty much made your mind up on what's going on.  The game does its best to lay it all out for you on a platter.  BUT, and this is a big but, as soon as you've finished playing it through, go back and play it again.  Some things will start to make a LOT more sense.  You won't regret it.  And believe me, after re-doing a chunk of the playthrough, you'll start to change your mind about whether the game has been altogether truthful with you.
The graphics are very pixelly and simplistic, with very charicatured actors.  However, the game uses sprite warping, film grain and other little effects to break out of the "pixel art" style that other games (like Home) use.  Most of the levels are grey, splashed only with colour to accentuate certain items, which works exceedinly well.    There's a lot of variety in the graphics.  The game doesn't rely too much on reusing stock backgrounds or items.   Each area is unique, each interaction unique, and there's a lot of nice gfx to show that the artists were really earning their pay (fog, coloured lighting, drifting trails, splatter.. all sorts).  The graphics are genuinely impressive.
The background audio is largely that weird discordant strings thing that horror movies use when things are going to hell in a handbasket.  It certainly adds a lot of atmosphere, and there are some moments where you're genuinely on edge, largely because of the sounds.    Occasionally a little music will play, or the background will change a little to highlight the change of scenery.
Since there's no vocal dialog, it's all text, there's a little b-b-b-b-b-blip sound which can be changed if the default is too grating. (I stuck with the default).   The text is well written, with few typos, and tells the story of the protagonist's fall from sanity well.   The different colouring of the text is reminiscent of Teletext subtitles, and helps differentiate speakers.
The controls are all keys, using WASD, E and space for everything.    This means I can sip my tea while playing, which is nice :) There's no mouse control.  Since the levels are side-on 2d, you just need left-and-right anyway!
The game has a lot of 'heart', and you'd have to be pretty soulless not to pity the plight of poor Mrs. Goodwin.  I was geniunely happy when the credits rolled and she makes one final appearance (you'll see).
The game takes a few hours to play through, but if you decide to play it through again, you can speed-run it in under an hour by just hammering the 'e' key to step through the dialogue.
I can recommend Distraint.  If you're not too jaded, it's a moving tale, with some little jump-scares, some horror elements, and a lot to make you look at yourself critically.  I really enjoyed playing it, and will certainly go and hug the first widowed granny I come across.  OK, it's not for everyone, but I think it's good for the majority.. :)
Remember: What goes around, comes around!

This game is a great arcade style game like the old coin ops.  You play as a robot and you have to eliminate all the enemy robots before you can exit a stage and move to the next one.  As you play you get powerups that make your robot shoot faster, recharge faster, have more armor, do more damage per shot, and so on, but you can also capture other robots which allows you to switch into them.  There's walls in the level that you use for cover while you try to destroy the enemy robots and there's a bit of a stealth component to the game too because robots won't come after you and attack you unless they can see you or a security camera can see you.  You can capture other robots and use them so it acts almost as a class selection would in another game and lets you adjust your tactics to the particulars of the level.  There's also occasionally boss robots at the end of the levels, around every 10 levels or so.
This is a blast for ten minutes to an hour here or there when you just want to do a little shoot em up and you can save at any time and come back for later so its a perfect game for casual play.  This isn't a hardcore game so don't go into it expecting to play it for 20 hours.  Its an arcade shoot-em up so you'll get a similar amount of play time to those kind of games, but you won't be dragged down by tedium just designed to slow down gameplay to make a ten minutes of action take 4 hours.

Yeah, I said it. It might be because it's been featured in a bunch of dirt-cheap bundles and so people might be inclined to give it a pass but DISTRAINT is bad. As a game it is stuffed to the brim with farcical "puzzles" that bring to mind the worst nonsensical crap that old adventure games had to offer (things like "find a can of gasoline so you can power the generator and turn on the washing machine so that you can pull out a glove to lure a dog back home!") while as a piece of writing it is not only absurdly predictable but completely incapable of finding its tone, regaling us with such hits as "GREED AM BAD, U MAEK PEOPLE SUFFER! Oh also we are going to play a loud noise when we reveal ourselves butchering this zombie elephant."
Eye-rollingly boring, weird for the sake of weirdness, incapable of delivering any tension or worthwhile gameplay; the one saving grace this game has is that each "level" is so small you'll have no problem figuring out how to use the mundane items you find to kickstart the improbable and barely sensical series of events that get you through the story. I extend my apologies to Mr. Jesse Makkonen, who uses the game's credits to address a cute little note toward the players, but in the end DISTRAINT is not scary, it is not thought-provoking and it is not even that entertaining. Truly the only question left in my mind after playing it is just how did it get so many positive reviews.

This game will be different for everyone, first off.  I myself, have a fear of man-made interiors, small-spaces, and darkness.  That comprises a good 2/3 of the environments in this game.  It felt very much to me like I was inside one of my own nightmares.  I loved the exterior/house sections too for world building purposes, but I was actually excited when the game switches to "descent mode".
The antagonist in this game is easily one of the BEST antagonists in any video game I have ever played.  This guy makes one of the most twisted horrendous plans that no one sane should able to even conceptualize... and actually partially accomlishes it.  All for the classic betterment of humanity.  I love the antagonist of this game.  10/10.
The sound is tear-jerking.  This includes bgm, voice acting, and random noises.  There's also a great deal of variation in bgm, from full out opera, classical, eerie ambiance, and then even ragtime loaded with political satire during the credits.
The voices and scripting are beautiful too.  This game is very poetic, like reading a good Edgar Allan Poe Poem.  Feels very quotable.  I also personally love how the main character refers to his family as "darling."  And like any good horror game, random noises attempt to keep you on edge always, though once you know you're probably not in danger you can numb yourself to the scratches, whispers, and footsteps.
Story.  This is one point that even some of the worst critics of this game usually give.  What makes this story so good is that it is relatable.  It poses a "what if" scenario, that is terrifying because it can be conceptualized in reality to a certain extent.  Not to mention it plays on a primal fear of losing control, and highlights the tragedy of some of the darkest ages of actual historical past.
I must mention the negatives, because indeed there are a few, which some people would consider these "game-destroying".  This game is somewhere in-between an interactive movie and an actual game.  You can indeed die if you're not attentive, are free to move around a limited environment, and there are a few pretty simple puzzles.  However there is no inventory, which means no typical Penumbra/Amnesia puzzles, worrying about your lantern oil, healing with laudanum (probably why it's hard to die).  There aren't many "jump-scares" or adrenaline pumping danger danger horror.  This game focuses on a deeper type of horror more akin to analyzing a deeply psychological nightmare than primal adrenaline reactionary horror.  Fine in my opinion to have those, but if you're looking for a danger around ever corner monster monster freak out session... don't expect to find it.  More saddening to me then anything else is the lack of the screeching noise whenever a monster is nearby... though the flickering light works pretty well too.
To me, this game is art.  The setting is beautiful and surreal, the sound is moving, and the story makes it hard for me to immerse myself in other shallower horror stories now.  If you consider the purchase of this game, make sure you're looking for an experience and not a jump-scare.

I am a fan of Clint Eastwood Western movie classic as well as of Spaghetti Western movies, especially those by Sergio Leone and Segio Corbucci (the director of the original Django movie starring Franco Nero from 1966). Call of Juarez Gunslinger is heavily inspired by those and really puts you in the shoes of a daring pistol and rifle wielding gunslinger. It is excellently executed, featuring robust FPS mechanic and a story that just brings the Wild West to life as a fan like me who is influenced from such movies as mentioned above.
While the actual campaign only lasts around 5hrs, it is never boring and presented in different chapters, each featuring one of those infamous Wild West scenarios. Additionally the game comes with a duel mode letting the player face off with all those historic personalities one comes across in the story, and an aracde mode where all that matters is a high kill streak.
Overall I can highly recommend this title to ever FPS fan and especially to every Western movie fan!!! It's time to ready those 6 Six Shooters, Winchesters and double barrel shotguns!!!

Honestly surprised by how much fun this game turned out to be.  That being said I had extremely low expectations. You're an aging cowboy so sometimes you need to go over things acouple of times when remembering the events.  As they player you have to adjust as game elements may suddently change as the main character realizes his story isn't correct.  It keeps you on your toes and provides a very good feel to the overall game.  Also if you couldn't tell by looking at the screen shots, this game is cell shaded.  So if you come across performance issues or don't like the cell shading you can very easily turn it off by simple modification of the config files.  The one negative that is worth mentioning is that the game is very short.  The levels are short but plentiful.  However there is alot of reused settings and assests, making the game feel even shorter.  Overall this game is fun for a couple of hours but dont expect more than ten hours total. I bought this game on sale for $5 bucks and would recomend it if it goes on sale.

The combat is what makes this game unique. Somehow they were able to work in both a real-time and a sort-of pause-and-plan type system. And it works. Very well. And on top of that, the customization of attacks (called functions) is unique.  Each function can be used as a main attack, or they can instead be used to add a modifier to another function to give it a boost. There may be only four slots (2 modifier slots each) and sixteen functions, but there's a lot of room to tailor your playstyle to what you want.
And the aesthetics. The music. The story. All frickin' beautiful. It gives off a nice sci-fi noir vibe. It's all beautifully put together. Honestly I liked it much more than Bastion. The only thing that I have any qualms with is the length of the story. I feel like they could have really expanded that out and explored the world a little more.

Let me tell a short story about the terrors of Pandora.
Bandit gangs never got along well, yet your gang managed to carve their own turf after a long battle with the rival gang. To celebrate it, you guys decided to storm the nearby settlement, pillaging everything, killing and doing much worse things to people that used to live there. Grabbing everything that's worth a penny, the entire gang rides home.
On the way back, one of the bandits spot a tall, lonely psycho. "Must be one of the other gangs." you say to yourself. Bad luck he's all alone. You order your men to prepare for an ambush. Everyone is in their place and with your order, they open fire. Once where he stood, there is now a thick cloud of dust.
Wait. Did that guy just emerged from the smoke as if that firepower was nothing but cotton candy? He's heading towards your gang while screaming at the top of his lungs. There is a bundle of dynamite in his hands and he's chucking it like there is no tomorrow. After shaking off the initial shock, everyone keeps firing. Psycho blows one of your men up and then pulls his shotgun, returning fire. one by one, your men fall.
You panic, pull up a flare gun and fire it into the air, requesting support from every single bandit nearby. the reinforcements arrive quickly, but this guy just doesn't know how to bite the dust. Lots of psychos swarm him, but he just lets out a maniacal laughter and pulls out his buzz axe, swinging it left and right. Limbs, guts and blood spreads everywhere. he just keeps swinging. He even hits himself.
In terror, you take a lucky shot to make him stumble for a moment, big mistake. He just spotted you. He starts to convulse, one of his arms makes an awful cruching sound as it grows into a gigantic size. the remnants of your crew falls left and right as he makes his way towards, you, it's then you realize; his entire body is covered with blood, bullet holes and much worse wounds. You have no idea what keeps him ticking.
As he lifts his axe to end your miserable life, your eyes lock. There is nothing in there. Nothing but pure, undiluted rage.
Lucky for you, you're not the bandit leader who just got hacked into bits, just like the rest of his crew. You're the Psycho who did all these, while screaming "I'M THE CONDUCTOR OF THE POOP TRAIN!" on the top of his lungs.
This is how playing Borderlands 2 feels like.

Firstly, I understand that I am probably going to get flamed and trolled to hell for not recommending this game. Secondly, I don't care. The original Borderlands had an interesting story and I felt like there was always a goal you were working towards. This is literally the same thing all over again 100% with just slightly better graphics, more guns and different heroes that have slightly different skills. The game is 5 years old and yet there's still a lot of areas where frame rates absolutely tank even with a GTX 1080 Ti. Yes, that's right some areas where there are a lot of buildings and individual objects cause the game to drop a good 10-20fps depending on whether or not you are in combat. I've tried tweaking the settings, but the point is I shouldn't have to.
To be honest I feel like this game is marketed at children who enjoy poop jokes, despite the fact that in Australia it has an 18+ rating and the game sports dismemberment. The characters are all hatable, their dialogue is repetitive, gun fights are repetitive, everything is repetitive. Run or drive to the marker, shoot up these guys, loot every case for a few dollars and some ammo and maybe a decent gun. Upgrade some stats so you can get 0.7% more health and 1.5% more damage if your life is <25%. Some bits of the game are interesting like the weapons that are actually unique but that's mostly it.
If you are seriously that interested in buying Borderlands, get the "Pre-Sequel" which is not only newer, it's actually better optimised. Just know that it's essentially again, the same thing as Borderlands and Borderlands 2. Same art style, same story, slightly different heroes, generally same weapons and slightly different game mechanics/perks. Just all packaged into another full priced title. I really am surprised how many people enjoy this series, so much that they are actually willing to basically buy the same game three times.
Inevitably this one is going to rot away in my Steam library for years to come. What a shame...

If you need a game to spend an (awful) lot of time on, then look no further. Final Fantasy XIV: A realm Reborn is all that you will need, especially with the huge amount of quests and side quests that the game currently has to offer.
Like any MMORPG, FFXIV ARR has different classes, that all work differently. Tanks being the Warrior (Maurauder) and Paladin (Gladiator), the healers being Scholar (Arcanist) and White mage (Conjurer), and finally, the DPS being Dragoon (Lancer), Summoner (Arcanist), Black Mage (Conjurer), Monk (Pugilist), ninja (Rogue) and Bard (Archer). Each class has plenty of abilities to explore, and all play differently, so there's definitely a lot of content there.
That being said, I don't think all classes are equally fun to play. Dragoons and Warriors aren't the funnest to play, but the fun classes definitely make up for that. My personal reccomendations would be:
Tank: Paladin
Healer: White Mage & Scholar
DPS: Monk, Black Mage, Summoner
Classes themselves are a lot of fun to explore, especially because the way the game handles classchanges: just simply change weapon, and your character becomes that class. No need for additional characters, or a lot of abra cadabra to change around a class, but very straight forward and easy. Even a casual outfit is possible, for in your "spare time", and hiding your weapons / headpieces on these is done with the single click of a button.
Besides combat classes, the game also offers multiple jobs to do, which you can also access with the same system. It's possible to craft your own weapons and armor with the different classes the game has to offer, or make extra Gil (= in game currency) with gatherers or with the same professions. Although not all of them are equally fun, there's plenty of fun to be had here as well. The only classes i don't really recommend here, except maybe for the gil, are miner, fisher and cook. Sadly, cooking seems a bit pointless in the game from as far as i've found out, except for slight XP boosts, or some additional effects.
The classes are easy to understand and straight forward. If you level one class far enough, you even get the possibilty to use certain abilities of one class on another, in a nice cross class system. Say for example you have a level 50 warrior, and want to use tank abilities that your level 18 gladiator has. It would be possible to have a couple of these abilities on your high leveled warrior, for more tanking badassery.
That's enough♥♥♥♥♥♥about the classes, now onto the juicy quests and most important of all, the badass l00t! :D
But in all seriousness, although there are a lot of "Go fetch", "travel 'round the world for me" and "go feed dem soldiers, guardian of light" missions, which unfortunately are boring and a lot of running around, the GOOD missions definitely make up for this. You can go into dungeons, trials (read bosses), guildhests (read tutorials) can farm F.A.T.E's (read events) and leves (read ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of xp for 'allowances'). Most of them definitely help level up your character, but when you reach max level, only trials, dungeons and raids would be in your interest, along with marks. These give you the epic l00t you were looking for :3
You don't have to l00t the defeated enemies, but drops will automatically be added to your inventory.

There's a two week trial to play the game. There is a free trial on Steam...just gotta type in "Final Fantasy XIV" and then it'll finally show up as a "Free Demo." Also when looking at reviews to get to know the game, ignore anything under 100 hours. They don't know what they'e talking about.
As it says for me, I've logged 440 hours at the time of this review (Thats bound to change very soon though). I'm downright addicted to FFXIV. Yes, there are points in which the game is tedious. Yes, there are certain things that make me sigh. And yes, the few cutscenes that are voice acted are terrible as the VA's suck.
First things first. Some of the negative reviews says the game is SUPER grind heavy. That's both FALSE and TRUE. It doesn't take long to get a single character class to 50 (Present max level though the DLC/Expansion that comes out this spring will raise it to 60 while adding an entire new area, new dungeons, raids, bosses, and 3 new classes). What takes long is getting your max Item Level Gear which is...130? I'm not too sure on that myself. I haven't hit ilevel100 yet on my main.
More on the Grinding. You can hit max level in under 2 weeks of moderate gameplay for one of your classes. That's not long compared to some other MMO's. Of course most other MMO's don't allow you to level EVERY CLASS in the game on ONE CHARACTER without the need for alts. What makes the game 'Grind heavy' is the fact that there's 9 Combat Classes and 11 Crafting/Gathering Classes. That's a total of 20 (Well 22 technically but those two share the same exp pool as its base class) different classes to get to level 50. On one character. And yes, there is a benefit from leveling all the classes. You can 'Cross Class' certain skills to other classes. Giving them benefits of different skills.
Some of the early dungeons are pretty boring but they're not really meant to be like really great. They're basically tutorial dungeons. Letting you learn the mechanics that you'll see extremely often in later, harder, and significantly more fun, dungeons (and raids.)
The crafting/gathering system is a love-hate thing. Though that's true of most every MMO. One of my Free Company minions focused almost exlucsively on the Crafting and Gathering Classes and almost hit 50 on all of them within only a few weeks time. If you're dedicated and manage your exp sources right (Levequests and crafting/gathering level appropriate stuff) your crafting/gatherers will level fairly quickly.
There's two different subscriptions too. So all those peope ♥♥♥♥♥ing about "Its 15 bucks a month" are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting you. 15 bucks a month is for the premium subscription that simply allows you 8 characters per server for a max of 40 throughout your Data Center. The Base Subscription, which is like...12-13 bucks? Restricts you to 1 character per server and a max of 8 in your data center. I'm not sure on the price as I have the premium subscription myself. The base subscription is cheaper then, say, WoW's subscription. And its worth it since you don't really need Alts. (I just really like the game. >.>)
As people will say, the game looks very nice. The music is fantastic (But what did you expect? Its a FINAL FANTASY game!). The story is interesting. Gameplay? I like it. It's solid. There's not really much to say about it. It's an MMO...Oh! I saw one negative review talking about monsters "Auto attacks" and there being to avoid getting hit by them unless it uses a move that creates a 'zone' that you want to get out of...that's not true. You can avoid getting hit by a monsters auto attacks if you STAY OUT OF THEIR RANGE. Which is understandably hard for a Melee Class or a Caster Class. But the Archer has no problem literally kiting a monster without ranged attacks around in circles. Ya just gotta becareful not to leash them...as they'll become invincible while they retreat back to their spawn area.
What else to say...what else to say...
Hm...JUST TRY THE FREE TRIAL! ITS FREE.

Pros:
- Intersting story that isn't hard to follow and has decently played out cutscenes.
- Collision/Impact style based tab target, Not the usual tab target where you can clip through people/npc/enemies, It actually makes you dodge attacks and not just stand there bored pressing 1 , 2 , 3 repeatedly untill the mob dies like generic tab target games.
- Brings back the old type of class systems where you can do everything on the one character, An aspect I personally love because it means you dont have to play through the same story over... and over... and over... to play the different types of classes available or master different professions - you only need the one character.
- Game lets me be a Ninja Catgirl.
Cons:
- Pay to play.
- Its still tab target.
- No open world pvp/Very little pvp content.
- Servers are pretty limited, Europe/Japan/NA.
All in all its a good game, Probably not worth the full price unless you plan to dedicate your life to it, On special i'd definitely reccomend it, The amount of content you can do on your one character is staggering and i'd imagine it would take multiple months to get to that level so you wont be bored quickly.
Take a week off work, Ignore your friends and social obligations and dive into the world of Eorzea, At the very least you'll leave with a miqo'te fetish.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.

I tried to like this game, I gave it so many chances (because I just love other Puppy-games), but I don't see anything fun here.
In a few words, Droid Assault is a game about dodging bullets. Of course, there are other gameplay elements which may seem interesting at a glance, but believe me, they are not relevant to success in the game.
The developers tried to make it look like there is a lot of strategic thinking involved in the game, but I will try to show why that's not the case.
You think that having an army of droids is cool? Trying to come up with different combinations, etc... Nope. You can control one droid at a time and the others do whatever they want (read: stupidly die all the time). Having one buffed droid is the only valid "strategy".
When you transfer to a droid, you don't know what you're going to get. Even when looking at a droid's information screen, the only thing you know for sure is how much health it has. Other pieces of information are either "ciphered" ("armour: kevlar", what does that tell you?) or just "lore" (affect nothing). At the same time, you have different ways for droids to interact: maybe some weapons work better against some armours... but we may never know, because there is a huge lack of information. Well, you could spend tons of time and compile a table with information on all the droids, deduce the meanings... but who wants to do that?
From what I remember, the bosses are just big droids with big guns, nothing too special.
But it's not all that bad. The game looks cool, I guess. Upgrading the droids can feel nice...
Droid Assault can be fun for a few hours, maybe for one playthrough, but it is not worth the full price.

Alright, first and foremost let me point out that I have recommended this game, which will contrast with what will sound like a negative review. If it comes off that way it's because I felt like Transistor could have been so much more, but standing next to Bastion it's withering in the shade. Overall it was an enjoyable experience, but at the end of the day I'm glad I got it on sale or I might have been very disappointed.
Let's start with the things I enjoyed about the game. The thing that jumps out first is that there's a lot of love behind this game. You can tell that Supergiant wanted to really connect with their audience by creating an immersive world and characters that you can sympathize with. The real-time/active-time combat tries new things while staying grounded in somewhat familiar territory for most strategy/rpg fans, and being able to 'socket' abilities into other abilities makes for some interesting emergent play-styles.
Now for the things I didn't find very enjoyable, or thought could have been done better:
First- about that immersive environment Supergiant wanted to create in Transistor. Personally, I felt like that was a total whiff. They should have called this game Esoterica, because it's filled with fluff that is never explained. It's like picking up a sci-fi book you've never read before and know nothing about- picking a random page in the middle, and reading for four hours. By the end you know more than you did at the beginning, but you're still lost for the most part.. you're missing fundamental information to make sense of the story.
As far as the characters go, I wanted to feel connected to them- I read every little bio and sought out every OVA station to learn more about the world and its inhabitants- but it feels hollow. Like they're trying too hard to live up to Bastion, which achieved greatness in both gameplay and storytelling almost effortlessly.
I found the "narrator" in this game to be completely obnoxious. In Bastion the narrator added a lot of flavor and backstory to the world, since as a third party witness to the events that were going down, he could provide information that the player needed to feel connected to the things that were happening around them. In Transistor, he just monologues.. it's like going on a road trip with somebody who can't make meaningful conversation and doesn't like the sound of silence so they read every billboard you see. Eventually you would rather swerve into oncoming traffic than hear that there's a Cracker Barrel in 2.7 miles.
The game itself is reasonably fun, if a bit repetitive (which is kind of a strike against it in its own right... how can a game with so much personality be repetitive after only 3 hours?). The ability socketing system is a very interesting spin on the whole 'play how you want RPG' genre. It's easily exploitable for those who want an easier time with things- but for players looking for a challenge can apply handicaps that award you with additional experience at the cost of a harder game. I would have liked to see a bit more variety here, but it's clear that they were designing a 4 hour game and not a 20 hour game.
I ran into a LOT of bugs, which was disappointing considering how late to the Transistor party I am. Supergiant has had ample time to fine tune the experience- but I was running into issues where all of the AI models were missing (you could mouse over them and get tooltips, but the models were missing). A few times during combat I was teleported outside of the "ring" and couldn't get back in, so I was locked into a combat state and couldn't end the fight- so I had to force-close and restart. And just pathing issues in general.. plenty of times I'd click on a point to run to, but Red would choose the most bizarre path to get to an unobstructed position. This happened frequently during combat turns, where the incorrect path taken would basically ruin all of the proceeding commands (attacks firing into thin air, etc). It wasn't so frequent that it was game-breaking, but it happened enough to merit mentioning.
And if you don't want any spoilers, this is probably a good spot to stop reading because I need to vent about something that happens at the very end of the game.
Still here? Okay. So one of the things I'd read about this game was that it had a "strong female lead" and that supergiant was doing a great service to female gamers with Transistor. Now, full disclosure- I'm a dude, so it's entirely possible that I don't get it. I fully recognize that I may in fact lack the extra "X" chromosome to understand what girl gamers are looking for in a game with a female lead. However, at the end of the game when Red chooses to off herself to be with this guy we (the player) know nothing about had my eyes rolling into the back of my head. I felt like it was a cheap romantic plug at the end of what could have been a somewhat interesting (albiet confusing) story. Here she is with the 'brush' that could remake the world- she could un♥♥♥♥ everything that the calimari or whoever destroyed. But instead she rebuilds a plaza, then sits down next to the narrator's body and stabs herself with the big blue sword. Poetic I guess? Maybe we need more context. Maybe the world isn't worth saving if they can't be together, but Supergiant gave us NOTHING on this guy. Not a name, not a backstory.. nothing. His bio card is "Unknown" with zero information.
Anyway.. It's worth playing. It has its problems, but it did not live up to my expectations at all.

Some games focus on the action, others focus on the tactical aspects, others the story - this game happens to do all the above. Transistor is a great example of a game that doesn't have to sacrifice actual gameplay to be art. Transistor was a bit of a pleasant surprise for me, I bought the game on sale and had only seens a few headlines stating that it was an amazing game - and it is. In all aspects it is.
The combat is interesting and diverse - the ability to freeze time to plan out your attacks in a semi-turn-based style whilst sacrificing a few seconds of vulnerability afterwards was very unique. The ability to increase the game's difficulty based on optional in-game options in exchange for more exp points was also a very nice tough. There were points where the game had gotten too difficult until I tried around 3 times, swapping my abilities and passive perks around to find the best combination but otherwise - the game was just difficult enough to be enjoyable.
The stoy however, takes the highlight. Rarely does a game make you feel for the characters, what makse this game interesting is that its entire story is almost told by a single male voice - no cinematics or animations, just a voice that speaks to the player's avatar Red. The amount of emotion conveyed was impressive and I enjoyed this game's story immensely due to it.

After what i feel is a decent amount of hours played i feel i can write a review for this game..
Lets start with its good points right? so here goes:-
FF XIV is a top shelf MMORPG, yes your have to purchase the base game and yes it has a subscription fee 'sigh'... but after much deliberation and playing pretty much every other MMORPG.  My friend and I came to the conclusion that in F2P games the most important content and utilities where microtransaction BS! and you just cannot progress.. not to mention the most vile and hatred filled gamers your ever likely to come across.. So we gave this one a bash and in all honesty for what your paying its a bargain ! and no im not a fan boy.. im speaking the truth.... theres no locked content, everything is available as long as your able to progress that far and level up high enough to reach the locations.
The graphics in this game are indeed Direct X9.0, but not by any means outdated ! i play many new games such as S.O.M / Farcry 4 etc... and this game is just as graphically pleasing if not a little easier on the eye as it all blends and texturises realy well. I run a Nvidia Geforce GT 740 2GB ddr5 card and get 40-50 fps all day long on the highest settings.
The music is well composed and fits in well with the FF Franchise to those who are familiar, however just sometimes it can grate on you when your not expecting it or suddenly gets louder...
Voice acting is some what scarce and when is around poorly dubbed but again something anyone familiar with FF will just over look this easily !
As for content the game is full of it ! Theres never a dull moment, with 18 Classes to not only choose from but swap to at any given moment you can never get bored... ive litterally gone from fighting to keep my A** alive to suddenly sat on a stool fishing for sardines !! all in space of a few seconds. get bored of fishing easy ?? no problem grab a pickaxe and follow me ! we can go smash some crountry side open and mine for ore and composites !! whats that you say ?? cant find your pickaxe ?? not to worry my friend, lets go train to become a carpenter. We'll have you equipped in no time :D and how about after that we head to the Culinary Guild and cook us up a nice dinner of rabbit pie with white pearl chocolates for afterwards.
Like a bit of slash and gash voilence ? become a Gladiator and Tank your way through whiles the Arcanist's and the Thurmatages watch your back with ranged magic and summons ...
And of course need not to be mentioned really (ITS AN MMO ITS IN THE DESCRIPTION) you can do this with your friends 95% of the way through... of course i say 95% because during some Guild missions and Campaigns missions im afraid your going to have to go it alone !!! But the people of Eorzea are a nice Folk and are willing to help out anyone who just speaks up !! Help is out there people.. your never alone here :D FF XIV is Cross-Platform compatible with the PC/PS3/PS4 platforms and you play along side them..
Bad Points to this game:-
Again i say "Subscriptions fees" but there not all that bad .. theres no locked content once you've paid and everything is at some point readily available..
Fast Travel can cost a fortune so be wary of how you travel !
Can seem Tedious at times, but once you discover everything there is to do youll never fit it all into a day :D
Overall i Can definetly recommend this game to anyone looking for an MMORPG but feel there all missing something ??

Papers, Please is a game made by indie developer Lucas Pope. In this game you are an immigration officer and your job is to guard the border of the fictional country of Arstotzkan to make sure noone unauthorized are allowed to enter.
The gameplay is easily summarized: You inspect passports and other documents to make sure they are correct and not forged. If you let through anyone incorrectly, you recieve a reprimand from the Ministry of Admission. Recieve too many and your paycheck starts suffering. Gameplay-wise, that is pretty much all you have to care about.
However, beyond that layer of mindless data processing is a human aspect. What rules will you bend and for what reason: Will you let the crying old lady reunite with her son even though her documents are missing? Will you take bribes to keep your family fed and warm?
The gameplay can get repetative. You check passports and wide range of different entry documents and keep track of the entry rules that changes from day to day. Is the birthdate correct on all documents? Is the name correct? Weight? Height? And so on and so on…
Still, the game is varied enough to keep my interest for two consecutive playthroughs. This is mainly because of the interesting people you meet and the sub-plots that keeps unfolding. I would definitely recommend you try it if you haven’t already.

Arreseted a murderer.
Denied a crossdresser.
Helped out the Arstozkan's equivilant to the illuminati.
Accepted $10 bribes.
Shut down a human-trafficking ring.
And told Jorji to get a proper passport FOR THE 4TH FREAKING TEAM.
All in days work for a border-checkpoint inspector.
GLORY TO ARSTOZKA.

Just Cause 3 is the sand-boxiest sandbox you could ask for, and is a game that lingers in my mind long after playing it. It’s a game that you see playing or someone mentions, making you think, “that was a ton of fun; I should go play it again!” We’re talking about a pure, unhindered, unapologetic sandbox of fun—giving you the tools to play how you want to play.
Now unlike Just Cause 2 (JC2), Just Cause 3 (JC3) takes a little more ramping-up to get into. When you get started, it will actually feel pretty clunky next to other modern FPS games. Movement and combat will feel limited, particularly if you’re coming from JC2 or from the fluid shooter mechanics of a dedicated FPS game. This can admittedly be a tough hurdle to overcome for many people, but STICK WITH IT! It gets better!
Rather than giving you all the tools right out of the gate, Avalanche has instead added a progression system that allows you to unlock abilities for your grappling hook, parachute, weapons, and vehicles. As you complete challenges and progress through the story (which is pretty good…writing isn’t the super strong point, but it’s absurd enough to be enjoyable), you’ll find that your abilities unlock fairly quickly. This is when the REAL game starts to really unfold: a play-your-way simulator of chaos!
The coolest things they’ve added to JC3 is the asynchronous multiplayer and the stat-tracking for almost everything you do in the world! For achievement-hunters like myself, this is awesome: you get a world of your own to explore while setting and breaking the records of your online friends as they set their own. You get to always push the limits, which is exactly what JC3 is all about.
Despite minor irks with the progression of the game, it is well worth the journey to play and unlock all the tools in your arsenal. The wing-suit is an AWESOME addition to the game—one of many improvements to create faster, more fluid, and more exciting movement in the game. I’d highly recommend giving it a shot, and would encourage you to pick up the add-on packs sooner than later to get the most out of what they add to the game!
