Transistor is the second game from SuperGiant Games, the makers of Bastion, and it shares much in common with their first game.  First, the visuals are quite stunning and appealing.  Second, the narration is excellent.  Third, the protagonist is mute.  Fourth, the story is always compelling you forward.  Last, the story is, sadly, on the short side (around 6 hours if you skip the optional trials), but it's still an excellent story; I'd much rather an amazing, compelling short game than a longer game that loses its direction, or my interest, along the way.  In addition to all of that, the game includes an excellent combat system and the voice acting overall is very well-done, and kudos to SuperGiant Games for doing what much larger studios fail at accomplishing - NPCs that drive the plot forward while talking just the right amount in well-acted voices.
The story puts you in the role of Red, a singer who has lost her voice and wields The Transistor, a talking circuit sword.  Much like Bastion, its predecessor, you travel around the world battling bad guys while trying to figure out what happened and how to stop it.
While fighting The Process, you get the pleasure of enjoying the battle system, which is quite well-done.
First, you may have up to four abilities hotkeyed to your active ability bar.  Each ability has one power-up slot, which can be used to make the ability more powerful in various ways depending on which power-up ability you choose.  As you level up, you unlock more abilities, more power-up slots, and more passive slots.  You can then take all of the abilities you have at your disposal and mix and match them in a myriad of ways to make a style that is both fun for you and powerful enough to get the job done.  Your choices are only limited by the abilities you choose to unlock and how much memory you have available (which can also be increased as you level).
Second, during combat you have the option of real-time or strategic combat.  You can run around the screen using your abilities live as they come off cooldown if that's your thing, or if the combat is especially easy, or you can choose to enter strategic combat and plan out an effective attack sequence and aim your abilities in the most advantageous ways.  However, the strategic combat option has a cooldown every time you use it, during which many of your abilities will be unavailable, so in between strategic rounds you'll need to become adept at evasion.
Last, if you find things too easy, you will unlock limiters as you level.  You can activate these limiters to make combat more difficult, and also to earn more XP from each battle.
If you enjoy RPGs, action-adventure, mystery, and/or strategic combat, then you have a reason to play this game, because it delivers all four in a well-balanced mix.

Another great game from developer Supergiant. I think Bastion really set the stage for the style we can expect from this developer, and it works very well. The story in this may not be immediately clear to many people, it certainly wasn't to me, but it does reveal itself over time. It becomes more clear on the second playthrough which I highly recommend.
Soundtrack and art presentation are absolutely beautiful here. If you find an area of the level soothing there's a button to let your character sing or hum to the soundtrack. I thought this was neat, and allows the player to separate from the combat for a while...maybe calm themselves if they're having trouble passing an area. I personally found the timed challenges to be infuriating at times.
Transistor is combat based using a realtime and/or jump-in jump-out strategy planning interface that you can use as long as it's not on cooldown. It's the players discretion on whether or not they need or want to use the strategy planner, or whether that's all they want to use. Combat pops up on you during progression as a virtual arena. Fast and swift attacks slowly chipping away at your enemies, or slow heavy attacks causing massive damage and immobilizing you for a few. Four main abilities with two sub-abilities each, you combine the abilities to create hybrid attacks. You also have four passives that you can slot any of your abilities into. The combinations are astronomical.
My problems with the game are gripes. The challenges had no apparent quick restart, just an end and re-enter the arena which took time. I couldn't find a way to view my currently assigned combos without hitting a checkpoint. Even at the checkpoint I couldn't find a way to directly inspect the combo, only the individual items in the ability selection menu.

Alright, first and foremost let me point out that I have recommended this game, which will contrast with what will sound like a negative review. If it comes off that way it's because I felt like Transistor could have been so much more, but standing next to Bastion it's withering in the shade. Overall it was an enjoyable experience, but at the end of the day I'm glad I got it on sale or I might have been very disappointed.
Let's start with the things I enjoyed about the game. The thing that jumps out first is that there's a lot of love behind this game. You can tell that Supergiant wanted to really connect with their audience by creating an immersive world and characters that you can sympathize with. The real-time/active-time combat tries new things while staying grounded in somewhat familiar territory for most strategy/rpg fans, and being able to 'socket' abilities into other abilities makes for some interesting emergent play-styles.
Now for the things I didn't find very enjoyable, or thought could have been done better:
First- about that immersive environment Supergiant wanted to create in Transistor. Personally, I felt like that was a total whiff. They should have called this game Esoterica, because it's filled with fluff that is never explained. It's like picking up a sci-fi book you've never read before and know nothing about- picking a random page in the middle, and reading for four hours. By the end you know more than you did at the beginning, but you're still lost for the most part.. you're missing fundamental information to make sense of the story.
As far as the characters go, I wanted to feel connected to them- I read every little bio and sought out every OVA station to learn more about the world and its inhabitants- but it feels hollow. Like they're trying too hard to live up to Bastion, which achieved greatness in both gameplay and storytelling almost effortlessly.
I found the "narrator" in this game to be completely obnoxious. In Bastion the narrator added a lot of flavor and backstory to the world, since as a third party witness to the events that were going down, he could provide information that the player needed to feel connected to the things that were happening around them. In Transistor, he just monologues.. it's like going on a road trip with somebody who can't make meaningful conversation and doesn't like the sound of silence so they read every billboard you see. Eventually you would rather swerve into oncoming traffic than hear that there's a Cracker Barrel in 2.7 miles.
The game itself is reasonably fun, if a bit repetitive (which is kind of a strike against it in its own right... how can a game with so much personality be repetitive after only 3 hours?). The ability socketing system is a very interesting spin on the whole 'play how you want RPG' genre. It's easily exploitable for those who want an easier time with things- but for players looking for a challenge can apply handicaps that award you with additional experience at the cost of a harder game. I would have liked to see a bit more variety here, but it's clear that they were designing a 4 hour game and not a 20 hour game.
I ran into a LOT of bugs, which was disappointing considering how late to the Transistor party I am. Supergiant has had ample time to fine tune the experience- but I was running into issues where all of the AI models were missing (you could mouse over them and get tooltips, but the models were missing). A few times during combat I was teleported outside of the "ring" and couldn't get back in, so I was locked into a combat state and couldn't end the fight- so I had to force-close and restart. And just pathing issues in general.. plenty of times I'd click on a point to run to, but Red would choose the most bizarre path to get to an unobstructed position. This happened frequently during combat turns, where the incorrect path taken would basically ruin all of the proceeding commands (attacks firing into thin air, etc). It wasn't so frequent that it was game-breaking, but it happened enough to merit mentioning.
And if you don't want any spoilers, this is probably a good spot to stop reading because I need to vent about something that happens at the very end of the game.
Still here? Okay. So one of the things I'd read about this game was that it had a "strong female lead" and that supergiant was doing a great service to female gamers with Transistor. Now, full disclosure- I'm a dude, so it's entirely possible that I don't get it. I fully recognize that I may in fact lack the extra "X" chromosome to understand what girl gamers are looking for in a game with a female lead. However, at the end of the game when Red chooses to off herself to be with this guy we (the player) know nothing about had my eyes rolling into the back of my head. I felt like it was a cheap romantic plug at the end of what could have been a somewhat interesting (albiet confusing) story. Here she is with the 'brush' that could remake the world- she could un♥♥♥♥ everything that the calimari or whoever destroyed. But instead she rebuilds a plaza, then sits down next to the narrator's body and stabs herself with the big blue sword. Poetic I guess? Maybe we need more context. Maybe the world isn't worth saving if they can't be together, but Supergiant gave us NOTHING on this guy. Not a name, not a backstory.. nothing. His bio card is "Unknown" with zero information.
Anyway.. It's worth playing. It has its problems, but it did not live up to my expectations at all.

The idea is to destroy all enemy droids while keeping your party alive, which is MUCH easier said than done. The game is a bit less about action skill and more about the managment of your droids, as some are faster than others, or have better defense, or have different weapons more suited for a situation. It's fairly easy for your droids to die, but it's also fairly easy to hack other droids if you have enough transfer points. The AI that commands friendly drones is fairly competent at killing enemies, but not so much at staying alive, so there is a constant need to keep them out of harm's way. Things get real challenging with boss battles and danger areas that throw tons of bots at you - I Think it's expected that you will loose some droids, which will unfortunately loose any upgrades they had. A very clever tactical, action game that use simple mechanics that just work. A challenging game, and I think I got to at least level 30 before I died, but I don't think I can improve much on my skill after my team nearly got wiped out the in the previous couple levels. If the idea of the game appeals to you, definitely get it, just realize there is a big challenge ahead of you in the later level (Ironically, the game seems too easy at the beginning).

Hello, I have about 1.5k hours on Smite (disregard my steam time for it since I got it for steam very late). I've played this game since season 1 and have seen it at its strongest and weakest points. This game for me was fun in that it offers a unique point of view that makes you feel much more immersed in the game and the skill shots make it feel so rewarding when you land them (and make you even more sad when you miss them, biblethump). Smite offers many gamemodes, so even if you're into the competitive conquest side but still want to play with your friends without them destroying your Elo, there's casual modes like arena and clash. Smite is open to both competitive and casual gamers. The Smite community, like any serious MOBA will have pretty rude players here and there. That's nothing new. However, I find myself easily making friends and finding players who ask to party up for games quite a lot. We're a pretty open community when it comes to making friends and parties.
Some things I don't particularly like about Smite are the matchmaking, servers, and balance. Matchmaking can be pretty ehhh. I understand players having a bad game here and there. Everyone feeds or does bad. However, at my playtime and such, I shouldn't be matched with players who just outright build wrong (Looking at you crit second item Neith). I know matchmaking isn't perfect, but there are times where it's plainly obvious they don't belong in this match. The servers for a while have been unstable. It happens here and there. It can be pretty frustrating and I find a decent amount of players lagging. As for balance.... Jesus. Smite has been pumping out new gods, which is a good thing but also a bad thing. I feel like they should first nerf the obviously too op gods before adding more gods to the game. I find that they always keep pumping out more and more gods without taking care to the obviously too op gods that currently exist in the game.
All in all, Smite has flaws that I find really annoying and can push me away from the game. I still do enjoy the game despite it. I don't play as heavily as I did before and will play a few games per week. I do recommend this game if you play fairly casually, but I don't recommend getting into this game all that seriously until they start to fix up their game more.

After hearing so much disapproval of this game, I've been reluctant to purchase it for over two whole years now. But come actually playing through it, I was not disappointed. Sure, there were a lot of interactive qualities that made The Dark Descent unique that they quite literally locked up here. (Seriously, most of the furniture and objects had real locks on them.) That didn't take away from my overall enjoyment of this game, though. I played Dark Descent to get scares, and after playing through it more times than I can count, I didn't expect as much of a scare factor from A Machine For Pigs. But boy was I wrong. This game made me jump and scream like a girl countless times. Not quite as much as Dark Descent, but pretty close. I loved how noticable the work put into the world's design and detail. Definitely an upgrade since the first game. The atmosphere was absolutely spot on, which is something Frictional or Chinese Room's games are naturals at creating. Eerie sound effects, ominous flickering lights, and claustrophobic corridors REALLY mix well if you're trying to create a scary game, and that's just what this game has. Really the only beef I had with this game is that it didn't quite live up to Dark Descent, which is pretty much expected. I mean, come on, how can you top the first game? As similar as these two are, it's still not even close, in some good ways and some bad. It was pretty relieving to not have oil as a concern, but I'm pretty sad they took out the sanity feature. It added more of a scare factor to Dark Descent that made it feel very different from this game's scary segments. Nonetheless, this game scared me enough, sanity meter not included. I was also not really into the story. It was too mysterious and hard to follow, and not very clear to me. To wrap this review up, try to ignore most of what I said. The more you compare this game to Dark Descent, the more disappointed you're going to be. This game is definitely not bad, but it's not the most spectacular thing you'll ever play. All that aside, this game is definitely DEFINITELY worth playing and I am very glad I finally gave it a chance, because it was a very spooky and fun experience. Recommended to fans of all horror games or horror in general.

“Papers, Please” allows the player to indulge in the fantasy of a border control inspector (quite similar to TSA). The game tackles a lot of interesting and controversial aspects of border security such as body scans and fingerprinting. The game has an inspection view mode which you use to compare sample data such as passport dates or names to existing rules or other data to find and resolve discrepancies.
There is also a very, and I mean very, big focus on memorizing information. You will need to remember just about every little detail about every little rule and you will need to continue to adapt this memory of yours to the ever increasing number of arbitrary rules that must be followed. Failure to follow procedure will result in warnings, fines, and a game over if you push your luck. Sometimes though, you will want to deliberately fail in order to help people out or achieve some other goal.
This game can get downright stressful during the post-review phase where you watch people entering/exiting the country with baited breath, hoping not to hear that telltale sound of a MOA citation being issued. Later on, you have to really be on your toes with all the various paperwork being juggled around and it almost seems like a relief when you find a stupid mistake.
This game is often heralded as an example of when indie games “nail it” on a concept, and I would agree. Papers, Please transforms a boring, repetitive task into something fun and challenging, while still retaining some semblance of story to keep the player pressing on just to see what will happen next.

DO NOT READ THE NEGATIVE REVIEWS. PLEASE READ THIS FIRST.
This is a very good hunting game. As a real life hunter, I enjoy the level of realism this game provides. It's not realistic in many ways, but it's not a hunting sim (even though I wish it was). That being said, it's certainly the most realistic hunting game on the market. It has a wide variety of environments, weapons, species, and equipment. It has incredible graphics, good AI, awesome online multiplayer, real-time competitions, interesting missions, decent skill system with acheivements, a photo gallery of your kills, and decent statistics tracking. The gameplay is fun while remaining somewhat realistic, but it does have a learning curve. Once you understand how the game works, you'll have a blast.
The negative reviews almost all come from people who did not read what they were downloading. They thought this was a completely free game without doing any research into it. theHunter DOES have a subscription based system and microtransactions, but it's not all bad. They just updated their F2P model and it is more than fair now. Keep reading.
As I write this review, currently there are 10 maps, 29 huntable species, and one species of dog you can bring hunting with you. When you download the game for free as a guest you are able to access all maps. However, you can only hunt 5 species for free (whitetail deer, pheasant, and three rabbit species). The free species are on all but one map. All other species require a license that you can either earn by doing missions for in-game currency (gm$) or buy with real money (em$). You can even earn em$ by doing sponsor deals (which I have not done, so I can't tell you whether or not I recommend it). You cannot shoot animals you don't have a license for. You are given two weapons (12GA Single Shot Shotgun and .243 Bolt-Action Rifle with unlimited ammo) and a few other items for free to start your hunting. This shotgun is legal for every species in the game as long as you're using the correct shells (birdshot, buckshot, or slugs), the rifle is legal for mid-sized animals including the Whitetail. Check the wiki for more information.
Between the missions for the 5 free species, you can earn plenty of gm$ to purchase a host of equipment to improve your chances of being successful, and even buy licenses for additional species. That's all without spending any real money. This route should be considered more of a demo to the full game, as it teaches you about the basics of what the game has to offer.
Once you're convinced that the full version is worth the money, you can purchase a membership bundle or subscription. Subscribers unlock all animals, maps, and unlimited free ammunition for the duration of their subscription. Bundles are the best value if you're just getting into the game, however. Bundles include a subscription and a host of weapons and equipment. I would HIGHLY recommend the Trailrunner Bundle ($49.99), which includes a year's subscription and a HOST of weapons and equipment. When your year's subsription is ending, you can renew your subscription for another full year for only $34.99. There are tons of extra weapons and equipment you can buy a-la-carte with em$ (real money).
I've spent an absolutely ridiculous amount of money on this game and I don't regret it. I love hunting and this is the best hunting game out there. You don't have to spend a ton of money to enjoy it though. You can have fun for free or take it up to a great time for $49.99. The subscription is fair and necessary because the devs are CONSTANTLY updating the game and adding new maps, species, and other features. Even if you don't want to spend money on the game, you can download what is a great free whitetail deer hunting game.
Before you go trashing a great game, do some research on what you're actually getting into. It is not fair at all to the devs or long-time players who want this game to be supported for years to come.
There is a wiki and forum for learning and getting involved in theHunter's great community. Happy Hunting, all.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is the newest and possibly final game in the Call of Juarez series. It's a follow-up to the critical failure of Call of Juarez: The Cartel, and because of the series' massive fall into relative obscurity, this game fell under the radar and recieved little attention.
You play as Silas Greaves, a fictional bounty hunter who was involved in many of the stories behind famous cowboy legends of the wild west. Your journey is told via narration of an older Silas reliving his experience to a cast of characters in a saloon, and his quips and interactions with the other characters surface frequently throughout gameplay, sometimes reacting to what the player's actions.
It's a fairly traditional first person shooter at first, it has solid shooting mechanics and a score-based combo system that rewards you for head shots, stylish kills, or getting multiple kills in a row without missing. It'll give you more points depending on how much style each kill Silas makes has. You can use these points to upgrade Silas's abilties in three different upgrade trees, "Gunslinger", "Ranger", and "Trapper". Each gives bonuses that cater towards different styles of play, but you can choose upgrades from any tree you want at any time. But if you want to get to some of the later abilities in one specific tree, you'll have to focus most of your points onto one skill-set.
Silas also has two active abilities that you'll be seeing most frequently, those are Concentration and Sense of Death.
Concentration is an abiltity you charge up with kills over time, and is activated using Q. Enemies become highlighted in Red, time slows down, and Silas's guns pack a bigger punch. It doesn't last long, but you can kill quite a few enemies without hassle if time correctly and your aim is true enough.
Sense of Death recharges itself over time automatically. Once it's filled up, if the player is hit with a lethal shot, Silas will be able to dodge the bullet if the player presses the correct key (either A or D, depending on which side of Silas's head the bullet is going towards).
Sometimes, Concrentration is automatically activated during cinematic sequences. In order to get more score in some of these sequences, the player enters a quick time event and must press the correct key to shoot multiple enemies and get a higher score. If the quick time event is failed, the enemies will remain alive and the player will have to manually shoot the enemies.
Other times, the player merely has to click the left mouse button and watch Silas do some gunplay on his own to reward the player for completing a section. Despite minimal interaction, it was pretty enjoyable to see Silas leaping from a bar window with duel revolvers, nailing several deputized hire guns in the head on the way down.
What you end up with is a solid shooter with easy to look at graphics,  well put together story telling and a fun upgrade system that encourages replayability.
For what it is, it's a great game, and I recommend it.

Borderlands 2 > Borderlands 1. If you liked 1, you'll like 2, and even if you didn't like 1 you may still like 2. The reasons for Borderlands 2 being better than 1 and a good game in general are the following:
1. Unique guns/shields that help to fundamentally change the way you can play the game.
2. Significant differences between classes - many RPGs have characters who are only nominally different. In Borderlands 2, you have classes that each have 3 subclasses where each of the subclasses is a truly nuanced version of the main character type.
If you like games like Fallout and The Elder Scrolls you may like Borderlands 2. However, it's important to note that Borderlands 2 is not exactly like these games. It has less side quests, and the sidequests feel far less meaningful than either The Elder Scrolls series or the Fallout series. Nonetheless, the main storyline is substantial and contains many hours of gameplay.
Though I recommend this game, there are some potential downsides. The storyline is pretty in depth, but I found the unexpected things to be rather expected and I felt like some of the characters could have had more depth. Additionally, I found the third act to be quite flat. Additionally, the unusual art style may dissuade some from enjoying this game.

BEFORE YOU READ ON: I would like to firstly state that the reason I am reviewing this game and not Scholar of the First Sin is due to this being the first Souls game I played and feel like it would be appropriate to review this game over SotFS as I am voting this one in the Steam Awards. I do NOT recommend you buy this game at all! The game got a complete graphical overhaul, mob placements AND you get all the DLC in Scholar of the First sin, so PLEASE buy Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin instead of this game! This game just has a special place in my heart and in all fairness, most of the points I cover in this review are still relevant in SotFS.
Brief: This game is a Dark Fantasy RPG with intricate combat mechanics, absolutely fair but punishing difficulty and best of all a rather vague, yet amazing Lore behind the game series in general.
Why would I recommend this game?
Firstly, let me start out by saying if you enjoy a nice difficult game that is not completely unfair in the sense that the AI is obviously conspiring against you, then this game is for you. It provides a fair challenge. It have a large selection of weapons of different types that you utilize in combat, whether it be PvE or PvP. PvE can be done solo or with cooperation with your friends. Same goes for PvP. And due to the large variety of weapons and the statistics system behind your character, you can customize a variety of builds unique to your choosing to use in PvE and PvP. Some can be viable, some may be just for fun. Either way, you control how much of a challenge you want.
The PvE: The PvE is great, though there is the odd occassional mob tracking issue, but don't let that put you off as it is rare enough to enjoy. The game requires you to learn the area you are in, this game is rather large and has a lot of areas to explore and conquer. You start off with a difficulty setting (which cannot be changed) called New Game. And each time you complete the game, you move onto New Game plus. Which basically causes some new mobs to be introduced in the areas you have been in, and makes mobs hit harder and generally increases the difficulty. The bosses you encounter in this game are a tough challenge, though some maybe a complete joke. The really challenging ones come in the DLC, with the occasional in Vanilla. Once you kill a boss you get their soul, which in this game is used as currency to buy items, level up and basically do everything. You can either use a boss's soul to acquire many souls (used to buy items etc...) or exchange it for a boss weapon which has unique move sets (usually) and quite a powerful set of stats.
The PvP: I never was much of a PvPer myself but trust me on this one, the PvP community on this game is HUGE! There are covenents you can join provided by the game that "matchmake" you in the sense (not directly- I will explain later on), which you use to defend a certain area against trespassers, or you "invade" someone elses world and punish them! How matchmaking works in this game is slightly odd and different to any other multiplayer games you have played in the past. Firstly, your character is undead- which means you cannot summon anyone to help you in the world NOR can you be invaded. You can summon someone to fight you AND you can put your sign down for someone to help you. Doing any of these will make you "human" which will: Make it so you can summon someone or be invaded by someone. These "signs" I talk of are points that show up to other players in their world. Imagine it like different worlds, each unique to one player. When a player puts a sign down (assuming they are within a certain range of the total number of souls the player has acquired),  other players can see this and chose to summon that person. That is the basics (I do not want to turn this review into a guide).
In Summary
The Positives:
+ Fair Challenge
+ Great Combat Mechanics
+ A Large Story
+ A Large World
+ A Proper "World" feel to the game (in the sense it does not feel like a lobby system)
+ Fantastic replayability
The Negatives:
- Mob tracking can be strange and a bit too predictable sometimes (not always)
- Some Bosses are a joke (they are way too easy for the stage they are at in the game)
- The Story is vague and will probably require you to study item descriptions or try to piece together the riddles of NPCs. (It depends on the person to be honest- there is a HUGE community of Dark Souls players out there that have put together the lore of the land)
- No clear direction (I personally do not find this to be a negative, I enjoy not knowing exactly where to go and exploring- HOWEVER: this game is not conventional and I'd imagine that most people would not like this.)

This game plays like that old 'Berzerk' game from Atari years ago.   Back then the graphics were drawn lines and small human-like block droids that sounded like the Daleks from Dr. Who.  While the graphics in this game 'Droid Assault' aren't exactly the latest frostbyte engine of today... I don't believe they're meant to be either.
The developer 'puppygames' has a number of games that have this same nostalogic feel.  Graphics are a big part of that.  They've done a good job of giving you that nostolgic  feel but also giving you a new game entirely.  This game may remind me of that old 'Berzerk' game but it plays like a modern arcade game.
You play the part of a droid that has to neutralize other droids within a given facility (map) while they also try to neutralize you.  You can neutralize them by destroying them or hacking them.  There are different levels of destructive power and hacking capabilities of each droid depending on the droid.  After you hack a droid...  it's yours and you can then use that droid.  You can amass a team of different droids and switch between them.  If one is destroyed, you can still control one of your other droids.  After all your droids are destroyed then it's game over.  The levels move along by defeating each progressively challenging level and then getting a boss level.
Movement was rather easy using WSAD for movement and using your mouse for aiming and firing with a kind of overhead view.  There's a number of games that use this method of movement and action for game play, so it's something you should prolly get used to if you haven't by now.  WSAD and left mouse button for firing... right button for hacking droids.  You have different levels of destruction and security for each droid and each droid is good for something that another isn't.  The idea is that you're able to utilize them as a team to do more havoc. The game gets progressively better as you learn to recognize the different droids and what their capabilities are.
It's a fun game.  I recommend for those 'arcade style'  junkies like myself.  Buy on sale of course.

Alright, I've had the physical copy of this game since the first month it launched and to be honest, I found it bland . . . At first. At release, it was like a brew of everything bad a total war game could have: bad optimization, wonkier than usual AI, bad diplomacy, politics that didn't work, tons of bugs, magical transports that can stomp legit navies, boring soundtrack, the list goes on and on. It was one of the games which I found too boring to play for thirty minutes, let alone finish a whole campaign.
But, I'll have to give credit CA. They fixed most of the bugs, gave it a massive optimization boost, reworked the politics, and added a free DLC campaign. While the stink of the game at launch lingered, instilling within people a prejudice towards the game that is still somewhat justifiable, this new iteration of Rome 2 is different from the one at launch.
Underneath the muck, the grime, and the sh*t that CA shovelled on this title is a streamlined game that is less tedious to play than the other titles. The addition of prompts, tabs, and UI made it easier to manage your empire, at least on the campaign map. The cultures have their differences from others, with the strong infantry of the Roman empire, the elephants of Carthage, the excellent cavalry and axemen of the tribes, the horsearchers of the east, yeah, CA did make the roster a lot more diverse, at least when compared to Shogun.
Though you can still sense the laziness of the devs in some ways where the game is presented, like the lack of beginning cinematics for the factions, the "parking slots" of the ships during naval invasions, and whatnot.
Despite this, the game is definitely worth it, but I recommend that you get it on a sale so that you can also get the piecemeal DLCs and get the full experience. At full price however, that's another story.

Although the lore, story, horror elements and gameplay are not as strong as its predecessor, "A Machine for Pigs" does offer a good (albiet watered-down) entry into the Amensia series. The environment is a nice change from "A Dark Descent", and is generally as good if not better than the dreary castle of the previous installment. Despite the great setting, the puzzles throughout the mansion, streets, engine rooms, sewers and complexes are essentially wheel-turners and lever-pullers.
Throughout the game, the notes and dialog honestly do a mediocre job at revealing the interesting world that you explore, leaving a lot of seemingly important things to the imagination, which can be a good thing but I don't think works well here. For every question answered, two more seem to open up. The monsters here are not as effective as they are in "A Dark Descent", essentially only giving us a few dangerous encounters. Even those encounters seem forced and almost cinematic. The plus side here is that the manpigs do fit the story of this game, and work well in conjuncture with the thematic "Industrial-Aztec-Sacrifice-Meat" elements of the game.
Although my review might seem negative, this game still delivers a short yet sweet atmospheric horror stealth-adventure with decent lore and good imagery.
I would suggest "A Dark Descent" over this game, but I think this still warrants a discounted purchase and playthrough if you're into atmospheric story-driven horror games.

First off, I loved the setting, I loved the atmosphere, I agree with others the design of the pigs was not exactly a masterwork in fright nor horror, but heck, anything that shreiks, chases you, and beats you up if it catches you will do the trick. No, the art was fine. Assume that every other element of the work fails. if that promise of art and atmosphere is still enough for you, stop reading this review and go on and buy it.
But once you've had your fill of the art, what's left is plot, and the plot, the thrust of the game, is totally craftless.
As is standard for amnesia, you discover partway through that you're supposedly someone who's done terrible things. The problem with that is the game spends the first three quarters letting you operate under the assumption that you are not that person, and developing an in-universe identity who's done nothing but try to protect his children. So, when the game tells you that you did something baffling and awful and there is blood on your hands, that you built a hell machine and oiled it with the blood of men, yes you, the person who probably baught this game because you were attracted to its strong anti-industrialist themes, this is the emotional reaction almost all players are going to have in light of this revelation:
No. No, I didn't do any of that. My hands are clean, and none of this has any relevance to me. I am not even slightly invested in the role.
And it really is all totally irrelevant to you because, as in The Dark Descent, the very empty explanation as to why our player character did these things seems to reduce to the influence of some black box alien artifact. You know, something that's explicitly not trying to analogize any real-world system, past, present or speculative future. Even if you were, against pragmatism, curious about this thin fictional construct, the game gives you basically no information.
Despite the familiarity of the industrial distopean setting, none of it is meaningful (beyond the premise itself, which is great, but that is conveyed in full by the cover text). It is not a commentary, or if it is, its angle is deliberately obfuscated. Not in a fun way. In a "there's no hint that there is any thematic puzzle here to be solved" way. If you think Dan Pinchbeck has said something meaningful, you could just as well be imagining it.

“Papers, Please” allows the player to indulge in the fantasy of a border control inspector (quite similar to TSA). The game tackles a lot of interesting and controversial aspects of border security such as body scans and fingerprinting. The game has an inspection view mode which you use to compare sample data such as passport dates or names to existing rules or other data to find and resolve discrepancies.
There is also a very, and I mean very, big focus on memorizing information. You will need to remember just about every little detail about every little rule and you will need to continue to adapt this memory of yours to the ever increasing number of arbitrary rules that must be followed. Failure to follow procedure will result in warnings, fines, and a game over if you push your luck. Sometimes though, you will want to deliberately fail in order to help people out or achieve some other goal.
This game can get downright stressful during the post-review phase where you watch people entering/exiting the country with baited breath, hoping not to hear that telltale sound of a MOA citation being issued. Later on, you have to really be on your toes with all the various paperwork being juggled around and it almost seems like a relief when you find a stupid mistake.
This game is often heralded as an example of when indie games “nail it” on a concept, and I would agree. Papers, Please transforms a boring, repetitive task into something fun and challenging, while still retaining some semblance of story to keep the player pressing on just to see what will happen next.

I've never been an MMO player. Briefly played Tera - liked it but found progression slow - and briefly WoW - disliked the combat, just felt like button mashing. I also played Mabinogi for a short while and really disliked the game's mechanics. One day I felt the urge to play one and I knew a friend was planning to start this so I bought it but neither of us started. 9 days ago a friend of mine was looking for people who wanted to start and I decided that if it was in my steam list I may as well try it out. I am now 95.9 hours in according to steam and I love it. I've just hit level 50 and got my Paladin armour and I'm still looking at all the content coming up. As I speak server is going down to patch even more content into the game. So here's the detailed review:
The story is a good one as far as MMOs go (based on my limited experience). I'd equate it to WoW in some ways as FFXIV builds off of an already established lore but is still extremely easy for new players to get into. I don't want to say much about it but Square Enix really put work into making a good story. It teeters a bit at times, especially around the middle (lv30-40 is a bit slow) but it's very enjoyable if you get into it.
Combat classes are fairly traditional: tank, support, ranged DPS and melee DPS. Still within these wider definitions, each individual class is fairly unique. To add to this you are not restricted to the classes that you pick at the beginning of the game. You will unlock the ability to train any and all classses as you wish which allows for a lot of flexibility. But "Oh, the grind ¬¬" you say. Nope, all classes trained beyond the first receive exp gain bonuses which really speeds up the process. This is alongside the quick levelling options which I'll discuss in a later section.
There's more though! All combat classses have a progression called a "Job" which is earned by reaching a certain point in the story, getting a class to lv30 and the corresponding second class to lv15, and then finishing the job quest. It's actually really easy to do and it encourages you to try a different role.
All combat classes are unique and don't overlap much at all which is great.
As for crafting classes, there's a fair few of them and I have limited experience of them right now but crafting itself isn't just sit there and wait for things to appear. There's an active process and is fairly enjoyable. Just like the combat classes, new skills are unlocked and it becomes a sort of strategic minigame. Quick synthesis for bulk items is available as well so you don't have to do it for each item.
Still I can see crafting becoming tedious. repetitive and boring at some point but that's no different from any other mmo. Also, unlike the combat classes, the crafting classes aren't really unique.
The combat system is targetted, which honestly I was sceptical about when first going in as I'm not a big fan of targetted combat but it grows on you. This is mostly to do with how the game feels since you really have to think about movement, positioning, skill orders, skill timing etc. from more or less the beginning of the game. This is a big deal and playing the first 20 or so levels in WoW feels boring and just mashing buttons in a certain order. The 2.5sec global cooldown adds to the strategic element of it too. You have more time to think and decide what move would be appropriate, but you also have a longer window to be punished for choosing the wrong skill. I honestly think this is way more fun and interesting compared to other games with a much smaller global cooldown.
Another important point is that this game is very controller friendly. It's on the PS3/PS4 with cross platform support so that would be why. I personally play with a controller and it feels very smooth. I don't feel too overwhelmed with skills and I've unlocked all of them for my job with 3 cross skills in use as well (I have 2 full hotbars but it's very easy to switch between them). It's down to preference in the end but the option is really nice to have.
There are so many different ways to level it's crazy. Though the main story quest is compulsory, there are loads of side quests available.
If you think quests are repetitive you can switch over to doing FATES which are events that spawn that give gil (money) and experience to everyone that completes them based on the level of participation.
If that's boring there are many different dungeons to do with solid exp gain on all of them. Duty roullete will give you bonus exp once a day so deffo worth doing that.
No? Then you can do levequests which are contracts to do certain things in certain places which you can get by using one of your levequest allowances (which refill regularly). Levequests are available to crafting classes too and are considered the fastest ways to level them.
Still not enough? Then Guildhests might be for you. These are very similar to levequests but you're put into a duty (instance) with a party and asked to do it as a group. There's a daily bonus on guildhest roullete as well so that's good.
Also, the first time you do a certain dungeon, levequest or guildhest you'll be granted bonus exp which is always a definite plus.
Still too slow? Not enough content? Too repetitive? Well if you're that hard to please then I guess I should tell you that there are these things called logs which grant bonus exp for doing certain things. A hunting log will ask you to kill x number of y, while a crafting log will give you the list of everything you can craft. The king of all these is the challenge log which refreshes weekly and gives you a lot of exp for completing tasks like "complete 3 dungeons" or "complete 5 levequests".
Honestly there are so many different ways to level that players can pick something that suits them and though some can get repetitive they're fun for the most part.
You only need to google the game to see the amount of post lv50 content. The game's been out for about a year and there are things constantly being added. The first expansion is coming out soon so keep an eye out for that. Most people will tell you that lv50 is just the beginning, and they're probably right. I'm only just getting into the endgame and I look forward to everything coming up.
Well. This is the one major downside I see to the game. It's very expensive. Though nothing new for an mmo, it is a pretty heavy financial commitment compared to most other steam games out there. Especially considering you can get Tera, Mabinogi, and loads of other mmos for free now. You can buy gametime online from other sellers for a bit cheaper but it's still expensive. I suggest playing the trial to give you a better understanding of whether you'll enjoy it. I highly suggest it and will be playing it, but I can appreciate that a few years ago I could never afford to play a game like this.
I honestly think this is the first mmo to seriously impress me with its ability to keep you interested. It doesn't overwhelm you, nor does it leave you with nothing to do. Bosses are often really cool and have interesting mechanics, even from an early point in the game. I really do feel that besides the price this game is practically perfect. It's a great game - buy it if you can.

This is probably the most poorly designed MMO I've played in years from a gameplay perspective. Lag is literally built into the combat system. Invisible walls are absolutely everywhere, there is an entire city of pirates, surrounded by ships and water, yet there is no swimming. You won't be on too many boats either.
That being said, the game is quite fun and addictive, the atmosphere is great, and the story isn't too bad. Do be prepared to do an inane amount of fetch and deliver quests, however (and the bulk of these will come from your "primary" quest line that advances the main story of the game). You will cross continents to fix jewelry, or gather ingredients for soup or perfume. There is teleportation, however, so it's not as bad as it could be. Be aware that this never ends. You'll still be doing trivial chores well beyond the level cap.
Aside from the continuation of quests at cap, the game does become a bit of a dungeon simulator, but this isn't all bad. The best thing about this game is a very strong sense of progression. There is always something to do, always something you can level, and the community isn't too bad. I haven't touched the PVP, but I've heard nothing good about it. There are PVP exclusive abilities as well. Really, just the combat lag is enough to make me stay away from it.
Overall, I'd recommend the game. It's fun for what it is if you can ignore the glaring flaws. However, unless you've tried everything else MMOs have to offer, or you just really like Final Fantasy as a franchise, you could probably do better.

Don't let my small game time dissuade you taking my review seriously, I have been playing since 1.0 and most of my logged hours are with the beta client which was patched to the retail client.
Anyway not really a review, but this is hands-down the best subscription MMORPG currently on the market. It may feel strange to those who aren't familiar with the Final Fantasy franchise, but to those who are (or are familiar with the original version of FFXIV) this game is now a huge success, and it's not hard to see why.
By adopting common traits found in modern MMORPGs, yet dousing it in Final Fantasy flavour, A Realm Reborn feels like an MMORPG while still feeling like a Final Fantasy game.
Square Enix are committed to continually updating the game as well, with loaded content patches being released every three months since launch. I hope they continue this trend.
Just be wary, you may not enjoy or appreciate the first 30 or so levels, but when you upgrade your class to a fully fledged job and can change jobs whenever you want (providing you are out of combat) and more importantly, when you experience the incredible amount of content that the endgame provides, you will realise that FFXIV is finally reaching the potential we all had hoped for.
I can't wait for the first expansion this Spring.

Some games focus on the action, others focus on the tactical aspects, others the story - this game happens to do all the above. Transistor is a great example of a game that doesn't have to sacrifice actual gameplay to be art. Transistor was a bit of a pleasant surprise for me, I bought the game on sale and had only seens a few headlines stating that it was an amazing game - and it is. In all aspects it is.
The combat is interesting and diverse - the ability to freeze time to plan out your attacks in a semi-turn-based style whilst sacrificing a few seconds of vulnerability afterwards was very unique. The ability to increase the game's difficulty based on optional in-game options in exchange for more exp points was also a very nice tough. There were points where the game had gotten too difficult until I tried around 3 times, swapping my abilities and passive perks around to find the best combination but otherwise - the game was just difficult enough to be enjoyable.
The stoy however, takes the highlight. Rarely does a game make you feel for the characters, what makse this game interesting is that its entire story is almost told by a single male voice - no cinematics or animations, just a voice that speaks to the player's avatar Red. The amount of emotion conveyed was impressive and I enjoyed this game's story immensely due to it.

Transistor is an ActionRPG from Supergiant Games, the same company behind the critically acclaimed Bastion. I never played Bastion so I went in blindly and I've not been disappointed.
The story is interesting, starting from scratch with few clues and evolving gradually during the playthrough. It's very linear but checking the environment as well and other functions will give you more elements to piece the whole thing together. Never predictable, will make you think and feel.
Even though this game is classed as an "ActionRPG" there's no actual need for fast reflexes as most of the battles will most likely happen in a turn() based environment. The player is gradually given new skills (from now referred as functions) and what makes the difference is the way they're used. You can have a primary function which will be an active skill, or can choose to use said function to support another function, increasing a specific characteristic. Functions can also be used as passives to give determined bonuses. This clever system allows for vast customization possibilities that will eventually fit most people playstyle.
The music is absolutely great. Whether in battle or just walking around, the sound will create the right mood, while the songs with voice make for fantastic cutscenes. The voice acting is also really good and well balanced. All the tracks will be unlockable in game by completing certain challenges.
- A high quality game under all aspects (story, gameplay, music) that was entertaining and fun to play from the beginning to the end. Definitely worth it's price.
+ good story
+ clever function system allowing many customization options to fit any playstyle
+ great music: the background tracks are good, the singed ones are amazing
+ great voice acting really helps definining characters personalities
+ smart challenge system that will help the user discover some interesting function combos
+ smooth difficulty ramp where the player can choose to add Limiters to increase the difficulty to it's own liking
+ achievable achievements. They require effort but unlike other games they're doable without spending 100s of hours
+ some replayability
- sometimes the tooltip during fights isn't accurate as it doesn't take into account knockups, cast speed and such
- can't skip cutscenes and most dialogues

So much doesn't make sense about this game that I don't even know where to begin. Granted, some of the scripting is rather colorful and quite morbid at times and some of the environments are ominous, but all that aside the plot essentially cannibalizes itself and ends up not making a lot of sense in the end.  So some guy saw some stuff in Mexico about humanity and the human condition in the present (1899 and thereabouts) and how cultures from the past apparently had the right idea with sacrifices and whatnot, and so this all gets him thinking that we are all just pigs...um....and that he needs to make a machine that turns us (I likely don't have this right, but after playing this you'd understand why) into manpigs - that doesn't give him the right to do the things that he did do and will do and does do...um...while you're(he) is playing through the game while trying to find his two sons (that he apparently loves though they were kept up in the attic).
Anyhoo, the beginning in the house is probably the best part as it's so ominous and is vaguely reminiscent of the glory that was The Dark Descent (and that was throughout its entirety).  Sadly, that is one thing this game is not - an Amnesia game.  As a follow up game to TDD, AMFP is utterly pointless and shouldn't even have 'Amnesis' in its title. I went into Machine for Pigs (MfP) with a bit of static in my ears.  My friends who had played the game gave me a very mixed feel on the game, plenty of negative to go with the positive, so I went in with somewhat lowered expectations.  I played Dark Descent years ago, and the Penumbra trilogy more recently, and right out of the gate it was obvious that though this game shared the Amnesia moniker, it was not a Frictional endeavour.
The only Chinese Room game I've played before was Dear Esther, and as much flak as that game receives I found enjoyment in the atmosphere the developers were able to build into such a short experience.  MfP helps the developers carry on that trend, but it gives them much more breathing room.  The extended length (~4-7 hours depending on your hurry) plays to the developers' favor and shows they can make a full length experience with a beginning, middle, and end.  The world MfP builds for the player is as much a social commentary on recent human history as it is a spooky romp through underground, industrial revolution England with tons of pig-based imagery.  While the ties to Dark Descent are minimal and fleeting, MfP manages to stand on its own as a new narrative in a new setting with new characters and still be captivating.  However, if you don't listen closely to the various notes and conversations scattered throughout the campaign, things can get a little confusing.  Even after beating the game I found myself googling portions of the plot to get a better understanding of what had just happened.
The main complaint I see/hear for MfP is that the horror pales in comparison to Dark Descent and I'm inclined to agree.  While Dark Descent terrified me from beginning to end, MfP suffers from the same issues as the Slender series in that after a certain point, prolonged exposure to the intiially "mysterious" creepies haunting you makes them significantly less mysterious, and minimizes their ability to inspire terror in the player.  However, I don't feel like it was Chinese Room's intent for the monsters to be the source of horror the whole way through the game.  Without going into plot spoilers, the narrative makes it a point to expose the monsters to the player to help make sense of the plot, and the horror stops being this abstract thing going bump in the night to an internal sense of fear and anxiety over the actions of the player.
With that last statement in mind, I can totally agree with the Bioshock comparisons.  MfP is every bit as deep as Bioshock Infinite, without the paradoxical nature of the protagonist running around gunning down hundreds of NPC's for the sake of AAA gun-play mechanics.
So if you're interested in an Irrational-style mind-trip, MfP is the game for you.  Just don't go in expecting to be scared out of your wits the whole way through.

text: Machine for Pigs is a fun and worthy successor to 2010's horror classic. It has some obvious problems, mostly to do with the linearity and lack of puzzles. Perhaps this was a choice by The Chinese Room, who made the snorefest "Dear Escher." On the other hand, it's not like the puzzles in Dark Descent were actually GOOD. So, if you're after the same thing I'm after--impeccable set design full of dark winding passages and horrifying creatures lurking just out of sight--you'll be pleased once again. In fact, this game has something that Dark Descent was lacking: a truly striking and effective story. It makes a surprisingly big difference, I found, grounding the protagonist's goals in a search for his missing children. And once you discover the true nature of the evil lurking in the tunnels under London, it will give you a lot more to think about than the rituals of Alexander ever did in Dark Descent.

To be honest I feel like this game is marketed at children who enjoy poop jokes, despite the fact that in Australia it has an 18+ rating and the game sports dismemberment. The characters are all hatable, their dialogue is repetitive, gun fights are repetitive, everything is repetitive. Run or drive to the marker, shoot up these guys, loot every case for a few dollars and some ammo and maybe a decent gun. Upgrade some stats so you can get 0.7% more health and 1.5% more damage if your life is <25%. Some bits of the game are interesting like the weapons that are actually unique but that's mostly it.
If you are seriously that interested in buying Borderlands, get the "Pre-Sequel" which is not only newer, it's actually better optimised. Just know that it's essentially again, the same thing as Borderlands and Borderlands 2. Same art style, same story, slightly different heroes, generally same weapons and slightly different game mechanics/perks. Just all packaged into another full priced title. I really am surprised how many people enjoy this series, so much that they are actually willing to basically buy the same game three times.
Inevitably this one is going to rot away in my Steam library for years to come. What a shame...

I'm so very conflicted about this game. Like many, I came in expecting a proper follow-up to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. That game set some extraordinarily high expectations, none of which are fulfilled in this sequel. Where the first game provided an ample amount of terror thru the use of clever level design, interesting puzzle-solving and a haunting atmosphere, A Machine For Pigs decides to ditch everything but the atmosphere. You won't find any difficult puzzles in AMfP; in fact, I can only think of one time where I barely had to use my brain to progress thru the narrative. The rest of the story is largely an on-rails narrative, in the realm of an interactive novel rather than a video game. Having played The Chinese Room's Gone Home, I had a feeling that the follow-up to Amnesia: The Dark Descent would be more focused on story-telling. I had no idea how strictly that model would come to define the folow-up to one of video gaming's greatest horror tales. A Machine For Pigs is a beautiful narrative, enanced by moody lighting and an emotionally stirring soundtrack. Though I was very dissapointed to find that many features from the first game were removed - namely, the sanity meter and the necessity to manage resources - I still found this game enjoyable and satisyfing. My best advice for enjoying this game is to understand that this is NOT a sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent in any stretch of the imagination. It is a stand-alone narrative featuring entirely new characters and a new setting. The gameplay mechanics are severely lscking, even compared to the minimal interaction compared to the first game, However if you are looking to try something different, and enjoy a good horror story, then A Machine for Pigs is worth your time and money. Just not $20 of it.

I can easily say Call of Juarez® Gunslinger was a fantastic experience that was well worth my time.
The fastest way I can prove this is that I bothered to 100% complete it (which requires 2 playthroughs and beating Arcade AND the Duel Mode). It took me 17 hours and I am ok with that. It was fun, I enjoyed myself the entire time.
Gunslinger has amazing combat, and while the weapon selections are limited (that actually isnt a bad thing) the game makes perfect use of them. I constantly swapped favorites and guns I initially thought "oh these are trash, why would anyone use these?" later turned into "Dang, this gun is game breakingly unfair and awesome." This happened repeatedly and now after everything I honestly think they are all awesome. They all have thier place and their uses.
You have your standard Revolvers (one for damage, one for speed, and one all around-er), your rifle (long range battle necessity) and your Shotguns (one Saw'd off and one double barrel shotgun). All one handed weapons can be upgraded to be dual wielded (which makes them less accurate but lets you pump out more bullets)
Oh also you get the ability to slow down time and do awesome stuff like shoot dynamite out of the sky after it has been thrown by either you or your enemies.
Gunslinger has an awesome Perk / Upgrade system that matches its extremely fun gameplay and further augments it to be even better. Upgrades come in 3 trees:
One for long range (mostly rifle upgrades)
One for Short range (mostly shotgun upgrades)
One for Pistols or Akimbo setup (mostly pistol based)
You can unlock perks ranging from reload 50% faster to just helping you find secrets. They all help and it is amazing when you unlock all of them together in New Game+
It is a well thought out upgrade system where upgrade paths branch off and merge together. Its a little hard to explain in words though.
The controls were great and everything is responsive. I know some people complained in the forums about mouse controls for the Duel System but I played with an Xbox 360 controller and I had no problems with anything in the game. (I'd recommend this style of play to anyone)
The story mode was fantastic. Amazing voice actors tell an incredibly interactive story. The events happen in the past and sometimes the narrator (your character Silas Greaves) forgets details or messes with his audience by putting in crazy details like you getting ambushed by 100 indians in the middle of a gunfight. Its really neat how the game merges the story telling aspects with the actual gameplay. Cutscenes are told in a comic book style but it really works for this game. The art is great and almost all of the characters are real people who lived and died during similar circumstances. This also goes for locations in the game. The game plays with history through the eyes of a drunk old man telling a story but these events are based on truth.
Speaking of truth the game contains Nuggets of Truth (that's seriously what they call them) when you collect them, they give you some honest historical information about the real people and locations the game contains. It is extremely interesting and may be the reason I first decided to actually 100% the entire game.
The 2 non story modes (Arcade and Duel Mode) are pretty cool too.
Duel Mode is simple, beat 15 gunslingers (all story mode bosses) in a pistol duel. The story mode already contains plenty of these so the concept isnt anything special but it is still really fun because of how well the duel system is done. It really has a real sense of tension as you closely analyze your opponents movement and hand position while struggling to control your own hand position and focus percentage.
Arcade Mode is a little frustating at first, especially coming from New Game+ on Story Mode. Mostly because Arcade mode makes you reunlock perks. Its not that bad, but it still upset me at the time.
Basically in Arcade mode you get a small section of a level from Story mode to run around in killing as many enemies as fast as you possibly can. The higher your combo the more points you get, and points get you gold stars. Get 3 gold stars on every challenge for an achievement. Its basically a score attack mode with preset perks instead of letting you be overpowered with every perk all at once (like in story mode)
Seriously, this game is great. I highly recommend it if you are looking for a FPS with some great story telling elements and incredibly fun gameplay.

I've never been an MMO player. Briefly played Tera - liked it but found progression slow - and briefly WoW - disliked the combat, just felt like button mashing. I also played Mabinogi for a short while and really disliked the game's mechanics. One day I felt the urge to play one and I knew a friend was planning to start this so I bought it but neither of us started. 9 days ago a friend of mine was looking for people who wanted to start and I decided that if it was in my steam list I may as well try it out. I am now 95.9 hours in according to steam and I love it. I've just hit level 50 and got my Paladin armour and I'm still looking at all the content coming up. As I speak server is going down to patch even more content into the game. So here's the detailed review:
The story is a good one as far as MMOs go (based on my limited experience). I'd equate it to WoW in some ways as FFXIV builds off of an already established lore but is still extremely easy for new players to get into. I don't want to say much about it but Square Enix really put work into making a good story. It teeters a bit at times, especially around the middle (lv30-40 is a bit slow) but it's very enjoyable if you get into it.
Combat classes are fairly traditional: tank, support, ranged DPS and melee DPS. Still within these wider definitions, each individual class is fairly unique. To add to this you are not restricted to the classes that you pick at the beginning of the game. You will unlock the ability to train any and all classses as you wish which allows for a lot of flexibility. But "Oh, the grind ¬¬" you say. Nope, all classes trained beyond the first receive exp gain bonuses which really speeds up the process. This is alongside the quick levelling options which I'll discuss in a later section.
There's more though! All combat classses have a progression called a "Job" which is earned by reaching a certain point in the story, getting a class to lv30 and the corresponding second class to lv15, and then finishing the job quest. It's actually really easy to do and it encourages you to try a different role.
All combat classes are unique and don't overlap much at all which is great.
As for crafting classes, there's a fair few of them and I have limited experience of them right now but crafting itself isn't just sit there and wait for things to appear. There's an active process and is fairly enjoyable. Just like the combat classes, new skills are unlocked and it becomes a sort of strategic minigame. Quick synthesis for bulk items is available as well so you don't have to do it for each item.
Still I can see crafting becoming tedious. repetitive and boring at some point but that's no different from any other mmo. Also, unlike the combat classes, the crafting classes aren't really unique.
The combat system is targetted, which honestly I was sceptical about when first going in as I'm not a big fan of targetted combat but it grows on you. This is mostly to do with how the game feels since you really have to think about movement, positioning, skill orders, skill timing etc. from more or less the beginning of the game. This is a big deal and playing the first 20 or so levels in WoW feels boring and just mashing buttons in a certain order. The 2.5sec global cooldown adds to the strategic element of it too. You have more time to think and decide what move would be appropriate, but you also have a longer window to be punished for choosing the wrong skill. I honestly think this is way more fun and interesting compared to other games with a much smaller global cooldown.
Another important point is that this game is very controller friendly. It's on the PS3/PS4 with cross platform support so that would be why. I personally play with a controller and it feels very smooth. I don't feel too overwhelmed with skills and I've unlocked all of them for my job with 3 cross skills in use as well (I have 2 full hotbars but it's very easy to switch between them). It's down to preference in the end but the option is really nice to have.
There are so many different ways to level it's crazy. Though the main story quest is compulsory, there are loads of side quests available.
If you think quests are repetitive you can switch over to doing FATES which are events that spawn that give gil (money) and experience to everyone that completes them based on the level of participation.
If that's boring there are many different dungeons to do with solid exp gain on all of them. Duty roullete will give you bonus exp once a day so deffo worth doing that.
No? Then you can do levequests which are contracts to do certain things in certain places which you can get by using one of your levequest allowances (which refill regularly). Levequests are available to crafting classes too and are considered the fastest ways to level them.
Still not enough? Then Guildhests might be for you. These are very similar to levequests but you're put into a duty (instance) with a party and asked to do it as a group. There's a daily bonus on guildhest roullete as well so that's good.
Also, the first time you do a certain dungeon, levequest or guildhest you'll be granted bonus exp which is always a definite plus.
Still too slow? Not enough content? Too repetitive? Well if you're that hard to please then I guess I should tell you that there are these things called logs which grant bonus exp for doing certain things. A hunting log will ask you to kill x number of y, while a crafting log will give you the list of everything you can craft. The king of all these is the challenge log which refreshes weekly and gives you a lot of exp for completing tasks like "complete 3 dungeons" or "complete 5 levequests".
Honestly there are so many different ways to level that players can pick something that suits them and though some can get repetitive they're fun for the most part.
You only need to google the game to see the amount of post lv50 content. The game's been out for about a year and there are things constantly being added. The first expansion is coming out soon so keep an eye out for that. Most people will tell you that lv50 is just the beginning, and they're probably right. I'm only just getting into the endgame and I look forward to everything coming up.

This is probably the most poorly designed MMO I've played in years from a gameplay perspective. Lag is literally built into the combat system. Invisible walls are absolutely everywhere, there is an entire city of pirates, surrounded by ships and water, yet there is no swimming. You won't be on too many boats either.
That being said, the game is quite fun and addictive, the atmosphere is great, and the story isn't too bad. Do be prepared to do an inane amount of fetch and deliver quests, however (and the bulk of these will come from your "primary" quest line that advances the main story of the game). You will cross continents to fix jewelry, or gather ingredients for soup or perfume. There is teleportation, however, so it's not as bad as it could be. Be aware that this never ends. You'll still be doing trivial chores well beyond the level cap.
Aside from the continuation of quests at cap, the game does become a bit of a dungeon simulator, but this isn't all bad. The best thing about this game is a very strong sense of progression. There is always something to do, always something you can level, and the community isn't too bad. I haven't touched the PVP, but I've heard nothing good about it. There are PVP exclusive abilities as well. Really, just the combat lag is enough to make me stay away from it.
Overall, I'd recommend the game. It's fun for what it is if you can ignore the glaring flaws. However, unless you've tried everything else MMOs have to offer, or you just really like Final Fantasy as a franchise, you could probably do better.

Don't let my small game time dissuade you taking my review seriously, I have been playing since 1.0 and most of my logged hours are with the beta client which was patched to the retail client.
Anyway not really a review, but this is hands-down the best subscription MMORPG currently on the market. It may feel strange to those who aren't familiar with the Final Fantasy franchise, but to those who are (or are familiar with the original version of FFXIV) this game is now a huge success, and it's not hard to see why.
By adopting common traits found in modern MMORPGs, yet dousing it in Final Fantasy flavour, A Realm Reborn feels like an MMORPG while still feeling like a Final Fantasy game.
Square Enix are committed to continually updating the game as well, with loaded content patches being released every three months since launch. I hope they continue this trend.
Just be wary, you may not enjoy or appreciate the first 30 or so levels, but when you upgrade your class to a fully fledged job and can change jobs whenever you want (providing you are out of combat) and more importantly, when you experience the incredible amount of content that the endgame provides, you will realise that FFXIV is finally reaching the potential we all had hoped for.
I can't wait for the first expansion this Spring.
