This was my first survival game and before saying what is good and bad, let me say why i chose this survival game over any others out there as my first:
I really like the medieval setting so that was a huge plus for me, i really like that there are no guns, that was a big plus for me, and the building mechanics give you complete freedom, you can build any base in any way you want, because you use individual blocks to build it. So that really seperated it from the rest for me, and there were Trebuchets and Ballistas and medieval weapons and torture devices. It also has a King mechanic whereby whoever is King can tax you, so people can go to war with the King to eliminate the Tax and potentially place their own Tax and takeover the Crown for themselves. I thought all these mechanics sounded like fun to try.
Pros:
- Playing in medieval setting with melee weapons such as longswords, axes and shields, and Spears, Bows and Crossbows are just plain fun among many other medieval weapons
-Collecting resources and building stuff and developing your base so that you never have to worry about water and food again and protection from wandering raiders and criminals is a very satisfying accomplishment.
-Maps are good, the larger map could use more features as it is very open, i guess they intended for the server to fill up and be busier with many bases.  The small map is great however, good balance of spacing for bases and map features like trees, resources, water, hills etc..
-Cutting down a tree never felt so good in a game, it is really surprising how enjoyable the atmosphere of the game can be at times for what it is.
-When you first raid someone successfully it is an amazing feeling, and you may actually become drawn into that and want to do it all the time. It kind of happened to me.
-Building your base in this game is very satisfying, you can plan out and design and build just about anything your imagination can conceive.
-King and tax system ads a new dimension to the game, that you may partake in or not
-Freedom to run around and create your own missions and goals, ability to strategise and play politics if you like that. You have the freedom to role play anything in this game, i have been a villain i have been a good guy i have been King i have been a Prison Warden, I have been a Butcher, a Farmer, some people have taken up Fishing, so there is much to try. You can be a warmonger or you can make friends with everyone, it is all up to you.
-You can benefit greatly from making friends in the game, but you can just as easily be incredibly successful playing alone and turtleing up. Both offer its challenges.
-Sense of accomplishment in this game is very high, and because you set your own goals it makes it that much more satisfying.
-You can be a nice guy or bad guy, it is up to you, people will be bad or good to you also completely at their discretion, while this can be a negative in some cases, there are servers where they don't allow killing on sight, so new players can ease their way into the game. If you don't want to be decapitated or imprisoned or hung or whipped or tortured, you may want to try the community servers first. Great that this option is out there.
-the game has levels of building blocks and weapons, so different materials provide different benefits as you collect resources to develop your base, equipment and unlock new things to build as you progress. So you can become more powerful as you play more and more.
- There are ways for you to change your apperance so you can change your identity in the game at any point if you collect the ingredients
-Ability to mute and block communications from annoying trolls, this was a great feature for dealing with those pesky people. It wasn't introduced until later, but its in there now, so its a pro
-Sieging a base with ballistas and Trebuchets, this is really when you know you have made it to the end game, when you are engaging in Trebuchet warefare, the game takes on a whole new level of fun
-Hand to Hand combat, it may not be highly refined, but its quite good for what it is, you can block, you can fake, you can do different kinds of swing attacks, it is absolutely great for a Melee fighting game, not too easy and not too hard.
Cons:
- Not enough Player vs Environment content, this is a real disapointment, there are some wolves, werewolves and bears on the maps but that really doesn't statisfy your hunger for more pve content.
-Really needs a secure trading system like other games, but like in life this game is ruthless, if you trust someone you do so at your own risk, they may betray you at any second if they want to. This is kind of good, but it can be devastating to new players who are tricked by experienced players.
-No horses, that would really have made this game so much better, especially if you had to feed them and water them and shelter them and keep them alive. Maybe even breeding.
-Farming system is poorly thought out and is pretty much irrelevant other than for the sake of saying you did it. They could have made professions and added value to it, by including trade routes and things of that nature to ad depth to the game
-Time commitment, you really won't get far or get much accomplished in this game unless you can put in a decent amount of time, so new players don't last long and there aren't as many people playing the game as you would want.
-Server wipes were kind of a problem when you were half way through a project and weren't able to finish it, but at the same time they were necessary, but because i kind of never finished some projects for me it was a negative since everytime i was working on a project it was pulled down and i had to start again, and after so many it becomes tiresome. Although when you do accomplish all your goals in a server, sometimes it is nice to start again.
-The game really required the community servers to give it more playability and the ping caps to prevent people and groups who would build in the kings throne and lock it up so well that it became impossible to penetrate. Although i did once break through with another person and that was very satisfying, the challenge was astronomical and only really possible because they went offline because of a pending wipe.
-Some initial bugs and gamebreaking glitches really hurt the game early on. Those are all cleaned out now, but the damage was done, many people left because people were able to break into their bases with glitches and they didn't know how to counter it, even though there were ways to build around it, many people didn't understand how it worked or how to deal with it. So the game really needs a re release to hopefully be played more as it does deserve it.
Bottom Line:
Great game with great potential that just fell short, hope someone takes this games concept and what it did and takes it to the next level, i would certainly be interested to play that game. The freedom a game like this provides is truly gratifying and even now i prefer a game that has such freedoms than a game that is linear and forces you to play down a path

Factorio is amazing.
The most similar things I can think of are certain varieties of modded Minecraft, and Factorio is better than them in almost every possible way.
Graphics: Not particularly high quality, but with the amount of bits and bobs that end up floating around, you can't really have super fancy graphics without hurting FPS.
Speaking of FPS, Factorio manages to simulate the MASSIVE machines, items, and other entities any decent factory will have without suffering any noticable lag whatsoever. It's an amazing feat of programming, and it greatly improves the quality of the game.
Sound: As with most sandbox games, I consider Factorio's BGM to be appropriate. Not particularly good, not bad, but fitting. I still usually choose to listen to other things while I play, but something is playing enough of the time that someone who requires auditory stimulation (like me) will probably be satisfied. The sound effects are similar: acceptable quality, and appropriate for the game.
Gameplay:

Pros:
-Factorio is a sandbox game based around automation. Most such games (in my experience) have less building complex systems and more waiting for resources. Factorio manages to mostly avoid this pitfall through careful balancing, meaning that you have to spend less time waiting, and can spend more time making and fixing things (which is the fun part of the game).
-Very active modding community. The large amount of mods available adds a lot of replay value, and the community shows no signs that they're stopping any time soon. It also help that you can install the mods easily by pressing some buttons in game, rather than having to fiddle with files manually.
-Active Developers that care. As is, Factorio could easily be released as a full game, but the Devs continue to add to it and improve it. Weekly rundowns of what they're working on let users be involved in the development process. The best part? Like the modding community, the devs show no sign of slowing down any time soon.
-MULTIPLAYER. While it's still not 100% optimized, you can play online with your friends. I've yet to try it myself (all of my friends that own Factorio have gotten bored of it somehow), but games like this are better played with friends. Just having the option is a plus.
Cons:
-Addictive. The vast majority of other reviews mention this, AND IT'S TRUE. Factorio progression requires you to set up large systems to produce and process various goods. As soon as you finish one project, there'll be another one ready for you. It's fun, and it draws you in.
If you have trouble remembering to do things like eat, drink water, sleep, go to the bathroom, go outside, etc. when gaming, it might be a good idea to stay away from Factorio until you figure out a solution to your problem.
Overall:
Great gameplay and a decent amount of replay value make this game one of the best games on Steam.
Don't forget to take breaks!

Transistor took me a little while to get into, but after the initial adjustment period, I became fully engaged. The aesthetics are absolutely stunning, from the particles and intricate details on every single attack to the vibrant colors and multitude of moving parts in the environment. The audio in the game is also top notch, with filters and effects (slowing down speech when entering a new Turn()) are used perfectly to enhance the gameplay. The soundtrack is also pretty amazing, but if you've heard of Bastion you should already know that.
The biggest draw in terms of gameplay is the ability to mix powers. Before I played that game, I thought the biggest novel mechanic was the Turn (the ability to stop time and plan out attacks), but I didn't really find myself using it all the much on my first playthrough. The mixing of powers is what I found most engaging. I spent hours drilling down to the set that most optimally fit my playstyle.
The story of the game is kept to a minimum on purpose, from what I can tell. A lot more emphasis is put on building an interesting world. The player is given little clues as to what the world was like before and why the events of the game are happening if they choose to read into it more. Otherwise, a player could just as easily skip all of the story and world building and still fully enjoy the game.
The one thing I found lacking in the game was the enemy variety. There aren't that many enemy types and the game reuses them frequently by upgrading their abilities to make the harder. This makes sense based on the fact that they are indie and chose to put their efforst into other parts of the game. It's not really a huge issue and finding different ways to beat the enemies using your mixed powers will keep you engaged all the way through to the end.
Speaking of which, the ending to the game is ABSOLUTELY INCREDIBLE! Whatever you do, finish the game! The final boss is one of the best final bosses I have seen in a video game to date! Even if the rest of the game were terrible, I would still recommend it just for that boss fight.
With great audio, visuals, world building and gameplay, there isn't really much else to ask for. Just go buy it!

Transistor, in my most honest opinion, is an incredible example of games as art. The combination of beautifully well-crafted landscape, architecture, color choice, music, storytelling and atmosphere come together to create this beautiful game. It's relatively cheap, it's not a long game, and it runs on a lot of setups, so there's not a laundry list of excuses not to play.
The combat, which is relatively its least interesting facet (in comparison to the rest of the game), has a lot of interesting experimentation to be done and allows for some interesting gameplay choices. Be aware, though, it is hardly a hack 'n slash like Bastion (Supergiant Games' previous game). It is more in line with a bizarre mix of 3d tactical combat with a mix of some 3rd person action elements. I'm sure some other reviews do a much better job of explaining the system and its quirks.
All in all, if you have any interest or stock in the idea of games as art, play this game. If you just want something interesting, I'd also tell you to play this game. If you want to play as a cute redhead with a talking sword that looks like a giant usb drive--oh hey, play this game.

TBH I am a little dissapointed. I bought this game cheap-as-chips on sale and so it wasn't the gushing user reviews that encouraged me to buy, however I do believe that they mislead me as to the quality of the game.
Let me start by saying that the game is not awful... that being said I found the story incredibly short and oh so predictable and the gameplay itself very linear and repititive and I in fact much preferred COJ: Bound in Blood.
I will say this the shooting can be quite enjoyable at times especially with the steam controller but the story constantly telling you what's going to happen or what didn't happen gets old really quickly. I personally am not a fan of the controller response on the duels and I lamented the loss of the bow and arrow/ throwing knives (from the previous installment) particularly the ability to make quiet kills. In this game instead you end up finding that you cannot approach the enemies in creative ways you best job is to treat it like a platformer and run in guns blazing because the enemy will only appear when you get close to them.
I found the cartoony atmosphere after a while detaches you from being absorbed into the gameplay especially combined with the constant narration. The story itself was very short I tried to be patient with the story telling but all in all you won't end up spending longer than 10 hours in the game.
Maybe I have been spoilt by the plethora of open world and sandbox games but the feeling of hand-holding I got throughout this title was infuriating to say the least. It's not to say I can't appreciate fixed level design as many other games get it spot-on but when you know you are simply going to face a stream of dull NPC baddies before repeating it over and over again the motivation to accept the direction of the level design becomes tiresome.
All in all... I am left to conclude that this game is essentially a shooting version of a walking simulator that took a healthy step backwards from the previous installment. Whilst the developers made a bold decision in their choice of colours and theme and method of revealing the story It feels like an exercise meant to attract acclaim rather than please the gamers who parted with their hard-earned money.
My answer is No to recommending the game at full price, buy it for a quid it will be over faster than two shakes of a sheeps tail and you will feel no better or wose at the end.

A good game in it's own right, Final Fantasy XIV is definitely a game worth playing. It has an intriguing story and lore, as well as a variety of classes to choose from, plus you can try them all with one character. And there is definitely plenty of content to enjoy, including with character customisation.
It does play like most tab target MMORPGs would, but there is a sense of strategy with the use of abilities, and good research and experimentation can lead to some fun times figuring out the best ways to play.

Honestly, if you're a fan of MMOs, definitely worth picking up.

Should you play FF14ARR? and more importantly, does it, in it's durrent state justify its sub fee.
First off, this is not the same FF14 that launch and crashed and burned so hard it practically legendary. Square rebuilt the game and pretty much fixed all the problems with it, and made one of the best MMO's I've played in a LONG time. But thats just how I feel. Your mileage will very most likely.
And hopefully they learned a leason about hubris as well.
Lets start with the visuals, as well as the look and feel of your character and Eorzea it self .Since its the first thing you will notice.
Square has, well ... been 'Square' in terms of the games graphical fidelity, of all the complaints you can level at Square skimping on graphics isn't one of them, and this game looks fantasic as a result. But in MMOs great looks rarely, if ever mean anything if theres nothing worth looking at. The citys, dungeons and out lieing areas around the main hub towns all look and feel, 'right', and coupled with the writing I'll get to in a bit, feels like a living breathing world of its own. The Animations look and as the apply to combat, feel good, hitting something feels good even at low levels. and the cutscenes bare special mention for the little details they added in terms of facial animations, animation your character uses them selves, and for me, watching my character visable react in an apropreate way to what was going on made me feel more attatched to my character. Even if they don't actually talk.
Writing wise, it is probably the best Final Fantasy in a LONG time, I'm not gonna take about the story, cause, spoilers, but I will say they worked the take down and rebuild of the game into the games lore in the form of 'The Calamity' which I thought was nice. The tone of the game is farly consistant as well through out the main quest line as well. The side quests on the other hand ... yeah ... just be aware Eorzea has some strange people living in it. From the side quest to unlock the character editor (lets you change your hair, hair color, tattoos/face paint) to ... Hildibrand ... (you really just need to expiriance the 'WTF ...' to understand it) the side quests can offer a break from the main quests some times heavy tone, and in a stroke of brilliance. The main quests, don't end at the current level cap of 50. The pace slows down a bit, but the story keeps going and theres still LOTS to do in the end game besides just run dungeons and Primals and grind gear.
Mechinicly, combat is not much to write home about sadly. Save a few things I think are worth of note. First of all. 'Skill shots' are a thing. Enemys of all stripes have one or two moves that leave a brightish orange shape (a cone, circle, or rectangle) on the ground/floor. this is a less then subtle hint to not stand there, and when you start getting closer to and into the end game, it starts getting more and more important to avoid them, this, coupled with 'possitioning' for some classes being important to maximize damage, it makes the battles feel much more fast paced and involved then the 'tab target' combat would allude to.
The other mechanic worthy of note is the Armory system. I ♥♥♥♥ing love this thing. In the simplest terms it allows you to switch classes (save a few situations like in the middle of a dungeon or raid or something of the like)  pretty much when ever you want. Tired of playing a tank? switch to DPS. Party good on Deeps but they need Epic heals? You can do that. All with the ease of equiping the weapon that class uses. Theres even an option to let you save your load out to list for even quicker changes.
You will need to unlock the diffrence classes by doing a quest, then important skills that class needs by following the quests you get relating to that class. For instance, the Gladiator, one of the Tank classes, won't actually get Flash, a group taunt till you do the class quest to unlock it. Personally I have no issue with this because 1) a lot of these quests teach how to use the skill you get and kinda how to play the class it self, and 2) as with the other story heavy quest chains in the game these are good, each class quest chain have its own batch of characters, some enjoyable, some ... in desperate need of a sharp kick to the teeth.
The Armory system applys to crafting as well, with Leather working, wood working, even gathering, being they're own seprate classes with they're own skills, equipment and quest lines to follow. I admittedly haven't really messed with this to much, I'm more then 'running around killing monsters' type of player. But from what little I've seen I like it. Crafted item quality seems to depend on a combonation of Skill usage, Item quality (pretty much every drop has a High Quality) and luck, I think, like I said not messed with it enough to say for sure. But I can tell you crafting in this game can fail, so theres reason to not half♥♥♥♥♥your gear and leveling if you want the really good stuff.
It might be odd to adjust to if your used to needing an alt to do certain things, it was for me, but ultimately once your over that, you'll probably not wanna go back to needing a bunch of alts, I know I don't.
The only, nit picky, complaint I have IS all the quests. Everything has a quest to unlock it. Classes are just the tip of the iceburge. Dungeons have to be unlock by going through the main story, or finding the side quest for them, all the side features like mateira (which I haven't touched at all past unlocking it) and even dying your armor color. All take a quest to unlock, and so on. Like I said though this is really nit picky, as I do actually like the added touch, it just gets tiresum sometimes to hunt down an NPC to unlock a simple thing that logically, 'I should know how to do', or a harder version of a dungeon or Primal battle.
So should you play FF14?
Unless you loath the idea of paying a monthly fee to play an MMO, (don't hold your breath on that here if your expecting it to go free to play) don't like MMOs to begin with (in that case why are you reading this ...) or are just to entrenched in your current MMO due to your social ties.
Yeah. It's a good game now, and I see no reason to let the stigma of its inital failed launch stop you from trying, what is a very well put together MMO.
But you don't have to take my word for it. The main site for FF14 has a link to a trial that lets you play from level 1-20 with no restiction on content, past the usual trail account stuff.

-TL;DR -
I would highly recommend playing the trial and then buying this game even if you just play the 30 day trial. It will give you plenty of playtime for you to decide if you like it and you should be able to reach a pretty high level within 30 days. It's worth it for those free 30 days.
-Long Review-
Final Fantasy 14: ARR offers stunning visuals, a fantastic music score, cat people and very heavy narrative questing. If you have played WoW and have a slightly biased viewpoint like me, try to give this game a bit of slack. I'm quite picky and noticed that a few things are a bit stiff in terms of animations and don't feel as fluid as WoW (IMO). But with that said, I loved the combat thoroughly. Playing as a Dragoon aka, wielding a polearm and doing the most funky moves ever, felt amazing. Each ability is uniquely animated and once you gain an idea of which moves do what, you can have a lot of fun dancing around your enemies. It keeps you moving unlike WoW where you are quite idle just hitting some buttons for the most part.
Boss fights are also a big highlight for me. They feel monstrous, edge-of-your-seat mode and have some great tactics. The only bad point is getting to those bosses. Some of the dungeons feel a bit long and winding and are quite boring to look at. Not all dungeons feel like this; some of them are beautifully laid out.
Gear and weapons are absolutely beautiful. Some of it can be a bit.... revealing. I questioned one gear set that made my character look pretty skimpy rather than beasty and well defended. But regardless, it was amusing running around in practically a thong for awhile. No one bats an eyelid.
The game is incredibly sociable as well. I found that the community overall was incredibly friendly and isn't literred with idiotic posts like other MMOs. If you are clueless in a dungeon, 9 times out of 10 people will be very willing to direct you.
However, you can get through FF14 to max level rolling solo. You can do almost everything solo bar raiding and dungeons.
Questing is very "go there, kill those, return with 8/8". There are a few moments where it can get INCREDIBLY annoying because you run back and forth about 6 or so times from opposite ends of the map. But the narrative is well written for most quests and the main quest line is lore rich and exciting to get through. There are some really beautiful in game cutscenes and mini boss fights as well.
But if you get bored of questing all the time, you can either turn to crafting or you can level another class for your character. Oh yeah, so unlike WoW and having multiple characters to have different classes, FF14 allows you to have every class within ONE character. Buuuut, you have to level them all up as you would with a new character. By doing this though, other classses abilities can crossover into your "main" class. E.g Dragoon and Maurader abilities can combine.
The game has spawn events in each zone that you can tag in and fight for with other people that just jump into the area, journals to kill certain enemies that then award big XP bonuses... Basically, there is always something you can do in FF14 if you are bored of the questing.
Personally I found it highly addictive, incredibly fun, beautiful to look at, sound and music is fantastic.. It's worth your time whether you are new to MMOs or not and whether you are an FF fanatic or not.

Many people didn't expect Amnesia: The Dark Descent to take off like it did. After receiving some praise from critics, the Youtube crowd took an instant liking to the game. It became a staple of letsplayers screaming and fans requesting to see their idols scared.
Hopes for a sequel were high and the announcement that "A Machine for Pigs" would follow in the footsteps of The Dark Descent got people hopeful. The end result, for some reason, disappointed a lot of fans.
Maybe this has more to do with me not truly seeing Amensia for many years, but I found Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs to be great. It certainly is different from Dark Descent, but it's no less tense or solid.
A Machine for Pigs deals with some incredibly disturbing and dark subject matter. This is almost the video game equivalent to that ridiculous scene in Pink Floyd's "The Wall" where kids are fed into a meat grinder. The plot line follows the dimentia of a man who obtains the orb from the previous game and goes insane.
To write it all out would utterly ruin the intrigue and mystery that surrounds every inch of this game. So I'll stop there and talk more about the game itself. Following in the vein of developer TheChineseRoom's previous game, Dear Esther, A Machine for Pigs is more about crafting and presenting a gripping narrative then it is with scares and gameplay.
There are still puzzles and enemies to deal with, but it's far simpler then before. Your interactivity with the world is cut down dramatically, so puzzles stop being about logic and deal more with you noticing an object on the ground. It's kind of sad, as I loved the mind teasers that were peppered throughout Dark Descent.
The enemy design is outstanding, but their AI is mostly the same (if not worse) then before. The Pig guards will run at you, but they can easily be outrun or simply dodged by shutting off your latern. It makes for moments that are definitely intense, but lack the kind of frailty that was so prevalent in Dark Descent.
That and a lot of the situations (both in puzzles and enemy encounters) feel like repeats of the first game. You get a similar confrontation with a water beast and often have to insert cogs and turn wheels to get the ball rolling. Towards the end of the game, you ride so many elevators that it almost becomes comical.
The presentation of everything is what really sells this. The graphics are nice and sharp and the music is just wonderful. A lot of scenes become transcendental in nature simply because of how every elements comes together. While the game doesn't ditch the diary pages from before, it's main narrative isn't hidden away by static screens.
You get constant narration from your character and some interaction with the game's antagonist. The voice overs are more compelling then the previous game and the plot takes an unexpected turn that packs a real punch at the finale. It's mesmerizing and makes for a great time.
My main gripe is just that a lot of the gameplay is stripped out. I loved exploring each environment in Dark Descent and figuring out how to progress. A Machine for Pigs is linear to a fault. Even in a big city, you only have one path to go on. Dark Descent reveled in giving you multiple things to do with no set guideline.
That aside, the overall package is just awesome. It may not be any more horror filled then it's predecessor, but it's definitely a worthy follow-up and a good experience. If you love dark, twisted fantasy, then don't pass this up.

- Houses and the atmosphere of the Elder Scrolls universe breeds many chances for RP.
- The community is less toxic than many other games, despite disagreements "world chat" is civilized most of the time.
- Low latency and fast fingers are a must if you want to compete at the 1% of PVE and PVP.
Cons
- Whilst having all default systems MMOs should have, ESO tries to stand out but stop halfway.
- The game mechanics for skills change so often that more than once I had my class be something different from what I choose three years ago.
- The same updates nerfs creative builds and in the end everyone gets holed up in the meta so the diversity, a main attribute of the Elder Scrolls series, slowly disappears.
- The Cash Shop got too greedy but that is the customer's own fault for purchasing. THERE IS NO PAY TO WIN though.
- The progression system is stagnant for high levels and grindy for lower levels.
- The guild system is way simplified and lack many of the features that make them great on Asian MMOs.
ESO was launched in 2014. My experience with AAA titles of big franchises going online is that they get better with time. LOTRO and SWTOR are fine examples of how they lacked on first years but now are filled with content and bandaids accumulated over time that made the game palatable. I think it will reach it's golden age in another 4 years.

Let me first start off by saying that I am a big fan of the genre: MMORPG.
I have played almost everything out there. Pay to play, play to win, free to play, freemium, take your pick, I've played em' all.
With that said, I have to say that Tree of Savior is one of the best MMORPG I have played, not only in recent times, but of ALL TIME.
Admittedly, I have played Ragnarok Online (since I've played literally everything), and have to say that it created a special love of hand-drawn art and customizable character progression.
Tree of Savior delivers fully in that regard. Beautiful hand-drawn art, beautiful sprits, intracate scenery and attention to detail that really shows.
And of course the character customization.
A lot of these 2000+ hours on record negative reviews are from people who have been burned by this.
Tree of Savior is not World of Warcraft. It does not hold your hand and let you know that in 200 levels, your build will be pure♥♥♥♥♥♥ Because of that, it is possible to totally mess your character up and force you to rage quit (then probably write a bad review of the game).
That being said, Tree of Savior, is one of the best MMO's for theory crafting I have ever played. A lot of the highest damage builds I have seen at end game, are extremely rare or "hipster". Of course, playing a cookie cutter build might sound boring, but it is not.
Progression is probably one of the better ones for any MMO currently out there. Solo-ing to high levels, party exp grinds, instanced dungeons, exp mission instances, its all there. The party exp grinds are especially fun and rewarding if you are trying out a rare build and because of how fast the exp is.
All in all, this game is not for your typical 12 year old noob, neck bearded care bear. The community definitely reflects the fact that in order to be successful, there is a lot of intellegence and thought required. Due to this, I think a lot of people can be a little closed minded, or elitist when it comes to character builds and such.
Huge recomend, I literally cannot understand why someone with a build that actually works would ever not recommend. This game is a labor of love, and you can feel the art, ingenuity, and experience that the development team brings to the table.
I have one very high level character, and am grinding up another character because this game is just that good.

Between social media, the forums, and fellow gamers, you'd think it would be pretty easy to always be informed about all the interesting games that get released. So, how is it exactly possible that I only heard about this game a couple of days ago, 16 months after its first release?
DISTRAINT is a small side-scrolling adventure game, with a very interesting psychological horror theme, well crafted using pixel art. I won't reveal much about the story, to let the player discover what it's about, I'll just say it's about life choices, and how much of an impact we can have on other people's lives without us even knowing. The plot is not very complex, but it's well written and always coherent with what I think this game wants to be (just a "window" on a difficult topic, without judging really, just willing to say "hey, think about this sometimes") so DISTRAINT not being extremely complex is a specific design choice, in my opinion. Puzzles are very easy, more designed to keep the flow going than to give a real challenge to the player, and the italian translation is pretty good. Graphics and sound are extremely interesting, both contributing to create the right vibe, from despair to anxiety or even hope. The use of colors and the dosage of lights and dark spots give life to a couple of very powerful moments.
I would not say it reaches the heights of "The Cat Lady" which for me it's probably one of the best examples of deep, mature, complex psychological thriller story, but it's definitely in the same ballpark. Thumbs up.

Transistor is a game that drives my heart into the world of cyberpunk and dystopian science fiction. It’s not just about gorgeous presentation and addictive combat, but I also realize the fault of human creation.
The more you advance in Transistor, the more you understand how the truth of the Cloudbank. Most of the time, Transistor is your main weapon and storyteller. Transistor also gives you strong narrative, telling what is going on, and comments on your interaction even each terminal is worthwhile to read.
As you fight against The Process, the main feature is shined out. Transistor’s combat can split into real-time approach and turn-based approach which give you planning phase to set your position, target, and set of skills. The variety of skill as you progress through the game make Transistor has unique combat and gives player’s choice to try out their own skill build. Even the limiter feature which works like player debuff, and test rooms offer challenge and thinking rather than spamming for win. However, it can be frustrated for cool down after turn mode is used as you may have to run around in small area while some enemies can constantly harm you. It is just minor issue which you can get over with once you get your perfect build.
Transistor is such a unique and great experience. Not just engaging combat, but I fell in love in polished art design, story, and memorable soundtracks which create what people like in the game. And I’m pretty sure you will enjoy much as I do once you get deeper into The Cloudbank.

Borderlands 2 > Borderlands 1. If you liked 1, you'll like 2, and even if you didn't like 1 you may still like 2. The reasons for Borderlands 2 being better than 1 and a good game in general are the following:
1. Unique guns/shields that help to fundamentally change the way you can play the game.
2. Significant differences between classes - many RPGs have characters who are only nominally different. In Borderlands 2, you have classes that each have 3 subclasses where each of the subclasses is a truly nuanced version of the main character type.
If you like games like Fallout and The Elder Scrolls you may like Borderlands 2. However, it's important to note that Borderlands 2 is not exactly like these games. It has less side quests, and the sidequests feel far less meaningful than either The Elder Scrolls series or the Fallout series. Nonetheless, the main storyline is substantial and contains many hours of gameplay.
Though I recommend this game, there are some potential downsides. The storyline is pretty in depth, but I found the unexpected things to be rather expected and I felt like some of the characters could have had more depth. Additionally, I found the third act to be quite flat. Additionally, the unusual art style may dissuade some from enjoying this game.

World of Goo is a short and sweet little game that is hard to dislike.
The well balanced physics-based puzzles are thoughtful and intuitive, making you feel rather smart for solving them without ever getting too frustrating or difficult.
The level design complements the art design and always varies, so while the basic mechanics remain the same, World of Goo manages to feel extremely fresh thoughout, never retreading old ground.
The mouse controls can be finnicky sometimes, but this will only frustrate the hardcore players attempting to 100% the achievements by completing all of the OCD variants.
That's my one major complaint with the game: a casual run-through is kept rather easy, while the OCD objectives (time limits, number of goo balls, number of moves, etc.) are very tough, and can be screwed up with tiny control mistakes or physics misjudgements. If you can ignore these optional objectives though, however enticing, you will find a game that remains very enjoyable, albeit somewhat easy, the entire way through.

While some descriptions of this game note, "significant lack of scares," don't be fooled.
By "scares", they refer to in-game sequences meant to cause sudden spikes of panic within the player, be they jump scares or enemy encounters. Amnesia: Machine for Pigs (I'll call it AMFP for short) is packed with scary moments, though they can be extremely subtle:
You may find yourself walking down a hallway, drawn by the need to explore, to search for clues- only to be stopped by a dead end. You then turn around and see something- an ornate pig mask. Was that there before? It couldn't be...and it's pointing somewhere. Who left it? When? Are they guiding you, or leading you to a trap?
The game paces itself nicely. Its heavy emphasis on story means forward progression is the main aspect of the game- because that's how you experience more of the story, and the story is worthy enough to be the game's main draw. There are plenty of puzzles, monster encounters, even what might be considered a boss fight or two. Yet, the most memorable qualities of the in-game experience remain story-driven: the atmosphere, heavy with dread. The music. The sound design (the distant clanks and clatters of pipes and chains really make you feel like you're inside a gargantuan machine). Most importantly, the revelations that the main character experiences come to him piecemeal, which allows the player to experience them in a similar fashion, as though gradually regaining lost memories. There are some plot twists that are easy to call out initially, but once you learn the manner of them,
Unfortunately, this emphasis on story is also what gives AMFP some of its most glaring flaws. The sanity meter from Dark Descent is gone. Although this makes surviving each level less tedious, it also makes the game less challenging. There is no penalty for dying. In fact, during the first hour or so the player encounters almost no enemies at all. Of course, they become more frequent and last longer as the game progresses, but this leads to a slight break in pacing during the middle of the game, about midway through Act II. This is where the game becomes the most puzzle-heavy. It's also why I stopped playing it for over a year before picking it up and swearing to finish it.
I'm disappointed I did, because shortly afterward, I reached the third act of the game...holy balls what a ride.
The implication of the machine's capabilities, and more importantly, its purpose, are truly horrifying. When I say horrifying, I don't simply mean spooky, I mean horrific on a philosophical level. There is a sequence that takes place on the streets of London in which the player sees the full extent of the machine's evil...one sight in particular was so disturbing, I actually cried out in disgust.
That's a horror genre win, as far as I'm concerned.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a really short game; I clocked in at around three hours.  To it's credit, even in this short time span I went through an impressive range of emotions.  First, I was unsettled and creeped out, waking up in a bed that was surrounded by an animal cage.  Next I was curious to learn who I was and what events had led to my precarious situation.  As I picked up and read some scattered notes I felt genuinely disturbed as they described surgical experiments and mutilation.  Roaming a labyrinthian sewer, I lost my way and confusion set in.  Then somewhere along the way I got tired of looking at bricks and pipes and I got bored.
The setting of A Machine for Pigs is intriguing; taking place in London (I believe...) around the start of the industrial revolution it's the Lovecraft tropes we know and love, but in a setting that's somewhat unique for the genre.  The character you control is the owner of a meat packing business, and the advent of automated machinery to replace human workers leaves him a little obsessed with streamlining the production line.  Under his house lies impossibly complex machines of death to slaughter the livestock.  And of course by “pigs” he means humans.  His kids take to playing in these death tunnels and have an accident around the pig people.  Discovering his twin boys' demise leads your protagonist further into madness, and he becomes obsessed with bringing them back.  The underground laboratories help his quest as he feeds more blood into his machines with the promise of quenching the insatiable appetite of an elder god residing in an abyssian pyramid.  His wife died, too?  Forgive me if the details are hazy, but this is one of those “pick up the notes” types of storytelling, and it also really doesn't matter that much because it's more about the atmosphere of the game.
And the spooky atmosphere is done rather well.  At first, anyway.  The early portions of A Machine for Pigs could reasonably be criticized for being nothing more than “boo, haunted house” jump scares, but these are quite effective and the strongest parts of the game.  Descending deeper into the earth you'd figure a darker madness awaited you, but no... it's mostly just recycled bricks and pipes and steam.  There's a real good buildup to revealing the pig-men hybrid monsters that stalk the halls, and seeing one for the first time is unnerving.  Unfortunately that's about all you're going to see in terms of monsters, and their effectiveness wears off long before the apocalyptic payoff of pigmen running rampant in the streets of London.  They become more nuisance than nightmare, obstacles between you and the solution to a simplistic puzzle you'd otherwise solve before you knew the problem.  Again, for a short game it seems like it's stretching itself too thin.
I started off fairly high on Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, but as I progressed I grew less interested.  It's been awhile since I played the original Amnesia, but somehow I remember much more about that game than the one I just finished.  It's almost like... no, ♥♥♥♥ it.
Going to a farm and petting a pig would be a scarier experience than this game.

I didn't know what to expect before I played The Elder Scrolls Online. I heard both positive and negative things about this game. Due to the fact that I played all the other ES games thoroughly and needed some ES content to satisfy my hunger while waiting for the next installment ES 6, I decided why not give it a go.
From the beginning I got quite excited, you really get sucked into the story the minute you enter. It is of course different to the other Elder Scrolls games, however I found this Online installment to be quite satisfactory and interesting enough to quench my Elder Scrolls thirst.There are a surprisingly huge amount of things to do, from the main quest to the side quests. Another plus about ESO is despite it being an MMO RPG, it is fit for any desirable playstyle, whether you want to explore Tamriel with your friends, or prefer to wander alone. Zenimax really had both types of players in mind here. From the fans from the offline series to people who are keen to play with others. As I prefer a solo playstyle this is perfect for me.  When I played the main questline I would often get so immersed in the world that I could not resist the temptation to explore and do other quests around me as well.  I noticed there are a lot of unique npcs as well, which for me personally is something that I enjoy seeing in an ES game.
The music was spot on in all the areas and really made me feel something wherever I went. The actual story is interesting and for those who have played Morrowind and Oblivion in particular you will often see a lot of connections in ESO which makes one feel nostalgic yet something fresh all together. Certainly this expands the world of Tamriel as we know it in a beautiful manner.  I also like the fact that you can make choices which can effect how people think of you and how the story plays out.
Now for the cons.
I acknowledge that the enemies have improved in the sense of combat. The patterns are a little more varied in ESO compared to former ES games. However there were quite a few times where I felt like I was grinding just to get to the next quest. But that's not really a major issue, overall it was fine.
To conclude ESO is a good game for any playstyle and may even surprise some of our hardcore ES fans. It's not as good as the usual ES game style but no doubt will satisfy the hunger of those eager for more ES content. And can be enjoyable to experience exploring all of Tamriel.

Factorio is an amazing logic puzzle that naturally grows more complex and difficult as you move along. Fun RPG with a twist. I really liked how avoiding combat was recommended and there was zero focus on grinding (as it would make you weaker). Combat is fun, with Gallium and charge attacks adding interesting new elements to combat. The story is  intriguing, and  is different from many RPG's.
The fact that you get weaker after every fight really makes the game interesting, and makes you wonder whether the treasure in that chest is worth fighting the monsters in front. On the whole, the game really captures the desperation of old age and fading power well.
On the downside, the game is short, and doesn't hold a ton of replayability value for me, but it was fun for about 10 hours. I got it on sale for 99 cents, and it was well-worth that price. I would probably enjoy replaying the game once and doing a few things differently, but that's about it.
On the whole, a very unique RPG with a couple of twists captured in an adequate, if not entirely sublime, world. Great for RPG fans who are getting bored of the usual grinding for gold and XP and looking for something new. 8.5/10

Let me tell a short story about the terrors of Pandora.
Bandit gangs never got along well, yet your gang managed to carve their own turf after a long battle with the rival gang. To celebrate it, you guys decided to storm the nearby settlement, pillaging everything, killing and doing much worse things to people that used to live there. Grabbing everything that's worth a penny, the entire gang rides home.
On the way back, one of the bandits spot a tall, lonely psycho. "Must be one of the other gangs." you say to yourself. Bad luck he's all alone. You order your men to prepare for an ambush. Everyone is in their place and with your order, they open fire. Once where he stood, there is now a thick cloud of dust.
Wait. Did that guy just emerged from the smoke as if that firepower was nothing but cotton candy? He's heading towards your gang while screaming at the top of his lungs. There is a bundle of dynamite in his hands and he's chucking it like there is no tomorrow. After shaking off the initial shock, everyone keeps firing. Psycho blows one of your men up and then pulls his shotgun, returning fire. one by one, your men fall.
You panic, pull up a flare gun and fire it into the air, requesting support from every single bandit nearby. the reinforcements arrive quickly, but this guy just doesn't know how to bite the dust. Lots of psychos swarm him, but he just lets out a maniacal laughter and pulls out his buzz axe, swinging it left and right. Limbs, guts and blood spreads everywhere. he just keeps swinging. He even hits himself.
In terror, you take a lucky shot to make him stumble for a moment, big mistake. He just spotted you. He starts to convulse, one of his arms makes an awful cruching sound as it grows into a gigantic size. the remnants of your crew falls left and right as he makes his way towards, you, it's then you realize; his entire body is covered with blood, bullet holes and much worse wounds. You have no idea what keeps him ticking.
As he lifts his axe to end your miserable life, your eyes lock. There is nothing in there. Nothing but pure, undiluted rage.
Lucky for you, you're not the bandit leader who just got hacked into bits, just like the rest of his crew. You're the Psycho who did all these, while screaming "I'M THE CONDUCTOR OF THE POOP TRAIN!" on the top of his lungs.
This is how playing Borderlands 2 feels like.

This is an early impression of the game. When I complete it I will update the review to reflect the full playthrough.
To start out, let me say I'm not a huge fan of RPGmaker games. They tend to be slightly uninspired and use generic tilesets. Many of them I feel should be cheap or free at best. This one is different.
This is the opposite of the fantasy JRPGs you've played. You don't get stronger over time, you get weaker. Your character is but an old man, whose time has already passed. You start out with the best skills in the game and over time you lose them, mirroring the desperation of age.
Your closest friend is a sentient shield who provides you with all kinds of information. You also meet some others along the way like a mercenary who admires you and a crazy woman who really likes to beat the crap out of people.
The major draw here is the writing. I don't want to spoil anything, but I've encountered a side-quest involving a little boy and his pet sheep that made me question if lying to children is wrong. If being in denial is better than knowing the truth. I've visited a forest full of floating eyeballs, and a town built against the side of an active volcano that could go off at any moment.
Damn this game's world is just fascinating.

Let me start by saying that I am and have been a big fan of the franchise and have played all games apart from Cartel (rightfully so ^^). My favourite had been Bound in Blood, however having recently played Gunslinger I simply cannot decide which one of the two is better. Techland are, without a doubt, a very skilled studio with a lot of potential and I am looking forward to a new CoJ game in the future.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is primarily a very fun and light-hearted experience with a lot going on and consistently good throughout. The game tells the story of Silas Greaves who wanders into a typical wild west saloon, where he is recognised as a famous bountry hunter and encouraged to tell a few stories. From the get-go you will notice the great voice acting as well as pretty cartoon-style cutscenes. After a brief loading screen you jump in game with a colt in your hand and Silas begins to tell his story. The graphic style of Gunslinger reminds me of Borderlands - cartoonish, but slightly more realistic. Throughout the game you will find yourself in various locations such as towns, deserts or mountains, which are all equally pretty and with a good level of detail. What distinguishes Gunslinger from its predecessors is the constant narration from Mr. Greaves which results in some rather comedic scenes playing out as the listeners try to throw in their versions of the story. Adding to the upbeat style of the game is the arcade style HUD which constantly shows kill awards for combos and such. I must say that I was a bit sceptical about this as it is a feature absent from previous CoJ games, however now I feel that it actually adds to the gameplay and to the overal style of the game. The gameplay itself is very fun with graphic headshots and lots of blood. Each gun has a nice punch to it, making taking down enemies enjoyable. Apart from that, there are unlockable skills grouped into 3 classes: Gunslinger, Ranger and Trapper, which give you special abilities such as dual wielding pistols or increased damage. You also have the possibilty to unlock special guns (basically nicer looking versions of existing weapons). I have not managed to unlock all abilities in one playthrough therefore I will certainly return to do that. Another aspect of the story, which was highlighted by the devs was the inclusion of famous Wild West characters in the game, such as Billy the Kid or Jesse James. Each one of these personas is presented in-game with a flashy cartoon-style cutscene. Lastly, another aspect which follows from the previous CoJ games is your classic wild west gun duel. I feel like this mechanic was improved over Bound in Blood, making it easier to see how good you are with specific stats (speed, concentration), which encouraged me to improve my skills.
Pros:
- pretty graphics and cutscenes
- good, light-hearted story with engaging narration, good voice acting and a twist :^)
- enjoyable gameplay, good feel of the weapons
Cons:
- the story is a bit short, took me approximately 4 hours to complete
- I guess you could have more weapons to play with
- honestly there is not much bad to say about the game, especially at its price
Overal, Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a very enjoyable experience and I would recommend it to both those new to the series as well as long term fans. Sure, the game is quite short, but it was marketed as such, having been released digital-only. At its current price of 14,99€ it is a no-brainer and definitely worth it. I am hoping for another CoJ game in the future to satisfy my Wild West hunger.

Very fun game.  I've listed a few annoyances but my only legitimate complaint was that there was not enough content...cleared twice and got every achieve in about 10 hours of game time (plus generous afk time).  Which considering the awesome gameplay, really had me craving more.
Things I loved:
- The novel Turn() concept, basically mixing turn-based RPG with real-time...you use the "Turn" function, performing all your moves instantly, then are at the mercy of the computer (in real-time) while it cools down.  Made it not feel like just another FF copy.
- Fun and interesting weapons that you can recombine for many fun and non-cookie-cutter playstyles as you level (e.g. stealth skill does one thing in a weapon slot, another when added to modify/upgrade an existing weapon, another when used as a passive).  Many playstyles are viable.
- The music is really awesome; the art is vibrant and the world is engaging, creative and interesting
- Difficulty level is challenging but reasonable (although I'm a hardcore gamer so the more casual gamer may find it more difficult--like one negative reviewer who clearly didn't understand the game revolves around the use of the Turn function!)
- Rewarding and fun challenge mode if you feel like levelling/camping/achieve-grabbing for a bit instead of progression
Things that got annoying:
- Unskippable and unforwardable cutscenes, and non-cutscene dialog scenes where you stand around and listen
- The story is decent, but the characters are definitely on the pretentious side.  (the classic story of a girl falling in love with her sword...)
- While the gameplay is awesome and accessible to all, the storyline, art, music, and feel are fairly girly which can feel off-putting if you're a guy
- On a similar note: the sword talking to you like his girlfriend all the time.  Every honestly 5-10 seconds he's stating the blindingly obvious, or tossing off lame tryhard one-liners, and if I had $1 for every throaty ".....hey".  And unfortunately he's the only narrator or story development, so while you can turn voice volume off, the game A) has all these random paues where you stand in place and he talks which now become very clunky and annoying, and B) makes no sense.  On replay in Recursion mode however B) is a non-issue so I picked problem A) as the lesser annoyance!
- Did I mention unskippable cutscenes??  Seriously.  Especially for a game where half the content revolves around a second playthrough, that's super annoying.  And the damn sword must have studied speech pauses from Shatner.
OK so that seems like a long list of annoyances...I guess what I'm trying to say is that the things a lot of positive reviewers loved (art, story, characters) I disliked.  But seriously the gameplay, difficulty level, and character/playstyle customization more than make up for it.

The gameplay is border control tedious paperwork. Verifying if different entries are coherent, checking for frauds or typos, asking people to provide more information. And then deciding if you let them through or not.
I have very little empathy to pixels, so I thought this was going to be easy. I would just accept people whose papers are fine, and then refuse people whose papers are not right even if they are dying and need an organ transplant.
But then the game got to me. There is so much more going on than just the little story of the person that comes to meet you. One person will tell you about another. Will give you something for another. Will try to bribe you, and you need the money to keep your own family afloat. There are events going on in the game's world, and it is subtly told through short sequences or short news reports.
I have to give a file to a spy. Someone else comes, and tells me that he is also a spy, and the next person looking for the file is a bad guy. He gives me another file so I can switch for the fake. Which file do I choose to give, who do I trust?
And then I start to care. A girl tells me that her abusive boyfriend that beats her up and might end up killing her is coming. His papers are alright, but I still refuse to let him enter, and get a salary sanction for my decision. The game won, I was not just proceeding as if they were pixels and I started to make moral choices and get invested in my role.
This game is not exactly "fun", but it is Art and worth trying to anyone that wants to see maturity in the video games medium. Very original, meaningful, and really well crafted.

First of, before I start this review let's go ahead and get one important/key factor out of the way...
THIS IS NOT LIKE THE FIRST AMNESIA.
Yes, this is not like the first Amnesia at all... this is due to the fact that FRICTIONAL GAMES, did not make
A Machine for Pigs. The IP was handed off to a developer team called THE CHINESE ROOM. THE CHINESE ROOM are the
ones responsible for creating this game and FRICTIONAL GAMES, was only involved in PUBLSHING (NOT CREATING)
but publishing this game. The Chinese Room are also the author's of the narrative driven game Dear Esther.
So in short, AAMFP is a game that is highly different than it's predecessor TDD(The Dark Descent.)
Let's do a quick run through of Pros vs Cons.
Pros:
-Good Atmosphere
-Good Story
-Good Graphics
Cons:
-Not as frightful
-Easier Puzzles
-The Tension that builds early is quickly lost.
The game itself is narrative driven, more so than the original Amnesia. The story presented in AAMFP is told and built quite well and solid in my opinion. It all led up to a more than predictable climatic ending however. The main difference I noticed between AAMFP and TDD is that often I found myself rushing through AAMFP content at times looking for the next scare/enemy interraction. There is significantly less interraction with enemies in AAMFP which in turn leads to long peroids of time where you're either exploring or solving mediocre puzzles such as changing a bulb, or turning a valve. It is during these extended periods that the fear and immersive dread that was originally built up is lost. However, I still found the encounters with the enemies to be tense at times.
Overall I feel that this game is worth it's retail value, I enjoyed it, I got a good imersion/scare out of playing it and the only real way to know how good this game is is to pick it up and give it a playthrough. As long as you're not expecting a Amnesia The Dark Descent v.2 I believe any true horror genre fan will enjoy this title.

From the first minute of gameplay, this game sets itself up to be a game that will have the player questioning every decision they make. From simple decisions such as to fight or flee, to weaving the story via their choice of words, this game excels in attaching the player to the story and the character.
The combat in this game is quite tactical, and this is thanks to the stance system. Without going into too much detail, it's basically a system that allows a player to alter their attack, defence, and magic-orientated statistics, as to minimise damage taken, and maximise damage output. Another thing that defines this game is the way in which the game deals with the effects of battle; As you fight, you're weakened. This system, yet again, makes the player think, and this is what truly defines the combat in this game.
The story, for me, is the best part of this game. Don't get me wrong, the design and combat are great, but the story offers something truly magnificent; it offers ideas that question our own values and morality. It shows us what all heroes eventually become, and this adds a layer of realism to the game; it reminds us that 'not everyone is a hero, and those who are, will meet the same end as you and I'.
Overall, this game is a very deep, yet enjoyable experience which truly does test the emotions and psyche of the player. Would I recommend this to a friend? Most definitely, in fact this game is a game that should be played by everyone, due to the ability it possesses, in allowing people to measure their 'acceptance of mortality,' as well being an enjoyable (and in many ways relatable) game to play.
Lastly, the developer, Kyle Ballentine, should be held in high regard for creating this game, and developing the themes within it. Neon Skies Studio should also be held in high regard for their brilliant job on designing the original art for this game.

Game doesn't need many words, it simply is that good.
Seriously though, the good and the not so good:
Good:
- Great art assets (handpainted style with neat cutscenes and backdrops, really helps the immersion)
- Phenomenal soundtrack (it's just nice, say what you will)
- Cool (boss) fights (you can play in real time, but turn mode is where this game really shines)
- Atmosphere in general is just really eerie
- Voice acting is also nice
- The story sounds interesting, I think 0o (more on Not so Good)
- Combat in general is pretty smooth
- Combo system is extremely interesting (haven't seen anything like it so far, basically you can combine all of your learned skills with one another and create "new" skills)
- Risk reward system implemented (you can basically make the game harder for you, but you also gain something from it like increased xp etc.)
- Death cheating system (basically, when you would die, you instead get another chance, but you lose one of your active skills. If you no longer have any active skills you will finally die)
Not so Good:
- The UI is closed off to you for the first 10-15 minutes of the game and you feel hopelessly lost. The game does not even let you look at the skills you have or what they do. Learning by doing. It's not too bad, but a little information wouldn't hurt. It may be off-putting for some. As the game progresses the UI opens up more and more and the game gets ever more complex
- There is no difficulty setting. Basically the game assumes you are on "easy" I guess and you can make it harder by using the risk reward system. Especially early on when you have no clue what you're doing and you encounter the first more difficult enemies the game can become a bit frustrating. For me this was the first boss fight. Some skill combinations are just not that suited here...or at all. For example I hate "Switch", because sometimes it doesn't seem to work and when it works it's somehow lackluster, but that could also be me being an idiot.
- No manual saving. You have to use the automatic save points. They are relatively near to each other. Every few fights or so...still
- The UI is clunky at parts. There are too many clicks involved and screens could have been consolidated. This is especially frustrating on the skills screen. You have to select the skill you want to add/remove, then click "add/remove", rinse repeat. This gets extremely tiresome, especially since you cannot see what effect the skill has on another skill if you do not click on "add" or "more details" first.
- While the voice acting is ok, there is only one voice and that is your sword....there seems to be no dialogue, which is sad
- The story is pretty confusing, as in you are somehow feeling as fighting inside a computer, but are you!? I'm not done yet, maybe this will be resolved, but basically the game tells you nothing at first
- Death cheating system described above is a blessing and a curse. If you lose a skill during combat you have to do without that skill for several fights after that, which can become really annoying. I also imagine to the point where you just keep dying, so perhaps it is better to just fail a fight instead of pushing through and ending up with 2 or 3 skills missing. You can replace those with other skills, but...it's a hassle and maybe not the best solution.
- Apparently the game is only about 4-5 hours long. That is not very long for the full price, but at a discount I would definitely recommend it. There is also a new game plus, which allegedly gives you access to all your combo potential and makes the game more challenging/fun, but...I would like to have that in the base game, not in a new game plus mode, which has me repeat the story again
- The levels are very nice to look at, but the game is extremely linear. You literally can only move in 1 direction. It's not too bad for 1 playthrough, but it might be annoying on the second in new game plus, because basically you could simply just string the battles together and be done with it...that is a bit disappointing.
All in all, a great little game, part game, part art project I think. Definitely worth a buy, just maybe not for the full price.

Never played Bastion before, so, first foray into games developed by Supergiant Games. Short game but enjoy it throughout.
Different powers (called Functions) as an active, upgrade or passive slot unlocks a whole new level of gameplay, allowing you to experiment with different attack combinations against different enemies.
Optional handicap (called Limiters) gives the player experience bonuses at a cost of harder enemies. Adds extra challenges to the battle but rewards the player accordingly. Also a test to the different Function combinations and its effectiveness.
New game+ mode retains the experience and powers obtained from previous walkthrough of the game. Allows experimentation of a different play style right from the beginning of the new storyline gameplay.

Good storyline. Characters associated with each Function gives an overview of the character's background story when the Functions are being equipped and used in different slots. The gameplay is border control tedious paperwork. Verifying if different entries are coherent, checking for frauds or typos, asking people to provide more information. And then deciding if you let them through or not.
I have very little empathy to pixels, so I thought this was going to be easy. I would just accept people whose papers are fine, and then refuse people whose papers are not right even if they are dying and need an organ transplant.
But then the game got to me. There is so much more going on than just the little story of the person that comes to meet you. One person will tell you about another. Will give you something for another. Will try to bribe you, and you need the money to keep your own family afloat. There are events going on in the game's world, and it is subtly told through short sequences or short news reports.
I have to give a file to a spy. Someone else comes, and tells me that he is also a spy, and the next person looking for the file is a bad guy. He gives me another file so I can switch for the fake. Which file do I choose to give, who do I trust?
And then I start to care. A girl tells me that her abusive boyfriend that beats her up and might end up killing her is coming. His papers are alright, but I still refuse to let him enter, and get a salary sanction for my decision. The game won, I was not just proceeding as if they were pixels and I started to make moral choices and get invested in my role.
This game is not exactly "fun", but it is Art and worth trying to anyone that wants to see maturity in the video games medium. Very original, meaningful, and really well crafted.

Final Fantasy XIV: The Journey To Waking Sands.
So, I played this game when it first came out on PS3, and retried it after a few patches here on PC.
Quite a few things improved... and quite a few did not.
My negatives first
Progression: You are forced to do the story quests if you want to really progress in the game.
Not entirely multiplayer: Every five levels (and for some story quests) you have to do missions solo. Why? This is an MMO.
Crafting: Awful. Just awful. Until level 50, everything you can make can be purchased from vendors. So dumb.
Market/Economy: It just feels empty. Since one character can do EVERY crafting/gathering class, it kind of devalues currency quite a bit.
Waking Sands: WTF?! Seriously, why don't they have a teleport stone in Waking Sands? You know, since I have to go there after every daggum quest.
Positives
Fishing: I loved me the fishing mechanics. It actually has fishing end game content. This point almost made me renew my subscription.
Community: The folks that play this game are actually pretty helpful for the most part. And with patches, you don't have to wait too long for dungeon queues (DPS times can get upwards of an hour, but who plays dps?!)
The game just feels empty. Soulless. Yeah, it's pretty. It sounds good. It isn't that difficult to start out (even through level 50). But it just didn't cause me to want more (except maybe fishing...)

I'm writing this right after finishing up the game. It's pretty short game but the quality of it is very good.
STORY:
The story is morally dark, depressing and very sad.
As a horror game, it's not supposed to jump scare you but to creep like a virus.
It's better if you read out loud the text.
GAMEPLAY:
There are some puzzles in this game, they were bit challenging but it shouldn't get you all lost as it's fairly easy to play.
It's impossible to die in this game if you are keep moving. The game is straight forward and game mechanics fit well with the story.
AESTHETICS:
Unique character design and pixelated art in film grain with dark sound design set the right tone for the story and dark atmosphere. Places you will visit are extremely dark so you always need to use the lantern. Horrible things revealed as you explore in places makes you wonder what happened. Nicely done.
OVERALL:
Excellent game for few dollars, the game is short but had me entertained for few hours.
The game is really depressing! I would recommend it to anyone looking to collect short horror games like this one.

Transistor follows a more Dragon Age pause action combat system. You will spend majority of your fights pausing using space and carry out your actions in the most efficent manner you can conjour up. I can't believe I haven't reviewed this yet, but my play time should speak for itself. Do not confuse this game with the atrocity that was XIV 1.0. Square Enix literally dropped a Bahamut meteor on that game to crash the servers and reimagine it as the beautiful experience it is today. Graphics are top-notch, at least if you have a decent enough rig to play it on high quality. The community overall is incredible, though your experience will vary by server, play times, and free company allegiance (FFXIV's version of guilds). Inter-played cooperation is mandatory for endgame content, and the game sets you up very nicely to learn your chosen role well by level 50. And then if you decide you don't like that role... all you have to do is switch weapons to a different class and try again.
Hallelujah, no more multiple characters to play multiple classes; I'm looking at you, WoW. Final Fantasy's job system makes it totally feasible to level every class to cap without having to jam up a server with 10 different characters, and you might be surprised by the number of people that do exactly that. Even the crafting system is much more interactive than others I've tried, and it's the crafters and gatherers that drive the game's economy. The sense of community is all-inclusive with plenty of experienced players willing to lend a hand to upstarts, though of course don't expect everyone to be this way. Like any game, this one has its elitists but the funny part is that some of those still haven't beaten the last raid.
The best pieces of advice I can give you are these:
1) If you buy the game, give it until around level 30 to start getting truly fun. That's where you unlock your job (as opposed to your class), earning you extra abilities, and it's where the dungeons start to get really fun.
2) Once you hit level 50, there is a HUGE learning curve jump when you get to extreme mode primals and the Coils of Bahamut. That's not to say these things are impassable, but you will have to buckle down and learn the mechanics rather than expecting a clear on your first try.
3) If you get lost, use the /sh shout function in chat. Talk to someone! I can almost guarantee there will be someone around to lend a helping hand.
4) Listen when people give you advice. 90% of the time, they say it because they want to help improve their server's experience, not because they think you're a n00b that sux.
5) If you're new to the game and chose the Brynhildr server, hit up Taliel Sicilian. ;)

An mmo with class!  I blame my friend Magmawk for this.
Graphics:
I have to say, everything is frakking beautiful.  This is literally the most beautiful mmo I have ever played.  It's not catroony coloful like TERA is, this game just look beautiful.  Not just is there a lot of detail on npcs and enemies, but even enviremnets look great!  The spells and special attacks all come with bright and colorful effects and really put pizzaz on your stuff!  In fact, the quest where you have to look for vistas is like the game saying "LOOK HOW BEAUTIFUL I AM!"
Sound:
The sound of this game is awesome.  The music sounds great and always feels perfect for the setting they play in.  None of the music is boring and I love listenig to it!  The attacks sound like they have impact and the monsters and npcs really sound good!  The voice acting is also very well done and amazing.  Turn the volume up on this one!
Control:
While I use a controller for this game (to great effect), keyboard/mouse also works quite well.  And the game lets you organize your skillbars to make even easier for you.
Gameplay:
While on your initial class, there is no shortage of quests to complete, FATEs to run, and Leves to do, as wel as hunting logs to complete.  WIth all that, it takes no time to level up.  Once you hit the level cap for a class, you stop gaining exp, so finishing no-50 quests becomes a waste of exp.  But you can switch to other classes at time, so exp is not wated.  And there are a LOT of classes to choose from!  But once you have completed most of the non-50 quests, the only good sources of exp come from FATEs and Leves.  And if you want access to the JOBs, you have to level up another class to unlock it.  Thankfully, there are many Level 50 quests that will keep you entertained.  From the Hildebrand quests to Crystal Tower and the Coils of Bahamut, you will have things to do for a long time.  And with classes like Culinarian and Armorer, you can get your crafting on and really make some money on the market, which is admitadly slightly broken right now abusable it is in making Gil.  My only issues are ;that the classes/jobs neatly fit into 3 basic catgories of TANK/HEALER/DPS with little way of customizing (only 2 tank classes, 2/3 healer clasess and 11 dps); and that it can be annoying waiting in a queue for a dungeon to launch (tanks and healers are usuallly rare).  Better have a group if you want to run dungeons for quicker queues.
There is some grinding on other classes, but it's not as much as other mmos and the story and dungeons are fun enough to keep playing over and over!  If you are looking for a truly great mmo, I highly reccomend this one!  It may not be free, but it is worth EVERY PENNY!

My original review was SO LONG that it became a novel…
That soon became a trilogy…
That was eventually released on blu-ray DVD.
