The game comes with a free month, which is more than enough time to give it a try. Despite the lackluster fighting IMO (read below), it doesn't detract from the overall gameplay. FFXIV is an absolutely gorgeous and vast world, and one of the best subscription MMO's I've played. I would recommend this game to any of my friends.
---
FREE-to-play MMOs are like highschool.
You’re often surrounded by people who could care less about you or the community, and only a select few people who do care.
One of the biggest reasons I play any subscription based MMO is for the community.
SUBSCRIPTION based MMOs are like university. You’re at a hub where like-minded people gather, who have paid for their entrance, and in doing so will most likely try their best to thrive; the only way to do so is to become apart of the community.
My first day on the server I was invited to a free company (a lesser form of a guild), and I was chatting up my FC mates like no tomorrow. We shared stories, got to know each other a little bit, and some of the max level players came out to help me quest for fun (they even gave me a free pet). We also went to the FC house and chilled in a hot tub, at which point we began to /dance naked without equipment. Needless to say, I felt like the community was incredible.
Granted, everyone will have a different experience and some might not be as lucky as I was (although I still vouch for the community since my brother and friend were in thriving FC’s as well).
I bought the game cause my friend said I could make a hot female character with an even hotter merchant retainer... He didn't lie.
But seriously, the graphics are stunning. So often did I catch myself stopping to take in the scenery before I continued on with a quest. And even more often did I catch myself marveling my own character (and others) during cutscenes. From equipment and weapons, to the vast cities and it's inhabitants, I could spend hours just roaming around taking it all in; and that's saying something.
I'll be honest, I'm very biased here, so I'll say it straight; I'm a huge FINAL FANTASY fanboy. From the lore to the cameo's, and all the familiarity that is FINAL FANTASY, I LOVED this game. But I'll try and be objective. IMO, this game isn't afraid to be cute and light, and neither is it afraid to be dark. This is reflective of the writing and plot, to the characters you meet and enemies you fight. Unlike most single player RPGs that become far too cute, or completely dark with no hope for salvation, or "try to hard comedic" with jokes that bash you're head in, this game is a combination of every world, and in nice moderation. I felt after my time spent in the game, I got to see its dark aspects, but never forgot how cute it was. Especially with the immense varying between areas. I adored how one city made me feel fresh and relaxed, while others made me feel rigid and attentive. The same goes for the characters you meet along the way. Even the monsters have great diversity. Although I'll stop there, because the sheer nostalgia of seeing a huge♥♥♥♥♥Malboro or Ifrit will turn this review into a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Alright this is the bad part, and might be a deal breaker for you. There was nothing wrong with the gameplay. In fact, I actually prefer FFXIV’s approach to the job system where all you need is 1 character to enjoy all the classes (this also removes the bs of having to start another alt if you messed up a skill tree or something). What I felt was this game was very REACTIVE as opposed to PROACTIVE. I was constantly waiting to react during fights, either waiting for my cast bar to finish and react with another skill, or reacting to a boss attack field by moving out of the way. Many MMOs have you proactively moving to avoid damage rather than reacting to a boss attack field. And those same MMOs don’t have a cast time for every single skill, thus creating a rhythmic flow to attack skill rotation (PROACTIVE) rather than waiting on dreary cast bars (REACTIVE). In general this made my gameplay feel lackluster at times. But this never detracted from overall gameplay. Mind you, mastering cast bar skill rotation (and skill rotation in general) is an art form all its own.
I would highly recommend this game. Even the gameplay which I just bashed isn’t a deal breaker (for me at least). There is nothing wrong with a reactive style of play. Keep in mind this review is just my opinions.
FINAL (fantasy) verdict:

Factorio is amazing.
The most similar things I can think of are certain varieties of modded Minecraft, and Factorio is better than them in almost every possible way.
Graphics: Not particularly high quality, but with the amount of bits and bobs that end up floating around, you can't really have super fancy graphics without hurting FPS.
Speaking of FPS, Factorio manages to simulate the MASSIVE machines, items, and other entities any decent factory will have without suffering any noticable lag whatsoever. It's an amazing feat of programming, and it greatly improves the quality of the game.
Sound: As with most sandbox games, I consider Factorio's BGM to be appropriate. Not particularly good, not bad, but fitting. I still usually choose to listen to other things while I play, but something is playing enough of the time that someone who requires auditory stimulation (like me) will probably be satisfied. The sound effects are similar: acceptable quality, and appropriate for the game.
Gameplay:

Pros:
-Factorio is a sandbox game based around automation. Most such games (in my experience) have less building complex systems and more waiting for resources. Factorio manages to mostly avoid this pitfall through careful balancing, meaning that you have to spend less time waiting, and can spend more time making and fixing things (which is the fun part of the game).
-Very active modding community. The large amount of mods available adds a lot of replay value, and the community shows no signs that they're stopping any time soon. It also help that you can install the mods easily by pressing some buttons in game, rather than having to fiddle with files manually.
-Active Developers that care. As is, Factorio could easily be released as a full game, but the Devs continue to add to it and improve it. Weekly rundowns of what they're working on let users be involved in the development process. The best part? Like the modding community, the devs show no sign of slowing down any time soon.
-MULTIPLAYER. While it's still not 100% optimized, you can play online with your friends. I've yet to try it myself (all of my friends that own Factorio have gotten bored of it somehow), but games like this are better played with friends. Just having the option is a plus.
Cons:
-Addictive. The vast majority of other reviews mention this, AND IT'S TRUE. Factorio progression requires you to set up large systems to produce and process various goods. As soon as you finish one project, there'll be another one ready for you. It's fun, and it draws you in.
If you have trouble remembering to do things like eat, drink water, sleep, go to the bathroom, go outside, etc. when gaming, it might be a good idea to stay away from Factorio until you figure out a solution to your problem.
Overall:
Great gameplay and a decent amount of replay value make this game one of the best games on Steam.
Don't forget to take breaks!

Dark Souls as a franchise is very unique. Many people who are thinking about buying this game, have probably heard stories about how Dark Souls is a brutal game. Well it is really hard at the beginning, but when you get used to the game, and when you get better armor and better weapons, it gets way easier.
So how the game works? Every time you die, you lose all your souls(Dark Souls money). If you go back to same location where you died you can collect your souls, but if you die again before collecting souls you will lose them forever. You can use those souls to level up and then upgrade stats, to buy stuff, etc. You can obtain souls by killing enemies, or collecting souls through items.
Now, enemies. You have normal enemies, and when you first start playing the game, you will realize that there are no trivial easy enemies. After a while you will get used to it. Aside from normal enemies there are bosses, and killing the boss in Dark Souls franchise is one of the most satisfying things you can do in gaming, since they tend to be really hard.
In this game you can play melee, you can cast magic or miracles, all depends on how you wish to play. Gameplay is pretty smooth in Dark Souls 2, kinda weird at the beginning, since it's littler slower than in other games, but it's amazing like in every Souls game. You need to worry about your equip load so you don't roll slowly or move slowly. There are bunch of weapon classes, and bunch of weapons. Swords, greatswords, ultra greatswords, axes, whips, shields, daggers, etc. Many miracles and sorceries too.
Multiplayer works like this. You can invade the world of other player with some special items, and there you can kill them while they are playing through game. You can play co-op with another two players, or phantoms. You can also post red sign on the floor and if someone calls you can duel with them. In invasion people usually don't play fair, they use enviroment, but in duels you play 1vs1. But that all depends on the player and on how he/she feels. Sometimes I played fair even in invasions, but sometimes I just wanted to have fun. In my opinion, Dark Souls 2 had best mutliplayer ever, even though it was a bit broken.

If you think this is Skyrim 2.0, you will be sad. But if you come to this game and play it with an open mind, you'll be surprised just how good it is!
The graphics are alright and the music is ambient and great, just like it's predecessors. The gameplay is mostly fluid, unless you have internet problems or play PvP with maxed out graphics.
The magic of this game lies in just how much content there is do to! There are thousands of quests with stories behind them, a bunch of delves, public dungeons, arenas, duels, PvP, crafting, harvesting, fishing, lorebooks collecting, exploring, NPC guilds and player guilds... it never ends! Another thing that also never ends is your character XP progress, even though past a certain point (which takes a long time to reach!) it stops granting you points to allocate in your passive trees, it will still be useful in the future when they release further content.
I think the biggest downside of this game is that there is too many things to purchase with real money and it ends up costing a lot really quickly... The game is pay to play ($20 USD) and a membership ($15/month) is really beneficial if you like crafting as you can carry an infinite amount of ressources on you. Then if you want to access all content in the game without a membership, you have to actually buy the DLC (in-game) with premium currency "crowns". But even there, you won't get all the content unlocked as they also release expensions which you can only buy as DLC on Steam (their only one so far is $30 USD with an option to pay $60 USD for a deluxe edition).
And it doesn't stop... There's the usual microtransactions which you can purchase for crowns (premium currency) and even loot crates (which gives a lot of unwanted items and some very rare good items) which you have to pay and gamble for. And functionalities like character slots, name change, appearance change, banker and merchant hirelings... Etc.
I would really recommend to stick away from this game if you tend to spend money you regret later quite often, because this is where this game could lead many people. Personally, I'm only going to stick to the occasional DLC and subscription purchases and I enjoy the game enough (and crafting of course) to unlock those.

I'm a bit of a sucker for the Call of Juarez series. The games all absolutely nail the wild west theme and are unrivaled in terms of six-shooter shooters. This entry in the series takes a more arcadey approach to the idea, giving you floating score indicators for kills and including a random slow motion special ability which can be upgraded with all sorts of devastatingly broken effects. It works though - without having to worry about balancing around multiplayer it's just some power fantasy fun.
I enjoyed playing a little bit of the score-attack Arcade mode after I was done with the story, though the duel mode didn't sit quite as well with me. Dueling in the game requires you to multitask keeping your mouse hovered over your opponent (which randomly floats off in random directions throughout) and keeping your character's hand in the perfect position over their gun holster with the A and D keys (and which also randomly floats away), which is awkward to say the least. There is also a measure of your reaction speed in that ideally you want to draw immediately after your opponent for the best outcome. It's a strange little thing. The idea is undoubtedly very cool but the implementation of it makes it extremely likely that you'll be seeing that game over screen during these sections repeatedly.
Overall, I love Call of Juarez because every time I come to play a game in the series it's a totally unique experience compared to your Call of Duty and such. This particular entry doesn't really stand out as anything special when compared to the first two games in the series,
and
, which are excellent, but is still a great if somewhat short time.

It pains me to write a negative review about something that I had anticipated for quite some time, but there are a few aspects about Transistor that irritate the hell out of me. I wasn't as smitten by developer Supergiant's previous game Bastion as some others, but the game was aesthetically beautiful and its mechanics, whilst simple, worked when paired with the often interesting narrative.
But Transistor is a swing and a miss this time around. Of course it looks and sounds beautiful, its unique visuals and haunting soundtrack being two of the game's biggest pluses, but that's where it ends. The story - well, what story, really? Honestly, the story seems to be deliberately vague as if that alone invites interest, but it's more infuriating than intriguing. I haven't finished the game yet, so perhaps this is a moot point, but the way the story is dished out to you isn't compelling me to finish the game any time soon. The world itself is innovative, but so sparsely populated that at no point does it feel truly immersive.
The combat system is initially interesting, given that you can play in a quasi-turn based style or real time, but after a few fights the flaws become apparent. The skill pairing and upgrade system is a little confusing at first, at least in my opinion, and I found that you ultimately rely on one or two attacks for most of your battles. Most fights end up being repetitive and dull. You move from zone to zone, from one fight to another in tightly contained areas, scarcely interacting with the world. There are some cut-scenes, quizzes and bits of text that are presented to you from time to time which I assume are meant to give us more information about the world, but Transistor falls into the same trap that a lot of games do with regards to world-building, which is that it tells us rather than shows us what we want or need to know.
Plus to add insult to injury, the narrator's voice simply rubs me the wrong way. Perhaps it's the delivery, the tone, or the echo-ey effect given to the sword, but I found it simply grates.
Transistor is a weird blend of okay-but-hardly-revelatory fight mechanics and a barely interesting story. It looks and sounds beautiful (if you ignore the narration) but is nowhere nearly as compelling as Bastion was. I absolutely wanted to like it more than I did, and given all the overwhelmingly positive reviews for this I guess I must be missing something, but in the end I felt let down by its mechanics and narrative. I will play it to the end, but am in no rush to do so.
PROS:
+ unique and gorgeous art style
+ beautiful, moody music
+ combat system tries something different with its blend of real-time/turn-based strategy
CONS:
- repetitive fights
- confusing skill system
- dull, deliberately obtuse story and weak world-building (though the world itself is fascinating in its own right)
- narrator's voice (for me) gets on the nerves

An mmo with class!  I blame my friend Magmawk for this.
Graphics:
I have to say, everything is frakking beautiful.  This is literally the most beautiful mmo I have ever played.  It's not catroony coloful like TERA is, this game just look beautiful.  Not just is there a lot of detail on npcs and enemies, but even enviremnets look great!  The spells and special attacks all come with bright and colorful effects and really put pizzaz on your stuff!  In fact, the quest where you have to look for vistas is like the game saying "LOOK HOW BEAUTIFUL I AM!"
Sound:
The sound of this game is awesome.  The music sounds great and always feels perfect for the setting they play in.  None of the music is boring and I love listenig to it!  The attacks sound like they have impact and the monsters and npcs really sound good!  The voice acting is also very well done and amazing.  Turn the volume up on this one!
Control:
While I use a controller for this game (to great effect), keyboard/mouse also works quite well.  And the game lets you organize your skillbars to make even easier for you.
Gameplay:
While on your initial class, there is no shortage of quests to complete, FATEs to run, and Leves to do, as wel as hunting logs to complete.  WIth all that, it takes no time to level up.  Once you hit the level cap for a class, you stop gaining exp, so finishing no-50 quests becomes a waste of exp.  But you can switch to other classes at time, so exp is not wated.  And there are a LOT of classes to choose from!  But once you have completed most of the non-50 quests, the only good sources of exp come from FATEs and Leves.  And if you want access to the JOBs, you have to level up another class to unlock it.  Thankfully, there are many Level 50 quests that will keep you entertained.  From the Hildebrand quests to Crystal Tower and the Coils of Bahamut, you will have things to do for a long time.  And with classes like Culinarian and Armorer, you can get your crafting on and really make some money on the market, which is admitadly slightly broken right now abusable it is in making Gil.  My only issues are ;that the classes/jobs neatly fit into 3 basic catgories of TANK/HEALER/DPS with little way of customizing (only 2 tank classes, 2/3 healer clasess and 11 dps); and that it can be annoying waiting in a queue for a dungeon to launch (tanks and healers are usuallly rare).  Better have a group if you want to run dungeons for quicker queues.
There is some grinding on other classes, but it's not as much as other mmos and the story and dungeons are fun enough to keep playing over and over!  If you are looking for a truly great mmo, I highly reccomend this one!  It may not be free, but it is worth EVERY PENNY!

The game comes with a free month, which is more than enough time to give it a try. Despite the lackluster fighting IMO (read below), it doesn't detract from the overall gameplay. FFXIV is an absolutely gorgeous and vast world, and one of the best subscription MMO's I've played. I would recommend this game to any of my friends.
---
FREE-to-play MMOs are like highschool.
You’re often surrounded by people who could care less about you or the community, and only a select few people who do care.
One of the biggest reasons I play any subscription based MMO is for the community.
SUBSCRIPTION based MMOs are like university. You’re at a hub where like-minded people gather, who have paid for their entrance, and in doing so will most likely try their best to thrive; the only way to do so is to become apart of the community.
My first day on the server I was invited to a free company (a lesser form of a guild), and I was chatting up my FC mates like no tomorrow. We shared stories, got to know each other a little bit, and some of the max level players came out to help me quest for fun (they even gave me a free pet). We also went to the FC house and chilled in a hot tub, at which point we began to /dance naked without equipment. Needless to say, I felt like the community was incredible.
Granted, everyone will have a different experience and some might not be as lucky as I was (although I still vouch for the community since my brother and friend were in thriving FC’s as well).
I bought the game cause my friend said I could make a hot female character with an even hotter merchant retainer... He didn't lie.
But seriously, the graphics are stunning. So often did I catch myself stopping to take in the scenery before I continued on with a quest. And even more often did I catch myself marveling my own character (and others) during cutscenes. From equipment and weapons, to the vast cities and it's inhabitants, I could spend hours just roaming around taking it all in; and that's saying something.
I'll be honest, I'm very biased here, so I'll say it straight; I'm a huge FINAL FANTASY fanboy. From the lore to the cameo's, and all the familiarity that is FINAL FANTASY, I LOVED this game. But I'll try and be objective. IMO, this game isn't afraid to be cute and light, and neither is it afraid to be dark. This is reflective of the writing and plot, to the characters you meet and enemies you fight. Unlike most single player RPGs that become far too cute, or completely dark with no hope for salvation, or "try to hard comedic" with jokes that bash you're head in, this game is a combination of every world, and in nice moderation. I felt after my time spent in the game, I got to see its dark aspects, but never forgot how cute it was. Especially with the immense varying between areas. I adored how one city made me feel fresh and relaxed, while others made me feel rigid and attentive. The same goes for the characters you meet along the way. Even the monsters have great diversity. Although I'll stop there, because the sheer nostalgia of seeing a huge♥♥♥♥♥Malboro or Ifrit will turn this review into a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Alright this is the bad part, and might be a deal breaker for you. There was nothing wrong with the gameplay. In fact, I actually prefer FFXIV’s approach to the job system where all you need is 1 character to enjoy all the classes (this also removes the bs of having to start another alt if you messed up a skill tree or something). What I felt was this game was very REACTIVE as opposed to PROACTIVE. I was constantly waiting to react during fights, either waiting for my cast bar to finish and react with another skill, or reacting to a boss attack field by moving out of the way. Many MMOs have you proactively moving to avoid damage rather than reacting to a boss attack field. And those same MMOs don’t have a cast time for every single skill, thus creating a rhythmic flow to attack skill rotation (PROACTIVE) rather than waiting on dreary cast bars (REACTIVE). In general this made my gameplay feel lackluster at times. But this never detracted from overall gameplay. Mind you, mastering cast bar skill rotation (and skill rotation in general) is an art form all its own.
I would highly recommend this game. Even the gameplay which I just bashed isn’t a deal breaker (for me at least). There is nothing wrong with a reactive style of play. Keep in mind this review is just my opinions.
FINAL (fantasy) verdict:
8.5/10

DISTRAINT is actually surprisingly good, like no joke I'm surprised by how good it is.
In DISTRAINT you play as Price, he works for a company which deals with real estate and you evict people from their homes when they can't pay the price to live there. As the game goes on you lose your sanity and the world around you becomes more twisted as the game goes on.
DISTRAINT isn't a jump scare fest and relies more on psychology to freak you out. It does that with freaky imagery, fantastic atmosphere and a really intriguing story to boot.
DISTRAINT at it's core is an adventure game. You can't actually die in this game all you do is explore and solve puzzles and some of them are quite smart, but there is one puzzle I dislike and that's the drug one in the last section of the game.
The pixel art style is absolutely amazing, everything looks detailed and most of the environments are absolutely beautiful. It's one of my favorite aspects of this game.
The games audio is also incredibly well designed, it helps build atmosphere in some sections of the game and in general it's absolutely fantastic.
Now I do have some negative aspects I'd like to address:
One of the main things I really disliked was some of the item placements, which it took quite some time getting, because they're placed in some really bizarre locations.
Some of the puzzles are kind of confusing as well, especially in the final chapters of the game. The game's puzzles up till the final chapter are sort of easy, but the chapter in the hospital had the probably the worst puzzle design. But the drug puzzle takes the cake as the worst puzzle, as the layout of the map and the entire puzzle is quite frustrating, but you understand it soon enough.
The game is also short. It's possible to finish the game a 100% with every achievement in 2 hours. After the first playthrough there's no replay value whatsoever as the game only has one ending.
Overall DISTRAINT is actually a really surprising game. It succeeds as a horror game and freaked me out and kept me intrigued to keep playing to see how the entire wraps up. Even with a few bad puzzles I loved my time with this game, not to mention I got this game for free, but I would have gladly bought it. I also can't wait for DISTRAINT 2 this year. So if you like horror games check this game out.
Final Rating:
8/10
Pros:
+ Intriguing Plot
+ Great Art Style
+ Amazing sound design
Cons:
- The last few puzzles are poorly designed
- Short

Bit Heroes is an automated dungeon crawl where you create an 8-bit hero to dwelve through 5 different zones in an attempt to go through repetitive dungeons, bosses and raids. It works on a rarity item and level up system where if you are of certain stats you will breeze through the stage. The objective is to make the game painful enough so that you will avoid grinding and pay cash for crystals which you can then convert into gold, energy and tickets.
Gameplay-wise, it's either pressing 123 and targetting your enemy or pressing the automate button. You take an action each time your action bar fills up and vice versa for the mobs. If you automate, you can just let the game run itself and it will complete the dungeon for you. As you complete dungeons, you can persuade monsters to join your party, pick up items and level up. There are only 3 stats, attack power that can improve your damage and heal, hitpoints and speed.
Conclusion, skip this pay to win game. It's another game aimed at squeezing out money from you by exhausting you with grinding. At level 10, you will get incessant ads telling you to buy a booster that will greatly increase your stats.
Note : The developer is Juppiomenz, a developer on Kongregate.

The game has been through a lot of changes since release, mainly related to the trade system restrictions that were set when the game started. I'll explain some of the important points regarding my experience below.
Trading was completely restricted when the game launched, personal 1-1 trades were only possible if you had a Token ( i'll explain what the token entails in the next point ) otherwise your only option to trade was using the Market, even then, trading silver was and still is impossible in 1-1 trades, with the recent patches they've lifted some of the restrictions. Allowing players to trade 1-1 without having a Token, albeit making the item untradeable if 1 of the parts don't have a Token or if their Token doesn't have any allowed number of trades left.
Most of the mid-game and late-game recipes, gear and materials were untradeable at start, with a recent patch, all of these items became tradeable ( although materials still becoming untradeable after trading them once )
The Token is a micro transaction type of ''subscription'', with it, you can access the Team Storage and have several in-game effects such as being able to learn specific attributes instantly without having to wait a a certain amount of time, reduced Market commission fee ( non-token being 30% and with token 10% ), +3 increased movement speed, increased amount of Market listings ( non-token allowing 1 listing at a time and token allowing up to 10 ), 30% increased EXP from hunting mobs, +30 allowed number of trades ( if they run out, it makes items go untradeable in 1-1 trades and it's still possible to stack tokens for more allowed number of trades ), +1 increased maximum buff count, being able to use Premium Emotes and +1 extra instance entry for missions and dungeons. People can still buy the token with or without cash, using in-game silver to buy it from Market.
The Market still has several restrictions to it, such as a wait time before the item gets listed ( from 30 minutes up to 2 hours ) and once it's been sold there's a wait time before you're able to collect the money ( it being 2 days ) unless you have a token, then there's no wait time, you also have to be lvl 40 and your ToS account has to be 7 days old in order to partake into Market and 1-1 transactions.
The Team Storage has also changed a lot in the recent patches, people are allowed to use it to store silver and items ( as long as they're tradeable or allowed to be transferred ) and send them to another of your alts, thing that wasn't possible when game launched, still you must have a token in order to use the Team Storage.
Bots have always been an issue with F2P market games such as ToS, bots were a truly painful issue the first few months after the game started, they still are however not as bad as before, nowadays bots get banned much faster and some of the maps aren't as clustered with bots as before.
Most of the rare items that drop in the open world such a monster gems, gear used for crafting BiS items and overall unique stuff, work under a system called Drop Per Kill ( DPK for short ) even though it's not confirmed, there might be a short variation of the amount of kills needed before a specific item drops, still, this system doesn't allow an item to drop more than 2 times right next to each other as opposed to luck based drops ( RNG ), the mob kill count is fixed to the channel you're hunting in, the kill count is also reset by maintenances and channel/server crashes making it very hard to get super rare quality items or items that require a high amount of kills, with the current spawn time of certain mobs and the decreasing population, this has been an issue.
It's possible and doable to level a char up to 200-220 by not relying on others for parties to do missions or dungeons of any sort, but as the game progress specially mid-game/late-game you have to group up to do mercenary missions and grind parties, the newest content patch ( rank 8 ) increased the level cap from 280 to 330, the new maps are pretty hard to complete unless you have a specific class or a group to be able to, this is a problem due to the decreasing amount of players, it's hard to find a party, namely mercenary missions in my case which start at level 100 and scales all the way to 330, queueing up with players of similar levels in order to start the instance, even though the queue system is cross server ( servers are divided in regions and said regions share cross server queueing ) it's not easy to find people unless it's at peak hours.

Transistor. Not too much to say, you spend less than 10 hours of gameplay per playthrough. But what the game has to offer is no doubt worth the money:
- 10/10 for game mechanics, balanced variety of functions (abilities) that you can upgrade with each other gives you your unique way of completing the game + there are some hardcore mods for those who seek challenge!
- 10/10 for the plot [no spoilers], you're playing as Red, a famous singer of Cloudbank who has lost her voice. And you definitely want to learn how the story ends. It's emotional. Believe me or not but I did shed a tear at some point.
- 10/10 for the soundtrack. The music is so outstandingly good. I am speechless, I really am, it's that good.
- 10/10 for the graphics. The art is amazing, the world is beautiful. Wandering the walkways of Cloudbank becomes addictive as you discover more and more of this wonderful universe.
Yeah, the game doesn't have any crazy 3D looks, multiplayer or whatever it doesn't have that you'd want, but it doesn't really need it. It is perfect. You should've stopped reading this already and gone play it.
Not recommending this amazing experience would equal heresy, thus I do recommend this game.
11/10, would Transistor again.

That art, That music, That game engine. This game is fantastic, leaving the only thing to be desired is a clearer storyline. Most of whats going on is explained in info biographies that you unlock, but even then i did not really know what was going on, but i still enjoyed the ride none-the-less.
The combat is rather robust, one of the better i've seen in a long time, the complexity and strategy behind combining and modifying moves adds alot of depth to combat.
Turn(), is a time freezing special you can do, that allows to perform a limited series of actions in an order you set, the balance to this, is your moves are disabled for a short time after.
in the 2nd playthrough you begin to unlock doubles of skills, which adds a whole new layer of depth to the game, i made an extremely overpowered layout that allowed me to one shot everything i came across with little to no effort, even with every challenge modifier enabled.
the combat system allows for so much creativity and combinations, it would take several more playthroughs just to try them all
my favorite build was:
Cull(), with breach or a higher damage output mod
Split(), with Jaunt and Purge
Void(), with get, and crash
Mask(), with ping for quicker cooldown
I used void() to pull all the enemies into a single point, which debuffs them, and stunlocks them down. I then use a quick split() into it to take out the weak ones and to apply the slow and DoT of Purge. I then used the Turn() special ability to get into a good position behind the enemy, i then hit Mask() for higher backstab damage, and Cull() them for a massive haymaker so powerful it one shots anything in the game save for "the spine". Split() with Jaunt allows me to knock the shields off dropped cells for pickup, or to kite enemies with the slow effect for defensive play until turn recovers.

It pains me to write a negative review about something that I had anticipated for quite some time, but there are a few aspects about Transistor that irritate the hell out of me. I wasn't as smitten by developer Supergiant's previous game Bastion as some others, but the game was aesthetically beautiful and its mechanics, whilst simple, worked when paired with the often interesting narrative.
But Transistor is a swing and a miss this time around. Of course it looks and sounds beautiful, its unique visuals and haunting soundtrack being two of the game's biggest pluses, but that's where it ends. The story - well, what story, really? Honestly, the story seems to be deliberately vague as if that alone invites interest, but it's more infuriating than intriguing. I haven't finished the game yet, so perhaps this is a moot point, but the way the story is dished out to you isn't compelling me to finish the game any time soon. The world itself is innovative, but so sparsely populated that at no point does it feel truly immersive.
The combat system is initially interesting, given that you can play in a quasi-turn based style or real time, but after a few fights the flaws become apparent. The skill pairing and upgrade system is a little confusing at first, at least in my opinion, and I found that you ultimately rely on one or two attacks for most of your battles. Most fights end up being repetitive and dull. You move from zone to zone, from one fight to another in tightly contained areas, scarcely interacting with the world. There are some cut-scenes, quizzes and bits of text that are presented to you from time to time which I assume are meant to give us more information about the world, but Transistor falls into the same trap that a lot of games do with regards to world-building, which is that it tells us rather than shows us what we want or need to know.
Plus to add insult to injury, the narrator's voice simply rubs me the wrong way. Perhaps it's the delivery, the tone, or the echo-ey effect given to the sword, but I found it simply grates.
Transistor is a weird blend of okay-but-hardly-revelatory fight mechanics and a barely interesting story. It looks and sounds beautiful (if you ignore the narration) but is nowhere nearly as compelling as Bastion was. I absolutely wanted to like it more than I did, and given all the overwhelmingly positive reviews for this I guess I must be missing something, but in the end I felt let down by its mechanics and narrative. I will play it to the end, but am in no rush to do so.
PROS:
+ unique and gorgeous art style
+ beautiful, moody music
+ combat system tries something different with its blend of real-time/turn-based strategy
CONS:
- repetitive fights
- confusing skill system
- dull, deliberately obtuse story and weak world-building (though the world itself is fascinating in its own right)
- narrator's voice (for me) gets on the nerves

I play games that have character generators because I don't like being shoehorned into any particular shoes. But despite having a character generator Eschalon does a lot of shoehorning anyway. The world is very contrived, and very shallow. It's like a themepark.
I tried to play as a travelling alchemy merchant and reluctant adventurer. Emphasis on reluctant. But was shoehorned into "adventurer" boots at every turn. This feeling I get from the game is no better summed up than when I encountered one NPC offering a very small job. It was one simple task; I was to take a recipe across the road. In any other game this would be conveyed as an NPC simply asking for you to do them a favour, (for example Ysolda in Skyrim asking you if you could keep an eye out for a Mammoth's tusk for them). In other games it's usually left up to you how you interpret your own actions, whether you're a vagrant looking for work, a sympathetic travelling merchant, a bard, knight, whatever - good RPGs don't get in the way of your role-playing. In Eschalon, even for a job as minor as this (taking a recipe across the road) the game couldn't help but make a show of it being a quest. Paraphrasing the game: "Oh whee, look at this shortest quest ever am-i-rite" *elbow nudge*. Yeh, Eschalon, you're like the infantile interpretation of a role-playing world; a cartoon of a role playing game rather than a role playing game. I really started to despise that so may of the interactions would result in either a generic "adventurer" quest or shoehorn you back into your "adventurer" boots via NPC dialogue. Thanks to Eschalon I now cringe the second I see the word 'quest'.
My attempt to roleplay as a travelling merchant/alchemist (in a game that has both mercantile and alchemy skills no less) was annoyingly awkward in other ways too. I discovered that if you are a divine magic user, empty potion bottles are like gold dust. This is all thanks to the dev's decision to make whether or not empty bottles are even stocked subject to the whimsies of Random Number Generation. In the 30 hours I've spent in this particular playthrough I've bought every empty bottle any Magic vendor has ever stocked, and been hoarding empty bottles from those that I've used (as I said, i have Divine magic so I don't use up many potions for healing) and bearing in mind I have not sold any potions yet at all I've been totally hoarding all empties I have 10 filled potions and a piddling 14 empty potion bottles! Such a great Alchemy merchant I can be, selling potions all across the land, erm 14 times yeh. And yes, while I can technically buy potions, use them and get the empties, It kind of defeats the point of being able to make potions if I have to buy potions!
While I'm determined to finish Book II, I will of course be done with the Eschalon series after this. Like I said, it's like a themepark; you can experience all the rides and have fun, and maybe that's enough for some, but for me its not. When playing RPGs I like to feel as if the world has an existence separate from my character. I like to feel as if it would still exist were I not there. In Eschalon everything is set up specifically around the player so that the world feels very cardboard. You can never escape the world trying to shoehorn you into your generic adventurer boots.
In addition to this there are awkward quest designs that draw attention to the limitations of the game design therefore breaking immersion. In one instance I needed salt to complete one of the main quests. Whether or not salt spawns in a chest or shop is subject to the RNG. I decided buying it in a shop was the optimal way of a acquiring salt, since I had seen it stocked in inns before I knew I needed it. Shops restock every seven days. Bear in mind that a society which has no mechanical refrigeration will be heavily dependent on salt to preserve meat so salt should be a commonplace commodity easy to acquire and as essential to society as water. And before I knew I needed it I saw it everywhere (but as soon as I knew I needed it it magically disappeared thanks to the fickle RNG gods). It took me almost two dozen weeks in game time of weekly visits to every shop in Eschalon to finally finally find a vendor that had salt in stock. After the salt incident, I found myself spotting the a myriad of peculiarities that draw attention to the world of Eschalon being incredibly inconsistent with itself more than actually being able to enjoy the narrative of my own journey. And so Eschalon all unravels once one thread frays.
Spoiler warning
In another example of the Eschalon world being self-inconsistent, I walked into a Dwarven mine described as impenetrable by any and all NPCs who had mentioned it, and not only did I penetrate it, but indeed did so by simply walking right past its occupants! Oh sure they would give chase the second they saw me, but they would follow me for about 10 steps and then give up, bless them. This suited me fine on the way down as I didn't want to harm the Dwarves since they had done me no wrong and were mixed up in this chain of events through no fault of their own. Once I reached the bottom of their mine I helped myself to a selection of their prized possessions and then turned around to make my way back to the nearest exit (conveniently located nearby I might add). Having been spotted by about three dozen Dwarves on the way down, I could have been forgiven for expecting that there would be an army of Dwarves rallied to stop this dirty human thief from making off with their treasures. Anti-climatically the Dwarves rallied a grand total of five Dwarves to stand between me and the exit of the lower part of the mine. And then having exited the lower part of the mine I walked right past a dozen more of the Dwarves I had walked past on the way down, waltzing out of the impenetrable Dwarvern mine without having to break stride once. Some scripted events such as finding on the way back out that Dwarves had overturned some tables and made some makeshift barricades to prevent my escape on the way back out would have been all that was necessary to give the illusion that the world was in some way more than cardboard. But no. It fascinates me that in a game that plays up the fact that you can take a non-combat approach if you want to, no contingency is ever put in place for that actually occurring. Events on the way out always seem to unfold as they would have if you had murdered everyone on the way in.
It's not a bad game, by any means, there's a lot that's good about it, but believable world building and self consistency is so central to an RPG that Eschalon's lapses in this area really harm it. So much of my character's story involved doing out of character things to make up for the flaws in the world design or finding huge discordance between the narrative of the NPCs and the actual state of affairs in the game world. As games go Eschalon had all the potential in the world to be something great, unfortunately it turned out to be miles wide but an inch deep.

With the release of SOMA, I couldn't help but think of this game. Seeing as I had not made a review for it, I am writing one now.
To be quite honest, I am torn about how I feel toward this title.
A Machine for Pigs is NOT A GAME. It is a first-person narrative. Its strong points are atmosphere, sound design, and story. What little puzzles there are are trivial and juvenile. The monsters are non-threatening and rather goofy at later periods in the game.
If you can appreciate a lackluster game for a pure story experience, I recommend this. Especially because Mandus' voice actor gives it his ALL. The final scene and monologue sticks out in my mind even today as one of my favorites. But as a game, this fails.
However, as a horror fan, this is definitely a unique piece of fiction. If you are like me who loves horror no matter its medium, this should be a treat. But don't expect the same caliber as its predecessor. It's actually a HUGE shame and disappointment that this has the "Amnesia" title tacked on to it as it has very little to do with the original title.

I've tried to enjoy Eschalon: Book II, and it really is a game fully inside my usual wheelhouse.  RPG... check.  Mouse-driven combat... check.  Unforgiving difficulty... check.  Sidequests... check.  Lots of interesting text to read... CHECK!
So why can't I recommend this?  It's the controls.  There is a simple flaw in this game's design that makes for a really poor experience when I play:
This might not seem like a big deal, but when I'm going to be playing a game for hours, this becomes painful quite quickly.  It isn't a click-fest like Diablo; it's both lots of clicking and LOTS of holding down the mouse button for long periods of time.
Otherwise, Eschalon: Book II is a quite excellently made game.  If I were to recommend an alternative, I would point to the recent Spiderweb Software games, which are probably superior to the Eschalon series anyway.

I do not generally like MMORPG's. They typically either have a clunky system, a boring story, the company nickle-and-dimes you to bankruptsy or a toxic community. ESO has excellent stories worthy of an Elder Scrolls title, nice graphics, a flexible and fluid system that allows for PVE-PVP-or Dungeon PVE builds or even some combinations. The community is generally friendly and helpful and full of interesting people. I admit there are a few jerks but life is like that. Most people are willing to help you out, even giving out Werewolf and Vampire bites for free (considering that otherwise you have to pay actual money for the privelage that's pretty nice of them).
And one of my favorite things about ESO is that beyond actually buying the game they don't expect you to spend more money, they'd like you to, of course but it is not expected of you. If you are not a subscriber you have access to all non DLC content (and any DLC or expansion content you purchased) but you do not suffer experience penalties, do not receive less gold, or items, you do not receive equipment from a source you can't use because you don't own the content. You can increase your in game storage with in game currency. You can also acquire mounts, pets and costumes in game without purchasing anything with actual money. And if you do subscribe you are rewarded bonuses like the beloved Crafting Bag, double bank storage, 10% experience and insprition boosts and crowns to spend in the crown store (9000 crowns for 6 month sub for instance).
Overall I really like the game. It has everything you could ask for. Good graphics, good stories, diverse and helpful community, PVE, PVP, mass PVP, dungeons, guilds (as varied in style, goals and methods as the people who found them) and overall good times. If you like the Elder Scrolls setting this game is definitely worth a try. I think you might be surprised. I was.

Final Fantasy XIV: A Realm Reborn is, without a doubt, the best MMO I have had the joy of playing. Of course, I grew up on Free to Plays that bombarded you with microtransactions everywhere you turned, and perhaps it's simply the feel of a clean  'I know exactly what I'm paying for' MMO that makes me love it so much.
The dungeon runs are smooth, and every single party I've been in has worked extremely well together. The only quip here I might have is how long some queues take, but if you're in a Free Company, chances are you'll have at least one person there to wait with you- which speeds things up considerably, might I add. Even when I was in a dungeon queue for over an hour, all I had to do was switch gear sets and work on my Blacksmithing. So really, I view the wait times as forcing me to get off my lazy♥♥♥♥♥and work on some more 'mundane' classes.
The idea of being able to play literally every class with /one/ character was, I'll admit, a little overwhelming at first. I didn't understand it all that well, but one of my companymates helped me out and showed me the ropes of juggling more than one class at a time. It's not that difficult once you're used to it.
I can't say much for the soundtrack, as I listen to music of my own while playing, but I can say something about the graphics. They're absolutely stunning. Some of the best I've seen for an MMO, honestly. Even little things, down to how clothes and hair blow when the wind picks up, and how your clothes will actually change texture if it's raining to actually make them look wet.
The community is actually surprisingly low-key, friendly, and helpful. I've only been playing for a few days and I've already made over 20 friends who've helped me understand quite a bit about the game. The only downside is I get a lot of whispers from spammers. They're easy enough to blacklist, which is another very well-implemented system, so it's not a big problem either.
Overall, I just really enjoy XIV. Maybe I haven't been playing long enough to say my piece, but it's a stellar MMO and if you're a fan of either FF or MMOs you should definitely check it out. Make sure you have enough for the monthly fees, because it'll have you wasting all your money.

Hey, hey. I've been playing Bit Heroes using its trusty phone application for a month-and-a-BIT (wink) now, prior to the Steam release. You'll also find it on Kongregate. It's essentially a turn-based mmorpg with a tier structure and rng (loot drops are randomly generated). So far, my only issue with the game is that the Steam version runs it too slowly, definitely recommend using it in the browser or on phone instead. Anyway, the gist of it is: Customise your character, fight monsters, make friends, and then fight monsters with them. Grind dungeons, get gear, find better gear, exchange old gear and repeat. Not only is there a lot of choices for multiplayer connectivity and also a global chat system good for meeting others around the world, Bit Heroes also offers the ideal in-game experience to a lone player. PVP with other folks to get prizes and helpful materials, or enter into the guild .vs. guild with a team of your very own (they do not have to be online for this). There are many currencies currently in the game, ideal for spending at the shop. Would you like to buy a virtual pet who can help you on your gamely travels? Save up! There's also the gauntlet, which offers a chance to find legendaries (really rare gear), and all my friends' favourite thing about the game- AUTO-pilot. Wanna go for a stroll, have a power-nap, or make yourself a coffee without pressures of walking away from the game getting to you? No problem, you can set any Bit Heroes minigame to run without you even having to touch the screen again. This way, levelling up is a breeze, and seeing new loot in your inventory is always a surprise! Through doing all this, you'll eventually gain enough EXP to progress far, and seeing as there is no such thing as end-game here, the possibilities are truly endless. I could go on about the game, but would rather keep some things a secret, because all-in-all there's just infinite things to do in Bit Heroes. -IGN:tachine

As I descended the lift towards the heart of the machine, it was nothing like I imagined. It was far more terrifying.
I truly enjoyed this game. However, there is no denying that 'A Machine for Pigs' is not as strong as its predecessor. The puzzles are far too simple, necessary only for maintaining an added level of interaction with the world. And, there aren't as many 'risky' moment.
In addition to this, a lot of gameplay elements from 'The Dark Descent' have been removed. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. The removal of many of these elements augments the game's focus on exploration. However, those elements are part of what made the puzzles in 'The Dark Descent' so strong, and the dangerous moments all the more frightening. And there are no new elements to bring everything together.
That being said, there are many moments where 'A Machine for Pigs' shines. The atmosphere, created through the carefully crafted environment, nearly stands on its own. Surprisingly, the lack of enemies sharply increases the anxiety; Imagination is potent.
The story is the strongest part of the game, arguably stronger than the original. 'The Dark Descent', while truly a masterpiece, told a story that was very cold and distant. In 'A Machine for Pigs', the story is uncomfortably, very human. Love and compassion are at the core of this story, at the heart of an impending madness. Painted sharply is a potent picture, not just about society, but also about people.
As good as the story is, the use of complex words and language often makes it difficult to follow at times (I must admit that the use of this type of language is a perfect match for Mandus). However, the story shines during the moments that simple language is used in a precise and clever way, leading to some horrific revelations.
'The Dark Descent' is a game where all elements came together perfectly, something that happens rarely, something that 'A Machine for Pigs' does not achieve. Despite this, I enjoyed it tremendously. For me, it is a worthy successor to Amnesia.

Alright, let me start off by saying that the first Amnesia was among my favorite games ever. While the scares got a bit predictable towards the end, the puzzles remained at least moderately challenging and the story that unfolded was just simply incredible. With the year delay on the release of Amnesia 2, I was really excited for this game. A small flag came up for me when I saw that Frictional partnered up with the devs behind Dear Esther (I don't care what anyone says, that isn't a "game" but a pretentious bunch of boredom thrown together to seem artsy).
I'm happy to report that The Chinese Room keeps up their air of pretentious stupidity throughout this game as well.
Let's start with a positive; the atmosphere is great. From the very beginning I was cautious around corners and appreciating the game.  But Chinese Room never gets past this point. They create a wonderful atmosphere, but when they ask themselves "now what?" I imagine everyone in the company just kinda shrugs and says "add more bloom effects."
There are no puzzles. With the removal of the inventory system, you simply pick up a battery and put it in a machine to open a door. It never gets any more complex than that.
There are no real enemies (besides the very small 45 second segment at the end of the game). There are stupid little pigs that walk around, but they move slower than you do. In almost every situation you can just kinda walk or run past them and you'll be ok.
As I love to say, The Chinese Room is pretentious as hell. The whole overabused theme of "we're all pigs in the machine of society," which was never original to start with, gets beaten over and over until even the most stalwart fans of these devs (which is probably the devs' mothers) have to be second guessing their taste in entertainment. But the way the narator talks, even at the end of the story, you realize that the devs really, honestly, truly believe that this is the most original metaphor that has ever been created in the history of mankind. What's truly sad is that the story itself is actually somewhat decent, I'd say nearly on par with the first Amnesia, especially with the twist. However, the ending sequence that explains everything is done in such a purposely convoluted way that it's almost as if the devs are trying to flaunt some level of intellegence to anyone who will listen. That purposeful air of arrogance from the writers comes off as overly-conceited, making it seem like they view themselves as exceedingly superior to the player.
Now, for the worst part; THE GAME IS ABOUT AN HOUR LONG. I played it through once, was convinced I missed something, played it through again, and realized that I had waited and extra year for them to scrap an entire game and give me crap.
There are good aspects here in what I would like to call a demo for a much better game:
1. The atmosphere is incredible until you realize nothing ever actually happens, which makes the buildup turn stagnant very quickly. There's no sense of danger to accompany the dark and forboding mood.
2. There's a "final boss" if you wish to call it that, which actually has the elements of a real game. Incredible, I know, it took every ounce of actual willpower that TCR has as a dev to make a real bit of gameplay. But it's essentially over in a minute and you never get anything else even remotely like it.
3. There's one little scene at the end where you walk around the streets of London. Again, this could have been incredible, with an open map in a phenominally made environment in a scary game where enemies could be anywhere. But wait, it's just more narrow corridors, the roads all blocked by boxes, and all of the action happening offscreen while you just walk around.
That's all this "game" is. Action is implied to be happening elsewhere, but you're lucky to even witness it. You just walk from one room to the next picking up batteries and putting them where they go to open doors for an hour, then you get the same motifs and themes beaten into you for a good couple minutes before it ends and you're sitting there thinking "did I really pay 20 dollars for an hour worth of boredom." Yes, I did. And I'm writing this review so you won't. If you're really interested in it, find a YouTuber who does Let's Plays without all the stupid 10 year old screaming and scare cams and other crap (I can't point you in the direction of one, pretty much everyone on YouTube over-acts like this, so I avoid the site entirely) and watch them play the game through.
Hopefully Frictional goes in another direction with Soma, otherwise I think I'm going to write this company off as a failure. I like Penumbra, and Dark Descent was a classic addition to the survival-horror genre. It's a shame they had to ruin what was shaping up to be a fantastic series of games.

The game significantly changes a lot of things from TDD, and those changes can be seen as both good and bad. Many steam reviewers appear to consider them bad, but I don't entirely agree. I'll address the pros/cons of the most common criticisms, starting by acknowledging that the game sets itself up for trouble just by calling itself "Amnesia" which leads players to expect gameplay matching TDD. So a lot of people are going to review it negatively right off the bat just because they loved TDD and it does not match that expectation. They probably should have called it simply "A Machine For Pigs" instead.
A lot of people like the sanity meter and will not like this change. I think this is a very positive change, though, as I never liked the sanity meter---i.e. the "fear level simulator". If a game makes you feel afraid, then you should literally, in your own physical body, feel fear. If you do not feel afraid, then it is very silly for a game to then tell you exactly how afraid you are according to the fear simulation meter it has given you. AMFP has the audacity to let the fear speak for itself rather than telling you what is or is not a scary or sanity-degrading situation. If the game does something scary at you but it misses, then AMFP's lack of a sanity meter at least has the honesty to let it miss. And if it hits, then AMFP lets you feel scared in your true amount rather than attempting to assign a fear value to it on a meter. So while the sanity meter certainly was a game mechanic, the lack of it is a more brave and honest approach to horror, if you ask me.
A common gameplay element of survival horror is the notion that there are certain resources useful for survival, but you only find a very limited amount of them, and they are in short supply, so there is always the fear of running out of those precious life-savers. Removing the tinderbox gameplay from the game removes a major gameplay element, but I have to say I didn't really miss it. Searching for and collecting tinderboxes gives you something to do, but light from the lantern was honestly never much of a survival advantage. Light is more comforting than helpful. AMFP opts to let you have infinite dim light for exploring but still flickers your light for scary effect when it wants to. Overall, I was okay with this.
This seems terrible at first glance, but it's no so bad once you realize they haven't so much nixed the inventory as translated it. For example, whereas before (I'm using a fictitious example here to avoid spoilers) you would do something like pick up a key and have it go in your inventory, then later select it from your inventory and use it on a door, AMFP has kept the same idea but put all of the interaction into the physical environment. So in AMFP, you would just physically pick up the key by lefting clicking it and holding, then carrying it over to the door while still holding it, then mouse over the keyhole, and the door unlocks. So there are still object-based puzzles. They just take a slightly different shape. This will annoy adventure game purists who like the fuzzy nostalgia of an inventory, but it's actually not bad. It adds a slight Myst-like quality to the game that TDD did not have.
This is something I've heard said of the game, and I half agree. There are DEFINITELY puzzles and some light mazing, but this criticism is correct in regard to how the game drops story info on you. There are definitely sections where the game makes you, say, walk down a long hallway while it arbitrarily revokes your ability to run and slows your walk so that it can force yet another audio log on you. You'll have to endure this more and more as you get into the final chapters. As a person who views audiologs as a cancer, I found this particularly irritating. Strange that they would also include audiologs for you to pick-up manually since they force-play another type of audio log on you half the time. (Not to mention all those diary pages littered everywhere.) But, as annoying as this was, I don't think it's fair or accurate to call it a walking simulator.
OVERALL GAMEPLAY: Focuses less on mechanics like resources and sanity meters. It puts more of the emphasis on exploration (some light mazing in some places) and on environmental/mechanical puzzles (somewhat Myst-like). There are some semi-rare enemy encounters, but as opposed to trying to use stealth to sneak around them, the game instead emphasizes running away, and in some cases "shaking" your pursuer by taking circutous paths or fleeing their patrol area. Enemy encounters feel kinda ambushy and confusing. Enemy encounters and constant audio/text logs are this game's major gameplay demerits for me.
★★☆☆☆
I'm only giving it two stars here, but not because it lacks good ideas. AMFP actually has some really interesting ideas. The thing that really hurts it, though, is that it has a serious case of too many cooks at the broth. I'll try to offer some generalized criticism without being too specific or dropping any spoilers.
You start with a really interesting concept that is vaguely reminiscent of the murders of H.H. Holmes, which is interesting enough in itself, but then the game starts dogpiling ideas and loses control of itself. It adds in some HP Lovecraft type ideas involving mysterious ancient rituals, and then throws in some Marxist themes re: class warfare / economic justice, but then it drops those ideas and goes in yet a different direction, and continues on in this way---a sample platter of ideas. The idea and appearance of the monsters takes some inspiration from Frankenstein, but I must admit that neither the idea of the monsters nor the appearance of the monsters is particularly scary, despite them causing a moment of panic when they ambush you. Then you also have the theme of a man struggling with schizophrenia, but then at other times the game seems to be vaguely interested in exploring a steampunk version of HAL 9000, but not quite. Man-vs-man, man-vs-self, man-vs-supernatural, man-vs-technology, man-vs-society. AMFP's story tries to do it all and ends up being a jumble of half-baked ideas as a result.
In addition to the story trying to do way too many things at once, it also insists on being cryptic. It wants to be cryptic in an intriguing way, but it's mostly just confusing. This is exacerbated by the way the writing even seems to contradict itself in some places in terms of chronology and also motivations. I won't spoil the specific plot point for you, but by way of analogy, how much sense would it make if Doc Brown saw Marty McFly's death in the future, and his idea to *save* Marty from his fate was to go back and torture Marty to death in 1985 so that he wouldn't die the normal way in 2015? SAVED HIM! You can expect similarly questionable ideas if you examine AMFP's story too closely.
TLDR: The story tries to juggle a hundred ideas at once while maintaining an air of cryptic intrigue about itself. The result is a bit of a confused mess. HOWEVER: despite the shortcomings in the story details, the game's general atmosphere while exploring and solving puzzles is excellent.
AMFP has an excellent spookhouse atmosphere and some myst-like puzzling. It is on these grounds that I recommend the game. However, prepare yourself for some stark differences from TDD and for a confusing, overwrought story with an identity crisis.

This one was a hard one to review, because I had so much mixed feelings because of its awesome predecessor, "Amnesia - The Dark Descent". "A Machine for Pigs" is not a bad game at all, it success in a variety of things while failing in many other ones. Moreover, it was just buried because of its previous game's shadow. In resume, "A Machine for Pigs" is not a "Dark Esther", it is more like a "Dear Amnesia", a truly dark and disturbing experience focused on exploration and narration.
The history is quite good. I mean, it is not as good as The Dark Descent, but was good enough to keep me interested in what was going to happen next. As its name reads, You start the game with no memories of what happened before you woke up. You must assemble the spare pieces of your memories by reading and collecting paper scraps that will help You understand what the hell is happening. It is a mix of some Lovecraftian concepts with a Silent Hill-esque progression.
As of gameplay, if You are looking for "The Dark Descent" mechanics, forget about it. In "A Machine for Pigs", Laudanum, Health Vials and Fuel are gone, Your sanity will not be affected by looking to the monsters, and life slowly regenerates. The lantern does not need fuel (Battery-Powered), and You will not have any inventory to carry those weird objects that must be used in the other side of the level. "A Machine for Pigs" focuses on narration and exploration, and sometimes in evading monsters, and its Puzzles can be solved as soon as You can imagine a correct order of use or just wandering around in search of an item that fits on a hollow space.
"A Machine for Pigs" has its virtue in the atmosphere and the sound effects, along with a sublime Soundtrack that fits in every moment, enhancing the experience in an awesome way. Graphics are not so good (sometimes, "The Dark Descent" seems to have better ones), but the level design is enough to forget this and just recreate in a Victorian London City. Again, the levels reminded me of some kind of Silent Hill, sometimes seeing a normal town and, when descending below the city, seeing underground rusted machinery and all kinds of neglected and forgotten objects.
In resume, "Amnesia - A Machine for Pigs" is not an Amnesia game. As I said before, it emphasizes exploration and narration, but believe be when I tell you it will give You varios moments of fear that will remind You of its former prequel.
Should You buy it? - Yes, but not at its original price! Get it on sale and You will not be dissapointed.

Overall, this was a pretty good game.  I recommend it to anyone.

So, this game... what do I think about it?
Emily is Away is a pretty good game to rid your boredom; in my opinion. The whole game should take around 30min - 1h to finish and after that, you can replay the game as much as you want. Each chapter consists of a conversation taking place every year starting in 2002 as last year of high school, where each conversation is like a social chat a lot like the ones we have nowadays. I like how it brings back the good old pixelated pictures as well as the trusty windows xp. The custom name and profile picture comes in as an added bonus to this marvellous game.
Although the whole game itself is pretty good satisfaction, however, I do believe there is room for improvements to be made. I have managed to find a few button faults where the hyperlink isnt where it should be located, so I was madly clicking randomly on the screen until I found and clicked it. Apart from that, there was no other glitches or faults that I could find.
For example, it would be nice to have some sort of development in the story plot with the 'reminder quote' on the bottom of the chat saying things like "Emily will remember that" or "You chose to have a conversation with Emma". I was confused that that it didn't lead to another conversation or come up in any later conversations as I thought it would be important later on in the story. Also, it would be great if maybe we could talk to someone else other than Emily in the game such as Emma rather than only being able to view their profile.
It would also be nice to have a bit more character trait and depth such as impatient Emily saying "hello?" if you haven't responded for ages.
I would also like there to be a bit more slangs for instance, 'you' into 'u' or incorrect grammars like 'ive' instead of 'I've'
All in all, Emily is Away is a pretty good game, I would rate it 8/10.

I am an introvert and practically asocial.  I much prefer single player games since I don't like interacting with people, and if I could be a hermit, I would.
That being said, I LOVE this game, as evidenced by how many hours I've put into it.  For the first few months I played alone--and it is very much possible to do so!--and just enjoyed running around Tamriel and getting to actually experience other cultures beyond Nord, Imperial, and Dunmer (and even those three races' have additional lore and 'revisiting' the same areas, granted hundreds-thousands years before the single player games).  There is so much to do in this game, and even with my main I haven't experienced all of the stories offered, not by a long shot.  The game play is a lot of fun, and while initially disappointed that I couldn't have the same freedom as I had in Skyrim (picking up weapons/spells and becoming whatever I wanted throughout the game) I got used to it, and even within the class systems there is flexibility.  Combat is fun and challenging enough without someone throwing their keyboard out the window during ragequitting.
For those who don't mind delving into the social aspect (that I inevitably did), most of the time people are civil and are very nice to beginners, and there are a ton of guilds that are very new player friendly.  Very non-toxic socially most of the time, and when it is toxic, just hop to a different zone or minimize zone chat.  I can count how many times I've had a jerk interact with me (mainly during dungeons) on one hand.  I have a love/hate relationship with PVP, but when I go in with the expectation of dying frequently and going with friends, it is a very enjoyable experience.  Bring your soul shards!
TL;DR: Be you recluse or social butterfly, solo-player or PVE Champion or PVP Emperor, there is something to enjoy about this Elder Scrolls game. 10/10; would be abducted and sacrificed by Mannimarco to Molag Bal again.

If you can get this game on sale for a decent bargin (like I did), I can't recommend A Machine for Pigs enough.
The experience takes full advantage of it's Victorian London setting and weaves a disgusting, unsettling, but surpringly poignant narrative. Representing a factory as essentially a slaughterhouse for the detritus is nothing short of genius, and the emotional ramifications of the player's identity within this setting particulary puts me at unease.
However, fans of The Dark Descent will certainly notice the huge step back in terms of challenge and gameplay mechanics with A Machine for Pigs. If you solely wish to engage in a terrifically written interactive experience, this might not be an issue at all, but gamers looking for challenge will find disappointment.
If I have any real issue, it's that there doesn't seem to be enough here for A Macine for Pigs to exist as a sequel of a monetary value equal to its predecessor. Many mechanics and concepts from Dark Descent are discarded with basically nothing to fill that void (Although personally I'm glad they did away with the Insanity mechanic). This does mean the puzzles don't outstay their welcome like they begun to in Dark Descent, but it's still ultimately a full fledged sequel with half the content.
But on the other hand, I still try to judge A Machine for Pigs (and basically all pieces of entertainment), not by its cost nor its quantity, but its quality. And A Machine for Pigs was a very satisfying nightmare to endure. It's short, but makes every single moment count for something substantial, and has a story and setting that is considerably more engrossing than Dark Descent's. The ending is also superior.
If exploring a living, mechanical embodiment of humanity's capacity for efficient, apathetic evil is your jam, I can't think of a better way to spend 4-5 hours. Well, obviously there are several. But you should also look into this game. When it's cheap.

In which theChineseRoom aptly demonstrate that walking simulators are not and should not be the future of videogames. I cannot recommend this game to anyone.
The game, while billed as a horror story, did not at any point make me anything more than slightly unsettled. For a game about a machine literally dedicated to turning humans into canned meat (spoiler warning: if you didn't already gather it from the exceptionally ham-fisted foreshadowing in the trailers, "pig" is Oswald Mandus' slang for "human being") you really don't get to see much of that. There's nothing remotely as revulsion-inducing as the blood transfusion scene from the first game, nor does it feel like the monsters are in any way as threatening as the Gatherers - this is perhaps because we have no context for what precisely they are other than twisted abominations.
Oh, also, the invisible water monsters are back but they're utterly wasted due to never being used in a context remotely as terrifying as in Dark Descent.
In fact, that there's little sense of danger anywhere in this title, as the game will respawn you instantly upon death, usually having despawned the monster that killed you as a courtesy. Horror games rely upon a sense of vulnerability and weakness, a feeling that the threats you're dealing with are difficult or even impossible for you to overcome. While there is indeed no way of killing any enemy in this game, simply letting an enemy kill you becomes a perfectly legitimate tactic if you want to progress to the next area of the game.
On that note, allow me to bring up how linear the game is. Gone are the hub areas which require you to solve a specific problem (create a flesh-dissolving acid, fix the broken elevator, melt a padlock, transfuse yourself with poison-resistant blood from a rotting corpse etc.) by solving smaller problems and accumulating tools that you find scattered around various levels. They are replaced with a linear progression of levels that seem in rather a hurry to speed you to the next plot point. There's very little in the way of side paths or secret areas to find, and although many of the original Amnesia's levels also had this problem, almost everything of any relevance whatsoever in A Machine for Pigs is laid out such that you couldn't miss it if you tried.
The story itself attempts an exploration of themes like dehumanisation, bereavement, self-righteousness, guilt and the merger of magic and technology, and don't get me wrong, it has some excellent ideas, but they're betrayed by a criminally ham-fisted delivery. The game tries to wring pathos out of references to the various atrocities of the 20th century, but all the while struggles to make its central characters relatable. Half the dialogue sounds like something out of an opera or a Greek epic, but without the human element that allows suspension of disbelief. We are shown the story, even told what we should feel about it and why, but we're never allowed to discover these things on our own and make our own decisions.
If Frictional wanted a horror game, they should have made one themselves. If theChineseRoom wanted an exploration of Victorian morality, they should have made one themselves. It feels like two different concepts and two different styles of game have been clumsily mashed together, and would have done better to be left seperate.
