A really unfortunate failure of a game. Had alot of potential, but failed, and I feel it may be due to the nature of the Chinese Room's involvement. Overally, not...a buggy game as I've heard, but not a pretty one. It's very different to Dark Descent. No inventory system, so much less player involvement, so much less /content/. I beat this game in only a few hours. My major complaint was that it was dull. I barely had to do anything, usually it was follow a linear path, flick some switches, then continue on my path now that I've opened a door. In between, I was told a story. Not necessarily a bad story, but nothing as nice as Descent. What's more disappointing is the graphics though. They look rather dated, the lighting engine is bad, and the entire game I feel like I'm staring through some sort of green or brown filter, that made it so hard to enjoy the scenery. That's a real shame too, because I'm sure I would have enjoyed the steampunk aesthetics and perhaps the game alot more. Overall, its completely on rails. I died once, perhaps twice, and it seems it might have been scripted, because of the spawn point. But I might be wrong. One time I got chased by a water monster, but all I had to do was follow the literally fenced in pathway to the exit that was only a few yards away.
Inventory and light source having fuel is removed. Few things in the environment are interactable. The optimization is poor, I had frame drops in random areas staring at walls or locks that I had to get past. The graphics are poor and seem filtered. Overall I can hardly recommend this, unless its on sale, and even then (at the time of writing its 4$) it's not really much. With the release of SOMA coming up, I can hope that Frictional has learned from the errors of this game, and will improve in their next title. They certainly did with Black Plague after Overture, and Penumbra being my personal favorite Frictional Game, I hope that SOMA will live up to the shoes that Machine for pigs failed to fill, and Penumbra never finished.
I almost forgot. On a plus note, Jessica Curry has composed a wonderful score for this game, and that's really the only saving grace. It is absolutely gorgeous, but in my opinion its better to just buy that instead of the game. You'll enjoy yourself alot more.

TL;DR: Short and sweet, a fast paced action packed western FPS, with a nice art style and a well told story.
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a little gem of a game. With the western setting you will adventure through the recollections of Silas Greaves. The world has a very attractive cell shaded look and mixed with comic strip styled cut scenes gives the game a beautiful tone. Using a set of iconic weapons to dispatch your enemies in an arcade shooter. The story is told in a fun and interesting way with environments changing with the story as it is being told. With upgrade paths and solid mechanics such as bullet time and one on one duels the small package fits in a lot of gameplay.
Positive features:
-Good stylised graphics
-Fast paced arcade shooter with varying weapons
-Fantastic soundtrack
-Funny and interesting story
-Collectibles that add real backstory to the game
-Very well optimised
Negative features:
-Confusing navigation at times
-Difficulty seeing enemies in certain areas
To conclude Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a satisfying game which doesn't overstay its welcome, fun to play through more than once with other reasons to return to it. A well told story and a well-made game.

Eschalon: Book 2 is a sequel to Book 1 and therefore similar in everything it does. There are minor improvements, like faster walking, higher resolution, more skills... but nothing of great importance. Eschalon is a turn-based role-playing game series with astounding graphics and sound. Unfortunately gameplay is a bit slow, even for an ultima-like game. Doing almost anything in this game is fun but one thing: Walking. And there's a lot of walking. Walking through forests, walking through beaches, walking through deserts... and even more walking. The game has interesting dungeons and towns, filled with many secrets and details, unfortunately other locations are there just to be walked through. That is why I would rate this game as decent: It's a very enjoyable RPG, except for tedious walking through wilderness.
No.  Just no.  They didn't fix anything, they just put out a carbon copy of the first game.  Nope.

Like the first game, the game's development was largely kept secret; the developers of the Eschalon series believe that most game developers release too much information about their products, spoiling the game when you eventually play it.

I've rewritten this review from it's original format. Current Review is based on Patch 3.3 of Heavensward.
Regarding Heavensward, EVERYTHING it contains is not unlocked until you hit level 50, other than possibly the Au'ra race. Unless it's on sale, you don't need to buy Heavensward for anything until after you hit 50 and want to continue the story and current endgame.
Short Version: Very fun game, if you go into it with the expectation to enjoy the ride, not just the destination. You CAN enjoy the destination, but you'll miss out on a lot along the way if you tunnelvision to the end.
If you're expecting anything groundbreaking, you may want to look elsewhere. If you want a solid MMO that might last you longer than the usual MMOs(I've logged many months on it and few MMOs I play last a month let alone more), give it a shot. Either way, with the Free Trial/Demo they have now, you have no reason not to at least try.
ARR/Base Game:
It's FFXI 2.0 with a better engine, system, proper smooth controls, but gameplay closer to WoW's systems. Not current "WoD/Legion let's hold hands and every class is equal" WoW, but BC/Wrath WoW before it went to complete♥♥♥♥♥♥
It's a little slow to start, but once the Main Story gets going around 20-30, it becomes pretty cool if you actually invest in and pay attention to the story. The 2.5s GCD that everyone usually complains about is something you don't notice, most classes have non-GCD skills, auto attacks aren't part of that and every mob in the game is balanced around it so it's not something you notice unless you specifically look for it. You'll still be mashing your hotkeys just like any other MMO.
Heavensward:
Continues the story quite nicely, adds no real gameplay changes but why fix what ain't broken? They did add 3 new classes, Dark Knight (meh Tank), Astrologian (a Healer they still don't know how to make useful a year later), and Machinist (DPS with guns and pet turrets, does well but complex rotations)
They're still doing a decent job keeping with their "Major content patch every 3 months" update schedule, with minor patches every month and a half to add a few things in the interim. The next Expansion has been announced but no major details on it at the time of this review, but people're making pleny of guesses as to the new classes and that it'll be focused on retaking Ala Mhigo from the Empire based on Squeenix's usual hinting in the 3.3 storyline.

Final Fantasy 14: ARR is probally one of the best P2P mmo's I've played in recent years, even moreso in my opinon than WoW etc.
I've put a fair few hours into this game and played to max level at the time I left (lvl50). This game offers so much content and so many ways of playing that it is worth the £7 sub fee per month. Admitidly I did buy this game during a sale ( I picked it up for around £6) and it was worth every penny.
However I can only base my review on my experience that I gained and of course you get what you want out of the game.
Things I loved:
-Each class levels up seperatly meaning that reaching max level with one class doesn't mean the end of the game.
-Being able to switch class just by changing weapon/crafting item means seemless fluidity.
-Being in a large Free Company (guild) is very enjoyable and many players are very friendly.
-Even if you are not a huge Final Fantasy fan this is still a great MMO.
-A nice loot greed/roll system that is done by class rather than all rolling on loot to stop people grabbing gear.
-Daily quests/trails/challenges.
-Fat chocobos.
Things I didn't like so much:
-Difficulty curve can be quite high and the ingame macro system isn't explained as well as it could be.
-High level dungeon grinding for high level gear can be tedious especially as some gear can only be gained once per week.
-All games have idiots and griefters on them, this is no exception.
-£7 can be alot a month if you don't have alot of time to play.
-Language barried can be a problem especially in dungeons.
-People farming the later story missions skipping the cutscenes ruining it for first timers.
Overall I can highly rate this game from a MMO point of view and while it does have it's downsides I put many happy hours into the game and met alot of nice people. Even if you are not a final fantasy fan, this game is a very nice MMO that is easy to pick up and enjoy!

DISTRAINT is a short adventure thriller game about distraint; you'll play as a guy who forces people out of their home because of various reasons. The game is played in various houses (mostly the victim and MC) and is displayed in minimal lighting with a minimal gore and shocking scene in it.
I don't remember the bgm in the game. If there are some, it must have been played in a very low tone. However, the sfxs are awesome. They don't sound weird at all and the shocking scene sfxs can really make you surprised.
The game uses 2D graphics and i have to say that the graphics are awesome. I don't really know whether it's because of the lighting or the awesome sprite (i believe it's both though), but the game gives off the scary vibe (although it's not really scary), especially when the shocking scene comes out.
The game story is quite sad (despite of its gore and shocking scene) yet logical. All dialogues are flowing smoothly and i took a liking to it.
The game itself plays in a sidescroller format and just like any other adventure games, you have to find some items and use it in the right place. I got some trouble at the start where the game seems to freeze (i can't do anything except by opening inventory, flickering lights, and opening the menu) which i believe is because i'm pressing the button too fast. However, it's not happening at all when i progressed the game further which seems very weird. The tutorial also need some work since they made me confused (and most of them make you can't move).
I was also confused at the controls at the start because i just skipped through the instruction in the main menu. It turns out that the default action button is E and i thought that it's either space or enter. I ended up reconfiguring the keyboard buttons because of that.
There are also some puzzles where you have to solve something to proceed the game. Luckily, they are quite easy to do.
The other thing that i want to point out is the fact that you can't have multiple saves and you can't go to the main menu once you start the game (there is an option to exit from the game though).
Pros:
- 8 areas
- Puzzles
- Dark and grim story
Cons:
- Confusing tutorial
- No exit to main menu button
- No multiple saves

I got this on sale for $5, and after playing it for over a dozen hours, I'm already thinking it's one of the best "indie" computer RPG's. It's like the older Elder Scrolls games, but with Ultima-style graphics and interface. It has a freely explorable world that is viewed in a 3rd person, top-down perspective. Resolution is limited to 1024x768. But I actually dig the graphics and interface. What I dig even more is how *challenging* this RPG is, and how you can build and play your character in very different ways to deal with those challenges. It's not an action RPG, like Diablo; it's more of a thinking man's RPG, like Elder Scrolls. (Eventhough a big part of that challenge can be a pain, dealing with darkness and thirst/hunger and equipment wear/breakage.) Combat is a tactical blend of turn-based and real-time. Keeping your character alive can be hard, especially if you're not paying attention and if you're not putting enough thought into how you build and play your character.

If you are a old school rpg fan that like turned based combat with survival aspects and many gameplay mechanics I recommend this. Polished, improved and bigger. The plot is decent, but perhaps there's less intrigue and mystery behind it than in Book I, as you don't have full-blown amnesia this time. You explore much further into your history than before, however. The combat's been improved a lot, but sadly there are still issues with balance. Mages are more overpowered than before, there are a lot of skills not worth investing in, while those skills that *are* worth investing in are going to need a lot of investment. It's simply not safe to play as a rogue and neither is it safe to play purely as melee or ranged. I can see a melee/ranged character working, but only when carefully planned and combined with tier 2 magic, min/maxing everything.
If you take one piece of advice, don't fall for the allure of the difficulty settings. Not because they're difficult or anything, but because you get nothing from them, aside from a higher score at the end. Play on normal or challenging.

I'll also preface by saying I just started playing this, so I don't have as much experience or knowladge as my brother, but I've been playing FF games and MMORPGs for many many years so it's not too hard to grasp.
I am a massive FF fan. Have been my entire life, and always will be. It's a tried and true series that I always come back to (whether it's Kingdom Hearts, the OG FF games or new ones) and I gotta say, this one holds up at the top. If you've been missing the high-fantasy style that the series has maybe "lacked" in the past few years, look no further. This is true Final Fantasy spirit.
To break it down simply:
-The combat it tab-target, but just feels so much more exciting. Every hit packs a punch that isn't there with most games except TERA.
-I don't pay much attention to story in MMO's since 99% of the time it's pointless fetch quest filler with some over-arching theme that really doesn't go anywhere till endgame, so I mean don't expect to be paying $15/month (or whatever I'm paying) for a crazy story.
-The graphics (which I got on max) are incredible, let alone for an MMO, but it's to be expected for an FF game. The character model detail is amazing and the world looks so clear at all times of day.
Here's where things get realllllllyyyyyyy rough.
Square Enix has the worst support/instructions/literally everything that isn't the game itself is the worst I've ever experienced.
Let me tell you a story.
I long while ago in a far off land, my brother bought FF14 on PS4 on my PSN account. Simple. Started playing till I kicked him off, so he buys it on my Steam. Simple. Well. No. Not that simple. One day I decided to start playing myself but because the PSN account is now linked to his SE account, I was unable to even change the USERNAME box on the FF14 menu when trying to log in. Okay, so I tried Steam, still, when I enter my details it asks me for a registration key (as if I didn't already own the game?) I've rewritten this review from it's original format. Current Review is based on Patch 3.3 of Heavensward.
Regarding Heavensward, EVERYTHING it contains is not unlocked until you hit level 50, other than possibly the Au'ra race. Unless it's on sale, you don't need to buy Heavensward for anything until after you hit 50 and want to continue the story and current endgame.
Short Version: Very fun game, if you go into it with the expectation to enjoy the ride, not just the destination. You CAN enjoy the destination, but you'll miss out on a lot along the way if you tunnelvision to the end.
If you're expecting anything groundbreaking, you may want to look elsewhere. If you want a solid MMO that might last you longer than the usual MMOs(I've logged many months on it and few MMOs I play last a month let alone more), give it a shot. Either way, with the Free Trial/Demo they have now, you have no reason not to at least try.
ARR/Base Game:
It's FFXI 2.0 with a better engine, system, proper smooth controls, but gameplay closer to WoW's systems. Not current "WoD/Legion let's hold hands and every class is equal" WoW, but BC/Wrath WoW before it went to complete♥♥♥♥♥♥
It's a little slow to start, but once the Main Story gets going around 20-30, it becomes pretty cool if you actually invest in and pay attention to the story. The 2.5s GCD that everyone usually complains about is something you don't notice, most classes have non-GCD skills, auto attacks aren't part of that and every mob in the game is balanced around it so it's not something you notice unless you specifically look for it. You'll still be mashing your hotkeys just like any other MMO.
Heavensward:
Continues the story quite nicely, adds no real gameplay changes but why fix what ain't broken? They did add 3 new classes, Dark Knight (meh Tank), Astrologian (a Healer they still don't know how to make useful a year later), and Machinist (DPS with guns and pet turrets, does well but complex rotations)
They're still doing a decent job keeping with their "Major content patch every 3 months" update schedule, with minor patches every month and a half to add a few things in the interim. The next Expansion has been announced but no major details on it at the time of this review, but people're making pleny of guesses as to the new classes and that it'll be focused on retaking Ala Mhigo from the Empire based on Squeenix's usual hinting in the 3.3 storyline.

Final Fantasy 14: ARR is probally one of the best P2P mmo's I've played in recent years, even moreso in my opinon than WoW etc.
I've put a fair few hours into this game and played to max level at the time I left (lvl50). This game offers so much content and so many ways of playing that it is worth the £7 sub fee per month. Admitidly I did buy this game during a sale ( I picked it up for around £6) and it was worth every penny.
However I can only base my review on my experience that I gained and of course you get what you want out of the game.
Things I loved:
-Each class levels up seperatly meaning that reaching max level with one class doesn't mean the end of the game.
-Being able to switch class just by changing weapon/crafting item means seemless fluidity.
-Being in a large Free Company (guild) is very enjoyable and many players are very friendly.
-Even if you are not a huge Final Fantasy fan this is still a great MMO.
-A nice loot greed/roll system that is done by class rather than all rolling on loot to stop people grabbing gear.
-Daily quests/trails/challenges.
-Fat chocobos.
Things I didn't like so much:
-Difficulty curve can be quite high and the ingame macro system isn't explained as well as it could be.
-High level dungeon grinding for high level gear can be tedious especially as some gear can only be gained once per week.
-All games have idiots and griefters on them, this is no exception.
-£7 can be alot a month if you don't have alot of time to play.
-Language barried can be a problem especially in dungeons.
-People farming the later story missions skipping the cutscenes ruining it for first timers.
Overall I can highly rate this game from a MMO point of view and while it does have it's downsides I put many happy hours into the game and met alot of nice people. Even if you are not a final fantasy fan, this game is a very nice MMO that is easy to pick up and enjoy!

Simple at first glance but delightfully complex once you get playing. I needed a light game for my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ school computer and so I gave this a try. I am pleased with what I got.
The premise is simple, you are an immigration officer tasked with reviewing the papers of incoming travelers. You will be given certain rules to follow but at the most basic you have to ensure that their names match on each document, that the region they hail from actually exists and that their picture and gender matches the person in front of you. Before you know it you will be handling 3 or 4 different papers and making sure expiration dates are good, that names match, that passport numbers are okay and that the seal is not counterfeit (oh and also that the person is not wanted by the goverment or that they arent carrying weapons!). Sprinkle in a few random events and odd characters, plus a simple economy system (you are paid per person inspected and you have to keep your family alive; there are a few "less than legal" ways to make money too) and you have yourself a pleasantly intricate game.
I am not one for challenging games but it doesnt quite feel that way. There are 20 different endings and each choice decides what ending you get.
In a sale, this game is a steal. The premise, the writting and the execution is fantastic, but do no expect great graphics (the game 47mb!).
If you are looking for an break from the usual video game or something to make you ponder what it would be really like to be an immigration office in an totalitarian state (because who hasnt?!), then this is your game.

Despite the warnings I went into A Machine for Pigs with bright eyes and an open mind. It only took about 10 minutes to crush that optimism.
The supposed sequel to The Dark Descent casts you as a Victorian-era inventor and industrialist, wandering his home in search of his rather ghostly little boys. The chase leads him into the sprawling factory complex he designed for automating the butchering of pigs. Now, Victorian horror is a rich vein to mine, and the setting of a mechanized slaughterhouse really can't be beat. So I hope you can understand the crushing disappointment that comes with seeing this setup wasted. In my first 90-minute session, nothing happened. Nothing. I wandered my mansion, I turned on some machines, I wandered a factory, I changed some fuses, I wandered outside, I turned on a truck, I quit. At no point did I encounter an enemy or anything even remotely threatening.
What I did encounter was a lot of poorly-paced jumpscares in the form of loud noises out of the blue and glimpses of scurrying NPCs. Understand that the original Amnesia did the same thing, but with a much better sense of moderation and coupled with an exceptionally strong sound design. A Machine for Pigs completely fails to build the same atmosphere, trading the mysterious whisperings and footsteps of the castle for the playful requests of ghost children (who basically exist to point you to your next objective) and awkward monologues recounting past events. Gone is the sanity system or the balancing of light and dark, along with the entire inventory system as well. You have an infinite lantern at your disposal, which you will need because the lighting in this game is a bit wonky, what with wall lamps and candles failing to cast any significant illumination. Hilariously, the game still uses the obnoxious visual sanity effects without the system... it just hits you with them at scripted points.
I was hoping there was an interesting story here, but the central theme is mangled worse than the creatures you catch fleeting glimpses of. The monologues and notes are disjointed and mostly unrelated. The attempt to write in Victorian styles also does more harm than good, making some notes near incomprehensible. In the end, there's none of the magic of Amnesia here at all. The atmosphere is botched, there's almost nothing to interact with and no reason to search the environment, and the story is nonsensical and poorly conveyed. I was certain there was no way A Machine for Pigs could be such a step down, but my goodness was I wrong.

Quick summary:
Bit Heroes is a mmo/dungeon crawler with a good community, a lot of unique features, and a great pixel art style but where it will lose most people, is the energy system.
Pros: as stated above, unique features, great community, a great pixel style, Progression is pretty solid, (even when you don't spend money) Fun and diffrent play styles, raids, dungeons, familars, pets, accesories, and more. Theres a discord (that I can't find the link to for the life of me) where people give there help, the devs do Q&As and more. The devs really care for their players and the game they made. There is a bunch of diffrent energys, and many ways to use them. You can use you friends in a lot of the battles. (not all though, and you'll find out why if you play *wink* *wink*) Also the devs are constantly making new things and giving the players stuff, f2p or otherwise (when they do its always equal as long as its not tied to ranks).
Pro/con: Auto system... most people only really use it though for stuff they know they can do 100%...
Cons: Energy systems, Rng is a B, if you spend money you will progress much faster mid/late game with raids, and even though the devs really do care about their game and their community, they have to make money, so they give you a lot of options to better yourself in game with real money.
Overall: If you can look past rng cruelity, and the sometimes harsh energy systems/micro-transactions, Bit heroes is a fun mmo with a lot of great people in it, backed behind good developers who are willing to give us plenty in return for us just playing their game.
PS: if you need help, go to the world chat and ask very nicely for some/ask for the discord and ask there.

You can't blast a rabbit w/ a .300 and get a score as its not an ethical round to take the game with.  The tracking is awesome.  The wildlife interaction is awesome.  The reserves are awesome. I actually got this game because I just finished reading Preacher and felt like playing a Western. Oddly enough, the series itself was partly inspired by the Saint of Killers from Preacher. Needless to say, I was impressed with what I played. I wasn't too aware of the series in the first place, but after playing Gunslinger, I want to go back and play the other entries.
You play as a man named Silas Greeves who walks into a bar and gains all the patrons' attention immediately. You then begin to tell them a story, and that's what you end up playing. As he tells his tale, you go through different typical Wild West environments, which change on the fly as Silas changes his story as he goes along, taking out whoever is in your way. Catching a bounty or getting revenge, everyone dies. And it never gets old, as you have a cool upgrade system that lets you earn experience points and use it on specific types of play styles. Ranged Rifle, Pistols, or Close Range Shotgun are available and mix up the gameplay very well. The story itself and voice acting was very good as well. Metal Gear Solid fans might notice Solidus Snake as Silas and Colonel Campbell as Ben.
If you have any interest in a unique shooter or a cool arcade like, over the top, action western game, I'd recommend it.

If the argument is made that video games cannot be art, one need not look farther than Papers, Please for proof otherwise. This is a fantastic, artistic game. It drips with atmosphere, the music is grippingly threatening, characters are empathetic, and you truly feel overwhelmed with responsibility - do the "right thing" by not accepting a bribe, or take the bribe in order to feed your family? It's the best kind of karma system, where your decisions have direct consequences, rather than an arbitrary "good vs. evil" meter. If I had any complaint, it's that I wish there was no time limit during missions, if only so I could take my time; however, the time limit does add to the intensity and it forces you to make hasty decisions, so I cannot rightfully criticize the game for that. I highly recommend Papers, Please.

Years ago I was flipping through TV channels and saw that Phone Booth was on. I was curious how a movie confined to more or less a single locale could be interesting. I didn't see it in theaters because I wasn't convinced, but watching it on TV was ultimately worth it. A decade later I saw pixel art style game advertised as a border crossing / document verification simulator. I'd like to say that my biases about judging a book by a cover had been eliminated, but let's be real, they haven't. There are and will continue to be plenty of pixel-art games worth the price of admission, but the subject matter of Papers, Please wasn't immediately exciting.
Papers, Please is as cathartic as it is tense and addicting. Specific elements of the game become almost Pavlovian, and the presentation immediately puts you in the inspectors shoes. It didn't feel like a far-fetched scenario from the stories that I've heard, but it was an immediate experience that always returns instantly whenever the game begins. From the soundtrack to the excellently implemented sound effects.

Here's the thing a lot of people aren't telling you. This game is not bad. It's not terrible. It's actually decently scary. The problem is, since it's called Amnesia, you have to compare it to the game that came before. THAT'S where the negative opinions come from. This game isn't broken, or boring, or unscary. It just doesn't come close to reaching the bar set by The Dark Descent. The first Amnesia game wasn't expected to be such a huge success. It was released when Let's Plays were becoming popular, so it gained it's cult hit status through that. This left Frictional Games in a situation where they needed to pump out a sequal that met this expectations they were unprepared for. So they asked for help. Chinese Room is great at atmosphere and enviornments, which this game has in spades. However the horror element is lacking. The monsters are scary for one or two encounters (Of the only seven the game actually has) and once you figure out you can outrun and outsmart them, they stop being a source of terror. The puzzles were simple in the first game, but they are ridiculous now. It barely ever goes beyond "Pick this up and carry it to this to continue," and they are few and far between anyway. They only people I wouldn't recommend this game to are people who still hold The Dark Descent on it's (deserved) throne of "Best Horror Game Ever." Everyone else could still enjoy this.

Once in a while, a great game comes out. That game becomes famous. And then, when a sequel comes out, it’s made simpler, easier and more “accessible”. That’s what happened here.
The only good things about it are the extraordinary voice acting and the story. The actors knew this was a serious game and took it that way and the story is good enough to keep you from uninstalling before you finish it.
You no longer have to manage which torches or candles you light up. There’s no more insanity, so you can be in the dark and look at enemies all the time you want. Puzzles are mostly just picking something up and taking it from one place to the other.
This game is also hardly scary. It only scared me three times in four hours.
It doesn’t have many jump scares, but you don’t need them to make a game scary. Some of the things that made the prequel scary were moments like hiding in a room and then, when an enemy entered the room, hoping he wouldn’t look at where you were. Or having an enemy chasing you and you knew you couldn’t outrun it. You had to close doors or setup obstacles on your way. The sequel has none of this.
My main problem with it is the difficulty. I’ve been playing video games regularly since 1993 (even earlier, if you count electronic games) and this was the very first non-racing/sports/strategy game ever that I finished without dying. And I’m not even that good. Before this, my best survivability record was only dying twice when I finished “Sonic Chaos” for the first time with Tails, when I was a teenager. When I became aware of my “invincibility”, I stopped being afraid of the pigs.
“Amnesia: The Dark Descent” will be known in History as one of the greatest horror games. “Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs” will be a footnote saying there was a sequel. Well, I hope Frictional Games made plenty of money with this use of the Amnesia name.

I think this is a really neat MMORPG. It distances itself from most others in how the developers appear to care more about the world and the lore of Tamriel, instead of pandering to those who demand a game which is entirely composed of mashing as many buttons as possible. The devs are clearly passionate about this world and really know their stuff, seeing as how there is a fairly blatant discussion of CHIM in the latest expansion. Furthermore, quests are rarely the stereotypical "go collect 35 bear pelts", and are all fully voiced with at least intriguing stories.
What I particularly enjoy about this game, however, is the level scaling; as your character levels up it get weaker rather than stronger, and you then supplement that weakness with higher gear. What this results in is the ability to travel anywhere on the worldmap and not worry about being too strong or weak. Of course, that isn't to say your character forever performs at the exact same level; endgame gear definitely provides advantages. But what this does mean is you have true freedom to explore at your own pace. And that really helps set this game apart from others.

This is certainly a decent MMO, one of the better ones currently available, however, I find I can't recommend it.
I really wanted to love this game, and the crafting was really great...at least until you got into higher level stuff.  It was with great sorrow that I realized that the higher tiers of crafting had some bizarre, invisible-except-for-certain-times-of-day mechanic putting my happy gathering spree to an immediate, screeching halt.  I understand the need to make things rare in order to maintain the economy, but seriously?  Faced with the choice of standing, waiting for hours for a single node to spawn or buying it from the market, buying it from the market seems a much better choice, at least, until you see the prices, and realise that it would take you just as many hours of harvesting regular things to sell to afford one.  I suppose this is 'balance' but it certainly wasn't fun, and crushed my hopes as a crafter.
The game will also 'force' you to participate in queue-for-group dungeon content to advance your main story quest, and I found unless you queued as tank or healer, you'd be waiting sometimes hours for a group (which may or may not even stay together to finish the dungeon!) just to advance your main, storyline quest.  I eventually made it to the end, but after that I was left with just a sense of overall disillusionment.  Add that to the pointlessness of the crafting at higher tiers, and well...
As I said, it is one of the better MMOs out there, but I don't feel it has anything for the 'long haul' - unless you fancy queueing for groups and sitting afk at node spawn points for months on end, which ultimately killed it for me.  Perhaps if you have unlimited playtime to do the time-sink routine it'd be worth a play.

For a two hour horror game, I'm more than happy to say this game was a fun little horror experience. Sure, it may be a little overpriced regularly since the game does only last two hours, but there's always sales happening, so it's not hard to grab it at a cheaper price.
Storywise, I liked Distraint a lot. The main character is human in his actions, especially with the moral dilemmas that he has. Personally, I liked all the surreal horror. It was done pretty well, and blurred the lines between what was real and what your character was just making up. There weren't a ton of jumpscares, and some of the scares were pretty unsettling (and that's coming from a person who isn't unsettled very easily). There was a great atmosphere that only got weirder as the story progressed.
In terms of improvement, the spelling errors and typos should really be fixed, considering how vital the dialogue is to the story. A misspelling really takes me out of the action. That, and some variations in the character's walking speed would be nice, considering there are times that you're supposed to be running away, and the character only does the same little waddle that he's been doing the whole game. That means to me that he's not scared, or everything else is just really, really slow.
Other than that, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game for $0.99 to any horror fan. It's fun, with a lot of things that you wouldn't expect to see.

Let me just start by saying that it took me just 4 hours to get through the game on normal difficulty. CoJ isn't a long game. It is, however, an extremley fun, brutal arcadey shooter with one of the most unreliable narrator
telling the story. Eh, I should probably start from the beginning.
Unlike the other CoJ's, Gunslinger isn't an open world roaming cowboy game. Instead, it's a more traditional 'on-rails' shooter, and leans pretty heavily on arcade elements; combos, 'Concentration' (Bullet time), Actual bullet time and the like. For the story, this makes perfect sense, the main character is called Silas Greaves, a now elderly bounty hunter who walks into a saloon in 1910 and starts telling his story to the patrons, getting more and more drunk in the process.
What makes this great is that it excuses the really, really crazy later game elements. He's drunk off of his♥♥♥♥♥ so the shotgun abilities start to make sense; they never were ornate, golden, unlimited-ammunition-with-no-reloads machines of death, he was just making up stories about 'em. And it's awesome.
Look. it's kinda pointless for me to keep rambling like this. Spend the money on an awesome arcadey shooter, or somewhere else.
*Pulls back the hammer on his pistol*

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a fast-paced, arcade style shoot-em-up set in the wild west.
You follow the story of Silas Greaves who has a vendetta against the man who murdered his brother. Along the way you will meet the legends of the fabled west such as Jesse James, Billy the Kid, and old Pat Garrett.
The environments consist of everything you want to see. From train robberies to ghost towns to shoot outs in saloons, Call of Juarez has all the sceneries covered. The art itself is quite pretty; the engine uses a cell-shading art style similar to Borderlands and gives it that comic book feel.
The gameplay itself isn't super in depth but the simplicity and speed keep the game fresh. There are three types of weapons: pistols, rifles, and shotguns - with each weapon having two subtypes. There is also a pretty sweet "concentration" mode where time slows down and you can take on an army for a few seconds.
The story unfolds in the form of a narration - similar in style to Bastion. As you journey through each level, Silas narrates the adventure in real time. The voice acting is superb.
Overall, for 15 bucks, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is more than a deal. It's a steal. It's better than many tripple A studio titles and at a fraction of the price (you can get this on sale for 7-8 bucks, sometimes even less). The art is gorgeous, the story is fun to listen to, and the action is fast paced and gritty.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger takes about 10 hours to complete. Additionally, upon completion,  there is a New Game Plus mode and an increased difficulty option.

Worst in the series if you judged dark souls 3 by it's potential. The best thing you will hear about it is the pvp. And even then you will have to go through the awful pve just to get the gear you need for pvp.
Dark souls is a series that is about both the single player experience AND the multiplayer experience. The game only focuses on the pvp and that is not how dark souls is meant to be. And when I mean focus, I mean priority. All of the games mechanics are made and balanced for multiplayer. Making the pve side of things even more abandoned than it already is, especially when you see that all the enemy placements are literally just mob spawns excluding the rare moments where they give you one lone enemy to introduce it to you before they gank the souls right out of you. From software attempted to make up for it with the "Scholar of the first sin" DLC.
The DLC is great, adding new gear areas making the pve experiences actaully enjoyable. But once you come to your senses you will become infuriated because the DLC should have just been the base game. It is that good compared to the original world and it makes it looks even worse.
In the end, this is a dark souls game the should only be played for the DLC and pvp. The base game pve should not be dwelled upon and its best to just get through it so you can get to the real good stuff. If there is anything you should linger upon its the lore of it, at least that will always be good. I cannot recommend this game because of its history. But if you are a fan of dark souls and you want to play them all, then I'd say it is worth it. Because it may not be the dark souls 2 that we should have gotten, but it is still a dark souls game.

After replaying Dark Souls 1 and then relatively shortly after playing this game, I now understand why people disliked it.
Dark Souls 2 is sort of 2 steps forward, 1 step backwards. I'll try to give some examples
Dark Souls 1 did have some balancing problems, especially with dual wielding, which are improved in this game. Being able to teleport to any bonfire is debatable. I like it, but I understand people who don't. The UI and inventory is improved, especially allowing to carry 3 weapons per hand and (I believe) 10 "belt" items.
But having to teleport to the central hub area just to level up (done by talking to an NPC, which always gives some lines of dialogue first...) - why?
The fact that you lose 10% maximum health upon death, up to a maximum of 50% is just stupid. You're making it even harder for people who are already struggling.
Getting hit through walls is somehow even worse than in the predecessor.
Most (all?) enemies do not respawn after killing them a sufficient amount of times. This is not Dark Souls like. Also it seems that the enemy placement was designed around that. Put together a big pile of enemies who attack you all at once (making sneaky counter/backstab builds much harder) instead of interesting 1v1/1v2 situations is just boring and bad.
I usually just fought them until I either still had enough HP after or until they no longer spawned.
Reducing the amount of invincibility frames from dodging is good in my opinion, as it requires more skill now. Also being attackable during backstabs is good in theory, but with the cluttering of the enemies it just makes backstabbing nearly unviable.
There's probably some other gameplay elements I forgot/can not comment on.
So much for the gameplay, now about some other problems.
First off: Why is there no Steam Cloud support for savegames? Even Dark Souls 1 had that after they moved away from Games For Windows Live (and before it still had cloud saves, but on GFWL obviously)
I pre-ordered this game (I regret it so much) because of how good Dark Souls 1 was (gameplay-wise... yes it was a subpar port, but I thought From Soft could improved upon this, which they mostly did to be fair).
Okay so some bugs were there on launch, of course, that's expected, but it took them a year or more to fix some bugs like:
-The first time you start the game, the "press start" screen ignored the volume settings - I ended up removing my headset for that screen because it was so loud*
-The weapon's durability degredation was tied to the frame rate, meaning that your weapons would break twice as fast if you're on 60 FPS
-Online was unplayable (not only for me, many others also had this problem). Insane lags. People invading you, doing nothing and when you attack them all of a sudden a bunch of hits from beyond and the invader teleporting behind you to backstab you... I ended up getting a P2P blocker because of that. (I actually don't know if this lag issue is fixed by now)
And then there's Scholar of the First Sin (SotFS), the "definitive" edition of Dark Souls 2. It's a full-price (you got a discount if you owned Dark Souls 2, however you did not get an additional discount if you had the Season Pass!), different version of Dark Souls 2 with a seperated online mode (seperated form Dark Souls 2 non-SotFS). It has some improvements like newer DirectX and 64 bit and I believe some small additional content, but I don't know, because I don't buy From Software products anymore.
Releasing SotFS and not giving me a fair discount for owning the game with all DLCs and basically taking players away from my (unplayable, laggy) online experience is just bad business.
Did I mention that you can't even transfer your savegame from DS2 to SotFS?
So to sum it up, it is (by now) a decent-ish game. It's still Dark Souls, but the first one just feels better. But do not buy this, not even SotFS, don't support this greedy, exploitative behaviour of the developer (and publisher?) and negligence towards their game!
P.S: If you, for some reason, still feel the need to buy this game, go for SotFS instead, because there you actually have some online players, but you should not buy it for more than 10€.
Do note though that Dark Souls 1 has, on average, more players than SotFS...
*edit: They actually still haven't fixed this bug. Please do not buy From Software products...

If the argument is made that video games cannot be art, one need not look farther than Papers, Please for proof otherwise. This is a fantastic, artistic game. It drips with atmosphere, the music is grippingly threatening, characters are empathetic, and you truly feel overwhelmed with responsibility - do the "right thing" by not accepting a bribe, or take the bribe in order to feed your family? It's the best kind of karma system, where your decisions have direct consequences, rather than an arbitrary "good vs. evil" meter. If I had any complaint, it's that I wish there was no time limit during missions, if only so I could take my time; however, the time limit does add to the intensity and it forces you to make hasty decisions, so I cannot rightfully criticize the game for that. I highly recommend Papers, Please.

Years ago I was flipping through TV channels and saw that Phone Booth was on. I was curious how a movie confined to more or less a single locale could be interesting. I didn't see it in theaters because I wasn't convinced, but watching it on TV was ultimately worth it. A decade later I saw pixel art style game advertised as a border crossing / document verification simulator. I'd like to say that my biases about judging a book by a cover had been eliminated, but let's be real, they haven't. There are and will continue to be plenty of pixel-art games worth the price of admission, but the subject matter of Papers, Please wasn't immediately exciting.
Papers, Please is as cathartic as it is tense and addicting. Specific elements of the game become almost Pavlovian, and the presentation immediately puts you in the inspectors shoes. It didn't feel like a far-fetched scenario from the stories that I've heard, but it was an immediate experience that always returns instantly whenever the game begins. From the soundtrack to the excellently implemented sound effects.

Bit heroes is an awesome example of how refined simplicity can provide countless hours of fun. The game provides players with a surprising amount of content that never seems to get old. I have always been wary of "The grind". Repetition in video games for me, just isn't fun. For some reason, though, this game never does. The admittedly few lines of dialogue are cheeky and witty. The amination is amazingly detailed, and remains true to the genre (Classic 8, and 16 bit games). The animations are even fairly cheeky at times. Join a guild, find friends to aid you in your quests, and try to find the best gear there is. The multiplayer aspects of this game are somewhat overexaggerated however. This ultimately means nothing to me, as the game is still just as fun anyway. The only time you are really playing in real time with other players is in the Boss Battles. Other modes, such as PVP pit you against other players' teams, but are controlled by the AI. That being said, there is still an amazing community within this game. very few games I've played have had the amount of players willing to help new players as I've encountered in Bit Heroes. The community almost makes this game in and of itself.
Possibly the biggest complaints you'll see for Bit Heroes are the energy system and the microtransactions. Bear in mind, that this is a port of a mobile game. Keep in mind also, that while you can certainly pay to advance quicker, you never need to. Most players in this game never spend a dime in-game, apart from perhaps the starter bundle (Which goes a long way to helping the developers of this game, and is worth ever penny at the point in the game it is offered).
All that in mind, I cannot recommend this game enough. Get ready for countless hours of adventures. I hope you enjoy this game as much as I have.

Played a while back for quite some time then ended up leaving due to lack of time. My IGN:SinfulOwl
I'll try to make this as short and sweet as possible.
1) Isn't pay to win, true you can pay to refill energy and attempt more runs of raids and such with it however doesnt guarentee that sweet legendary gear your hoping for. I've seen players refill raid shards back to back running up to 200 raids with no loot (except experience ). I've also seen free to play players run a few raids and get some loot. Up to RNG my friend.
2) In regards to low amounts of energy or rather people complaining about there being nothing to do. Your energy bar limit raises as your level increases. You also have the ingame chat rooms which are called World Chat 1,2 and 3. Each housing several moderators to ensure spam and guildlines are followed. The chat rooms are excellent places to make new friends and possibly add high level players to help you progress easier.
3)Friends, they are needed. Depending on what your doing will depict if you can use your friends or not. Pvp only allows the use of yourself and your familiars ( creatures which can captured either by luck of rng with some gold or persuading with gems). GVG means yourself and your guildmates can be used to fight other guilds. Dungeons can be completed either with familiars or friends. Raids as well however the higher the difficulty the more chances you'll need stronger friends. World bosses are events that randoms people can join or you can invite friends to join to partake in a boss battle. There is also another two modes which alternate given the weekly reset timer which both permit yourself and the use of your familiars only.
4)Familiars, every creature you'll fight can be captured. However gold or gems are needed. Gems for a guarenteed capture and gold for chance of capture. It's recommend to save your gems for only legendary familiars as the more common ones are more often encountered.
5) Guilds, excellent places to meet and join like minded people to play and talk with. Guilds also provide special perks depending on what your guild chooses to invest in with guild bucks ( which can be obtained from GVG events and such). You can invest in more guild member slots, more energy, more raid shards, higher percentage to persuade familiars, etc.
6) Discord, this game has it's own discord channel which offers help and questions, talking with devs, giving suggestions that the community can vote on, art channel for fan art, general art, game mechanics to discuss the tiny details and numbers,adding channel to get free adds from higher peeps, hunger games to have a chance at higher lvl friends,etc.
7) Would i recommend this game? Yes, yes i would. I played for roughly a year and loved it. I met some amazing people and was a part of one the top guilds ( Ironthrone). I laughed, i got mad at rng and took parts in events. Ultimately i spent most of time as Free to play and i enjoyed it, so give it a go and see where you end up at. If you do decide to start playing do say Hi to Pavu, MrOwl, TeaOwl, Deadfall, or anyone from Ironthrone for me. Just tell em SinfulOwl said hi :)

Every sentence I structured had no effect no matter how well crafted and thought out. Loosing hope and giving up sitting to wonder what if for the rest of my days. The fact that no matter how hard you try you have to be the one who eventually says "Goodbye" That is hard. This is certainly a decent MMO, one of the better ones currently available, however, I find I can't recommend it.
I really wanted to love this game, and the crafting was really great...at least until you got into higher level stuff.  It was with great sorrow that I realized that the higher tiers of crafting had some bizarre, invisible-except-for-certain-times-of-day mechanic putting my happy gathering spree to an immediate, screeching halt.  I understand the need to make things rare in order to maintain the economy, but seriously?  Faced with the choice of standing, waiting for hours for a single node to spawn or buying it from the market, buying it from the market seems a much better choice, at least, until you see the prices, and realise that it would take you just as many hours of harvesting regular things to sell to afford one.  I suppose this is 'balance' but it certainly wasn't fun, and crushed my hopes as a crafter.
The game will also 'force' you to participate in queue-for-group dungeon content to advance your main story quest, and I found unless you queued as tank or healer, you'd be waiting sometimes hours for a group (which may or may not even stay together to finish the dungeon!) just to advance your main, storyline quest.  I eventually made it to the end, but after that I was left with just a sense of overall disillusionment.  Add that to the pointlessness of the crafting at higher tiers, and well...
As I said, it is one of the better MMOs out there, but I don't feel it has anything for the 'long haul' - unless you fancy queueing for groups and sitting afk at node spawn points for months on end, which ultimately killed it for me.  Perhaps if you have unlimited playtime to do the time-sink routine it'd be worth a play.

"If we make it big and loud and dark poeple with think it's scary!" Surprise. No they wont. Pewdiepie will be happy to do a promo where he overeacts, but this game is not actually scary.
The puzzle elements are gone, the atmosphere isn't subtle, the monsters are laughably easy to deal with, the twists are very easy to predict and there really isn't a proper conclusion. This game wanted so badly to be The Dark Descent but never actually realized what made TDD so good.

So I guess i'll break this up:
PVE:
Questing:
Story: The questing is incredibly boring if you don't want to listen to the story as it has you doing literally the exact same things over and over again just reskinned and in the end nothing really changes. On top of all of this you have no real choice (just the illusion of choice) and in some cases you're simply asked "Do you want good reward? Choose bad guy option." "You want slightly less good reward? Choose good option." although granted they don't straight up say this it's worded differently.
Rewards: The EXP and Loot do not come anywhere close to just running Dungeons all day or grinding at one spot for levels and you're forced to run Dungeons if you want decent loot at your level.
Mobs:
Mob Placement: Mob placement feels like they looked at a MMORPG that literally plays itsself and only requires clicking to accept quests and turn them in (auto pathing and auto fighting) called Sword Art Online and said "Yes we want mobs to sit in weird locations in groups as well."
Mobs Themselves: Quite bland and boring just reskins of each other with new attacks. They chase you to the end of the world attacking you and turn around and run away when you try to attack them. On top of this there are locations where mobs do almost no damage to you and where mobs will 3 shot you and are grouped together in like teams of 6. Wouldn't be too bad if you know... they gave MORE exp than the others?
Mob Attacks: All have an attack that stun you so it makes running away difficult, all have an AOE attack that you could care less about and they say you can stun them to stop it, and all have an attack that the game recommends you block (50/50 as to if the attack will knock you down and stun you).
Bosses:
World Bosses: Quite possibly the best part of it really. They seem to be somewhat challenging and in most cases require you to as you'd expect attack with a team.
Normal Bosses: Incredibly stupid. Many of them also require you to either be an absolute god at playing or to have multiple people attack them with you or you can simply just be max level. They have stuns that stun you forever and then attack you until you're almost dead and some of which even though are ranged and take quite a while to get to you freeze your character (of which apparently you can block vomit with a staff?) and stun you.
PVP: Haven't tried.
Misc: Feels incredibly dumbed down for console. There is this terrible mechanic that ruins a sense of progression where all it does it make your items and stuff weaker as you level instead of just making items get better as you level. Out of all your skills only a hand full are useful and quite a few are pretty much required to be using in all situations. No different styles of playing. Game also has a terribly overpriced trashy system to "help pay for the servers and staff, etc" because apparently $40 and a $50 DLC can't that effectively feels like a mobile game and because of this they have incredibly long times on everything forcing you to come back every day to make them hope you continue playing the game.
Overall: I am only playing this game because my friend gave me it from his Humblemonthly along with a 15 day ESOTrash membership. I would personally spend probably a maximum of $5 on this game and the DLC (of which i'm assuming is the same garbage as the base game).

Hell yes do I recommend this game.
Graphics:
Not the photorealistic super-graphics of many AAA titles (or at least, attempted photorealistic) this game has gone for a painted style to it. In my opinon it is absolutely GORGEOUS. The colours are well chosen and blended, the enviroments are suitable atmospheric and the lighting is always good for the scenario, wether you are running in terror from a Jerk, slinking through the back alleys or going through the blindingly bright areas of process country (No, we can't stop here).
Music:
Arguably some of the best tracks I've heard in a while, the game goes from fast and tense battle music to a haunting orchestral piece in a cutscene. Many of the track even seem to be affected by the enviroment, when the process are out in force expect your music to be techno-influenced as if the process even got the music.
Enemies:
Ah, the process. As with everything else in the game they are beautifully done from the teleporting she-b****, broodmother of the younglady to the ground smashing tank of the Jerk to the carpet bombing cluckers every enemy is interesting and unique.
The names themselves are rather fun too as they are named on the fly by one of the characters. For example the shielding enemy is named a "cheerleader" after the transistor pokes fun at them, calling them that. The Jerk (one of the toughest non-boss enemies) is called that because frankly it is one.
They also work very well together, each enemy filling a niche of it's own. There is no overlap and you will see every enemy in a different light, I love fighting the youngladies and Jerks because they're interesing and hate fighting the fetches because they're little ****s
Battle system:
The battle system of Transistor is simple yet complex at the same time. I wont go into a huge amount of detail but you get functions, each function has an Active (used as a move), Upgrade (used to improve an active) or a Passive (Used to improve you) ability.
Load() for example is an explosive move. It creates a bomb when used as an Active, it makes other abilities explode or have a larger area of effect when used as an upgrade and will randomly spawn bombs when you use it as a passive ability.
Jaunt() is a teleportation move and if you upgrade Load() with it then Load() will auto-detonate instead of needing to be detonated with an attack. If you upgrade Jaunt() with Load() however then Jaunt() will create an explosion where you teleport to.
Every single ability is unique and different to every other one and you will be constantly mixing and matching. Some will look awesome but turn out to suck and others will look boring but turn out amazing, I'll leave you to find out which is which.
Story:
I'm not going to comment on the story much or I'll give it away. It's the kind of game where it's impossible to say anything without spoiling it. Suffice to say it is a very good story featuring all the classic themes of revenge, justice, loss, fear, desperation, success and everything else that makes a good tale.
Summary:
Stop reading this and buy the game. Now. Don't make me find you.
Seriously though this game deserves every good review and metacritic point it gets. It's damn cheap compared to other major games and a damn sight better than a lot of them. I rate this 9/10.
//WARNING//
The only reason I'm not giving this a 10 out of ten is that it can be confusing at times to know which functions are good or not. For example Ping() can be a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use and Jaunt() is too valuable to use as a passive or upgrade.

I stood there, wreathed in flame. A stupid smile was on my face. I was experiencing (with unrepentant joy) the awesome power of having both energy shields, and a flame thrower. Wave after wave of enemies mindlessly flung themselves at me, each one died like the last: Drowned in a sea fire. Their screams of anger and despair melded together in a cacophonous symphony of pain within my headphones as I sprayed their nests with liquid death. They had fought Valiantly. Desperately. But had not been enough. All was silent now. I could here the wind blowing, The quiet, near non-existant ambient soundtrack hit a somber chord. Smoke was still rising. During my rampage, a forest to the east had been lit aflame. The fire spread throughout it, a blazing wall of destruction, keen on consuming the whole of the forest. Left behind were only a scant few charred, smoking husks of what once were trees.
Low on power and ammo, I decided to make my way back to the car so I could return to base and resupply.
But I had... Difficultly. The world had changed in the few minutes that had passed since I had left it. As I passed the innumerable corpses and husks of earlier conquests... The once lush and green forests that i had litterally needed to hack through to proceed were gone. Replaced only with barren, charred wasteland. As I became more and more lost in my own destruction, I began to feel a twinge of guilt. I was just one guy, and yet here I was, destroying an entire world, and for what?

As much as it displeases me, I still have to review shovelware from time to time. Don’t get me wrong, no one’s forcing me to write about them or even activate these Steam keys that “stink” from a mile away. It’s my choice since I stick to my plans of reviewing any genre and topic eventually. This is Steam in 2017, folks. Quality Assurance is a myth over here. If it’s on the platform and I’m in the mood to write about it, I probably will. Just don’t expect me to mince words. The wonderful debut of Aaron Roller and PilotLumba Gaming. They’ve got a bright future ahead, I’m certain!
Aren’t you eagerly awaiting a story? Well, Space of Darkness delivers! What exactly, I have yet to unravel that mystery either. The game starts as abruptly as it ends. So we’ll just read the objectives, ok? “Robots attacked the spaceship, find a weapon fast!” Will it be a laser rifle, a plasma shotgun, Doom’s BFG itself? Nope, it’s a deadly yet still stylish, kebab knife that has the mystic power of also acting as a boomerang for some reason. You whack it at some really brain-dead hovering drones. And they lived happily ever after. Or not. End of story.
No cinematics, no explanation, literally nothing in terms of a plotline or narrative development. Even the now infamous “The Slaughtering Grounds” had  Golden Joystick Award-worthy storyline by comparison to Space of Darkness. Was it that hard to slap a text wall with some generic information about a John/Jane Doe having to save humanity from R2-D2’s inbred cousins or something? Anything would have been better than a subtitle-like objective.
Aaron somehow managed to mess even Unity Engine’s legendary stability on my system. The frame rate was all over the place and interesting enough, the game would not actually scale to lower resolutions other than my monitor’s native one. The textures did scale to a certain point, at least enough to run the title at a bearable frame rate. I won’t lie, it doesn’t look like a Digital Homicide asset flip. That is what angers me more than the time I wasted playing Space of Darkness. Its visuals are decent enough and could have carried even an abysmal storyline, if there ever was one implemented at all. In its current Early Access stage, it can only be regarded as a subpar tech demo.
I honestly can’t remember hearing anything worth mentioning. Did it have a soundtrack? I won’t reinstall it and spend another 10 minutes listening more closely. There was no voice acting or sound effects, so it might just as well have featured some piano songs playing in the background, silent movie-style. I would have rated it higher if it did.
If only I had more than 4 levels to talk about. And even then, the space ship “walls” were prevalent across all four stages, from the flooded one to the mysterious fog and trees. Inside the ship. That was the biodome section, right? No dome or anything to contain all that moisture, but we’ll call that a minor plot hole when compared to the absurdity of the situation itself. All you do in Space of Darkness, is to travel from one end of the short levels to the other, while hitting the drones with that space sword or whatever. You have to hit them faster and sooner than they can bump into you and somehow kill you in the process. Sounds like a world of fun already!
Only that it’s really not. And it’s the kind of experience that makes you question your own life decisions: “Should I really attempt game development? I know Valve will accept nearly any sorry excuse for a game on their platform, but I really don’t want to embarrass myself that much and release something in Early Access that could be completed by players in less time than it takes to microwave a TV dinner.” After 15 minutes (I must have spent at least 3, waiting for some Easter Egg or joke that would provide access to more levels) I was greeted by a screen which informed me that I “won the game”. Not even a “You’re winner”? Ok, I guess all we can do now in Space Darkness’ case is to wait for more delightful levels to be added in subsequent updates.
It took me longer to write this than actually finish Space of Darkness. Might have been “poetic justice” to rate it for as many minutes as it lasted until its last level, but I won’t stoop that low. It’s in 3D even if it runs like liquid derrière, so I’ll be generous. I cannot overlook however that it charges far too much for its bad joke of a gameplay. I know that I avoid speaking of actual value and pricing in my recent reviews, but you’re getting ripped off by this title even if you pick it up in a bundle. It goes without saying that I recommend you steer clear of it and play Tetris or some Angry Birds instead. You’re welcome.
+ It’s a 3D tech demo?
- Early Access that’s so brief and broken, it becomes insulting.
- No Steam Trading Cards nor Achievements.
- No story, no coherent gameplay.
- No redeeming points either.

I have to say, Space of Darkness is probably one of the worst games I have ever experienced. I understand that a lot of low standards are placed onto games in early access because the games aren't complete, but you have to at least have some form of standards in placement for something that can be purchased, and Space of Darkness is nowhere near ready for even early access standards, and it worries me that this game is meant to be put out as a full release come November.
Space of Darkness is a first person survival horror game taking place in a starship which has had some kind of slaughter occurred in regards to the crew by some robot race which is never really explained fully, and it leaves the player as the only survivor and you have to fight your way through to the end of the ship, or at least I think that's the goal as the game can't actually be completed in its current state.
As explained before, your main goal is to go through the ship fighting robots that sometimes are set in place and sometimes awkwardly spawn in as a form of attempt at a cheap jump scare, and that's just about where this game's horror elements stop. There isn't even a ridiculously loud music queue, it's literally just a robot popping into existence and that is it, you might think with not seeing the game that I'm making the scares sound worse than they are because they can't be as bad as what it is that I'm describing, but I'm being serious, that's literally all there is, an enemy popping into existence.
The game also has a really out of place aspect in which the character has a hunger bar, but from what I've played of the game, there is no food on the ship, so you can't actually increase your hunger bar, and also even if your hunger bar depletes, it doesn't seem to have any negative effects. I fail to see why this kind of game even needs a hunger bar, especially when it doesn't do anything, when it isn't exactly open world where you can freely scavenge and monitor the food you've collected where you just need to keep moving and killing the robots on the ship.
The graphics are really bad and almost unbearable to look at. The ship is full of a lot of muddy textures with things that barely represent what they're meant to represent. Ontop of that, the game has an annoying shiny reflection coming off of almost everything in the ship, which makes the game look even worse as there's not too many forms of cohesion with the muddy textured objects having realistic lighting placed on top of them and almost blinding the player and obscuring their vision further.
There's not really much to talk about in regards to the sound as there's no music or little to no sounds to speak of. It's dead silent throughout the majority of the game besides the main menu which has your generic horror music playing on top of a tacky looking menu screen, and the rest of the sounds in the game are either the saw blades of the robots playing at an insanely loud volume or your wrench colliding with the robots.
Now, in the introduction I mentioned that this game can't actually be beaten, and here I'll explain why. Firstly, it's impossible to kill one of the robots without taking some form of damage, the robots move faster than you so you can't run, the robots aren't startled when you hit them with your wrench, so you're literally given no choice but to just run up to them and hope that they take away as minimal amount of health as possible, as the health they take away is random. After playing a few times, the minimum I saw them take was a quarter of my health, and the maximum they took away was two thirds from one hit. There are a great number of health kits scattered around the station, but 60% of them either can't be picked up or when they are picked up, they don't restore any of your health, so in reality, in the first two rooms, out of the 15 health kits in the first 5 areas, I'm willing to say that only 5 of them actually worked. Due to the low amount of health kits that work and the high damage rate that the robots do, the game is impossible to complete. The only tactic that I applied that got me further along the route than usual was to use the kits sparingly and doing trackbacks to the first area which is the only area where the health kits actually work. Also, it isn't only the robots that take health from you. Randomly, and for no explained reason, when you're going down the corridors, you will get hit by nothing and never see what hit you, and that will take away a lot of your health as well.
So, with saying that, the play time is worthless since the game can't be beaten and as a result, there's no real replayability factor due to how low quality the game is.
Space of Darkness is a game that is unbearable to play through and due to the sheer amount of flaws and unbalanced mechanics in the game, it is rendered unplayable in its current state, and with that being said, there is no way that I can recommend this to anyone.
Final verdict: 1/10

Realm Reborn is a sequel to the previously released Final Fantasy XIV, which wasn’t received very well, and this is even conveniently explained in the game’s plot: there’s an apocalypse which ravages the whole realm and begins a new era. Personally I hadn’t played the previous game but this sequel is said to offer significant improvements over the original across the board, it's essentially an entirely redesigned game of its own.
The plot is fairly generic save the world kind of stuff: you are an adventurer brought into one of the game’s three big city-states with a special ability to attune to crystals which hold some great ability to hold off evil. You perform tasks for the city-states and eventually rise to become an envoy between them and even serve them. Similar to single-player games, the main plot and many of the other quests are filled with cutscenes, and in the main story’s case, the significant ones are also voiced. It’s all easy to follow and they’ve tried to put a bit of story into everything, for instance all of the game’s class guilds have a storyline of their own that advances as you gain levels and do guild quests.
However this kind of plot is well suited for MMO and something as complex as Final Fantasy XIII’s super messy plot obviously wouldn’t work here. Rising in guild ranks and joining armies feels like an accomplishment, and you get treated to far more heroic stuff like taking on massive primals (think summons from previous Final Fantasy titles) rather fast. The game overall plays much like a singleplayer game story wise: the story is focused on your personal character and many plot advancing quests have certain “duty” sections that can only be completed with your own character, such as taking on a boss battle. This can be reversed too in some cases: some boss battles and dungeons instead put you in a party with others. Most of the game can be soloed if you want, but the option to do stuff in a party is totally there too, you’ll only ever be separated for brief periods at a time.
This focus on your own character is what sets the game apart from other MMOs in my opinion and makes the game more interesting. The cutscenes are also no worse quality than in singleplayer FF titles and the game’s graphics and particularly animation are fantastic. All characters are lively animated and seeing your character pull off all kinds of stuff like stupid faces in cutscenes is really fun and involving. The game is also really well optimized, running on a large variety of systems and even having its own preset settings for laptops for instance that take your specs into account. The user interface in the game is really good too, super easy to use and slick looking, I was never at a loss to find something.
Gameplay is similar to other MMO titles and the difficulty level is really good across the board, you will be challenged at every level and you can always find more dangerous or easier opponents and quests. As a nice twist your character can be literally any class in the game – you can use and level any one class at a time, provided you have joined their guild, and certain class abilities can also be used by other classes. For instance, Gladiators that have leveled Conjurer can cast Cure, which they normally wouldn’t have access to, so cross-classing a bit is encouraged and even required to get Jobs (specialized mid/late-game classes) later on. To swap a class you just swap to a different gear preset, which you can create lists of. At the most basic level you just need to change a weapon to switch to another class.
The game is easy to get into as well, there’s a 15 day free trial that offers leveling of a single character up to level 20, but you can cross-class him/her as much as you like, and it’s definitely enough to get a good look at the game. The free trial is best played with a friend that already owns the game though, because you cannot set up your own parties in it, but other subscribed players can invite you to theirs. Marketplace and trading functions are limited but otherwise there’s no significant restrictions. The game is available as a digital download on the website and on Steam, as well as on PS3 and PS4 on the consoles, the multiplayer is cross-platform, and new buyers of the game automatically get 30 free game days. Steam users will also be happy to know that the monthly subscription can be paid with just Steam wallet money, assuming you also bought the game from Steam.
TL;DR
It's great. Don't compare it to Square Enix's other new FF games. It's a traditional MMO game with Final Fantasy flavor and one well designed one at that. I enjoy it tons more than the recent main series FF games. And I wrote this review originally for something else in mind, if you're wondering why it's so long and detailed. :P Give it a chance, it deserves more PC Steam players. And, it has a ton of content in a large world. I still feel like I've barely scratched the surface of what it has to offer so far at the moment of writing.
