I'm sure many of you by now know all about how Dark Souls 2 didn't live up to it's expectations as a sequal. And you're right. There are so many things wrong with this game that it wouldn't even be worth identifying them. You can find everything elsewhere. I'll mention a few, but this isn't a slag-fest.
As a stand-alone game itself, DS2 is actually quite fun. The game controls have been improved since DS1 and the game runs much more smoothly. The stats etc have been streamlined and over-all it feels more coherent than it's counter-part. Gameplay in DS2 is superior, as is the online match-play. No more will you have to wait around for an hour+ to find your friend's summon sign and invading other players is a much more common occurance. Weirdly, of all the 3 Dark Souls games, DS2 is the game I return to the most. It's easier to pick up and play than it's other 2 titles, perhaps due to the level design? DS1 was a game you really had to concentrate on and be very wary of your surroundings. It had an atmosphere which couldn't be ignored, and you felt in constant danger. DS2 doesn't have that unfortunately, and instead encourages the quick run-through style of play.
The inclusion of Soul memory baffles us all, and as a gameplay mechanic doesn't work whatsoever. Invasions and co-op should just have been left with regards to your over-all soul-level. It's much simpler. Plus, for some reason, From Software don't ever seem to be able to do covenants right. None of the covenants in DS2 are particularly worth joining (with exception to the Sunbros), and the way in which the game forces the player into PvP arenas to rank up in a some of them is just aggrovating.
The biggest downfall of this game however is level design. The levels are too short, too easy, and aren't coherent with an open-world game. Levels also feel very linear. The story is almost non-existent, though this is conclusive with other games of the franchise, and it jumps around all over the place, hoping to cover it with the often repeated line "...without ever knowing why".
Despite all these pit-falls, and there are many more things that weren't mentioned here, I would still recommend this game.

ESO is balanced on needing very specific "Traits" on your weapons and armor in order to be effective in combat. The problem with that is it turns gear acquisition into a total grindfest - even though essentially everyone needs certain traits to play the PvP unhindered, for example. They attempted to "rebalance traits to promote variety" and that didnt really do anything except nerf the most popular/effective weapon trait into being essentially non-usable.
Clockwork City DLC was a big disappointment. 'Trait Conversion' is the worst system ever introduced in any Elder Scrolls game. Conversion requires 50 consumable items called Crystals, found at the end of long dungeons, to change the trait of *ONE* item. The problem here is Crystals are not a guaranteed drop, so you could potentially play 100 dungeon runs and find zero of them.
TLDR: they intentionally overhyped Clockwork City and Trait Conversion, whille both were essentially garbage. And while the base game is decent, the inevitable disappointment/frustration is not worth the massive time and/or money investment.

I think the best way to love this game, is to see it not as an elder scrolls game, but the best MMORPG there is at the moment. So much better than WoW and others. Supergiant Games seems to be the only developer attempting to go beyond the cookie cutter story.  Gaming itself is plagued with such similar experiences between each game that it's beginning to be hard to tell any of them apart, but Supergiant cares about the story they want to tell and that alone is worth being a part of it.
This is a heart-wrenching love story in a sea of dude-bro action movies and "an ancient evil awakens" pancake batter video games.
It's a shorter game, but it can be difficult at times (unless you feel like breaking the game with a very specific attack combination). (Check out my Stormblood expansion/DLC review for more up to date thoughts of what I think)
Realm Reborn is a sequel to the previously released Final Fantasy XIV, which wasn’t received very well, and this is even conveniently explained in the game’s plot: there’s an apocalypse which ravages the whole realm and begins a new era. Personally I hadn’t played the previous game but this sequel is said to offer significant improvements over the original across the board, it's essentially an entirely redesigned game of its own.
The plot is fairly generic save the world kind of stuff: you are an adventurer brought into one of the game’s three big city-states with a special ability to attune to crystals which hold some great ability to hold off evil. You perform tasks for the city-states and eventually rise to become an envoy between them and even serve them. Similar to single-player games, the main plot and many of the other quests are filled with cutscenes, and in the main story’s case, the significant ones are also voiced. It’s all easy to follow and they’ve tried to put a bit of story into everything, for instance all of the game’s class guilds have a storyline of their own that advances as you gain levels and do guild quests.
However this kind of plot is well suited for MMO and something as complex as Final Fantasy XIII’s super messy plot obviously wouldn’t work here. Rising in guild ranks and joining armies feels like an accomplishment, and you get treated to far more heroic stuff like taking on massive primals (think summons from previous Final Fantasy titles) rather fast. The game overall plays much like a singleplayer game story wise: the story is focused on your personal character and many plot advancing quests have certain “duty” sections that can only be completed with your own character, such as taking on a boss battle. This can be reversed too in some cases: some boss battles and dungeons instead put you in a party with others. Most of the game can be soloed if you want, but the option to do stuff in a party is totally there too, you’ll only ever be separated for brief periods at a time.
This focus on your own character is what sets the game apart from other MMOs in my opinion and makes the game more interesting. The cutscenes are also no worse quality than in singleplayer FF titles and the game’s graphics and particularly animation are fantastic. All characters are lively animated and seeing your character pull off all kinds of stuff like stupid faces in cutscenes is really fun and involving. The game is also really well optimized, running on a large variety of systems and even having its own preset settings for laptops for instance that take your specs into account. The user interface in the game is really good too, super easy to use and slick looking, I was never at a loss to find something.
Gameplay is similar to other MMO titles and the difficulty level is really good across the board, you will be challenged at every level and you can always find more dangerous or easier opponents and quests. As a nice twist your character can be literally any class in the game – you can use and level any one class at a time, provided you have joined their guild, and certain class abilities can also be used by other classes. For instance, Gladiators that have leveled Conjurer can cast Cure, which they normally wouldn’t have access to, so cross-classing a bit is encouraged and even required to get Jobs (specialized mid/late-game classes) later on. To swap a class you just swap to a different gear preset, which you can create lists of. At the most basic level you just need to change a weapon to switch to another class.
The game is easy to get into as well, there’s a 15 day free trial that offers leveling of a single character up to level 20, but you can cross-class him/her as much as you like, and it’s definitely enough to get a good look at the game. The free trial is best played with a friend that already owns the game though, because you cannot set up your own parties in it, but other subscribed players can invite you to theirs. Marketplace and trading functions are limited but otherwise there’s no significant restrictions. The game is available as a digital download on the website and on Steam, as well as on PS3 and PS4 on the consoles, the multiplayer is cross-platform, and new buyers of the game automatically get 30 free game days. Steam users will also be happy to know that the monthly subscription can be paid with just Steam wallet money, assuming you also bought the game from Steam.
TL;DR
It's great. Don't compare it to Square Enix's other new FF games. It's a traditional MMO game with Final Fantasy flavor and one well designed one at that. I enjoy it tons more than the recent main series FF games. And I wrote this review originally for something else in mind, if you're wondering why it's so long and detailed. :P Give it a chance, it deserves more PC Steam players. And, it has a ton of content in a large world. I still feel like I've barely scratched the surface of what it has to offer so far at the moment of writing.

Once upon a time, I had a life.  Then I discovered Factorio.
800+ hours in-game later, I surfaced long enough to write a review before going to catch a few hours of desperately-needed sleep...
If you are at all OCD, this game is for you.  If you like Minecraft, this game is for you.  If you like to be able to design layouts and optimise the flow of things, (yes, you guessed it) this game is for you.  If you like fast-paces action shooters with state-of-the-art graphics... well, this game may or may not be for you but, as so many others have said, if it appeals to you then Factorio is like the gaming equivalent of a crack pipe.
You start with just a few iron plates and a couple of other items, and a whole (infinite) map to explore.  The first hour or so is pretty boring, running around and collecting iron plates out of your furnace, chopping down trees for fuel, setting up miners and smelters, but then the tech tree starts to kick in.  Automation.  Logistics.  Defenses against the pesky native spawns.  Electricity.  Oil processing.  Trains.  The list goes on, and each level introduces new and wonderful things to build and play with.  CIrcuit networks!  People have built entire CPU models within the game, not to mention the automation facilities that you can put into practice with a bit of work (okay, and an understanding of Boolean logic or some in-depth forum research) :-)
Eventually, you will get to launch a rocket.  "I win!"
But... you know, I could have built that base a bit neater.  And a LOT bigger.  And it would be kinda cool to launch more than one rocket.  Or one rocket every 10 minutes.  Or one rocket a minute.  Oh yeah, then there are the mods which introduce all kinds of other stuff if you ever get bored or dissatisfied with the vanilla game.
£15?  The sheer amount of entertainment that I have received from this game would make it cheap at 5x the price!

I'd recommend this game based on what it's meant to be. At its core, it's a shoot-em-up arcade game.  That being said, I didn't enjoy it as much as I hoped I would.
Pros:
-The graphics are beautiful, and very well done. A shout out to the graphics department in charge of the game.
-It's got a very artistic way of portraying the story; Graphic novel style, combined with the narration of an old cowboy telling his story.
-It's not an easy game, and at times requires trying different routes and tactics to accomplish your goal.
-There are some great history-bits found as secrets throughout the game. I love me some real-life learning.
Cons:
-Linear, shoot-em-up. There's not much depth to gameplay.
-A few path bugs. I remember a boss getting glitch stuck inside an environment element, where I was able to hit him safely without him being able to move or shoot back. There were also a number of places where I'd find my own character stuck and unable to move.
-Sometimes, the controls would bug out to where I couldn't aim, crouch, reload, etc.
-It got repetitive pretty fast. Even when trying to branch from the norm, as in the case of duels, it didn't feel like there was much depth or learning curve.
-One last thing that bugged me. In the Xbox 360 version there is the option to turn off swearing and blood, which didn't port over into the PC version. Now, I understand plenty of gamers believe the more gore, the merrier, but I appreciate the chance to share the game with kids and family. Given it's an option in the console version, I'd appreciate seeing it ported over.

Dark Souls
Demon Souls
Dark Souls III
Bloodborne
Dark Souls II
*Note in mind I haven't played Bloodborne or Demon Souls, but I have watched videos on them and from what I've seen of the mechanics, enemies, graphical style and stability, that's how I'd rank them.

400+ hours I've put into this game, largely because I'm a fan of the building mechanics and the pve elements that you can find on certain community servers. Had a blast playing the game, building massive bases solo and had the odd problem with hackers or greifers coming in and taking my stuff. Nevertheless, I always thought that this game could have been a lot more than it was. A game that could have rivaled some of the best given its unique deliverables like the building system, the crests etc. Alas, it was not meant to be. Although I still hope that the devs maybe revisit the game, or that they open it more to the modding community to do something greater with this game, because this game caters not only to the pvp, but also to the pve element. It does a lot of core thing correctly, but now, I wish there was more time spent on creating more content for this game. Maps, game modes/styles, more things to build, harder things to create, more elements of siege etc. With this being medieval based, the roleplaying capabilities could have been far more than what it is today.
Would I advise buying the game? At full price, not a chance. While on sale, maybe. If you're into building, check out some youtube videos and make your decision on that basis. Pro's: The game is beautiful. Even on medium settings the game looks great and runs smoothly. The story is actually enthralling and is keeping me interested and I don't find myself speeding through text and skipping cinematics. Atleast, not for the main stories lol. The monsters are really well done and there are a wide variety from cute and cuddly (i.e the Cactus monster thing...) to the scary *** demons.
The dungeons are fun and it seems that most of them tie in with the main story so you in a sense have to unlock them. Same goes with getting your first chocobo
Cons: There are some things that really do bug me in this game which may be just superficial on my part. The first is how the map is. When zoomed out to look at a regional view all you see are name blocks with lines directing which zones are connected. It's not like a google map view that you find in most mmo's. Along with that is trying to find where to go with quests. Some mmos if you have quest lets say 3 zones over, will usually point you to the nearest exit from the current zone into the next. This game doesnt seem to do that. If you have a quest in one zone over, sure it will show you. But if it is 2 zones over then you need to go and track it down.
The zones themselvs I wish were not instanced. Even parts of the main cities are instanced. I personally like complete open world games. Or at the very least, the main cities should not be broken into instances.
Getting a mount is kind of a pain. You need to progress to roughly lvl 20 before you get the quest to get a mount. Then you need to go farm some tokens in order to get a certificate. That part isnt necessarily hard just annoying. Even if you have the collectors edition and have the two mounts already, you need to get the normal chocobo first before you can use them.
My biggest gripe however, is the use/lack there of of voice over for the games. Some main story cinematics will have voice overs, some dont. Some times you will have voices then all of a sudden you dont. It's not my sound card, or computer, or whatever, it's the developers that didnt put in voice acting for the whole game. I hope they do add in more sometime down the line.
Overall though this is a very well done game and I am impressed. Even with the nuances I am enjoying the game immensly and definitely recommend playing it even if it's just the trial.

Believe it or not but Final Fantasy 14 is a serious waste of time. While the classes and job system is extensive, it's also pointless.
You get the option to raise base class jobs like Lancer, Marauder, Rogue, etc etc. And through combinations of main/secondary class levels you unlock jobs like Paladin, Black Mage, Dragoon, which seems like a cool concept but
The entirety of this game consists of leveling from 1 to 50 over and over and over again, doing the same method over and over and over again. Your free stat points might as well be dumped ALL into Vitality to have any sort of use for your huge variety of jobs. Strength doesn't help mages, barely helps rogues. Dex doesn't help mages, barely helps melee. Int doesn't help either of the 2 classes before hand.
Your Jobs can sound pretty coo like who doesn't want to be a warrior Monk and master hand to hand combat? Or who doesn't want to be a Dragoon like Kain? Except Melee DPS classes are trash. Tanks can show the same dmg output but have tons more utility and survivability.
Every class and every job in the game shares the same 2.5 second base cool down for abilities. You can't combo wombo your abilities. The fact that a giant heavy armor wearing sword and shield toting tank can attack just as fast and often as a cloth wearing rogue or monk is just stupid. There are ways to lower these cool downs but the amount of effort to make a seeemingly noticable difference hurts your other stats to the point it's not worth it.
A ton of dungeons are part of the main storyline. And you HAVE to have a party to do these dungeons. Yeah you can invite friends who can sync but people don't do that because there's basically no point in it. You can wait 30 - 60 minutes easily for a dungeon to pop JUST so you can go on with your quest line, to have another dungeon immediately after with another prolonged wait.  Dungeon system in this game sucks.
But wait there's more! The mounts, and mount armor, that you get from collector's edition are useless! While this game has a cool concept of having a mount that can fight by your side, it cannot be the Fat Chocobo or Coeurl. They do not fight. Meaning you're not going to have these out any time soon. There's really no need from them since you'll most likely be using the travel system to teleport all over anyway.. And the fact mounts are actually pretty slow. barely faster than walking speed.
Also you buy these things and expect to get to use them immediately, after all they are just mounts. Nope. You have to do the main story line into the 20s just to unlock the mount feature. And into the 30s to unlock the mount companion feature. And by then the only mount you'll have around is your basic choco to fight by your side.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. The sequel to the critically acclaimed Amnesia: The Dark Descent, with a papa like that, you'd have to imagine the son would live up to the reputation, in some aspects, I believe it does, others not so much.
Pros:
-The atmosphere is quite unsettling, much like the first.
-The voice acting got a major upgrade from Alexander telling Daniel not to stray thirty times with his over-the-top voice.
-Manpigs are a bit disturbing and the noises they make are terrifying.
-Decent reference or two to the first game.
-Music was completely amazing and help create so much of the feeling of this game.
-No naked guys.
-Like the first one, I was fine playing this in the middle of the day with people around, but at night, alone and with headphones completely changes your views to how it should be viewed.
-Was that a pig snuffing I just heard?
-In layman's terms I was scared multiple times while playing this game.
Cons:
-Sanity bar, health, puzzles, tinderboxes, oil and challenge were all thrown right out the window.
-Every puzzle consists of put x in y to open z door.
-Monsters were not as disturbing or creepy as the original slack-jawed, strap-wearing fatty we all know and love.
-Monsters were very slow.
-Plot was confusing and I didn't really get it and ended up looking it up to fully understand it.
-Lantern is replaced by flashlight thing that doesn't require oil and you can keep it on for as long as you'd like, and has the added bonus that it flickers when a piggy is nearby so you basically know when there's something close.
-Piggies looked silly during multiple parts of the game and it took away from the feeling of it.
-Most of this game felt like you exploring a machine while there's something lurking there rather than a struggle to try and find your kids.
Overall, this game is nowhere close to the standards that the first game set. But on the other hand, I was scared quite a bit, the best way to put it is that ATDD was The Empire Strikes Back while AAMFP was Revenge of the Sith. Anyone who liked the first game and likes the series should play this, and I personally believe this game recieves more hate than it deserves. If it's on sale, or you really, really, REALLY want to spend $20 on this, please pick it up, it was a good experience and deserves to be loved for what it is, not hated for what The Dark Descent brought forward to the horror genre.

This game has the most hours on any game on my account so you can see I love eso and that’s saying something when eso has more hours than Skyrim. This game sticks to the elder scrolls legacy by letting you do what you want. Want to completely ignore the story? You can do that (excluding the tutorial) Want to murder civilians? You can do that. Everyone is nice and friendly and will usually help you. The class and race selection is nice. The classes are not overly limiting to your playstyle either. You can be a dragon knight with a restoration staff equipped. You can be a sorcerer with a dual wield weapon. The list goes on and on. I have played this game for over 200 hours and I still have barely scratched the surface of content that eso gives. I cannot give this game enough praise for what it is, but that’s enough about the good things let’s talk about some negatives. Firstly the justice system is flawed. For example if you were to kill a person with no witnesses remaining, you would still get a bounty unlike the other elder scrolls games, but this is minor problem that I personally don’t mind too much. Secondly the lore is a bit off in eso. For example another mild problem is that the argonians and the dark elves should not be in the same alliance as the dark elves have enslaved the argonians for centuries. Again mild problem, but it makes the game a little less appealing for lore fanatics like myself. The third problem with the game is the pvp. This is more of a personal problem. I don’t get why people like it so much. You have to ride a mount if you don’t have one already the travel time is insanely long to get from castle to castle and once you get to an enemy base it is really easy to die and have to go through that travel time again. To top it off the fast travel system in pvp will only work if the castle is not under attack and if your alliance controls it. Again this is a personal problem that I have with the pvp. If you like pvp that’s fine it’s just not for some people like myself. In fact, you can choose to avoid the pvp all together if you wish. Finally, crown crates. Where to start on this one. Crown crates are Eso’s biggest flaw. Crown crates are boxes that give you exclusive items in exchange for real money. They are a ripoff I’ve seen a guy named Deltia’s gaming (great channel by the way) buy $100 dollars worth of crates and not get a single item of the highest rarity (can’t remember the exact name) Simple fix, just don’t buy crown crates. In conclusion eso is an incredible game that has a few flaws after all no game is perfect and eso accomplishes much and is one of my favorite games of all time. My suggestion: get eso!

Alright. I used to play Bit Heroes alot on the Kongregate version, and I had fun. I became a moderator for their World Chat and I enjoyed playing the game and seeing new people. At some point, the game came out on mobile. Alot of new players in the World Chat, which of course, includes trolls and spammers. I also started feeling like Bit Heroes became less and less enjoyable for me to play. I was a simple F2P.
Later, the developpers gradually added more P2W content, and the difference between F2P players and P2W players became obvious. The game isn't fair, and if you want to actually progress and catch up everyone else, you need to get out your wallet and spend alot of money on the game. Fun stuff.
The gameplay itself isn't exactly bad, but due to how it works, it becomes VERY repetitive. Add to that the fact that you won't always obtain what you want due to the game being a rather generic grinding game. Sure, you can level up, but it becomes slower as your progress more, to the point that a F2P will only level up once per week. Of course, P2Ws have the upper hand here! They can run a dungeon as many times as their wallet will allow them to!
As for the equipment, getting armor isn't bad, but upgrading it becomes more and more tedious. Especially the Set items, that requires an insane amount of grinding to even upgrade once. Getting a good pet/accessory will usually require to be extremely lucky or be willing to pay money! If you aren't one of these two, well too bad, your gear will keep sucking and you will have a much harder time in high level pvp.
You also need to note that friends/guilds are actually very important in this game. When you first start, you won't really need them, but the more you progress, the more you will need them. Sadly, the friend limit is 100. Doesn't seem too bad at first, but for a game with alot of players, it can be troublesome. You will usually need to stick out from the bunch to get the best friends for late game, which is pretty hard to do as a F2P.
To finish this review off, I'd like ask the developpers a question: Why did you put the game on steam if you originally said you wouldn't put it? I believe that publishing the game on steam was a bad idea, as this game is better played on mobile. Most players that will actually play this on steam long enough will be old timers that will sell items from other games to spend the money they got on BH. Not to mention that there are no ads (and no ads rewards) on Steam, which again, doesn't help F2Ps.
While I like the artstyle and some of the music, I don't like the game. It feels like you are PUNISHED for not spending money on it. Of course, some old timers may disagree with me, but if you want to play a game and expecting to be able to progress well without having to pay money, this is not the game for you.

I'd recommend this game based on what it's meant to be. At its core, it's a shoot-em-up arcade game.  That being said, I didn't enjoy it as much as I hoped I would.
Pros:
-The graphics are beautiful, and very well done. A shout out to the graphics department in charge of the game.
-It's got a very artistic way of portraying the story; Graphic novel style, combined with the narration of an old cowboy telling his story.
-It's not an easy game, and at times requires trying different routes and tactics to accomplish your goal.
-There are some great history-bits found as secrets throughout the game. I love me some real-life learning.
Cons:
-Linear, shoot-em-up. There's not much depth to gameplay.
-A few path bugs. I remember a boss getting glitch stuck inside an environment element, where I was able to hit him safely without him being able to move or shoot back. There were also a number of places where I'd find my own character stuck and unable to move.
-Sometimes, the controls would bug out to where I couldn't aim, crouch, reload, etc.
-It got repetitive pretty fast. Even when trying to branch from the norm, as in the case of duels, it didn't feel like there was much depth or learning curve.
-One last thing that bugged me. In the Xbox 360 version there is the option to turn off swearing and blood, which didn't port over into the PC version. Now, I understand plenty of gamers believe the more gore, the merrier, but I appreciate the chance to share the game with kids and family. Given it's an option in the console version, I'd appreciate seeing it ported over.

What happened? That's really the question you'll be asking yourself after 2 hours playing this. Where did the dark, creepy and melancholic atmosphere of The Dark Descent go? Where did the fear go? The constant surprise? The panic? That "oh God I have to go through this new room" feeling?
Everywhere the player looks there's nothing but a singular lack of ambition. Everything feels like the devs didn't have any money. Like they had to recycle elements and then recycle them again and then some. There is no originality in design or locations. There's maybe three different monsters. The game doesn't take any chance, with anything.
Remember the genius "water part" in The Dark Descent, probably made with one corridor, one splash FX, one water texture and a bit of scripting? How scary it was, how it had us screaming in front of our screens trying to escape that thing? Here you will find nothing like that. A Machine for Pigs is flat, without any surprise or change of pace. Boredom lurks at every corner. The story takes ages to become interesting and after a while, inevitably you stop caring - you don't even want to know anymore. Art wise, this game does look good and you'll see some cool details here and there - but it's stale. It's long, it's boring, and you've seen it before. The Chinese Room made Dear Esther: why didn't they keep doing what they were good at - exteriors? Why do you have to suffer the neverending black corridors, levers and buttons?
If this game were a ride, it'd be the one that takes you to visit Grandma in your countrisde hometown. It's a safe journey that isn't exactly unpleasant but that isn't fun and that will create only frustration - because you could have been somewhere else, doing something more interesting rather than being here, waiting for the ride to end. You could've been eating a pizza. Watching something on Netflix. Playing a more exciting horror game (Amnesia: The Dark Descent; F.E.A.R; Outlast; Alien: Isolation; Cryostasis; Scratches; ...). Hell, you could've been sleeping.
Let's wrap this up. I love scary games. I loved the first Penumbra, I loved The Dark Descent. I also love dark tales, creepy 19th century literature, superstitions and pseudo-science, and anything Edgar Allan Poe.
But this sucks. :(

If Supergiant Games can be counted on for anything, it's convincing you of its world through very small details. Transistor has that in spades, even moreso than Bastion. The music, OVC terminals, and stained-glass visual aesthetic paint a stunning portrait of a world fragmenting into pieces. But likewise, the story must be pieced together as well - no omniscient narrator this time. For me, finding these story snippets and inferring the connections between them was rewarding, but I can see how for some it might be too much breadcrumb trail and not enough gingerbread house, especially in comparison to Bastion.
The combat system in Transistor is definitely enjoyable once you find the right synergies, but also very challenging until you figure those out (or look at a guide). I like that Supergiant used the trace files and the test rooms to encourage you to switch things up - experimenting with different loadouts and finding what works for you is the only way to succeed as challenges increase. That said, while generally you can play to suit your preferences, some synergies and loadouts are definitely stronger than others, so you might find the combat less balanced than you'd like. Turn() is also less powerful than you might expect, and it takes awhile to find the right rhythms and strategies. But when you do, man does it feel awesome!
All things said, I enjoyed it enough to play twice, and I'm actually finding it more enjoyable the second time. If you want a game that will challenge you with surprising complexity (and a game that will look and sound gorgeous to boot), Transistor is absolutely worth the money.

Supergiant is steadily becoming one of my favorite developers.  Bastion was amazing enough, but Transistor went even further with the strength of its art, music, sentimental narrative (Cunningham's voice is become quite iconic in its own right!), and more than anything, its mechanics with the customizable ability system, setting it apart from Bastion entirely.  Both of their games make me realize why I now prefer smaller companies in gaming: a smaller number of dedicated people making a smaller game seems much more likely to never lose sight of their creative focus, and the end product is often a more memorable and rewarding experience than an big budget pile of trendy mediocrity where things either drag on to the point of tedium, or abruptly end in unfulfilled disappointment.
My only regret is that I can't SPECIFICALLY explain why I love Transistor so much without spoiling what makes it so memorable, so I'm stuck with being vague.  All I can say is that I was extremely happy to play this game, despite...well, if anyone's finished the game, they know.  After the emotional reaction I got from Bastion, I would expect no less from Transistor.  They delivered exactly what I was hoping for, and let's just say there's a very good reason why I refused to buy this game without the soundtrack bundled in.  I only wish I could get an artbook to go with it.
I really wish I didn't have to be so cryptic, but this is one of those games that you just do not spoil.  It's just so refreshing to see a game like this.

If Supergiant Games can be counted on for anything, it's convincing you of its world through very small details. Transistor has that in spades, even moreso than Bastion. The music, OVC terminals, and stained-glass visual aesthetic paint a stunning portrait of a world fragmenting into pieces. But likewise, the story must be pieced together as well - no omniscient narrator this time. For me, finding these story snippets and inferring the connections between them was rewarding, but I can see how for some it might be too much breadcrumb trail and not enough gingerbread house, especially in comparison to Bastion.
The combat system in Transistor is definitely enjoyable once you find the right synergies, but also very challenging until you figure those out (or look at a guide). I like that Supergiant used the trace files and the test rooms to encourage you to switch things up - experimenting with different loadouts and finding what works for you is the only way to succeed as challenges increase. That said, while generally you can play to suit your preferences, some synergies and loadouts are definitely stronger than others, so you might find the combat less balanced than you'd like. Turn() is also less powerful than you might expect, and it takes awhile to find the right rhythms and strategies. But when you do, man does it feel awesome!
All things said, I enjoyed it enough to play twice, and I'm actually finding it more enjoyable the second time. If you want a game that will challenge you with surprising complexity (and a game that will look and sound gorgeous to boot), Transistor is absolutely worth the money.

Supergiant is steadily becoming one of my favorite developers.  Bastion was amazing enough, but Transistor went even further with the strength of its art, music, sentimental narrative (Cunningham's voice is become quite iconic in its own right!), and more than anything, its mechanics with the customizable ability system, setting it apart from Bastion entirely.  Both of their games make me realize why I now prefer smaller companies in gaming: a smaller number of dedicated people making a smaller game seems much more likely to never lose sight of their creative focus, and the end product is often a more memorable and rewarding experience than an big budget pile of trendy mediocrity where things either drag on to the point of tedium, or abruptly end in unfulfilled disappointment.
My only regret is that I can't SPECIFICALLY explain why I love Transistor so much without spoiling what makes it so memorable, so I'm stuck with being vague.  All I can say is that I was extremely happy to play this game, despite...well, if anyone's finished the game, they know.  After the emotional reaction I got from Bastion, I would expect no less from Transistor.  They delivered exactly what I was hoping for, and let's just say there's a very good reason why I refused to buy this game without the soundtrack bundled in.  I only wish I could get an artbook to go with it.
I really wish I didn't have to be so cryptic, but this is one of those games that you just do not spoil.  It's just so refreshing to see a game like this.

Dark Souls II receives a lot of unwarranted hate and dislike. While the second installment in the Souls series (third if we count Demon's Souls), is not as great as the first one, It's certainly worth a playthrough if you're a fan of the series.
Let's start off with the positives. This time around, the PC version is not a complete mess, it runs very well and even the keyboard controls are manageable, even though I'd still prefer a controller. They've improved co-op as well, by introducing a special ring you can use, to make it easier to summon your friends. The game is also bigger than Dark Souls 1, though as you'll read later, this is a negative as well. Out of all the Souls games I have played, Dark Souls II offered the most variety in armour and weaponry, making it better than both Dark Souls 1 and 3 if you wanted to do a cosplay or challenge build.
Now for some of the negatives. There's two big issues you'll find in this game. The first one is that they chose for quantity over quality. There are more bosses and areas than ever before - but none of them stand out as much, which is a real shame. Many of the bosses are forgettable, thanks to being similar in either design or moveset. They've also decided to make the game more difficult in an artificial way. By placing more groups of enemies together and by allowing enemies to do full 360 degrees spins, just to face you.
And while they introduced a special ring to help you summon your friends more easily, they also gimped online connectivity as whole, thanks to Soul Memory.
For those who don't know what Soul Memory is, it's the combined total of souls you have ever acquired, regardless of if you used them. This works in a tiering system, if you're in a higher tier, you will not be able to invade or summon people from lower tiers, and vice versa. At first, this completely killed the online after a certain point. With the introduction of Scholar of the First Sin, though, another ring was added which disabled any soul gain. This way, you'd have to sacrifice a ring slot, but at least you wouldn't end up in a lonely, high tier without anyone to invade or summon.
+ Tried something different rather than piggyback off Dark Souls 1 (which is what 3 did).
+ Most variety in weapons, movesets and equipment.
+ Improved the ability to summon your friends with the special ring.
+ Solid port and controls.
+ 90% of all DLC is great in level design ánd bosses.
+/- Replay value is higher thanks to the variety in weaponry and such. But since the world is much less open than in Dark Souls 1, you'll end up going the exact same routes most of the time.
- Soul memory, albeit fixed with a workaround, was still a bad decision.
- World, bosses and story are far less interesting.
- Soundtrack is not as impressive.
- Added difficulty for the sole purpose of being difficult.

Having played ESO a couple of years ago and logging over 300 hours (honestly not a lot) over the years not on Steam and watch the progression of the game, I can only say positive things about ESO.
When ESO originally came out, it was buggy, not really balanced, and a big cash grab. That's quite frankly why the game originally was a big let down. However, over the years, they've made many major improvements. Some of the major improvements include getting rid of the mandatory subscription model, making everything scale, allowing players to venture over all of tamriel without getting to max level. These changes, along with more omptimization really made the game a lot better.
As for the gameplay, it is a very typical MMO style game. There is melee, magic, and archery as the three combat styles. You have a bar of spells you can use (5 normal, 1 ultimate). Some spells are support spells, some spells are combat spells, some spells are situational spells. There is a roll dodge feature so that you can avoid certain abilities, and the sneak ability comes in handy especially during multiplayer (I will talk about multiplayer a bit later). You can group into a party of up to 4 people to do quests on a normal basis, with a full raid party of up to 24 people (6 groups of 4). Generally for the PVE only, you can also do everything solo no matter what class you are. Additionally, like many other MMOs, ESO has a crafting system that is rather nice. Whether it be increasing enchating, alchemy, smithing, woodworking, etc. there are a wealth of noncombat skills to level up and gain experience in.
A little on guild side now. Similar to other MMO games, you can join a guild to interact with people. There are dungeon guilds, PVP guilds, trading guilds, casual guilds, etc. You can even make your own guild as a personal extra bank for items. Trading guilds are a great way to make money faster by selling your ingredients or items (way more than NPC merchants will buy them for). You can also use guilds to buy ingredients or items you need or want. If your guild gets rich enough, you can even bid for a guild trader.
The game also has a really awesome dungeon system where you can do them in a group. There are the basic dungeons that you can go in with 4 people and simply kill monsters till the end. But there are also bigger, harder, and more experienced dungeons that require a more tryhard team. Some dungeons are even scaled to the point where you should be going in with a 12 man party sometimes (trials I beleive). Dungeons are a great place for loot and keep the game interesting, whether it be casually or more tryhard.
Lastly, the best part of the game is probably the multiplayer. When I say the best part, I actually mean it. The basis of multiplayer is that you are part of your faction, whether it be daggerfall covenant, aldermini dominion, or ebonheart pact. Each faction holds keeps and buildings that can be captured by another faction. Each faction also starts off with 2 elder scrolls each, and these can be stolen/captured. Now this might not seem that good, but trust me it is. There are trebuchets, ballistas, flaming oil, etc. for sieging and defending. Imagine this but with a full 50 v 50 v 50 in a three way battle. I have actually gotten to the point the battle is so big that my sound cuts off. That is truly some good stuff. Additionally, the multiplayer scales your player, so even at lower levels you can enjoy multiplayer to a degree.
Overall, the game has gotten much better since I originally started playing, so much that I bought it again for steam. I would highly recommend any person who is a fan of MMORPGs and not stuck with World of Warcraft to consider playing ESO.
TLDR: ESO is a very improved game from what it originally was with a good PvE, fun dungeons, and AMAZING multiplayer.

Reign of Kings (RoK) is almost like a tragedy; what's present is the making of a good game, but the tragic part is the developers have "released" the game, and appear to be finished with it. It seems their intentions are no longer on developing and supporting game content.
At this point, the game feels like it's in a Beta state - movement, animations and character models are clunky and unrefined. The content available in the game feels shallow, and also in need of refinement. This is terribly unfortunate, because, despite the state of the game, there's plenty of fun to be had. If more time and effort had been put into the game's development, it would feel much fuller, vibrant and even more fun.
What RoK offers now is a stable, albeit shallow and clunky, medieval sandbox survival experience. While it offers a fair amount of variety in resources, materials and crafting elements, it doesn't offer, or receive, the same developmental support that will ensure a lasting (fun and interesting) game experience. Furthermore, the combat, while serviceable and modestly entertaining, is in need of work; animations are horrible, and both armor and weapons could use balancing (to make the system more interesting, example being: the speed difference between fully nude and clad in full steel armor is roughly 6% - essentially, there's no pros, or cons, outside of armor value between armor sets).
But, again, RoK isn't a wholly bad game, and, in fact, it's pretty fun for the most part. It just feels unfinished. That's the best, tl:dr, way of describing the game: unfinished.
I paid $5 for the game, on sale. At that price, it's worth the money. However, for the full $20, I just don't think I can recommend RoK. Ultimately, it's an unfinished product, that while fun, isn't worth the price of admission. If you can get it for $10, or less, then I say, "sure, go for it."
Again, TL:DR - Fun game, albeit feels unrefined and unfinished. Only worth it on sale, not at full-price.

Short summary: don't buy it or play it. Not worth your time or your money. Oh, you want to know why? I'll lay out some points below, but in brief: they removed or botched every distinguishing characteristic of the previous Amnesia game (and Frictional Games in general), and replaced those characteristics with . . . nothing. What you're left with is a series of spooky but poorly realized environments and a scenario/story which has a lot of potential but isn't fleshed out or conveyed very effectively. If you love the original Amnesia, play it again. Or play one of the fan-made scenarios (there are some great ones). Or play the Penumbra games (they're very very good). Just don't play A Machine for Pigs.
Things you should know about A Machine for Pigs:
• Lots of cut and paste art assets. You'll see the same paintings, desk lamps, sacks of inexplicably fresh potatoes, chairs, desks, barrels, crates, and wall textures everywhere. This would be fine in a 1st person shooter or something where environment is secondary, but inexcusable in atmospheric horror where you are supposed to be piecing a story together based on environmental cues.
• No interactivity. In the original Amnesia and other games by Frictional, you could pick up most small objects, open every drawer and cupboard, and push around most larger objects even if you couldn't lift them. In addition to being the basis for some great puzzles, the physics system created a much-needed sense of *presence* and gave life to the environments. (Rooting through a pile of rubble, throwing items off to the side, to find a useful item underneath, is more engaging than clicking on an item sitting on a shelf, for example.)  You can’t even jump on top of most low objects nor crawl under most gaps.
In Machine for Pigs, you can pick up chairs, and you can open *some* desk drawers and doors. That's about it, except for puzzle-specific objects. Most egregiously, the game is full of "doors" and "cabinets" which you cannot interact with in any way. In Dark Descent, you could try to open one and it would at least rattle and maybe you'd get a message that it's locked. In this game? Nothing. Your cursor doesn't even change when you mouse over the door or cabinet. It's basically a wall with a door texture on it. This reduces the game to a "pixel hunt" where you move your cursor over every object and surface in a room to figure out which thing is interactive (usually nothing is).
• No inventory. There are no items to collect, examine, combine, and use to solve puzzles. There are no tinder boxes for lighting torches, and your lantern never runs out of oil so there is no need to find lantern oil. Not a problem on its own, but combined with lifeless, non-interactive environments and it means there's nothing to actually *do* in this game.
• No game mechanics. No sanity or health or lamp oil to manage. Few enemies and they mostly appear at pre-scripted moments for chase sequences. You never have to make any risk/reward type decisions, and this makes the game feel very low-stakes.
• Story and scenario are not sufficiently realized. I think they needed a bigger budget and more time for this. Won’t go into details but suffice to say it’s a grandiose premise which could have been the basis for something great, but this is not how it panned out.

I got 'AMfP' as part of an Amnesia bundle for pretty cheap during a sale and went into it ahead of time knowing about the lukewarm critical reception. Maybe if I had paid full price during its initial release with high expectations I would have been let down but in the end I thought it was a good game.
To be sure, it's not as good as the first one. With the first game I actually had to stop at various points because I was too nervous to progress into a darkened area. There's only one scene in this one where I felt close to that level of scared. This game simply isn't as horrifying this time around. It's also a considerably shorter, more streamlined experience -- there's less interactivity, puzzles, etc.
Another thing that disappoints me was the lack of a custom story option. The original Amnesia has hours and hours of replay value that this does not because of it. The game is different enough than the original that there's potential for a number of custom stories using the elements present here.
On the positive side, the game is still an effective and atmospheric experience. I would stay the story is stronger this time around. The protagonist Oswald Mandus plays a much bigger part in his own story than Daniel did in the first one and as such his his character arc is more rewarding in my opinion. The game's world is beautiful and haunting to look at; I stopped several times just to take in the scenery. I normally don't talk about music in games but Jessica Curry's soundtrack really adds to the story.
The developers had the unenviable task of following up 'The Dark Descent' and to their credit they took a risk as opposed to simply copying the formula of the original. Not all of it works but I still have to applaud their efforts.
If you're all hesitant I would wait until this is on sale but I do recommend you try it out at least once.

Pros:
+Suprisingly addicting gameplay, conisidering that you feel like you're at a day job
+Sufficiently intiguing story
+Twenty storyline "outcomes" dictated by player decisions
+Amazing auto-save system.  At any point in the story, you can go back and restart from any previous level WITHOUT saving over the original playthrough's saves, essentially creating an alternate save "branch".  Once you see the save menu, you'll wonder why it's not the standard for all games.  Makes achievement hunting a breeze.
Cons:
-Low replay value.
-No music variety.  The songs works, but by the end it got annoying.
-Player controls are unlocked like character abilities.  For example, at the beginning of the story, the approve/deny stamp is brought out by clicking a small tab at the side of the screen; later on, you buy the "desk upgrade" that allows you to open the stamp with a keyboard button (a much more convenient and logical control for the most used function in the game).  This makes a second playthrough quite annoying, since your muscle memory adapts to the button controls.  Seems like a gimic that should've been scraped in testing.
Oddly, I felt that it was too long.  The idea works, but "checking passports and ID's for consistency" is simply too repetetive of a task for a 5-6 hour playthrough.  I just think it might've been cleaner if it were shorter.  By mid-to-late game, I stopped having any fun and only played through it because I felt invested in the story.  Still a thumbs up for a unique and well-executed indie title.  At $5, go for it.

The game starts off with the same problem of many modern FPS, with a very boring tutorial and story. You get interrupted a lot with quick timed events and story. Moreover some levels are poorly designed, so you may spend lots of time finding were to go next. Fortunately there's an option to permanetly guide you. I strongly recommend activating this option. Basically in the first episode you spend a lot of time with annoyances rather than just shooting.
After the tedious tutorial the next levels have a much better flow. During the game the main character tell you about his story but this does not interrupt the game flow at all and even gives the game some character. You always have lots of enemies to shoot. While there are still some quick timed events during the game they're really quick and shouldn't bother much.
The bosses aren't great. Most bosses have lots of energy and just hide and shoot with their companions appearing sometimes. There's also a western shootout at the end of most levels. It's just one of those accuracy and timing mini-games. Overall bosses aren't interesting and easy to defeat.
There are some unnecessary features in this game. First there's the typical items to collect. Collecting things is just a waste of time. There's a skill that allows you to slow time down either manually by pressing a key or automatically when you're almost dying. I didn't need these skills to beat the game so it just made me feel like the game is holding your hand too much even in the highest difficulty. There is already automatic recovery so automatic time slow down is just an exaggeration. Finally there are upgrades. The upgrades don't give much of an advantage and neither give an incentive to get them all.
It is a short game and it really shows. Being a short game is not always a bad thing but in this particular game finishing does not leave you with a sense of accomplishment. It didn't really bother me that much because that's what I expect with modern games. Unfortunately games with good sense of accomplishment are rare these days.
Anyway I recommend this game for those who like linear FPS. Just don't expect genius work.

Red pulls the sword out of the man’s body. The sword talks to her, but she doesn’t speak back. She lost her voice and he lost his body. It was an eventful night. The sword is obviously too big for her, she drags it around, but somehow manages to muster the strength she needs to wield it in battle. The city of Cloudbank is being destroyed by a cybernetic virus called the Process, let loose by a shadowy organization named the Camerata. Red, a famous club singer, is a target of a failed assassination. Other prominent Cloudbank citizens have become unfortunate targets as well. But why? Transistor manages to deliver an interesting premise that takes place in a sci-fi world that fuses programming languages with a dystopian alternate reality to create something wonderfully unique.
Narrative exposition is actually pretty light, most of the storytelling comes from Transistor, the titular sword who comments on everything that is going on. Terminals scattered across the city provide updates on the latest news. You can also learn additional information about the various characters by unlocking new weapons and limiters. Along with the beautiful visuals and great soundtrack, the storytelling paints a striking picture of the intriguing setting. However, it doesn’t really do much with it. Aside from the enemies and the dead bodies you stumble upon along the way, the city is barren. There is no interaction with anyone until almost the very end. Despite all the strong production values and wonderful artistry, Cloudbank still somehow manages to feel a bit empty and distant.
The vast majority of time is spent in combat. You may confuse it with a turn-based combat system at first, but it’s really a real-time system. You can fight the Process’ minions in real-time without interruptions, but that may prove difficult. So the game offers you to use a “turn” which is in fact just a slightly more elaborate pause. During this turn, you can plan your moves including movement, abilities and weapon strikes. Once you’re satisfied, the game will then play out your orders. After that, all your abilities are on cooldown for a set amount of time during which you have to avoid enemy attacks by either taking cover or running around positioning yourself for your next “turn”. It takes a while to get into the groove of things, but once you get used to it, you’ll find it a very enjoyable and flexible system.
What makes the combat really interesting is how you can use each of your functions (abilities and attacks) on a primary, secondary or passive slot. Each function provides different abilities or powers depending on which slot it occupies. This system enables plenty of combat experimentation sometimes leading to unexpected results. The game will also sometimes force you to experiment and swap out functions because losing chunks of life points leads to a function overload rendering it unusable for a while. My problem with the combat system isn’t really down to the combat itself, but rather the fact that the game doesn’t provide any options to tailor it to your preferences. For example, having the option to automatically initiate a turn on enemy sight and/or end of cooldown would have been really helpful instead of having to constantly keep track of the cooldown bar as you’re trying to dodge incoming attacks. Also, displaying your current function setup on icon mouse-over would have helped to be aware of your powers. Considering that you swap them out so much, it’s easy to forget what you’re using as you can only inspect your functions in detail at checkpoints.
I walked away from Transistor with a feeling that a bit more could have been done regarding the design, gameplay and storytelling, but despite that, I found it to be a highly enjoyable and thoroughly unique action game with stellar presentation and an engaging emphasis on player experimentation.
Highlights: Art direction, soundtrack, combat experimentation
Downsides: Lack of options

After nearly 1700 hours spent on this title, i can say this is by far my favourite Total War game, and maybe my favourite game overall. Mods add a huge amount of replayability and make the game much more enjoyable than vanilla. However, even with said mods, it's far from perfect, there are a lot of cool features that were lost from Rome 1 and Med 2. Since those two are the only TW games i have played besides this, my comparisons are based on the differences between them. Rome 2 has better AI, especially in battle, but the campaign map, including empire management, feels lacking comparing to those old titles: i don't like the province system, it removes all the fun of seeing a city grow and become rich, strong and, in general, important to maintain. Diplomacy is better (but still not great, the AI is often as stubborn as a mule); sadly no family tree, but i can get over this, 'cause at least here we have politics; speaking of politics, it's not a very well designed system, but i hope the new patch will improve it; civil war mechanic is not that amazing, and only two factions get benefict from having one. Early game can be really hard, especially on Very Hard and Legendary difficulties becuase of the insane "cheats" the AI gets, while in late game you can just steamroll the whole reamaining map due to the broken auto-resolve (heck, you can just recruit auto-resolve stacks and conquer the world without having to manually resolve a single battle, which might make you think that 4th tier units are not all that good). This is like the opposite of Rome 1 :/
Battles are less fast-paced, units take longer to break, and cavalry is far less effective at doing so. The only reason i recruit cavalry is for killing skirmishers, which the AI loves to spam. The only units that may wanna go behind the enemy lines are skirmishers: when all the enemy melee infantry is engaged, it's easier to kill them by shooting them in the back.
If cavalry was the battlefield king in Rome 1 and Med 2, now this role belongs to artillery (ballistas are the way to go): its accuracy is insane, and it excels at smashing cavalry. With the cinematic view, you can aim and shoot yourself, with an even greater rate of fire, and completely annihilate the enemies if they're already engaged and you're shooting from just behind your line (that's why i always place artillery very close to the front line). In sieges, they can trap several enemy units standing on the walls by destroying adjacents towers and exiting points. Naval battles are meh: again, artillery is king, and all you need in your fleet are ballista ships. They smash enemy ships at distance and can ram the remaining ones wtih ease. They can even bomb an entire garrison army to death, or lure them offshore and sink their transports (which is the simplest way to kill them).
The food mechanic is just tedious, i always find myself expanding towards the grain settlements, which give +1 food per level for every single settlement you own. This has made all my campaigns almost the same: I always end up with a small empire that include Dacia, Pannonia, Thracia, Illyria, Macedonia and Hellas, from which i can start building up high tier armies and procede to steamroll the remaining objectives. I recently started to use a mod tha completely removes food, so i can no longer focus on said grain settlements and go conquer what i want.
Dilemmas are not consistent, you can take the same choice for the same event end get a different outcome every time.
I won't say anything about multiplayer because i'm a singleplayer guy, i literally never fought an online battle or started a coop/vs campaign.
Last thing i wanna say... Yes, it is true that Rome 2 suffered from a bad launch, i myself didn't play it until more than six months after its release even though i pre-ordered it, but now it's completely fine, i can't remember the last time i incurred in a bug or glitch, if we don't taking into account the (rare) frame drops in big sieges. Maybe the "ships sailing on sand" still exists, but last time i saw that it was more than a year ago.
So, that's it: I definetely recommend this game, even at full price. DLCs, on the other hand... Get those only when they're on sale, they don't really add much for their price, especially culture packs.
Recommended non-overhaul mods: 4TPY, No AI agent, Reduced Corruption, Better Campaig AI, Balance Through Realism, Decreased Replenishment rate of Mercs pool, Faster Cavalry, Faster Research, Force March removed, Sell your Slaves.

There are changes to the somewhat standard format in place since Napoleon TW. Armies must be raised and led by a general. This keeps tiny reinforcement armies from clogging up the map and helps the AI from getting too confused by the possibilities.
Pros:
-Field battles are lots of fun
-I found siege battles generally more fun than in previous TW games
-Transporting armies across water is easy. You just tell your army to go into the sea and they build transports to go there. Almost too easy to do so (see cons)
-Sea battles: ramming enemy ships and watching them sink will make you cackle with glee!
-AI on campaign generally seems a bit smarter than previous games
-New province system is interesting and has potential
Cons:
-Cities and settlements on the campaign map are ridiculously huge and project a massive area of influence. In smaller territories, you almost can't avoid fighting in them, making a large number of your battles siege or settlement battles.
-Sea transports for armies should have some cost. It's too easy to transport and use them as a professional boarding fleet. Perhaps making your ground troops have a sea sickness penalty during boarding actions?
-Sea battles are really annoying. Your ships will rarely ram twice by rowing backward and forward into the same ship. The AI fleets do it all the time.
-Experience for generals and agents needs to be fixed or the timescale does. You will rarely get them highly ranked, at 1 turn per year and the experience you get, they die too quickly.
-Campaign AI seems to get confused when fighting wars across the seas instead of over a direct land route. My Roman war vs Carthage was disappointing because Carthage just wandered around the seas with its land army in transports which allowed my true navy to pick them apart.

Having played ESO a couple of years ago and logging over 300 hours (honestly not a lot) over the years not on Steam and watch the progression of the game, I can only say positive things about ESO.
When ESO originally came out, it was buggy, not really balanced, and a big cash grab. That's quite frankly why the game originally was a big let down. However, over the years, they've made many major improvements. Some of the major improvements include getting rid of the mandatory subscription model, making everything scale, allowing players to venture over all of tamriel without getting to max level. These changes, along with more omptimization really made the game a lot better.
As for the gameplay, it is a very typical MMO style game. There is melee, magic, and archery as the three combat styles. You have a bar of spells you can use (5 normal, 1 ultimate). Some spells are support spells, some spells are combat spells, some spells are situational spells. There is a roll dodge feature so that you can avoid certain abilities, and the sneak ability comes in handy especially during multiplayer (I will talk about multiplayer a bit later). You can group into a party of up to 4 people to do quests on a normal basis, with a full raid party of up to 24 people (6 groups of 4). Generally for the PVE only, you can also do everything solo no matter what class you are. Additionally, like many other MMOs, ESO has a crafting system that is rather nice. Whether it be increasing enchating, alchemy, smithing, woodworking, etc. there are a wealth of noncombat skills to level up and gain experience in.
A little on guild side now. Similar to other MMO games, you can join a guild to interact with people. There are dungeon guilds, PVP guilds, trading guilds, casual guilds, etc. You can even make your own guild as a personal extra bank for items. Trading guilds are a great way to make money faster by selling your ingredients or items (way more than NPC merchants will buy them for). You can also use guilds to buy ingredients or items you need or want. If your guild gets rich enough, you can even bid for a guild trader.
The game also has a really awesome dungeon system where you can do them in a group. There are the basic dungeons that you can go in with 4 people and simply kill monsters till the end. But there are also bigger, harder, and more experienced dungeons that require a more tryhard team. Some dungeons are even scaled to the point where you should be going in with a 12 man party sometimes (trials I beleive). Dungeons are a great place for loot and keep the game interesting, whether it be casually or more tryhard.
Lastly, the best part of the game is probably the multiplayer. When I say the best part, I actually mean it. The basis of multiplayer is that you are part of your faction, whether it be daggerfall covenant, aldermini dominion, or ebonheart pact. Each faction holds keeps and buildings that can be captured by another faction. Each faction also starts off with 2 elder scrolls each, and these can be stolen/captured. Now this might not seem that good, but trust me it is. There are trebuchets, ballistas, flaming oil, etc. for sieging and defending. Imagine this but with a full 50 v 50 v 50 in a three way battle. I have actually gotten to the point the battle is so big that my sound cuts off. That is truly some good stuff. Additionally, the multiplayer scales your player, so even at lower levels you can enjoy multiplayer to a degree.
Overall, the game has gotten much better since I originally started playing, so much that I bought it again for steam. I would highly recommend any person who is a fan of MMORPGs and not stuck with World of Warcraft to consider playing ESO.
TLDR: ESO is a very improved game from what it originally was with a good PvE, fun dungeons, and AMAZING multiplayer.

i have gotten a little ways in to the game and i have got to get a few things out there.
first off, this game is great for ridiculous fun provided you dont expect any degree of reality or story. of course if you are looking at these games you are probably already aware of this. so far at least this is not a big problem to me, i wasnt expecting serious so i am not disappointed there. its actually quite funny, in the way the cheesy action films are funny.
however, there are a couple of things that have really got me angry so far, not a little annoyed or frustrated, outright angry. there is a lot in here that is really poorly explained, controls are touched on in the midst of a mission and then if you forget you have to go back into the controls menu and look them up. i am not bad with this kind of thing normally but i have had to do so several times already. this is largely due to the fact that the controls are, i can only assume deliberately, unlike any other game i have played. they seem to have gone for the "well we will do it toally differently" mentality. you get used to them eventually but it just continually comes off as backwards.
the vehicle controls are terrible, really terrible. i know keyboard is far from ideal for driving but i have never had so much trouble before. powerful cars and bikes seems to suddenly spin out one second then not respond the next. some of the vehicle based challenges are daft thanks to the controls. plus the physics in the game are bizzare and you may be able to ram your way over a rock but then a pebble with send the car flying into the air spinning around wildly. it makes no sense, even in a game where sense is not really the point. flying around with the grapple/parachute/wingsuit are a lot better and the heavy stuff like tanks is more civilised though, which makes up for it somewhat.
then are bases, which can be great fun but you come across objectives that are a little more involved than 'shoot it until it explodes' or 'drag it over with the grapple'. which would be fine but they get mentioned in easily missable dialogue and then the markers appear and disappear seemingly at random. which really winds me up. so be prepared to use google sometimes to find out what you are meant to be doing.
most infuriatingly, and this has caused me to rage quit several times already, you can get stuck in a never ending attack. enemies can call reinforcements which if you kill the caller before the timer runs down you can lose your wanted level. so far so good. however, i found myself regularly wiping out everyone in the area and then hearing the reinforcements are coming in, kill everyone again and watch like crazy for the icon and yet again the phantom call goes out again. its not that i am missing the last guy either, i have been 100% certain that everyone in sight is dead, including civilians just in case, yet it still happens. leaving you in an increasingly difficult yet entirely inescapable situation which stops you from doing anything else unless you die or quit. that is not fun in my book, it just seems like a broken mechanic but it has so far had a huge impact on my time with the game.
so to sum up, if you like the outpost capturing antics of farcry 4 and assassins creed but dont worry about stealth, and like the destruction and humour of GTA then you will probably like this game. if you are easily annoyed or impatient then you may find this very aggravating. i would recommend it becase so far the funny bits and the crazy bits are outweighing the rage inducing bits, but i would be ready to stop and take a deep breath every now and then.

A Machine for Pigs is what you get when you take the Amnesia and Penumbra games and make it more streamlined and environment heavy rather than puzzle and physics heavy. While it's a beautiful wretched game, it isn't up to par compared to the other two.
I won't spoil too much (though honestly the plot is even more bare bones than its predecessor) but there's a lot to take in and explore, but again, greatly simplified. There's no inventory, enemies can persue you though not very far and aren't as numerous, puzzles are rather obvious, and exploration is at a minimum.
That doesn't keep A Machine for Pigs from getting a recommendation though, while it's more limited, there's vast amounts you can leave to your twisted imagination and the scale is quite epic. The biggest thing it ends up doing wrong is making itself an Amnesia game considering its predecesors are superior in many ways. It's more of a standalone than a sequel, an episode rather than a complex game. But again, hardly a terrible thing. If you're interested, a sale would probably whet your appetite.

This game is like "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" made with half the gameplay time and half the development effort. Even if this game wasn't part of the Amnesia series I wouldn't recommend it because it's not good even as a standalone. I almost wonder if this game was pushed through development way too fast in an effort to piggyback on the success of the first one.
A lot of the things that made the first Amnesia so good are gone: No sanity changes, no inventory, far fewer scares, and a much less interative environment. Something about the physics feels off and when your character slows to a snail's pace during voiceovers way too often it's very annoying. I'm halfway through the game and I've rarely seen monsters, I'm practically skipping through the levels without feeling threatened and have thought several times about shelving it and just watching a Let's Play instead.
Don't buy it at full price, it isn't worth it. On average, people beat it in 3.5 hours, so even based on gameplay time alone I don't think it's worth $20. The Amnesia 1 and 2 often go on a combo sale for a few bucks during summer. If you really want to play, I recommend picking it up then. And if you don't play it at all, you aren't missing out.

As a player acquainted with Strategy games (Sid Meier's, Total War Series etc.) but new to MMORPG, I find TOS a good experience:
- The graphics is really nice, except for some bugs, such as the turning heads etc.
- The audio is good, though my girlfriend, who was a big fan of Ragnarok, says Ragnarok's songs are more beautiful but I can't really judge as I haven't played it.
- The storyline is well-written. Those commanding good English and caring to read will be additionally entertained.
- The game mechanics is ok, although introductions of some new Classes and nerfing of existing Classes or Skills have disappointed a number of players (not including me.) Daily activities are too many, though, for compulsive-obsessive players (including me.)
- The community is ok, especially if you belong to a Guild of like-minded players or if you are a nice person yourself. (Talking about Guilds, I would rather IMC incentivize the Guilds more to GvG, for example give them some inconsequential rewards for participation.)
- Bots are surely present but they haven't interfered with my gameplay, so I cannot really tell if they are a real problem.
But the biggest weakness of TOS is the latency, especially in the Cities. I hope mankind will have the right technology to overcome this entirely in the future.

A horror game that made me a little tense at times, it has a really good story about morals. Basically it's about a guy who, in wanting to achieve success in life, seized the properties of 3 people for the company that he is working for (I learnt that distraint is an actual word that means "the seizure of someone's property in order to obtain money owed, especially rent").
Throughout the game, we see how he starts to lose it after the first distraint until the point that he feels that he needs to quit his job after the third distraint... I will leave it at that but suffice to say that the story was something I enjoyed a lot, particularly the twist that I didn't foresee at the end which left me in awe, especially when I replayed the first part again (while trying to get some achievements that I missed in my first playthrough) and could appreciate the connection between the start and the end...
Gameplay wise, you are basically going around talking to people, finding and using objects and it has some puzzles along the way akin to those you see in hidden object / point-and-click games. Perhaps the only drawback is that the game is quite short (probably about 2 hours) but for a game that is almost single-handedly created (from game design, art, music) - the main source of help was from his wife who contributed some ideas - it's a brilliant effort and definitely worth some time and a few bucks to support the fella. =)

Transistor is an isometric, half-turn-based, half-real-time, sci-fi game made by the same devs as Bastion, and it's a pretty bloody good game.
As expected from Supergiant Games, Transistor has fantastic art style and music, interesting setting and story, and a very melancholy vibe throughout. You fight by planning out your actions to maximum effect during a "Turn()" phase, then watching them play out, all the while dodging enemies in real time during your recovery phase.
The combat not only has a ridiculous amount of customization and depth— as you try out different combinations of different offensive and defensive "Functions" in active slots, upgrade slots, and passive slots— but also ties crucial story information to said gameplay experimentation. Each "Function" details the story of a particular character in the world of Transistor, and by using each Function in a different way, you unlock more information about that character. Overall a great way of world-building and encouraging player experimentation.
The only major complaint I have is that Transistor employs in media res to a rather absurd degree. The game throws you in to the story immediately after♥♥♥♥♥♥has gone down and leaves you there to piece together the story bit by bit from sporadic dialogue and flavor text. You'll be well over half-way through the game before you can really piece together the basics of what's going on.
That aside, I highly recommend Transistor for its fun combat, cool setting, interesting story, and fantastic art style.
