First and foremost, this game is incredible, and I would absolutely recommend it. The plot is clever, thematic, and flows beautifully. The visuals and music are perfection. The game is just missing something, and it took me a while to but a finger on what it was.
It's people. The game is really lacking some sense of humanity. The streets are empty, and so the world feels lonely. I tried really hard to feel a part of it, but I couldn't. There just wasn't any immersion walking through lonely streets. I made the excuse that I was sharing in Red's isolation, clinging on to the narrator's voice as our only anchor to this world. But that's all it was -- an excuse. In reality, every time I turned a corner, I was just hoping to run across someone new in the streets, anyone, even bodies. Just something to convince me I was walking through what was once a crowded city.
While the characters are deep and brilliantly crafted, their character development is sort of shallow and vague, and the lack of backstory behind their relationships really doesn't give enough credit to how interesting their story actually is. I would have loved to be more emotionally invested the game, but I just wasn't, and I think it's a by-product of how intentionally vague and desolate the Transistor world is.
For example, at first, I thought the narrator was a stranger. Then it became obvious that they knew each other. And then he started babbling and I was like, "this dude got friend zoned so hard." And then you find out they were lovers! I wish I came in having some sort of backstory on their relationship, because without a perspective of who they were before, you can't really appreciate the transition most of the plot is built around them coping with. And that detachment really cuts at the heart of what the game is about. I still have this feeling like I missed some sort of intro video, you know? The only backstory they give on the founding incident is maybe three seconds of a parallax scene where you can easily infer, but it is not stated, that the narrator was Red's lover and jumped in front of the blade to save her life, and then he just gets drunk and goes on and on about how much he loves her, without any word or indication about his feelings being reciprocated by Red until the end and then you're like, "the ♥♥♥♥ just happened." Even reading all the terminals, I was completely caught off-guard and felt a bit in the dark. "Okay, I guess that's what happens then. Uh. Yeah. What." But once I figured it out, it was like, "Holy ♥♥♥♥ that was beautiful. I wish I could have appreciated it more..."
So after my first playthrough, I loved everything I understood about the plot, but had some pretty big questions, so I went to the forums. The plot, once you wrap your head around it (and especially if you have experience with programming), is elegant on a level I haven't seen in a video game since the Bioshock series, but with a lot more class. I recommended it to a ton of my friends, but felt stupid being like, "Yeah, and read this thread to figure out what's going on with the plot." Like with a game this brilliantly crafted, I shouldn't have to do that. Before they started playing, I had to think about what information I could tell them to make them appreciate the game in ways I didn't have the opportunity to, but then what information I had to withhold for them to really have the proper experience of playing the game without it being ruined by spoilers.
I would love to play the game again, if only for the chilling music, but spending so much time trying to figure out how to appropriately explain things before my friends played it left a bad taste in my mouth, and I really can't bring myself to open it back up. But with a few minor changes, this could easily be one of the most perfect games I've ever played, and I went out and bought all of the studio's other games because of it. If there was a sequel, or director's cut, I would buy it. As it stands, I paid like $13 for the game, and I felt that was completely fair. Would I pay $20? Probably not. But with the sort of changes you could suggest in a 15 minute conversation with a developer, polishing up the combat to make it a bit less repetitive and making the world/backstory more immersive, I would gladly ask everyone I know to shell out a full console price of $59.99.
All and all, a wonderful game, and I would definitely add it to your wishlist. I've seen it go on sale 3 times in the last few months, so you could probably get it for a bargain if you don't mind waiting.
TL;DR, Play this game on the highest difficulty, read the forums for a full plot synopsis after your first playthrough, it took around ~24 hours of gameplay to achieve 100% completion, and the game was so good I literally did that after work in 3 days. 10/10 would buy the developers a beer.

Though I'd say Skyrim is still king of teh Elder Scroll series, ESO seriously gives it a run for it's money.  I've already put over 100 hours into this game and I've only scratched the surface of it.  The map is HUGE and is still being updated and added to.  Tamriel is massive, and with ESO you are able to explore a vast amount of it, and hopefully the rest of it on down the road.
I think my only "dislike" with the game is the combat.  It feels a little wonky and almost goofy in a way.  It's just sort of awkward.  It's either you fight 1-2 enemies at a time and it's boringly easy, or you fight multiple enemies and it becomes insanely difficult as your health drops terrifyingly fast.  This could just be me and maybe I'm just bad at this game though haha.
I 100% love the looting system in the game as well as the leveling system and skill system and all that jazz.  I really enjoy the lock picking mini game for treasure chests too!  It took me a few tries before I got the hang of it but once I did it was actually quite easy and pretty fun.
I also love the variety you can have with your clothing, armor, costumes, helmets and masks.  You can even dye your clothes and armors different colors (I believe my character is currently hot pink....).   I would have liked a bit better or at least more definitive variety in the weapons but that's not a big deal.
The quests in the game like other ES games or Fallout even can be a little boring and tedious at times.   But it's almost always worth it in the end when you usually get decent rewards.
I plan to get the Morrowind DLC at some point too.
Overall a very solid game that's fun and addicting.

Overall, A Machine for Pigs is a pretty good, if short game. The story is interesting, and the settings are well-designed (and certainly more visually interesting than the dull castle of The Dark Descent). If it was just called "A Machine for Pigs", I would have no problem giving it a positive review.
The problem is that it's not called A Machine for Pigs; it's called Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, and so the developers are actively encouraging me to review it as an Amnesia game because that's what they're pitching it as to the customer. And in that regard, it's kind of awful. It's important to understand that this game was developed primarily by The Chinese Room, the developers of Dear Esther (which was an interesting story-based exploration game with gameplay summarized as a walking simulator), and not Frictional Games, the creator of the Penumbra and Amnesia games. I've already made it known that I consider Amnesia to be a worse game than the Penumbra series, and this game just takes it a step further down. The worst parts of Amnesia are well in-tact, so you can fully expect to frequently get wobbly vision during setpieces and to constantly get slowed down and visually impaired while the narrator dishes out a bit of story, which consistently kills both the pacing and the atmosphere. But everything else seems to be fair game for the cutting board, since there's no longer a sanity system, you don't have to manage resources like fuel for your light, and you don't even have an inventory. There isn't a puzzle in the game any more complex than "put the coal into the coal chute ten steps away" or "pull the lever", which makes it hard to say that there are even puzzles in the game at all. Enemies are almost nonexistant, with the grand total of actual enemy encounters being about 6, and being generous, taking up about 3 minutes of the 3 or 4 hours it takes to complete the game. They're not even particularly good or long encounters, either; in one particular instance, you suddenly drop into an area with an invisible water monster (which was more or less shamelessly ripped from The Dark Descent in place of actually making something new, with only a single note giving a half-hearted explanation of why it exists in this game), all you have to do is run forward in the only other direction that isn't towards the water monster. The path to the ladder to escape is literally gated by siderails, so it's almost impossible to actually fail the segment. And that sentiment applies to all of the game's sparse encounters; each of them is a very scripted, very setpiece-like instance where the monster shows up, you hide in the designated hiding place, the monster walks by, and you continue your merry way. It's very safe and guided, and you never really get the feeling of being in any real danger. The game does a lot to try to build up atmosphere, but it falls flat after the first thirty minutes or so because you very quickly realize that the game is never actually going to pay off on the tension beyond quick fleeting glimpses of a monster or a sudden banging noise that has no purpose other than to try to get a jump out of you (which makes up about 2/3 of the game's "scares").
Ultimately I would still recommend this game at a heavy discount, since all things considered it's still not the worst horror game on Steam (though that isn't saying a whole lot, considering thanks to Steam Greenlight even Bad Rats is no longer the worst game on Steam) and it does have an interesting plot, but if you're looking for more of what you've come to expect from Frictional Games then either wait for SOMA or download Penumbra: Necrologue.

A disappointing combat system leads to frustration and headaches.  I was really looking forward to this game and it's such a letdown.  Transistor's combat alternates between clunky and infuriating.  The game is both incredibly short and entirely too long. The music is great, but can only be accessed in-game in the challenges area.
Transistor feels like a long demo, or something Supergiant games cut their teeth on before making the glorious triumph that is Bastion.  I'm actually very disappointed that I bought this game. I wanted to like it, but it really just made me want to play Bastion again and pretend this never happened.

Transistor portrays an excellent story over an incredible world, that, states very nearly nothing, forcing players to have to piece it together through the limited dialogue of the supporting cast, and story logs from the abilities.
The combat of the game is very unique, yet slightly reminiscent to that of Parasite Eve, with an incredible 38,416 potential uses for those functions.
As for aesthetic, this is one of the two areas that the game outshines any and all competition (arguably, even that of Bastion) with a purely phenomenal and atmospheric soundtrack, that goes along outstandingly well with the awe-inspiring beauty of the visuals. Another game in which Darren Korb shows that he has the complete inability to make a bad song.
Great art, very enjoyable gameplay and an amazing story! Supergiant Games succesfully made another must-play game.

But of these seven hours registered to my account, 6 went into updating game and applying patches. Now, I do understand that the massive amount of data equals massive amount of megabytes and that ever changing universe does gets updated pretty much often, but somehow, I would like Bethesda to understand that I'm 31 year old working male with family who can't spend free hours of his life looking at their update progress bar.
Therefore, I am deeply sorry, but pushing gigabytes of updates every single time I launch TESO just ain't gonna work.
Thank you.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I can't reccomend this game enough.
Now, you may be thinking, "but you only have like 160 hours!1!!1" and you see I had this game on steam pinned to my taskbar and whenever I launched this game from my taskbar I guess it didn't contribute to hours, but let's get to the review.
I believe the whole game is great, from quests to story to alliance mode, it has it all. I could go on and on about the pros, but first let me start with some cons.
EARLY GAME
Now this is the make or break part of the game for (what i've seen to be) a lot of people. Due to the fact that I enjoy the Elder Scrolls series and it's lore so much that it was a given I would enjoy this. However, I've seen how tedious the early game can be with your low level gear and abilities which doesn't make combat that fun. I also believe the starting quests for every alliance are a bit tedious and just boring. However, if you get past this you should be able to continue to climb ranks, do dungeons, join guilds, make friends, and so much more.
BOREDOM
For me this was a huge problem because I just felt that my progress was so slow and I didn't really think I was getting anywhere. So, as you may imagine, I stopped playing for about 3 months. Side note: This was after the Morrowind release and I had been playing that for a long while, then got bored. I'm back into the game now however for some the boredom problem causes them to just quit the game and never come back.
CROWN CRATES AND MICROTRANSACTIONS
I was perfectly fine with all the microtransactions considering that a lot of them were cosmetic and the food and some other gear could be made (not as good as the crown goods but still good enough). Then crown crates came around. I have a huge pet peeve with these. Crown crates I feel like are the ultimate cash-grab, and here is my problem: you can only buy the rewards in the crates with currency you get from destroying the stuff you get from crates. I think this is absurd. Let's look at the Overwatch loot box system for a second. The currency you get in the boxes can be used to buy skins you may not have gotten in the loot boxes. This is fine, but imagine the only way to get this currency is to sell skins for an absurdly small amount of the currency to buy the skin you want. Since they don't have enough currency/skins to sacrifice, they buy more loot boxes. You get such low crown gems from destroying the items it's arguably not worth it.
Now, this seems like a lot but there are so many more pros, and as I said earlier I could go on and on, but here are the highlights:
FUN WITH FRIENDS
You have no idea how fun this game is with friends. My friends in real life don't play this game so I had to find some friends online who played this game, so I joined a guild that was advertising in the ESO reddit discord. I haven't left the clan since. I have made so many good friends in their, and we all love to play eso together. It's what being a guild is all about.
EXPLORE ALL OF TAMRIEL
In and out, you had no idea how entertaining this is. From the realm of Molag Bal to deep underground to the Clockwork City, you name it, it's most likely in the game. Each area has a unique story, many quests, dungeons, locations, oddities, and so much more. Each area is unique and when you walk into a town, you really get the sense of what the town is like. A busting trade center close to a bay or a large city where everybody works as a community. Each area is more than worth the visit.
SO MANY ADVENTURES
You can be taken to Daedric planes, a Lich's former school, a crazy Argonian alchemist's puzzle city, and so much more. Dungeons and Trials are very fun, especially with friends from the story they tell, the unique bosses, and the amazing loot. You always have something new when you enter a dungeon, even if you've already done it before. There is no one set way to do a dungeon, which brings me onto the next point.
CHOOSE YOUR OWN PATH
I don't think my words can do this one justice. The game never makes you do one thing, you can go off and do whatever you want, whenever you want. Especially after you complete the main storyline, the sky's the limit. Even with your race and class selection there are so many different ways to make combinations with classes, races, and roles. For example, templars are considered the healer however it is also pretty common to see a templar DPS who doesn't do healing whatsoever. Another example is the dragon knight. The dragon knight is a class that is the tank, however my main character is a dragon knight who focuses on fire magic and combos using the fire magic skill line dragon knights get. This character is also a dark elf due to their potency with fire damage.
All in all, you can do whatever you want in this game. Make a combo PVP rogue to help push your alliance forward or be a dungeon healer who fuels the fight. You decide.

Dark Souls: An action RPG-franchise known for being hardcore and immensly satisfying to a decent enough gamer...
Yeah, I can safely say that this franchise has earned its good reputation. Dark Souls 1, which I played on the 360, got everyone's attention when it came out, because it basically told you what the different buttons on your controller do, and shrouded everything else in mystery. I've always considered myself a good gamer, but Dark Souls 1 put that ego to the test...
I remember how I kept walking into the wrong place at the start, believing the skeletons in that graveyard to be the first opponents outside the tutorial area. I was so frustrated with how I couldn't seem to fight them without dying over and over. And then I eventually figured out: I was in the wrong place. There was a subtle path leading up the hillside, towards the actual first area, which I had completely missed first time around...
Things didn't get much easier once I learned how to navigate myself though. Whenever I thought I had figured out the enemies or controls, something new always came up, forcing me to go in over my head, or grind like an idiot for days on end. And even then, the first "real" boss was a pain to beat. But man... I was so happy to beat that Taurus Demon.
So I played Dark Souls 1 for months on end, mastering the game and its intricasies, and learning just how useful or useless some things really were. And then I heard that Dark SOuls 2 was coming out, and I was hyped! The sequel to a modern masterpiece, it had to be good!
And so now here I stand with DS2 in my hands...
I really can't tell you all there is to know about this game, since I haven't beaten it yet nor have I looked up the various things beyond my current point. What I can tell you is that this is a good game... Maybe not as focused or charming as the first, but just about everything is improved upon here. The combat is more varied and balanced, a thing which in itself is a tremendous achievement, the progression is more streamlined and of course: Praising the sun has never been quite as convenient.
There are a few things which irks veteran players in this entry, mostly the lifegems which can make the game a little too easy if used well, and a lacking structure to the level design. But frankly, those are minor things that won't bother most of us. And I for one enjoy the levels, even if they are a little disjointed.
Normally I'd tell you the most important things you should know about gameplay when I review games, but since the Souls series is built around trial and error and control mastery, I feel like there isn't much to say. You need to learn how to dodge well, when to block and when to roll, what weapons, spells or styles are the best in any given situation and decide for yourself whether you want to risk the multiplayer features or not. I've found a decent balance myself, but that's my way of looking at things. Yours might be different and should be decided by you as opposed to me. There are a few hints I can give to new players though:
1. Don't wear armour that's too heavy, or you'll find the essencial skill of dodging being bogged down by what is commonly referred to as "the fat roll."
2. Don't limit yourself (or your character) to one style of combat. It's good to have a certain amount of focus on your skill set, but you'll likely come across some enemies which your preferred method of attack won't work on and then it's good to have a different approach on standby. As Bruce Lee once said: "Be water my friend."
3. Develop your skills so you'll have access to some form of ranged weaponry or magic. Trust me, it's practically essential.
4. Prepare to die: It's not just a motto, it's a mindset. When you know you'll likely die, you'll soon find it much easier to try new things and cope with losses. It's inevitable that you perish at some point, unless you're a stupidly skilled and lucky player, so always keep a level of stress and steel in your focus and you'll find things flow so much better.
Follow advice, and you'll understand why some say the game isn't necessarily as hard as everyone claims.
So the only question remaining: Which Souls game should you play first? Well... They all have their own pros and cons concerning gameplay, story and multiplayer. But personally, I recommend DS2. It might be more complex than the original Dark Souls, but this complexity adds to the level of control you have over your character. And frankly, it's also somewhat easier. The only reason I haven't finished it yet is that... Well, procrastination! Anyway, it's a good starting point.
And btw, I know that a third DS-game has come out, but I haven't had the oppurtunity to play that one yet, so we'll see if my opinion changes over time. But from what I've heard it has pretty much the same feel as the original, so take that as you might...
Now with all that said... I'm going to get back into it. Praise the sun!

This game is an absolute blast. It has a distinct arcade-like style to it, with over-the-top action, rewards for being flashy, and so forth. Anyone who played old light-gun games in the arcades can get a kick out of this one. Aside from that, the story is surprisingly interesting, and told in a really interesting and often funny way. The game has a surprising amount of depth, and lots of great little design choices like how if you blaze through a level without too much trouble, the game will offer to up the difficulty automatically. And it perfectly captures the old romanticized version of the good old Wild West. If you like shooter games or the old west, definitely pick this one up.

There is a good reason why this game is bundled with the Far Cry Blood Dragon. Until I started Gunslinger, I thought it was done to boost sells for the game from the series which fate was uncertain after unsuccessful Cartel. But that's not the point. In fact, now I'm in doubts which one of those two bundled games is more providing with the spirit of the 80's.
Remember the scene from the "Back to the Future 2", where Marty plays the Wild Gunman in the cafe? Gunslinger is all about that sequence. Where Far Cry Blood Dragon is the modern FPS filled with neon and such landmarks and tombstones of the past as "VHS"... Gunslinger is only looking as a modern game. In fact, it is just an arcade with cowboys shooting each other for a fistful of bucks or without any reason at all. "Ma foi, je me bats parce que je me bats", said Portos... and this bravado stays in our blood, no matter how civilized we are.
There won't be cool distinctive features of the generous western shooters such as the Call of Juarez 1&2. No real-deal ballistics, no such variety of tools and gameplay sequences... You just run'n'gun, but boy, that one is pure and delightful experience! Some people blame new showdowns... certainly they wouldn't stand even 10 levels in the Wind Gunman (and I was good behind the 100th level on my NES back in time).
So - yeah - I like the game just as it goes. Fair challenge, fair experience, fair price... Nice story and solid gameplay. Good Western show on your PC, and I think it is much better than you can get from the Disneyland tour or just idle watching young Eastwood or Bogart movies. My mark is 8/10.

The sad thing concerning Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, is that your appreciation of the game might be entirely based on your previous experience of Amnesia: The Dark Descent (or lack of)
I expected the second Amnesia to be a "same but different" kind of survival mystery / horror game. And it was not. No real pressure is put on the player in this game (except at the end).  No oil or sanity management. No terrifying enemies. It seems that many things has been toned down to lift up the story.
So. Is the story good ? Well, it's decent. It's disturbing at best. There is so much foreshadowing that you can figure out the whole thing (but that's good planting nonetheless). Most of it is told though notes, voice recordings, memory recalls, voice over and telephone... Unfortunately, I did'nt relate to the character and the thin gameplay wasn't helping.
Except the sheer size of the "machine", there is to few intriguing level design. The puzzle are not always related to the plot. All in all, I found myself cruising through the level and reaching the end. Hopefully, the game was short enough to let me enjoy another one.

I went into it with an open mind and after reading some of the reviews below, it seemed like the game was fairly different from the original Amnesia. Ok, fine - not necessarily a bad thing. However, after an hour or so in, I began to feel slightly frustrated. As I played the game more and more, it dawned on me: this game feels like a chore to play. The problem with this game is that it feels like it goes on forever without really giving you anything in return.
The story is predictable and you can pretty much call the ending after the first hour or so. The game lingers on far after you'd expect it to end to the point where it becomes abusive. I felt like I was forced to endure some beginner in creative writing's 1200 page narrative. By the end of it, you've been bashed in the face with the theme so much that you're almost apathetic to the game's final ending, and even after the ending, there are still loads of unanswered questions.
The gameplay can be essentially described as follows: Go from point A to point B, walk into a bunch of scenes that play some spooky audio triggers, go solve some generic puzzles that will be require you to move your mouse more than require you to think. Occasionally, some enemies show up, but it's not until half-way through the game and even then, their AI is so painfully bad that they're not even intimidating but almost comically stupid. Unlike the original Amnesia that gave you plenty of scares and brief moments of high-tension, this game lacks nearly all of that horror charm.
It's made by the same developers as Dear Ester, so if you liked that then you might enjoy this game. I just think that Dear Ester and this game feel more like walking audio tours than actual games. That's not a problem if the writing is especially strong and you actually care about the characters (e.g. Telltale Games), but this is not one of those games.

If you loved Bastion, you'll love this game. A lot of the structure (and a few story elements) carry over, giving you a feel of familiarity. This is not a Bastion rehash however, as the music, the art, the setting, and especially the combat put it apart, making it a marvelous game. The only problem? Too short. Aside from that one little thing, Transistor is definitely worth your time and money. (And if you are musically inclined, the soundtrack is worth the purchase as well.)

Transistor is an innovative game set in the future on a different planet with a decently developed duo lead - Red and the Transistor, and an amazing art style. This game is different from Bastion, if you've played that game before, in a way that its less hack and slash and more based strategy and timing. Additionally, the backstory and the climax are both different in a way that Bastion's backstory was of a great destruction and Transistor's is of slow corruption. The idea that there is a computer program taking over and essentially hacking the whole world is quite interesting as there arent too many games with that theme. However, the linear storyline discourages the player to play it five times over again, regardless of how good the art style is.

To put it simply, this game is an amazing and immersive experience that I will not forget. From the beautiful and emotive soundtrack to the spot on voice acting to the intriguing and stylized atmosphere, every aspect of this game comes together in such a way that draws you in more and more as you go. The story is mysterious and well written; you get thrown into circumstances that you can't understand, with abilities that are unexplained, but quickly more and more details come together to add a little bit more to the puzzle and give you context and understanding...but not enough to prevent you from being surprised on multiple occasions with where your journey leads.
As far as gameplay goes, it's an interesting twist on the traditional turn based style. If you enjoy turn based combat and playing strategically, I definitely think you would enjoy the mechanics Transistor employs. Also, if by chance you've played Arcanum, it's oddly similar to the fast turn based option available in that game. Don't let the fact that it starts out a bit confusing put you off; it is very easy to adapt to and you get guided a bit more once you get to the first save point.
Literally the only downside to this game in my opinion is that I quite simply did not want to stop playing. Luckily, despite the main story taking only approximately 10 hours to complete, it actually does have decent replayability thanks to NG+ so I am looking forward to playing through it again at some point.

I stood there, wreathed in flame. A stupid smile was on my face. I was experiencing (with unrepentant joy) the awesome power of having both energy shields, and a flame thrower. Wave after wave of enemies mindlessly flung themselves at me, each one died like the last: Drowned in a sea fire. Their screams of anger and despair melded together in a cacophonous symphony of pain within my headphones as I sprayed their nests with liquid death. They had fought Valiantly. Desperately. But had not been enough. All was silent now. I could here the wind blowing, The quiet, near non-existant ambient soundtrack hit a somber chord. Smoke was still rising. During my rampage, a forest to the east had been lit aflame. The fire spread throughout it, a blazing wall of destruction, keen on consuming the whole of the forest. Left behind were only a scant few charred, smoking husks of what once were trees.
Low on power and ammo, I decided to make my way back to the car so I could return to base and resupply.
But I had... Difficultly. The world had changed in the few minutes that had passed since I had left it. As I passed the innumerable corpses and husks of earlier conquests... The once lush and green forests that i had litterally needed to hack through to proceed were gone. Replaced only with barren, charred wasteland. As I became more and more lost in my own destruction, I began to feel a twinge of guilt. I was just one guy, and yet here I was, destroying an entire world, and for what?

After a long wait you sit down down to begin work on the newest jigsaw puzzle from one of your favorite jigsaw makers.  Right off the bat the pieces feel comfortable and familiar, reminiscent of the maker's last product.  Before too long you have a framework of the puzzle complete, and you've enjoyed every moment of it.  At one point though you are holding a piece in your hand and you want to place it, but you are super-confused because you are certain that you are holding a piece from the previous puzzle, which was completed and broken down and stored away years ago.  But nope, you are pretty damn certain that it's the same piece from the prior puzzle, but you are able to find a space on your tableau to fit it in.
You soon accept that this new puzzle was designed to borrow heavily from it's predecessor, but now all the joins between the pieces aren't clean.  The material slightly overlaps, or doesn't quite meet along the borders.  It's not too long until you've exhausted the last piece, and resting flat on the table is the product of your labors.  It's very atmospheric and polished, but the strong current of blemishes make you think that maybe your copy is a misprint, that the tools that machined the parts were miscalibrated.
You check the box for an address to return what you are sure to be defective pieces.  No address can be found, but there is a note in small print.  Tilting the box just so to avoid the glare of an overhead light, you read this message: "Take this product as it is, and trust us that you are just missing something.  Or, you can take your imagination, and smash it against the puzzle until the gaps fill in and the overlaps smooth out."

So much paywall! Oh man, this game... You have to pay for the ESO plus membership if you want to have access to all the DLC. Werewolf and Vampire skill trees behind a paywall. EVERYTHING is behind a paywall and behind the damn monthly fee. See, If I am going to have to buy everything individually and need to ALSO pay a huge $14.99 a month fee just to have access to all the game, then why the hell do they charge for the game itself?! Bottom line, this game is just a money hole and literally no one who values their bank account should even consider this. I got mine from the Humble monthly bundle so I didn't actually intend to ever get this game.
Now that I have gotten it, I actually do absolutely ADORE playing the living heck out of it. It is just enough to keep me sated till Bethesda sees fit to grace us with an Elder Scroll VI. It is a LOT of fun but unless you get this game for way less than $10 and have the self-control to NEVER pay for anything they want you to pay for I would still avoid it. Even considering how much enjoyment I get out of it, if I had the choice, I would have simply never gotten it. You would literally be spending hundreds of dollars to just get the actual game content and this doesn't include ANY pets, ANY armor sets, ANY of the houses, quite literally just gameplay areas. They even penalize you for not paying the exorbitant monthly fee by making all of your crafting, enchanting and alchemy supplies take up inventory space as well as take 10% of the experience away from you.
Very little MM in this MMO. The chat window is so small I literally can't read it on a 65 inch TV 7 feet away from me. Now I am going to go play some ESO while complaining heavily at their shenanigans while spending nothing in the crown store and NOT being an ESO Plus subscriber out of principal...

Ok, not going to lie, I do have this game for my PS4 as well. I enjoy it quite a bit, but my wife plays it so much on the console, I figure I'd get it for PC. Right off the bat I have to say that the game runs much more smoothly and has better graphics on the PC version.
I have been a fan of the Elder Scrolls for a long time (my first was Morrowind on the Xbox). I enjoy the freedom the games offer to the players. I think that freedom was carried over into ESO for the most part, but there are limits as to what you can do and where you can go. Depending on what type of character you have and how you want to play the game, you'll be spending a lot of time grinding out XP from dungeons, crafting weapons, armor, potions, etc., or PVP battles.
I was dissapointed that some features of the series were removed and made into DLC. I was always a fan of playing as an Imperial, but I really didn't feel that I should pay to play as a race that's been included since I've known the series. I also do not like that the Thieves Guild and the Assassin's Guild are DLC as well. I feel that Bethesda has focused more on crafting than the overall stories of their last few games.
I will say that, overall, the game is fun. The quests do get a little repetitive after a while, but if you supplement in dungeons and PVP, it's enough to keep you busy. I would purchase this game on sale, though the $20.00 it's listed at is still a good deal.

Every factor of Transistor is either gorgeous, unique or both. 5-6 hours excluding replayability makes it rather short, but more than worth it nonetheless. Buy and play it already!

To put it simply, this game is an amazing and immersive experience that I will not forget. From the beautiful and emotive soundtrack to the spot on voice acting to the intriguing and stylized atmosphere, every aspect of this game comes together in such a way that draws you in more and more as you go. The story is mysterious and well written; you get thrown into circumstances that you can't understand, with abilities that are unexplained, but quickly more and more details come together to add a little bit more to the puzzle and give you context and understanding...but not enough to prevent you from being surprised on multiple occasions with where your journey leads.
As far as gameplay goes, it's an interesting twist on the traditional turn based style. If you enjoy turn based combat and playing strategically, I definitely think you would enjoy the mechanics Transistor employs. Also, if by chance you've played Arcanum, it's oddly similar to the fast turn based option available in that game. Don't let the fact that it starts out a bit confusing put you off; it is very easy to adapt to and you get guided a bit more once you get to the first save point.
Literally the only downside to this game in my opinion is that I quite simply did not want to stop playing. Luckily, despite the main story taking only approximately 10 hours to complete, it actually does have decent replayability thanks to NG+ so I am looking forward to playing through it again at some point.

Where to begin?
First off I am a huge Final Fantasy fan, I own and have played through every FF game to date. My alias is Mog and I typically go by Moogle Assasin7. That being said, this is my SECOND favorite FF title to date. Don't get me wrong though, I do have some gripes about this game which is why it's only my second fav.
What you need to know about this game is that you have to buy it and it has a subscription (BOTH are required to play). I didn't realize this until my free trial ran out. Very dissapointed that they left that tidbit out of the discription. However, I still play because its awesome.
Next is the game itself. Very repetitive... you tend to do a lot of the same stuff over and over. The trick is to mix up your game play and switch up your focus. There is a massive amount of story and there is always something to do. Voice acting is great. Plus the devs are constantly adding new content, which helps keep you engaged. Community is great, I have yet to have a problem with a single person. It's easy to drop in and out. This is nothing like FFXI, you CAN actually progress through the story line and you'll do it almost completely solo.
I use a midgrade laptop that runs on windows 8.1 and it handles fine. (usually around 11fps) I know that isn't alot but this game doesn't require much. Biggest drain on fps is the hunts.
Bottom line 9/10 for massive amout of content, easy to learn, hard to master, great story but repetitive. Totally worth the 15 bucks a month. Highly recommend.

=Updated Piece under updated heading further down=
Fun up until you hit around level 167 then struggle as the quests only provide you with 1.5 levels and the zone increments go in 3's. Even following a leveling map to ensure going through all zones in order I came up short on exp to the significant point of requiring 4 levels to unlock the next quests of the map, then it would require another 4 again. Unfortunately they have next to no options to obtain these levels unless you want to suddenly spend days upon days getting exp from enemies that give around 0.001% per kill. Other than that it seems you are limited to an insignificant 5 dailies that will get you around 1/3 a level so this would screw you over for at least a week. How this oversight came to be is a huge flaw and a great way to lose players, along with the various other major issues.
From a balance perspective, this is extremely unbalanced and some skills seem to promote botting. I happened to come across a strange skill that involved ghostly shadow orbs all over the zone, rapidly taking all mobs and multiplying without interventation. If you are trying to do a quest and these are present, you are essentially screwed while the bot just continues to farm endlessly. If you are not playing a DPS class and choose a healer, expect a painfully slow journey with long CD's and very little way of doing damage. To screw you over more, there are "air" mobs (they hover) and are unaffected by anything you place on the ground such as healer squares.
Don't expect any form of information from the game, it explains absolutely nothing unless you somehow stumble on it or someone tells you. After 60 hours I am still not sure if there is an enchanting or upgrade system or where higher gear comes from without painfully farming the materials for it (very painful for a healer to kill the air mobs that are usually required). The world is large and has so many zones that are not connected and make navigation next to impossible without a detailed map you can locate on Google that will cover the zone order. Oh, also don't expect to be able to reset stats or skills without real money, if you mess up there is no free respecs.
The last major issue is performance. The game seems to have severe lag issues as you can press a command and it happens anywhere from instant - 3 seconds. The FPS stutter is also severe enough to make you sick. These issues and so many others could be nullified with some optimization and testing but it clearly doesn't seem to be a priority (again, just think back to that skill perfectly designed to allow botting), it seems to be a cheap attempt at offering up a game and hoping to make some micro transaction profits with no maintenance or care for the game.
The one positive experience here the music and what even kept me around, some great techno music you might want to locate and download. The biggest issue though that forced me to stop was no more quests left or maps to explore to level up and doing 5 dailys a day for a week just to play the next map is not acceptable for an MMO.
===========Updated Piece=========
After SLOW progression to get past the choke point, the game gets a bit better till you hit around 225, then you once again come to a halt as the only way to level is A) your 2x daily mission B) Quests that will net 1 level requiring you to grind out the other 3 via dungeons (good luck finding any with 2+ hour Q's) or hope for an event that offers exp. Oh, and if the game freezes upon loading screen one of those daily passes is consumed. Once you reach these levels though you quickly realize... there is no real "end content". The whole game ends up consisting of just grind leveling till you hit 300 or so then can run what looks like 1 dungeon. So after all the torture and time consumption, there has been no purpose to go through such a grind compared to other MMO's where you can do end game raiding/dungeoning/battlegrounds/etc.
=====================================

Game Length: 2/10 - Easily 100+ hours to get to around 230 at least, but this is long in a bad way with no purpose

This game gets trashed for not being as scary as The Dark Descent and, to be honest, it's not. It's not scary in the "traditional" sense, almost at all. There are of course the parts where you walk about and sneak past monsters, but you quickly realize that they are not as much of a threat as the monsters in Dark Descent were. You don't feel the same urgency and need to survive as in Dark Descent either.
This, however, is not necessarily a bad thing.
The horror mechanics of The Dark Descent have not been removed in this game, they were replaced. Like Daniel, you enter into a horror of your own making but instead of fearing for your life you end up fearing yourself. As you read more and more into the story, you realize what person the protagonist, you, are and what you are capable of. You do not, however, get a complete picture. Not even at the end of the game do you know everything and that is where the terror comes in. You want to know what exactly is going on but at the same time you fear finding out what you've done. Not to mention that everything you do find can be interpreted in a myriad of ways.
A Machine for Pigs is, largely, fridge horror. For those who don't know, fridge horror is a realization you have about something you paid no attention to at first, perhaps in a story or a TV series, but then one day, many months later, you just go about your life but upon completing some mundane task such as opening a fridge door, a realization strikes you about the gravity of that tiny detail.  A good example is realizing that, in the Harry Potter books, Harry's pain due to his connection to Voldemort is stronger not with time but with destroyed Horcruxes (aka with Voldy getting more of his soul back) - never stated in the books outright, but clear once you put two and two together.
Machine for Pigs has many moments like these, where you just register them and move on, only to realize days, weeks or months later what they actually meant. I myself did not find the game particularly scary and just wrote it off as a nice storytelling device, but luckily I didn't decide to write a review until now, as it would likely have been negative.
TL;DR this game isn't scary. It's terrifying. Not in the Outlast "atmosphere+jumpscare" way or A Dark Descent "impending doom+wtf is going on" way. It's terrifying because you need to discover the past while at the same time fearing what that past is. And then when you think it's over it'll hit you by surprise with a sudden realization that everything you thought you knew was a lie.
This is a brilliant game.

Manning a checkpoint and stamping visas may not sound like gripping gameplay but Papers, Please somehow manages it. With your family on the brink of starvation, political trouble brewing and a cast of characters whose lives you briefly glimpse (and possibly permanently alter) the impetus to be alert and make the right choices is very strong. It's a very hard game to put down.
The graphics may seem basic but they serve the dual purposes of paring back extraneous detail to help you concentrate while simultaneously reinforcing the dreary Cold-War era atmosphere. The moral quandaries you frequently find yourself in (you can barely go a day without being offered multiple bribes for a start) don't usually have clear right or wrong answers. Indeed, whenever I lost (often) I didn't get the impression it was because of any moral failings on my part, just making choices (or mistakes) with harsh consequences.
On the subject of losing, this game has one of the best save systems I've seen. It saves at the end of each day so that you can go back and restart from any day of any playthrough you like. You can go back and fix a mistake you realised from two days ago, or try something different or whatever you like and it displays it all in a way that is easy to navigate.
I'll finish by saying that this game might not be for everyone but I have personally loved it. If the idea of a game that's a bit different, that will make you think, that can actually draw you into the life of a poor worker stuck between a rock and a hard place, this is definitely worth a try. It won't break the bank and it will definitely leave you with an impression.

I'm a long time Total War fan, the original Rome is one of my favourites (hundreds of hours I would guess), along with Medieval 2 and Shogun 2.
Rome 2 (un modded) is a complete disaster from the first few turns and I found I was only struggling to play it hoping it would get better and justify spending money on it.
Issues you might have:
1) Tone is hard to explain, but Rome 2 is VERY "Hollywood". It is like at every turn someone was saying; "It needs to be more like the movie 300, the kids love that stuff. Make every single moment more epic". This has infected everything and its a complete farce, there is none of the humour or pragmatism of the first Rome. Every unit/army on the campaign map keeps making vague roaring or yelling noises instead of anything meaningful. And the loading screens make me roll my eyes every time.
2) Historical accuracy is so uncool. In the opening turn (just one quick example) you can have a mercenary company of entirely female roman gladiatrices (the games encyclopedia entry even says there has never been any proof found of female gladiatrices in the history of the empire). It just hints that you can field some very weird stuff pretty quickly.
3) The music attempts epic but is so forgettable.
4) Stances sound great, but in practice constantly wreck everything because you are human and forget to change an army stance from last turn now they can't reinforce, or they are guaranteed to be ambushed next battle.
5) Dynasty management is gone. Now you have a collection of generals from different roman families... And you can't tell them apart. They are such non-characters you really don't care about wether they live or not, you just need them around.
I could go on. But I am finally enjoying the game with mods. DEI mod on the steam workshop completely changed the game and made it worth playing. But tellingly, that is a complete overhaul of mechanics. There are smaller mods that tweak out frustrating elements of the base game and make it more enjoyable like; original rome music, original rome families, better unit and character cards, better generals and better traits.
Bottom line: the vanilla game is garbage for a long time fan, but the mods on the steam workshop go a long way to making it enjoyable finally.

Also, there are 20 different endings, so it's absolutely replayable. I'm not somebody who particularly enjoys replaying games immediately after finishing them, but I found myself playing days over to see another ending, without ever feeling like it was a chore.
Overall, a brilliant game that had me hooked almost instantly. Glory to Arstotzka!

Papers Please was a highly immersive, beautifuly executed game that conveyed a dreary feeling of hopelessnes. In my review below, I break down the game into categories and analyze it thoroughly.
STORY (Spoiler-free):
In "Papers, Please," you play as an unnamed border processing guard in the distopian country of Arstotzka, and it focuses on bureaucratic efficiency. I personally loved its story telling and thematic choice system. The entire game presents you with mind-racking choices that have to be made throughout gameplay, but the primary dilema focuses on whether or not you will care about others and their woes, or only look out for you and yours. For example, on one occasion you have the option to wave the rules to reunite a pair of lovers (one of whom has invalid paperwork) but doing so will give you a citation, and can potentially cost you crucial money to keep your family happy & healthy. Choices like these kept the tension high, and present the player with a moral conundrum. Many of the choices you make throughout the game influence the ending in a huge way, with most of the endings differing in content drastically. This highly increases the replayabilty of the game, as you'll want to experience all of the different endings. Overall, the story was well done, oozing with atmosphere, and I give it a 9/10
GAMEPLAY:
The Gameplay of "Papers, Please," is simplistic, but effective. This is a stress management game, as the goal is to process as many people as possible in the time allotted. As a game should, the gameplay becomes steadily more complex as more layers of paperwork are added for you to check. It starts simple, only having the player check the person's passport, but gets progressively harder as you begin to start checking work permits, discrepancies in various papers, etc. Although the gameplay can become repetitive as time goes on, the new layers added on help to prevent total stagnation. It may nopt be to everyone's liking, but I found it effective and fitting. All-in-all, the gameplay gets a 7/10 from me.
ART & MUSIC STYLE:
The graphics in "Papers, Please," are simplistic and old-school. It has an almost SNES style of graphics, and it looks pleasing to the eye. The art style conveys the bleak, distopian feeling of the game witha heavy gray color palette, and it adds a fitting atmosphere to the game, as it takes place in a circa 1980 distopian, communist, Eastern European country. Although I can see how the art may not be for everyone, so look at the scfreenshots for exampes of the graphics that are to be expected in the game. The music in the game is low, dark, but paired with a slowly increasing melody of some kind of stringed instrument. It sounds very Eastern European, almost Russian, and is paired well with the setting. When both of these are combined, it paints a picture that fits well with the story, and builds a strong atmosphere. The Art & Music gets an 8/10.
CONCLUSION:
"Papers, Please," is a well done game, and I applaud the creator for doing such a fantastic job. Even though the gameplay is simplistic, the tension is high and the feel of the game is complementary to the setting. The experience that I had while playing this game was one of intrigue, nail-biting intensity, and mind-breaking dilemas. It's not for everyone, and I think it's best suited to a more story-driven gamer, (as the gameplay consists of little fighting and is mainy reading and the occasional button press) If you enjoy a fun experience that is story driven, unique, and dripping with atmosphere, "Papers, Please," is for you. "Papers, Please," was a gem that should not be passed up on, as most the gameplay sucks you in and addicts you, and this was one of the best games I've played in a while; so for that reason, my "Papers, Please" overall rating is a 9/10, and I highly recommend it to people who enjoy thought-provoking games, as this is a thinking man's game.
Thanks to anyone who read this, it took a while, and I hope you enjoyed my analysis of the game.

Where to begin?
First off I am a huge Final Fantasy fan, I own and have played through every FF game to date. My alias is Mog and I typically go by Moogle Assasin7. That being said, this is my SECOND favorite FF title to date. Don't get me wrong though, I do have some gripes about this game which is why it's only my second fav.
What you need to know about this game is that you have to buy it and it has a subscription (BOTH are required to play). I didn't realize this until my free trial ran out. Very dissapointed that they left that tidbit out of the discription. However, I still play because its awesome.
Next is the game itself. Very repetitive... you tend to do a lot of the same stuff over and over. The trick is to mix up your game play and switch up your focus. There is a massive amount of story and there is always something to do. Voice acting is great. Plus the devs are constantly adding new content, which helps keep you engaged. Community is great, I have yet to have a problem with a single person. It's easy to drop in and out. This is nothing like FFXI, you CAN actually progress through the story line and you'll do it almost completely solo.
I use a midgrade laptop that runs on windows 8.1 and it handles fine. (usually around 11fps) I know that isn't alot but this game doesn't require much. Biggest drain on fps is the hunts.
Bottom line 9/10 for massive amout of content, easy to learn, hard to master, great story but repetitive. Totally worth the 15 bucks a month. Highly recommend.
Update as of June 2017
Built myself a custom pc and I'm pulling 80+ fps, game content has grown exponetially and I'm even more impressed now than I was before. The repeatition is there but not nearly as bad. If you're just trying to decide if you should buy this game, I still highly recommend, don't wait for the trial to end.

This is another cell-shaded game but unlike most other games out there this one is a western. With excellent graphics, excellent sound, good music, good voice acting, good level design, generally good controls and a whole lot of other stuff that's good, if you want to play a first-person perspective action game western this is the best game to get. But be warned, this game is HARD. Especially the first time through.
The Good:
+The graphics are rendered in a sort of cell-shaded graphic-novel style but the game is bright (unless it's nighttime) and always fairly colorful. The between action-sequence cut scenes are done in a nice western comic book style too. Despite the cell-shaded graphical style, there is still a great amount of nitty-gritty fine attention to detail throughout. Textures in this game are particularly crisp. The game's contrast is very high and so shadows can seem very, very dark in otherwise bright areas (but the degree of contrast can be adjusted easily in the game's easy-to-use menus.
+The sound is clear and crisp and excellent (and the gunshots sound very realistic. Remember the way guns sound in the Terminator 2 movie? The guns in this game sound a lot like they did there. Loud and reverberating).
+The voice acting is good and the overarching narration is well-written, often spontaneously changing the tactical situation as the somewhat hap-hazard and fanciful (and miss-remembered) narration continues on. The unreliable narration often affects gameplay in very creative and very funny ways.
+This game has a great sense of humor throughout and rarely (if ever) does this game take itself seriously. Essentially the narrator seems to be spouting a bunch of garbage and the gameplay (and you, the player) have to adapt to the historically inaccurate garbage the narrator spouts. An excellent idea which has been very well executed here.There are funny jokes throughout and the game is made even funnier the more you know about the actual, historically accurate history of the American Wild West (because then you will have an even better idea of how far off this game's plot really is).
+The game attempts to educate those who are unfamiliar with the actual facts of the wild west by letting you find little "nuggets of truth" in hidden places throughout the game which tell you the more historically accurate version of what happened in the old west. Essentially this game spouts a bunch of garbage and knows it and does it anyway and then humorously informs on itself by telling you that it's been spouting garbage all along.
+The items and upgrades your character comes across are all wild-west classics (though guns are not called by their actual proper names) and nearly every single type of weapon you might expect to see in a western is in this game. Indeed, this game is also purposefully packed full of humorous western story cliches from beginning to end.
+This game has 2 endings (though yet again, which one you get is entirely dependent upon what choice you make at the very end).
+There's a nice mode which lets you play through the whole game over again to unlock the special abilities you probably didn't get to unlock the first time through. Despite the fact that I wanted to play this game through a second time (mostly because it is so funny and fun) a single playthrough of game didn't feel too short to me, particularly because it was so challenging for me the first time through (without any special abilities unlocked yet). My first playthrough lasted only a little over 7 hours though (If I remember correctly).
+You can go into bullet-time and dodge bullets while firing your own weapons and this aspect of gameplay is particularly well done. When using a Gatling gun in some sections I was reminded of that scene from the first Matrix with Neo firing the minigun on the helicopter into the building. The way bullet time is handled in this game can really be almost that cool. To make matters even more funny, enemies sometimes react and exclaim about how you just did the impossible. I heard enemies say things like "He can't dodge a bullet can he?!" and "That's impossible!"
The Mediocre:
+/- Yet again, which ending you get should be decided based on how you behaved throughout the entire experience, NOT based on a single choice at the end of the game (in this case the choice is given to you with the help of a menu no less).
+/- This game is very, very challenging the first time through even on normal difficulty. The tacked-on arcade and duel modes are even more challenging than that. Only after you upgrade your character and play through the game a second time is the game anything approaching easy when played on normal difficulty. I think the very first level on my very first play through of the main story mode was the hardest part of all.
+/-The game often feels like it gives you some freedom but mostly, any freedom you have is illusory. Stray too far off the path you are supposed to take and the game will restart the level at the last checkpoint and say you have strayed too far away from the story. When it comes down to it, this game's areas have a very linear design but at least they don't always feel that way.
+/- The gore is certainly bloody, making use of big Mortal Kombat style splashes of red which vanish almost as soon as they appear but enemies never, ever lose limbs or organs and blood never stains anything (including you). Bodies always stay in one piece. More realistic gore would have made the game even more edgy and tense but it might have distracted or detracted from the game's humor but I doubt it (just look at Pulp Fiction for example). At least corpses don't ever vanish in front of your eyes.
The Bad:
-Boss fights come in two varieties. A good kind, where you fight against an unusually tough enemy like you normally would and a really, really bad kind; wild west gunslinger duels. I played through the whole game with a mouse and keyboard and with these, the duels were frustratingly difficult and had amazingly poor (and confusing) controls (especially amazing considering how good the controls are during all other parts of this game). I really wish the gunslinger duel aspect of the gameplay wasn't in this game at all and was replaced with something more conventional like a more intuitive rhythm or timing method of doing the duels. Unfortunately these overly difficult, frustrating duels crop up fairly often at the end of each segment of the game.

This game seems so innocent. You build a simple production line to manufacture red science. Reasearch stuff. Okay now you can build automated mines and more complex production lines. But now you aren't being supplied enough copper ore for your furnaces to keep up with the demand from the assemblers. So you go and find a solution to that issue...
Many hours later you find yourself hunched over your keyboard trying to fine-tune the arrival of your copper ore train so that your oil train can scoot in and offload before your oil refineries shut down causing your entire petrochemical industry to grind to a halt, stopping you from producing the ever needed plastics for your rocket parts while simultaneously halting your research efforts due to a lack of blue science modules.

This game is quite good and unique in its own way. Papers, Please is basically a checkpoint simulator, but it's not boring. It's probaly one of the most stressful games I have ever played. To start with, you not only have to wach over an entrance in what can be compared to Soviet Russa with increasing amounts of paperwork and immigrants. Now the word paperwork in a video game is probaly a turn-off for most, but stick with me. You do go over a lot of paper, but that's the challenge. You have to scan almost every little thing, and I have been fooled many times by a fake height or birthday. It also includes moral choices, as there are some people who come to the checkpoint with sad stories, like reuniting with a lost lover or needs an operation. But these people don't have the right papers, so you can either tell them to get lost or let them through. But it will cost you money, and at the end of each day your paycheck is spent on rent, food, heat etc. If you don't pay your rent then you lose. All in all, a fun game for those who like a good puzzle and a little drama.

I thought this game was great. It was very tense in the beginning, and I flipped when I first saw one of the pigs (but that might not be saying much as I'm a total wimp with horror games). The music/soundtrack is beautiful and haunting, and the story was very well done. And I felt the graphics had improved from the first game.
There are definitely some problems. It does differ from the first Amnesia game in many ways. I liked that they got rid of the inventory system. I was bummed that there was less interactivity with the environment, but I could understand that with the loss of the inventory, it might have made finding the right items difficult. The loss of sanity meter was also disappointing to me, as I thought it a defining feature of Amnesia, but with the loss of the lantern I can see why it would be a moot point.
I also agree with a lot of other reviewers when they say that they lost a lot of what made the first Amnesia so great with this game. The puzzles are pretty straightforward, with no real searching involved. And you are never being hunted by the pigs the way you were with the monsters of the first game. For fans of The Dark Descent, I can see why they are disappointed.
Still, if you are able to enter the game with an open mind, I think you'd find an enjoyable experience.

A short, but inspired game. It literally walks the line between turn-based and action rpgs, and you must decide which one to use - executing a Turn() allows you to complete a string of commands much more quickly, but leaves you unable to act for a brief period of time.
The beauty of it is enhanced by a handful of functions to use in one of sixteen slots. There are three types of slots:
Primary - functions assigned to these slots have direct affect on the field.
Secondary - functions assigned to these augment the primary it's attached to. Each Primary has two Secondaries.
Support - functions assigned here have a perpetual or reoccuring effect.
The story was a surprising joy; while it doesn't break any ground in its plot, it's still well told with clever plot devices and evokes a genuine feeling through Red's actions and Transistor's words. The soundtrack helps carry it along in ways that can only really be summarized thusly: You can find the moody soundtrack on youtube, but the studio recommends not listening until the game is finished - not as a dare, but because it's the soul of the story.
As of this writing, I played through the game twice in 20 hours. I also unlocked every achievement offered in this time. They're definitely easy to acquire, but they draw your attention to the nuances of the story and the gameplay mechanics  in a masterful way. Despite how easy it is, the difficulty continues to ramp up on successive playthroughs as you unlock copies of functions you already have, creating even more strategic options. It's quick and chaotic, and without Turn(), you won't survive many encounters.
This game reminds me of what I loved about my SNES days and allows me to relive a time when I wanted to understand what was going on in the character's head. For me, the shortness of it made for an awesome lazy weekend and left as quickly as it began.
I bought it on sale, so it doesn't seem fair to discuss value. Would I buy it at full price? Yes, if it INCLUDED the soundtrack. Definitely worth putting on your wishlist, because any discount on it will make it a Goodbye().

If you're a fan of playing Minecraft in peaceful mode, and just wanted a bit more depth, this game is for you! The core mechanics of mining is similar to just about any survival game, but quickly scales far beyond any survival game I know of. It's as if you blend zachtronics' infiniminer with a 2D minecraft, with baddies and everything.
The learning curve is in waves until you're able to request via logisitc robots everything be delivered to you. That said, its fairly accessible to the user despite the user interface and tech information from in-game being non-friendly. Set the enemy area size to none when you start your first game and just dink around. Unless you die to critters, or get run over by your automated train, you can carry on with factorio games forever.
The only thing I wish (beyond a more intuitive interface) is that the game be in 3D instead of 2D.

Transistor is one of those few games that feel unique. The last few years I have only got this feeling from two games, the first one was The Banner Saga, and now Transistor. This is a game that when I sit down playing it I don't wanna stop, but I dont really want to continue either, because i'm thinking: The game is probably quite short.
However, for this story the amount of time was perfect, not to short and definitely not to long.
This is a very interesting RPG-game with a deep love story, in a city where very weird things are going on.
I must say that at first I was very confused, but the longer I played it the longer I was drawn into the story and into the world of Transistor.
Together with the exellent art-style and magnificent soundtrack this game made made me more immersed than what I usually get in games, atleast since I got older. I remember that I as a kid more often got this feeling, the feeling I got from Banner saga and now Transistor. I guess that is because I get used to it, to the way games play and the way a gaming story most often adapts.
Romance or more rather love is a huge part of the story, or it basically is and I don't feel many games use that as their spine. More games should, since it's a powerful tool to usurp our feelings. I want my feelings to get usurped by games, I really do.
This game has two main characters, one is Red, a strong female character who are fighting to get back her voice, which was stolen from her by Camerata, which is a group you don't know much about, but their intentions were at first good, but power might have corrupted them. The other protagonist is "the" Transistor, the weapon Red uses. who throughout the game is trying to help you as much as possible.
The fighting is very interesting, as you play you will find more and more moves, or attacks that you can use during these fights. You can fight as time goes, or you can enter this... "V.A.T.S" system (If you know Fallout 3 & NV) where you get to plan your moves ahead of you and then fire them all at once without the enemy having the time to respond. However that leads to a cooldown so you can't attack for a few seconds after. I found this system very usable at times, but mostly I tend to... forget it? Or maybe I just don't appriciate it enough. It has helped me sure, but I want to kill the enemy "myself" If that makes sence.
Whenever you get beaten enough you'll lose some attacks, which will return later on when another cooldown has counted down to zero. The most interesting part with the attacks are that you can put them together, you can strenghen one by adding the others, that however cost a few points so at the same time you have to look at a bar that show you how much points you've spend on this. While leveling up you can choose to increase that bar, or add another support slot for your weapon, etc.
I would dearly recommend this game to anyone who would like to try something different, but still very beautiful and worthwhile.

I don't know how they did it, but these developers made what's basically a bureaucracy simulator not only fun, but addicting. You play as a simple man whose only job is to check the papers of immigrants and make sure everythings in order, and these papers get more complicated as the game goes on. While at first you only have to maybe check a passport or two to make sure the city is valid or there isn't a typo in the name, near the end you have 3+ different things to juggle around on the tiny space of your desk, terrorists to worry about, forged passports, rebels that want in who you can either aid or send away, and moral decisions (do I let this woman in with her family, who I met just a couple hours ago, and get a dock in my pay? Or do I send her back home, possibly to never see her husband and kids again? Do I arrest this person because their card says they're a male, when my X-ray showed they were biologically female, and because one of the guards is bribing me to arrest more people? Or do I just reject them and let them be on their way?)
And during all of this, you're timed. The more people you let through who had everything in order, the more money you get to feed your characters family. They need heating, food, and medicine if their sick, and you need extra money to pay the rent.
Really, though, this game is a blast. And with around 20 endings, it'll definitely last a while.

It's funny--in the age of ultra-realistic graphics and sprawling even-the-kitchen-seek AAA titles, the games I remember most are often the games where I can do the least.
Here, you see people at a checkpoint, then try to keep your family fed and warm at home. People might invite you to post-workplace events ranging from the sordid to the friendly, but you don't go there. They might claim to have interesting lives, but you don't know for sure if you're lying. All you know is the documents they have, the stories they tell, and the regulations that dominate everyone's lives.
Strangely enough, I found myself loving this game's side characters, precisely because I had to imagine their lives, and also because their lives are so obviously more interesting than the task of comparing yet another passport number to yet another government-issued ID.
This isn't the most fun of gameplay (though, despite its similarities to a rather sub-par desk job, the gameplay is strangely hypnotic and relaxing.) But it's a fascinating narrative exercise, and experiment in empathy.
I got to the end of the game once after a few hours of gameplay, and I may not re-play it. But I also can't imagine forgetting it. This is an interesting little restrained story of the game.

A fantastic game from 2013. While it may look bland upon first glance; you are a border inspector checking passports and documents to decide who enters and who leaves and it isn't the best job to have in real life. In the game however this job becomes interesting as you encounter various characters that can affect you and events that you can choose or choose not to take part in. All of which change the course the story takes.
I like how the game presents choice in the game. So if your roleplaying as yourself in the game you make the decisions you think are right. Or you can roleplay as something else and do what the character you are roleplaying would do.
The atmosphere and asthetics feel right. The simple graphics give it an old time feeling that go well with the setting in the game. The main theme and sounds throughout the game are unique.
The only bad thing i can really see about the game is that it may get repetitive on multiple playthroughs in the story mode as many events take place on the same day everytime. Although you can set yourself some challenges to spice it up a bit like a no mistakes playthrough. You may notice the same npc's in the same playthrough as well. Although you can set yourself some challenges to spice it up a bit like a no mistakes playthrough. The game has an endless mode as well so events are randomized and there are other game types in there.
Overall it is a fantastic game to playthrough at least once just for the experience. It may not be appealing to some people but give it a shot.

If you're looking to buy this game, I'd say wait.
The core concept is very neat. But as of right now, this "game" is barely functional. Constant crashes, the controls are sluggish and horrible and you have to exit OUT of the game to even configure them (the options menu is embarrassingly bare). The "combat" is non-existant (just point at enemy and spam the left click on your mouse), and apparently it likes to reload my auto save out of nowhere just randomly, making playing the thing even more difficult if it doesn't decide to crash in the first place. The performance also isn't great, but it's the least of its problems when compared to all of the above. Either way, as far as basic presentation goes, it has failed every aspect of it, which is disappointing for a game that has apparently been in Early Access for over 2 years. I would have figured these kinds of things would at least be somewhat ironed out by now.
I wish this game well and hope that in the future that it will be a game worth trying again, but as of right now, it's suffering from far too many Early Access pains to even be worth playing, if you can even get it to work properly. As of right now, it has a very neat concept, but that's the only real appealing thing it has going for it. Hopefully the actual gameplay will become appealing some day, too.
