The Elder Scrolls Online is an amazing game that add's a lot of content for 19.99, as this review is for the base game I won't get into specifics of dlc, solely going to say that if you aren't willing to spend the extra 90$+ to get all the dlc that you aren't going to miss out on anything too major but if you do spend the money you will get the content easy.
While you shouldn't go in thinking you are about to play Skyrim v2 you don't need to get into the game with the mind set that you are in for a completely different game, it's simply an Elder Scrolls game made with a few major differences (some that people wished for in Skyrim).
You get 8 character slots and three character deletions which recharge over time, and that is enough to play one character for every race (if you want to make a build for every race.  It does feel rewarding to make more characters and build new play styles.)  This means that if your first character isn't as fun as you thought it would be you can have unlimited chances.
Speaking of character builds, you are almost completely free to make whatever you wan't.  This is an aspect which feels extremely Elder Scrolls, while the original classes are there to set you on a path, you can do whatever you want. Nightblades who cast Thunder Storms, Healers who wield warhammers, etc.
Main Story is fine, if a little weird when you see a million other chosen ones running around, but if it isn't your cup of tea there are alliance quests, side quests for each area, and dungeons to delve into.
Due to the extremely large player base which grows every day you are going to have a guild for anything you want.  PVP, Roleplaying, Trade, Aformentioned Dungeons, even just genuine exploration.  Even if you never sign up for a guild the people online are for the most part friendly.  You can recieve help, tell stories, joke around, even just complain and most people with respond and talk to you.
Tldr;  Elder Scrolls Online is a large game with an even larger player base of friendly people. It's also a MMO-ElderScrolls hybrid which brings the best of both worlds to create a vast sandbox where almost anyone can find something they enjoy while also grouping up with friends to explore both beloved and completely new areas of the world of Tamriel.  Despite the complaints of DLC/Micro policy from some in the group you can have just as much fun with the one time purchase of 19.99 with no sale (although there are plenty on this site), and only need the DLC if you're absolutely dying to see a certain area.  50 Hours  with not a cent spent on microtransactions or Dlc and I still don't feel like I need a DLC to warrant clicking back on.  Definitely recommended for any MMO/ElderScrolls fans looking for a new adventure!

I know, negative reviews on overwhelmingly recommended games won't win me any popularity points, but hear me out.
It breaks my heart to not recommend this. I had really high hopes due to how amazing Bastion was, and I went into this knowing that it is nothing like Bastion, so my dissapointment doesn't stem from that. Let me start off by saying that the combat customization is pretty neat, the art is nice, and the music is really nice.
- The story just isn't that good. Futuristic world is being destroyed by virus-type-invaders and your sword/companion is the key to beating it. The ending is very predictable and there isn't much character development at all. There is such little story that I can't even expand on that without spoilers because of how little story there actually is.
- The atmosphere is pretty but has very little variation. I got really tired of seeing the same grey blocks over and over.
- The enemies have very little variation. You have turrets that buff/heal, fast dogs, floating objects that shoot beams at you, a mortar, am aoe tank, and guys that spawn suicide bombers. Not much else, the listed enemies all look exactly the same throughout the game; the only difference being small buffs as you progress. There are three bosses, each more forgettable than the last.
- The combat is very tedious, and because (as above mentioned) the enemies lack variation, every fight feels the same. There are some great ways to customize your skills and buffs, but everything just feels the same. Since your last shred of action bar can perform skills that would normally take a huge chunk of action bar, every turn you take is just skill stacking just the right way so you can get the big one in at the end for free. It just feels exploity.
- The backdoor area (a special zone where you can access challenges): probably my least favorite thing about this game. The trials are all (save for one) time consuming, tedious and pretty pointless. I did all the trials with very little to show for it other than maybe a level and a half and music tracks unlocked, which as far as I can tell, can only be listened to in the backdoor area.. A place that quickly becomes chore zone. Every time I finished trials, I was more than ready to leave.
- No replayability. There just isn't. Restarting with all your skills would be nice if the skills weren't so bland. It's just doing the exact same thing over and over again a second time.
-The game is incredibly short. I have 7.7 hours logged and I even took my time. I explored thoroughly and didn't move between areas until I knew that I had explored the whole area. I read all the dialogue and accessed/read/listened to/replied to all the terminals and still only got 7.7 hours out of it with no interest in or reason to begin ng+.
- One of the things that irritated me the most is this game has an amazing soundtrack.... but it is hardly utilized in the game. When your in combat, you spend most of your time in a pause-type attack planning phase.. during that phase, the music is replaced by the same humming.. so you spend a lot of time listening to that one track that is her humming the same tune over and over. When you're running around/exploring, the sword is talking the whole time (not a bad thing) and you cannot hear the music at all.
The game was probably overhyped to me, which is probably why I feel as dissapointed as I do. If you love SuperGiant and love hearing Logan's voice (like me) I'd recommend getting it on sale. Otherwise, you might be dissapointed.

A short, but inspired game. It literally walks the line between turn-based and action rpgs, and you must decide which one to use - executing a Turn() allows you to complete a string of commands much more quickly, but leaves you unable to act for a brief period of time.
The beauty of it is enhanced by a handful of functions to use in one of sixteen slots. There are three types of slots:
Primary - functions assigned to these slots have direct affect on the field.
Secondary - functions assigned to these augment the primary it's attached to. Each Primary has two Secondaries.
Support - functions assigned here have a perpetual or reoccuring effect.
The story was a surprising joy; while it doesn't break any ground in its plot, it's still well told with clever plot devices and evokes a genuine feeling through Red's actions and Transistor's words. The soundtrack helps carry it along in ways that can only really be summarized thusly: You can find the moody soundtrack on youtube, but the studio recommends not listening until the game is finished - not as a dare, but because it's the soul of the story.
As of this writing, I played through the game twice in 20 hours. I also unlocked every achievement offered in this time. They're definitely easy to acquire, but they draw your attention to the nuances of the story and the gameplay mechanics  in a masterful way. Despite how easy it is, the difficulty continues to ramp up on successive playthroughs as you unlock copies of functions you already have, creating even more strategic options. It's quick and chaotic, and without Turn(), you won't survive many encounters.
This game reminds me of what I loved about my SNES days and allows me to relive a time when I wanted to understand what was going on in the character's head. For me, the shortness of it made for an awesome lazy weekend and left as quickly as it began.
I bought it on sale, so it doesn't seem fair to discuss value. Would I buy it at full price? Yes, if it INCLUDED the soundtrack. Definitely worth putting on your wishlist, because any discount on it will make it a Goodbye().

Transistor is one of those few games that feel unique. The last few years I have only got this feeling from two games, the first one was The Banner Saga, and now Transistor. This is a game that when I sit down playing it I don't wanna stop, but I dont really want to continue either, because i'm thinking: The game is probably quite short.
However, for this story the amount of time was perfect, not to short and definitely not to long.
This is a very interesting RPG-game with a deep love story, in a city where very weird things are going on.
I must say that at first I was very confused, but the longer I played it the longer I was drawn into the story and into the world of Transistor.
Together with the exellent art-style and magnificent soundtrack this game made made me more immersed than what I usually get in games, atleast since I got older. I remember that I as a kid more often got this feeling, the feeling I got from Banner saga and now Transistor. I guess that is because I get used to it, to the way games play and the way a gaming story most often adapts.
Romance or more rather love is a huge part of the story, or it basically is and I don't feel many games use that as their spine. More games should, since it's a powerful tool to usurp our feelings. I want my feelings to get usurped by games, I really do.
This game has two main characters, one is Red, a strong female character who are fighting to get back her voice, which was stolen from her by Camerata, which is a group you don't know much about, but their intentions were at first good, but power might have corrupted them. The other protagonist is "the" Transistor, the weapon Red uses. who throughout the game is trying to help you as much as possible.
The fighting is very interesting, as you play you will find more and more moves, or attacks that you can use during these fights. You can fight as time goes, or you can enter this... "V.A.T.S" system (If you know Fallout 3 & NV) where you get to plan your moves ahead of you and then fire them all at once without the enemy having the time to respond. However that leads to a cooldown so you can't attack for a few seconds after. I found this system very usable at times, but mostly I tend to... forget it? Or maybe I just don't appriciate it enough. It has helped me sure, but I want to kill the enemy "myself" If that makes sence.
Whenever you get beaten enough you'll lose some attacks, which will return later on when another cooldown has counted down to zero. The most interesting part with the attacks are that you can put them together, you can strenghen one by adding the others, that however cost a few points so at the same time you have to look at a bar that show you how much points you've spend on this. While leveling up you can choose to increase that bar, or add another support slot for your weapon, etc.
I would dearly recommend this game to anyone who would like to try something different, but still very beautiful and worthwhile.

Dark Souls 2 was the first Souls game I really played. Now, much later, I feel like that was a good thing. The rest of the series has so far felt way more punishing, harsh, complex... you name it. I jokingly call this one the "babby's first souls game" among my friends. Not that it'd be easy, but at least I'm pretty decent in it, which is something I... really can't say regarding the other Souls games.
I don't want to talk too much about the other games, but Dark Souls 2 is definitely one of the more, if not the most, straightforward and simple games in the series. Not once did I feel overwhelmed by the bosses, the lore, nor the areas. There were moments when I felt frustrated, but that was a rather refreshing kind of frustration, rather than being annoyed and wanting to ragequit. The AI definitely was dumb at times, but that didn't really make the game any less enjoyable — especially as a dumb AI is sometimes actually harder to predict and plan for.
The atmosphere of the game is incredible. Not all the characters were all that interesting, but the areas looked beautiful, or scary, or calming... some really giving a strong impact. The first time I entered
, I was legitimately scared. That thumping sound, the all-consuming darkness... I swear it took me a few minutes just to take my first step into the area.
In the end, I went ahead and got all the achievements (which, too, was rather easy compared to the other games in the series) as I wanted to keep playing even after defeating the final boss and playing the NG+ for a while. NG+ definitely had a lot of replayability, as even the small changes gave the second run a fresh feeling to it. This game really ended up sucking me in, and now I'm stuck playing both Dark Souls and Demon's Souls, and about to start Bloodborne. Yet I don't feel like playing any of them all that much, as I'm afraid they'll make me feel bad in games. Woe is me.
On another note, Dark Souls II: Scholar of the Sin is a thing, too. It's somewhat more difficult, but nothing special. I'm, of course, playing that one too, as Dark Souls II became more or less my favorite Souls game, as it's the one that introduced me to the series. Now, I know that it's not even considered to be a part of the series, especially the lore, but I don't mind. I already know this, I just like the game, and I like the other games, too. It's just, the first one is always the first one, and you can't change that.
I wasn't particularly interested in the game after first-play but someone else probably will like it.

Total War: Rome II, a magnificent experience that can best be described as a strategic slaughterhouse; set in Ancient Rome with a significant emphasis on historical accuracy, you’ll wage war all across the mediterranean with legions ready to give their lives on your command. Considering this is still a Total War game, there’s a wealth of mechanics you’re guaranteed to have seen before, and more than likely will see again, so don’t expect a significant amount of innovation here. This is to be expected, and I think that even just by improving upon what had already been established in the first Total War: Rome game, that in itself makes the sequel a worthy purchase. However, this is not to say Rome II is perfect or without flaws of its own, as even still bugs manage to persist from the abhorrent launch which afflicted the game right from the start. Rome II also has some moderately frustrating AI problems, made exponentially more so seeing as this is a strategy game and a crafty AI can cut the fine line between a lasting classic or, like the fall of Rome, a tragic failure.
Now as you may imagine, Rome II involves enough fighting to satisfy even the most battle hardened legionnaire and is what you’ll spend the majority of your time doing. Arid deserts without a man in sight, gallic jungles brimming with ferocious tribesmen, and all the high seas in between, you will make these environments ring with the sounds of battle. There’s maps aplenty and, while you may fight two battles in a similar forest, you will never fight two battles in the same forest. Each battlefield has its own land features and you’ll have to strategize how to best use these to your advantage in order to prevail against whatever foes may come. You may think that this is the place where strategy would become crucial but to my disappointment I found that actually, in more advanced cases, it was the exact opposite. Yeah, it’s crucial that you use some basic strategy such as hitting your enemies flanks with cavalry while they attack your main line, but if you want to go for a strategy even slightly more advanced, such as using part of your force to set an ambush in the treeline, you’re all out of luck. I’ve tried many times to lay an ambush among the trees and every time without fail, the AI seeks out my men and annihilates them before any plan can be executed. You may think that this is just poor planning on my part, and there’s a good chance you’re correct, but it’s pretty suspicious that even when I place hidden units far behind my main force, the AI still seeks them out relentlessly as if they knew they were there from the start. This highlights a massive problem within Rome II: The AI can never function strategically in the same way that a human player could, meaning that they’ll never use much strategy and instead try and engage you in a head on brawl. This removes the element of preplanning from battle strategy and instead forces your focus on how you’ll handle your men and adapt tactics once the bodies begin to litter the field. While this is certainly a major issue, it still doesn’t take away from the sheer magnitude of just how breathtakingly enjoyable these battles actually are. I found myself fighting battles even against foes I outnumbered almost five to one just because it’s so satisfying to control such immense armies, feeling like a general barking orders and implementing grand strategies. There’s substantial variety in unit design and function for each faction, which always allows you to form any army to attempt just about any strategy you want, and especially helps with managing difficulty. If you’re having too much trouble then you can simply make some modifications to your army, toss in some new units, remove a few more, and head right back into battle, hopefully with better results. No matter the flaw and no matter how big it may seem, in the end the battles of Total War: Rome II still feel massive and brutal: just as they should be.
When you aren’t busy fighting you’re going to be managing your empire on the map screen, where you can view your various cities and the buildings within them, as well as the terrain and just about everything else pertinent to your rule. There’s a variety of factors which are going to contribute to either your success or failure in running an empire in Total War: Rome II, chief of which are food and public order, both aiding or hindering your rule in their own ways. Neither can be ignored, unless you’re a ruler who prefers endemic levels of starvation and rebellions sparking up in every city as opposed to peace and prosperity. Food, as any poor peasant may be able to deduce, is critical to not only keeping your settlements from slowly starving themselves into an early grave, but also for raising more armies and feeding those that already exist. You’ll produce more food by building the respective food-producing buildings, though I often found myself extremely hard-pressed to actually gather the food I required. The problems with this food system don’t seem to make sense, one winter you’ll have the perfect amount of food and the next you’ll somehow find that half of your stores have gone missing. This alone can, and will, cripple you by making you unable to form armies large enough to adequately defend your lands, as well as making soldiers in the existing armies desert. This doesn’t happen than often and the problem’s also negated by the sheer enjoyment you get of managing your massive domain, though nonetheless when it does occur it feels cheap and unfair. As for public order, this is a lot more straightforward and less confusing since you can hover over your cities and see exactly what is influencing them, rather than having to guess as you would with the food system. Throughout your gameplay you’re going to have to constantly monitor these two factors, lest they get out of control, wreaking havoc all across your lands. What impresses me the most is that I found myself often just looking at the map, planning what I wanted to do, and actually having to make strategic decisions on how I was going to march my army, where to, and at what pace, among other factors. The overland map truly impresses upon you the feeling of being an ancient general poring over a war map to ponder and plan his next conquest.
Total War: Rome II may have had a frankly pathetic launch and has some flaws even still, but neither of those can eclipse just how indescribably enjoyable the battles are, making up for it all.

Horror, blood, elephant, 2D pixel's graphic and a cup of cofee. Money rule the world and feelings are buried under the ground. But, only with money, you will be never fully happy and you will never give a true sense to your life....
This short story is more than a game. This is actually a full morale lesson for everyone that will play this game in the correct way.

The game is a 2D based "adventure" where you play the role of a worker for a expropriations agency.
The gameplay itself is pretty much linear with several puzzles in all the situations. There will be only one way to play but I really suggest to play this game twice not only for the hidden achivements but to understand better the story itself.
The choice of the music is really sweet and helps a lot to transmit feelings to the player. It will even give you the chills during the "horror" parts.
Graphically don't expect a lot of "sweet effects" but the choice of the colors and the "noir" style gives a quite good look to the narration.
You can play this game both with keyboard or a 360 XboX controller.
In the end: for being a game made from a single person with the help of his wife this is a quite amazing experience. Again, as I said in the beginning, do not buy this game if you are simply looking for fun or you will never fully enjoy this game.

- - - - Nominated for the 'The "I Thought This Game Was Cool Before It Won An Award" Award' recognising the amazing effort of the one man dev team (aka Jesse) to make this wonderful little game in just 3 months! - - - -
Basically Distraint is an indie 2D horror game where the 'horror' aspect is mostly provided by the twisted human condition- surely the most terrifying of all demons! It often follows a metaphysical thread, blurring dreams and hallucinations with reality- and really commits to it too, which in essence is vital to its' success.
Suspense is king here and at appropriate times it provided a jump, or a dropped a twisted revelation you didn't quite see coming. The moments in between are sprinkled with subtle humour in dialogue and interactions that reminded me of getting the giggles playing games like Final Fanasy IX. The art style is fantastic in my opinion, and the dev clearly has a talent for giving flavour to the environment and characters.
The game also provides one particularly excellent and memorable mind bending spacial/ temporal trippy puzzle sequence that rivals Braid at its very best (drugs, all the drugs).
There isn't much to criticise, but being nitpicky, I found most of the puzzles and inventory items to be a bit too 'neat' and convenient- not an uncommon problem in adventure style games. All of that is forgiven when it throws out some funny dialogue when you try to put some item where it clearly doesn't belong. I love it when a game has a dig at you, the player, for beng dumb or whimsical.
I would highly recommend this one. I got it on sale but I think it's well worth the full price.

A spectacular redemption of the original Final Fantasy XIV, A Realm Reborn turned one of the worst MMOs of all time into one of the very best. FFXIV: ARR combines elements from RIFT, WoW, Guild Wars 2, and a whole host of MMOs to create a fabulous gestalt of MMO mechanics, one that offers more and more the further you go. While TOR is still my favorite MMO due to it's excellent storytelling, FFXIV is definitely my favorite MMO in terms of it's mechanics, though the story here is pretty good too. Set a few years after a fiery apocalypse destroyed the land of Eorzea, the world is just about getting back up on it's feet after the cataclysm. However, the warlike and expansive Garlean Empire has other plans, seeking to subdue the violent and destructive Primals that make their home in Eorzea: by any means necessary. While suffering from a lack of voice acting and an exceptionally slow start, the mysteries and questions of the FFXIV story are compelling enough that you want to see how it all turns out. Overall, while it doesn't have too many ideas of it's own, FFXIV's polish and quality are more than enough to compensate. Looking for the pinnacle of the hotkey based MMO? Look no further.

TL;DR: It's awesome, the devs are awesome, get the game.
I am the guy who searches endlessly for a game that doesn't feel like all the others I've played. When I came across this one, I was just as skeptical as I usually am. I watched the videos, read the description and reviews, and hoped this was as good as it sounds.
Yes, it sure as hell is.
This is the best Early Access game I have ever come across. The devs are actually being devs, focusing on fleshing out the game before making it look pretty. Gameplay is seriously fun, and unlike games such as Black Death, it's easy to figure out what to do without a tutorial, complex without being too complicated, and if you aren't reckless you will stay alive for a very long time as you gradually become more powerful. The levelling and skill system is perfectly balanced, with AI teaching you new skills if they themselves know it. This is a beautiful game, without needing crazy graphics that are the main focus of most modern games.
There are bugs and glitches, but there was only one that interfered with my gameplay, and do you know what that was? I tried to equip a bow and it vanished. Oh no! I just made another and it was fine.
The English in the game has errors, which isn't a big deal. AI glitch through structures, but that's nothing new. This game can also be a resource hog, especially if you play with the default settings. I've had upwards of 2GB of memory being used up by this game, and it is a bit laggy as a result. I hope this will be improved somewhere down the line, but it's still playable.
This game is a flat $10, and even less if you get it during a sale. Buy it, try it, and gift it to a friend. You won't regret it.

I got more odds and ends but thats all i could think of when writing this review. All that being said, its a fantastic idea for a game. Its nearly one-of-a-kind; a world that builds itself around you is something very few games have played with. Dont tell me about games where your decisions help craft your outcome, a grand majority of them were probably pre-written story lines that were made to connect.
In this game, you are truly a nobody. You know very few skills (that you get to chose) and some stuff depending on your skills, which is kind of nice. Items, such as tools, have actual value. i.e. if you lose your axe, you cant just smith up a new one like *snap* that. Better hope you can find a local smith somewhere or a shop that has actually has one in stock.
Which brings me to another fun concept. Markets work by supply and demand and that applys directly to each settlement and their shops. For example, smiths dont just magically have all the armor and weapons you could desire plus all the materials to forge your own. No. You want something? You either make it yourself, or kill someone who has what you want. Want to do more? Find and teacher and learn that sh!t you bum, knowledge doesn't just appear...sorta. NPCs wander about until they find a settlement they want to join.
Do you know who you are and want to be? Perhaps a....
- Ravaging Marauder that sacks settlements and terrorizes the commonfolk?
- Quiet farmer that keeps his village fed and runs a bakery?
- A noble pilgrim warrior that hunts down bandits?
- A clever business man that built and owns every shop in 7 settlements?
- A true Jack-of-All-Trades, that has mastered all the available professions?
- A humble smith that owns a small shop by the shore?
- A ne'er-do-well that robs travelers?
Go ahead and pick one or write your own story, the choice is yours.

Yes the game has a slow development rate.  Yes it has been awhile since last update.  But not yet long enough in my opinion to declare the game abandoned.  I very much like this game and like where it is headed.  But it's never going to get there if people don't support it.  Games get abandoned when financial support stops coming in.  Financial support stops coming when impatient people whine and cry about bugs and long development times and other impatient people listen to them.
For $10 the game is currently worth it if you have the machine to run it.  It is resource intensive to older processors, leading to a host of problems that are not necessarily a problem with the game itself.  I started playing this game on an older computer and the lag and bugs were intense.  I since bought a new pc and tried it again and it ran like a dream.  If you like the idea of this game and you are not living paycheck to paycheck, then support it.  Especially when it goes on sale.
Ultimately it comes down to this: if you don't have disposable income, don't buy EA games then whine about the bugs and development rate.  Review a game as bad if the GAME IS ACTUALLY BAD.  If gameplay sucks, or the devs make poor choices, or the game is not what is advertised, THAT is what reviews are for.  Giving a good EA game a bad review for slow development is like investing money in a company then telling everyone that company sucks and not to invest in it.  You are shooting yourselves in the foot.

So, I've been recently playing "Reign Of Kings" so I thought I might give my first impressions on it.
The aim of the game is survival, similar to DayZ and Minecraft except there are a few catches: One, you can make guilds and conquer areas to make bases and such. Two, you can theoretically start wars against other guilds. And three, you can become the literal King/Queen of the server.... that last part is so damn awesome to me!
So, you start the game pretty much naked with a wooden club and a few bandages. Me and my friend gave this a go and yes, the gameplay was slow and we didn't know what we were doing. I've replayed it since then and have managed to make a very simple base with some supplies. Once you start going places the game becomes much more immersive, allowing you to craft armour, weapons, cages to lock in other players, banner, instruments and all sorts!
I had a few times in my playthrough talking to other random players through voice chat. Even if you're not big on roleplay, I definitely recommend choosing a roleplay server for the entertainment value and immersion.
I ended up making this base for a solid four hours if not more, meaning I should probably work on getting some sleep.
Overall I think the game does have it's annoying bugs and glitches, and has it's slow moments, but regardless is a really enjoyable and rewarding game that defines what a medieval simulator should strive to be!

Papers, Please is a interestingly fun game to play. When I first seen this game, my initial thoughts was that it would be boring but how wrong I was. You take on the role of an immigration inspector that controls the flow of people entering.  Among the many people entering, looking for work are hidden smugglers, spies, and terrorists are rampant. Taking a look at the provided documents by travelers and the Ministry of Admission's primitive inspect, search, and fingerprint systems you must decide who can enter Arstotzka and who will be turned away or arrested. It takes time to look through the documents and then cross checking them with the book and instructions you have been give to decide if you will approve them passing or not. A really different and interesting take on something for a game. Brillient game to play and have fun with.

Papers, Please is the game that made me think I'm a terrible person. This game simulates a life in a totalitarian regime where you work on the border, deciding people's lives.  If you do good and let people who don't have a passport but want to go over the border continue, your pay will be deducted. If you don't have money, your family will starve, and if you don't have money to pay the bills you will be arrested. On the other hand, if you don't help the people you will feel like you are a terrible person. I made this mistake once in the game, and never again. I destroyed their regime, saved my family, but alas my son has died.
I would recommend this game to everyone to check their moral codex, and especially to people in rich countries, so they can know what is like living in poverty.

Looking at the Distraint Steam page, it looks like a cute little horror game that maybe has some cute scares worth checking out, so that's what I did. What I experienced was a blood-pumping, dark, thrilling, serious-themed game that surely caught me off-guard until it's ending.
In Distraint, you play as a young man called Mr. Price, who has been promised a job promotion, but first he has to kick some people out of their houses due to the lack of rent payment (because that's his job). This is the whole concept of Distraint. Sounds simple and not engaging at all? It may be, until we realize that the game is not just about kicking people out of their houses, it's about the guilt of Mr. Price for ruining the lives of other people, just for his wage at the end of the month. Taking a trip through Mr. Price's mind resulted in what can be one of my favorite horror titles in recent years.
The bobble head looking characters with little arms and legs do make you judge the game prematurely and they do take a bit of time to get used to. I didn't even care about it when I got engaged into the story, it's really a good one. I absolutely love the retro look of the game, which reminded me of other indie horror titles like Home, Claire and Lone Survivor. Like those games, the gameplay is fairly simple. You explore 2D environments, you find an item, and you put the item where it should be or give it to someone. It's pretty much a stripped down Point & Click game focusing mainly on story with no difficult puzzles, only quick and simple ones.
The visuals aren't definitely what made this game so good. Story elements aside, it was the sound effects and soundtrack. My goodness, I can't praise the audio in this game enough. It's what got me anxious of what was on the other side of the doorways. The most atmospheric and tense sections of the game always had the help of an engaging soundtrack. The camera even zooms in and out sometimes automatically to make you feel tense and insecure, since you do not know what's behind you at all.
It's one of those games where most story elements don't make sense at all, but as you progress the bigger picture starts to reveal itself before you, and suddenly everything makes sense. The writing and story as I've mentioned is superb, and it's safe to say Distraint has one of the darkest endings I've experienced in video games yet. Players can complete the game in just 2 hours, so paying 5€ may cause hesitation, but it is definitely a good price. I got it in a bundle and it was totally worth the price I paid. At last but not least, quick shout out to the developer for having a great taste in music as shown in the credits! 8.5/10

It could have been fun. But there are no dedicated servers, so one of the players is chosen to serve as host, which usually results in a terrible connection and a lot of lag. Once the game notices that, it looks for another host. The original host is kicked after the host migration (because the game obviously has to be as annoying as possible), and the thing starts all over again. If no other host is found, everyone is just thrown out of the game.
There is also no way to kick or ban the hackers, which is great fun as well. The same thing goes for hacked lobbies - sometimes, you join a game that is modified, meaning some weapons can't be used, the game mode is different, your settings and stats can be changed and other things. Of course, there's nothing you can do about it.
Dedicated servers would fix that as well. Of course, those are impossible, because Activision says so. Giving you the ability to play the game mode you want without lags and with the ability to ban hackers could actually make this game fun! We obviously can't have that.
So: If you're lucky and get a host with a good connection, you can play the Team Deathmatch mode. No one bothers to queue for other game modes, because there's not enough people playing them - of course, hacked lobbies do have other modes from time to time. And if you're really, really lucky, maybe there's no hacker in the game either, so you can even enjoy it.

Honestly, I never review games. All I do is READ them, but this game really caught my eye and I truly believe it deserves one.
Final Fantasy XIV has to be one of the most fun MMORPG's on the market to date. You jump right into the story and feel like you're listening to someone read a really well written book. It draws you in and makes you want to hear more and more with every passing hour.
First off I would like to point out that Final Fantasy XIV has one of the most beautiful soundtracks I have ever heard in my entire gaming life. It fits really well with every location you reach, and the battle music is one that will bring back memories for all the Final Fantasy Vets who play .
Second, I would like to say that the graphics quality is out of this would for any MMO to date that I know of. it may only be DX9 but they gave thee game a full graphics overhaul. Playing on the lowest settings gives you STANDARD DEF CONSOLE graphics, but when you crank up the settings, BAM! you look close and every bit of clothing has texture, every shadow is perfectly cast, and the over all exicution is remarkable.
Finally I would like to say that after over 200 hours of in game time, I have made many friends. The community is wonderful. I remember when I was about a level 14 White Mage, I was taking on a level 17 monster and I was low on health. Another Healer out of the blue healed me and a Black Mage helped me defete the enemy and gave me about 5000gil to buy better gear. Everyone playing this game seems to help one another as best they can whenever needed and that is probably the best part of it all.
Personal Rating for this game would be a 9/10 just because sometimes when you stop playing for about a week or two and come back to it, you may get confused on where to go and it leaves you to figure it all out. but other than that little disadvantage, I have to say that this is an all around perfect game. And the edition of multi class gaming on one character makes it stand out from all MMOS I have played.

Disclaimer: While I wouldn't usually recommend a game like this in its current state, remember that it's still a VERY early alpha stage, and that - while I believe the developers are committed to work on it - there's always the risk they will simply stop working at it. A small team means real life issues could put the word *ABANDONED* in the development process at any given time. Then, you'd ask, why a recommendation? I'll explain as best as I can.
The game has a wonderful and quite rare (in modern gaming industry) core concept: you're just SOME settler on a "virgin" island. You are not a chosen one, you're not a jack of all trades and you're not the center of the world. You're just whatever you might start as (a blacksmith, a builder, a farmer - pretty much anything you could be in a medieval society) and become with time and experience. The introduction takes place onboard a galleon which, for some reason, has cannons and a distinctively 17th century appearance - while the settlers cannot obtain such technologies, at least not at this stage of development in the game.
When you leave the ship... you can do pretty much anything you can think of. You can avoid other settlers or befriend them by joining a settlement and doing quests for the community. You can live on its outskirts as a farmer, miller and baker. You can also (and this is where the game might eventually shine as a really bright gem) be the founder and leader of a town that will eventually grow, with your help but also on its own. The AI, even if it's still a little barebones, is quite impressive already. The small hamlets expand rather slowly, realistically... and things do not just appear out of thin air... settlers have to work for every log, every stone, every piece of iron. The city building part of this game, all in first person, looks really promising already - and you can spend some nice hours building the "perfect" settlement.
The game is still really raw in the three other fundamental aspects:
-Combat Mechanics. They are somewhat similar to Morrowind's but far less polished and easily exploitable. If you manage to catch and tame a horse, you can basically kite everyone for miles and just shoot arrow at them until they eventually succumb. Archery by itself, though, is VASTLY underpowered and hunting is a terrible chore, due to both the ineffective bow and arrows damage output and their erratic pathing. Same with swordplay, it's clunky and definitely needs a LOT of work in order to be considered acceptable in a 2017 (even in a 2010 or 2005) title.
-Exploration and Survival. There are ruins, yes. But they're all exactly the same, except for some minor differences. Don't expect any procedural goodness down there, for all you'll find are iron deposits and a mysterious chest at the end of the "tunnel" which might contain something useful or just a handful of coins. There are also no real "wow!" Moments while exploring the vast but not procedurally generated island... while graphically pleasing and not too buggy, there are no interesting landmarks, no mysteries to uncover and no XP or rewards for simply roaming the land to chart the area. As for survival, there is really no risk of dying of either thirst (not implemented) or hunger, because food is plentiful (berries, mostly) and because a settlement won't simply starve to death because they failed to build a farm before winter started. There's nothing actually threatening you OR a settlement aside from the rare appearance of a wolf or a bear.
-Factions and Diplomacy. While there are bandits (basically hostile small groups of settlers who aren't actually a threat unless you approach them, they do not raid other settlements or prey on travellers at the moment being) they're still only partially implemented, and so they're a non-threat if you avoid them. Other settlement can trade with yours (or with the one you're part of as a simple citizen/blacksmith/baker... and so on) but as long as you don't actually form a war party and physically assault members of other settlements - killing their leader seems the only way to make you the de-facto leader of another settlement at the moment - you won't be harmed. There won't be envoys or emissaries. There won't be any kind of league or federation. No Kingdom will be formed, no King will rise from the most powerful settlement on the island.
From what you've read, you might think: "What is this guy on? After all he's said he's giving this game a recommendation?" And yours would be a quite valid point - as I said this game wouldn't usually be on my recommended list. But it is, for a very simple reason. The potential for it to become a MASTERPIECE is there. Everything is there, the graphics are raw and unpolished but already good, the development is slow but every patch is quite massive, factions and kingdoms are on the way and, let's be honest... what other game really allow you to be a total nobody who can become ruler of a whole island by your own merits? Even if you're not fully convinced... make a little leap of faith, that's my suggestion for you. It's not pricey at all, and the promise it holds is something I've never seen before in 25 years of gaming. The community around it is also very friendly (although this is strictly a singleplayer experience) and OREOL, the developer, seems really eager to create something special.

Just look at the average playtime compared to other games and it will be an easy decision.
But aside, this game is soooooo much fun. One common misconception I have heard from people is "oh. that looks just like minecraft but worse." That is compltely incorrect. This game is nothing like minecraft. It is all about automating different procedures and building a complex factory. Instead of "handcrafting", you are required to build machines (assemblers) that will make parts for you, and then you must design a system to tranasport those parts into other assemblers to build even more things! It is a puzzle game, a logistics game, and a defense game (if you don't turn on peaceful).
And best of all, the multiplayer is amazing. Unlike many other games, this game has an extremely supportive and helpful community, and the servers aren't just full of players who destroy things. The team challenge brings this game to a whole new level, and even just a normal multiplayer server is extermely fun to see how fast things get built up.
There is no reason why you should not purchase this game, especially for only $20, you will get far more out of it than any other game. Buy it now.

It's been a while since I've played a game where my first 8-10 hours of gameplay were interrupted only by necessary breaks.
This game has construction well beyond any Sim City game combined with the crafting / resource gathering and real time movement / combat well beyond Minecraft.  It is also very much an idle game  However, unlike most idle games it really makes you work for it. It provides the ability to automate nearly everything.. which you have to do if you want to do anything interesting.  It also has Zerg expies and mood inspired by Diablo 2.  And graphics from Total Annihilation. Finally, for me it evokes nostalgia for the original Roller Coaster Tycoon.
The game is surprisingly well designed and well done. You'll probably enjoy this game if you like building complex supply/demand routes while defending them from increasingly belligerent zer.. aliens.  I'm on my second world, as I created the first world with less aliens and, after those initial 8-10 hours of "practice", figured I could use the challenge and that I'd need to farm the aliens to feed the labs.
The only thing really "missing" from the game is something to do aside from killing aliens and building things.  It's also a bit tedius that most of my main base is devoted to feeding an array of labs.  But I don't really care.  I've got plans for a new factory complex that's gonna solve my resource problems (for now).  And on my last recon I saw that a big alien nest has been setting up uncomfortably close to one of my lone oil pump outposts.
So I'm gonna go take care of those things.

I loved Amnesia: The Dark Descent, so I had high hopes for this one. Sadly, my expectations were lowered in my time with it. Put in the simplest of terms, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is disappointing as an Amnesia game. As a story-focused adventure and modern horror game, it's recommended. It's a good effort from Dear Esther developer The Chinese Room, and the atmosphere is still much better than many modern horror games. It can still creep out and possibily scary you. But as a sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, an absolutely terrifying delight of a horror game, it comes up short in multiple ways. Many game elements were removed, including the inventory screen and Lovecraftian-inspired sanity meter. The inventory screen leads to overly clunky puzzles, while the sanity meter is a sadly missed feature that removes the balancing act between light and shadow. The game is also made somewhat easier by the lantern having an unlimited power supply and the complete removal of tinderboxes. Finally, while the story is nicely written, it seems to follow the same pattern of the story in Amnesia: The Dark Descent. This essentially boils down to the phrase "not an Amnesia game". While cliched, it is sadly true. It just doesn't feel like the original or like a game from Frictional Games. It's clearly a sort-of successor to Dear Esther, and it does work on that level. So, if you're looking for the horror equivalent of Gone Home or Dear Esther, then Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs will satisfy. But otherwise, you're better off with the first one.

DISTRAINT, is a short story psychological horror as advertised, I bought this game for under a pound ready for my horror month of streaming. I don't often have much expectation for such cheap games, but I must admit, I was totally blown away with the awesome work here. The game runs well, has simple controls and a nicely designed options GUI, if a little confusing at first, I picked it up in two to three minutes. As for the game itself, this crafted work of art was brilliant in so many ways. The graphics design really set the tone and atmosphere for the game, the audio was incredible, provided me with a few jump scares and again aided in setting the mood. The story was of the right length for a game like this and told an interesting story, tackling some deeper routed issues in a very unique way. The puzzles we're simple yet interesting and worthwhile. I would highly encourage you to buy this game if you are into short story and puzzle based horror games. Myself and the stream came away blown away, further amazed when the developer built this on his own in just three months, a bright example of small devs changing the market in a big way. The key words used by the stream we're unique, interesting and graphically pleasing, all aspects I feel have been well rounded in this game. Congratulations to the dev for making this awesome game, which may prove to take my streams 'obscure game of the month' title.

I enjoyed this game, though I found the end of the game a bit disappointing.  I'm sure others will disagree and love the ending.  The game is very tense, great atmosphere, and has an intriguing story woven into it.  I noticed that many people compare this game to Dark Descent, so please note, this isn't a sequel, but a game that should stand on its own merits, and it has many.  The first half of the game is very Lovecraftian (and I mean that in a "The Rats in the Walls" or "The Picture in the House" way, not a "Call of Cthulhu" way).
WARNING, POSSIBLE SPOILERS FOLLOW
What I didn't like, judge for yourself is this would be an issue for you, was that it began to stop being as much horror, and turn more into an action game towards the end.  While you still have no ability to fight, your character is set "like an angel of death" to stop the evil that has been unleashed, which is a giant pseudo-magical GLaDOS-scale steampunk machine.  And by GLaDOS-scale, I mean this machine has to take up a good chunk of the underground of London.  And it was supposed to be built secretly, in the 1800's.  Further, for the plot twists, I either saw them coming a mile off, or my ideas were better.  Further, the Amnesia spoken of in the title is never explained.  The main character seems to know everything about himself, except what's convenient to the plot.  I just wish the game had ended on a more horrific note, instead of reaching a really epic scale.
This criticism aside, though, it is a great game, and I heartily endorse it.

I wanted to like this, I really did. But the troubles start before you've even properly begun. The game is full of bugs. Forums are filled with people (myself included) trying to figure work-arounds for issues like constant in-game lag (has nothing to do with the quality of your rig or having the necessary audio/video drivers updated), random graphic hitches that filter the screen in a blue, washed-out color, and audio stuttering. Some of the fixes work, though mostly for temporary periods. If you do manage to run the game properly after all that:
PROS:
+ The environment is great. The mansion is atmospheric, spooky and interesting to explore.
+ The voice acting is very good.
CONS:
- First and foremost: The game is just not scary. It's not Amnesia. It's Dark Esther. It's not survival and stealth, it's exploration. There's next to no tension.
- The tinderboxes (requiring you to work on conserving them for light) are gone. Instead you have a lantern that never goes out. Considering that the mansion is pretty well lit 90% of the time, I found I hardly needed to use it (even with Gamma turned down)
- The sanity system is gone, and with it the tense effort to remain sane in the wake of prowling monstrosities.
- The monsters. The pigmonsters are not scary. They're just silly looking. They don't pursue you with the intensity of the creatures in Dark Descent and you can look at them without fear of insanity, which whittles away the mysterious fear factor very quickly.
- The story is just dull. There is some possibility in the beginning that it might go in a certain, disturbing direction based on the narrative given, but it turns out to be pretty boring and a bit nonsensical. The characters just aren't very interesting. You don't really care very much.
For the money you pay, I really can't recommend this one. If you must, buy the steam code for it on 99Gamers for cheap, instead of throwing $22 out for it.

Papers, Please is an ambitious game that takes the concept of a dystopian society and the strict controls that are placed on the borders and tries to make it an interactive experience. It's times like this I wish there was the option for a neutral rating on Steam because whilst there are a few positives to the game there are a lot of negatives that I personally disliked about the game.
Starting with positives the nitty, gritty pixelled style of the game is a throwback to the 1980s where this game takes place and adds to the charm of it. It's really great but the downfall of this is that sometimes it can be hard to see if there really is a discrepency that you're expected to pick up on. The music in the game is fantastic (when it plays) and adds to the atmosphere of a society controlled by a strict regime. I literally cannot fault the music; it's perfect for this kind of game to be honest. The save system works on a timeline basis meaning you can go back and replay days and basically create a split timeline which is something that I appreciated as it meant I didn't have to go back and play through parts of the story I'd already seen. It's innovative and something I would urge other game devs to follow this format for other story intensive games with multiple endings.
There's very little humour to the game but one of the characters, Jorji, is a light in an otherwise bleak world and it made me smile whenever he popped up into the booth. Cobrastan is best country.
Unfortunately what does let the game down is that after the 2 hour mark it begins to feel more like a job than an actual game and the fun factor completely dies off. Perhaps this was the intention of the game but if you're like me it ends up killing whatever motivation I had for the game. If reflecting the boring job of border control was the game's intention it did a great job at that. The moral choices that you're expected to make sometimes feel cheap and I felt no sympathy for the people I turned away (in fact I took great delight in detaining anyone I could much to the horror of my boyfriend who claims I'd ruin many people's days if I this was my real life job). I'm a sucker for stories that pull at my heart strings and leave me feeling depressed but Papers, Please failed to illicit any of those emotions from me.
There are two main stories that you can follow and one is dull and boring whilst the other has a little more action orientated. The former just drags an already dull game downwards. Even whilst playing through both storylines there's very little difference between the two other than choosing to take someone's passport or not, etc. Some variation and more consequences would have been fantastic.
If I look at this game as a game I genuinely cannot recommend this unless you delight in sorting through mounds of paperwork. As a statement this game reflects life in a country being torn apart by conflict and the strict regimes of an oppressive society great (although it's still not fun to play). I'd recommend buying this on sale because you're either going to love it or turn around and absolutely dislike it to the point where playing feels like a chore.

First off I'd like to start by saying I honestly wasn't expecting a lot going into this game. That being said, I was very wrong. Transistor definitely takes the advantage of setting to mood and feel of the game right out of the gate with it's stylized graphics and it's killer soundtrack and it only gets better from there. The gameplay is pretty fun with it's "Turn()" function adding a whole new strategic way to play through the fights but also causing you not to be able to attack a short while after the attacks that were planned have been executed. It feels more than just a simple RPG in my opinion, for the fact that if you just run at your enemies gung-ho right off the bat, you are more than likely just going to end up overloading all of your functions and dieing. Instead, you have to plan your attacks, combo them together and try and stay out of enemy fire. Each enemy that is in each fight completely effects the choices that you will make and I love it, sometimes it pushes you into a corner where you've lost all of your functions and you just have to see what you can do with your standard attack. The attacks, or functions in this game, are really well put together. The fact that each function can be smashed together with another one, causing the effect of the attack to completely change is amazing. Each function can have 2 other functions attached to it to give the attack a different behaviour. Even putting a function into a passive slot will have a different effect then putting it into an attack slot or an upgrade slot. This game is my #1 game for 2014 and I would highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a killer gaming experience. A game for those who love tactical RPGs and for those who love a decent story with an amazing atmosphere.

Summary: Great game for a sale price, a little short for full price. If what you've heard of the combat sounds interesting to you, and you enjoy atmospheric storytelling, you'll enjoy this game. Otherwise, wait for Supergiant's next venture.
Details:
Transistor is a game of two equal parts: atmosphere and combat. There's just nothing else here.
The atmosphere is potent. Your city is being devoured by a mysterious force. You are compelled to seek revenge by a familiar voice that seems to be coming from a giant glowing sword. All the places you used to know are abandoned - either evacuated, or compromised. Four aristocrats are responsible. Make them pay.
Does that sound interesting? If so, good. That's half of the game already in your pocket.
The combat is intriguing. It is alternately frustrating and exciting, and complicated enough to keep you tinkering for quite a while. If you're the type that endlessly combined weapons and upgrades in Bastion, looking for a fun exploit, then this game will thrill you. There are 16 "functions," which can be used as either attacks, modifiers of attacks, or passive upgrades to your general behavior. There are memory limits, so you can't go completely nuts, and it takes a long time to level up to the point where you can maximize your potential (two playthroughs at least), but it's clear exactly how much potential for fiddling there is.
Actual gameplay consists of either real-time attacks (mostly slow, vulnerable, difficult to maintain) or Turn() attacks, where you stop time and run a short "program" of sorts, enacting a small handful of commands to deal strategic damage. After a Turn(), you're vulnerable, able to use an extremely limited pool of techniques, so plan well.
Eventually, you start optimizing and exploiting. You find the attack that stuns, weakens, and poisons an enemy all at once. You start clusterbombing and oneshot-crit killing. The game continues to provide ways to reinforce experimentation. You start upgrading attacks with copies of themselves. Things get weird. After a third playthrough, you have basically seen everything the game has to offer.
This might take you 20 hours, more or less.
If that sounds like a combat system you want to experience, and the playtime seems worth your dollars, then wait for a sale and buy this game. I did. And I'm happy with my choice.

Adding to original:
I'm almost 19 hours in at this point, and still on my second playthrough. Granted, some of these hours come from me being afk and leaving the game running. I know people that have completed the game in less than 5 hours or so, but I just keep taking time to read each bio, complete each achievement, and generally replay the game. This is, all in all, a very excellent game. The soundtrack is just as wonderful as the game. Art is wonderful, gameplay is very much dependent on your cycle - my first playthrough, I relied very heavily on a feature called "Turn". Turn pauses the game and allows you to plot out each action. Honestly? Buy this game. You won't regret it. It's worth every penny and every hour you put in. You will have feels. You will be emotionally attached to the sword. You will probably yell profanity at the screen.
You will regret nothing.

I didn't know what to expect when I'd first launched Transistor. It loaded up and I was thrown directly into the game. No main menu, no company logos, right to the action. If you could call it that. I'm torn with my feelings for the game. The story, music, art, and atmosphere are all top notch. Absolutely stellar, and I couldn't help but be totally absorbed into the world while I was playing. The characters were interesting, and the world fascinating, if a bit vague. However, what I'm not so sure of is the gameplay itself. The game had an odd mix of half action RPG and half tactics type combat. The combination itself is interesting, however I feel as though it wasn't executed well enough to be entertaining throughout the entire game. It was clunky, and I felt the game didn't provide enough information to me whilst in combat (either in real time or in "turn" mode). The game also seemed to have an issue with ridiculous difficulty spikes at certain points, however these may be attributed to my own incompetence. Although in other areas, after a bit of progression, the game felt far too easy. The game features a host of abilities which you are allowed to switch by way of these stations posted through out the games world. With a good enough combination, you're able to plow through enemies without any issues. In some instances though, no matter what combination you have, certain encounters remain headache inducingly difficult. With this inconsistent level of difficulty, it made the combat turn into either a slog through tedium, or an infuriating exercise in brick wall head banging. Overall, despite my lack of enthusiasm for some of the mechanics, I'd definitely recommend this game. It, despite its flaws, still manages to be interesting and engaging. The story is well worth it, and perhaps the gameplay is better suited for someone other than myself. It is also worthy of note that the games length depends upon your investment. It took me about 5 hours, without completing any of the side objectives, whilst I'm sure completing all of these would yield longer play times.

Transistor's an odd sort of game. If one was to analytically break down its components, one would be hard pressed to find anything that is perhaps truly innovative. Certianly it lends a lot to Supergiant's last game, Bastion (another excellent game. Spoiler there? Oh well...), but Bastion's strenght wasn't in innovation, really.
Transistor's strength lies in its excecution, in smoothness of purpose and design. Of doing what it does not with originality of gameplay, but doing it WELL. One does not simply walk through a series of rooms, idly connected to create a singular pathway. One is traversing a city, and there is no doubt that you are. The enemies start out simple and have such basic "gimicks", but they soon not only gain new ones, but start to have wonderful and frustrating synergy at the same time.
Even the concept of new abilities really has nothing 'new' per se, but dovetails neatly together in such interesting ways. A single ability can either be used as a primary attack technique, or it can provide an enhancement to another technique, OR it can provide an overall passive bonus. Simple, yes? And yet both elegant and effective: A single new technique suddenly opens up all manner of new tactics.
Did I mention the music? If there's one thing that Supergiant seems to have locked down more than anything, it's soundtrack, and it shows in spades here. The songs fit the ambiance of the levels, adding that little extra to mood, and frankly they dammed well stand on their own, without even a game to be set to them.
Are other games "more innovative"? Probably. Are they "Newer, with sharper more realistic graphics?" I suppose.
Do those games let you sit back at the end of a session and just marvel at what you've seen and done and heard, and think "That was Beautiful"? I don't think so.
Don't cheat yourself. Don't watch a playthrough, don't watch spoilers. Get the game, and experience it.

I really wanted to like this game. It's a throwback to what I enjoyed most about MMOs before everything became an amusement park with quest spam. The core gameplay and setup are great and I think it could have been one of the best MMO's out there, but its execution falls short.
I won’t go into the negatives on how the trading restrictions go with the token item, since this is what the devs thought might be a legitimate way to solve the bot/real-money-trading problems most MMOs have. I'll just say that in the end it did not work out and turned out to be a really bad decision that many players ended up disliking from the get-go.
The main reason why I cannot recommend this game starts here. When you first spawn in the game, this is where they hook you. There are tons of low level mobs in the starter areas that die within 1-2 hits. It’s very fun and satisfying to mow down monsters and watch them explode into pieces and collect the money and items they drop. When you think of a game where the core is to grind monsters to level up (along with quests of course), you would think that you’d be playing like this the whole way getting more challenging, but that setting changes drastically shortly after the first/second dungeon. Mob density gets extremely low and that fun atmosphere of destorying piles of creatures before you starts to become tedious. Imagine playing a high intensity action RPG game like Diablo II or III, and when you reach a higher level the mobs start to take more hits as they should, but instead of killing hoards of 30 skeletons they condense it down to 2 or 3 with experience getting shallower and shallower as you go. The only reason why I didn’t quit sooner is because dungeons fulfill this problem, with many mobs available and a good amount of strategy needed, it’s simply fun. But here's the real issue with dungeons, you have a global dungeon limit, so that fun is short lived. This might be okay for the average person who maybe spends about an hour in game, but for those who want to spend more time slaying, you're gonna have to wait.
The second main reason I cannot recommend this game is how the game runs. I've never complained about how a game runs before in my lfie, granted I have a nice system that usually runs most AAA 3D games on high/ultra, so it’s very sad to see a game with this art style and caliber run so poorly on so many systems. Alone it’s easy to hit 50-60 FPS while killing low density monsters, but when you get into dungeons with a full party of effects and more mobs on-screen, you can drop well below 25 FPS often. Towns also have the worst FPS drops due to the amount of players on screen at once. I purposfully look for channels with no players just so I can move around. I can only imagine the frustration of PVP with this lag. You know, I can deal with some ports having 30 FPS locked, but if your game goes below that during the core of gameplay, it's simply unacceptable.
There’s a ton of good stuff in this game. Like I said, the game feels fun to play when you don’t lag, especially in dungeons when there’s plenty to fight. The stat/class system is one of the most interesting out there, giving you lots of freedom to be whoever you want to be. I personally understand this would be hard to balance without lots of trial and error. You can buy buffs/upgrades/repairs from other players to make your leveling easier, which is neat if you want to solo for a bit and it’s an interesting way for other players to get money other than the normal MMO routes. Being able to teleport to finished quest NPC’s is great since it eliminates downtime. The art style and music for this game I should mention is top notch for fans of the genre like me. I should also mention that this game doesn't feel P2W at all (at the time of this review). If it is, it's the least I've ever felt in a FTP game ever. The community on Reddit is pretty cool too, as it really shows that people wanted this game to succeed. I did too.
At the end of the day, if the game isn’t fun as early as mid game due to the FPS/mob problem then what is going to keep players playing? I’m fine with it being a grind game, but you have to make the grind fun and you have to give players things to do (I didn’t touch end game since I’m not there, but it appears to be pretty shallow there too). If FFXIV can turn around their game, I think TreeOfSavior can too, but I highly doubt the devs would re-release this game after fixing it. If they did, I’d be interested, though I’m not holding my breath since the speed at which they make improvements we’d probably have Half-Life 4 and flying cars by then. It’s saddening to see so much potential thrown out the window, because they’ve built a very solid base, but sadly, it may already be too late.

Silence of the Sleep was a refreshing break from the horror genre with its unique pacing and animated cast. The developer went on to create DISTRAINT in a scant three months as a challenge, so it would hardly be fair to expect the same level of detail. What's surprising about DISTRAINT is not that it still manages to be as beautiful or harrowing, but that it manages to cram a solid story into its short runtime as well.
You play Price, a pleasantly bobble-headed little fellow with the unpleasant job of repossessing property. He's only three claims away from being made a full partner at his firm, but as you might expect they don't exactly go as planned. You'll experience his tale in simple side-scrolling adventure fashion with only five or so buttons to guide you; left, right, use, inventory, and light. They're all you need to navigate hallways, solve simple puzzles, and speak to the other denizens of your dreary world.
Do not be put off by the Charlie Brown-looking people, because there's still plenty of menace to be found in DISTRAINT. The atmosphere is what makes the game, with looming shadows cut by dusty sunbeams and sickly lights flickering against decaying walls. Even with the limited interaction you're sure to feel trapped in Price's terrible world, a fitting fate given where the story goes with his weary conscience. There are quite a few surprises and sudden spooks to look out for as well, which will keep you on edge for much of the game. And it's not even all straight horror, as there are few instances of macabre absurdity and even humor sprinkled in.
DISTRAINT will last you just shy of two hours, but its a more complete and meaningful game than most twice its length. The writing is snappy and cuts right to the point, the characters are colorful and animated with charming bobs and sways, and the scares are well-earned. In the end the only thing I could have asked for was more time with Price and his acquaintances, but the poignant ending is worth seeing it all come to a close so soon. Anyone looking for a good story with some tense, creepy moments will be happy with this one.

This game does a few things differently from the original Amnesia that I didn't agree with. Unlike the first Amnesia, the environment can't be interacted with unless absolutely necessary. Closets, dressers, and nonessential doors have enormous locks on them and can't be opened, and the props lying around can't be picked up or moved unless they are explicitly used to solve puzzles. While this does prevent you from getting lost, it really hurts the immersion factor. There is no more inventory or sanity meter, and although you can die from taking too much damage, health isn't visible. Monster encounters are also a lot less frequent than the original game, and since the environment is static they seem a lot easier to avoid. You very rarely feel threatened or vulnerable so the game doesn't do a good job of being scary.
However, the atmosphere is fantastic, and the visual style and sound design are a bit better than the original. I had heard that the story has nothing to do with the original, but it does in fact make several references, including namedropping Brennenburg early on. There is a pretty interesting plot here with good pacing, a few twists, and I felt compelled to keep playing to find out more about the mythos of the world. This game has a stellar soundtrack with excellent voice acting and beautiful music that lends an imposing feel to the world and really emphasizes the impressive setpieces and more dramatic moments in the story perfectly. I also enjoyed the grim industrial complex a bit more than the dilapidated castle from the first game.
In all, I felt pretty good about this game. It was a good experience despite the lack of interaction. As long as you aren't looking for a real immersive "horror" experience I definitely recommend playing it, there's a lot of cool things to see and an interesting world to learn about if you're willing to explore. Plus the soundtrack is gorgeous. You might want to wait for it to go on sale though, it's not very long. I hope I can look forward to seeing more Amnesia games in the future.

Honestly, all this "indie" garb is new to me. Games that speak a message and look like they could run on a Sega CD are fine by me, though. Back when I was growing up, indie meant the budget aisle at Circuit City, and NO ONE had any insight or comments on the stuff they put back there. Today, there's specialized awards for games that, six years ago, wouldn't be considered games!
Papers, Please is one of those games. Which means this isn't a game. This is a "life hard-ship simulator".
Have you ever wished you could live in a Soviet country during the Cold War? No?! I didn't think so.
Have you ever wanted to do mundane tasks, much like the day job you fill to pay for video games? No. Me either.
Have you ever listened to someone's opinion, only to realize you don't share it, and you've wasted your valuable resources to compare? This is exactly it.
Papers, Please is supposed to tell a tale. But... I finished the game. I was thrown into prison. The end. I was done.
Why should I have to play the game 19 other different ways? Linear storytelling, in this case, would have been better. When your game is based around pushing documents around, it tends to get gruellingly boring. I don't care about plot when I've been doing paperwork for four hours.

Ok, so this is my first review and I feel it's worth mentioning that I do like Dark Souls 2 however, I think it's ultimately a waste of money for reasons I will list.
Pros
- It is challenging and unforgiving (don't burn your effigy in the campfire, that's not how you use them)
- It is beautifully designed and graphically stunning
- Because of the challenging nature of this game when you do succeed you feel like a bad*** and there are few games that offer this same satisfaction
Cons

The gameplay is unique: it revolves largely around the turn() mechanic, by which the player plans out their moves in advance.  While it can be quite satisfying to see a successful turn() executed, it leaves something lacking in immersion, and  I found myself unable to play more than a hour-or-so long session.
But with that said, the game is still great.  There's a lot more to the story than what is fed to the player, and encourages digging deeper to uncover the truth.  Transistor and its characters were unpredictable, and the story had me wanting more of the land of Cloudbank in which it takes place.

Transistor is a fantastic game. The gameplay is fantastic and interesting (especially with the unique Turn() mechanic that freezes time and lets you plan your actions), the story is intelligent and makes you think rather than spoon-feeding you answers, and it is a very rewarding experience overall. If you like intelligent stories and a game that's more of an experience than something that you could play for hours, Transistor deserves your money.
However, as somebody who's just gotten done with a marathon of Bastion (Supergiant's other unique, story-driven game), make sure that you're not going into Transistor expecting a sequel or even a spiritual successor. There are a few similar things -- a charismatic-yet-silent protagonist in a bleak, desolate post-apocalyptic world; reliance on (mostly) a single character to narrate; fast-paced combat and a very open-ended upgrade system. Aside from those, though, Transistor is entirely unrelated to Bastion. But by no means is that a bad thing; it's just a likable formula that works applied to a different area.
Complaints about Transistor are hard to come by until near the very end. (Thus, there are abundant spoilers to be had in this paragraph). The ending comes very quickly, and though there is a very cool and challenging final boss fight and a fitting conclusion, you'll definitely be wanting more, as it's about a five-hour long story. The ending doesn't give you even a binary choice about the very end, either, and sadly the only ending is one that a lot of people will find bittersweet at best, and something that mars the entire experience at worst:
.
Although Transistor could be a little better, no matter what, your jaw will drop countless times while playing. I would definitely reccomend this to almost anyone.

Fantastic game. The gameplay is amazing and compelling; it opens up for different ways to deal with situations since you can attach different abilities as either active or passive abilities, and it's a joy to mess around with different ability combinations. For instance you have a dashing ability which deals no damage, but you can add different abilities that compliment it, like shocking orbs that scatter around and deal damage. Or you could draw enemies closer to your starting position. The atmosphere is stunningly beautiful, and the music is fantastic, my personal favorite being the beach challenge theme. If you liked Bastion's music, this game's soundtrack and Bastion's was produced by the same person, Darren Korb. The only flaw I see is that this game is short; the story can easily be beaten in around 4-5 hours, but damn is it good while it lasts! Despite the short story there's still a fair amount of replay value, including a NG+ mode and Limiters that spice up the difficulty (in similar fashion to Idols from Bastion). This could keep your attention for a while, especially if you're into getting achievements like I am.
