Alright, I have never reviewed a game on steam before now but I feel Kingdoms merits a full review.
Review: This game is definitely worth the time and effort to play. It's challenging to figure out at first but once you get the hang of it you'll quickly start to survive better and progress through the game quickly. However there isn't much game to play just yet and that's okay. This feels like a great MVP (Minimum Viable Product) and I actually enjoy getting a chance to play a game just like that.
Suggestions to Developer:
Play Skyrim with Frostfall and Camping installed, these mods to that game really added some depth that I feel Kingdoms would ultimately benefit from. You're almost there already, with a need for eating, but the added fight against the elements would also be nice along with the ability to carry a tent with you as though actually exploring and camping down for the night.
AI tweaks towards more clustered settlements and a more common landing spot for ships would really help. Perhaps it could be an old ruined dock that can set up the possibility of exploring ruins and caves for stories and treasure. Perhaps a town/settlement could build a dock to attract more ships to it.
The jobs board is an interesting concept but I think it actually hinders NPCs more than it helps right now. NPCs don't seem to pick up jobs they'd be suited for and sometimes the AI doesn't update an NPC as having a home when they asked for a shop or tavern. Perhaps buildings for NPCs could be less freeform and a little more structured? Such as they'll try to focus housing towards the center of the town and businesses along the roads? Which brings up roads, it would great to have a dev switch to turn them off. They can slow down gameplay and don't really have the biggest benefit to the player at this moment. I'm sure there's a plan in place but it's not a feature that adds robustness to the experience of the audience, so a toggle to keep it from happening would be nice.
I love crafting in your game and I would not change a thing! I'm sure once it's been released and more widely played there could be some revisit to the recipies or the system, but right now it doesn't need fixing at all.
Please keep developing this game, this answers all my prayers when it comes to a game and after downloading I have sunk my teeth into it with over 5 hrs of play and soon there shall be plenty more. The Living AI system is exactly what games of tomorrow need and I pray you will continue to push forward with it.

This time period is my favorite of all Total War games, so take that for what it is worth. I also did not pick it up at launch, but waited for awhile after and so I do not have the memories of any problems that came along with launch.
I thoroughly enjoy the game and the many campaigns it offers. For the most part I like every change they made to the campaign aspect of the game, especially the province system and how only province capitals are walled and can result in seige battles. The politics system is 'take it or leave it' at times, but I feel on the whole it is a positive, same with Agents.
The battles are my favorite, with the exception of battle speed. I honestly dont know if I hadn't played MTW and RTW prior if I would love this game's (and STW2) battle system near as much as it is just so incredibly short at normal speed. This game will hand you a flimsy bit of wood, a broken bit of metal, then point you at a dude the size of a house, with a mace bigger than your whole body, and tell you to go kill him. You will die. A lot. And you will LOVE it!
This game is brutal, infuriating at times, but incredibly satisfying when you finally kick the♥♥♥♥♥of that one boss that was throwing your ragdoll all over the boss cavern. There's nothing quite like it anymore either. Games have become far too easy. Far too "casual" to use the vernacular.
This game is the counter to that. It starts hard and you can increase the difficult as much as you like either by starting New Game Plus (NG+) over and over, getting harder each time, or you can use items at the game's bonfire's that will increase the difficulty in that specific area permenantly. There are advantages to doing this, however, and many items / spells etc will only drop / become available on harder NG+.
The community is also one of the more helpful that i've found. It being a mainly single player experience, but with the opportunity to do some "jolly co-op" by summoning allies to help fight difficult areas or tough bosses you feel you want a hand with. You can also go help others in order to gain various benefits. There is also the option to be a dickbag and invade other players with the sole purpose of killing them and stealing their humanity. Either way it's all tied together with the fantastic combat system.
The gameplay is brutal but fair. Even fairly "basic" enemies can still kill you far into the game if you mess up your block or dodge or parry. But equally you can read their patterns and learn how to deal with them without taking any hits once you're practiced.
There is so much to explore, so many side quests to uncover, secrets to puzzle out, hidden walls and illusions to find. You can play as a high strength / dex blademaster build then change your mind and respec to a full on fire throwing lightning slinging magic user when you feel like it using a (somewhat) rare consumable.
On the topic of magic.... spells in Dark Souls are JUST as punishing as weapons. If not MORE so. There are some insanely powerful spells in the game and the limited uses per spell before you need to rest at a bonfire allows for them to be balanced. The sheer insane variety of ways to play and different builds available makes it a game i'm STILL not bored of, and STILL discovering more and more about. I've not even started the DLC's yet and i'm over 150 hours in on my main character.
Sadly bows are somewhat lacklustre in the Souls universe which i attribute to balance reasons. They tend to require a lot of stamina to shoot compared to similar weight melee weapons, and their damage is pretty limited for the most part. There are some greatbows that launch treetrunks at people and can do heavy damage, but are so slow to fire and in pvp will leave you an easy target. I've always loved archery and all things bow related in my games, but even with the limited power of bows in Dark Souls II i'm happy with my Hunter's Blackbow +10's damage output. It's the fastest firing bow and takes less stamina than most. I combo it with poison arrows and can poison 90% of enemies in 1 volley (how many arrows i can fire before out of stamina) which is extremely useful in certain areas. Even with my love of bows, and normal preference for ranged classes, i don't find myself caring in DSII. The melee weapons are so varied and satisfying to use that i'm perfectly satisfied to use a mix of ranged bow shots to pick off tougher enemies / thin the pack, before taking out the rest with my swordplay.
The whole game just feels so incredibly satisfying when you get good, and even when you "think" you're good, there's always the other player invaders to show you how wrong you are :P

Be prepared to get frustrated and desolated on your insade, but the feeling to have overcome all this is totally worth it.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs plays a bit differently than The Dark Descent, making both good and poor changes. Gone is the inventory system, any item you need or want to move you must move with the mouse. Gone is the sanity system which helped the first game to scare so many. The source of light you have (a lantern) never runs out, and there are far fewer enemies who are also far less dangerous than the ones from the original. Despite some of these changes however, AMfP still manages to create a masterful horror experiance with a deeply psychological and disturbing story line, grotesque and nightmarish images and creatures, and an amazing sound design that rivals that of the first game. While AMfP may not be as jaw droppingly terrifying as the first game, its own horror will do far more than simply make you nervous. This is pure psychological horror as it should be, and I am proud to list this game amongst my favorites along side the legendary Silent Hill 2.

Negative:

* The duel idea (aka boss fights) is cool, but I wish they could have built on it with more variety (additional minigames, maybe both duelist are unnarmed, but there is a gun near each one so they have to catch it and shoot first, or during a duel some henchman jumps in to save his boss, so you have to get rid of him first before shooting the boss, etc...)
Verdict: A-

My Bite Size Review - Call of Juarez Gunslinger
The Good:
+Story is amazingly told - voiceover from guy in a bar
+Cell shaded art style looks really nice
+Mid level - real time - map changes based on story being told is cool to see
+Lots of guns
+Different builds (dual pistols, sniper, etc) for your cowboy
+Enviroments are varied and look great
The Bad:
-Dueling is a minigame style event in the game that has very weird controls
-Short game (but not really worth noting since the game is only $15, well worth the price)
The Verdict:
If you are going to release a modern western game, you either have to go realistic with it (Red Dead) or really ham it up with funny names and bullets and booze and everything. This game does the ham it up option really well. The story telling steals the show here - as your character tells his story of his pervious tales to bar patrons. Levels and enimies change in real time as the story is told and it really makes for an interesting game.
The only dark spot on this game? Is the dueling event that happens usually at the end of each level against bosses - the controls on PC were really weird and honestly I never got used to them. I only got through each duel by spaming gun fire and getting it overwith.
But the gameplay and graphics and story are really good and all in all this was just a great little gem of a game.  Highly Recommended.

Kingdoms is surprisingly polished for an early access game.  The $10 price tag is worth giving it a try.  It's challenging in the settlement-building aspect.  You can choose to start your own town, live in an established town, become a bandit, a wanderer, or build your own farm.  You can raise and control an army.
The AI is very smart, especially for an early access game.  The game even generates roads from one settlement to another.  The more perks your offer in your town, the more npcs will want to settle there.
The game encourages you to travel and trade, because some things can only be acquired in other markets.  You can also sell goods in other markets.
Multiplayer will be implemented.  Global politics.  Massive armies.  IF you can manage your resources and get people to follow you.
The envisioned end-product for this game is impressive.  I've already received more than enough compensation for the $10 I paid.  I'd really love to see this game reach the finish line.

I know this game is early access, so I am going to give this review with that in mind.
For a $10 game, this is worth it.  There is probably only 10-20 hours worth of game time for it's current content (Nov 2017) but I do hope the developers keep at it.  They are very responsive to the community, care a great deal about their game, and are quick to watch for any reports of bugs, glitches, or areas in the game people get stuck.
I honestly think the towns develop way too fast and building is essentially too easy.  You can all too quickly get the best gear in the game.  Once you open a trade house it's pretty much smooth sailing.  Suggest lowering the number of people who arrive on the island and maxing out their frequency.  Possibly giving more direct control over where houses get built in the town for each citizen, too, would give more for the player to do... perhaps plotting a piece of land for where the new residents live so the AI can decide what house to build and where on that plot of land.
Great game, though, and looking forward to seeing how much further they develop the game.

Alright, so I'm going to give this game a very cautious "recommended", as in its current state, it is quite far from being a "game" in its own right.
I would classify it as a settlement simulator with a pinch of RPG and an ounce of strategy game. It aims to be a lot of things and the roadmap is impressive to say the least, as if all the options are ever implemented, it would radically change the way RPG's are played. I don't yet know if I should be confident or scared about the future of Kingdoms. It aims very, very high.
So far, what you get is a pretty pleasant simulation which enables you to build your own settlement and attract settlers, help them to fulfill their needs and be rewarded with skills you can learn from them. This concept is most definitly very refreshing and efficient. You can also opt out of creating your own colony and simply join an established settlement and interact with the people, go on hunting trips, trade and more. You can even choose to be a bandit and plunder other settlements. There is gameplay in this little pearl, but once you've reached a certain point in the game, there are no more real challenges to entice you to play more of the same level. Instead, you'll very likely start a new game and experiment around.
Controls are a bit wonky and as someone has already said, if you plan on using weapons often, combat will be a lot of hit and miss directed by luck more than skill (even if you level up the said skills). Building on the other hand is fun and if you take up the heavy task of establishing your own haven, it will feel even more rewarding. Tending to the needs of your people gives you a real purpose in the game and is surprisingly fun. Even though there's a bit of a grinding involved (deforestation at its best).
Graphics are... how could I put it gently? Not awesome. Character creation only lets you make people who look like 5th generation inbreds, the environments range from boring to sometimes nice, but don't expect too much in terms of visual eye candy. It's early access stage and you'll either live with it or plainly hate it. Also, if you play long sessions, involving a lot of NPC's on the map and roads being created, the game will slow down considerably. Reloading helps, but after a while, you can feel the frames dropping again. Sounds are, well, OK and when music does play, it fits the ambiance rather well.
Overall, this is a game to carefully invest in. If you don't mind waiting for the dev(s) and updates, you should give it a shot. But if you can't stand unpolished games which are not entirely ripe to play, think twice about putting your money into it. I've made the jump and I hope to have done so to see this game thrive and become a killer of RPG/simulation games.

Short Story:
Good Game, buy.
If you want a more detailed review, read on:
This isn't an "online Skyrim" that you can play with your friends, although some people have managed to perceive it as such, even after playing for many hours.
My favorite thing about this game is that while there are subscriptions and in game currency, it doesn't have to effect gameplay. Most MMO's, if you don't have a subscription, and I don't know.. Cartel Coins, you wont have as much fun and wont have cool stuff. I have played this game without a subscription, and I can say that there isn't a massive difference, you can level up almost as quick and still do hundreds, if not thousands of hours worth of gameplay without it. The biggest perks of a sub are dyes and the crafting bag ( having played before the crafting bag, I will tell you that it is worth a sub all on it's own.)
A lot of negative reviews I've read have to deal with download space and time... It's that way with all MMO's, know what you're getting into.
All the others have to do with how Bethesda and Zenimax are greedy for offering in game currency, those people obviously have no grasp on how the current climate in video games are going, specifically in mmo's (loot crates, pay to win, microtransactions. etc.). I'm not saying they're totally wrong, but I hope they have a nice bed living under that rock. I personally don't mindpaying a bit extra for added content as the game goes on, the people making the content have bills after all.
I've seen a few bad reviews about offering Morrowind as a paid DLC. My first point on that is to refer to my previous statement on not understanding what is driving profit in a lot of games these days. My second point is that I have not bought Morrowind, and I can say that it has not effected my game in a negative way AT ALL.
Pros:
Amazing graphics (for MMO) on high end machines, still playable on low end machines.
In game paid currency (crowns) doesn't mean pay to win.
PVP is an absolute blast
All MMO zone chats are toxic, but this is less toxic than most
An almost endless amount of things to do
You can make a viable build out of any race and class
Getting in depth with builds can be a lot of fun
Awesome voice actors
Fantastic Add Ons
Cons:
Load screens can suck during high traffic hours.
PVP can be a bit zergy (Can also make for a lot of fun though)
Can be a bit grindy if you let it.
Builds can often change based on patches
Not having enough time to spend playing the game
Overall I would recommend to a friend.

What can I say?  This tiny gem of a game truly surprised me.  I walked into Papers, Please with low expectations.  After all, the game is about running a border checkpoint, how hard can that be!  Boy was I wrong!  Needless to say, I was completely blown away. Sure, there is an innate challenge towards operating a border checkpoint, however the real depth of the game is its ability to convey deep moral dilemmas through its characters.  You'll find yourself torn between moral choices day in and day out, all while just trying to feed your family and pay your rent.  And as you make these decisions, everything comes together to build a complex story that can end in one of 20 ways.  In my opinion, it is worth its entire cost and then some.  If you have your doubts, buy it on sale.  The experience is well worth every penny.

Decided to update my review, just because I love this game so much + my last one didn't do it justice. Going to break the main points down, so it's easier to read.
GAMEPLAY:
Like most MMOs, you have the holy trinity of dps, healer and tanks. In this game they are divided into classes, which can further specialise into jobs. Cross class skills are used, so lets say I'm a White Mage at level 60, I can use cross class to access some skills from other classes/jobs I've leveled. Classes/Jobs are also handled differently. Your character can switch between any of the classes/jobs as they get unlocked, allowing you to completely change your playstyle should you choose to in the future. There's even classes like Fishing, Blacksmithing or Alchemist if you want to work the markets, or help your Free Company build an airship! Gameplay is like most MMOS, except it can get quite challenging as you get to a higher level. IMO this game has some of the hardest content from any MMO out there. There's the typical "Run around and quest" style gameplay, you can do a main story, there's lots of little "sub stories", trials, dungeons, fates in which many people randomly team up to complete a mini objective etc. Gameplay wise the game definately isn't lacking. The actual combat is quite good, players aren't just taught to stand still and smash buttons. There's lots of movement during fights, as you move away from aoes, deal with specific mechanics to handle bosses and move to specific locations to help team memebers. Apart from the obvious leveling gameplay, there's a lot of other things to go and enjoy. There's sightseeing logs, hunting logs, Gold Saucer events + a lot more.
STORY:
What surprised me the most about this game is just how good the story is. Not just from an MMO perspective, but from a Final Fanasy one. Generally, it's put together really well. Ofcourse there are a few tedious bits, but for the most part it's extremely enjoyable. The story helps guide you to places you should level, introduces you to more of the world and characters in it. Another thing to note is how well some of the characters are built up throughout the story, you really get to know + like them. Again, content wise you're definately not short, especially with Heavensward just released. There's easily more than 50 hours of story content available at the moment, and the best thing is that it's constantly being added to through content updates. The story is split into mini chapter type things, some with overlaping issues, so certain issues don't overstay their welcome and it doesn't get stale.
VISUALS + OST:
This is a Final Fantasy game. Even people that haven't played Final Fantasy know that a lot of effort is usually put into these 2 areas, and it applies here. Visually, the game is extremely impressive, especially now with DX11 support. The zones and enemies are extremely diverse, filled with a true sense of imagination and thought put into them. The music complements each area well, with a great range of types used. Lots of different types of musical styles are used for certain situations, from J-POP, smooth jazz and heavy metal. Even if some music tracks don't fit your fancy, theres bound to be plenty more that will.
ENDGAME:
Decided to give this it's own section aswell, as most people are interested in this. There's a ton todo at end game. There's tons of dungeons, raids and extreme primal encounters you can fight for gear, mounts or glory. Some of these get extremely challenging, to the point that you'd need to form training parties to help train yourself + your team to beat an encounter. There's also a pvp arena, which I confess I haven't used, dailies through beat tribe quests or doing any of the logs I've mentioned above.
OVERALL QUALITY:
IMO The overall quality is just great. There's so much todo content wise, it's just unreal. With so many possible playstyles and things todo it's hard to not reccomened this to any MMO or Final Fantasy fan. I'd honestly reccommend it just for the story alone. This review really doesn't do it justice, so if you've read this and it's interested you I'd really reccomend watching some videos of it on youtube(Just don't spoil the story for yourself!) and checking out the free trial. Just be warned, this game is an absolute timesink that will steal your life.

Here is 90% of the game:
1. Walk around empty environment looking for a level/valve to pull to open up a door to advance.
2. Every 5 minutes, an earthquake or meaningless ambient sound or pointless voiceover flashback will cause the screen to go blurry and slow your character to a crawl for a couple seconds.
That's it. I'm not joking. That's almost the entire game. There aren't even any items, inventory, or resources to worry about. I would have been fine with this since that aspect of Dark Descent annoyed me, but they didn't replace it with anything interesting here. There are free horror Flash games with more depth and interaction.
Even though I didn't like Dark Descent, at least there was  the interest in pushing forward in order to find out why your character was in this environment. You had amnesia with a note from yourself telling you to kill some man, and you spend the game finding out why. In Machine for Pigs, you have a plot that's pointlessly obtuse only to distract you from how boring it is. Your character wakes up and mumbles something about the children running into the basement where apparently you set up an industrialized slaughter house. Most of the notes and journals you pick up are confusing and worthless to sheddding any light on anything. They're just there to waste your time and try to trick you into thinking there's some DEEP MEANING to this pretentious naval gazing nonsense.
Just worthless. HOW bad is it? I honestly think this might be a worse atmospheric walking simulator than Gone Home. Yes, it's THAT bad.

It's nothing like the original - but that's not necessarily a bad thing. The Dark Descent featured challenging puzzles, pulse-raising ‘run or hide’ decision making, inventory management and constant danger. A Machine for Pigs holds none of these accolades, however, it’s still a good game! It has an interesting story with some horrific themes running throughout. It really makes you feel like you are trapped within the innards of some mechanical beast.
There are a few terrifying and jumpy moments before you actually encounter a pig-monster face-to-face... Until you realise that they are a totally pointless gameplay mechanic. Normally, in games where you must rely on either running or hiding from enemies (e.g. the game’s predecessor or Outlast), there is normally some general indication as to where to run or hide. Whether this is done by backtracking to previously seen areas, or running towards illuminated exits. With other games there is fun to be had in evading danger, but not in a Machine for Pigs. The pig-monsters spot you instantly and you can rarely outrun them! This is all okay though because if you get killed, you simply black out and spawn further on in the game, as if the encounter never happened... What’s the point?
As soon as I hear a pig’s squeal, this is normally my reaction:
“Oh blimey! It’s a pig-man! And he’s spawned right behind me again! I guess I’d better run ahead!”
*runs ahead*
“Oh-no! There’s nothing here! You know what?... Sod this! I’ll just take a beating because I have no idea what is going on...”
*stands there, gets beaten to death by pig trotters and respawns*
“Ohhhhhhh so I was meant to run down that ridiculously dark corridor that was obstructed from view by that massive pipe! Stupid me!”
Literally, I’d say 2 out of 3 pursuits could pan out like this. The action is AWFUL. The "puzzles" literally rely on pressing buttons, replacing power fuses or turning steam valves. That said, simply looking at the machinary is a joy to be had and interacting with it can be quite fun!
The game’s redeeming features are the story and the atmosphere. I’m not going to say much about the story, but it is really good! The themes expressed are extremely dark and the way everything unfolds is rather marvellous. Whoever designed all of the machinery did a really good job. The large growling machines and the spitting steam pipes twisting all around create a very immersive portrayal of 19th century industry. Brilliant ambient noises with the accompaniment of eerie music makes you want to jump out of the nearest factory window. There are some instances at the start that had me bricking myself.
I personally don’t believe this game should have been called “Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs” because it is hardily like its predecessor. The only thing that is the same is that you can open draws and doors, and wind steam valves with mouse actions. That’s it! Everything else has changed. The game feels more like a scary industrial Dear Esther. However, I can totally understand why the developers would want to capitalise on a series.
Essentially, if you want an incredibly immersive and very artistic story-based gaming experience, this game is probably for you. However, if you want a heart-pounding survival horror – don’t even think about it. It’s nothing like the previous game and your money would probably be better spent on Outlast, if you haven’t already played it.

Amnesia: a machine for pigs mixed reviews represent the afternath of the clash between the Amnesia franchise fans and Dear Esther sequel hopefuls.
Amnesia fans wanted more of the 'scary' Amnesia series while and Dear Esther fans such as myself craved more of Robert Briscoe's unique style from its debut, genre defining title. In the end, neither really received what they wanted, although thankfully the game certainly is more of a ''walking simulator' than a series of cheap scares.
The production values might not be stellar but remain relatively high throughout the adventure, and for the most part, the title delivers a solid gaming experience for the 5 hours or so it takes to complete it.
7/10. Bring Robert Briscoe back.

Distraint is a good example of a classic indie game, that was created first and foremost for the sake of the story which the author wanted to share with everyone. It combines a bit of a direct narrative, a bit of environmental storytelling and some atmospheric sound design to deliver its message.
The message in question in this kind of games games is a highly subjective thing, and if you're interested in the game, you better make your own opinion of it, but my version comes under the spoiler:
Distraint has a sound story, not those pretentious "boy longes for a girl in a platformer game" setups you see these days. And because this game is a one man effort, its every component (be it graphics, puzzles, sound, or visual effects) is really consistent with the storytelling, providing a very solid overall experience.
Technically, this game is a 2D adventure with a dystopic setting and lots of horror elements.
The game has 4 main levels (based on story arcs), with an addition of several smaller levels made for the sake of artistic exposition. Don't worry, though, Distraint is not a walking simulator - you'll have to solve multiple puzzles to progress through each of the main stages. There is also a nice degree of funny interactions you can make by applying items from your inventory to unexpected targets. After each story arc is done, you return to the protagonist's apartments to wrap things up.
Speaking of the horror elements, they are made not so much to scare you, as to make an accent on some point of the story or develop a charachter trait. Overall, it works well, the game doesn't create suspense, but rather a feeling of phantasmagoria, and does it quite elaborately, so it doesn't fall apart as a bunch of random nonsense. Also, the game has some really good findings in horror department.
Even though Distraint has a relatively slow pace, it really makes you wonder what will happen next. And what happens next really can come off as a surprise - or as a deppressingly accurate prediction.
Currently, SteamSpy estimates Distraint to have around 32k owners, and it definetly deserves more attention. If you miss the feeling of the game made by a single author, you should definetly play Distraint.

It's developed by only one man, and it shows. Don't get me wrong, developing all this on your own is an incredible feat, but the game is lacking in a lot of different areas. Let me tell you how the first 5 minutes are, so you can get an idea of the game:
After starting a new game using a menu that leaves a lot to be desired, you appear on a shipwith a group of NPCs. The ship is a ship from the age of sail, a XVIII century looking ship, with various decks of canons. And the game is suppoused to be medieval. When the ship reaches the coast, you just jump out of it. No ramp, no stairs, nothing, just a 15m jump from the top deck to the ground. Fourtunately, there's no fall damage, because that fall would kill you in any other universe.
Now, why didn't the dev use some kind of medieval looking ship? Something like a scandinavian longship, for example. If would keep the medieval aesthetic, and just jumpinng out of it would make a lot more sense. It's not really that big of an issue, but when it's the first impresion you get from the game, well, the dev could have put a little more thought into it, no?
Well, the thing is that he couldn't, because instead of making a small game with a lot of care and details, he chose to make a big one, a really big and ambitious one, but there is only so much a single person can do. The result is that the game feels lacking in almost every corner. Combat, building, farming, NPC behaviour, hunting, map generation... I struggle to find a single aspect that could not use some serious improvement.
I like the concept, I admire the dedication of the dev, but the game is just not good.

Decided to update my review, just because I love this game so much + my last one didn't do it justice. Going to break the main points down, so it's easier to read.
GAMEPLAY:
Like most MMOs, you have the holy trinity of dps, healer and tanks. In this game they are divided into classes, which can further specialise into jobs. Cross class skills are used, so lets say I'm a White Mage at level 60, I can use cross class to access some skills from other classes/jobs I've leveled. Classes/Jobs are also handled differently. Your character can switch between any of the classes/jobs as they get unlocked, allowing you to completely change your playstyle should you choose to in the future. There's even classes like Fishing, Blacksmithing or Alchemist if you want to work the markets, or help your Free Company build an airship! Gameplay is like most MMOS, except it can get quite challenging as you get to a higher level. IMO this game has some of the hardest content from any MMO out there. There's the typical "Run around and quest" style gameplay, you can do a main story, there's lots of little "sub stories", trials, dungeons, fates in which many people randomly team up to complete a mini objective etc. Gameplay wise the game definately isn't lacking. The actual combat is quite good, players aren't just taught to stand still and smash buttons. There's lots of movement during fights, as you move away from aoes, deal with specific mechanics to handle bosses and move to specific locations to help team memebers. Apart from the obvious leveling gameplay, there's a lot of other things to go and enjoy. There's sightseeing logs, hunting logs, Gold Saucer events + a lot more.
STORY:
What surprised me the most about this game is just how good the story is. Not just from an MMO perspective, but from a Final Fanasy one. Generally, it's put together really well. Ofcourse there are a few tedious bits, but for the most part it's extremely enjoyable. The story helps guide you to places you should level, introduces you to more of the world and characters in it. Another thing to note is how well some of the characters are built up throughout the story, you really get to know + like them. Again, content wise you're definately not short, especially with Heavensward just released. There's easily more than 50 hours of story content available at the moment, and the best thing is that it's constantly being added to through content updates. The story is split into mini chapter type things, some with overlaping issues, so certain issues don't overstay their welcome and it doesn't get stale.
VISUALS + OST:
This is a Final Fantasy game. Even people that haven't played Final Fantasy know that a lot of effort is usually put into these 2 areas, and it applies here. Visually, the game is extremely impressive, especially now with DX11 support. The zones and enemies are extremely diverse, filled with a true sense of imagination and thought put into them. The music complements each area well, with a great range of types used. Lots of different types of musical styles are used for certain situations, from J-POP, smooth jazz and heavy metal. Even if some music tracks don't fit your fancy, theres bound to be plenty more that will.
ENDGAME:
Decided to give this it's own section aswell, as most people are interested in this. There's a ton todo at end game. There's tons of dungeons, raids and extreme primal encounters you can fight for gear, mounts or glory. Some of these get extremely challenging, to the point that you'd need to form training parties to help train yourself + your team to beat an encounter. There's also a pvp arena, which I confess I haven't used, dailies through beat tribe quests or doing any of the logs I've mentioned above.
OVERALL QUALITY:
IMO The overall quality is just great. There's so much todo content wise, it's just unreal. With so many possible playstyles and things todo it's hard to not reccomened this to any MMO or Final Fantasy fan. I'd honestly reccommend it just for the story alone. This review really doesn't do it justice, so if you've read this and it's interested you I'd really reccomend watching some videos of it on youtube(Just don't spoil the story for yourself!) and checking out the free trial. Just be warned, this game is an absolute timesink that will steal your life.

SUMMARY: Transistor is a precise, intelligent RPG focused on action combat and a deep story.  Appropriate for fans who like deep, stats-tweaked, customized action with a story behind it.
It's the story of a city that's always changing.  A singer who can't sing.  A man who's dead but alive.  And a sword that's not a sword - the Transistor.
Transistor is best thought of as a "thinking actioner."  The basic formula of the game is to enter an area, find some narrative and extras, then engage in a fight against highly different enemies.  Over time one unlocks various abilities that lets you customize combat in extremely deep ways - and without customization and careful choice of abilities and how they work together, you will fail.  The plot makes you think, the combat requires you to do the same.
The core mechanic of the game is that the mysterious Transistor picks up personality traces that give you new combat moves, and leveling up unlocks new options and abilities.  These moves can be combined with each other, one move attached to another to give it new effects.  Moves can even be slotted to provide passive bonuses.  This allows for extremely deep customization and development of your own combat techniques - and in a few cases, lightniing-bolt moments of realization where you see a combo you can use or should have used.
However those moves?  They're from personality traits of the deceased.  As you uses them in different combinations, more story is unlocked.  Mixing it up in combat lets you find out more about what's been going on in the setting, the ever-changing city of Cloudbank.
And how is the story?
Frankly, impressive.  It's a tale told via characters, from the mysterious man trapped in the Transistor to the personality traces you uncover.  The story is thus highly personal, and really draws you in, rife with issues of art and creation, moral ambiguity and fads, and permanence versus change.  Excellent voice acting brings everything to life.
The people that said the ending made them cry?  You'll see why they did.
If there's an issue with the game it's that it's precision may not be for everyone - if you're not ready to figure out your combat techniques and your timing and the use of the freeze-plan Turn() ability, it won't be for you.  You have to put in effort to figure the right way to fight your enemies, and if you're not willing to do that, it's going to feel like a chore.  Neither the plot nor the combat or customization are laid-back affairs.
Also the combat IS the game.  If you're not up for a fight, then you won't enjoy this.
The game is short, but it doesn't overstay it's welcome.  It also has replay options and lets you add new challenges (with corresponding increases in experience).  For people who love highly customized action, you'll probably enjoy it.
I consider Transistor another success for Supergiant.  Thoughtful, character-driven, well-told, it really takes you into the setting and pushes you.
And maybe, just maybe, makes you a bit sad and melancholy.

Distraint is a psychological horror adventure game which not only offers the player a good portion of unsettling tension, but also has its humorous moments. The games narrative and great pace will surely drag you in, and what's gonna keep you there are the many, many emotional moments. Interestingly enough, the latter manages to be both one of the games strengths as well as a weakness.
In my opinion, Distraint's biggest shortcoming is the extremely black and white view on a morally gray situation where in reality, you won't find those cartoony sides of pure good and pure evil. I personally believe that a slightly more balanced and objective viewpoint would have strengthened the story, and it would still have been able to create a just as gripping experience. It might even have made the story even more thought-provoking.
Distraint's simple but well made art style, full of personality and just the right color scheme, creates a beautifully grim atmosphere and gives life and a soul to the characters, making you care about the ones whos lives you as Price comes to affect. The gameplay as well as the puzzles are straight forward (though I have to admit that I was stuck in one of the puzzle sequences for an embarrassingly long time). It's a linear game, but because the story and the emotional trips sticks with you after you've finished them, you might want to experience it all a second time.
It's worth noting that the game is a one-man project. You can tell a lot of effort was put into this and its price (no pun intended) is low for what it offers. I'm looking forward to see more from this developer!

First thing first. I really wish they'd make this game a one off payment with earnable in game cash that is actually worth something.
Then MAYBE have a few deluxe items for the really hardcore pay-to-win type.
As it is this game really is pay-to-play....
On a good note though - If you are a keen hunter IRL this is as close as it gets! I'd actually call it a hunting simulator.
And about 90% of the players (paying members - not guests) have all been friendly hunters also. Eager to talk about both game tips and their experiences in  real life.
The environments and scenery are great. However, Australia has a lot more to offer than the Mars like landscape portrayed.
Wind swept leaves are indicative of the wind direction and strength, which if you don't pay attention to could spoil your stalk in a heart-crushing split second.
Distance scaling and graphics are also quite good. I normally play on high or very high settings to really feel immersed in the hunt.
The range of equipment is good. Not great, but still comprehensive. And there is the ever annoying fact that you have to pay for
. And I mean like $3 for a Jacket, $6 - 10 for a rifle, $5 for a blind, $1 or so for each duck decoy the list goes on. If you wanted to be kitted out to hunt everything at maximum effectiveness, it would cost you around $150  and that is a generous estimate   :s      Though, if you are a keen hunter this won't deter you as it is a great time and if you space it out (I normally buy about $15 worth of in game money every pay) a solid collection comes along nicely and this leads to great replayability (or really just continued playability).
Gameplay is challenging (as is hunting in real life - a thing that a lot of people don't understand, hence the mostly negative reviews) But, with challenge comes great reward and there is a strange satisfaction when you take some trohpy photos of a monster Red deer you successfully roared in, or a massive tusky boar that was taken whilst greedily eating the baits you left earlier in the week. Sitting in a blind with your retriever calling in a flock of ducks to attempt landing within range of your 12GA is truly a buzz. The same goes when you finally land your binoculars on the perfect buck after seeing many does and spikers. It always gets me raring to go on a trip in real life haha.
Conclusion:   If you are an avid hunter or just love the sims and games this is great. If you think you can just join a server and run around culling animals like it's Call of Duty in the bush you're going to be butthurt like the rest of the reviewers.

I don't do the MP, so this is all about the SP. I put about 160 hours into this game on PC, completed all the missions multiple times on the highest difficulty, and have almost all the achievements. If I can do that, then better players like you will do great for sure. Overall, the game was not a waste of money, but it is sad to see a great franchise focus on the features I like least. I haven't bought a COD game since this one and based on watching other people play them, I am glad I didn't. If you want the best COD experience, COD4 or COD2 will serve you well. Never played COD3 since I don't own an Xbox or whatever console that was exclusive to.
If you liked COD: Modern Warfare, this game will appeal because it is pretty much the same game with lots of minor changes. It expands on the trends that set COD4 apart from the original WW2 shooters that COD was built on, expanding the special operations focus and focusing on bond-style villains weaving fancy plots to run the world in some way.
Technology also is greatly emphasized; COD4 was built on real weapons in wide use in the early 21st-century, while COD: MW2 makes commonplace what is rare or simply theorized even today. Most guns now have electronic sights instead of ironsights, automated weapon systems like sentry guns play a prominent role, and remarkably efficient UAVs with more firepower than a B52 menace the skies. If you want a more sci-fi than real-world experience of "modern warfare" then you have found your game. Incidentally, the poor RPG7 rocketlauncher remains a big part of the battlefield and remains unable to hit anything more than 30 feet away without a huge dose of luck. So much for modernity!
If you like the classic "common soldier fighting for his country" theme of the original COD series, you will be in for some, but not complete, disappointment.There are maps where average soldiers still fight average soldiers from other countries, but where they are fighting often requires considerable suspension of disbelief. What is clear is that COD: MW2 is continuing the trend of the franchise towards special ops missions where the real story revolves around elite special forces units who battle sinister evil geniuses weaving great conspiracies. Common soldiers like Paratrooper Martin and Sergeant Moody are very much passe. If you want Splintercell without the stealth mechanics, this will do something for you.
Like COD4, maps are tight enough to keep players from getting too lost and open enough, most of the time, to let players do more than simply charge straight into killzones. Some maps have tedious bottlenecks that will frustrate, so expect a few ragequits unless you are a masochist like me. So far, the grenade spam problem that makes many COD games very annoying is not too strong here; certainly not as bad as COD: World At War. You will have time to rest between rushes without too much fear of an endless rain of grenades appearing out of nowhere to punish you for your laziness. Infinite respawns are pretty reasonable in this game as well, so you aren't always going to lose for not having rushed after that last enemy getting shot.
One huge feature that greatly limits the appeal of this game for me: NO PC CONSOLE! COD consoles have always been fairly limited in their utility compared to games like Halflife, but for reasons that make no sense to me, IW has decided that players don't need consoles and so now players have no ablity to fine-tune their game settings, use cheats, or even fix some issues that could have been done in the past with five seconds of typing. This massively reduces the playability of the game for me. Before this game, I loved to see the beautiful animations and graphics in slow-motion. Can't do that here and that makes me sad.

Let's get thigns straight: this is a Horror game, not a Terror game. ATDD is a Terror game, a game that exists to scare you out of your wits. This game is nothing like ATDD in terms of terror, but this game can immerse you and envelop you and disturb you in ways equally terrifying. This game was my single most favourite experience of 2013. Even though it lasted just under 3 hours, I have since played it twice over. Everything about this game is incredibly intricately designed. The atmosphere intoxicating; and the music, oh the music that gets inside your head and controls your thoughts.
Do not buy this game to be scared and have a bit of a laugh like ATDD, buy this game to play in a dark room, undisturbed with headphones on and the volume cranked to obscene levels. Read each note carefully, and build your own picture on the events of the game's story. Connect with Mandus, and experience his journey through his own creation in (I would say) the best psycological horror game to date.
This game is not a game, as such; it is an experience, to be experienced, not so much played. It may as well be a book or a film, but there is not as much personal connection with the character in those mediums. I wholly recommend this game to anyone who is serious about their horror stories, and really everyone old enough to play it. You cannot miss this. Although I do recommend waiting for a sale as it is a tad expensive. Or steal it off a mate, if you liked it, great! if not, so what? you didn't lose out reall, except for a few hours, maybe. So go one, give it a try, and you might even become a pig yourself!

Do not expect this game to be a sequel of the great Amnesia: A Dark Descent. While ADD was scary as hell and had a great sanity/resource management system, A Machine for Pigs takes away all of the inventory and resource management.  It doesn't have the sanity effect either which is really the only aspect I miss.  The puzzles are pretty easy and really only feel like slight detours to story progression rather than some of the puzzles in ADD that were tricky or hard to find the solution to.
What AMfP has going for it is atmosphere and story; which imo are far superior to ADD.  The pacing is spot on, the music and sound effects are perfect, and there was a great feeling of dread from start to finish.  The story is a satisfyingly gruesome, disturbing, Lovecraftian tale about evil and redemption. The environment and monsters are creepy as hell, but not quite as horrifying or difficult to defeat as those in ADD.  Overall, I loved how terrifying ADD was and it's sanity meter was a fresh idea for the horror genre.  AMfP is a different game then its predessesor and I love it for different reasons.
Don't pay attention to negative reviews trying to compare it to ADD. It is a beautifuly crafted horror story that will stay with me way longer than the first Amnesia. I give it a solid 8.5/10.

Dark Souls II is a fantasy third person action RPG game, developed by From Software and published by Bandai Namco, releasing worldwide on PC, 360 and PS3 in April 2014. The story takes place in the grim fantasy world from the original game, Lordran. This time around you visit different areas and play as a new character.
If you have been on the internet at all in the past few years you will already know what Dark Souls is known for, gruesomely hard unforgiving game play. The original game was probably one of the hardest games I have ever played which tested my skill not only as a gamer, but as a person. Whilst the game play mechanics in Dark Souls II are basically the same comparatively allowing the player in full control of building the character they want to play due to a different levelling system being incorporated. Of course the most important aspect of Dark Souls is the combat and again it is done very well. A lot of the regular mob fights are interesting and varied, you do come across a slight repetition issue when you find yourself being killed by the same monster over and over again but it gives you that little extra incentive to progress.  Boss fights throughout the game are all extremely well-tuned and designed encounters – I’d say the boss fights here are more memorable than the original’s purely because the scale and size of them is gigantic in some cases.
Another really key element to Dark Souls game play would be the exploration of the game world which is essentially entirely open for you to explore right from the beginning of the game; whilst it may not be the wisest thing in the world to go exploring the later stages it is possible if you want to though. I was more inclined to go searching for treasure and loot this time around too; whether it was because I was completely enthralled with the armour and weapon designs that I wanted to keep finding more, or because of how well the maps are designed.  The game does very little to aid you by telling you where to go which leaves you in a rut sometimes. I have to admit I did resort to using a walkthrough and wiki throughout my play through; I know I know, I’m such a wimp – I honestly don’t think I would have been able to beat the game without it though, so for the purpose of this review I’ll take one for the team here!
Graphically Dark Souls II has been improved over the original, I tried to find the official game engine being used online but even so long after its release I’ve not been able to find a reputable source of an answer but all you need to know is the game does look much better than the first. There are still a few textures which are low quality, but character models, animations and scenery all look gorgeous. The little voice acting that is available is done really well; almost too well – you can really feel the deprived thoughts of the characters in the game through their monotone and dull voices which I found to be quite an immersive factor. It was a little off putting when characters were quite obviously talking that their mouths weren’t moving through which was a shame to see from a game of this standard.
I have to say I found the original Dark Souls to be more of a challenging game compared to II – I think the main factor behind this is the fact that the PC port for this game wasn’t completely broken compared to the first. The controls work right off the back which is always a good sign.  That being said boss fights are fundamentally easier though; with some mechanics more clearly than others on how to combat them, or maybe it’s because I finally “gitted gud” at Dark Souls. You can also tell how less of a challenge I found it, given that my first run through of Dark Souls II took almost half the amount of time than the original game, spanning just twenty one hours – remember that I had a wiki throughout the run so if you are going for a true experience you are easily going to be pushing the fifty hour mark. You’ll also get plenty of replay ability from this title due to a new game+ mode being introduced this time around.
There is also a much improved multiplayer side of the game too; one element of this is the ability to leave notes and hints around the game world for other players to see, as well as being able to see people’s recent deaths around you too which is always amusing to see someone run straight off a bridge; it never gets old regardless of how many times you watch it.  You’ll also get other players invading your game world which is…well, a different experience to say the least.
Like I said above, this is a much better PC port of the game; there is already native controller support which is brilliant as the game is played waaaay better on a controller compared to a mouse and keyboard. Whilst there are limited graphical options, I was quite pleased to see that I was able to run the game at 4k resolution and on full graphics the whole time and I was able to remain at 60 FPS the whole time. This wasn’t even running SLI so it is an extremely well optimized release.  I did find it slightly annoying that I wasn’t able to turn off the online though, you are able to opt out of it on console in the options menu, but it seems to be constantly online for PC – you can get round it by launching Steam in offline mode, but I still want to be online on Steam, just not in game as it does get annoying when someone ten times higher level than you keeps invading your world to poke you up your bum with his massive sword time and time again.
Right from the beginning of this game I actually found it to be a worse Dark Souls game compared to the original due to it not being overly challenging, but that being said I had more fun playing this game than the original; I know it probably doesn’t make sense but this felt more like a finished product that works off the shelf and I was able to finish the game to completion within a matter of a week and I enjoyed every minute of it. I would have like to see the price drop a little bit over the course of the past two years but you are still getting a game that is a joy to play from start to finish here. It is also worth noting that there is a different version of Dark Souls II, in the form of Dark Souls II Scholar of the First Sin – whilst this is an improved version of the game, both graphically and technically, the game’s worlds are also slightly different. This review is for the original Dark Souls II release.

Dark souls 2's base game is similar to the first where the main objective is to explore the level going through monsters to reach an area boss. Some of the bosses were very imaginative and had a cool way in which you can approach the fights, whereas others were a bit disappointing and a couple were just a rehash from early game. The game is better ported than the first but still isn't great. I would strongly recommend controller as trying to use a keyboard just results in things like "press {Xbox b} to roll" even though you specify you are using keyboard and mouse. However, the game feels much smoother to play and controls feel more responsive. I also didn't experience any lag issues throughout the entire game.
Now this is going to sound strange but I was actually a little disappointed at the games difficulty. It actually felt a bit too easy. I probably did 1/5 of the bosses first try and around 2/3 within a few tries. In fact there was only one boss that gave me a lot of trouble and I was very happy to beat. Nowhere near the level of Ornstein and Smough. Just something about the boss difficulty was lacking. This game felt more of a woo I beat another boss. Whereas almost all of the bosses in the first game gave me a lot to think about and left me feeling a massive sense of accomplishment after beating them. I only got that for maybe 2 bosses in this game.
Having said this I cannot deny that this game is absolutely excellent. Once you get into it you'll get incredibly immersed in the world and you will be playing for hours at a time. That's how you tell it's a great game.
Overall, I really enjoyed dark souls 2 and would recommend to buy.

It's a story game. But, it doesn't sacrifice gameplay for the sake of it. The story is mostly told by cutscenes and dialogue. The cutscenes aren't that long and don't intrude with the game. As you progress further into a level, dialogue relating to what you're doing will play. It's a well told story about a man being in certain places, killing certain people, exacting revenge - the usual. It's got an arcade feel with the points system, but doesn't punish you for missing out on points. You can go at your own pace, cradle yourself behind cover as much as you want until the damage goes away. The game doesn't mind. It's got ALL the time in the world. But, the pressure and tension are there. You WANT to continue going and learning about this man's story. The name escapes me, right now, but whatever. I imagine it's myself, because I wish I was that cool.
My one complaint is the standoffs. I get it's classic cowboy schtick, but I just shot about 50 of this man's friends in an unfair fight, can't I just pop a cap in this man too? No? Fine. It's not really a problem, it's just a little quip.
I love this game, it's a great way to just spend a few minutes (the save points are plenty) or an afternoon (if you want to pound through the whole game).

An old man walks into a bar (no joke) and sits down with some strangers to tell stories of his days as a bounty hunter on the trail of revenge to kill the men who killed his brothers. As he tells each story you get to play through that tale, shooting up bad guys old west style. If you ever remember playing West Bank on your Amstrad or C64 or maybe remember Wild Guman from the Back To The Future movies then you might enjoy this one. While it's definitely a modern FPS most of the shoot outs play out near cover with bad guys popping up or running into play turning the screen into a hail of gun fire as you mow down opponents much like those old gaming classics. As you wade through enemies you'll get to fight bosses with gatlin guns and have quick draw shoot outs. It's not a revolutionary game but its good wild west fun. Grab it when it's on sale :)

I picked up Distraint hoping that it would be one of those little 16-bit-esque games with a killer soundtrack that helps carry the graphical style, and to some degree that's what I got, but not so much that it blew me away. The story is very unique, and I wonder now whether that uniqueness is part of what left me feeling like I was just grinding it out in the end, because I was never really emotionally invested in the protagonist's "victims"? The horror was underdone, and I say that because Distraint starts off strong, but by about 2/3 of the way through it pretty much ceases to exist. In a lot of ways this makes it feel like you are playing two separate games - One that has the bones of a great shock-horror, and then later it is watered down to a semi-emotional scrolling sim with plenty of drug use. Likewise, the soundtrack starts off pretty well, and then just dulls down with the horror aspect of the gameplay.
The reason I can't be super harsh in my evaluation of this game however, is that it was only a three month project start to finish. Yes it shows, and yes it is a little more frustrating than if the game was just completely rubbish the whole way through, but it is still pretty well on par for games around the $2-$3 mark even though they would have had far more time invested in most cases. Distraint is solid enough of a game that it asks the question of other games in its price range, "What did you actually deliver for all that time you spent?" And rightly so, it's the question I'll be asking from now on too!
Great concept, solid ending, but it's a shame it was rushed.

Distraint was programed by one person over the course of a few months, but you would never guess it from playing the game. It is extremely well done, capturing its intended atmosphere perfectly. Despite being a shorter game it offers a rich and rewarding story that sticks with you. While not the scariest game to ever exist, it did make me jump a few times. There were also a few times where I found myself hesitating to proceed. Both of which are truly admirable feats in side-scrolling games.
Pros:
>Solid story that keeps you wanting more throughout the game.
>The style and feel of the game is distinct, well done, and matches the story perfectly.
>Teaches the player a valuable lesson in the form of a short story.
>Smooth gameplay, does not have any weird bugs or glitches at all, easy to stay immersed in the game.
>Steam achievements and controller support.
Cons:
>Does not save to the Steam cloud

First thing first. I really wish they'd make this game a one off payment with earnable in game cash that is actually worth something.
Then MAYBE have a few deluxe items for the really hardcore pay-to-win type.
As it is this game really is pay-to-play....
On a good note though - If you are a keen hunter IRL this is as close as it gets! I'd actually call it a hunting simulator.
And about 90% of the players (paying members - not guests) have all been friendly hunters also. Eager to talk about both game tips and their experiences in  real life.
The environments and scenery are great. However, Australia has a lot more to offer than the Mars like landscape portrayed.
Wind swept leaves are indicative of the wind direction and strength, which if you don't pay attention to could spoil your stalk in a heart-crushing split second.
Distance scaling and graphics are also quite good. I normally play on high or very high settings to really feel immersed in the hunt.
The range of equipment is good. Not great, but still comprehensive. And there is the ever annoying fact that you have to pay for
. And I mean like $3 for a Jacket, $6 - 10 for a rifle, $5 for a blind, $1 or so for each duck decoy the list goes on. If you wanted to be kitted out to hunt everything at maximum effectiveness, it would cost you around $150  and that is a generous estimate   :s      Though, if you are a keen hunter this won't deter you as it is a great time and if you space it out (I normally buy about $15 worth of in game money every pay) a solid collection comes along nicely and this leads to great replayability (or really just continued playability).
Gameplay is challenging (as is hunting in real life - a thing that a lot of people don't understand, hence the mostly negative reviews) But, with challenge comes great reward and there is a strange satisfaction when you take some trohpy photos of a monster Red deer you successfully roared in, or a massive tusky boar that was taken whilst greedily eating the baits you left earlier in the week. Sitting in a blind with your retriever calling in a flock of ducks to attempt landing within range of your 12GA is truly a buzz. The same goes when you finally land your binoculars on the perfect buck after seeing many does and spikers. It always gets me raring to go on a trip in real life haha.
Conclusion:   If you are an avid hunter or just love the sims and games this is great. If you think you can just join a server and run around culling animals like it's Call of Duty in the bush you're going to be butthurt like the rest of the reviewers.

Having said this I cannot deny that this game is absolutely excellent. Once you get into it you'll get incredibly immersed in the world and you will be playing for hours at a time. That's how you tell it's a great game.

The amount of classes is good, but lacks some core ones (2handed dmg dealer most noticable, or dual wield damage dealer outside rogue/ninja which will  be introduced shortly after I make this review)
The story is quite lacking -some- times, but is quite epic at others.
Lack of addon support.
While these may seem as deal breakers to some the game has insane features on other departments, offering deep customization on things I didn't even know it's possible to customize. And I say that, having played all the popular (and not only) mmorpgs out there.
The overall design is just FLAWLESS, and for that the game designers have my utmost respect.I don't just mean that about the graphics. The music of the primal encounters, and other major fights are just epic, well made, inspiring pieces.
The boss encounters do have very interesting mechanics at time, but - as everything - once you conquer them they turn easier.
The game offers a LOT to do, and it's fun as long as you interract with others.
Getting into a good Guild (Free Company) is a great tip for newcommers. Many players are helpful and offer tips, and you can forge relationships which is up to you if they last.
The social experience is there, and that's a part of MMOs players neglet a lot as they blindly rush towards endgame.
I know I did that, and I've got ~450 hours played in about a month that I started this game.
That said, this game is addicting, much like any mmorpg you enjoy (won't name other popular ones)- mmorpg players will understand.
The monthly subscription is not even worth mentioning as everybody who has played mmorpgs before knows there's a vast difference in game quality, support, and other features when a game has subscription. What you pay for, you get.
Should be mentioned that the game itself is relatively cheap and comes with a 30 days sub-free to try out.
There's also a trial version available in which you can play for 2 weeks with max level 20 (and other restrictions).
I'm quite sure a game for a console costs more(about 3 times as much) and it's a 1 week experience tops.
In a market where going Free to Play seems like the only option to maintain a game, this game grows.
Credit for that goes to it's nice comunity, it's regular updates, it's low downtimes, it's nice optical and accoustical experience, and most importantly to the fact that this very game in it's 1.0 version failed horribly, shut down, and was Reborn, as the title suggests, into what is currently one of the greatest of it's kind.
Additional awesomeness points go to writers/translators or whoever named the Quests and FATEs in the game (FATE = Events that happen randomly in the world) - The naming is just great, at times I found myself just laughing at the screen with the things I was reading.
The game is so well written I cannot even begin to explain.
Overall, I feel the game was one of the most worthy purchases I've made in quite a while.

I won't lie, I was skeptic. Heavily skeptic. Like, I thought this was worse than Dead Island skeptic.
Square-Enix's track record has been far from amazing in terms of Final Fantasy titles as of late. Final Fantasy XIII almost cemented my lack of trust in them, and watching the disaster that was XIV 1.0, I just stopped keeping track altogether. They'd lost their magic much harder than I could imagine.
This game is lucky I knew someone else who was into A Realm Reborn. At first, I had to laugh at the fact he was still paying for a lousy, broken, boring MMO, but then I started watching. I hadn't realised XIV had ended it's world and restarted again, and I was confused when I found the game to be a lot more interesting than I remember. It shut me the hell up.
I decided to dive into this head first, give it a shot, see if it would be something I could get into. After all, I knew people playing it already, it would be a party based activity, something I haven't done in a while.
But as you can tell by the amount of hours currently sunk into it, I didn't really need to know anyone prior.
This game sunk it's teeth in. Hard.
I'm not someone that comes from a massive MMO background. The last one I had played and gotten into was almost 10 years ago. It would be difficult to know if I could recommend this game over other MMOs, or even other games. Although you would probably do this anyway, I recommend looking at gameplay footage and deciding for yourself. I can personally say I've had more fun with this than I was expecting, and keep coming back.
Community is pretty good (on Cerberus anyway, and from what I've found from watching other players). Yes, there are a few bad eggs, but considering the MMO and other online games I've come from, this isn't a problem. Every community will have the ragequitters, the griefers and the thieves, but they are so scarce. PvP is probably the main place you'll find these people, if at all.
There are a handful of nitpicks, most of them are rather minor, such as the voice acting at points sucking the emotion out of a moment, usually in a single word (this seems to be a SE staple(seriously stop hiring the worst actors to play big roles)) and the HUD does not scale with windowed mode, so it's very easy, if you're running a smaller window, for your screen to get cramped with icons, even if you do shrink them down. But they are nitpicks, nothing that stops the game for me at all.
All I can say is, there is a large chunk of time that I have sunk into it and I do not regret it*.
*okay I regret it a little. I could've been saving the world or learning to speedrun a game or something else with the time I've spent on this.

Strikes a very satisfying balance between RPG and action game. Classes and skills themselves are very simple, much moreso than ones you'd often find in other MMOs. The simplicity allows for the player to focus harder on individual fights rather on stats and builds. This means that, assuming you're properly geared, you have only yourself to blame for death or messing up. You didn't put an extra point in a bad stat, you didn't level a bad skill, you just messed up, and the next step is learning how not to do the same thing again. Or you lagged. Titan HM/EX, every time.
Mechanic memorization may not be everyone's cup of tea, but in my opinion it is much better and more satisfying to clear a boss or a raid because you knew what to do, when and how, rather than because you're a big bad min/max'd dude with perfect stats and a perfect skill build. You get to where you are through practice, through learning, through experiencing. You can't just invest a bunch of time/gil into BiS gear and expect to do good at everything if you haven't tried it yet, and that's why I really love this game.

This game recieved a far harsher reception than it really deserved.  Of course, this is entirely understandible considering it was sold as the successor to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, when it's not even made in the same style.  A Machine For Pigs was not even made by Frictional Games.  It was made by The Chinese Room, a developer previously only known for Dear Esther.  Now, it would be entirely reasonable to respond to that statement with "the devs responsible for Dear Esther made this?  Well, it's probably a peice of♥♥♥♥♥♥"  However, far from what the horrible steam reviews would suggest, translating The Chinese Room's style into the Horror genre (and adding some gameplay) is quite effective.
Aesthetically excellent, and narritively intreguing, this is ultimately an unsettling and worthwhile experience, despite it's poor gameplay.  However, while I appreciate the slow burn, the monsters are infrequent enough that the game gets dull at times.  Also, I found the journal entries ruined the immersion, as they were super flowery and eloquent.  When did I supposedly write these?  When I was wading through blood?
Thoroughly unsettling, often thought provoking, but makes poor use of gameplay, and is sometimes too slow.
Worthwhile despite it's flaws.

Well, where to begin. Let's just say that when I first played this game, about a year and a half ago or so, I hated it. With a passion.
I thought the controls were broken, the pvp unnecessary (and forced) and the challenge all artificial and totally based on whether you manage to avoid hitboxes/trial and error.
Now, all of that is true, but there is a secret to understanding dark souls that I have just recently come across.
The thing about this game, is that it has a lot of potential, if you just know how to look at it.
I came back to this game several times expecting better things over and over again, and I was wrong multiple times.
Until this time. You see, the earlier playthroughs I had done, I had never once tried to use a particular kind of weapon combination/strategy that turned out to be well worth the effort invested into it.
I don't claim to be an expert in everything that this game has to offer, or all the strategies in all the game, but there are three things that everyone who plays this game that were frustrated beyond relief need to understand.
1. If a tactic/strategy that you are using doesn't work, do something else. The main thing that I personally changed was that I had, up until recently, only used slashing swords. Thinking about it for a while, I realised that thrusting weapons tended to be more efficient. I picked up a solitary rapier from the blacksmith in the game (after using the shortsword as a makeshift one) and never went back to anything else. I have killed multiple bosses just with this sword, and have won every pvp duel that I have fought (I'm bound to lose eventually, but this is a lot more powerful than what I used to do).
2. Fix the controls to what YOU want. All the main controls in the game can changed (the combos themselves can't), and what I ultimately was able to do was set the attacks that I wanted where I wanted on the mouse (left click for right handed weapons and so forth) as well as setting the blocking button close to the movement keys and the lockon button (extremely important). Even though I don't use a controller, this setup is almost perfect, so if you put the effort into it, it can really pay off.
3. Just relax and have fun. It's only a game, and don't worry if you die, the penalties (even though called insanely harsh) are not that bad. All that happens, is you lose your currently acquired souls (but can retrieve them from the place you died) and take a small hit to max health (as well as some other features such as gnarly zombie face rawr). But in all seriousness, all of that can be reversed with a human effigy. So, if you're dying to a boss multiple times (my personal favorite of annoying bosses is The Pursuer), don't worry about using an effigy to bring back your max health, just get the ring from the end of Heide's Tower of Flame (which reduces the max health reduction to 75% instead of 50%) and just keep at it until you win.
I understand that a lot of controversy has surrounded the game's different releases as well as various problems with how the game was essentially released twice with little difference in between among other things, but I just got the basic game and finally because I put real effort into enjoying it, I can proudly say that this game is actually good.
I know not everyone likes it for various reasons, but if you want a game that is relatively realistic and fun when you finally get a good strategy going, check it out.
