This game lacks quite a lot to make it the most deep mmorpg around.
It has low variety of endgame armor models, low varity of impressive graphic skills (unless you're a monk class).
The grind is there, but it's not as painful as it could have been.
The amount of classes is good, but lacks some core ones (2handed dmg dealer most noticable, or dual wield damage dealer outside rogue/ninja which will  be introduced shortly after I make this review)
The story is quite lacking -some- times, but is quite epic at others.
Lack of addon support.
While these may seem as deal breakers to some the game has insane features on other departments, offering deep customization on things I didn't even know it's possible to customize. And I say that, having played all the popular (and not only) mmorpgs out there.
The overall design is just FLAWLESS, and for that the game designers have my utmost respect.I don't just mean that about the graphics. The music of the primal encounters, and other major fights are just epic, well made, inspiring pieces.
The boss encounters do have very interesting mechanics at time, but - as everything - once you conquer them they turn easier.
The game offers a LOT to do, and it's fun as long as you interract with others.
Getting into a good Guild (Free Company) is a great tip for newcommers. Many players are helpful and offer tips, and you can forge relationships which is up to you if they last.
The social experience is there, and that's a part of MMOs players neglet a lot as they blindly rush towards endgame.
I know I did that, and I've got ~450 hours played in about a month that I started this game.
That said, this game is addicting, much like any mmorpg you enjoy (won't name other popular ones)- mmorpg players will understand.
The monthly subscription is not even worth mentioning as everybody who has played mmorpgs before knows there's a vast difference in game quality, support, and other features when a game has subscription. What you pay for, you get.
Should be mentioned that the game itself is relatively cheap and comes with a 30 days sub-free to try out.
There's also a trial version available in which you can play for 2 weeks with max level 20 (and other restrictions).
I'm quite sure a game for a console costs more(about 3 times as much) and it's a 1 week experience tops.
In a market where going Free to Play seems like the only option to maintain a game, this game grows.
Credit for that goes to it's nice comunity, it's regular updates, it's low downtimes, it's nice optical and accoustical experience, and most importantly to the fact that this very game in it's 1.0 version failed horribly, shut down, and was Reborn, as the title suggests, into what is currently one of the greatest of it's kind.
Additional awesomeness points go to writers/translators or whoever named the Quests and FATEs in the game (FATE = Events that happen randomly in the world) - The naming is just great, at times I found myself just laughing at the screen with the things I was reading.
The game is so well written I cannot even begin to explain.
Overall, I feel the game was one of the most worthy purchases I've made in quite a while.

I won't lie, I was skeptic. Heavily skeptic. Like, I thought this was worse than Dead Island skeptic.
Square-Enix's track record has been far from amazing in terms of Final Fantasy titles as of late. Final Fantasy XIII almost cemented my lack of trust in them, and watching the disaster that was XIV 1.0, I just stopped keeping track altogether. They'd lost their magic much harder than I could imagine.
This game is lucky I knew someone else who was into A Realm Reborn. At first, I had to laugh at the fact he was still paying for a lousy, broken, boring MMO, but then I started watching. I hadn't realised XIV had ended it's world and restarted again, and I was confused when I found the game to be a lot more interesting than I remember. It shut me the hell up.
I decided to dive into this head first, give it a shot, see if it would be something I could get into. After all, I knew people playing it already, it would be a party based activity, something I haven't done in a while.
But as you can tell by the amount of hours currently sunk into it, I didn't really need to know anyone prior.
This game sunk it's teeth in. Hard.
I'm not someone that comes from a massive MMO background. The last one I had played and gotten into was almost 10 years ago. It would be difficult to know if I could recommend this game over other MMOs, or even other games. Although you would probably do this anyway, I recommend looking at gameplay footage and deciding for yourself. I can personally say I've had more fun with this than I was expecting, and keep coming back.
Community is pretty good (on Cerberus anyway, and from what I've found from watching other players). Yes, there are a few bad eggs, but considering the MMO and other online games I've come from, this isn't a problem. Every community will have the ragequitters, the griefers and the thieves, but they are so scarce. PvP is probably the main place you'll find these people, if at all.
There are a handful of nitpicks, most of them are rather minor, such as the voice acting at points sucking the emotion out of a moment, usually in a single word (this seems to be a SE staple(seriously stop hiring the worst actors to play big roles)) and the HUD does not scale with windowed mode, so it's very easy, if you're running a smaller window, for your screen to get cramped with icons, even if you do shrink them down. But they are nitpicks, nothing that stops the game for me at all.
All I can say is, there is a large chunk of time that I have sunk into it and I do not regret it*.
*okay I regret it a little. I could've been saving the world or learning to speedrun a game or something else with the time I've spent on this.

Strikes a very satisfying balance between RPG and action game. Classes and skills themselves are very simple, much moreso than ones you'd often find in other MMOs. The simplicity allows for the player to focus harder on individual fights rather on stats and builds. This means that, assuming you're properly geared, you have only yourself to blame for death or messing up. You didn't put an extra point in a bad stat, you didn't level a bad skill, you just messed up, and the next step is learning how not to do the same thing again. Or you lagged. Titan HM/EX, every time.
Mechanic memorization may not be everyone's cup of tea, but in my opinion it is much better and more satisfying to clear a boss or a raid because you knew what to do, when and how, rather than because you're a big bad min/max'd dude with perfect stats and a perfect skill build. You get to where you are through practice, through learning, through experiencing. You can't just invest a bunch of time/gil into BiS gear and expect to do good at everything if you haven't tried it yet, and that's why I really love this game.

TL:DR a decent FPS with a Wild West setting. At times it feels like any other generic FPS but its setting, clever playing with the story and having stuff like stand offs is enough to give some enjoyment. Worth picking up if you enjoy Westerns and the Wild West type of setting
Full Version:
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a FPS with a Wild West setting. You play as Silas Grieves,a bounty hunter, and in the game you come up against some of the most famous outlaws of the period such Jesse James and Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid. While the game is mostly standard FPS gameplay it does have a couple of cool features. The best one is the quick draw  stand offs you have at several points in the game. It works by having you try and hold a reticule over your opponent to increase your focus as you wait for him to draw. As soon as he reaches for his gun you have to quickly press the fire button which slows everything down as you try and move your reticule over the opponent and fire before he shoots you.  Its really well done and does well to convey the tension of a stand off.
You also have the ability to slow down time to shoot down enemies and also a Last Breath mechanic when your health is low where things go into slow motion and you have to dodge a fatal bullet.
As well as story mode you've got an arcade mode where you have to get as high a score as you can, and a stand off mode where you have to win a series off stand offs with only 5 lives.
Good points:
- the Wild West setting is great especially as there arent many Wild West themed FPS on PC. Its also quite cool to have the events of the game tie into real life events and people like Jesse James and Billy the Kid.
- the game starts off with Silas entering a saloon and telling the people in there his stories about his past. This is used in quite a clever way as the story you experience shifts and changes based on what the people listening to Silas are imagining. For example at one point he says "the enemies jumped out like Indians" and you find a load of Indians shooting at you. However Silas points out that they weren't Indians, they just jumped out like them and the scene rewinds and the enemies are now bandits. It does stuff like this frequently and its a refreshing way to experience a games story.
-the stand offs are probably the best part of the game and really manage to recreate the tension you'd expect in that situation
Bad Points:
- some sections can feel quite dull and similar to each other.
-there isnt much weapon or enemy variety and while its understandable given the time period the game is set in, it doesnt help prevent the game feeling repetitive at times. However dual wielding a couple of old style revolvers still feels pretty badass

A little gem I was expecting to be this enjoyable, I am by no means a good FPS player and wanted something to just jump into quickly have a short bash then back to normal life. This Wild West show bowled me over and here are a few of the reasons…
Excellent Voice-acting, nice visuals and terrain with brilliant maps (although I noticed one was a reuse, may have been more not sure). Excellent music with a real Wild West theme. The narration does well to keep the campaign play through engaging, and doesn't take itself too seriously and this deserves a special mention as it was spot on (some of the lines made me chuckle and the story telling was brill). Nice historical bits of history that are enjoyable to read through collectables. Solid, entertaining gunplay mechanics. Nice upgrade trees all fairly unique depending on play style. Frequent checkpoints, useful for someone who dies (A LOT) and is pants at FPS. Extra features such as mini game duel (which I loved!), and arcade game.
I could mention the negatives but I would just be picking this game is well worth it even more so when on sale, thumbs up from me!

Distraint is a very short horror-adventure about a man and his life choices.
I found the horror aspect to be lacking. The jump scares fell flat on their face for the most part due to poor execution and choice of graphics style. However, the game did fine with setting a creepy and unsettling atmosphere. I can think of one moment that was kind of gross.
The gameplay is very simple and doesn't require much from the player. You'll mostly be walking around and solving the occasional puzzle. Some of the puzzles can be confusing due to the mental state of the character which means that solutions might not appear logical in the normal way. You'll be doing some weird things. You might also become very stuck at certain parts like I did.
The strongest part of this game is the story which suffers slightly from subtle English errors in the form of missing words for some expressions and one idiom that is reversed. The story does have some good moments, especially towards the end of the game. One of them was touching and the other made me think, "No way."
Overall, the game seems like an okay experience and made me want to finish it despite having some difficulties with a couple puzzles. The price point is really up to the person, but if you're on a tight budget and are looking for many hours per dollar spent, this game is clearly not going to live up to that expectation.

Thisis by far one of the best MMORPGs I have ever played. If you're thinking about buying this game, keep in mind, it's nothing like Skyrim, and it's certainly not Elder Scrolls VI. It's a much more different experience than playing Skyrim, but it's still really good. The game mechanics are typical of an MMORPG, the combat system is intricate and smooth, and there are enough classses to suit anyone's playing style, whether it's a templar, healer, mage, nightblade, or anything else. The leveling system is alright, but some may find it slow; you'll probably have to look up good areas of the map online to level up your character. The story is good, but you'll find yourself doing the exact same main story as every other player in the game. This is normal for an MMORPG, it can't really be avoided, but this doesn't make it bad at all. My favourite class is the Templar class, as you can heal yourself, use magical fire-based attacks, and it goes with just about any race. Choose the class that suits your palying style, and pick a race with traits that complements your class. For example, the Imperial race is the best race for a Templar, but you'd have to pay extra money for the Imperal race. Good luck if you're joining the game, and have fun!

I also recommend you guys trying Sorcerer or Warden, both are a hell of a lot of fun to play. Sorcerer, to me, is a bit more powerful than I expected, but no complaints there. lol
My only complaints about this game is how they added level scaling to the overworld, it kinda just takes away the challenge, you know? To clarify, as Dark Souls 2 is the considered the odd child of the series, I'm only not recommending THIS version of the game since I believe the "remaster" Scholar of the First Sin version is better. Get Scholar of the First Sin instead of this.
So instead of a full review of the product I will give a more detailed idea what SoTFS does better, but first I will need to go over the CONTROVERSY.
For the uninformed, Dark Souls 2 has a rocky release history. The announcement footage of the game featured pitch black areas that required the torch, beautiful graphics with tons of pretty particle effects and shadows being cast off every lighting source. It was surprising that something like that could even run on last gen consoles.... but it was too good to be true. The release looked very little like that, the infamous LE PREPARE TO DOWNGRADE.
Many people argue that there was no reason for this downgrade. I have a unique perspective on this as I'm someone who was able to play the original infamous demo version of the game at Comic Con. The game looked pretty yes, the dark rooms added tons of tension since you didn't know what was lurking ahead of you yes, but it ran very poorly. Many people argue that the reason for the poor performance with that version was cus they ran the demo off xbox 360 Dev kits that run games worse than the actual console. Now we will never know the reason for the downgrade Officially, but I think it's clear that the downgrade happened because it ran so poorly on last gen consoles.
Now Dark Souls 2 has one area that is dark and you need a torch for, and you get to experience the tension there, but areas like in the demo that were dark were not dark anymore. Since there's this whole torch mechanic it's makes it basically useless now that it's gone. Why was it removed? Speculation, but since you need to hold a torch, people who mainly 2hand weapons would be at a disadvantage, theoretically. But being the whole point that you're gimped during these sections, and that you need to light these lighting sources to go 2Hand is a good tension in my opinion and removing it entirely and LEAVE THE WHOLE TORCH SYSTEM STILL IN THE GAME never made sense to me.
This is where Scholar of the First Sin comes in. First of all it attempts to add more graphical fidelity into the game, and while it's basically just SWeetFX injected into the game by default that game does look better and less flat. And, areas are dark again! The torch system actually has a use in SotFS since there's various dark rooms again. Thus with an Attempt to amend the "le prepare to downgrade" graphics and re-add a, imo, important mechanic, those two alone make me recommend Sotfs.
The last change is that enemies/items were rearranged. How it felt to me was that the difficulty spikes of the game got moved around, so some areas are easier but some are now harder. Nothing really soured me even though the pacing was changed, but a few areas were vastly improved. A late game level that was unnecessarily annoying was changed to be wayyy less annoying and for that I would again recommend Sotfs over the original release.
For the final kicker, DLC is not included in this one, it's a seperate purchase. Sotfs has all the DLCs already included, and actually incorporated in the game instead of just giving you a key to the area when you buy it.
Dark Souls 2 was created by the B-team of From Software while the main peeps were creating Bloodborne, but even as someone who preordered the PC copy and preordered the season pass, I never felt duped really. It's not a true Dark Souls 2, it's more of a side story, but I didn't hate the game because of it. Making Scholar of the First Sin a complete seperate purchase with seperate servers to split the community is when I felt duped as I saw no reason to do it. And it really should of been a free upgrade for all the people who owned all the DLCs already, but during one Steam sale the "upgrade" discount price for Sotfs was $5 which I bought with money I made from selling CSGO/TF2 stuff so I effectively got a free upgrade... Still the only thing to make me sour from all of this. So.. GET SOTFS OVER THIS.

Yeee-haw, y’all.  This was more fun than I reckoned it would be.
It’s a solid game.  Lots of action & Wild West nostalgia.  Plenty of shooting.  Tumbleweeds.
The story is told as a series of flashbacks from the perspective of a Bounty Hunter named Silas.  He apparently had run-ins with some of the more colorful names in history, and each ‘chapter’ of the game plays out in relation to these characters.  I played the first chapter, in which I assisted Billy The Kid when he was pinned down in Stinking Springs.  He and I barely made it out alive, but ended up in jail.

The game looks great, just like a comic book, in my opinion.  The graphics are so ornate, that sometimes it’s hard to tell where an enemy is when they’re hiding behind cover.
Most of the time, the game plays like a shooting gallery.  You crouch behind your cover, and they hide behind theirs.  You then spend the game trading shots at each other, hoping to take them out before they hit you.  It’s well done, if you like that sort of thing.

Similar to some other first person shooting games, this one includes a slow-motion ‘bullet-time’ powerup that can be used when you want to catch your breath or take out multiple targets in a hurry. ‘Concentration’ builds up over time, and can be turned on when you want to use it.  A nice feature of ‘Concentration’ is that while under the influence of Concentration, everything becomes shaded in black and white, except for your enemies, which are highlighted in red.  I found it useful for times when I just couldn’t tell exactly where my opponents were hiding.  A quick burst of Concentration, and not only could I immediately see the bad guys, but they were standing still and vulnerable.
At the end of most chapters of the game, you meet up with someone who apparently needs dueling.  You face each other down, waiting for the other to draw…  Meanwhile you’re trying to keep your ‘focus’ on the target; a targeting reticle slowly drifts around the opponent, which the player must keep on target.  Finally, in an honest duel, the player waits for the other gunslinger to draw, at which point you quickly reach for your own gun, and if your focus was still on target, and you were quick enough, you live to see another chapter.
Overtop of the gameplay is a great vocal narration track that changes depending on the gameplay.  “I finally made it to the back of the farmhouse”,  or “Finally, the stables were in sight”, or, after I accidentally shot a chicken: “I figured that after the fight, we could fry us up some chickens.”.  Very colorful and moves the plot along nicely.
There are also xp skill trees with several different paths to consider.  There’s a short and long ranged option, plus a jack-of-all-trades option to choose from.  I chose the long-range option, which gave perks like more aiming time when using long rifles.
The game features many secrets to be found and collected.  “Nuggets of Truth” items are scattered throughout the game in the form of old-West baseball-card type collectibles.  I found one that gave the bio and background of the sheriff that took down Billy the Kid.  I have no idea how much truth were in these “Nuggets”, but they were interesting to read.
What I liked:  The collectibles are a great idea.  They make you wonder how much of the storyline is based in truth, and how much is fiction.  The graphics are great, there’s a style there and they really made it work.  The voice acting is humorous and well done.  This all ties together to make a great atmosphere.  The gameplay is fun and fast paced.
What I didn’t like:  Sometimes I felt like I couldn’t tell what I was shooting at, and I felt like I had no control over the situation.  Others, it felt like the only thing stopping me from getting headshot after headshot was my own ability to move the mouse.  I didn’t like the variation.  I think the environment had a lot to do with this.  The enemies are usually wearing dark brown or black, and they hide in the shadows a lot, and blend in quite well.  This makes it hard to tell if you’re shooting at anything or not.
This one really surprised me.  I wasn’t expecting to like this one much, but it was fun.  I think I’d play this one some more.
Thanks for reading.

Have you ever played Mount&Blade before, and wanted the option to live a simpler life? To be a farmer, earning honest gold, rather than commanding armies to slaughter men, and profit from the spoils of war? Then this game is what you're looking for!
Currently, you can help building up someone's village, or explore a randomly generated world and manage your own village. Survive by gathering berries, farming crops, and hunting animals. Watch out for wolves, bears and bandits! Chop, mine, cook, craft, tame and more! Set up a shop to sell and buy things, or visit the shop of one of the NPC's.
And if you like being a leader, you can form an army anyway. Sieges, large scaled battles and politics are on the way!
A downside (just like M&B) is that the game can become repetitive. Once you know how everything works, you may switch to the rogue life, killing friendly NPC's in towns. However, there's going to be politics, families, livestock, pets, guilds and even multiplayer.
Let this happen! Support the developer and buy this game. Know how to play it so you can focus on these things once they arrive.

If you're interested in this title it's probably because you played Amnesia: The Dark Descent and were really hoping for a proper sequel, but sadly A Machine for Pigs by comparison is inferior in every way. The world doesn't have that same sense of despair, the monsters are a lot less scary even to look at, infact I want to know how some are a threat because some of them are smaller than you? The story leaves a lot to be desired and it started to lose me a little past the halfway point. The game has had many featers striped away including interaction with enviorment the like rummaging through the drawers and closets, So a sense of exploration is removed. The sanity meter was removed so you can look at the monsters and have that sense of horror removed because you can visually study the creators. The only thing this game does right is it sets a the atmosphere properly with its environments but thats about all it does. I really tried to look at this game for its own merits and not compare it to much to its predecessor, but its rather unavoidable. Even if I did A Machine for Pigs is just simply a short and basic indie survival horror game played once then abandoned. I understand this game was developed by The Chinese Room and that would explain the lack of content because The Chinese Room are known for making experiences more than games.

Cards on the table... the art style and he soundtrack were not my cup of tea. This is the most important consideration if you are considering buying this game.
I wouldn't criticise either aspect as it's totally subjective, lots of people lap it up.
So my review is based on the gameplay and the story.
The gameplay is extremely repetitive and very dull with a grand total of about 7 or 8 different enemies you will face in the entire game.
The mechanics have depth and potential (and in fairness, a big dollop of imagination and originallity) but it took me up until the game was nearly finished before it all clicked into place with the upgrades, downgrades, perks and anti-perks you can assign; it's really not very well explained. So I can see why people say they get more out of this on the 2nd play through.
The story is obviously a matter of opinion, but mine is that it was a load of pretentious twaddle, I kept hanging on waiting for a twist that never came. When the end credits rolled it dawned on me that I really had wasted an entrie afternoon with this. Instantly forgettable.
It seems to be really cool to like this game and I don't want to seem that I'm just being contrary, but I can honestly say not only did I not enjoy this, but the only thing compelling me to play to the conclusion was the overwhelmingly positive reviews that had convinced me to purchase it.
Conclusion
If you fall in love with it straight away then great, the aesthetics are clearly a huge part of the appeal here.
If you're not getting into it after 30 minutes, don't expect it to change your mind in the following hours. It doesn't change.
My God, this game is so damn good, and the finale made me cry. Love Supergiant Games.

A mess of a game,  sure it can be fun to play but its severely buggy and heavily monetized.   The "free" to play method is also severely restricted, making it so if you intend to play you need ESO+ subscription - without it you are heavily limited in bag space, bank space..yada yada.
The bugs are fairly severe and it seems the publisher don't give a crap about fixing them (what else is new?) Mobs knocking you through the world are common, or being knocked to the other side of the zone are also common,  the players have just settled on calling these types of bugs as 'features' now instead of complaining,  another common bug is mobs disappearing completely especially when too many players are around.
The auction system is also terrible, requiring you to join a trade guild if you want to sell....even the simple fact of searching for new gear isn't easy, its a terribly convoluted system and even with addons, barely helps and then, we come to the heavily monetized aspect..
Pretty much here, Beth/Zeni wants to sell you 'everything' // every major advantage you can think off has a price tag, some of the more major advantages like mobile banks/merchants clocking in at $50 each.   I forgot to add that the monetization is essentially a triple threat -  #1 Monthly full price subscription #2 Crown Store #3 Loot boxes......that sends a clear message of greed on behalf of the publishers.
The positives are few to be honest,   sure there is alot of content and ESO+ subscriptions get all the DLC for free (Consider the subscription as season pass) and a bunch of crowns each month, so you could get some of those major advantages if you sub long enough..

When starting the game you get to name yourself and the island, choose the maximum population (2.000 people!!!), how fast new people arrive, the length of the day/night cycle and how many animals per squar kilometre there are. After that you can customize your character's face, race and gender as well as pick your starting skills that will decide your future professions on the island.
After a short time loading you awake on board a ship heading for the coastline of the gigantic island in front of you. You and about 20 other people get off and go their own way. Some set up a settlement, some become bandits, some get mauled by a bear or wolf. Such is life in The Zone.
Depending on your starting skills you can be a productive part of society by providing lumber for people's houses, building structures, opening a tavern, keeping a farm, crafting items as a blacksmith or opening a shop. Or by protecting the town with your trusty sword or bow from animals or bandits. Maybe even attack other towns with people you recruit? Or start your own settlement?
Currently the game has all this to give you plenty of hours of entertainment. However... it needs work but that's to be expected as this is a tremendous undertaking for a (I think) three man team.
Some of my personal observations:
- occasional lag, could be due to the amount of activity happening. Developers, did you code in for the game to only load and render the immediate NPC's? This way you reduce a HUGE amount of lag and keep the game performing like a clock. The "off-screen" NPC's could be set in Unity to just not render until within 250m of the player?
- The User Interface (UI) could use a loving hand, it's clear and structured but it looks dated and is sometimes not nice to look at. Ditch the parchment and make everything a bit smaller. The "book" needs to be less yellow and the text should lose the drop shadows and use a rectangle background.
- Combat needs reworking, right now it feels like a placeholder and has no excitement.
This is not meant as something bad, but to help Kingdoms grow into a beautiful game!
I wish you all good luck at Oreol! :)

I never played the first Borderlands game, but all I know is this: I LOVE THIS GAEM.
4-player co-op option, an absolutely absurd amount of guns (few of which are really endgame viable, but more on that later), 4 free distinct characters (with an added 2 from DLCs), an abundance of good DLCs and enemies, dynamic skill trees that you can tailor to your own playstyle and relatively addictive Legendary farming.
Need I say more?
Borderlands 2 has great replay value. 1 (well done) main story, three difficulty levels and 4 (or 6 with DLC) characters to max out. For each difficulty you encounter, your enemies get stronger as you do, providing great challenge (and fun) as you play. Legendary drop rates increase (MOAR LOOT) as you go higher up, allowing you to wreak havoc and violence more efficiently and colourfully. Of course, if you have the DLCs, the replay value skyrockets, MORE LOOT to scrounge up and MORE STORY!!1!!1
The many different characters and personalities in this game draws you in, from Sir Hammerlock's dignified demeanour to Miss Moxxi's various husbands and endless innuendos. Even the villain, Jack, has a well-developed backstory. Even if you hate him for killing off [Bleeped to prevent spoiler], you can still
sympathize with him. The poor guy is just trying to do what's right in his eyes, anyway.
Now to the gameplay. Gunfights can get hectic, trying to stay in cover while trying to utilize your abilities to kill basically ANYTHING you see. You
die a
in the first few hours into the game, but fret not! Progression is quite smooth, provided you don't try to speedrun through the game (those who do, I salute you). Weapons are very diverse, some exploding when you throw them at your enemies and some more capable of killing
instead of the enemy.
However, the further you go along in the game, the harder it becomes, rendering some weapons useless. Although this problem is mainly when you venture into the Overpower levels, it can also be a problem in Ultimate Vault Hunter mode as well. By then you would only want the best Unique or Legendary weapons to even stand a chance against these enemies. The grind (OH THE GRIND) can get a little repetitive, but then again, it's called
for a reason.
Would I recommend this? YES! ABSOLUTELY! Get some friends to play with you if you can; it's
more fun. I'd even recommend getting most of the DLCs (Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep, mainly).
I enjoyed this game. The story, characters, zones, and loot make it fun. Grab a couple of friends and kill baddies together for even more fun.

Phenomenal game.  The creepiness was greatly upped from the first game, and it had a great atmosphere throughout.  Also, the setting changes, which makes it refreshing and a lot less repetitive than the original game.  Multiple monsters, and a very gripping story.  Better than the original, by far.

Amesia -- what a wonderful trope for a videogame.  In the original Amnesia, lacking any reference to the character I was inhabiting, I imbued him with my own values.  Surely he was a good guy in a bad situation.  Maybe a victim of what was going on, rather than an instigator.  Is was a glorious surprise to learn what a cretin my character really was.
In A Machine for Pigs, I went into it assuming I was a cretin.  And the game didn't waste much time proving me right.  It's a short, but tense ride into the depths of depravity.  I loved it.  Yes, there were points where the hall crawling got a little tedious, but the dark, intense atmoshpere and my desire to finally understand what was underlying the whole terrible affair kept me plodding forward.  The writing (letters, journal entries, voice overs) is outstanding.  It's the kind of writing that generates visceral reactions.  Spectacular.
The journal is really the only thing that removes the immersion.  A little icon appears in the lower left corner of the screen, which tells you to hit esc and read the journal, instantly bringing you back to the fact that you are merely playing a videogame.  Hopefully, the game designers can figure out a more immersive way to do this in the future.
A lot of you didn't like it -- you miss the sanity meter, the inventory and puzzles, the searching for lantern oil.  I can see why.  But I think it is a matter of preference.  To me, all that stuff got in the way of the story and the exploration aspects, which are really the main point of the game.  Are the puzzles straightforward?  They are.  That's good.  There are monsters in the game who cannot be killed.  But they were never caused overwhelming frustration... just kept things nice and tense.  That's good too.   I do miss the sanity meter, particularly the way the screen morphs when the protagonist is fightened.  So maybe bring that back next time.  Maybe.
So, for me, this was nearly perfect.  And, if you like a good immersive horror story with terrific writing, spooky environments, and a main character who is a mystery through much of the game, you'll love this one.

Where to  begin with Transistor? It is a strikingly beautiful game that goes beyond the conventional bounds of what is typically considered to be standard in the sci-fi game genre. Done in a lush style, Supergiant Games utilizes a vibrant futuristic art-deco style that is as much of a character as the protagonist. Gameplay is similar to that Supergiant's first game, Bastion, with skills naturally being acquired as you level up and allowing you to add limiters to make the game as hard or as easy as you would like. Skills can also be arranged and combined together, allowing for experimentation, as well as unlocking finer details about the world Red, the protagonist, lives in. The story is fantastic and remarkably emotional for a relatively short game. Details are not missed in Transistor, with everything from style to soundtrack being considered and working together to create a truly stunning game.

A game I was attracted to thanks to its appealing aesthetic, Transistor ended up being muc more enjoyable than I anticipated; mostly because of its unique atmosphere. The gameplay remains very basic, but you play this game mostly for its artistic side rather than the rest. The story does not lack of interest, but the way it is developped asks for a second run to completely understand since it is more intricate than it seems at first.
The level design is relatively basic, but the style is very unique and appealled to me. The cutscenes in "parallax-ed" artwork convey the mood very well provided you don't mind a comic-style narration. The visual effects in-game are really tasteful, not overwhelming, and if you take time to just look at it there are many eye candies you can find. It is refreshing to have something that stylized for an indie game that is not pixel art.
A good variety of themes that revolve around elctronical sounds and floating voices, never overwhelming so as to keep you in the game, but always matching the situation, whether it is in combat or just wandering in the city. The voice covers are mostly limited to two characters, but they are enough. Your companion regular monologues really help you not feeling alone in the otherwise empty city.
Most of the gameplay revolves around the combat system. You can trigger the "Turn" mode on to stop time and take actions that will be resolved instantly when the mode is triggered off. Each action takes a certain amount of an action gauge, depending on its power. It's easy enough to enjoy without too much practice, and offers enough complexity to try some interesting combos once you have enough abilities. The rest of the time, you stroll around a colorful city and enjoy weirdly shaped plants. This part of the gameplay is more of contemplative experience rather than a real gamin one.
The story is not easy to grasp as it is unveiled like if you already know some parts of the universe you are part of. The opposition between Red and the Camerata (no spoiler here) is obvious, but the way the city works and what role the Process has in it is foggy at best when you play the game for the first time. I recommend to run it a second time to really enjoy the intricacies of the scenario as well as the full capacity of the combat mode and all the challenges it offers.
Transistor is a great game overall. Don't expect super-production-like content, it is not its purpose. Play it for what it is, as a unique experience of few hours. If you enjoy it the first time, you'll enjoy it more the second. It has everything a good indie game needs. The only downside I found was the way the story is unveiled since I needed to run the game again to completely grasp it.

Take one Silent Hill loving game developer with no real knack for writing and no real understanding how psychological horror works. Give him quite good art and sound design skills. Don't explain to them how and why puzzles are done in story-driven games. You get Distraint. A game that desperatly tries to tell a psychological horror about guilt and EVIL CORPORATE SYSTEM that is so EVIL and INHUMANE using the most hamfisted SYMBOLISM and incredibly boring gameplay.
This is a purely story with "puzzles" horror game (which has manual saves seemingly just because either developer couldn't figure out how to make autosaves work or just because the engine they chose is pretty bad at autosaving), where you just walk back and forth small locations in 2D perspective trying to find the next trigger for the next thing to happen to procede to a next location and repeat the process ad nauseam. There little rhyme or reason to a lot of things that happen with game never really understanding that you can't mix totally unreal situatons with real situations without any thought and hope that it creates a surreal feeling instead of the mess you just don't care about.
"Puzzles" are usually "guess what silly item combination you need to do" kind with several pointless minigames, including one that isn't a puzzle but a guessing game. There are countless moments when you just don't know what game wants from you, either because you need to revisit some place for no reason and some new interaction is now available, or because you need to use an item in some illogical way (often the former). Game constantly tries to bombard you with YEAH EDGY moments for no reason, with blood, guts, drugs popping up and making you sigh and roll your eyes instead of feeling any kind of tension or surprise. It's just there. Evil people are EEEEEVIIIIL. Any attempts at some symbolism are silly at best.
It's a really really silly game that could've been fine if it was even shorter or went for a dark comedy twist. Instead, it's too long (for being around 2-3 hours game), too messy and stupid and isn't worth your time. There are better examples of 2D horror adventure/survival horror like The Last Door, Home, Lone Survivor or, hell, even also TOO EDGY and silly The Cat Lady is more worth your time than this.

A lot of people don't like this entry in the series. It's easier than 1 and 3, less inspired, the bosses are usually disappointing. I suppose that's all somewhat true, it really is. The bosses ARE mostly easy and uninspired, many taken straight from tried fantasy tropes (a woman with a scorpion for a body -- a woman with a snake for a body). On top of that, some of the earlier bosses are absolute jokes as far as difficulty is concerned. Some of the later ones too. And yes, a lot of the rooms you'll be exploring are pretty unadorned, just stark cubes with enemies in them. Uninspired environments.
So that's all true, so why am I recommending it? Well honestly, the most major way in which the game didn't disappoint was in the massive choice it gave you over the path you take through it. From the starting city there are multiple paths you can take through the game at any point, and this only grows as you continue to explore. If you're stuck on or bored with an area or a boss, you can take a break and explore someplace else. Not only that, but the different areas of the game are, in my perspective, very well differentiated. They're mostly very visually unique, each with its own feeling and challenges and secrets to figure out. They also all fit together nicely, lending a very cohesive feeling to the game.
So yes, as I said, there are disappointments, but when I think about games that have stayed interesting playthrough after playthrough, this is near the top of the list.

I my opinion this is a must own for any fan of mmo's or rpg's or mmorpg's. Now I know that all other games of the genre  have open worlds and let you do whatever you want but this is the first game I've played in a long time that made the world feel free to me. There are no restrictions to anything, be whatever race, clan, class you want. And it is so easy and simple to get the hang of any aspect of it so it will be very welcoming to anyone who doesn't normally play the genre. Best part for me though are the crafting and the gathering systems. While every other game I've played has only needed a level req and a click before leading to a long boring animation that leaves you to do nothing until the character is done, this one has a minigame for crafting that gives you a chance to fail(Which is a rare occurence unless you mean it to happen or you don't pay attention) or even make the item you are synthesising into a higher quality. If you don't want to keep playing the minigame though, there is a quick synthesis option that makes the character do the work on his own. He won't strive to fail or improve the item though it can still happen. This let's you get a drink while your character does the work for you. As for gathering, it isn't a struggle or a fight with other players. Even if you trigger the minigame in the same spot as another, you will not take anything from them nor they take anything from you. All of this makes the mind numbing exp grinding into something fun and stress free. Changing classes is as simple as changing the main hand weapon from say a lance to a sewing needle so you can go from thrusting attacks to stitching together armor just like that. There is still so much in the game I have yet to see and I plan on seeing it all. I cannot reccomend this game enough. It is such a huge improvment on other mmorpg's and it is worth your time and money.

This isn't so much a game yet, but rather a proof of concept.  I definitely recommend it for two reasons:
The game immediately sets itself apart from the rest with it's leveling system and overall feel.  Health doesn't increase, and while there isn't anything stopping you from getting all the skills, it would take months of leveling.  This particular system will be MUCH more appropriate when either the AI is improved or multiplayer is implented.  As is, the drawback is that you really can't count on NPCs to get anything done for the settlement.
This game has the potential to be absolutely incredible if even rudimentary versions of the planned features are implemented.  Again, the proof is here.  We can start our own village, kill other village leaders and claim their villages as our own.  We can become bandits and kill and loot villagers.  It all needs to be refined a little, but that's the whole point of early access.
Bottome line: don't pay the $10 hoping for gold.  Pay the $10 for a few hours of good fun and to support this game.

I don't really write reviews, but I'll be damned if I don't write one for this masterpiece. It may be short, but it sure is sweet. With the perfect balance of Borderlands-esque humor and art style, mixed with the sheer beauty of the west, it's one of the most enjoyable games that I have ever played. The combat is tight and frantic, with extremely satisfying gunshots and explosions.
You'll meet a ensemble of many legends of the Wild West on your journey, and you'll kill most of them. Though Silas' story may be a bit exaggerated, you will discover "nuggets of truth" along the way. These nuggets are little snippets of the true history of the West and it's outlaws.
While a part of me wishes that it was much longer, I think the shortness of the game is actually one of it's strengths. It doesn't outstay its welcome - it doesn't lose its focus, its charm, along the way. From start to finish, Gunslinger is satisfying and fun, with great combat, hilarious dialogue, and a truly epic tale... the tale of Silas Greaves.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a Wild West first-person shooter with cool and interesting mechanics, such as the legendary bullet time and you may enter a "last breath" type of scenario (if you've filled certain requirements), where you can dodge the bullet that would've killed you and if you dodge the bullet, you've cheated death and you may continue.
This game also features a skill tree feature, when you rack up enough points, you get to invest those points into skills, you've got three skill trees to invest the points on, so make sure to choose wisely.
The gun play feels very satisfying, but it might get repetitive.
This game has three game modes to play, Story Mode, Arcade and my personal favorite, Dueling.
Story mode is pretty straight forward, it's an interesting story that tells about an outlaw, called Silas Greaves, who tells his story from his own perspective. Along the story, you might stumble upon a few comical jokes here and there. The story is solid, and has an interesting ending. Although the story mode isn't that long, but the game offers re-playability to unlock all of the skills you didn't unlock in the first playthrough with New Game+ and with the hardest difficulty, if you've got the guts.
Arcade mode, you just rack up points and build your combo as large as possible until the level ends.
Dueling mode is an amazing game mode which is a showdown. In order to defeat your opponent, you must keep your hand close to your weapon and keep your focus on your opponent and draw your gun after he's drawn his, if you're playing hororably, that is.
I recommend this to everyone who likes western styled games, it's a wonderful game!

- The 3rd person perspective; It has a different perspective than traditional MOBAs which I quite enjoy.

I personally do enjoy the game, especially with friends.

DISTRAINT:
~~~~~~~~~
McDade, Bruton and Moore is a company that repossesses homes. Your name is Mr. Price and your first job is to tell an elderly lady she is going to have her house repossessed. How do you feel about it, Mr. Price? Any guilt, Mr. Price? Are you ready for more, Mr. Price? Because you have to make the hard decision, Mr. Price!
Distraint is an adventure / psychological horror game where you play Mr. Price, a repo man. This is truly an interesting game to say the least, as your character is going to do his duty all the while experiencing these sombre feelings called guilt and sadness for doing so. I really like the way these feelings are shown through the dark and dusty artworks. As you progress through the game, you will find objects in each location, helping you to advance through the story.
Realistically, these items are part of simple puzzles. Mr. Price goes through dark corridors armed with a lantern; he will discover properties step by step, which gives you the sensation of what is going to come next. Great stuff.

The atmosphere is sorrowful and suits Distraint perfectly. Visually, the game looks good and I really like the character’s animation. For me, Distraint has been well thought-out and everything you see and feel fits very well.
The controls are really easy to use as you will really need to use W,A, S, D for movements, E to use an item and SPC for your inventory.

Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Great Artwork
-	Great atmosphere
-	Good Story
-	Achievement & trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~

-	Game is short
In Distraint, you will experience all sort of emotions and feelings. A very well executed game that deserves to be in your game library!
8.5/10
Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

Dark, both literally and story-wise, but worth the price of admission. Distraint is one of those games that's worth playing once, maybe twice for achievement hunting (much like The Park). The art style is interesting, and brings with it a feel that another style wouldn't have. Some puzzles can be frustrating if you don't happen to go just the right way under just the right circumstances or click just the right thing that often feels arbitrary once you finally discover it, but there are Let's Plays on Youtube if you're really stuck and looking for a hint. The story is the real heart of this game.
Not recommended for people who trigger easily, but then you're probably not looking for a horror game if that's the case.

After playing (at this point) 117 hours of the game, most of it, without any mods, I can say without a doubt that I love this game. The vanilla game is fun but it gets way too easy pretty quick when you play as Rome, you become a juggernaut and once you take the Nile, your food rationing days are over and all will bend to your will.
Mods like, Divide et impera (DEI), GREATLY improve on the core concept of this game. It takes a few days and failed campaigns to get used to the new mechanics but the reward for sticking with DEI is immense. There are many more viable options for your generals, admirals (yes, even admirals are viable now), armies and towns. Want a general to stay at a rebellious province with a garrison army, not the towns army, a real army stack that specialises in fighting on its own territory? Well now you can.
TL;DR.
Recommend this game to any TW fan, but get yourself the DEI mod.

Darkly atmospheric and beautifully rendered, I thoroughly enjoyed this one, dare I say, more than the first. It abandons the point and click Hidden Object Game mechanics in favor of exploration while masterfully building tension. That's right, it's not a HOG like it's predecessor, which was innovative for it's time and we can still see it's legacy in a brillant masterpiece like Outlast. This one is much more polished and focuses on a cinematic audio that will have you taking off your headphones and turning on the lights to make sure that was from the game and not from the burning carbuncle eyes snorting in the darkness at your window. Often hiding the horrors, it knows that what you can't see will bend your mind on all fours to imagine far worse than any engine can grind up and reanimate. The porcine genius of it all is the sqealing progression of a story line that will raise the bristles down your spine as it roots around, huffing and snuffling, in the fetid mire of your psyche.

This game.
oh my god this game.
Don't think of it as a sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent (which is also amazing), but rather a new experience in the same universe.
TDD was an absolutely frightening affair which was at times hard to play if you scare at all easily, but this is a whole other beast. Its monsters aren't as instantly unsettling, it's chases aren't the same speed, frequency or volume, and if you don't pay attention it could easily be just a few hours in a kind of spooky building.
But this game is utterly terrifying.
If you really pay attention, listen to the words, read the letters, hell, do some research, get on the message boards, there is a lot going on here. The Chinese Room is not only proving to be a very able development house, but one of the smartest videogame developers out there.
There's a lot of Lovecraftian games out there, but this is the only one that scares me as deeply as anything Lovecraft actually wrote.
It's poignant, beautiful, seductive, manipulative, fever-inducing madness.
If you just want a good scare, it's not bad at all. If you want to experience a story, it's absolutely brilliant.

There are a few restraining facts that should be known about Distraint before making a decision to invest time or money into the experience. First and foremost it’s a small game in every respect. It’s made by a one man team in a very short time and that show in everything from the length of the story and the assets used to the somewhat unpolished UI.
Mr. Makkonen is also Finnish and while obviously being quite fluid in his English there are some weird sentences and grammar not spotted in the proof reading. Sometimes it also feels like nuances in the dialogue has been lost in the translation.
With those reservations aside however I very much enjoyed the few hours it took to complete. The narrative feels fresh and the characters, while not overly complex, feels human enough to care for.
The story itself is about a man whose life choices doesn’t add up to his own moral compass, and the internal consequences of a life lived not true to oneself. The graphical horror could be said to represent his deteriorating self image, and the ending while quite obvious felt like a natural conclusion to the story.
Highly recommended for fans of Makkonens unique style and fans of psychological horror looking for something very different.

So first time writing a review bout games on steam, but since I liked this one i suppose it's about time.
I'll start with the cons to FFXIV, but please read on cause i do recommend this game to others.
- The fact that the game is a p2p game. Even though the Sub has 2 options, for those who can afford to buy the game but can't continue the Sub each month it's a big downer
- A strange latency issue which i was told it's cause of where their servers are.
- No F2P model at all. If i could make one suggestion to the devs for this game it would be to design an F2P model with a Sub option since that's the way a lot of modern day games are going.
Now for the pros and i won't list them all or this would be a 4 page essay.
- Gameplay is easy, but exciting at the same time with having to watch and learn the mechanics of monsters and bosses to dodge frontal and AoE attacks.
- The ability to have 1 character be all classes and gear each one the way you want to gear it.
- The crafting system and gathering system is very interactive.
- Dungoens/Raids have never been this interesting and mind blowing before. It's not just watch for the red carpet mechanics. You got to watch what the bosses do, what they spawn and even how things are placed and killed.
- Funny, emotional and down right heart touching quests. The main story will grab you and never let you go, but even the side quests have that effect.
- The guild system and community group system is ground breaking. I love the fact that there is your guild system with quite a few costumize options and a housing system for the guild including player housing (recently added), but ontop of that you have linkshells where whole bunch of people from different guilds or even guildless can form a group to chat with and share things with each other.
- Everything you loved bout FFXI is still in FFXIV (classes are being added slowly as well) Even though a few of the classes are different from FFXI, there is a lot of the game style and even some class mechanics that was brought over from FFXI.
So even though it has a sub, if you can afford it then i would suggest playing this game over a lot of p2p games out there.

I once saw a Let's Play of this game and immediatly fell in love with it. 'Papers, Please' is like nothing you have ever seen before, you play as an Immigration Inspector deciding the faith of the people in the communistic country of Arstotzka.
You have to carefully check passports, work permits, vaccination papers and so much more and carefully decide who you will  accept and who you will decline and do not take your decisions lightly either! everything you do will impact your game.
Besides immigrants you have have to help your family survive the cold winter in lonely Arstotzka and deal with tons of unforseen events such as terrorist attacks, rebellions and serial killers, make sure you make the right decision because it could be your last!
What might turn you on?
- Multiple possible endings, strive for the best one!
- Incredible atmosphere, the music and colours of the game truly set the right mood.
- Wonderful characters, you just WANT to help some of these people, you will care for them, you will betray them.

What might turn you off?
- Heavily text based game, it involves a LOT of reading.
- Hard, even though the premise might be simple,
this game is really hard and most of  your family won't live through your first play through.
In the end, would I recommend this game? Well if you prefer heavy action based games, super intense RPG games or multiplayer madness shooters then no. Do you love the indie type game, those games that are just so weird you love them for being unique and giving you that playstyle no other game could ever give you? Then hell yeah!

I'm a very cost-conscious gamer.  I find that the Tamriel Online + Morrowwind combo pack to be not a very good value.  After about 5 months of playing this game off and on, I've decided that the heavily quest-oriented aspects of this game make it feel like a quest-on-on-rails type experience.  Really, every area has a single main quest line.  Pretty much once you've done that, there's absolutely nothing else to do in that zone.
After level 20, the progression seems to slow way down.  Maybe I'm not in the right area, or doing the right quests, but with the dynamic scaling, it's difficult to judge from the content where you should be.
The story and writing are pretty good; better than competing MMORPGs.  The graphics are adequate, maybe a bit overdone for my tastes.  Even the combat is reasonable. or at least I can adapt to it.  But I've basically stopped playing this game.  It just isn't fun and there's little variety in things to do.  The story lines in the individual areas make me think that I'm playing a soap opera -- every zone's story seems overly dramatic and over done.
The price I paid (Spring 2017) was $60.  I got a lot of content, it just all feels the same.  There was too much DLC that wasn't included in the TO+M package, and a player really needs to pay the monthly subscription to achieve anything.  For that reason, I don't feel that I got value for my money.  That prevents me from recommending this game.
If your money means anything to you, this isn't your game.  If you choose to play this game, be prepared to buy almost every DLC and pay for the monthly subscription.

Hello everyone! I am writing this review to help those of you on the fence either pull the trigger and buy it or not, so here we go!
So, let's start with some of the good stuff:
Kingdoms has a lot going for it. Yes, it's in Alpha and very incomplete, but what is there is very fun. Surprisingly addicting, actually. Simply put, you start by exiting off a ship bringing you and a group of settlers to an island that is inhabited by no one. Little by little, settlers will go off on their own and found their own villages and towns, and you can too if you chose the neccessary perks at the beginning of the game to be able to do so.
You can build houses of various designs and sizes (again, all of your options rely on having or not having the relevant perks to unlock them. This goes for everything buildable and even DOABLE in the game), build smithy's, taverns, shops, common houses, stoneworker's houses, woodworker's houses, farms, gardens to grow crops and even a windmill to mill wheat down into flower, a bakery, which you can use to bake the flower into bread, and more. You can do what you want. Interestingly, the AI isn't half bad, with NPC's doing work and building their own houses or they can hire you via a job board to finish it for them. There is a little economy in each town and you can totally be part of it.
I built and run a shop in my town, and I go exploring and find different foods, healing plants, cut some wood, mine some stone and iron, grow fresh produce, etc. and then put it all in the "storage" in my shop which puts it out for sale. NPC's will actually come to shop at various times and make purchases. When something is bought, yes, it actually disappears from the store inventory and you will have gold waiting for you in its place. You don't have to stand and wait in your shop for people to buy things, either. The honor system works: They take it, they pay for it. You can also visit other people's shops and spend some gold to put that money back into your village's economy.
Put some villagers on guard duty, or add them to your ranks of soldiers in your army (soon, an update will allow politics and wars between different villages!). There are animals to hunt, wild horses that you can tame by placing a saddle on them, mining, woodcutting, archery, swordsmanship, and various other skills to increase as you level up and get points. As hard to explain as it is, the grind is strangely addicting and satisfying. Plus, when new boats bring more settlers and they come to live in your town, more houses start sprouting up and you get to watch your city grow! You can even become a bandit through gaining certain skills, or "perks", and can build bandit related buildings.
Now, some bad:
Of course, there isn't a whole lot to do other than what I said above. You can find "ruins" thoughout the world that are little more than a couple structural bricks next to a cave entrance. The caves are very linear and short with no enemies that I've seen in them yet. There is iron in here and nothing else, unless by random chance you get a cave with a chest at the end. The game is unfinished, so it isn't optimized very well and will have frame slowing as your town grows, even with a decent machine running the game. Graphics aren't great, but that's to be expected. There is no depth to mining; you can't mine underground or for that matter, anything other than designated clusters of stone on the surface and designated iron ore clusters in the ruin caves.
Unfortunately, the building system is very thin. You can't custom build anything the way you want, it's all "prefabs." You can also tame horses but there is no option for building stables or a barn and there are no livestock. Another issue is that the "tutorial," which you'll only find by clicking aimlessly through tabs and finding the entry to read, is not a tutorial at all. It explains practically no real mechanics of the game, many of which I am still confused about after quite a few hours under my belt. The interfaces for the most part are poorly set up, confusing and difficult to read, with no explanations about their functions. On your job board, which you can use to manage and tax your town, there are small icons next to the name of each settler. If you click them, they change from red to green, but there is NO explanation about what it does, so I have no clue and that's frustrating because it seems important. Lastly, which is probably not a big deal to many but is to me is the grammar of in game messages. Any text in the game has tons of grammatical errors, such as leaving out several entire words and sometimes leaves out so many words and is written so poorly, I literally can't understand what the game is actually trying to tell me. It drives me crazy and makes the game feel that much more...cheap or amateur.
Either way though, this game has a lot going for it and I can't wait to see how it develops. What it DOES have is fun and somehow manages to keep me playing even though I don't really like "grindy" games, which, given the lack of things to do outside of building, farming and mining resources, this game very much is right now. They aren't asking much for it, so I would pick it up and give them some support to get it to an even better state sooner!

FFXIV can be a little slow on the uptake, but once you get rolling you get hooked.
The greatest part about the game is that only one character is needed, and can freely switch between jobs (after they are unlocked). Each job must be leveled separately, but there are plenty of quests, overworld events, and dungeon/pvp queues to help you level each one. Daily and weekly quests and awards also speed the process along. Every job plays somewhat the same for the first few levels, and then they become much different, and there are enough that finding one or several you enjoy is easy.
Some generic MMO concepts are still present: pick a faction to gain reputation with, fetch quests, kill x of monster y quests, etc. Some pay required for certain things, but it's not needed to succeed in game, mostly just cosmetic or mount/pet related items.
The one thing I dislike about the end game content is the lack of new dungeons/raids. As you level, you gain access to new dungeons and several are only available to max level players, yes. However, much of the gear progression for end game involves redoing previous dungeons and summon fights, only on a harder difficulty, twice! The fights do change and more know how is needed to complete them, yes, but the idea of having to redo them over and over and over just becomes tedious. But what is end game content of any MMO other than repeating content until you get the gear you need?

I believe this game is one of the best games I've played. Looking around the mistakes and issues that they had at the beginning states, the game by itself is incredibly fun. People fail to see that this is only approximately 1/3rd of the game, and the "lategame" they mention is no where near late game. Due to the lack of staff in IMC they are not able to roll out the updates as quickly as players want. Coming soon there will be a level cap update, with rank 8. Players will soon be able to start to 'define' their characters, the early game may not play a big part into late game as people may intend. However, the class creation system is one of the best ever, imo. I just think that you have to plan, and anticipate changes in the future, all in all you should create a character for yourself, not for the meta. You may get bored of a meta build in the future. I think it is a learning process. I've made many of characters, reaching approximately 230-280 in level range, just to restart and do it again because I wanted to change a little detail. Each and everytime I restart I notice something I missed - considering I like to 100% every map, and do every quest it's really fun for me to find something new about the game.
I do reccomend this game to people who are willing to commit, grind, and be determined to reach the late game. However, this game isn't for everyone, which saddens me.

Excellent short arcade FPS western. Great voice acting and characters to love. They bring in many true cowboys from history and weave them into a fun and action packed fictional story. The game can be beaten in around 7 hours but the whole time it's fun.
The story is told while you play as Silas Greaves, the main character, narrates his run ins with the various cowboys looking for the men who murdered his brothers. He tells the stories to a group of patrons in a bar who doubt his accuracy of his story telling on occasion. There are laughs to be had a twist to be discovered.
There are collectibles that are cards telling you real history of the wild west. Great things to find and read if you love the wild west. You will also earn xp in the game to level up Silas to make you and even better gunfighter. After beating the game it unlocks a new game + and true west modes. This adds some good replayability to the game if you are one who likes to try and achieve the highest score you can for each level.
Also when you find one of the main cowboys you can be thrown into a duel. You control your hand over your gun to try and build speed up for a quicker draw and also a reticle over the enemy to build your focus for better accuracy. The goal is to draw faster than them and win the duel. Once you hit about 75% accuracy though you can draw first and shoot them but you could get a dishonarble kill which doesn't get you bonus xp.
It's a great game to play and not be passed up. I definitely recommend this awesome game.

It's been sitting in my library for ages now. Dead, untouched.
Message 1
"hey bro wanna play factorio? I just got these sick♥♥♥♥♥drones and thought you could help me set the area up!"
My mouse stutters as I move it towards the program.
I enter the abyss.
It's been hours, i'm not sure what the factory even does anymore. I have forgotten the common goal, the new one to only expand.
Expand...
Expand...
Expand...
The factory grows larger to overrun the area that is the "planet". But it isn't a planet, its a dead wasteland with many, many acres of metal. The factory seems to be an organism, growing on its own, at the command of the owner. It is a maze of conveyer belts and pipes. Steam fills the air, the wiring of all the electric cables twisted like a ball of yarn. Trains run up and down the spine of the organism we have created. It seems to only thirst for the growth of its own being. It has consumed me, my only focus is expanding the glorious monster.
Then they arrived.
Their presence was a chilling sight, their intentions were even worse.
We destroyed their home, their native land, and their resources had been dried out by us.
Their only goal was to take back what we had taken from them.
So I took wo building walls, turrets, and defense mechanisms. They were of great value to the cause, but required much extension and resources. But this was okay, for with some travel resources were infinite.
It's been 3 days. The rocket is ready.
Beneath the depths of the earth lies a maze of infinite tubing and pipelines. Above is a mess of wires furnaces, arms, and conveyer belts. Acres and acres of storage tanks and buildings outline what was once a small area of land to be pillaged and industrialized. Miles and miles of track lay before us, and what has been done is done. It is time to go.
Liftoff is succesful, below you can see everything as you are now miles above the land. The factory is so massive it takes much of an altitude to see as much as a quarter of the cement and aluminum labyrinth.
It is done... The game is over.
Peace has been acheived within, and I can finally rest.
10/10

Dᴀʏ 1
I've just spawned in, I have this furnace and a burner mining drill, and a stuffed pony I've had for my entire life. I place the drill down and start mining, and eventually create an electrical system to do it without fuel.
Dᴀʏ 2
I've started researching new technologies to enhance my automation. I start building turrets, walls, and automated assembly machines for automation. Eventually, I automate all of these.
Dᴀʏ 3
Aliens have attacked, and all of my assemblers have been destroyed. My mind is itching from having to handcraft the assemblers instead of having them be automated.
Dᴀʏ 12
My base is now approximately two miles wide and a three quarters of a mile tall. I've got railroad systems bringing oil back and forth to the central processing system. Three friends join me and we hop inside tanks and kill the aliens and take their artifacts to use.
Dᴀʏ 27
Finally researched rockets, and my team is about to launch one tomorrow. We're all so hyped for it, that we create a circuit network firework show out of lamps that activate once the rocket launches.
Dᴀʏ 28
We launched the rocket, and it went perfectly! We've sent a satellite to space and we've got information on everything on this planet. But we're not done yet
Dᴀʏ 54
We don't have enough resources to satisfy our factories anymore, we can barely produce 500 electronic circuits a second.
Dᴀʏ 57
My friends have quit, I was fired from my job and my girlfriend dumped me, my life is in ruin. But I must continue. I must get more resources!
Dᴀʏ 59
Furnaces are no longer running, my steam engines have stopped, my solar panels cannot receive any more light due to the amount of pollution in the air. But, there is one way I can get my factory back. I must fuel my boilers. Desperate to continue my legacy, I walk over to the boilers. I check my inventory for anything I can fuel it with, and I find something. After a couple deep breaths contemplating on if this will solve my power issues, I pick up the stuffed pony, and I put it inside the boiler.

text:
TLDR; Basegame lacks depth, good mods amply compensate for this.
Basegame:
The game as it is has been fixed from most of its starting bugs, and still looks quite good. The map is nice, the historical period is amazing, and the battle system is very nice. However, the game is shalow. It is quite easy to play, and as you grow bigger it gets even easier. The building system is very easy to learn, and you can easily outsmart the AI in battle. Upping the difficulty to make the AI get a ton of legions, be super aggresive and have buffed unit stats is possible, but I recommend another option.
Mods:
There are a ton of mods for this game, produced by a still very active modding community. I would highly recommend playing this game with one of the two major overhaul mods: Divide et Impera, or Radious. Both add depth to the game, but my preference goes to DeI, which I'm currently playing with. Everything is overhauled in this mod, new historical units, the AI is better, there is a supply system and a population system. For me DeI adds the depth that I missed in the basegame, and since its enterily free I highly recommend you to use it.
There are also graphical mods that make the game look nicer (I recommend GEM and Aztec lighting), and a ton of smaller mods, with which you can customize the game entirely to your taste. I would say that a fully customized Rome 2 can be a very good game, and since its entirely free, I do recommend getting the game.
DLC's:
The DLC's are generally not worth the money, except when they are on sale (I bought mine 75% off), and you specifically want to play some faction. The DLC's are not needed to have a good experience with this game, and I would only buy them if you have played quite a lot of hours, and want to try out some new factions or campaign maps.

FFXIV can be a little slow on the uptake, but once you get rolling you get hooked.
The greatest part about the game is that only one character is needed, and can freely switch between jobs (after they are unlocked). Each job must be leveled separately, but there are plenty of quests, overworld events, and dungeon/pvp queues to help you level each one. Daily and weekly quests and awards also speed the process along. Every job plays somewhat the same for the first few levels, and then they become much different, and there are enough that finding one or several you enjoy is easy.
Some generic MMO concepts are still present: pick a faction to gain reputation with, fetch quests, kill x of monster y quests, etc. Some pay required for certain things, but it's not needed to succeed in game, mostly just cosmetic or mount/pet related items.
The one thing I dislike about the end game content is the lack of new dungeons/raids. As you level, you gain access to new dungeons and several are only available to max level players, yes. However, much of the gear progression for end game involves redoing previous dungeons and summon fights, only on a harder difficulty, twice! The fights do change and more know how is needed to complete them, yes, but the idea of having to redo them over and over and over just becomes tedious. But what is end game content of any MMO other than repeating content until you get the gear you need?
As a long time fan of the FF series, nostalgia hits hard when fighting/riding/playing with all the different monsters and creatures from the universe. The fat chocobo mount still makes me smile to this day.
Didn't play the game as much as I'd like, but if I ever have the time again, I'll gladly go back.
