Papers. Please is an indie game that puts you right into the seat of a border crossing with the power to approve or deny entry into your country. The country you work for is seemingly a dictatorship/communist country where the government has absoulute control of the population and you are assigned your job. The game starts out simple and you get different goals every level on who to let in or deny entry to from your government. It seems like a simple job to look at a passport and approve or deny it, but as the game progresses and based on how good or bad you do things change. I would really advise this game to either TES fans or to people who like MMO but try to find something a bit different to play.

To be fair, I've played Call of Juarez twice in easy mode. The game has many qualities, even if some aspect of the gameplay are sometimes confusing or frustrating.
First, it's a story-driven game ("aka constrained"). It's like a journey into the legends of the Wild West along with bounty hunter Silas Greaves. The recreation of the old west is pleasant and inventive. If you pay attention to the story, the game ending might not be a complete surprise, though.
The most pleasant part of the gameplay is (in my opinion), to shoot with two revolvers in your hand. You can still aim and there is no strange "left click for left gun / right click for right gun" scheme. Just click and deliver.
Two other mechanics are also interesting : Focus (time slows down and enemies are highlighted) and Cheat Death (time slows down and you can either lean left or right to dodge bullets). You feel like the real deal.
On the other hand, the game suffers from the fact that sometimes you just can't see who's shooting at you unless you expose yourself to receive a bullet and track down the shooter (the same problem that plagues ROTT Redux).
A last note about the Duel section. The game mechanics completely changes here, you have to position your hand to gain speed, and place a moving target on your opponent to gain accuracy. Once you feel you you have enough of both, you can either shoot before your opponent (not honorable) or shoot after he has drawn and dodge a bullet (honorable). Even if the mechanic is inventive, you really cannot capitalize on it since a duel is kind of draining (especially if you loose) and can drive you out of the game.
But it's a good game anyway :) At least one I enjoyed from the CoJ serie !

You control Price, a man that has just started working as a repo man for the McDade, Bruton & Moore firm: you are their face when people need to be convinced of letting go of their property, you're the one doing the dirty part of the job and Distraint asks you how much of your humanity you're willing to let go to be successful.
You'll be playing through three different distraints plus a few more sections, exploring rooms, gathering objects and using them to solve simple puzzles: Distraint's gameplay might be pretty straightforward but is backed up by a very good story and great atmosphere.
-the 2d pixel graphics are simple but feature a great style made up mostly through the smart use of black and white with a few contrasting colours in between
-really nice sound design and great soundtrack
-the art, sound and music all contribute to a greatly eerie and disturbing atmosphere where reality is interrupted by gruesome visions
-a quite good story and narrative dealing with morality and the consequences of one's decisions
-the puzzles are, for the most part, very easy and straightforward, so don't expect much of a challenge
-the bobblehead-like faces might not be everyone's cup of tea and they're a bit lacking in expressiveness
-the layout and timed puzzles of the third restraint can easily get confusing and leave you a bit stumped
-quite short, expect around 1,5/2 hours

I really, really enjoyed my time with Distraint even though its gameplay might be basic, most of the puzzles were a breeze and its linearity means there's little replay value unless you're achievement hunting. But the game's story and narrative are really good and can easily keep you engaged as you go through different distraints and see how Price reacts to what he has to do. The visions that sometimes break up reality not only serve as a great way to express Price's feelings but are also appropriately creepy, gruesome and serve as an important part of the plot.
When you consider that Distraint was an one-man project completed in just a few months I can only congratulate the dev on the result: Distraint is an effective and engaging psychological horror and an easy recommendation.

This is one of the games where I really would need a neutral review option, since Transistor has a lot going for it, but ultimately it ended up disappointing, therefore it will be a thumbs down from me on this one.
I loved Bastion, the previous game by developer Supergiant Games, so Transistor was an easy purchase, both games share a lot of similarities in art style, storytelling technique and atmospheric world building. However there is one major difference, while Bastion at its core was a very good action RPG that got elevated into something greater by is innovative narration and fantastic audio-visual presentation. The core gameplay of Transistor on the other hand is a weird turned-base tactical combat with a single character and modular skills. All the elevating elements are present around it, if you strip them away, what would be left is underwhelming, the combat is not as deep as it aspires to be, the difficulty is set too low (at least on the initial playthrough) and since the story is strictly linear, there is not much motivation for making use of the New Game Plus option. To be fair, towards the end the gameplay deepens a bit once your heroine levels up and acquires more skills, but it is too little too late, by then the story is almost over and I really can’t appreciate the design decision to make the character builds and fights more fun in additional sessions only. It is frustratingly hard to actually time the correct start of a turn and in between you run around like a headless chicken due to very un-precise mouse movement, the way you lose skills when your life-bar is depleted encourages experimentation, but gets annoying fast, since you basically spend too much time in the clunky menus re-assigning four functions after every second battle or so.
It comes down to this, I did not enjoy the fights at all. The game is short enough to make me push through, the story is interesting enough to serve as motivation and there is much to appreciate along the way, from the gorgeous world design over the phenomenal driving soundtrack and the quality of the writing behind the transistors voice. But it all goes only so far if the core gameplay is completely no fun for the majority of the playtime and there is not much to do besides walk from fight to fight and read some environmental clues.
I am still interested in what the talented people at Supergiant Games come up with next, but whatever it is, I hope they do not forget the most important principle of what makes a game a good game: gameplay first. I need to enjoy the interactive sections as much as the narrated ones, if there is a mismatch as evidently the case with Transistor the overall judgement has to be a negative one.
Pros:
- fantastic music/voice work
- immersive environment design
Cons:
- shallow repetitive combat
- annoying heath system
- linear and short
- gameplay deepens only in NG+

Well, I'll get this out of the way:  No, it's not as good as "Bastion".  Is it a good game?  Yes.  It can be a bit obtuse and difficult to figure out (both story and gameplay-wise), but it's fun.  It also doesn't overstay its welcome at about 4-6 hours.

Combat: A+, unique and creative, giving you a set 16 fucntions you can form together TO MAKE VOLTR- I mean to use in different and interesting ways.
Visual: Supergiant Games never skim on two things, one of which is visuals. Some of the combat visuals can get a little overwhelming when executing commands, but the ambient occlution makes them game look and feel as if Cloudbank has some form of actual physicallity.
Music: The other unskimpable thing is music, and yeah no when I have to buy the soundtrack immediately after finishing this game the first time and hum a majority of the songs without even noticing, you know ♥♥♥♥♥ good.
But yeah, Transistor’s the kind of game that made me immediately jump back in to take on NG+. Exploring the combat in more challenging scenarios. Doubling back on the areas that I’d missed the first time through, and try to fill in the gaps of the story. But most of all, THE MUSIC UUGH.

This is a beautiful game with an excellent soundtrack. If you were a fan of Bastion, you will probably also enjoy this game.
Transistor has an interesting combat system, in which you can plan a sequence of attacks ('functions'). Functions can be used to upgrade other functions or provide passive effects, so there are various ways that you can mix-and-match to suit your playstyle. You can attack without using the planning mode (there is a cooldown period between uses) but it doesn't seem like you are intended to play this way.
I very much enjoyed the storyline (as well as the exposition of the narrator, voiced by Logan Cunningham) and I think the techno-noir art style is absolutely gorgeous.
My only disappointment was that the game is rather short; there exists a New Game+ mode which carries over your unlocked functions, and a few optional challenges ('Tests'), but otherwise not much else in terms of replay value.

Is this better/worse than the original Dark Souls? I don't know yet; I'm planning to play every Souls game eventually when I get the time.
What I do know is that regardless of its comparisons between other Souls games, this game is still excellent, maintaining the wonderful core mechanics of the Souls games, having excellent New Game+ incentives, and just being excellently fun.
However, there are obviously flaws that even I can point out:
-VERY bad at giving the player direction. Often you'll have to find your next objective through guesswork or looking guides up on the internet.
-Obviously, hard. There are a few moments that can feel unfair, but often you can beat these bits by taking a different approach or in some cases doing a completely different, equally important objective, then come back once you've become more powerful.
-Multiplayer isn't what I'd consider "Dead", but it's nowhere near as lively as it was at launch, and Scholar of the First Sin doesn't help. SotFS revamped the entire game's enemy/item placement, but the original game and SotFS are incompatible in their multiplayer, completely splitting the community. Thankfully there's quite a few AI phantoms you can summon, and their colossal tankiness makes them excellent distractions while you heal up or whale on the bosses. Oh yeah, and don't worry; You can "be wary of message" all you want! message ahead therefore praise the sun!
-Bad lore and worldbuilding especially compared to what I've seen from the other Souls games. Even if the lore/worldbuilding was good, Souls games don't exactly fit into traditional storytelling, instead choosing to be as obscure as possible with the story, telling the backstory of the world through item descriptions and insinuations by the rare character you meet along the way. IMO this is a very entertaining and unique approach, but definitely not for everyone.
-Plenty of features that "Ruin" the PvP and so on in people's eyes. Don't get me wrong, PvP is always fun, it's just that actually encountering a player is a rarity outside of hotspots like Threshold Bridge. This goes WAY further than the problems I've mentioned earlier about multiplayer being partially dead. The features also ruin co-op; you can't help or hurt other players if the amount of souls you've collected isn't comparable to the amount they've collected, for example; this means you can't go back to early bosses like the Pursuer and help early players out with those if you've already beaten the game. Multiplayer features are great, but sadly due to these problems actually finding someone to invade/co-operate with is a rarity. Only on about 10% of bosses did I even see any summon signs for other players.
-Artificial difficulty. There aren't that many examples of this, and most examples are either manageable or completely optional, but I can't lie; I've never beaten Ancient Dragon purely because I find the fact all of his attacks will oneshot 90% of character builds utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥te. It's nowhere near as rampant as some salty hipsters may try to tell you Dark Souls is all about, but when you find it it is annoying, and the temptation to just cheese it with your crossbow will slowly grow more and more tempting.
-Some really easy bosses. Not an issue in the DLC, though, and some bosses in the main game did give me a challenge. There's none at the Pinwheel level of pathetic, but several bosses like Dragonrider, Royal Rat Vanguard and especially Prowling Magus/Congregation are pretty easy kills. For some, obviously, this may be a good thing; For players who want a bigger challenge, they can always join the Covenant of Champions or get the DLC which, in the tradition of Souls games, is always host to the most challenging fights in the game.
In summary, Dark Souls II may or may not be as good as it's predeccessor, (Primarily in terms of worldbuilding and plot) but that's no reason to dismiss it as a bad game. Play it if it seems like your thing!

It's a shadow of the first game.  The story is predictable for fans of thriller, mystery or horror stories.  The sense of immediate danger is strangled by bouts of hand holding with an AI that turned out completely gimped against the trailer showcase.  I wanted to like it.

MFP did a good job with their storyline, but the game overall wasn't as scary as the first amnesia. I still had fun playing through it.

Although not as good as the original, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs certainly does not disappoint.
Honestly, I'm not sure why this game has so many bad reviews.  People were complaining about pointless activities the game has you accomplish, however I did not see any of those here.  The monsters are plentiful, however the game provides a nice equivalent between hiding from monsters and enjoying the atmosphere.  Some said the game was short, however I think if the game was any longer, it would simply be a drag.  In fact, half way into the game I thought I stumbled upon the ending, only to soon learn it was just the middle.
The story is. . . interesting.  Not a bad one, but non-sensical.  The world in Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is truly evil, possibly more-so than The Dark Descent.
All in all, I would say pick this one up.  Though, for the $20 price tag, I would suggest waiting until a sale.

Finally tried this, and was let down. From the start there is no feeling of immersion, fear, nevermind horror. Runs very poorly on my computer, which is admittedly old, but which still can run much prettier games like Farcry 2 and Fallout New Vegas. This one looks worse and runs worse than either of those.
Main reason I don't recommend this is a very poor sense of immersion. You can pick up some objects, but everything else is static. I threw a chair on a table with bottles and cutlery, and the chair just slammed into them, nothing happened. Also, although I didn't play for too long, there was no sense of urgency, and I just didn't care about the story at all. I just walked through the house, heard some rumbling and saw lights flickering. Not scary, nothing to do with horror.
Also, some triggered events were just really annoying. Blurring effects and limited movement, and for what? Atmosphere? I wanted to like this, but really I can't.

No jokes. This game is just a bad sequel.
I can't recommend this game as a successor to Amnesia TDD. The feel is very different from the original, obviously, since it was developed by Chinese Room. There aren't many good puzzles, half of the monster encounters are scripted nonsense, it also lag spikes constantly no matter what setup you have due to bad sound design(?) (it loads each sound effect on the spot, from what I can tell) And it's also very short. The Dark Descent gave me 15 hours of gameplay, I played through this twice and it only gave me 4 hours of gameplay per playthrough. The story is 'acceptable', and pretty dark if you're into that sort of♥♥♥♥♥♥ although only people that really take their time to absorb themself into the nonsense of pig metaphors will understand. Which, isn't really worth the time, to be honest. It's not all that good anyway. 6/10, Buy it if you're a hardcore fan of the series, Frictional's games or the HPL engine!

BEFORE PURCHASING WATCH THIS
I love this game. The nostalgia is awesome, the classes look great, the gameplay is challenging, the crafting system is inspiring, but there is about a 20-30% chance this will be a permanent thing happening to you 80% time after using fixes. No this is not a graphical error, this is the problem with Server-live hosting which is rarely used in mmos for this very reason. Sometimes the fixes make the issue livable but in my case it still happens even on a cream of the crop desktop.
This Game is all other regards is great. But that issue makes end game content either incredibly hard or in cases like titan hm or ex impossible. After reaching this point I am heavily considering quiting over this issue. As you can see I logged plenty of play time up to the point where it is debilitating. At endgame with all or most players ragging on you just because they dont have the issue, even vote kicking you over something you cant control is beyond infuriating.
In conclusion: If you dont play end game content in mmos, this mmo is perfect for you. If you dont have this issue this game is an EXCELLENT and FUN time. If you get this issue, you will have to be carried through instadeath AOE fights unless you really luck out on positioning.

The Elder Scrolls® Online: Tamriel Unlimited is pretty good.
I will be honest with you, I've played only the Skyrim game of TES series. Had a few hours in Oblivion and Morrowind too, but not enough to say that I've actually "played" it.
Not a big fan of MMO too, I find grinding very borring.
However, this game has a very descent balance between MMO stuff and TES stuff. It does feel like an Elder Scrolls game.
Yes, combat will feel a bit weird at first, classes as well, though you really can shape your character to be anything you want. Race and class define only 4 of your skill trees, while you still have skill trees like "Two handed", "Dual wielding" or "Bow" that are accessible to any class and race.
I think, the best way to play TES Online is to experience it as a single player product at times. Just to go explore the world and complete some side quests on your way. And once you wish to spice it up, do some MMO stuff like dungeons or PVP.
There is also a controversial side to this game: paid content. Yes, game already costs $20 (the cheapest package) and it has some in-game purchases that are not only cosmetical, but can give you some advantage as well. I, personally, did not find anything game changing though.
I would really advise this game to either TES fans or to people who like MMO but try to find something a bit different to play.

TL;DR: The game isn't worth the massive costs you'll wind up paying for it in order to enjoy it.

Cons

SMITE on it's own is a fantastic game. It includes God's from various religions giving the players an understanding of the various religions and somehow making it seem cool. The concept of SMITE is the same as any other MOBA, attack the towers with "minions" and push to the end goal whilst gaining buffs and help from "jungles" and "stores". This is the core aspect of the game but isn't the game all together. There are many modes and many God's to chose from. Apart from the core objective of the game, there is a mode that is, imo, the best part of this game. Arena. It's where you are pitted in a team of 5 and must face against another team of 5 in a deathmatch type of mode where the main objective is to kill the other team to remove some of the points from the "bar". Alternatively, guiding minions to the other team's portal can lower their points as well but is more difficult to do.
In conclusion, I love this game very much and I think that it is better than LOL and DOTA purely because of the playable characters, third person view, fun gamemodes and it's overall controls of the game(being able to move with WASD. Can't do that with LOL or DOTA.).

It no secret that I've been a fan of the Total War series since Rome: Total War. In fact, the Total War Franchise was one of the game series that got me into RTS games. So now that the dust settle after the horrible launch Rome II had, let see if the game is worth playing.
Gameplay:
If you played a Total War game before then you know the formula. A campaign map where you manage the economy of the faction you play as and build up the forces for your armies. Some new features added since Rome include army stances that change how far an army can move, make them harder to spot so they can ambush, raiding enemy lands, etc. Each stance has it strengths and weakness. Also in Rome, you could build wall around any settlement. That been done away with in favor of a province system. Each province has a capital city that can have a wall and several cities that cannot have wall. It does feel a little limited. But once a whole province is in your control you can get benefits for the whole province.
With the campaign map, you have battles that you can fight in with your armies from the campaign map. This is where you get to control your units, maintain formation, use abilities, etc to win the battle. Simply bringing the best units is part of the challenge. You must be ready to flank the enemy and do rear attacks to best destroy and route the enemy. Battles are my favorite part of this game. When you have 2 large armies going at each other in the field or a huge army laying siege to a great walled city. You get some spectacular moments.
Graphics and Sounds:
The game looks great and sound just as well during battles. I would recommend the Gore and blood DLC, not so much for the blood, but the gore it satisfying. Nothing better than seeing limbs and heads on the ground.
Final Comments:
I can’t really speak on what the game was like during launch since I bought it after all the launch bugs have been dealt with. But what I can say is this is probably one of my favorite total war game in the whole franchise. Granted the DLC feels pricey and should only be grabbed upon a sale, but it worth it once you have it.  Let see if the Google translation gods have blessed me in this phrase:
Veni, Vidi, Recensuit!

Call of Juarez Gunslingers shows the story of a retired justice fighter - a man of the law, who breaks the law himself, a true cowboy of the Wild West. The story is very well built up, with great "boss battles" and some betrayals. It successfully shows how the Wild West were days of harsh struggle and gunfights that came out of nowhere. Almost every mission is to do with someone you have to kill for a bounty - it was a common sport for cowboys in that time.
Throughout the mission, I had picked up some collectibles. These were often cowboy hats that gave some information on the game menu about certain people. I just thought I'd mention collectibles as they are a really good essential to good campaigns. Collectibles allow gamification to be relevant, meaning that the players can really get to explore the full creation from the creators.
The campaign contains lots of cowboy stereotypes, such as the clothing they wore and the way they spoke to each other. These stereotypes are good for historical knowledge and teach the gamers who play with some Wild West knowledge. I had also noticed that some of the bountied names from the campaign were actually real criminals and outlaws in the Wild West in real life.
The cutscenes in the game are cartoon and are effective by the use of camera zooms and camera shots. For example, some of the cinematic shots were extreme close ups to show extreme emotions on the characters' faces. The voice acting was also very good.
Western music was used during the game which really helped the game stick to one symbol, which is the cowboy. The music was successful in creating tension by intensifying at certain moments. Animations and player rigs are really smooth in the game, so job well done to the creators!
The ending of the game was really exciting and gave an option, a bit like the Walking Dead games would give you. You know... "kill this dude... or kill the zombie that's about to eat him..." - I don't know. :3
Anyway, I really like that the game gave more than one way that the game could have ended. It really is quite a unique part of this game.
Overall, I would say this game really is fun to play and I personally had a blast playing it. I'd be more than happy to play other Call of Juarez games, too! I would recommend this game to any people that enjoy story-rich games and first person shooters. The gunplay is actually quite exciting! :)

I hadn’t heard of DISTRAINT – released in mid October 2015 – before, but now, it is easily one of the best games I’ve played this year. I mean, EASILY. EASILY!
I’ll start off by saying that the music and sound effects in this game are fantastic. Everything goes off at just the right moment, and I can tell that all of the music was meticulously chosen for each scene to evoke just the appropriate emotion.
Read the full review at:

Distraint - /disˈtrānt/
"The seizure of someone's property in order to obtain payment of money owed, especially rent."
Mr. Price has one job: he is the man who tells you that you’re going to lose your home. Yes, he is
guy. To his credit, he seems to have a conscience, and that is where the psychological horror comes from here. We see him struggle with his own demons and his own decisions, as he races towards a promotion.
Distraint will take you to a world that is obscure and ruthless, yet its inhabitants are charming characters with oversized heads while tackling various themes such as greed, compassion and depression in a compelling and unique fashion. It takes some unexpected turns, but doesn’t rely on disgusting imagery to weird you out, as this game has more fun playing with your mind. I wouldn’t say that this is a frightening game, but a few jump scares are executed pretty well. This is a particularly good thing in story-driven games, especially when its aim is to convey a message to the player. No need to worry about dying either; the worst that could happen to you is lingering on a puzzle.
Speaking of puzzles, they are relatively simple, yet clever. Some involves a considerable amount of walking back and forth, and some segments also introduce innovative ways to progress further into Price’s living nightmare ( I won't spoil it here). And the gameplay is... well, you can walk from left to right and vice-versa, the controls are pretty standard: W,A,S,D to move, E for the action button, F to use your lantern and spacebar to open inventory.
To sum it up, Distraint is short but sweet. It's a game with an intriguing storyline and a decent sense of humour among the horror.  It’s a carefully developed and intriguing video game, made by one man that is worth your time.

This game made me feel a kind of pain I haven't felt in a while.
First of all, it is not guaranteed that you feel the same if you play through this game. Basically, this is a nightmare that some people have actually gone through. Just imagine a friend that you actually like, but you're good friends and you don't want to screw the friendship you already have. You keep talking for months and years and that person ends up meaning way much more than you could have ever expected. As it happens in this game, the person actually likes you too but you can't just act as you would wish.
Some mistakes happen, some problems surface, and suddenly your friendship is hanging by a thread. This is where you realize how much that person means to you. And then you realize it's probably too late to say what you feel. To say what your heart felt but your mind denied. In the end, you did nothing wrong, You tried to be the best you could for that person. And still, suddenly, everything you thought you did right starts to feel so wrong. Please note that this is a long distance friendship/relationship. And everything you try to say from this point on won't matter. Because the other person just doesn't care about you anymore. You can't meet them because they won't even agree to that and you're left with such a hole in your life. All you can say is
1. goodbye
2. goodbye
3. goodbye
From that point on this friendship you relied so much on no longer exists. Imagine trusting one single person so much and have that person do this to you. I guess this is a issue that mostly affects people with some degree of social anxiety, so I understand if you don't feel as emotional as I did playing this game.
For the game itself, it simulates that struggle described above in a 2002 style, with the AIM messenger and all those cheesy descriptions and icons that everyone back then had (and some still have today).
It's kind of hard to recommend this game, as it can be a saddening experience or a completely boring one, depending on which spectrum you are. But I'll recommend it anyway. Give it a try.

. This review is a mix of bad and good things (mostly bad) about the actual Tree of Savior and some of these may change in the future.
I've been playing ToS since the first day of the official free to play launch, I enjoyed doing quests for the first few weeks with friends, but after a month or so all of them left the game 'cause it wasn't fun anymore, even with the repetitive quests, (you will only start to grind with a party past half way through your journey) FPS drop and tons of bugs I kept playing, it was more of an achievement hunt than actually having fun, all I wanted was to reach max level with at least one character to see the end-game content and this is what I've seen...
The end-game content is close to none at the moment, the only thing you can do is run lower level dungeons and try to get something out the bosses, oh the bosses! They look more like piñatas, the AI is terrible and the only challenging thing about them is their HP, that's the only difference between high level bosses and low level ones. Besides dungeons you can climb the Earth Tower.
It's basically the generic daily time sink for players to log-in everyday, you have a limit of 2 tries per day and every 5 floors (max is 20) you have a chance to get a boss box (contain loot) you can either decide to keep climbing or just stop at any of those (5, 10, 15, 20) to secure the box, each floor means a different bland challenge, but to be short I'll just mention the first 5 ones.
DPS test, kill 150 mobs in X minutes.
Protect the "statue" (you can just use a barrier and don't move for 5 minutes, don't worry, the mobs won't be able to reach you nor the statue)
Kill a ghost mob and receive a buff to kill a totem in the middle of the room, just use 5 barriers (one for each player of the party), pull the ghost, kill it and destroy the totem without being touched by the mobs.
Just run in circles without using any skill (literally).
Kill the boss and that's it.
PS: You have to do that for 20 days to get a single part of the set (unless you want to pay to re-roll your boxes with in-game currency).
PvP is not something you can do all the time, 3 times a day the PvP opens for 1 hour and then closes, you cannot make a pre-made party with your friends, everyone is having issues with FPS drop (even with a great PC you will experience it anyway), lots of bugged skills and so on.
GvG happens twice a day for 1 hour, since it's 30 players in the same place using skills everywhere, you can barely move due to huge FPS Drop and bad optimization.
You can see players abusing exploits here and there to get stronger and not getting banned even with screenshot/video proof, tons of bots and RMT, since the game has been losing an average of 3,5k players every month the company won't ban players even if they abuse it.
It happened due to a few players complaining in the forums, since IMC doesn't play their own game they decided to remove it. The company literally killed the open gvg battles implementing the "Neutral guild option", before that any guild was at the mercy of joining a war. Players could declare war to a guild once they find their tower (you could hide it anywhere in the map, anywhere!) or even play as a spy selling information on tower locations (can you see how much content that feature creates?), you had to choose between protecting your tower or attack the enemies, once the battle starts both sides are able to kill the opponent anywhere in the map besides main cities, unfortunately there is no reason to do it anymore.
If you enjoy testing builds and leveling up a bunch of characters to max level this game can actually be kinda fun, it has a huge amount of classes and you can mix them together, but once you get to max level you either create another one or get stuck on the nonexistent end-game.
The whole game feels like a box, you will never feel actually free to explore due to a hundred of invisible walls and bad designed maps.
Somewhat discouraging but it prevents inflation in the game market which is good.
Any class is able to complete quests (it doesn't mean you won't struggle a lot) but it will be extremely hard to find a group to run dungeons without friends since no one is doing them anymore due to the huge decrease in the player-base.
If you like build theory and creating a bunch of characters it may be fun, but once you get to end-game content you will realize it's close to nonexistent.
PvP and GvG are fun but due to constant FPS drop it became unplayable.
Repetitive quests, huge monthly decrease in the player-base
, tons of bugs, terrible FPS optimization, BOTS, players exploting bugs here and there, claustrophobic level design, good features being removed, encourages solo-playing, bland PvE with bad AI
.

Closest you're ever gonna get to a truly solid MMO experience.  I came from TERA, i promised myself i'd never play a game with tab-target again.  But here I am, 150+ hours,
While questing you'll spend a lot of time blazing through quests, and for the most part, I didn't feel bored by the story, the combat was engaging, and he quest themselves were decently written and weren't tedious to manage or complete; my only complaint is one must resort to FATES once they hit hit that point of "GOTTA GET TO 50 ASAP"
Luckily endgame content in FF14 makes you work for your gear, but makes it easy to accomplish and is not a time sink (for the most part)
One can attempt to hunt monsters with a full 8-man raid, along with many other raids to get specific currency to obtain that gear, and it takes a good 5 hours to get all that currency for decent gear to PREPARE for endgame content.  Once you're properly equipped you start facing many challenges that do take skill in your class, and communication with your party to accomplish, such as Hard Mode versions of boss fights in the story mode whilst you were leveling.  The main thing to note about this game is that it is very hard to NOT suck at your class, every class is incredibly unique, espcially when one is allowed to get a job (Specializing in that class role) but the game makes it very easy and simple to do a specific role without much screw ups, levels 1-49 preapre you with very brief 30-40 minute dungeons that give you a proper conditioning to be a healer, tank or get a sense of your DPS rotation, so you won't get your♥♥♥♥♥handed to you when you first start out.
Free Company's are FF14RR's guild system, and it not only serves as your help hotline, it serves as your home as well... literally, FC's are allowed to acquire houses for all their members for a small payment of... 2 million gil.... >.>  and 10mil if you want a swag pad, FC's in turn give you plenty of leveling bonuses for new players, and the more new players do FATE's, the FC in-turn ranks up in their residing Grand Company of 3 Grand Companies.
Get this game, it's a full package, engaging story, plenty of customization (More hairstyles when you're lvl 20 C:), and traditional but SOLID gameplay.
You won't be dissapointed if you love MMO's.

is a very unique game. 3909 Studios knows how to make a game about simply manning a checkpoint into questioning the ethics of Arstotska while simultaneously questioning my own morals. Through the game things don't get easier. In fact, its quite the contrary. You'll find yourself getting beat over the head with family needs of food, medicine, and heat. All requiring money to obtain, money you don't have. In the beginning of the game I was just a worker keeping criminals and other evildoers out of my country. Then the rent wages went up, my family was getting sick. I noticed that as time went on I started to get more and more desperate for money, accepting bribes whenever I could. I was slowly becoming the person I was originally supposed to keep out. It may be too repetitive for some, but as for me though, they spiced things up enough for the game to not grow stale. The musty pixel art sets the tone in this beautiful game. 3909 Studios did an amazing job, and I look forward to see what else they come out with in the future.

Smite is a really well polished moba, it has a different spin on the tradditional moba by using real life religious gods such as Zeus, Odin, Loki, Thor, Apollo and all sorts of well known gods, it puts them in a 3rd person perspective rather then the usual top down view we've come to expect from moba's.
Smite does a lot of things right; Here i'll name some of the main things that will be very appealing for a new player to the game or the moba genre in general,
-Level up rewards (this includes favor points, limited skins, limited gods,)
-Seperate first wins of the day (in moba's a first win gives you extra ingame currency, smite has a seperate one for every map/mode)
-Playing as a god, you sometimes really feel like a beast when you just get a massive lightning storm off with Zeus, or hunt someone down with your chariot as Apollo
-Quick fast paced action, this moba is based a lot around action and fighting.
-Basic attacks arent point and click (I love this♥♥♥♥♥♥xD)
Some things are a bit worrying however,
-Every damn god has a dash, pretty annoying for assasins ;)
-The majority of female gods are really objectivied, take it or leave it I guess, doesnt bother me personally too much but it is worth noting.
-Performance is a bit poor for low end pc's, the game isnt super taxing but for the lower ended systems you can get severe framerate issues
-A standard moba community (generally pretty toxic)
-Communication, smite uses voice lines for most of the communication, seeing as you can't really use the map, remembering all the combinations is a pain though.
-Shop is a bit chaotic at first
Overal though Smite is a nice breath of fresh air, I jumped in recently again and purchased the god pack. Having a lot of fun with it especially with a friend or two.

This review will be split up in categories, to show how good each section of the game is. In each category I will shortly explain each of the points.
- Very satisfying gameplay. The way you control your god feels very good and can be quite fun, even after many hours. Even though the core elements of a MOBA are still there, it feels like a 3rd person action game, which means it appeals to both fans of the MOBA genre and people who want a cool, fun experience.
- Interesting representation of ancient gods. For me it is commendable that they managed to present gods from 9 different pantheons (as of now) with a lot of detail, having a somewhat accurate appearance, a lore feature which allows players to read the backrounds of all gods and encourages some of them to look for more details. At the same time, Hi-Rez is not afraid to release skins that are definately not faithful to the mythology, but are meant to be simply cool.
- Extremely well made sountrack. Even though some of the tracks in Smite are variations of the same theme, they managed to make them in a way to go for a different touch in each version, depending on the pantheon. Still, leaving those aside, the game has a lot of high quality themes that fit the tone of the game and in fact can be appreciated even by outsiders.
- Outstanding in-game chat. The text chat is nothing special, but the voice chat is really convenient. During Smite matches you can open your voice menu (using the V button) and quickly find different messages like "Enemies in the right lane", "Be right back" etc that are read for your whole team to hear. Needless to say, this is a great feature that helps speed up the process of communicating with your team.
- Nice visuals and level of graphics. Considering this is a free to play title, from a visual standpoint this game has succeded. The god models look pretty good, the environments have some detail, textures are (almost) always clear and in general it seems satisfying to look at.
- Good application of the free to play model. This is one the rare occasions where a game that is free to play does not depend on spending either money or insane amounts of grind to compete with other players. In order for you to be competitive, all you need to have is the required skill necessary. That being said, you do depend on your teamates as well, but nevertheless if you are good enough you will at least guarantee that you will do your part sufficiently.
- Leniency in collecting in-game currrencies. This game uses two types of currency, favor, which is mostly obtained through winning matches and gems, which are mostly obtained through paying real money. There are bonuses for getting those currencies, like free favor/gems for logging in on consecutive days or for completing daily quests. That allows players to collect gods/skins in a shorter period of time without having to play all day. It should also be noted that there is the Ultimate God Pack, a feature that unlocks all current and future gods for around 20-25 euros/dollars (price varies depending on where you live). Although getting every god is not necessary to play the game, having every single one that is out or will be out for that amount of money is a good deal.
- A variety of game modes. There are 6 different maps (with the corresponding practice and co-op modes), as well as a Match of the Day feature that, as the name suggests, changes every day and is inspired by recommendations of the community. Naturally, there are also 3 ranked modes on these maps (Conquest 5v5, Joust 3v3 and Joust 1v1). The different layout of the lanes, the towers and the camps in those maps means you can alternate between them and reduces fatigue.
- Well designed watching option. In the "Wisdom" tab, you can quickly find current Smite streams or god guides and watch them while the game is running. Granted, you could just open your internet browser and search it there, but it is a neat feature which should be mentioned. Also, the spectating mode is pretty handy.
- The community. This is not the worst community in any game (it is FAR from that), but at times the playerbase can get pretty bad. As I mentioned earlier, the game has a voice chat available, which can be spammed a lot when people are upset. This creates issues, since you don't want to listen to pointless messages, but at the same time muting the player completely can cause you to miss important warnings. Not to mention the intentional feeders/leavers/blamers that are matched with you from time to time. Overall, it is better than many games and probably better than most MOBAs out there, but still the room for improval is there.
- The matchmaking. Sometimes, in order for Smite to find players to match against one another, it has to expand the window of matchmaking between players. Simply put, in normal matches there is a chance you could be matched with players way higher or lower than you in terms of skill. Not only does this make certain matches very unbalanced, but it creates another problem. Punishments for leaving god selections are very severe, because making it more bothersome when people leave in god selection discourages that behavior, thus decreasing the chances of leaving and the time people need to find a game. Unfortunately, when you find teamates in normal games that picked a weird team you don't want to spend time playing with you have to consider staying and potentially wasting your time or leaving and risking at best a big duration as a deserter or at worst a ban. I have even heard that someone got banned once for not clicking accept in time when a match was found.
- The balancing. In comparison to other competitive games with multiple characters, it is relatively better in that regard, but still, for most of the gods what occurs is going through a period of time of mediocrity, then receiving a buff and becoming pretty strong and then maybe a nerf that brings them back to their original stats (or even lower). I am aware that you can make up for some of the god's weaknesses with a certain level of skill, however when the opponent's skill level matches yours and he/she is using a more viable god you are at a slight disadvantage from the start.
- The servers. Servers in Smite have been unstable as long as I can remember them. Lag spikes and disconnects are issues that happen from time to time in games (not very often but on occasion). If I am not mistaken, this issue has been mitigated over the years, but it remains one of the most important ones, as you will get a disconnect from a game because of the servers around once every month.
- The recent implementation of Easy Anti Cheat (EAC). EAC is known in the field of gaming to be a big failure of an anti-cheat software. It is riddled with problems, such as not allowing the game to run if you have unsigned drivers, disconnecting players for no reason, banning more innocent players than cheaters (which combined with the irreversible nature of the bans is an awful issue), failure to even stop all cheaters, having properties of actual spyware. Even though the community complained, Hi-Rez included EAC in a recent patch and unsurprisingly, a huge amount of people reporting having trouble with the game since, even though most of them were not cheaters. History proved that EAC was disastrous in other games in which it was implemented (the stories regarding For Honor were even worse) and it was proven very bad in Smite as well.
I was really torn about this decision, because I really, REALLY wanted to recommend Smite, since I've had a lot of fun with this game. However, I decided in the end not to recommend it as the existance of EAC is so menacing that it counteracts all of the advantages Smite has (even though they are greater in number). If EAC is ever removed - highly unlikely - this game would unquestionably be recommended.

Distraint is a short psychological horror title in which you play the role of Price, a young man whose job is to seize the property of others. He quickly discovers that he's entering a decent paying career at the cost of his own humanity.
The game is full of hidden meanings (even Price's name), and the story is something that almost everyone who has had a job can relate to. Myself personally being a slave to call center careers for the past decade, I certainly know how the protagonist feels and the story really hits home for me. The graphics and gameplay style will easily remind players of titles such as Lone Survivor, Claire and Home. However, Distraint has a personality and concept that is unique to itself. The atmosphere in the game is heavy, brought on by dimly lit corridors and a pressurized ambiance that gives an overflowing sense of dread for the entirety of the game.
Distraint is an outstanding indie horror title that does its job of instilling fear and dread into the player. The puzzles are very easy and the game is very short, your initial playthrough may take anywhere from 1-2 hours to complete. Subsequent playthroughs will see 30-45 minute timeframes. There are a few grammatical errors within the dialogue at times, but the game is bug and crash free.
The price has dropped significantly since launch, and Distraint is worth every penny of the $5.49 CAD asking price; it even goes on sale for $1.09 quite regularly. Additionally, it's very impressive that one person created this game in a little less than 3 months; the same creator behind Silence of the Sleep. If you're looking for a good horror title to spend some time with this Halloween or cold winter season, look no further.

I just finished playing through CoJ:Gunslinger so the experience is fresh in my mind for this review.
The whole storyline playthrough took me around 5 hours, and honestly it wasn't bad! The story itself isn't anything amazing, I dare say it may even be rather forgettable after a few days, but overall the fun wild west shootouts and satisfying/solid feel when hitting a target made it definately worthy of a recommendation. The game didn't manage to inspire any emotions relating to the story the protaganist is telling despite there being the availability for it (I don't want to give any spoilers so the details here will just stay this vague), but it wasn't boring or badly voice acted/written either. I think the developers put their time into the combat mechanics of the game as a priority and that side of the game was more than enough to pull the average storyline through to the end.
The gameplay was solid, well voice acted and the cutscenes were short and sweet, nothing too long that made me bored.
The variety of weapons basically boiled down to 3, a rifle, a pistol or a shotgun, and I felt like each of the weapons felt satisfying to use, though dual wield pistols felt abit clunky at times, I stuck with the single pistol if I had to use it, otherwise I used the rifle with a sawn off shotgun as a secondary weapon which worked nicely and proved to be fun.
I'm a veteran of fps games having played them for many many years, and yet the game still provided a challenge that I found highly enjoyable, and there's multiple difficulty settings to spice things up if you want another playthrough.
Replayability - It was good but now that I know the story it's not something I can realistic imagine playing through again. It was an enjoyable 1 time experience but there's nothing pulling me back in to try it again since it would just be more of the same, maybe just on the hardest difficulty mode.
Choices - There was only 1 choice that the player was asked to make and it was in regards to whether the main bad guy gets to live or die, I chose live and it was a peaceful end to the game. Don't expect to have any impact on any part of the 'world' like in other RPG's and it's not that kind of game, it's not a persistent world and quests/missions are given directly to you without needed to be collected. It's basically an old-school storyline shooter like the old Medal of Honor series.
All in all i'd say it'd be a shame if you missed out playing through this game, but i'd recommend grabbing it while it's on sale or on offer as a bundle (I got it from bundlestars) as based on the short amount of time it took to complete and the linear enviroments that leave the player with little to no decision making required, it's not really worth more than 5 euros in my opinion, but for that price it's a great game.
Overall rating - 6.5/10: It didn't wow me and the story was forgettable, but the combat was fun and the enviroments were pretty.

Wall of text incoming:
I think it goes without saying every game has its drawbacks (COD games most of all, and it doesn't get any better as the game ages), but this is a Call of Duty game and it's one of the most-highly praised ones - the storyline is engaging, multiplayer is fun, and the Spec Ops mode is challenging (if that's more your speed). Weapons in the game are fun to use and each one has their own little niche for different players, whether you're a rush-in-and-hit-'em-hard type, or a-sit-back-and-let-them-come-to-me kind of player.
Biggest gripes I could come up with for this game are the scant amount of perks available at the start and how much of a grind it feels like to level up. The most redeeming feature are the maps - most of them are fantastic and well-designed with different overwatch spots, cross-ways, multiple routes to take for flanking or getting to the objective, and a lot of maps force you to play differently than you would on other maps. Also, if you're at all familiar with the map Favela, for some reason it never comes up in map circulation anymore; it's weird.
If you're a fan of Call of Duty and you won't mind the chance to happen upon a modded lobby in multiplayer, dealing with players liberally using grenade launchers, or those players using the cheapest tactics they can so as to get that Chopper Gunner/AC-130/Nuke, then by all means get this game and have fun with it.

Kingdoms:
Kingdoms is a nice open world sandboxy game where you just do what you want.
I greatly enjoy the genre so i picked up this game, and here is what i think:
Negatives:
-It turns in to a real pain to level up around level 14 and some things like master blacksmith take 80 points (8 levels worth of points) so i can start to get a little bit grindy
- (minor) The bow seems to be like 20lb pull, because that arrow drops like a rock.
- Combat (with people) is horrible right now, you can just walk around behind them and they wont turn around, so you can just stab them right in the back a few times and you won.
Things that i am neutral or very slightly annoyed about:
+- NPC's will camp the bulletin board and swipe jobs before you can even get a chance to do anything. Not a huge issues, but when you are the town builder, it sucks to have those jobs taken away.
+- You cant build others houses. I dont enjoy seeing half built houses for weeks, but i cant finish others houses unless i have been assigned to
+- I would ****ing love if i could commision work from the blacksmith. I'd pay throught the nose if i could do it.
+- Due to the level grind, if you camp in the town you made, youll come to a standstill level-wise, so you have to explore or something, which doesnt really suit me.
+- if you start as like, a blacksmith, or something, it takes a long time for a town to get the capitol to build a blacksmith place, so you either need to level up and learn worker, or start with it, taking away from your blacksmithing, or other such skill.
Enough moaning though, Here is what gave the game the positive rating.
++++ Absolute freedom to do as a please. This one is huge for me. I really enjoy things being open-ended.
++ build what you like where you like as long as  you have the skill, and if you do, you can sell your houses
+ smithing is a pretty neat mechanic, i enjoy the way its setup currently.
All in all, i do enjoy  the game. Its got some quirks, but the genre and style make up for it in my opinion. That may not be how you feel, if you need set goals, this game is a little bit lacking. However, if you are fine just being dropped into a world and making your own path, this game is great.

I started playing The Elder Scrolls about 13 years ago (TES3) on PC. I bought it used with all expansions at a liquidation sale, having no knowledge of it prior. I have put countless hours of gameplay into the series since. I took a hiatus from any serious gaming for years to focus on other priorities and I've just recently found the time to game again. I got this game as part of a bundle and was ridiculously excited. I've been unable to pry myself away from the computer, longing to return to gameplay when I do. My sleep schedule has been ruined. The graphics are fantastic, the gameplay has kept some of the most unique and awesome aspects of TES - lockpicking, theft, bounties, in-depth foraging and crafting, and a fairly interactive environment. The combat system is flawless. Skill trees based on guild/race/class/etc makes for ridiculously customizable characters. I haven't had any pvp experience yet, but I personally favor faction-less pvp. ESO has one area (Cyrodiil) where levels 10+ can fight based on their respective alliances. I have always preferred a worldwide pvp system based on level ranges (a la Everquest's Zek), but ESO may still change this preference. I love love love this game so far and definitely recommend it.
UPDATE: (There are skill trees based on weapon and armor choices, pvp performance, staff choices [resto, destro, etc]) - unbelievable level of diversity in customization! PVP did indeed exceed my expectations. It is a constant war to reclaim Cyrodiil, featuring a specific currency for items to repair various outposts and towns as well as siege weaponry. There are PVP and scouting quests to couple with the constant siege experiences. Blown away by the quality of this game.
UPDATE: Customer service is lacking.
UPDATE: Battlegrounds PvP is amazing. Morrowind expansion is crazy nostalgic. A lot of buildings and their layouts and Vvardenfell's inhabitants appear to be ripped right out of Elder Scrolls III and polished for the newest generation.

Dark Souls II is a sequel to the cult classic Dark Souls game and it unfortunately lacks every subtlety that made the first game such an intoxicating experience. To explain these subtleties would be to ruin what makes the discovery process so fun, but I will respond to anyone who wishes to know what I think in a personal Steam message.
As a story telling experience, it lacks the reason to be it's own story (The DLC sort of corrects this problem.) As a combat experience, it lacks the tight mechanics that made the first one fair and engaging. The hitboxes are not as the appear at all, there is input lag on movement, and a well-designed mechanic -- rolling -- is hidden behind a stat called "Adaptation." Its level design is good, but lacks the metroid-vania style *world* design that makes it replayable. The game feels nearly as linear as a game like Darksiders does. Forgettable bosses that are just 2/3rds big armoured people with formulaic attack patterns. Dark Souls II is a pretty good Souls-*like* but pales in comparison to its predecessor. I couldn't, with good concsious, reccomend anyone looking to understand what souls is *about* by reccomending this game.
As a personal aside to establish what my opinion might, or might not, mean to a review reader, I purchased the original Dark Souls four times. Once on console, twice more for friends looking to get into the game, and once on PC. I pre-purchased the deluxe edition of Dark Souls II on console and afterwards the PC version. With collectively 700+ hours into the souls series (1, 2, 3 and Bloodbourne) I still don't reccomend Dark Souls II. I would reccomend Dark Souls II *last* if you want to know what Souls is about.

For the people who don't want to read a whole review, TL;DR, I'd definitely say this game is worth it if you just want a pretty fun arcade shooter that won't take you a week to finish (I beat it in 4 hours).
Going into this game, I didn't expect much. I picked it up for cheap during some sale since it looked like something dumb that I could stream for friends and we could laugh at it. I had known that the previous Call of Juarez games weren't particularly great, especially the one where you play as 3 different characters in modern days. That one is pretty lame.
After having it sit in my library for months and months, I finally got around to starting it up to stream for a friend while he worked. I went into it, again, expecting to laugh at how dumb it was, but before the first level even ended, I realized that it was actually a really solid game.
Now, don't get me wrong. It's obviously not GOTY every year, but it's FAR from a bad game. I actually really enjoyed myself. It's short, it's pretty easy, there aren't tons of guns, and none of the mechanics really stand out from any other FPS game. But what it lacks in innovation, it makes up for in charm and excitement. The old west setting and environments are awesome. Dual wielding revovlers and gunning down an arena full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cowboys or bank robbers is super satisfying, the game has no trouble with really making you feel like the badass outlaw that the story makes you out to be. The visuals are real nice, and although the shooting isn't too much different from your average arcade shooter game, the point system really makes you feel like every shot, every combo is impressive in some way or another. In addition to this, there is a quickdraw minigame in between most missions that is actually pretty tense while you're doing it. If you're not quick enough, or don't have the ability to multitask, focusing on both your enemy and your own gun, it'll be tough, you might even have to repeat it a few times. I'm not sure if this is a complaint or praise, maybe I'm just bad at the game (this is extremely likely). There are even loads of collectables if you're into that kind of thing, like I am.
The story is neat. It's funny, it's engaging, and it's sometimes even really tense, especially near the end of the game. Without spoiling anything, it's geniunely hilarious when the narrator's story gets interupted halfway through, and in doing so, a boulder gets moved out of the way, or a path opens up in between some trees, or a box full of guns and ammo falls from the sky and into your lap, because of the unreliable narrator. It adds a lot of charm and humor that tons, if not most, FPS games fail to provide.
As I've said before, the only real complaints I have are that it doesn't really have anything new or interesting in terms of mechanics to show for, but I get the feeling that the creators weren't really going for anything like that. It's short enough so you can marathon it in one night like I did, or take 2, MAYBE 3 sessions to beat it. I played it on Hard difficulty for my first playthrough, and I only died a handful of times, most of which were just falling off a cliff stupidly, or messing up the quickdraw minigame. Very few deaths were a result of dying in combat, which is either a testament to how good I am at games (I'm not), or how easy the game is.
Overall, if you want a short but sweet, fun, dumb arcade shooter game to crank out in an afternoon or two, this is a great choice.

While normal enemies are perfectly fine, boss fights are absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing ridiculous. The bosses take forever to kill, and just one bullet from an enemy gun is enough to kill you. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t? Definitely. Prevalent in the game? Absolutely.
It's frustrating as hell, and limits progression. Sure, the game itself? Fun, if you're willing to overlook the fact that bosses and duels are ♥♥♥♥ing impossible on harder difficulties as not only are they overpowered, but they have minions that almost appear to be extensions of themselves - one shot and you're ♥♥♥♥ing done.
EDIT: Okay, so after calming down - the game is truly fun, don't get me wrong. The unreliable narrator approach is brilliant and entertaining, the characters are likable, and gameplay is usually very well balanced given that the player has some sense of 'reload and take cover'; however, one thing this game does horribly is boss fights. They introduce 'flimsy barriers' which are covers that can be pierced by enemy bullets, thus rendering them completely useless. And guess what? The one or two covers that are there are usually positioned in a spot where all of the enemies can shoot at you, making you the absolute easiest target ever.
All in all, the game is fun. Buy it on sale or as part of a bundle, as you probably won't get much time out of it; however, just the experience is great (overlooking the terribly balanced boss fights).

Transistor has an amazing audio-visual style and a strong emotional story. The gameplay is fused into its sci-fi world, and everything about it is blended with jargon from informatics, computers, programming, technology etc. The combat system is evolved, engaging and suprisingly deep and diverse.
(1) Art-style is awesome. (2) Music is fantastic, original and merged with the story. Red, the protagonist, is a singer who has lost her voice, and for that reason there's a dedicated "Hum" button, where the game pauses and Red hums to background music! (3) Combat system is a very interesting and well balanced blend of real-time with pause-and-give-orders: You can fight in real time (which is hard!) or you can use the "Turn()" command to give orders which are then executed sequentially by Red while her enemies are slowed down (nearly stopped). After that, Turn() requires several seconds to recover before you can use it again; it the meanwhile you can't use any abilities and just need to run around in real-time avoiding enemies.
(1) The story can be confusing. Despite the very few characters, it's often hard to understand why Red, the protagonist, does what she does. It took me two playthroughs and reading a thorough guide, to understand what was going on. Nevertheless, you can "breeze" through the game just for the feeling without losing much, but understanding the story adds to the emotional experience. (2) The sci-fi jargon --informatics, computers, programming, technology-- can also be confusing. I have some skill in the department and it wasn't all that easy for me either. The GUI is good at explaining things, but you gotta spend some time to check things out. (3) The game is not good at revealing the depth of its combat system. Also, with the main story being relatively short, you can reach the ending and beat the game without needing to grasp the mechanics. My second playthrough (NG+) was much more entertaining, as was doing all the optional "Tests" offered.
*** Comparison to Bastion: I liked Bastion's narrator better, as well as the delivery of the story, which was way simpler. Also, I believe that Bastion was better at hooking you up into its gameplay. Transistor has much better combat system, but it's not so good at hooking you up. Transistor's visuals, music and "world" are much more interesting.
*** I played this for more than 20hrs, completed the story twice (first play-through and NewGame+) and got almost all the achievements.

I'll start by saying the recommendation comes with some caveats. If you're looking for a hardcore MMO experience with balanced PvP and epic PvE, I wouldn't recommend this. There are too many framerate issues when lots of other players are on your screen, the population on EU servers is kinda low for reliable PvE, and the social functions are lacking. Updates are slow, fixes are even slower, 80 classes would be hard to balance even for more involved devs...so yeah there's definitely problems.
But if you like levelling, if you like grinding for progression, if you like researching and building the perfect class, and the sense of achievement that comes with reaching a milestone in class progression (fun new spells! new cute outfits!) then you might find the game fun. Considering it's free to play, I don't feel too bad sinking hours into doing just that. If I paid for an MMO, I would be less forgiving.
The visual design is great in my opinion. The maps, while some are samey, are quite beautiful. The music is great. The class outfits are cute and nicely varied. The huge amounts of different class builds is great, it adds a lot of variety. 4 character slots is not quite enough to fully satisfy that, but given I've sunk 100 hours into the game so far, I wouldn't feel too terrible about buying a couple more slots.
The combat feels smooth, but the controls aren't brilliant for mouse and keyboard. If you like playing with a controller, then I hear that's optimal. Sometimes it won't let you click on quest items etc with the mouse and you have to switch quickly to auto controls so you can use spacebar instead, then switch back. That's honestly the most annoying thing about questing.
I enjoy this game, and if someone was looking for the same things I am looking for in games, I think they would enjoy it too. But if you want a seamless MMO and dedicated, balanced, end-game content, I would not recommend this.

Pros:
~Simple, yet incredibly enjoyable combat revolving around AOE. It feels very impactful, and in my experience only got boring during super long play sessions.
~Insane variety of classes, many of which I have never seen attempted before in an MMO.
~Lots, and lots of bosses, both optional, and required by the story.
~Class Circle system which allows the player to specialize in several classes at one time, and forcing them to plan out their next advancement.
~Reminiscent of the original Ragnarok, but still has plenty to set it apart and make it its own game.
~Extremely helpful community, in my experience.
~Consistent, and well-written story.

Other: Slightly chibi graphics, for those of you who are into that kind of thing. Personally, I don't have a preference.
Cons:
~Suffers from many of the basic flaws that many Korean MMO's have.
~Somewhat grindy, but I honestly don't mind because of the combat.
~Gold sellers (unfortunately)
~Occasionally you'll run into large groups of bots gathered in small areas, killing monsters as they spawn, and then teleporting away. This can occasionally make things frustrating when you're trying to quest, but most monsters can be found in several places around the map anyways.
Overall, if you're willing to look past the grind and the bots, Tree of Savior is one of the best f2p MMO's out there rn. From strategizing for your next advancement, to testing it out with impactful, and flashy combat, there's always something to do. I won't lie and say that this game is revolutionary or anything like that, but it's certainly unique enough to provide you with at least 10 hours of fun.

It's a decent game that's fun to play with friends, and a enjoyable time waster solo when you do not want to put much thought into what you're doing. Listening to new albums and watching shows while not in dungeons, drinking, and other activities are highly reccomend while playing. It's not for everyone, but it's free so it's worth a try to see if you're someone that would enjoy it.

We currently have a world of medieval NPCs that have varied costumes and looks, they chop trees and build houses and shops, they buy and sell things in the shops, they hang out in taverns and sleep in the common house or their own homes. Well, I purchased this yesterday and dropped 7 hours in it since then. It's about to get deleted off my drive for now, as I have things I NEED to do, and they're going to take a back seat to Kingdoms unless I take drastic action.
Without trying to get clever or funny in this review, let me say that the game reminds me of what you'd get if you took Mount and Blade and Settlers of Catan, along with a sprinkling of The Guild series, and put them in a blender. You essentially start out with a few odds and ends, and have to figure out how to make a go of it pretty quickly (hint: learn what berry bushes look like, and consider taking a couple of levels in agriculture). I started out with a swordsman who had a level in merchant (whatever it's called in the game, I forget). Didn't realize I needed worker to build a building, but was able to get that when I levelled up. After building the store, I decided to get into the farming business and built a farmhouse, along with a dozen garden plots. Nice, freeform gameplay, especially if you're looking for a "medieval tech colonial life simulator."
Given that the game is still in EA, it's playable and fun to mess around with. My concern for it, at this point, is that there is a lot of room to grow, mechanically speaking, and it's a small dev team. Some things still feel weird, like having a shop where no one works there, or not being able to hire someone to work in your fields. I'd assume that minting coin will come along at some point, but for now, "coin" just magically appears out of thin air. Also, as far as building structures go, is a castle going to be feasible for the AI to build, and is it going to look out of place to have ten villagers and a giant, empty castle? Also, there is a lack (so far) of any kind of medieval class structure and interaction - while Kingdoms feels a bit more Renaissance to me, the common and noble divide was still strong, and feels like it should be an integral part of the game system. The island is massive, which feels like it would somewhat limit interactions, especially with a small population. Also, acquiring deeds to build in an established settlement, as well as being able to tear down a house, seem like a must. I am concerned about modding, as it's not easy to implement, and Unity 3D is a little lacking in that department. Carts and wheelbarrows would also be a nice edition. While some of this is on the roadmap, with any EA title, there is still a question of whether it will ever be implemented, or what form it'll take in the final version.
The upside is that I think the game has a lot of potential, and that it is solid and interesting enough to fiddle around with, even in the EA stages. Most of all, I had a lot of FUN going foraging for new seeds to plant in the garden, keeping my crops planted, and carrying a load of lettuce down to the store. You read that right. FUN, and I tend to be a pretty jaded gamer. For the price, it's a steal, too, and will hopefully continue to drive the development of the game.

As a big fan of good, subtle horror, and amazing stories, I was a huge admirer of "Amnesia: The Dark Descent", and when I heard about the second game, I couldn't contain my excitement. That was sort of my first mistake. Having huge expectations after the first game, I sadly had to be let down. This does not mean the game is bad, this just means, that after "The Dark Descent" it probably just had to go downhill. And even though I would love to judge the two games separately, comparing the two is sort inevitable.
On the up side, I believe the story in this game is way more interesting, heart touching, and creepy at the same time, than the intricate, but slightly… “whatever” story in the first game. It is more personal, and emotional, and the outcome is way more disturbing.
The music has definitely left an impression, and I still listen to "Mors Praematura" from time to time, cause the atmosphere it created was divine. Graphics are noticeably better, as the game is a fresher release.
Yet, as I moved through the empty house, as I watched Mandus' story unwind, I felt complete peace. And this is not what you want to feel, when playing a horror game. Maybe I have developed a strong resistance to scares, cause of my love for horror, but as hard as the game tried - I just could not get scared.
Even though I love the design of the monsters in this game (whom I will refrain from calling by their name, in case you would rather be surprised), I found it hard to fear them. Found them extremely disturbing, but also had a strong sense of pity for them. They just couldn't get me in the "oh crap, oh crap, oh crap, running away" mode, that the first game had me in most of the time.
Also the puzzle difficulty in this game is very low, and doesn't require any real thinking skills. Which can be considered an advantage by some, but for me is again, very disappointing.
So in conclusion, I would suggest playing this game for the interesting story, which left a strong unease in my heart, and the amazing music that stays with you for a long time. But if you are expecting getting really scared, or a good mind boggling puzzle, you will probably be left with a feeling of letdown. All in all, not a bad game, just probably not what you would expect.

Don't let the name fool you. This game is barely even a spirtual successor to Amnesia: The Dark Decent and is vastly insuperior. You may remember that The Dark Decent was developed by the brilliant studio, Frictional Games. However, for reasons unknown to me, they let a different studio delevelop this game. That studio, is The Chinese Room, who destroyed this game by removing most things that make an Amnesia game so great.
One of my biggest gripes with this game is the overfocus on story. In my opinion, The Dark Decent was brilliant because it balanced story with fear. This game, however, removes the fear that made The Dark Decent as scary as it was. In The Dark Decent, you constantly had to worry about the loss of your one ally, light. You could easily run out of lantern fuel and tinderboxes, leaving you blind like a child to whatever danger was headed your way. It was part of what gave the game its atmosphere, the constant worry of losing light. Well, say good by to that. In this game, you have an electric lantern which never runs out of fuel, and lightbulbs that are already lit for you. You could very well say that alone ruined the game, but that's only the start.
The monsters. Holy ♥♥♥♥ing balls, the monsters in this game are a massive dissapointment. Not only are they no longer scary in appearance, but they no longer carry a threat either. In The Dark Decent, you had to hide, you had to run, and you had to stay in the dark when a monster was around. Rome 2 had a rocky start. For about a year after release the game was in horrible shape. CA/Sega released the game as "finished" when there was still 18 months of game-breaking bugs to fix in patches, rough edges to smooth over, and a large amount of DLC that should have been included in the base game.
HOWEVER, now that its over, Rome 2 is perhaps one of the best total war games to date, even now in 2017. I absolutely recommend you buy this amazing game.
It takes a little while to figure out what you're doing and why certain units/tactics are more effective than others, but once you do its an extremely immersive experience that really throws you into ancient times.
What I like so much about this game is how many great balancing features this game has which Attila and Warhammer got rid of. I believe the Total war franchise is getting increasingly easier (and therefore a lot less fun) from Rome 2 onwards, so Rome 2 is an interesting balance of the difficulty and immersion of older Total wars, with the features and graphics of the newer ones.

There are better games that have developement teams dedicated to gameplay rather than just E-Sports and Cash Shops. (Dont mind the cash shops and the cool skins, but when you play 6 matches in a day and get stomped each time, you can't get enough points to get the cool stuff.) Most losses came from playing with people who had no clue how the game worked, didnt buy items, ran in and died everytime, or could not follow up anything. Soooo, I would recommend trying the game out, but don't spend any money unless its a game you really really feel your gonna be dedicated even when matchmaking sucks the soul out of you. As for me, I've had much more frequent fun, close games with Overwatch, Dota2 and LoL.
