Short but fun.
Review disclaimer; I only played story mode through on the easiest setting.
I ultimately got this game in a bundle but it has caught my eye for a few dollars on sale before too. For those kind of prices, it is a downright steal. The visuals alone (once the comic border and FOV was tweaked via config file editing) are worth those bargain prices of admission. This game is a looker first and foremost. My extremely short 4.6hr play time through the story mode is actually extended some by me just stopping and staring at scenery. The gun play is satisfying and some bullet time features and a decent enough perk system keep things interesting enough throughout. The story telling and narration directly influencing gameplay and the level's landscapes was an interesting angle to take and I mostly enjoyed it. Far from perfect but very interesting. Overall the atmosphere was really immersive, I could feel the dust of the desert and smell the trees in the mountains.
It isn't all good. The game takes the quantity over quality approach to enemies. They show themselves, they run for cover (or don't) and shoot periodically. That's it. You slaughter hundreds and hundreds. The difficulty options don't change much, they just shoot more and take more. The duels that take place are going to be a love or hate experience for most anybody. I personally found them clunky and not very enjoyable. And then there are sprinklings of quick time events. I can take or leave QTEs but I know they don't get some people too excited. The length of the story would be a bit tough to swallow if it wasn't for the bargain of a bundle. Then the provided video options are far too minimal, but some config file editing expands your options. The game does run smooth and fine though so it is an acceptable port if that's what we're labeling it.
Overall its a gunslingin' romp of a good time through some gorgeous levels that I can comfortably recommend for under the $5USD mark. I think a cover system, less but more tactical enemies, a longer campaign, and cleaned up duel system could've made this an all timer. The good is that good that greatness is within it's grasp. It just left me wanting more. Not in a way that makes me want to repeat the story mode again or play the arcade mode. But in a way that I wish there was just a bit more to it.

I played Total War since the original Shogun.  This series took a hit with a sub-par Empire edition, but rebounded maginificently with Shogun 2, which I still play fairly frequently even after 6 years.  Rome 2, however, is a bit of a let down for me.  First, I was hoping CA would take the franchise in an unexplored direction, like possibly the 3 Kingdoms era or 30 Years War, or Great Northern War, or Mongols (not as a sidebar to Medieval, but as the focus of the game).  Yet the 'C' in CA seems to have run its course.  There are so many other eras of history they could've zeroed in on, but I guess that dead horse named Rome hasn't been beat enough.  Secondly, they actually had some great concepts in this game, but simply underexecuted.  Overall, the game is OK, but CA isn't supposed to be putting out OK stuff so this one really had me bummed.
They attempted to introduce a degree of role playing by increasing the importance of generals.  Armies are led by generals.  The practice of building leaderless armies as was allowed in previous TWs is no longer possible.  I'm OK with and even prefer a design where the leaders are so important you develop a bit of an emotional tie (like ROTK VIII or XIII).  I found dealing with leaders and worrying about all their stats and how it affects the area to be more of a distraction.  IN the end the leader was no more than a face with some associated numbers.  You can succeed in all aspects of the game with not so great leaders and I eventually stopped wasting time considering what leaders to put in charge.  I just clicked the first one my pointer fell on.
I was also fairly excited over the idea that there are multiple political factions within the overall faction.  I didn't realize when I started playing that I would actually have situations where I put another faction's leader in charge of my Armies.  They tried to implement something akin to the intra-factional rivalries like they had in the first Rome.  I think the first Rome (fantastic game by the way) had it right.  Just make the intra faction rivals into their own playable faction.  If we're going to recycle old ideas might as well recycle some of the good ones.  I still have yet to see a civil war start in any campaign I've played or even any slight negative affect from having another faction's leader in run my Army.  I'm just not sure what the point was to the way they did it.
Another issue with the leaders is you only get so many slots to form a legion.  Again, I think they did this to improve the role playing aspect.  So, if you build a strong economy, get super wealthy, and think you're going to build a bunch of armies you will be suprised to see that you in fact cannot build all the armies you want.  This is actually a ridiculous restriction considering how the Romans raised and lost and raised and lost and raised and lost armies when Hannibal went on his Rock the Vote Tour in Italy.
The 'Hero' agent also seemed pretty cool at first.  But that turned out to just be another icon on the board to account for and increase the time you spend managing details on each turn.  The heroes are interesting, but ultimately their payoff is too minimal and unexciting.  I think an excellent improvement to the hero agent would be if once inserted into your army they were actually associated with a specific unit and given certain boosts and abilities to that unit and other units within a given proximity to that unit.  Other than that, they act more like saboteurs/shinobi type guys who degrade an enemy's army.  They've just taken previous agent functionality and wrapped it in a new skin.
The buidling tree is typical of what you see in other similar games, just packaged differently.  But I do enjoy the variety in the buildings and the ability to assign developmental focuses in different provinces.  I appreciate the fact that I can't conquer an area 500 miles from Rome and immediately start recruiting high quality legionnaires.
The naval combat in Rome started out very fun.  I loved ramming my enemy's ships.  But after awhile it became repetitive.  Overall I still like the naval combat, but the novelty wore off quick.  Even better, I love the fact I can land my ships on shore and use my crew as an Army.  That is an excellent feature I believe they got right.
Again, you will have fun playing this game at least in your first few campaigns.  It isn't a bad game.  It's just that my expectations for the Total War Series are very high and this fell well short.  I would not recommend this game simply because CA needs to be sent a message that customers aren't going to accept a product that largely pieces different aspects of previous games together and only scratches the surface of that increasingly meaningless first word of their name.

An honest review:
Okay, so a lot and I mean a LOT have been disappointed with Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. So, you right now, reading this, might be wondering "Should I get this game?" Well, here is the answer. (In details)
The beauty of this game is not in the scares, nor the chase scenes, nor graphics but also with the story itself. It does have its moments, and it does have its creepy scenes, just not as good as Amnesia: The Dark Descent. The true beauty of this game is in its story. The story of this game in my opinion is just really nice. There is a lot of hidden symbolism that I think everyone should appreciate (I do) What makes this game unique is the fact that this story can be/is related to our modern lives in a way or another. It also relates to our parents and grandparents. What I liked about this story is that we can all relate to it somehow which makes it a little better. The story in Amnesia: The Dark Descent is amazing as well but I have not seen such similar hidden symbolism. Those messages throughout that adorn the story make it stand out. Sure it may be a little complex to comprehend and maybe the story may not be explained as much due to some reason which I will explain a little further but it is a really good game if you look at it in a different perspective. Okay, so this game somehow relates to political movements and actual tragic events that happened where some people might be offended if elaborated in the game. Those who understood it appreciated it and those who did not understand the hidden messages and symbolism found that it made no sense and that the story sucks as well. I really liked this game due to its story.
If you are looking for:
-A game that will make you feel scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
-A game that has terrifying chase scenes.
-A game that has extra ordinary graphics.
-A game with complex puzzles that will need you to think heavily.
-A super long campaign that will take more than 10 hours of gameplay.
Then this is not the game for you.
If you are looking for:
-A game that has some terrifying scenes but not the scariest out there.
-A game that has a beautiful story with hidden messages throughout long notes found during the gameplay.
-A horror game that concentrates on storyline more than to try to spook you.
-A game that has an average length of gameplay (neither short nor long).
-A game that has descent graphics yet not the best out there.
Then this might be the game for you.
Honestly, I don't like pointless games that just want you to feel scared for the sake of it. Also, for the people who say they could have added more scare scenes and some enemies that cannot be avoided easily then I will have to say it may have worked but then it would seem to be a little unnecessary. I mean, like in some games out there where they just overload with jumpscares and that after a while gets frustrating. (In Amnesia: The Dark Descent the amount of scares and chase scenes is just perfect) but in other games like Outlast or the DLC of it to be exact feel a little repetitive and just too sloppy. You would only like the game if you want to feel scared. Also Alien: Isolation is an example that the scares just feel that they are too much and you keep dying constantly. Luckily, I like both haha, games that make me feel scared and games with good stories! Anyway, if you are planning to buy this game but not too sure buy it now when there is still a sale! Happy holidays!

I will be making this relatively short review a positive one for one reason alone.
That is that it's not a review of an Amnesia sequel.
Much more so than its predecessor, the game feels and acts like an interactive movie, being 110% linear with less exploration than a retired Indiana Jones trying to find his way to bed. It is, like previous titles, heavily narrated at certain points, and most of the story and background story is told through this narration, or pieces of paper. While it does indeed have a very interesting story, any survival horror game should focus on a mix between both story, gameplay/immersion, and ambiance, one of which is lacking almost entirely to most players because:
If you go into this expecting an Amnesia experience, you're going to be extremely disappointed and left with horrible gameplay that is impossible to immerse yourself in the way you're used to. But if you remove the word "Amnesia" from the title, and focus on it as a standalone survival horror game, it tries and does a relatively good job compared to other titles of the genre when the game came out. Inventory, oil, insanity, all is removed from the game because believe it or not, it ruined immersion at the worst possible times, by making you fall over and gurgle at the mere sight of an enemy, tumble around the dark tediously clicking everything... Before falling over and gurgling at the darkness, or by just leaving you clueless and aimlessly wandering back and forth until you find that one thing you use once and never again to unlock the next area of exploration. This game removes all of these tedious, immersion-breaking aspects and leaves you with a fully immersive game that does not feel like a traditional game at all.
A Machine For Pigs is an immersive experience above that of The Dark Descent... If you have not played The Dark Descent. And if so, I would recommend that you play this before playing The Dark Descent, as this game WILL disappoint you, should you play its predecessor first.
Remove "Amnesia" and I give it a solid 8/10 as an independent horror game. Should I have reviewed it as a sequel, I'd have given it a 2-3/10.

Papers, Please is certainly a unique and interesting experience. The game tasks you as an immigration inspector at the border of the fictitious country of Arstotzka. You job is to approve or deny entry into the country based on whether there are discrepancies in the paperwork presented. Although it may sound like something you should be paid to do in real life, it is actually quite addictive.
Papers, Please starts off a little slow, but as you progress it becomes increasingly more interesting. As you continue to approve or deny entry, the game presents you with subplots that keep you interested. I find that this is the highlight of the game. For instance, some people may ask you to deny access to another person down the line, explaining that if they are approved they could be killed by them. This presents you with an interesting moral dilemma: Deny that person access, even if they have the correct paperwork, and take the penalty for an unauthorized denial, or accept that person anyways to avoid penalty. This plays into the other aspect of the game which is maintaining the health and welfare of your family. You are paid based on how many people you correctly process. Although you are allowed two mistakes per day without cash deduction, you still only make a certain amount of money to pay for food, rent, heat, and medicine.

Each level is broken down it days. You are presented with a time limit to correctly process as many people as you can. This provides you with another interesting choice: skim through the paperwork and risk taking penalties, or be meticulous and thorough. I found that a happy medium between both was the best option. Although I usually made a few mistakes and took a few penalties, I was able to make a decent amount of money at the end of the day. This encompassed with the moral dilemmas presented means you are never bored.
The only problem that I had with this game was that sometimes I felt a little overwhelmed with all the decisions. In addition to regular inspection and subplots, each day added additional rules that you have to follow. For example, on a new work day, all immigrants from a certain country were required to be searched every time they came through the checkpoint. It may not sound like much, but with all the other things to consider, sometimes it can be easy to forget.
On the flip side, at the end of a hard day’s work, you are tasked with deciding what to spend your money on in regards to your family. You may want to save 20 credits for later, but your family goes that day without eating. There is no time limit on these choices. This offers another interesting gameplay element, but it is also a welcome break from the timed work day.
Although the graphics look like this game is from the 16-bit era, the presentation is flawless. The gray backdrop of the inspection checkpoint makes you feel like you’re actually working a desk job in a Soviet-like country. The closest thing I can compare it to is the movie adaptation of 1984.  The further notion that you were chosen to do this job by a labor lottery helps solidify this. Also, this may be a subtle detail, but having desk in front of you in which to drag and drop paperwork, pull out approval or denial stamps, and look at your rulebook adds to the realism of the experience. This makes the game feel less like…. well…. a game and more like an actual job. Having the ability to actually hand people their paperwork instead of pressing a button simply makes the illusion more real.
All-in-all, Papers, Please is certainly a game at least worth trying, although the $10 price tag is a little steep in my opinion. It may seem like a simple game on the surface, but it is actually a thought provoking experience. The only players that I think should stay away from this game are those who do not like racing against time. If you are looking for a more relaxing indie experience, I would not recommend this game. Otherwise, Papers, Please is a fun and interesting experience that any gamer would enjoy. This absolutely deserves my recommendation.

World of Goo came out during a time where physics-enabled flash games and independent indie puzzle games were all the rage. This trend may have largely fallen out in recent years, but World of Goo stood on top of the mountain of mediocrity, largely for two reasons. Firstly, the game was polished; every level is interesting, provides a thoughtful challenge, and the game's overall structure is well-paced, so there's little frustration and a good rate of 'oh, I get it' moments, which steadily takes you from being confused as to the mechanics to understanding every possible combination of gooballs. Second, the game has an interesting emphasis on storyline; you wouldn't expect a silly, random puzzle game like this to have much in the way of story, but World of Goo manages to have a strong atmosphere and a subtle narrative worked into the levels that makes the experience far more driven and cerebral than a straight puzzler would be. World of Goo is well worth the time it takes to see it to the end.

Over the last couple of years I have regularly asked myself why I keep getting involved with early access titles. The reason why is that every so often you uncover a real gem. Kingdoms is without doubt one of those. It is rare in my gaming life, which spans decades, that I have come across a game so well put together with its gameplay, music and sheer concept. I have enjoyed the hours I have already spent ingame immensely, and fully expect to spend many hundreds more. The way the AI developes the town, the way you have' wow' moments from the scenery at dusk or dawn, the overall impact of thunderstorms and the freedom to play the game the way you want to all combine for a really compelling game.
All of these wonderful points though are secondary to the most vital piece needed for an early access game to come to fruition, and that is the developer. In all my years of gaming I have not found a developer so devoted to a project as this one is. It isn't so much a project, it's a labour of love. It has already been a privilege to see what he has accomplished since the  game launched over 18 months ago. It is perhaps unique in my experience to see a developer so devoted to his dream and still producing updates, comunicating with his community, and driving his game forward at this stage of the games development.
Don't let the fact that this is an EA game put you off. This one is special.

This game made me fall in love with Rome Total War again.  Literally.
I put countless hours or enjoyment into RTW and M2TW back in the day.  Empire Total War was a disappointment for me and I drifted away from the franchise, but when I learned that R2TW was out I returned to the fold, assuming that I'd get an updated version of the experience I loved so much with RTW.
Sadly, my hopes were dashed.  R2TW somehow misses out on all the joy that RTW captured so well, and I'm not quite sure why.  I played it for a while back in 2014 and didn't continue for long.  Picked it up again recently to see if I could figure out what the problem is, and gave up again after about a week.  It could be the Stacks of Doom that all the AI factions seem to have, far outweighing their territorial resources.  It could be the lack of so many of the cinematic elements that made the original so movie-like (most notably the absence of Jeff VanDyck's excellent score), or the general inscrutability of the game design that makes it difficult to know what's going on in one's empire at any given moment.  But the sum total is that playing the game just isn't *fun*.  I'd say the only improvements over the previous version are the snappy graphics and the increased faction variety and detail.  Everything else felt like a step backwards.
Just in case I had rosy spectacles where the original game is concerned, I blew the dust off my old CDs and reinstalled RTW.  And I have to say the magic is back!  Even with the old-fashioned graphics, RTW is still a blast to play.  Now if only I could get a version of RTW with the newer graphics and factions...

Final Fantasy XIV is a beautiful game. The world design is wonderful, bringing life to new areas with each update. Dungeons are fun, interesting, and easy to get into. While there is a primary storyline, which you need to follow to unlock different aspects of the game, a lot of the side quest are unique and very filling. When I say filling, I simply mean that there is a lot of "stuff" to do. From slaughtering cacturns, to exploring new areas; each quest comes along with an interesting narrative.
When I first started to play, I joined up with two pals from beta. They were significantly higher level than me, but were able to help me by lowering level to match my own. It really made the game more fun, and we got a few good laughs out of the dungeons. They had me join up in their Free Company, and now I've got lots of people to just hang out with and dungeon run with.
Sure the cost isn't exactly cheap, but it is easily worth the monthly fee. Besides that, the only real issue is that even on the lowest graphics, it can still slow down a computer to a crawl.

FFXIV is an entertaining, consuming and user-friendly game. Square Enix has made it very easy for the people that like to play a variety of different character classes. No need to keep different characters going, just swap out your primary weapon (or tool) and poof, you've changed class. The limits on what you can hold are so high (especially when you acquire the two free retainers) that managing your inventory isn't a problem.  And there are regular adds of both new features and new game areas to keep you occupied for a very long time to come.

Beautiful and Addictive-
The world is breath taking and emersive. Sound track is Light and easy to listen to , though can be repeative- FF fans will reconize several key sounds ie the victory music in boss battles.
Character customization- is deep , you can spend hours tinkering with every detail of your hero, near impossible to find two characters that look the same (Which is a great thing!) well except for some of the npc but thats fine. There are also Vanity quests you can do at about lvl 15 that will alow you to dye your clothing and change your hair and makeup/tattoos. They are abit hidden but there are guides that show you where to find them.
Class customization- is easy and fun. At level 10, after completing corisponding guild quest you can change classes  and pick up craft/ gathering jobs. there is also a cross skill mechanic which allows you to customize your skill sets. You can unlock class jobs buy getting one class to level 30 and another to level 15. Also I found it nice that there is a exp bost for secondary classes based on the lvl difference between it and your highest class. It was wonderful to only have to have one toon to try all the classes- As simple as changing your weapon.  (Granted I like having a few toons just bc I think certain races look funny as certain classes and I like to create tooks for a specific look )
Questing is fun and fresh - You dont feel a grind. though the traveling between the three main continents can be a bit tedious, especially if you die in Grandia and forgot to set your home crystal so you revive all the way back in Limia. Highly recommended, albeit short title.  It's hard to have a compelling story in a single player shooter, but Gunslinger gets it right with its interesting narration throughout, as told to a bunch of bar patrons.  As the star gets called out on overembellishment or recalls missing pieces, the game changes with it; paths open up, the weather changes, or even entire sections are replayed.  The campaign is short (took around 4 hours on hard), but it is a perfect length I think for a story like this and it doesn't overstay its welcome.
The shooting is also solid and while there isn't a whole lot of weapon variety, the pieces provided do make you feel like a gun slinger.  A few iterations of bullet time round out this western; nothing cooler than making a split second reflex button press and dodging an otherwise fatal round.
Worth a look if you've got a few hours to kill (the game also has speedrun/leaderboard items to add to longevity).

Cons:

As a Korean MMO, one should expect a game with a lot of grinding and Tree of savior is no exception. There is grinding, especially the higher up you go, but there is a little grace added to the usual formula by adding EXP resets. Every so often, the amount of exp required will reset to a ridiculous low value which gives the player a short break from all the grinding.
Questing in this game is also somewhat of a grind. I find myself, and most other players I've met, simply spamming through quest dialogues. I would suggest that part of the reason the quests are a grind is attributed to the fact that the lore of the story is only appealing to a small minority--at least in its current execution. The quests are hit and miss, some are pretty interesting, while some are just bland extermination or fetch quests.
Leveling is very interesting. By completing quests, you receive EXP cards which can be consumed immediately or used a later date to give you fixed amount of Base/Class EXP. This is a very interesting addition to a leveling system which helps ease the need to monster grind. Exp Cards also drop rarely from monsters and can be obtained through the PVP reward shop. I didn't find leveling too difficult. I would advise new players to look at leveling guides, specifically a quest leveling guide, and proceed from there. This game can be quite harsh if you go in blind--unless you're just trying things out.
The environment is excellent. Beautiful artwork in not just the characters, but the terrain as well. The game is somewhat open world, but the quest line, and leveling progression is extremely linear so it won't have same feel as Ragnarok Online fur example. The environment though is definitely a strong point for me.

World of Goo is an excellent game (primarily) about building triangular-based structures by stretching Goo Balls. The goal is to use whatever utilities possible to get a certain amount of Goo Balls to a pipe. And the game introduces QUITE A LOT of goo ball variations (from balloons to flingy Goo Balls). The game's story-telling via the Sign Painter and atmosphere are little things that leave an impression. The soundtrack is also amazing and fits perfectly with the setting you're put in.
I've only had a few problems with the game. The first being its reset system. You're only given a couple of chances to rewind time, and most times you have to do it twice since the first sends you to a time when your structure is still falling. I've found myself restarting levels when I was at the end and made one mistake often. The second is the difficulty spike during the end-game. It's possible (I did it, after all), but the first level of world 5 must've taken more than an hour and halted my craving to play for a while. Also, OCD goals (getting the maximum amount of Goo Balls possible to the end)...I'm not touching that. But if you like a really tough challenge, go for it! Finally, the game takes dominance of your screen, so don't expect to do anything else on your computer without leaving the game.
Overall, World of Goo is great due to its consistent freshness of mechanics as well as its nerve-wracking and sometimes emotional gameplay. It's one of those indie games that isn't as recognized as it should be. Go give its creators a sale at whatever price you think is worth it ($10 isn't bad for the 6 or so hours it took to beat)!

It's an easy to learn game, with helpful tips and flavor-text for skills, proffessions, buildings, etc. The only learning curve will be for adapting to the current stage of combat, which is constantly being worked on. Unlike your typical hack and slash RPG, this puts an emphisis on how you are a part of the world, not the prospective overlord that can single-handedly cut down armies. You will start out on par with your everyday NPC and will have extreme difficulty fighting hostile wildlife. Over time, you will get better equipment, better skills, but still have the same amount of HP, which means that while you can do more damage, and the damage you take is less, it will ultimately come down to your skill.
The A.I. is a fresh take on survival/rpg/city-builders. You impact the world, but this world is very well and happy to exist without you. If the player takes zero action with any of the settlements that are randomly built by these A.I. NPC's, they will still build, thrive, and eventually follow their own individual destinys. You are a part of the world, not thee world.
Overall, this could go on for many paragraphs, but the end point is this; It's a good game, but it's Early Access, so if you want to be a part of a growing game, with an outstanding community, and a dedicated developer, then hop on in. It will be an adventure, as new content comes out. Don't expect to be thrown into Mount and Blade, Skyrim, or any other major known title just yet. It's moving towards being a game of reknown, with elements from many different titles, to include the ones above. First person combat, with 3rd person coming in the future. Army leading, village development, ranks, titles, etc.
If you like... Mount and Blade, 7 Days to Die, Subsistence, Elder Scrolls, Life is Fuedal, or any others like that, then I would strongly suggest trying out; Kingdoms.

This game made me fall in love with Rome Total War again.  Literally.
I put countless hours or enjoyment into RTW and M2TW back in the day.  Empire Total War was a disappointment for me and I drifted away from the franchise, but when I learned that R2TW was out I returned to the fold, assuming that I'd get an updated version of the experience I loved so much with RTW.
Sadly, my hopes were dashed.  R2TW somehow misses out on all the joy that RTW captured so well, and I'm not quite sure why.  I played it for a while back in 2014 and didn't continue for long.  Picked it up again recently to see if I could figure out what the problem is, and gave up again after about a week.  It could be the Stacks of Doom that all the AI factions seem to have, far outweighing their territorial resources.  It could be the lack of so many of the cinematic elements that made the original so movie-like (most notably the absence of Jeff VanDyck's excellent score), or the general inscrutability of the game design that makes it difficult to know what's going on in one's empire at any given moment.  But the sum total is that playing the game just isn't *fun*.  I'd say the only improvements over the previous version are the snappy graphics and the increased faction variety and detail.  Everything else felt like a step backwards.
Just in case I had rosy spectacles where the original game is concerned, I blew the dust off my old CDs and reinstalled RTW.  And I have to say the magic is back!  Even with the old-fashioned graphics, RTW is still a blast to play.  Now if only I could get a version of RTW with the newer graphics and factions...

The good:
Great time period, total war game
Lot of interesting factions
Moddability(although worse and severely limited in comparison to pre-shogun2 titles due to lack of moddable encyclopedia/no built-in viewable database). There are some great mods, such as DEI.
All in all, everyone can see the hours I spent with this game (though they may not entirely represent actual hours played), so I probably got my worth of money out of this - but there are some things that if improved would make whole game instantly better:
The bad:
1) Zooming out of battle is essentially like minimizing all the objects, without any significance of the overall mass - imagine that because if you fly in baloon and would be looking at lot of grassland, you may miss the lonely tree here and there, but you would certainly see a forrest - In Rome 2, you should be able to see mass of units and mass of pikes, but everything becomes hardly visible at all if you zoom out, and you are no longer able to distinguish even pike units from swordmen. Sadly this is the case even with relatively minor zoomout. So you are in fact limited to about two views - one which is too local, where things look great but it's difficult to control whole battle, and one which gives you overall view but where you actually can't see/distinguish what's where unless you mouse over units.
2) No build-in/moddable units/building browser. Seriously, if this would be the case with older titles, things like Rome Total Realism, Europa Barbarorum(1/2), Deus Vult, A Proper Empire, and many others would have no chance to exist, because most of their content just couldn't be there. Even for unit mods, you can't check modded unit stats, unless you install special mod that extends the unit card information. It's just very sad and ridiculous and not at all worth anything (in ancient history they claimed that it makes maintaining it easier, but that just doesn't make sense if they need to maintain actual content locally anyway - it means they must have extra service running which also isn't going to be free. There just isn't anything good about that, local unit/building/skill viewer should be brought back - even as bad as the current one is, just allowing local one and moddable one would be a huge difference.
3) Bultings capped - same as previous point, this puts severe limitations on moddability, though this one at least isn't as nonsense as 2)
4) No "Guard" mode - at least that's back in Warhammer, in RTW2, your only two options with missile units are fire at will which will not always make best choices, or if you target enemy unit(such as archer unit behind infantry line) and rout it, your own missile troops will happily follow it all though mass of phalanx battle line. There just isn't any justification for dropping that function.
5) Faction part of the game, is not very satisfying - there is almost no control. This got somewhat improved in Atilla, as did many other things(but still no guard mode).

TL:DR Was a disaster on release but CA did manage to turn this one around eventually and its worth playing now. Has a few contentious changes over previous titles but whether you dislike those changes or not will come down to personal preference.
Full Version:
I've owned Rome II since the day it was released. It was initially an absolute mess with bugs and balance issues and it stayed that way for quite a while. However with the release of the free Emperor Edition upgrade the game became a lot more enjoyable.
Rome 2 had quite a few big changes over previous titles. One of these being a more limited number of armies and fleets. Armies are now recruited by first recruiting a general and then recruiting units to his army. You are limited to a certain number of armies with that number increasing as your empire grows. This does mean no more endless single unit stacks running about the map but it means your armies could be more spread out as your empire grows and you may need to prioritize if fighting on multiple fronts. This change was pretty divisive so whether its a good change or not is down to preference.
Another big change comes in city and province management. Provinces are new with each province made up of 2-4 cities. Control a full region and you can issue an edict which will boost public order or production for example. Cities now have limited building slots so you need to balance what you build. Again this was pretty divisive and some may like this change and other will hate it.
In terms of the battles I feel this is the games strong point. The battle and unit animations are great and much improved on previous titles although I feel it doesn't improve massively over Shogun 2 which was brilliant in this respect. But battles are still enjoyable and can offer a fun tactical challenge.
Another area I think the game does well in is diplomacy. There are more fleshed out factions and its possible to build good relations so you dont have factions breaking alliances or peace treaties as frequently as they did in old games.
Downsides are that units dont feel as diverse as they used to. Although the game is trying to be more historically accurate I miss some of the "crazy" units like flaming pigs from Rome 1. Theres also a lot of DLC for this game. My recommendation is only get it if a faction or campaign interests you. They go on sale often enough so pick them up cheap.
Overall despite a very rough start I think Rome 2 has developed into a great game and its worth a try if you've enjoyed any of the other Total War titles.

An unsatisfying, extremely short, mostly non enjoyable, very linear, disappointing sequel without any challenging segments that can be a downright bore.
Some good I can say is that the story does eventually culminate in something that feels as big and grand as they were aiming for. Also, some of the environments and machinery looks very good. But really, I just finished it and I'd be really hard pressed to come up with anything else. And both those come with a hitch or two. The story isn't engaging until it's been built and fails to deliver on the whole "Amnesia" aspect. And the game is horribly optimized so you can't really enjoy anything when it comes to the graphics or gameplay. Perhaps I was the unlucky one with the perfectly wrong setup but I could not get this game to avoid frame rate drop offs (big ones) on any graphic settings at all. At least 30mins of my gameplay time is adjusting settings. No matter how low and small or how high and big I went the frame rate got beat in to the ground at random spots. And thus detracted from the already shallow gameplay and the pleasant environment visuals. But while this was the most glaring and annoying issue, I can't say my review would change much if the frame rate was a steady 60FPS.
Nothing drew me in. You walk. You run. You climb a ladder here and there. You pull a lever. The gameplay is as shallow as it gets. You never have to think or complete a puzzle. You can only interact with what you need and usually its just a couple feet away from where it goes. There's absolutely no mystery as to where you're going or what you should do. Just no confusion at all, no "Amnesia" if you will. While the environments look great there's a lack of atmosphere built. Maybe the sound is just average? Maybe the special effects are lacking? I do not know, but it just lacked the atmosphere the first game created as a whole. An hour in I was already looking forward to the end as it began to feel like a tedious chore even though it wasn't really tedious. If that makes sense haha... I just couldn't get drawn in. There was no intensity or panic. I never felt threatened. Even when enemies have a rare appearance in the game a little jog in a circle around an object will buy you the time you need. Just no threats in the game at all.
As a standalone game it doesn't offer much at all and as a sequel it is downright awful. I applaud the effort and was able to enjoy some late game moments as things built up in a grand way and the story was more valuable than gameplay. But as someone who just enjoyed Amnesia: The Dark Descent I couldn't be more disappointed in Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs.
Throw an absolutely atrocious price tag on top all of this and I can comfortably tell you to avoid this game.

Pros:
1.)  This game is exceedingly beautiful.  The art style is vivid, colorful, and appealing.  The characters look as though they have some Manga/Anime influences, which I really find intriguing.
2.)  The music is once again, like Bastion, superb.  It sets the mood of the story.  It makes me want to keep playing.  I have the soundtrack, and have listened to it for hours already.
3.)The mechanics are definitely interesting as well.  The game is pretty much a tactics game mixed with RPG and RTS components.
Cons:
1.) I don't dislike the story as a whole really.  But I feel that it is lacking.  It seems to be rushed and just kind of ends.  Maybe a play through ng+ will add something to it?  Fingers crossed.
2.) The Cameratas.  They are supposed to be the villains of the game, but I never really got the "ooo these people are d!cks".  Having finished the game, I am rather dissapointed in them.  They felt more like bullies on the playground than the grandmaster schemers bent on changing the world to their whims.
3.)  The battles with the lower-end creature bots were on par at times with the (few in number) boss battles.
Overall
I think this game deserves a chance.  It is definitely an interesting concept.  The Art and Music are what really sells me on recommending it.  The movement and battle mechanics are good.  I can understand why this is getting  majority popular votes, but there are just some things that I believe could have been made more cohesive. (story, bosses)

I thought going in this game would not appeal to me because on the surface it looked too shallow, with a limited graphics style and a top-down approach. And underneath the hood it seemed too complex, a machine-maker for those that really wanted to scale up their experience but maybe a little too much for my general gaming tastes. I was wrong. While the graphics are simplified and pixelate when zoomed in, and the technology can get overwhelming to try and wrap your head around the first time through, it plays out relatively smoothly. There's a large tech tree, a large world to work with, enemy pressure and complex logistic issues you'll need to engineer your way through to progress to the next key products in your chains. And you don't even feel obligated really to pursue a single path. There is an overall goal you're pushing for but there's a lot you need to do between start and then, and you can generally take your time, think and build your way through it without even needing to pause the game.

Pros:
+ Game graphics, from characters CG illustration to background and landscape, are really beautiful, really surprising me.
+ Story-wise it's decent (not the most amazing you can find but it's not really bad-written).
+ Variety in class-combinations, making the gameplay for each player unique (aside from meta, that is).
+ Nice soundtrack (I think more ESTi would be better though).
+ The gameplay mechanics are amazing at least. The EXP curve, Lv. Card leveling, crafting, hidden mechanics... it makes the game really enjoyable!
+ The leveling is getting easier with recents events, though (as of 11/24) /o/
Cons:
- Poor support server-wise for brazilians at least, as the host server migrated to USA, making ping such as ~230ms pretty much normal... it gets worse as LU!G lost interest in the game.
- Most of the mobs are recolor versions of themselves... really, the name, moveset and everything are the same, the color is the difference mostly.
- Although grinding here is much less massive than Ragnarok IMO, there are level caps that you are forced to grind, mainly Lv. 210+, starting from Alemeth. Not really a bad point, but some players may be annoyed by that (I guess mainly Mabinogi players?).
- BUUUUUUUUGS, really, there are a lot of glitches in the game, from simply trespassing the elevator from sprite-freezing in charging skills, requiring me to change channels, that got reduced, actually. As I play with a Paladin, I can say that I have one useless skill (Conversion, that may bug dungeons or not even work) and Barrier, that sometimes doesn't work properly...
- REALLY unbalanced. Silver-making classes (Alchemists, Squires, Pardoners) have a huge tax while selling their services, being a poor way of making money. Swordsman class is really nerfed PvE-wise and in PvP any wizard-class shines, as spells can't miss nor be dodged and their damage are enough to 1HKO an entire party (really). Classes that should get fixed (Paladin, for example, and most of SM classes IMO) are left alone to rot... although they're trying to fix this with Rank 8, those stuff has not changed yet.
It is worth noting that in Cleric-classes some classes are pretty much excluded from gameplay as their signature skills (Barrier, Daino) are sold by Pardoners and SM that don't own at least Rank 1 in Peltasta aren't interesting in party, as the DPS role most times are covered by Wizzes and Archers.
- Some core mechanics from the game are really annoying, like silver-trading is impossible, team storage is Token-only (premium, purchasable from the market tho), trade has restriction and limits, need to lose a Rank 7 to create a guild (Templar).
- There is a fair amount of gold sellers, bots and bug exploiters. Gold Sellers whisper-spam a lot (and, tbh, even in shout they do this), and bug abuse is pretty common in SA, ranging from purposeful channel crashes to seemingly glitch-abuse in refining (seriously, I've seen a weapon +15 with not a single failure, and more surprisingly a shield, and it's said there's a Kepa Pendant at +50, aw c'mon).
- Really, like, REALLY bad optimization. Even tweaking graphic configs, on a (for now) GTX 760 my FPS tends to get nearly to 10, or lower in cities/PvP. Heck, even grinding it's really annoying.
- Devs seem aware of bug exploits, and still they only release some cash shop stuff and don't aim for objective things. This game hyped a lot of players, ranging from ~54k player peak to more or less 6k (according to Steam Enhanced), and yet they put a Lesser Panda Companion to exchange for PvP points, but due to daily obtainable points amount limit, it'd take more than a year to obtain it (50 points per day, 20k points the pet... yeah).
(UPDATE, 26/09) - Excrulon, one, or most probably the best addon developer in Tree of Savior, has just ragequitted as IMC Dev Team is rather incompetent. Although addons are entirely optional, it complements the game with essential features (e.g.: exp calculator, mobs HP/details are shown, mob kills for Vibora EXP Card rewards, etc), so when his addons get incompatible once again it's pretty much over, as other developers aren't so inspired as him.
(UPDATE, 27/10) - Rank 8 is launched, making most Rank 6 and lesser ranks obsolete in damage output terms and turning wizard lifes significantly harder as most new mobs have such a high MDEF that magic damage output is 1 mostly (specially for Sorcerers). IMC now plans to implement gachapon in TP shop (something I'd consider an explicitly cash-milking) even though a lot of bugs are still not fixed (Sorcerer's Morph bug, that still exists since CBT iirc for example).
For most people (and for me too) it is a game with such a high potential ruined by bad devs, and I'd not be surprised to ToS close its servers before someone get that panda pet... (EDIT: seems someone from Silute has nearly enough points to obtain it... oh well ;-;)
Overall grade: 5/10

This game is free, this game is amazing and it is tons of fun when you manage to play it with your friends. Overall a great experience that mainly focusses on two modes. Objective mode where you have to traverse a set of objectives with slightly different item locations/objectives on other playthroughs and Survival mode where you have to survive waves of the undead while protecting a base before getting evacuated.
What seperates this game from any other zombie shooting game is the little tweaks that make this game more "real" and harder to play on first tries. First off it's impossible to kill all the zombies in Objective mode, you have to find a way around them or kill a majority with melee weapons before proceeding. Your inventory is limited, you never know when you need those bandages or if a few extra bullets will prevent the bleeding through shooting.
You can get infected and you can fend the infection off with pills, putting a timer on your actions. You have to look at your ammo count to see how much ammo you have and what ammo type you need for your gun. So randomly picking up ammo with your limited space is not a viable option.
Also even if you are experienced with this game you WILL die sometimes, you can get bitten 3 times and nothing can happen but the smallest slip can let you get infected. And the faster infected look like the rest so their arrival can be unpredictable. There are enough spaces in the maps where being caught alone certainly means death.
Overall this is a great experience, for the same price you can stare at a brick wall or play League of Legends. Both eventually drive you insane, so why not have a go at this?

Since this joke review somehow managed to get attention, i'm going to patch it up a little bit so that it could be useful to potential buyers, here we go.
ESO is an elder scrolls game made into an MMO, it does have most of it's feature from elder scrolls games, but had to give up a few to accomodate with the MMO part. You will be assigned to a faction after making your character, and each faction got their own main story line, there are so much zones and quests, finishing the main story line would definitely cost you at least 100 hours or so, but it doesn't end there, after finishing the main quest, you will be able to travel to other faction's starting zone, and be able to do their main quests as well, basicaly tripling your main quest line gameplay(not counting dlcs and special zones).
--Story--
While people does argue a lot about the story, and some parts of the community said that the story is so bad, i think that the story is... okay. It might not have the best wriitng, and some voice acting doesn't really go well with the dialogue and situation present, but i think that the story doesn't deserve to be called the worst, it's not great, but it's not that bad either.
+Hundreds of hours worth of main story gameplay.
+All dialogues are fully voiced.
+Choices do matter, you can save or kill some quest npcs.
+Memorable npcs(CadwellBestNPC).
-Bad voice acting at times.
-Weird voice acting at times.
-Story might feel generic or boring at times.
-Will feel linear at times.
-Gameplay-
Gameplay is very nice, it has a lot of ESO elements, but had to give up a few to lessen the strain of it being an MMO, such as ragdoll, all killable NPCs, etc. Also, the game allows AddOns, and most of these AddOns are very effective to make your gameplay dozens time better.
+Intense gameplay, filled with dodge, block, and weaving.
+Gameplay carries a lot of depth.
+Highly customizable, with champion points bringing more customizable elements to the game.
+Great level scaling, lowbies could be as contributive as a high level player on dungeons together.
+Good group finder system.
+Intense pvp with sieges.
+Game changing AddOns
-No ragdoll.
-Doesn't feel much like a sandbox.
-Aiming doesn't really matter since projectiles will auto track like in those generic MMOs.
-In game mails often requires the player to change zone before being able to receive them.
--Optimization and Service--
The service and optimization for ESO is great, recently they have done an optimization patch and it enables the game to be playable even on my potato laptop which costs like 400$, and the customer support does answer queries and help players.
+Highly optimized.
+Customer support is not bad.
+Not much server problems.
-Recurring launcher problems.
-Huge game size(70 gigs).
--Community--
From my hundreds of hours of experience on this game, the community is fairly nice, i've rarely seen someone being toxic on this game, people would help each other if they could, and lots would give advices to newer players such as which addon to pick, and how to play the game properly.
+Can join up to 5 guilds.
+Mail is very straightforward and easy to use.
+Guild is account wide.
+So much things to do in group.
-Trading is very... bad without the help of an addon.
-No proper serverwide auction house.
-Even with the help of an addon, trading is still very tedious.
All in all, ESO is a very good game, it's not perfect, but it's still very fun to play with a lot of contents and ways to play the game.
Wish there were ragdolls tho.

An excellent game, I highly recommend it.
Positive Aspects:
- The game is exactly what it says it is. There is no false advertising.
- The game hits the right balance between complexity and simplicity. Specifically: you can automate just about everything. So, if you build your factory correctly, you only need to do any given complex task [once] and never again. This keeps the game from becoming repetitive.
- The ability to craft something in your inventory signigicantly helps from being bogged down by minor details, such as needing just one more unit of that resource and having to run to the other side of the map to acquire it.
- The game is actively being worked upon and the updates actually [improve] the experience.
Negative aspects:
- Honestly, the only real negative aspect I can mention is the lack of a proper ingame tutorial. However, seeing as the game is still in Early Access, this makes sense. It would be a huge waste of time to create a tutorial now for functionalities that are going to change by the time of the final release.
Additionally, there are quite a few video guides and online tutorials available, so whenever you get stuck not understanding how something works (which does happen farily frequently, initially), you can find help in a matter of minutes.

World of Goo is deceptive in how simple and casual it is in the beginning. Using sticky balls of goo, and later other materials, you will build bridges, towers, and other structures in order to complete each level.
What the game does best, however, is consistent innovation in both puzzles and atmosphere. The world is trapped somewhere between cartoonish, dark absurdism and a very light, humorous satire. You will be using goo to aid in a product launch, to judge in a beauty contest, and to destroy the Internet (it makes sense in context). As simple as the story is, it makes the most of the small parts it has.
Gameplay wise, World of Goo is difficult, but never unfair. A few of the later levels took half an hour or more of trial and error, but almost always this was due to ignoring a vital detail, taking too many risks, or simply failing to build a stable structure. Completing a mission, however, never fails to bring a sense of accomplishment, and often zooms out to see the proud structure now standing (or, humorously, the structure collapsing right after the level is complete).
I don't play a lot of puzzle games. Often times I become too frustrated to really enjoy myself. World of Goo, however, was too appealing for me to give up on, even as the later levels did their best to send my balloon-supported bridge into the bottomless pit after five minutes of making it PERFECT.

Guys, I don't even know what to say. I bought this game a while ago, but only now decided to do a review and noticed that the full price is $9.99? If you're like me and have been robbed a few times by EA survival games that promise but don't deliver, then you will want this game. I believe in these developers, they've done massive work non-stop since they returned to the game. Don't even look at the recent updates, go to the forums and look in the patch notes. This game has the biggest potential by far to become one of the best survival games ever. I've been following progress on other survival games like Forest, Out of Reach, The Deep, Subsistence, Savage Lands, etc. and I believe this game will outshine them all.
What I like the most (Pros):
+ Levelling System and perks - not many survival games have this, and it gives feeling of progression
+ Building: very different from other games in that it doesn't take alot of grinding to achieve (although this might change), and as result you can build potentially a village in 1 real day.
+ AI interaction: NPC will cut trees, build their own homes, buy and sell goods, and much more
+ Quests: It's a nice feature, although there's not a lot of quests currently
+ Army: you can hire NPC's to be in your army and you can give them commands, which is very unique to this genre of games.
What I think needs improvement in existing features (Cons):
- Combat is very rudimentary and needs more animations
- NPC models are also basic-looking
- The UI and inventory need lots of work, for example to eat you must drag and drop food from inventory to your character model.
Finally, this game will eventually have multiplayer, and probably sooner than Rising World (at least this game has character model). For the price advertised and the content it offers, I can't recommend this game enough, it's simply a steal when compared to other survival/building games.

Factorio is a game about designing a game you don't have to play. Automation is the key here, and you design a factory on a desolate planet to leave the game you're currently playing which at some point, if developed correctly, plays itself. It rewards ingenuity through sheer laziness, the hallmark of industrial civilization. Mining by hand takes too long, so you build a driller, which needs fuel, so you develop a system of automated feeding belt. You need other materials to make these, and the next thing you know it's 2 AM.
I have actually no idea if this game is any good. It's compelling and addictive, but I don't know if I would call it "good" or "fun". You have to be a very specific type of person to "get" this, and I'm definitely that person, but I'm not sure if I have it in me to go the distance with this one. I garnered an unhealthy obsession with this title for more than 50 hours, and I left it mainly because I felt like I was playing but not progressing very far. It will draw you in like few other titles, and hours will melt away, for better or worse. You can spend hours chasing a problem to its source and then forget what you were originally trying to do.
What the gameplay loop boils down to here is to solve a continually escalating series of problems you create with innovative solutions you design. This is a puzzle game at its core: how do you go from coal miner with a pickaxe to developing a rocket engine; the industrial revolution in microcosm. It's infuriating, challenging, time-consuming, and kind of brilliant.
PROS:
- Fair escalation of difficulty based on your own pace
- Mentally challenging puzzles
- Fascinating exploration of automation mechanics
- Sandbox world allows experimentation
- Extremely moddable (and recommended)
Cons:
- Needs a better tutorial, especially for rails, circuits, and blueprints.
- Once you figure out an optimal solution you like, gameplay can become a tech tree grind
- Fiddly, annoying interface at times
- Overly complicated tech trees that don't show progression very well.
- Difficult to correct crtical errors early in game
- Defense from enemy mobs is a chore
- Large maps are annoying to navigate on foot

I honestly thought I wouldn't like this game for many reasons. I wanted to try it though due to its success here on steam. I have to say this is one of the best games I have played this year. Now let me go ahead and clear up a few things I was worried about before purchasing the game.

- I expected a large learning curve. There really isn't one. Now that's not to say that the game isn't challenging, it definitely has its challenges. Learning the game has a very natural progression. This is aided by the fact that everything in the game just makes sense. The mechanics of the machines you can build are all well thought out and provide for a great experience.
The game is just an insane amount of fun. It really challanges you to continue making a more efficient factory. The addicting factor comes from expanding your factory and improving effiencey. This game is all about efficency. You find one way to accomplish a task, and then continuously refine that method making it more efficient.
If you have even a slight consideration of buying the game, just do it. You will easily know within the first hour if the game is for you.

Also, Duels mode, if you couldn't get enough of a minigame about watching your own and other people's hands. This is a masterpiece.
I've always loved games that tell the story through every single element of the gameplay, and Transistor is no exception. You can choose how much you learn about the characters involved in the story, which is told through the voice of the Transistor for the most part. The voice acting is superb and embellishes an already-compelling tale. The soundtrack--don't even get me started--the soundtrack is massively beautiful, adding to and improving upon the story and world of the game. The visuals are both vibrant and not distracting. And the ending...the ending is exceedingly well-done and satisfying to me as a gamer, and as someone who'd gotten invested in the characters.
What really set this game apart for me was the combat system. I am usually a FPS gamer, so this was a new and intriguing experience. By customizing your chosen 'functions' you're also able to customize how you fight the enemies. In addition to that, the turn mode is REALLY interesting. It takes some getting used to, but the transition period is not overly long.
All in all, Transistor has rocketed to a spot on my list of Top 5 games. This game is a work of art, simply put, a work of art to be appreciated and revisited. I only wish the base game were longer, but it felt perfectly timed.

It's just dumb fun.
You have unlimited trigger bombs, RPGs are lying all over the place, the non-story missions are basically "go to this town/base/harbor and blow up all the red things," and the DLC adds some really awesome stuff (though it's a bit much at full price.)
60 seconds after you press Start you're standing on the wing of a bush plane with an RPG in hand, blowing up SAMs who can't seem to get a lock.
I only have two gripes... and frankly if the rest of the game weren't so much fun they'd be deal-breakers.
1. There's a scoreboard that tells me of 30 strangers who've beaten my score on challenges every time I start the game or load an area. I just... don't care, but there's no way to turn it off.
2. There's no minimap. I cannot imagine who thought it would be a good idea, but every time I'm flying around in circles looking for the last destroy target, pausing every ten seconds to pull up the full pause map, I curse them.
Here's an idea: Get rid of the meaningless scoreboard and put a minimap in its place!
And a bonus gripe: No way to rebind gamepad controls, and the options menus in general are pretty barebones.
It's not a good game, I don't think. But in the end, it's a ton of fun. Wait for a sale though and pick up the DLC pack, it's not worth the full price.

Similar to shogun 2 army movement restricted to destinated paths. Good for chokepoints/ambushes, you no longer witness african desert totalwar.
Province system good design but too gamey: only capitals are walled causing funny iterations like walless Syracuse or Jerusalem. Limited slots also restrict viable designs: almost every province would have similar templates except certain larger four-town provinces with ports where it would naturally be advance/elite troop centres;
Stances almost felt too gimmicky; camps near useless, ambush nice touch but hard to achieve passively, successful ambushes often due to attacking AI's tendency to speed-spam with forced-march. AI with Cav-only army is raiding hell for players in frontier factions neighboring steppe/eastern factions.
Generals/admiral system limits number of armies. Meanwhile no more stack spams yet richer/stronger nations are nerfed.
Cheap levy multiple stack with auto resolve can win most battles. Army tradition too gamey and op- level 7/8/9/10 traditon with 18-24% meele plus charge buff can make eastern spearmen withstand legionaries. with a cav charge from behind for massive damage.
Almost no point to research military first-actually almost no point doing any research as you might as well spam levy stacks and conquer away—as long as you place non-family members on admiral duties with their own boat on patrol duty only, then civil war will be a breeze.
Year-per-turn renders generals' development irrelevant as they die within 50 turns. no longer turtle friendly I mean you surely can agressively steamroll but often you will soon stop playing altogether as there are very little point to continue/sense of fulfillment.
Politics dumbed down, family tree non existant, promotion is a must with op tax bonus/reduce upkeep almost felt dirty to activate but are neccessary to maintain family control via ever-increasing gravitas.
Nice navy action with good variety (you wouldn't get to play them after Attila which itself is a toned-down version)
Graphics as spectacular as always; phsysics arguable (lumps of men versus formation, cavs with their momentum nerf no longer launch dirty pesents as easily as before/ Horse Archers reduced effectiveness (no longer OP?) and Cav-heavy army might become micro-management hell for some. Exotic weapons often gimmicky (scythed/ chariots/elephants near useless. Dogs meh, often you would just levy spear spam plus some fast cav to anti missle and slingers to anti armor)
DLC actually fine imo (as long as you get it on sale)-but without flushed out briton/germanic/slavic factions is sad. Caesar in Gaul/Hannibal at Gates are fun campaigns, Wrath of sparta less so.
Generally speaking while onsale this is a must-buy for people who wishes to conquor the world with levy spears. With regular pricing this is only for hardcore historical totalwar fans. Even that can ignite heated disscussions (army reform/composition/overhead spears/lorica segmentatas)...
From Shogun II to this Rome II is a sudden step of complexity. So be prepared for that, and you will be able to enjoy this game.
All you need is to move with two full armies and auto-battle. There is no spirit left from Medieval 2 or Rome. There are no heroic battles. Generals are dying like flies.

I have mixed feelings about this game.
Pros:
- Setting. Choosing nostalgic athmosphere never fails if you want to make a good game. Not everyone's going to understand, but those who will are going to be excited and thankful for such media.
- Gameplay. (if it can be called so) It's simple, yet at the same time I find it unique and outstanding. It's not just clicking for options you want to say, it's like you're actually interacting with Emily, by "typing" messages to her.
Cons:
- Plot. It's linear. To be honest, I was expecting more interactivity with plot, so I even tried to complete game four different ways. Then I noticed it's all mostly the same no matter what yo choose. It's disappointing, to be honest. It's definitely not how visual novel should be
- Characters. Both Emily and protagonist seem childish and annoying to me. Tons of vague messages, way too obvious hints, avoidance of clear answers/questions... It's like from cheap early-teen drama. How is this possible to be that irresponsible and flabby? They don't seem like people who are going to graduate college. To be honest, they don't seem mature enough as High School students to me as well. I didn't feel sorry for them at all. Maybe a little bit for Emily when she got into abusive relationships for the first time, but later when she choose to get along with her abusive boyfriend again, I thought whatever. Just whatever.
And protagonist? Pretty much boring descent dude who tries to be a typical "nice guy" sometimes.
I guess, cons outweight pros to me.
HOWEVER, I do recommend this game for setting, athmosphere, simple yet interesting "gameplay" and a lot of references.
4/10

So, I've always been a fan of MMORPGs and I'm no stranger to the Elder Scrolls either...
After over 200hrs of playtime, I'd easily recommend this to anyone who enjoys either. The leveling system allows for a LOT of flexibility in your build and progression, and even offers some unusual options for these kinds of archetypes, like Mages can tank, Healers can wear heavy armors and there are many other examples of this kind of freedom to build and play the way you want to. PvP is fun and balanced, and its one of the most relaxed and awesome communities I've ever experienced. Crafting system is easy to learn, difficult to master and very interesting, with the use of styles to allow you to change your equipments visuals. Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a straightforward first-person shooter where you're following the story of a seasoned bounty hunter who seats in a saloon and tells it to patrons, sometimes venturing far away from reality.
Good things about: Story is good. Shooting mechanics is interesting and allows leveling up skills according to three different play styles: pistol, rifle, shotgun. Cel shaded graphics looks good. After completing the story (or instead of playing it altogether) you can still play two different mini-games, one is called "Arcade" where you clean a small location in  a timely manner, another is "Duel", where you, well, duel. There are "secrets" in the game that add good chunk of EXP when you find them and complete backstory. They are not too obscure to find and sometimes just lie in front of your path. Speaking of path...
Things I didn't like:
1. Rails rails rails. The game has a single path. If you stray away from it, you die. That was ok in the time of Call of Duty 2, not ok in the time when Fallout 3/FNV, Skyrim and Borderlands are long past.
2. Ambushes. Every now and then someone ambushes you. Every time they circle you instantly from out of nowhere and start shooting while you have no place to hide. It's *kind* *of* in accordance to the story, but quite frustrating to the player. "What should kung-fu master do when he's surrounded by enemies? Kung-fu master cannot be surrounded by enemies, or he's not the one". People came from behind where you, one of the best bounty hunters, just massacred dozens of bandits?
3. One autosave. You missed the secret before killing a boss? You shoot too fast and got dishonorable killing? Your loss. But if you die midgame, it's all forgiven, let's start again. And yes....
4. You'll die. It's not final, as the game will load previous checkpoint, but you will definitely die. Because something falls on you. Because you spent 2 seconds picking up that secret (yes, either secret or you're dead). Because you fell down 10 feet. It's fatal, don't jump down, that's not Borderlands, guys, that's Wild West, where you instantly heal but cannot jump from the ladder. It's somewhat convenient when you die just after checkpoint (there are a lot of places like this because level designers KNEW YOU WILL PROBABLY DIE NOW), but can we just get rid of this stuff in games? Please?
5. Duels. Duels are goddamm stupid and make no sense from gameplay perspective. You move your cursor for 30 seconds and then click "fire". If this was supposed to be enterntaining, then I'm going to tell you it's not. It's definiteluy not. Stop putting non-optional minigames in regular games. Just stop it. Stop it.
6. Killing ghosts. That level. They come from every direction, they cannot be killed in just one shot except by headshots and you can hardly see them in that bloody fog. That level was so frustrating, I cannot even tell you how. Games should entertain people, not make them suffer.
Anyway, this is a solid game, enjoyable for the most part. Much much much better the first one (I lasted less than an hour, good thing it was from a humblebundle).

This game is a stunningly beautiful work of art. Gorgeous artwork and soundtrack along with engaging storyline and interesting characters set the dystopian mood perfectly in my opinion. Combat mechanic is challenging enough so that you won't pull your hair out but requires you to play smart and try new things. Difficulty ramps up nicely, too.
The game is a bit short but can be remedied by Recursion mode which is basically a NewGame+, and skill UI can be annoying at times but if you don't mind putting extra one or two steps to your gameplay, you'll get used to it.

This is a masterpiece.
I've always loved games that tell the story through every single element of the gameplay, and Transistor is no exception. You can choose how much you learn about the characters involved in the story, which is told through the voice of the Transistor for the most part. The voice acting is superb and embellishes an already-compelling tale. The soundtrack--don't even get me started--the soundtrack is massively beautiful, adding to and improving upon the story and world of the game. The visuals are both vibrant and not distracting. And the ending...the ending is exceedingly well-done and satisfying to me as a gamer, and as someone who'd gotten invested in the characters.
What really set this game apart for me was the combat system. I am usually a FPS gamer, so this was a new and intriguing experience. By customizing your chosen 'functions' you're also able to customize how you fight the enemies. In addition to that, the turn mode is REALLY interesting. It takes some getting used to, but the transition period is not overly long.
All in all, Transistor has rocketed to a spot on my list of Top 5 games. This game is a work of art, simply put, a work of art to be appreciated and revisited. I only wish the base game were longer, but it felt perfectly timed.

Final Fantasy XIV is in a tight spot. Following the poorly-received Final Fantasy XIII and carrying on the legacy of Final Fantasy XI, it has a lot to live up to.
And originally, it failed to live up to this. With 1.0, it had a lot of major issues including XP caps, lack of group activities and general bad design. This was a major problem that could've caused the death of the game.
However, Square Enix did something different. Instead of following the generic "Make it Free-to-play" model, they set out on rebuilding the game. Almost completely scrapping the original game and rebuilding it from the ground up, they made a game that can serve as the true XIV that people wanted. This is A Realm Reborn.
Following the failure of 1.0 and the implementation of ARR, Square Enix decided to keep the universe of 1.0 semi-canon, with ARR following on. Set 5 years after 1.0, there was a catastrophe that served to bridge the gap between the 1.0 world and the ARR world. With many features such as landmass, NPCs and areas staying almost identical to that in 1.0, the whole storyline is completely a new, almost sequel to XIV, with gameplay vastly improved and expanded to meet those of other modern MMOs.
The storyline, although generic, does follow the Final Fantasy formula of an evil Empire ruling over the world with an evil agenda, and you and your companions have to fight against them. With this, it is almost a retelling of Final Fantasy VI, with many story elements shared across the two universes, and this is strengthened in the expanded storyline with locations and characters having similar names.
The characters within the game are all pretty unique, although it does have it's own versions of "Biggs", "Wedge" and Cid". Each character in the world feels fleshed out, with most having their own questlines and stories separate from the main storyline. This serves to flesh out the universe and make you feel like you're in an actual world rather than a half-baked MMO.
Although the storyline is a major aspect of the game, it does serve mainly to unlock additional content, although this is in no way a bad thing. The storyline quests give a good step on leveling up your first character, guiding you through the leveling process whilst not serving to hand-hold the player. Although it is easy to gain levels through quests, it would not be easy for a character to max out by simply completing quests.
Instead, the game has a number of different ways to level up, mostly these are through group events.
Firstly, one of the most commonly encountered events are FATEs. There can essentially appear anywhere in the field, outside of towns and other sanctuaries. FATEs have a simple objective, often something such as "Kill all of x enemy", "Kill x boss" or "Collect all of x". Usually they involve beating on enemies until the quota is met, which is pretty satisfying. These give the player additional XP and Gil. Mostly these FATEs are level-limited, so many higher-level players would not be inclined to do older FATEs or do them if they are max level, however this has been changed through late-game content that requires players to return to areas and perform in FATEs, meaning that they are available for everyone and serves to keep old content fresh.
Secondly, are Leves. Similar to FATEs but for single player, you are assigned them in each town by a special NPC with a unique tasks such as "Kill x and collect their item" or "Plant an item at x". These are pretty fun to pass the time and have a number of benefits, similar to FATEs.
Finally, the most common way of leveling up is through Duty Roulettes. Once a day, the player is given a boosted XP and Gil bonus by performing in the Duty Roulette. By choosing to do this, you are randomly assigned a party for a Duty, which can consist of a dungeon, a Trial (Boss fight) or Guildhest (Similar to FATE and Leves). These are unlocked as you progress through the story, and as it is random you can get assigned to any duty that you have previously unlocked. This means that a maxed player can get assigned to a level 20 dungeon. This ensures that the game is kept fresh and that new players can progress through lower level dungeons without the risk of there being no available players, which is also reinforced as an XP bonus is rewarded for all party members who participate with members who are new to that duty. As you progress, more and more duties are unlocked including high and extreme level, with their own rewards. In addition, once the player hits level 50, an additional reward becomes available as a substitute to the XP.
I currently have 150 hours registered to Steam for this game, and have just completed the main storyline. There are countless other things that I must complete, as well as the content unlocked in the latest update coming soon. This will add large amounts content which serves to increase the playability for both high and low level players.
Square Enix are very good at announcing and presenting new content to the games, with regular livestreams showing off new content to keep up the hype. This builds good relations between both the players and the company. In addition, the moderation team of the game (GMs) I have heard are very helpful, and can resolve most issues. In addition, in the two times I have contacted Square Enix support I have received an adequate response within a few hours.
In all honesty, the game is great. Although it is different from other MMOs I have played, it does have a great playerbase who will help newcomers with any issues. I fully recommend this, even if it's only for the 30 day trial.
