I wrote this as a recommendation some while back though now after much consideration (and noticing it's still priced at US$20) I have changed my stance. Starting with the positive, AMFP is very well developed in its storyline. Though its predecessor was disturbing enough, AMFP tackles on much more deep and *real* issues surrounding war, isolation, opression, paranoia and other dark and disturbing themes. In no way are they generically produced, in fact I was surprised by how well put together they were throughout the entire story even if not everything was particularly original. The art style of the graphics and the soundtrack fitted brilliantly with the combination of horror/suspense and some steampunk, giving a lot of the level design a sense of beauty.
Here are the issues though; it's hardly an actual "game". Granted, I'm not the biggest fan of the term "walking simulator" due to it often being used to smear titles that are actually good. In this case however, this is very much what AMFP is. Monster encounters are too infrequent, and when they are there the Monster AI is amazingly pathetic and will patrol a few steps before changing to another direction, barely moving away from the 4sq metre space it's within. The only AI that was interesting was the "boss" during a rather fast-paced second half and even then, not nearly as unsettling and intense to face as a grunt or brute.
The gameplay itself is significantly stripped down, with no tinders, sanity and inventory system. Even the environment/object gameplay/physics interaction is reduced! Although TDD was linear, it provided many hubs and general areas that let you explore and proceed at your preferred order without any significant invisible walls. AMFP not only has more invisible walls and tighter paths than a COD game, but even includes areas with object placement that are ideally designed for hiding and stealth yet never present any real danger or reason to check them out. Strange how the developers admitted they previously included more maze-like areas only to tarnish exploratory freedom for no clear reason. The story is not just shorter, but also doesn't include alternative endings like before and the voice-acting is overall bellow average and does little justice to characterisation in an otherwise ambitious tale.
I'm almost thankful that I had Outlast to look forward to alongside this as AMFP was a significant disappointment after months of high anticipation. It's really not worth more than 50% its current price. In its own right, AMFP is an interesting adventure game with a few puzzles and disturbing atmosphere. As a sequel to TDD or just a general survival horror action-adventure it is deeply lacking.

Let me start of by saying, if you're looking for a game that is exactly like The Dark Descent, A Machine for Pigs isn't it.
While, I will admit that I would have liked to seen some more aspects similar to that of TDD, I'm still a fan of AMFP. Why? Well, because there's so many jumpscare horror games out there nowadays. Jump scare horror games while, yes, do scare you, are very easy to make and take minimal effort. The Chinese Room could've very easily done just this and given us a half-effort game full of cheap jumpscares. But they didn't, instead they decided to take time and make a game that will do more than give you a heart-attack, it will, instead send chills down your spine and leave you feeling disturbed long after you've finished it.
The atmosphere is spot on, the ambiance is great, the story is chilling and the main character is interesting and extremely complex. I won't give away details about the storyline but, if you're concerned about this game not being connected to TDD at all, it is, don't worry, you just gotta be quick enough to notice it ;). So, overall,  AAMFP is a fresh take on the Amnesia franchise and is one those games, where you honestly have to play for yourself to really develop a good opinion on it. Honestly, it's no TDD but, it's still a great game and worth a play. 7/10

Don't treat this like an Amnesia game, and I can guarantee you'll enjoy the hell out of this game.
This is probably the best horror game I've played since...
Well ever. And for reference, I've played Silent Hill 1-3, Condemned Criminal Origins, Alien Isolation, and System Shock 1-2.
Graphics:
Not the best in terms of optimization, but it makes effective use of late 1890's English Industrial architecture to create an incredibly grimy world. I honest to god felt the need to take a shower after playing this game. Textures are a bit inconsistent in quality, and the scenery changes are a little jarring. Effective use of lighting, even if it looks a little off.
Sound:
Incredible. Voice acting is great and the writing is likewise. Sound design is near-immaculate, nearly every effect fits the world and it's atmosphere. Music is fantastic.
Gameplay:
Minimalist. Doesn't feel like an Amnesia game in this aspect, as the original's point-and-click-esque gameplay has been stripped to the bone. No sanity meter, no lantern fuel, no inventory management, and the puzzles never really go further than "bring object X to room Y about ten feet away every 20 minutes or so". The linear nature of AMFP may turn off many, but it works with the story enough to not be too much of a problem. Not a whole lot of replayability. I played through two 6-hour playthroughs and felt kind of done with the game, I'll probably never play through again. The actual monster encounters are few and far between (easily countable on your hands the number of times you're actually in danger), but the few it does have are effective.
Story:
Grim as hell and with the best ending in a game since Spec Ops: The Line. Might come off as pretentious to some, and the pacing is a little bizarre, but it's definitely one of the highlights of this game. The atmosphere is brilliantly done, and by the time the game is over, you really feel like stuff happened and you were responsible, which is more than most games can claim.
OVERALL:
8/10
Not recommendable to:
People who think horror games are just for jumpscares and intense moments of fear. AMFP delivers a couple of those, but not nearly as The Dark Descent. AMFP knows what it's trying to be: a horror game. It's trying to horrify you a dark story and some really ♥♥♥♥ed up visuals and events, where The Dark Descent kind of fell flat. If you liked TDD for it's gameplay, go play Outlast or Alien Isolation.
Recommendable to:
People who liked Silent Hill 2 but hated its puzzles. Atmosphere is key, and both SH2 and AMFP have the best in the genre.

Upon completion of Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, I found myself rather baffled... This game presented me with an intriguing, thought-provoking, entertaining and most disturbed tale that really had my mind racing all throughout and even after, as well as my heart for much of the second two thirds of the game. The gameplay is rather simple, in a good way; unlike the first game, you can't manipulate most of the objects in the game and there are no mechanics pertaining to the player (i.e. inventory, sanity, etc) except for health. Most of the game involves solving moderately challenging puzzles (not so easy as to be boring, and not so hard as to require the aid of the internet), with a few action scenes wherein the player must flee monsters or escape pipes filling with hot steam. The level design is relatively realistic and rather expansive in multiple cases, and the graphical design of the game is rather excellent. The actual graphics are somewhat average -- this was not a game intending to boast its graphics, but some of its textures are noticably low quality, and the same goes for some unimportant static meshes. These things aren't too prevalent however, and shouldn't bother most people (I just happen to be the kind of person that examines the textures, models and graphical FX closely in games whenever given the chance).
Overall, excellent game. Simple, but entertaining, scary when it intends to be and involving an excellent, deep, thought-provoking and twisted plot.

The game play for miner mayhem is very basic. The games platform is a 1-D base platform where you stand still moving back and forth hit the ores in front of you. The way to hit the ores is simple you move back and forth using the arrow keys on the keyboard.
But there is a slight challenge to all of this, you have obstacles attempting to stop you from mining. But if you’re very careful and fast you can pass these obstacles, which will lead to mining faster and getting a much higher level.
When mining the blocks away to moving on the next objective you are timed by a bar with red inside of it. The slower you go the higher chance you have at failing the level. But if you’re capable of going faster without hitting any of the obstacles, going faster will keep the red bar full so the timer won’t run out. But once you slow down it will begin to drain extremely fast.
Now when most people see these types of games they wonder, what’s the objective to the ending of it? What makes us keep going. Well the developers in this game sadly couldn’t deliver achievements or badges so they did the next best thing possible. What’s that you ask? In-game store where you’re able to purchase different miners as you increase your levels and blocks hit. A small but cool little objective which was added.
In side of this shop / player skin area there are several different skins you can unlock. Now to properly unlock these skins you have one of two ways of unlocking them either A. Reach a high score or B. chop an insane amount of ore. Either way you’ll be playing for a long time to unlock some of the skins inside of the game!
Minery Mayhem was created by a group commonly known as Anarchy Enterprises. There website is covered in newer games they have created. They are also known for older games known as, Coffee Simulator and Moon Simulator. Along with its newer games Tiki man, Ant War and several other games.

When it comes to making games and keeping them going for years ahead are having the basics. Good content, achievements, objectives. This game is lacking a few of those things but still has a great concept behind it.

TLDR: This is a story-based MMO that has had a rocky start, but in the end is better for it.
Having watched this game while it was still 1.0 status and having just finished my time in Vana'Diel, I was rather hurt by the 1.0 iteration the team had put out considering they had experience in the MMO market. I staved off my urge to hop in to the 1.0 version of the game (which was a blessing and a curse). Deciding not to saved money in the long haul, but new comers to the game might be somewhat lost as a large deal of the story from 1.0 was washed away by the 2.0 offering of the game and is very briefly touched upon at the start of the game.
Now, compairing the two as a game side by side; 2.0 wins by a landslide. This offering of the game was a playable game. While my only gripe is that not enough of the 1.0 story was transfered into the new version of the game, it can not be overstated that the 2.0 version of the game was vastly improved from the 1.0 version (see the original review by Gametrailers to see what 1.0 was like).
The game moved to 2.0, a new direction with the story, the game play, and that direction was ushered in by the now lead developer Yoshi P. He literally set the old world on fire with the new story and set the stage for what was to come at the new end-game for 2.0. It would not be until patch 2.2 (and a steam sale) came out that I'd finally make the (rocky) delve into the game.
Over time, more story was tacked onto the game. Deepening the story of Garlean Empire, and the beastmen races that sought the destruction of the alliances of Eorzea. We saw a game burn down for the mistakes of the past, only to rise from the ashes of it's former self that in time would go on to have it's first expansion released: Heavensward. The last time we saw something similar in the entertainment industry was Firefly and it's movie, Serenity.
If you are looking for an MMO with a great story and familiar elements from your childhood, you need not look any further than XIV. We the community look forward to fighting at your side. :3

The Total War series has had some games that are better than others, but generally these games have stayed at least decent enough to be worth playing. Rome II is the best in the series. It not only takes what has been a generally very historically-accurate series and goes in-depth enough to entertain history enthusiasts, but with an excellent variety of factions it would take years of non-stop gameplay to completely wear out the game. There are always new tactics to learn, and with the possibility of choosing anywhere in ancient Europe, Northern Africa, and the Middle East, you have thousands of potential battle locations. I love this game - the balancing is exceptional and it faces none of the issues attributed to earlier games (such as Medieval 2's somewhat broken morale system or Empire's lack of variety) while at the same time maintaining the classic gameplay that has been lost in the new Warhammer games. It combines some of the best part of city/civilisation building games like Civilisation V in the world map in campaign with a slightly more complex but much more fun battle system reminiscent of unit-based rts like LOTR: Battle for Middle Earth 2. I heartily encourage you to get this game, although the pricing (particularly on DLC) is a little on the steep side so you may wish to wait for a sale. This happens often enough - one time it was on sale during the summer sale and then again the week after that sale ended as part of the weekly sales - so you shouldn't have to wait to long if you wish.
Now to address some concerns:
1: Repetitive multiplayer. Oftentimes people are turned off by Rome's multiplayer, as there is a tendency to periodically focus on a particular strategy, which can get old rather quickly.  However, this is an issue with the community, not the game itself. People often like to look at other people's strategies, and unfortunately this often builds into one strategy or another becoming overused - usually as a tactic capable of beating the previous favorite becomes well-known. It is possible to win any battle with roughly equal forces on either side regardless of what tactic your opponent takes. This is because the game is actually fairly well balanced, unlike what some would have you believe.
2: Pricing: I agree, this is annoying. A large number of factions and some side features are locked by dlc. This is pretty much the only downside to this game. Again, wait for a sale. When this game goes on sale, the sales are usually pretty good.
3: Repetitive AI. One replayability issue the game does face is that the AI is only so smart. As such, higher difficulties usually mean the AI is merely smarter about recruiting and management, not so much in actual battles. This is mostly due to the fact that we can only program AI to be so smart, particularly since this is a slightly older game. I personally have not had a problem with this, but if you find the AI to become boring as you become more familiar with the game then I recommend inviting a friend to join you. The campaign is in fact two player, either coop or competitive, so if the AI doesn't provide enough challenge then invite a friend or simply leave the slot open. There are plent of people still playing the game, and usually there are open lobbies waiting for a second player and players waiting to join campaigns, so you should have little trouble finding someone to play against.

This game is largely unimpressive and an absolute disappointment compared to its predecessor.
Admittedly, the removal of the HUD, that is, the inventory menu, and all indications of just about anything, including loss of health and sanity (the latter of which was removed entirely), had a positive effect on immersion compared to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. However, this was quite possibly the ONLY potentially positive difference made between the games, and I use the word 'potentially' very hesitantly. Why? Because, and you can ask ANYONE who has played both games all the way through at least once, a lack of information and indication on your status in the game also causes a bigger lack of things to worry and stress about. And let's face it, what good is immersion if the gameplay itself is tedious and incites no feelings or emotions in the player other than absolute boredom, especially if you made the transition from the first to the second Amnesia video game? In the first Amnesia game, you were always constantly made aware of your health, sanity, objective, and situations/surroundings. The more you let your loss of health, sanity, and light sources get to you, the more you focused on your objective in the forms of memo and journal notes, and the more time you spent being chased by monsters or traversing through eerie environments, the more you'd have genuine feelings of fear, stress, and even despair the more you 'got into' the game.
Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs has a huge problem with all of the above. Health is no longer indicated in any clear or visible form, which honestly has more of a penalty on immersion to begin with. Let's face it, if you're physically hurt, you're aware of it, because of the feelings of pain. In this game, all you can do is 'make your best guess' on your current physical well being based on your memory of how often you were hurt before and how long it had been since then. Sanity has been removed completely, further decreasing the levels of difficulty and immersion while playing, making the game itself even easier than it already is. All that's left is lore and exploration, and a video game composed of nothing but lore is NOT a video game, it's a walking simulator. Objectives are generally more confusing at first glance compared to the first game, but at the same time, they're very easy and tedious due to the fact that they are all marginally you having to walk around to specific points and interact with specific things. That's it. Goals and objectives in this game are basically normal everyday tasks in a slightly creepy environment. Speaking of environment, the next topic, the overall 'feel' of the game simply doesn't seem to fit within fear or horror anymore, and is closer to that of a creepy, almost surrealistic cliché. You loved the original Amnesia and want more, but do not mind a weaker plot and the loss of limited light sources or puzzles.
The spiritual successor to Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but not quite of the same calibre.
I'm undecided about 'A Machine for Pigs' - It's certainly got the Amnesia style and it's a pleasing change to see it taken to a more 'Industrial Revolution' style setting, than attempt to recycle the original. The smart, yet empty, house and the networks of industrial machinery are unpleasantly eerie and set the tone nicely. Crackling radios, the creaking of valves in the distance and the solitary ring of an isolated telephone... certainly a well-crafted environment.
The problem, however, is that a large portion of what made the original scary has been removed. The tinderboxes/lamp are replaced by a lantern with unlimited fuel. Whilst the new mechanic
get used to good effect on a few occasions - There's no longer any dread, no longer any fear and rationing. You don't lose sanity, so the darkness is more an inconvenience than a threat now. The only fear now is what you're likely to stumble upon, which isn't quite sufficient to carry the game on its own. Unnerving, yes - but lacks the same intensity and immediate danger.
The puzzles / environment interactions have also been largely stripped from the game. Whilst I appreciate looking in your inventory and collecting items might detract from the plot: It wasn't an issue before, so seems odd to remove it now. You're left with a more linear path and just having to throw switches / carry objects from A to B.
Truth be told, the main appeal seems to be the story... but that too, has taken a kicking. It feels reminiscent of those films where you're shouting "don't open the door you idiot!" You're being lured deeper into a nightmarish factory by a weird voice who keeps ringing your phone to go "Hurry. You must come quick, it's your kids..." and the schmuck of a protagonist going "Sounds legit. Shall I come unarmed and unaccompanied?"
It works as a horror, but not much as a thriller. It's still fun to play, but it lacks the same exciting tension as before.

It breaks my heart to say it, but this game is NOT good!
Long story short, this game is a "horror" version of "Dear Esther," which was the previous game made by developers The Chinese Room. If you are not familiar with that game, its basically an interactive novel, which could also be said of Amnesia: AMFP. The problem with this type of game is that it isn't scary!
I played Amnesia:TDD and loved it and I waited a year to play AMFP. I read the reviews, both good and bad, and I knew that this game didn't play the same way as TDD, so I wasn't really expecting a sequel to that game. I was ready to play AMFP as its own game and I desperately wanted to love it. However, regardless of how you look at it, whether you compare it to Amnesia: TDD or you take it as its own game, Amnesia: AMFP is neither scary nor fun.
First, let me talk about the gameplay: It's extremely simplistic. The primary point of the game is to turn on/off a giant machine or factory. You would think this would offer a lot of opportunities for organic puzzles as you figure out how to operate a complex machine that you have no memory of creating, right? WRONG. I was never confused about what I was expected to do because the game is extremely linear and usually the switch your are supposed to flip is the ONLY switch you can touch! To make matters worse, whenever you enter a new area, you get a journal entry telling you exactly what you are supposed to do, even though you will already know because it's so obvious.
The second part of the gameplay is avoiding the pigs, which are the main "monsters" in the game. The pig monsters were absolutely terrible for two big reasons: 1) they are NOT scary, and 2) they have terrible AI and are extremely easy to avoid. Every time I entered a new area I attempted to find good hiding places in case the pig monsters would appear, but 80% of the time it was unnecessary because they wouldn't show. That is probably the worst aspect of the game: you rarely ever see the pigs. The few occasions in which you do, they are stupid easy to avoid and don't even kill you instantly, so you can actually run away from them while taking damage and escape!
The other element of the game that matters is the story. The story is comprised of documents found throughout the game as well as "visions" or scary moments that you have in-game. The creepiest part of the game is your character's two children, which appear and do creepy stuff every now and again. Everything else, just isn't scary. The pig's are scary for about the first 30 minutes of the game and after that, you just get used to what they look like. The storyline makes very little sense and your character's motivations are unclear. It is hard to give an example without spoiling, but the best I can give is the pigs themselves. It is extremely unclear why the pig mosnters exist and what the purpose for their creation is. Ostensibly, they are supposed to kill people, but the giant machine already does that on its own, so why the pigs? This question is never fully answered and even after going on the wiki and reading the full explanation, it still makes no sense.
Overall, I was completely devastated by how completely bland, boring, and uninspired this game was. If there is a third game in the works, they need to keep The Chinese Room far away from it!

KINGDOMS... what is it? I'd call it a cross between Mount and Blade and The Guild because the focus is more on building and crafting than on combat.
Ever since I played Mount and Blade for the first time I've been looking for more medieval game worlds that thrive  without interaction by the player. Sadly most devs in this genre are incapable of programming such complex NPC's so they slap hollow buzzwords like "player driven" onto their games as if that is something to be proud of. Kingdoms, even in this very early version is a rare exception that managed to impress me.
A few things that Kingdoms does that I haven't seen anywhere else (yet):
- NPC's build new cities (they don't just run pre-made ones)
- I can start as a humble peasant if I want to.
- NPC's build a trade based economy from the ground up.
- If you want to learn a profession you need to find a teacher that has mastered it. Makes sense, doesn't it?
- You aren't the only one trying to strengthen their position. NPC's will build shops, become leaders, etc.
A few things to keep in mind before buying the game at this stage of development:
- It's nowhere near done yet. The "Early Access" warning is there for a reason.
- Much of the more complex NPC interactions (social hierarchy, faction warfare, etc) is still under development.
- No multiplayer at the moment, but in the works.
- No roads inside of towns or between them. So expect long travel times until you get a horse.
- The game starts you off with you and around 20 other immigrants on a ship. There is currently no option to start with a few cities already in place. So it takes some time before the economy takes shape.
- My biggest annoyance at the moment is that abandoned building scaffolds can't be removed after the NPC disappears for an irreversible reason such as death.
Overall I'm very excited about the future of this game. The groundwork looks impressive and I'll keep dropping in from time to time to see the items still on the development roadmap implemented.
I really hope that the devs will keep motivated and eventually deliver the ultimate medieval simulator!

A few days ago I loaded it up and to my suprise I was not on a hillside surounded by bears, I was on a ship flying towards a coast! Everything was new, I flailed, I noobed, I died, I fell in love. The game of my dreams had arrived.

You can't appreciate this game with only 20 minutes of play, you need to go to the discussion pages and look at the tutorials to play it correctly and get a proper start. It is early access and that means it has quirks and is not wiki-ed and walk throughed. I promise you this, if you like civ / kingdom builders with a focus on rpg style progress you will find a hidden gem here.
You arrive on an island aboard a sailing ship in the 1400's with 20 other people looking to start anew.
You may be a founder trained in the scholarly arts that allow the starting of your own settlement...
You may choose to be a black smith or a hunter, a swordsman or an archer who wants to join a coloney and do your part. Maybe you are a farmer at heart who wants to start a farmstead with wheat and a windmill and the whisleing winds.
You are not alone, ships arrive regularly bringing new people who want to make their own colonies, You will need the help of the others who have come, to learn new skills, to trade and sell your goods, to defend your settlement, or to go to war and take the other settlements by right of arms.
With a huge island of up to 2000 NPC characters, full seasons, and up to 150 animals per square km there are caves of wonder with rare resources and dangerous beasts mingled with wild horses amid wild plants to harvest and sow.
King, bandit, farmer, or artisan, you decide your fate and the fate of your kingdoms...

I spent hours the other day with a friend on our first time on a server.  We clubbed sheep, made some decent tools, eventually got decent armor and managed to get a cobblestone fortress.
Eventually, we managed to get lumber work done along with lots of iron so we could start making an iron fortress.  I read online you have to set doors to "Family only" or anyone can unlock your doors.  So of course, I made sure to lock our door.
5 hours later... we've got chest after chest FILLED with raw materials, weapons, loot, iron and were smelting like crazy.  We decided to take a break for the night, we felt absolutely OP considering we were doing great against other players.  We ended up going after a couple newbies and got some iron, head back to the base and get ready to log off.
I stash all of my good loot (5 hours worth of gathering, crafting, looting) in our new iron chests.
My friend makes an iron reinforced door and removes the old one.  Doesn't lock it.  I've already logged off at this point.  We log in and someone unlocked the front door and took everything.
10/10 would lock the door again.
Pros:  The crafting system is pretty great.  I love that you can upgrade existing stations instead of having to get rid of the old stations.  Mekes more sense.  I LOVE that you can reposition things.  It's helpful with rebuilding a base, upgrading, or MOVING a base.   The map is easy enough to understand critical places/landmarks that you don't /need/ a map to figure out where you're at once you get the hang of the area.
Cons: Hit boxes for things like animals with certain weapons are kind of odd.  Instead of aiming direct center when you're close to something, sometimes you kind of hit off to the side which is kind of odd.  I think the whole locking thing is kind of annoying.  I think by default, doors should be LOCKED for family or player only, and have the ability to unlock if the player so desires.  Automatically unlocked for all players is just begging for all new players to get raided and make silly mistakes that cost them hours of gameplay, or even vet players who make a new door and forget.

Factorio is a game about designing a game you don't have to play. Automation is the key here, and you design a factory on a desolate planet to leave the game you're currently playing which at some point, if developed correctly, plays itself. It rewards ingenuity through sheer laziness, the hallmark of industrial civilization. Mining by hand takes too long, so you build a driller, which needs fuel, so you develop a system of automated feeding belt. You need other materials to make these, and the next thing you know it's 2 AM.
I have actually no idea if this game is any good. It's compelling and addictive, but I don't know if I would call it "good" or "fun". You have to be a very specific type of person to "get" this, and I'm definitely that person, but I'm not sure if I have it in me to go the distance with this one. I garnered an unhealthy obsession with this title for more than 50 hours, and I left it mainly because I felt like I was playing but not progressing very far. It will draw you in like few other titles, and hours will melt away, for better or worse. You can spend hours chasing a problem to its source and then forget what you were originally trying to do.
What the gameplay loop boils down to here is to solve a continually escalating series of problems you create with innovative solutions you design. This is a puzzle game at its core: how do you go from coal miner with a pickaxe to developing a rocket engine; the industrial revolution in microcosm. It's infuriating, challenging, time-consuming, and kind of brilliant.
PROS:
- Fair escalation of difficulty based on your own pace
- Mentally challenging puzzles
- Fascinating exploration of automation mechanics
- Sandbox world allows experimentation
- Extremely moddable (and recommended)
Cons:
- Needs a better tutorial, especially for rails, circuits, and blueprints.
- Once you figure out an optimal solution you like, gameplay can become a tech tree grind
- Fiddly, annoying interface at times
- Overly complicated tech trees that don't show progression very well.
- Difficult to correct crtical errors early in game
- Defense from enemy mobs is a chore
- Large maps are annoying to navigate on foot

Bigger, better, and more bombastic than its predecessor, "Modern Warfare 2" is an excellent production. All of the good elements (the basic gameplay mechanics, environments, sense of "epicness," and so on) have been pushed up at least one notch.
At the same time, the debatable elements have also gone up a notch. (This doesn't negate the "better" statement above. "Modern Warfare 2" is a one-trick pony, but it does that one trick in a way that feels generally more developed than the original.) I felt even a bit more constrained than I did in the original, with missions boiling down to "move, shoot a bit, find an opening, repeat." Because the thrill ride is so pre-planned, there just isn't room to try anything really interesting. This is especially unfortunate late in the game, when a certain mission that could have been an exercise in innovative defense turns into little more than "find a good corner and bang away." The early-game mission with strong stealth elements feels like a tease of what could have been - it was truly interesting, but nothing like it comes up again.
And, at the very end, the game tosses out its core mechanics in order to present a certain dramatic narrative. "Press X repeatedly to view the cliffhanger ending." Sigh.
These issues aren't deal breakers by any means. As a metaphorical "theme park attraction," this game is certainly worth playing. You just have to realize that this particular piece of software isn't really any more than that. The developers certainly made a title to be proud of, but there's something sort of...intangibly "shallow" about how it all goes down.

(EDIT:This is a review, not a tweet.  It is long.  I could say "game good" but I prefer to review what I experienced.  My apologies for those who don't like to read long things.)
186 hours in, as of this review.  First, as we all should know, this is not a Final Version.  The game is in Early Access.... and there is a Beta branch that owners can sign up for, to get a cutting edge version of the game.  That said, changes and repairs are quick.  The dev team is small, so the project is taking as long as it takes.  That doesn't mean that progress is slow.  It just means changes are regular and not huge and sweeping.
The game is growing.  There are aspects of the game that get tested out in the Beta branch, before they make it to the Main branch.... for example, update 17.3 still didn't have horses.. but as of update 17.8, mounts have been added.
What does all this mean?  It means that the game still doesn't have an Autosave feature, and it may never have one.  This is a Survival game among other things.  Sure... you can save whenever you want, wherever you are.  But if you forget to save, and get mauled by a bear... that's on you.  If enough users request an Autosave feature, it might get added.... but the Kingdoms community seems to be OK with not having one.  So it is vitally important to take note.  If you purchase the game, you should expect to participate at some level in the community here on Steam... if for no other reason than to read up on the latest nuggets people uncover about the game.
The game looks nice... and visual tweaks are always being added.  Construction isn't done piece by piece... building scaffoldings are placed, and then materials are added to the scaffolding.  NPCs will place scaffoldings, or post requests for them... and other NPCs can choose to place them.  The NPCs in your town, or any town, will take a hand in shaping how it looks and comes out, if you allow them.  It is possible to stay ahead of them, planning out where everything goes.... but the game is still in Early Access.  Things like roads, lights, fences... that is still ahead.
Combat is, basic.  On the one hand, it is very easy to go into a fight where there is more than one combatant, and you end up damaging them both.  This can make things difficult if you are attacking a wolf or bear that is engaged in combat with an NPC.  If you damage the NPC, you've made an enemy.  The system of communication with the NPCs... what they say, the scripts they follow... that is still all being worked out.  However, there is a certain precision that can be applied in combat to ensure you only hit what you are aiming at.
Kingdoms isn't an action game.  There is action, but early in the game it is more likely to result in the player's death.  Kingdoms is a 1st person Kingdom simulator.  Eventually, you are expected to build.  Whether you start the game geared towards exploration, or construction, or combat, or hunting... eventually you are expected to drop scaffoldings and put wood and/or stone into them.  You can create your own town, or you can find the leader of a town and take over after killing them.
You'll need food.  Berries and seeds are scattered throughout the landscape, but they will only fill hunger needs or heal wounds in large quantities.  You'll need to have things to sell to purchase food in towns... once they get to the point where they've got a bakery or a store that is selling food sold to it by a local farm.  Yes, there are NPCs that can start farms.  Once there is a working store in a town, that farmer will begin to deliver produce to the nearest town's stores.  Kingdoms is a survival game, if you choose to play that way.  That is only one aspect of the game.  You could grow your own food, if you choose to learn the skills.
Crafting is continually being fleshed out.  You have the ability to customize your melee weapon, should you choose to make your own.  There are multiple foods that can be grown from seeds, and produce can be used to make more seeds to plant in farm gardens.  Wheat can be grown, turned into flour, baked into bread, pies are in the works, and there is an alchemy path that can be followed.  Leather must be created from skins collected from game.  Bows, arrows, armor, saddles, axes, pick-axes... all can be crafted.
Guards can be hired.  Soldiers can be hired.  Both can be equipped with the same gear you can make for yourself.  They can be assigned to guard posts, brought with you, told to attack, etc.
Taxes can be levied.  Your town's inhabitants have money, and they will spend it for food or materials if they want to.  Some will purchase a house you create, others will pay to have a scaffolding built, while still others will choose to place their own.  They want jobs to do, and will purchase businesses much the same as they choose where to live.  They might place their own shop scaffolding, or they might purchase one you make and put up for sale.  They will work, and take their goods to the local stores.  Some NPCs will even make their money by purchasing goods at one store at a low price, and selling them to another store at a higher price.  I've watched them do this with Berries, when I flood the market with them at my personal stores in my towns.  I'll collect a few hundred, drop them in my store, and watch the people flock to get them AND sell them at a higher price at nearby stores.  The economic system is being flushed out, and developed.  There is a system in place to set a Town Store... which will lead to trading missions to other Town Stores.  Money is important early on, and will only continue to be important.
Purchasing the game now means being patient while it is developed.  Anyone purchasing Early Access should know that.  However, bugs aside (and they are being found and fixed), the game is coming along nicely.

Fighting mechanics I have never seen in a game before. Graphics and sound are just masterful. Not a lot of content packed into though. I Would highly appreciate DLCs/content patches. The game is extremly linear, but due to the artstyle, soundtrack and virtually infinite combinations of Functions (Spells/Skills) this game never becomes boring.
I will explain what functions are below
Your spells are called Functions. But Functions can't be only used as skills. They have 3 purposes.
For instance you have the function called Get(). What it does is it basically pulls enemies to you as far as its range goes and deals damage to them. There is another function called Breach(). What this does is it shoots an arrow which penetrates all walls and enemies and deals massive damage. You can use Breach() to strengthen Get() to make Get() penetrate enemies and be usable through walls! Combine it with one more function for instance Crash() to stun them once you grabbed them to you! But what if you don't want to use Get() neither as active function, nor to use its abilites to strengthen another active function? Use it as a passive permanent buff! If you use Get() passive, what it does it pulls Cells (Pickups you have to collect after killing an enemy else they respawn) from further away to you so you don't need to take care of them anymore! It is not a huge bonus but it is free and it makes unwanted functions useful.
There is A LOT more to talk about the game's mechanics

So let me start this off by saying I haven't played this game for a long time by any "normal" standards. I don't particularly consider 30+/- hours (my current time while writing this) a good amount of time for "this" kind of game as I have barely scratched the surface, and I realize that. Please keep this in mind as you read / if you read any further and know that these are the points I feel are relevent to the game currently (See date posted). I see a lot of negative reviews and I dove into the water regardless when I normally would stay away. As of now I'm glad I ignored those posts and I wanted to add my two cents with a thumbs up. I'll update this if anything changes however.
TL;DR : It's good despite its flaws and I've had too much fun so far to call it a bad game. Try it for yourself.
________________________________
PROS:
- Beautiful.
I have an art degree, I appreciate art and the quality of certain things. Water-color, meet pastel. Have a baby, name it TOS. Feed that kid cake everyday.
- Sound / Music.
I dig the sounds in the game. It's pretty clear for all your actions and the music is magical.
- Control.
You can use a mouse, Keyboard, or controller (kinda). The UI setup for controller is primarily for combat and a few simple things like map teleportation. When I need to use the mouse/keyboard I don't use it for long.
- Class Variety.
Nothing is gender locked. Classes spread like freakin' trees and your mom's legs. The farther you get the larger variety you get to choose from.
- Story.
Evil jim-jam does evil thing, something Tree, something goddess. If this is your kind of ride there's plenty of track on this text train.
- Community.
These people, especially those who have been here from the "start" are passionate. I've lurked around the "main" forums a bit and they LOVE this game. I see a lot of "Guild Towers" so I assume there are plenty of those around as well and apparently you can have a "base" in "any" map and that's pretty darn spiffy.
- PvP
I am NO WHERE NEAR the end game. I assume PvP is at the end game. I LOVE PvP. This may change to a CON instead of a PRO if I find anything broken or annoying with it but I'm NOT THERE.
- Enemy Variety.
I have not come across a "clone" yet and I can't tell you how many maps I've blasted through. They are just a joy to watch and I find myself sometimes plowing through a map just to see what's next on the other side.
- Skill Point Distribution.
Put the stats where you want, how you want, as much as you want. There are plenty of skills that allow for a variety of builds and unless you look up a "build" I assume that no one is going to have the same thing. I've got a Healer class with more beef than a GMO Cow.
- Weapons / Armor.
Sure you can get a bonus for having a "full" set of armor types but you can slap on what ever you want. There are SOME restrictions for weapons but I still get a good variety to choose from that align close with my class and I think this still squeaks out as a positive.
- Crafting / Collecting.
Lot of recipes for armor, weapons, spells (in a way), items. There are CLASSES that are devoted to this stuff. Enhance your weapons and armors with sparkly gems and big "+" signs. If you complete a "collection" with materials you get permanent buffs to your character from Health to stats.
- Free.
It's free.
...You need more than that?  I think people tend to take this for granted especially in an age where we are flooded with F2P games constantly. Don't like it? Don't spend money.
________________________________
CONS:
- Grind.
I "grew up" playing Korean MMOs so it's like breathing to me but I put this here as I assume no one else actually likes this. I think I got about to level 30 when I first noticed it but it's shoving its genitals all in my face at level 70+. Nom nom.
- Character Image / Costumes.
When you change your class your character image will gain a "costume" for that class. Beyond purchasing other "costumes" with real money there is no other variety to your image.
- Bots / Gold Sellers.
Boy there's a lot. From what I see in game and what I hear in forums you'll be seeing them for quite some time.
- Content / Gameplay.
Whack a thing or finish a quest; This is your grind. There are many like it but this one is yours and it's all you get until much later in the game. (I assume.)
- Enemy Distribution.
Some maps are great. Some suck hard. Prepare your butt.
- No Resets.
If you "mess up" a character, pick the wrong class, choose the wrong skill or stat you're stuck with it. Unless you pay, there's nothing but the "Create new character" button.
- No Direction / Need to Research
Going in blind, I had no idea there were more than 4 classes, what other classes lead to, what stats fit skills for those classes. I think this is good and bad, but mostly bad. It almost made me un-install in the first 30 seconds of the game. Wiki the game FIRST. Check out the classes and play with the builder. Why can't this just be in the game?
___________________________
Conclusion:
ToS is a beautiful game with a lot of creativity and heart. Despite the "normal" draw-backs for a F2P model it somehow feels good to play without any immediate indication that a player has to put money in to continue that enjoyment. It's creative without being heavy handed and allows players to smash monsters or complete quests to earn levels. It's a grand adventure solo and probably even more enjoyable with friends. The depth of progression choice without restriction is a breath of fresh air and is a fantastic carrot on an otherwise familiar stick.

Kingdoms is an early access open world game that seems to focus less on the open world part and more on building a little virtual "Kingdom." As this is in early access, I did ran into some bugs, including random lag spikes that freeze the game every once in a while, glitchy physics, poor ai, (I mean seriously you can go behind a settler when fighting them and sometimes they wont turn around to fight you back) and loading crashes, yet, Iove the concept and the execution of the game's mechanics. One thing I love is the leveling system, it gives a satisfying way to grow stronger without making you feel overpowered even at higher levels, which is a problem with something like Ark Survival, and the more direct approach to the "you can do more as you level up" game design type is interesting as well. Another complaint I have is the building, I'm not saying you should have to build houses piece by piece instead of just clicking a button, I'm saying it should take a lot more resources to build things, it would make the game a lot more accomplishing since it is a fairly easy game when it comes to one of the most vital parts of the game.
Overall, this is an early access game, not finished, so treat it as such, you will get a lot more enjoyment out of the game acting like it is an unfinished product, hopefully the problems with the game will be fixed, this is an active developer and I'm sure things will be improved. But, for now, I am going to give this a 7/10, I enjoyed the game, although how much these issues effect you differs from person to person, I was able to deal with these issues just fine. I recommend it.

**UPDATE**
I can no longer recommend this game to anyone as it seems the developer abandoned it still in Alpha.
**OLD REVIEW**
This game has huge potential! If you like the genre I HIGHLY recommend you support its development!
Also it is already at a very stable and enjoyable stage. And, it is very low priced at the moment. IMO the final release should have a higher price. It is worth it.
In the sea of "survival/building/open world" games currently on Steam, Kingdoms is refreshing for its focus on building and development, and a good single player experience for those tired of the pvp garbage of games like Ark, Rust, etc. It has a full functioning town/economy/crafting system with political and war system coming.
The game is like Mount & Blade, in the sense that it gives you an open sandbox to play your own way and make your own story. In fact it is exactly like M&B when it first came out. The graphics and overall content can still go a long way but the concept is amazing! Like M&B this game can stand the test of time, specially if it opens itself to the modding community after release.
The dev is very engaged and active, and very interested in community suggestions.
You can be:
. The lord of a town you have built from scratch or taken by force (the core gameplay activity)
. A crafter or a farmer setting up shop and trading with several villages to build your fortune
. A trader buying and selling as you travel the land, helping towns flourish through trade
. A hunter living in the wild and selling your furs and meat
. A builder taking on contracts from the local town to build houses and shops for payment
. whatever else will come in development and is in your imagination
PS: this seems to be a one man development effort. I see way too many of the usual negative reviews that forget to take this into account saying it has been out since 2015, or the typical review that ignores they are playing an alpha...

"World of Goo. The second best puzzle game I've ever encountered. This challenging puzzler had me playing for HOURS just to get OCD in one level. There is one complaint I have. Oh, I'm sorry, that other review of this game was posted during the time I had goo for brains, I apologize. Here is my new, more serious review for this game:
As Yoda would say: World of Goo, an interesting Indie game, it is.
It's a medioacare puzzle game that involves building with goo balls, nothing more to say. What you see in the game screenshots is what you get. Basically what you do is build towers and things using these little goo ball guys. The annoying thing about this game is its physics engine, it's too darn realistic, every damn thing I build eventually (but not all the time) ends up crashing down, it gets relentless.
The game doesn't really have a story. A story is there, but it's just hard to notice it.  You'll be too busy fixing your falling buildings and such.
What I like about this game is its variety of building materials, with each one having different effects. The Ivy Balls unfortunatley don't stick as much as I thought they did.
This game has basic game mechanics and some frustrating things in it, but those things can be tolerable.
The only thing that bugs me about this game is the WoG Corp 300 goo-ball limit, it makes me nuts. And also the OCD side-missions are somewhat demanding, so it might take you a while to finish a level in a certain amout of moves/gooballs/time before you start ripping out your hair.
This game is ok, but I wouldn't say it's a Steam (or PC in general) classic.

I recommend The Hunter for anyone that has ever wondered how hunting really is. It's a free game that allows people to hunt Whitetail Deer, pheasant, and all types of rabbits. The graphics and realism of the animal's detection system is as realistic as hunting can be. Hunting is a game of patience & stealth and always has been - elements that are accurately instilled into this game. Don't anticipate collateral noscope headshots playing this.
~Pros~
-Amazing Graphics & incredible terrain with 60-80 fps
-Diverse hunting terrains from swamps to dense forests to the arctic circle
-Great AI and animations that replicates animal's mannerisms in real life
-Very realistic ambient sound effects that are unique to each map
-Surround sound footsteps, calls, & noises help narrow down your prey's location
-Play with friends (for free!)
-9 of 10 maps have something huntable for free accounts
-Realistic Ballistics
-Licenses to hunt other animals can be acquired from completing missions
~Cons~
-(Biggest)You need to pay a monthly subscription for licenses to hunt any other type of animal
-No lump sum payment to just buy the game for all of its content - you must pay monthly.
I have only played the free version of this game and still enjoy it everytime. It is a very relaxing experience that grows in intensity once you're stalking your prey. Once you get your first kill, you'll want to come back for more.
Give it a try, after all, it is free!
---------------------------------------------------UPDATE------------------------------------------
Recently purchased the 12 month Trailrunner subscription ($50) and I could not be happier! They give you 8 guns & an awesome bow, excellent camo clothing, callers, 3 deployable towers, a tree stand, wind indicator, a tent along with licenses to hunt every animal & host your own server.
I absolutely love the stealth aspect that comes with stalking your prey. Using the bow is even more challenging since you need to get very close to your animal to get the best shot. Never thought I'd enjoy the bow better than guns, but when you can silently take out a flock of turkeys/deer/elk etc. it is very fun.
I'll continue to revise this review as time goes on.

In the first Amnesia game, you were trapped in a surreal castle followed by a dimensional monster while being chased by aquatic ghost monsters and former humans, deformed into monstrous servants. The kicker, though? You were to confront the owner of the castle, an alien disguised as a human noble, from another dimension which defies all imagination.
The dimensional guest we are to confront has a motivation for his perseverence in all things. He wants to traverse the dimensions, back to his beloved. After centuries of studying cultures, creatures and the very human nature.
This would be a short and unimpressive description of the a fascinating plot which the first game has. Do the fans even care about these things? No, no one cares about the plot reasoning. They just want jumpscares so they can record their own stupidity on youtube.
What A Machine for Pigs did, it cut out the cheap jumpscares and introduced a hard-to-digest storyline and a character which most fans can't comprehend or relate to in any way possible. The reaction? Not enough jumpscares.
Bottom line, the PewdiePie generation has the last word in any horror game which actively tries to be more than a jumpscare-dispenser.

So let me just get this one or two line summary out of the way first since it's probably a common question. In terms of atmosphere and story this punches Dark Descent in the face, takes its wallet, then pushes it down on the ground again when it tries to stand up. In terms of gameplay it's missing a few things. Including the high level of world object interactivity that made a lot of people fall in love with Amnesia and Penumbra, the inventory, the nightvision and the sanity system.
The monsters, at least in the beginning, don't inspire the same pure existential terror that the Brennenburg servants did. Likely because they aren't as explicitly humanoid like the servants were. But that's okay since even by Amnesia standards this game doesn't focus on enemies. The game is actually better for it too. No doubt because the guys who worked on it are masters of atmospheric gameplay (they're the guys who did Dear Esther). This is also why I wasn't really hurt by the lack of barricading and things of that nature.
Otherwise though it's great. Amnesia is a series that is special to me because it's one of very,
few video games that have actually creeped me out on a noticeable level. This one succeeded at a few points and quite possibly did a better job of it than the Dark Descent during one sequence in particular.
The story as a whole is great. It's delves even deeper into the mind of a broken man even more than The Dark Descent did. Things get weird. I'll say that much. And it. Is.
.
I can't say that you'll like this if you liked Amnesia or Penumbra. Because again one of the major things that made me fall in love with those is missing here. But all in all as a horror game (seems like that is a diluted name these days doesn't it? Usually it's another word for "jumpscare ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t") it's one of the best and in that regard I can recommend it heartily.

After three long years of scouring every nook and cranny of Lordran in anticipation of conquering a new crumbling, pestilent fantasy world , Dark Souls 2 has arrived and we are prepared to die again... and again. While this entry in the Souls franchise takes place in Drangleic instead of the familiar Lordran, players will still take control of a chosen undead to rise up and light the bonfires to stave off another age of darkness. Standing between your humble avatar and the salvation of the damned landscape that surrounds you are numerous terrifying monstrosities and unnerving NPC's who are prone to articulating unnerving and ominous warnings.
In foul and crumbling Drangleic where Dark Souls lays it's scene, King Vendrick thrust his kingdom into ruin after declaring war with the Giants across the sea. Using their souls to construct his castle, Vendrick earned the ire of the giants and plunged his kingdom into chaos with the survivors of the fray turning into undead who must fight to maintain their humanity lest they turn hollow. While the narrative still unfolds in the nuanced manner that characterized past Souls tales, players will noticed Dark Souls 2 features a more refined story. There is still much to be left up to player's interpretations with many details to be found in item descriptions and conversations with the various citizens of Drangleic. Series veterans will find many allusions to the previous games and a few subtle tie-ins. As is customary in the Souls series, cut scenes are limited, mainly used to introduce the lethal bosses that players will encounter, thereby never interrupting the pace and flow of the game.
While Dark Souls 2 does try to draw players in by being a bit more accessible, it would be foolish to think that the series has gone soft in an effort to sell more copies. Drangleic is quite a bit more difficult and unforgiving than Lordran or Boletaria from Demon's Souls and those looking for a challenge will be more than satisfied. As someone who has personally beaten both Dark Souls and Demon's Souls numerous times, I'm not afraid nor ashamed to say that I died on more than one occasion in Dark Souls 2. Deaths can feel a bit more cheap and sometimes unavoidable; but the game manages to get away with it by offering an unmatched sense of reward, compelling players to continue even after the most egregious deaths occur.
Veterans will also breath a sigh of relief upon realizing that Dark Souls 2 has not been made more linear to increase it's mass appeal. Upon reaching Majula, the game's hub location, players are given minimal guidance and are left to their own devices; being simply told to seek the king and gather four powerful souls. The NPCs that you encounter in your travels will congregate in Majula offering goods and services for sale as well as other means of upgrading your character. Certain actions can also result in slight upgrades to the town area in Majula an incentivize return trips. These features add a sense of community to the harsh and lonely world and each change to Majula feels like a milestone in the progression toward the game's conclusion. While having a constant safezone to visit as a reprieve from combating the monstrosities inhabiting the games locales is welcome, the tedium of being forced to return to Majula to level up isn't exactly among Dark Souls 2's strongest additions.
Once players decide to leave Majula, they can tackle the available areas in any order they wish though clever design choices ensure that players are on the path that they need to be without feeling as though they are a sheep to be corralled by the game's level design. Unfortunately, while the game world in Dark Souls 2 is larger than it's predecessor, it's suffers from a sprawling design that leaves it feeling less interconnected and forces players to rely on fast travel much more.  You won't find as many of the clever short cuts as there were in Lordran and as such, Dark Souls 2 provides players with the ability to fast travel from the onset. There are some positives that come from this design choice however, the larger world makes exploration more exhilarating and there is much greater variety in the game's areas. The secret areas and items are more obscure than ever and require plenty of searching to find. Rather than simply having illusory walls that you have to strike to open, the inclusion of walls that need to be activated by enemy attacks, or explosions make them all the more difficult to find.
Combat is fundamentally unchanged but is far more refined. Changes to various classes provide more viable play styles than before. Shields are far less powerful than they were in previous games making dodging and rolling more important as well as making the temptation to dual wield or two hand a weapon for more powerful attacks while foregoing a shield altogether more appealing. These changes wouldn't mean much without a cast of dangerous and disgusting enemies to test your sword and board or casting skills against. Fighting even the lowliest enemy involves a bit of strategy and care and groups can really be a test of skill as you manage your stamina and methodically butcher them. Torches have also been added which are held in your left hand in place of a shield. They can be lit by any bonfire helping illuminate your way in dangerous areas.  Lamps lit by your torch stay lit for the duration of the game, and certain enemies will react differently to light as well, such as a certain long-armed monster that will run and hide when approached with a torch or act far more aggressive towards players without one. When an epic orchestral theme starts to play in favor of the normal ambient noise, it's likely that you will find yourself standing toe to toe with one of Dark Souls numerous and varied bosses. The boss fights are more intense than ever showcasing the game's unique game mechanics. While a lot of the bosses felt similar in past games, each of them feels unique and different from one another in this installment. From requiring quick reflexes to killing enemies in a specific order as well as positioning and memorizing attack patterns, there is no shortage of new and innovative challenges in Dark Souls 2. The optional bosses add another degree of difficulty as they’re quite a bit harder than the final boss of the game.
The art direction has been improved from the other Souls games, as the environments offer greater variety and feel more distinct from one another. Thankfully, this entry relies less on the gloomy interiors of previous titles and features some brightly lit locals that maintain the atmosphere of loneliness and desperation that characterizes the series but aren't as fatiguing to travel thought. Games like Resident Evil and Silent Hill seem to have an influence on this installment as well, as visiting a village filled with crazed villagers and traveling through a foggy forest are quite memorable. Some areas are absolutely stunning though the tech powering Dark Souls 2 is still rather disappointing. Textures can have horrendously low resolutions in some areas and  some really poor tiling can is noticeable on certain structures.
If you’ve never experienced the frustration, wonder, and excitement of the Souls games, now is as good a time as any to start. Bertolt Brecht once said, “Do not fear death so much but rather the inadequate life.” and we here at Analog reviews say, “An inadequate gamer is one who has not experienced Dark Souls.”

As a huge fan of Demon's Souls and Dark Souls, I looked forward to Dark Souls 2 with anticipation. While many of the initial issues with the game were patched out, the game doesn't quite live up to the series' standards. The graphics just don't seem as impressive as its predecessors, and the much-lauded lighting system is wholly absent, rendering the torch mechanic virtually useless. The story is incredibly convoluted and confusing, leaving many giant plotholes and other issues.
Basic combat is incredibly frustrating, based on numerous changes to how it works. Movement feels floaty and awkward, and rolling is fairly ineffective until you level up your agility stat. Stamina drains extremely quickly, and low stamina slows your character's attacks down, which feels sluggish. A "sweet spot" system makes certain weapons much harder to use, and therefore less preferable and less effective. You're repeatedly ambushed by unreasonably large groups of enemies, and the broken poise system means you can be staggered by the simplest, weakest attacks. The game is missing some obvious shortcuts that would have enhanced the experience and made it much more pleasant to retry failed boss fights, and the geography of the game world is nonsensical. Parries and backstabs are slower and less satisfying, coupled with silly-looking animations.
Healing is a poorly balanced combination of consumables and Estus, the system from Dark Souls. Numerous boss fights are either ripped straight from Dark Souls, or barely modified versions of bosses from Dark Souls. The leveling system is tied to a character, which makes no sense given that bonfires still let you do everything else they did in Dark Souls. You have to mash through four lines of dialogue every single time you want to level up. Default keyboard/mouse controls are absolutely ridiculous. For example, your most common attack, referred to as R1 by many, is mapped to the right mouse button. You are intended to click the right mouse button as your default, most commonly used attack. Obviously this is absurd, and a sure sign they had no idea how to map controls for PC games.
Overall, I found it a disappointing sequel that didn't know whether it wanted to follow in Miyazaki's footsteps, or venture out and do its own thing; ultimately, it became a messy mish-mash of both. Occasionally I return to the game, hoping I'll feel differently, but I find playing through the game a chore.

Fighting mechanics I have never seen in a game before. Graphics and sound are just masterful. Not a lot of content packed into though. I Would highly appreciate DLCs/content patches. The game is extremly linear, but due to the artstyle, soundtrack and virtually infinite combinations of Functions (Spells/Skills) this game never becomes boring.
I will explain what functions are below
Your spells are called Functions. But Functions can't be only used as skills. They have 3 purposes.
For instance you have the function called Get(). What it does is it basically pulls enemies to you as far as its range goes and deals damage to them. There is another function called Breach(). What this does is it shoots an arrow which penetrates all walls and enemies and deals massive damage. You can use Breach() to strengthen Get() to make Get() penetrate enemies and be usable through walls! Combine it with one more function for instance Crash() to stun them once you grabbed them to you! But what if you don't want to use Get() neither as active function, nor to use its abilites to strengthen another active function? Use it as a passive permanent buff! If you use Get() passive, what it does it pulls Cells (Pickups you have to collect after killing an enemy else they respawn) from further away to you so you don't need to take care of them anymore! It is not a huge bonus but it is free and it makes unwanted functions useful.

As a student of Greek and Latin, I automatically love this game for its historical character; you can either follow the footsteps of great Roman dictators and commanders and bit by bit conquer entire Europe, with some Middle East and North Africa on the side, crush the Romans as Carthago or start another Persian war.
There are, however, some issues with historical accuracy: the AI seems to behave rather randomly at times, for instance with Syracuse declaring war on Rome in turn 2 or 3 or Massilia having conquered their way into the Balkans. I personally would love for an option to make factions behave the way they did historically as this is something that really bothers me.
Furthermore, some dlc content could be available as updates to the vanilla game, instead of requiring you to pay for it (such as the blood and gore dlc and some minor faction and unit packs)
These minor issues put aside, I do enjoy the game to a great extent and would recommend it to anyone interested in playing historical strategy games, although I'd recommend buying it during a sale.

This game is an example of why steam needs a "Maybe" recommend. While not a bad game in its own rights, its just not what I was expecting. I played Bound in Blood and it was a blast, it had a great western storyline and some really cool gameplay mechanics.
However, Gunslinger just isn't nearly as good as Bound in Blood. There's nothing here that was fun enough to keep me excited about it. After 2-3 levels you know the whole game. You go through a railshooter type level killing 100s of badguys, and then end the level with a stand off against some popular western outlaw. It gets old really fast, and nothing really gets added to the formula. I was curious to see where the story was going and that was the only reason I kept playing.
Even the story had its issues too though. It was very cliche, and played off that old west style of story telling about larger than life cowboys who took on all the baddest outlaws and survived. However, putting all of these big names in the story ruined the appeal to it, and by the end of the game I was just rolling my eyes to all the stuff that was being told. I get what the game's story was doing, it just didn't work out. I saw the ending from a mile away, and using Eisenhower was just unnecessary, and frankly just dumb. I just felt it was a letdown all together, and felt like I wasted my time playing it.
If you're looking for a mindless Shoot-em-up this isn't a bad game to get for that, but there's much better games to waste time shooting people western style.

I have never been so actively repulsed, frustrated, and ultimately angry at a online game.
For starters, there are constant issues for the optimization of streaming data in this game. Expect your connection to buckle under this game, for playing this game while on teamspeak proved an impossible feat. It was impossible to connect to any server - official or community, local or overseas - while running any other program that used any considerable amount of bandwidth. Most every other game I have ever played can handle teamspeak 3 in the background in addition to music streaming and other things, but this game is not up to that task.
Onto what little gameplay I experienced, it is lackluster. Gathering resources is an abhorrent, boring task. At the rate of collection and simply finding resources to collect, this game is worse than most other survival games in many regards - even those noted for their occasional sparsity of resources. The gameplay itself, in what little was experienced, was terrible on all fronts - especially the receiving end of 'combat', which is a complete disaster. The combat combined with the latency and bandwidth issues made it possible for me to be attacked with a six inch dagger from over twenty feet away, ruining any chance of response and making fights entirely one sided.
But the community -- oh, dear lord, the community. If you for some reason purchase this trainwreck of a game, stay away from official servers. They are plagued with people who are playing on the wrong servers and have horrible ping, scream in voice chat and fill up with text chat with intelligible conversations. In addition, this game is worse than DayZ with regards to the KOS mentality, with the combat system contributing to the problem due to its non-parity and numerous engine problems.
The only possible positive this game can muster to draw from its♥♥♥♥♥♥crusted pile of dung is the graphics, which are good for the intensity they place upon the user's system and the tradeoff of apperance. But it numerous drawbacks with a sort of pseudo-motion blur being pervasive, even after disabling motion blur itself, with pixel dragging and visual distortion on numerous levels of graphic settings.
Save yourself the money, and just go buy Rust.

An incredible evocation of the bureacratic nightmare of 80s communism. One of the very rare games that actually forces you to make hard ethical choices. Much deeper than its simple interface suggests.

Papers Please is a great game. It's basically a game where you control a checkpoint at the edge of a country and you can decide whether people are let in or not. Simple, right?
Well, if it was THAT simple, it probably wouldn't even be on Steam.
The country you work for, Artzstotska (I bet I spelled that incorrectly) apparently has a lot of issues, and it gets to the point where billions of documents have to be checked before you can clear them for entry. One tiny mess-up, and you can get fined, warned, or worse. And at the end of the day, the money you make is immediately spent for your family so that you and your family can stay alive. I actually found myself really concerned about my family while I was playing this game and felt overwhelemed as if I was actually a poor man not doing so well in a communist country.
Also, I'm not very good, because my uncle, wife, and son died :(
That would STILL be boring if it wasn't for the immense variety of people that come in. Some are smugglers, some are reporters that I can't let through, some don't have the right papers but beg and bribe me, some have stories, some cuss at me, some threaten me, and some launch terrorist attacks. Personally, I'll let anyone in that will bribe me enough to compensate for my violation fees, and detain anyone because I made a deal with a security guard to have half of his bonus whenever I detain a person with him. I am now trained to use a gun to deal with attackers, and I am a very good shooter. Secretly though, I am part of a special underground operation that aims to take down the horrible government and I recieve messages from them every day.
This game has a lot to offer. Seems simple at first, but when you get into it, it turns out to be really great. Papers, Please is a true storytelling masterpiece.

A concept that is basically running immigration for an eastern-bloc country during the cold war. Sounds boring as hell, right? So deceitful it is then, because few things are more addicting. While playing, I kept finding myself thinking "Just one more day, one more then off to bed". Five hours later, it's 5AM and I'm due at work in three hours. No regrets here, either. The gameplay is simple but deep, and the story branches like a visual novel. Plus it's the only game I've ever played to truly make me actually feel -BAD- for doing what the game tells me to. Video game history teaches us that morality is black and white. Papers reveals how evoke it with more gray area than I ever thought a game could, and it's crazy how easily it does so.
There's a reason this game was voted GoTY by so many publications, and touted as simply amazing by gamers far and wide. Quirky, fun, addictive - you owe it to yourself to play this gem. GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA!
