I have played completely through the Penumbra series and Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and so I was waiting to see what they would do with A Machine for Pigs. I did all my research on The Chinese Room, and read the interviews with them during the production of AMFP. The trailers looked even scarier than TDD and the atmosphere seemed to be a huge upgrade with the new sounds, the thrill of new monsters, and a whole new story. If you have seen the trailer when the thing starts bashing on the door, and the player hides under the stairs... that never happens in the game. It seemed as though they had something great going in the trailers, so two thumbs way up for the making of the trailers, but two thumbs way down for creating false and misleading trailers. If you're looking for the same thing that they had in the trailers even, you will be sorely disappointed. Is that wrong -- to expect a trailer to reveal the actual game? They might as well have released trailers for Outlast and called it A Machine for Pigs, it would have been the same thing as what they did in their own trailers: revealing content that doesn't even exist in the game.
This game is all about story and atmosphere, yes, but even then it was a poorly designed horror game. If anything, advertise it as a creepy or an eerie game, and the reviews would have been higher. Those of you who have played Dear Esther knew how The Chinese Room does their games, and a few poeple came from Dear Esther to AMFP, only because it was TCR that was making it. When they took over for the AMFP project, they did not announce it as the 'indirect sequel to Dear Esther' they made an official announcement that said, "The indirect sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent." Those of us who played TDD, wanted this from AMFP because that's what we were told we were getting; they did not say anything about changing the series completely, they did not announce their switch from the Amnesia title to stage their own Dear Esther 2, they simply said, "it will be an indirect sequel to The Dark Descent." I think I can speak for the majority of TDD fans in the fact that we were mislead and were sorely disappointed in the butchering of the Amnesia title. If they had posted this as the indirect sequel to Dear Esther 2, the reviews would be higher, yes, but that would be because the wave of purchases would have come from fans of Dear Esther rather than Amnesia fans.
*Possible Spoilers*
Now, taking the view point of this being it's own horror game, regardless of whether or not you've played TDD or Dear Esther, if you want a game to take you by the hand, through every 'puzzle', and lead you through a dark and eerie story then this is a game for you. If you want an immersive atmosphere open to exploring and puzzle-solving with hiding spots to be made ahead of time and rooms to explore for hidden secrets: DO NOT GET THIS GAME. If you do not need to be in this room, the door will be locked. If there is a 'secret' item that you need to progress in the game, the door will be unlocked, and probably wide open, too. The puzzles are as difficult as this: there is no inventory, if you can pick up the item you will need it at some point, if you do not know where said item goes -- throw it around the environment -- it will automatically attach itself to where it needs to be as if pulled by a super magnet (not even exaggerating, I've done this one several times), if there is an open area -- that's where you go. The puzzles are basically solved for you without giving you the challenge of needing to solve them, just pick up the one and only thing that can be picked up in the room and carry that over to where it looks like you should go. You can't even pick up crates, boxes, or barrels in this game. If your lantern flickers, something is about to happen, or you're looking directly at a monster, no matter how far away it is. Found a monster? Run and hide and hope it does not find you? No need. Just run around, in circles if desired, until the monster gives up and stops chasing you; you'll know when they stop when the music stops, then you can continue at a brisk walk through the area until either your lantern flickers or the music starts up again.
I tried to play this game as it's own game. I did my research before it was released; finding out everything I could about TCR and the types of games they make. Even then after the first half hour of playing, I slowly got less and less scared. The atmosphere in the beginning of the game was amazing inside the mansion, with the secret passages and the hallucinations. Even the monsters were scary at first. For the first half hour - hour, I was finding the hiding spots, taking mental notes of where different things were at, immersing myself into the game and the atmosphere, and moving through very slow and cautiously. After I found the first monster I said, out loud, "That's it?" I kept waiting for a new enemy to show up, or a better chase to happen... but nothing new showed up. What really lost it for me was when I was taken into the prison area where all the monsters were locked away. I realized at this point that TCR did not want the player to fear the monsters, but only fear dying.
These are giant manpigs, capable of destroying doors in a matter of seconds and able to sniff out your general location, according to the trailers and the way they look in-game. What they really are: these are monstrous manpigs that have been created to wreak havok and bring in a new age of these 'evolved' creatures and eliminate mankind... but their weakness: doors. Simply shut your doors and they cannot get you. Run around long enough and they will give up; and boy will they give up, too -- when they give up, you can even walk up right behind them, lantern lit and making all the noise you want, and they will simply ignore you for a while until they feel like chasing you again. Walking into this area lost all forms of scary, and killed the atmosphere completely. The holding cells are a realization that they cannot break down doors to get you, and when they see you in their territory they don't even care.
What they could have done to make a better game and get better reviews: don't try to bring in the Amnesia audience for the Dear Esther game. If you make a game to be a Call of Duty sequel, don't give them a Halo sequel. What you claim to be draws in the audience that is going to like your game. The reviews would have been astounding, not because people would not have been disappointed, but because those of us who were told it was going to be Amnesia 2 would not have bought it knowing it was going to be Dear Esther 2, and Dear Esther fans would have flocked here. Those that loved the game are saying not to think of this as Amnesia 2 and that's why the majority of people were disappointed. The reality is that that was not the only reason there was disappointment. We were told to expect Amnesia 2, TCR did not mention anything about Dear Esther during production of this game, and they made all their trailers reveal it as a complete upgrade to everything Amnesia. They mentioned nothing about being a complete overhaul of Amnesia to create their own Dear Esther 2, and they mislead everyone. They tried to collide two different types of audiences into one game without including things from both games. If you're looking for Amnesia 2: don't get this game, if anything just get some custom stories and mods for TDD and that's the closest you'll get to Amnesia 2. The Chinese Room: don't declare a new Call of Duty, advertise a Call of Duty, and make a new Halo. Clashing these two fan groups will destroy your reviews and disappoint those who wanted a new Call of Duty just to please those who wanted a new Halo. TDD and AMFP are similar to each other in the same ways that Halo and CoD are, but they are two completely different games and should have been advertised and kept seperate.

Very original Game. Yes you need it, simply because it's such a unique thing, but not for 10 bucks. I've spent approximately 20 hours with it - and that includes time spent replaying the game. I may get back at it one day.
Now that we got that out of the way - the Review.
STORY:
So you are an immigration inspector at the border of an exagerated communistic nation. Maybe it isn't even THAT exagerated, but the situations posed and the narration make for a deeply comical - but critical - atmosphere. There is a lot of Orwell's "1984" in this game (yea like EVERYBODY talking about that nowadays... OBEY!... but it really fits! *ducks*).
GRAPHICS:
The graphics are retro-simplistic but good. I like the graphics, they get the job done.
GAMEPLAY:
Now this is where Papers Please defines itself - well apart from the bizarre scenario it imposes upon you. You have to grant people access to your country - or deny them - based on the correctness of the formulae and documents they present to you. You need to check if their Birthdate, Gender and Photograph match and make sense - and the further you progress - the more things need checking. For example after a certain day all immigrating workers also need a working permit, and the game expands upon this more and more the further you go.
If you make a correct decision, you earn money. If you make too many incorrect decisions - you have to pay a fine. Simple as that.
Paper checking is done by dragging and dropping the documents on your tiny desk (you well need to do A LOT of paperwork readjustments on your tiny wooden table in the late game) and comparing the given documents to the "Rules and Regulations". If there are inconsistencies, you need to highlight a the incorrect thing in the passport (or any given document) and the corresponding rule that states that it is incorrect. Simple as that, but it sounds utterly confusing in text. After you have done this - the passport needs to be stamped with either "Access Granted" or "Denied".
Basically it's like a paperwork simulator!
Based on your successes at the job, you then need to make sure you can pay for your family's nourishment and the heat in your apartment. So if you have a bad day - they might just starve to death and you are game over. And just to screw you up, occasionally it turns out you need to feed your sick uncle and mother or whathaveyou.
STORY2:
Now i know, i have already talked about the story, but this game's gameplay is like its story that's why i pick it up again. It's an odd interweaving of events that make your decisions of letting people through - or not - matter. Basically every immigrant has something unique to say (the writing is excellent btw), but some of them are even more unique and the plot is dictated by whether or not you let them through. But there is no indication that this is the case, which is what makes this game so awesome in the first playthrough. You have this really weird feeling sometimes that the games got you by the balls, and you have this strange fear of screwing up. It must be the weirdest thing i have played and there is nothing i can really compare it to - but it has this really deep atmosphere, like in Gothic 1 - the first time you played it 15 years ago. That's as accurate as i can get, and i know comparing it to a 3D open world RPG from 200X must seem ridiculous, but that might just prove how crazy this game is.
AUDIO:
Super crisp paper sounds. I mean seriously. Stamping a document in this game is as satisfying as firing a gun in an immersive fps! So odd...
Now i know this review might not manage to sum up the game in it's entirety - but due to the fact that it is very story reliant, i would probably start spoiling the fun if i wrote more. Just get it and be surprised by it.
GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA!

This is actually a tough one.  Because... is it good?  Yes.  Is it good enough to recommend to others?  Ehhhhhh....
Graphically, it looks better than the original.
The story is quite twisted actually.  It has an interesting atmosphere too and pretty good voice work.  But... is it scary?  Ehhhhh... compared to the original?  Nope.    Compared to Outlast, definitely not.
Where Outlast took the high paced scary parts of Amensia the Dark Descent and ramped it up a few levels and threw in  a ton of jump scares, A Machine for Pigs went the other direction.  Things are more slow burn.  I don't think there are any jump scares either.  It does have a delightfully twisted story though, but the monsters that chase you are too goofy to be scary in my opinion.
Avoid it if you're looking for a pulse pounder.  Consider it if you like slow but twisted stories.

I started playing this and luckily I ran into the poor design and customer support before I spent more than 10 euro on this game. It is a good game for collectors but severely, severely grindy.
It's not just killing mobs over and over, but in order to complete collections some of the mobs have normal drop rates for grinders, about 0.1% but the problem is that the mob may only have 2 spawn ever 5 min. So not only do you have to kill 100's of the mob, but you have to spend an enormous amount of time doing so. Better to have many spawns with a lower drop rate.
But the real killer is the poor game design about some things. You can enchance your weapon in player shops, but to do so, you have to unequip it. If you forget to re-equip it and it gets sold to an NPC, good bye item. There is no buy back feature and if you ask for support, they don't even have a "this is your one get out of jail free card". Yes, this is what happened to me, I accidentally sold my weapon that I'd spent days grinding for. So good thing it happened to me early in the game so I know not to waste more time on a game that not only has poor design but also lacks customer support.
It's not all bad though, they occationally clean out the bots and the spammers. The graphics are nice and the controls refreshingly simple. The classes are highly varied so you can design as you like, but as usual when there's a lot of class choices, only a few become really viable.
If they would fix some of the design flaws or improve customer service, I could recommend this game, but in it's current state, I cannot do so.

As a student of Greek and Latin, I automatically love this game for its historical character; you can either follow the footsteps of great Roman dictators and commanders and bit by bit conquer entire Europe, with some Middle East and North Africa on the side, crush the Romans as Carthago or start another Persian war.
There are, however, some issues with historical accuracy: the AI seems to behave rather randomly at times, for instance with Syracuse declaring war on Rome in turn 2 or 3 or Massilia having conquered their way into the Balkans. I personally would love for an option to make factions behave the way they did historically as this is something that really bothers me.
Furthermore, some dlc content could be available as updates to the vanilla game, instead of requiring you to pay for it (such as the blood and gore dlc and some minor faction and unit packs)
These minor issues put aside, I do enjoy the game to a great extent and would recommend it to anyone interested in playing historical strategy games, although I'd recommend buying it during a sale.

So, I was gifted this game by someone I don't particularly well, as they had a spare key, so I wasn't exactly expecting a 10/10 game, but I can safely say I was pleasently surprised. I'll go through all the important things one by one.
Graphics - They have a sort of borderlands feel to them, but are quite clunky. On max settings the game is really beautiful scenery and setting wise, and most poeple should be able to run this on high settings, as it doesn't require a huge amount of power (which is another a good thing).
Storyline/Dialogue - This is one thing I wasn't hugely impressed with. It was kind of like; do this, do that, not one big linked story. Despite this, I did find it fairly amusing how it was kind of like obviously made up/over exaggerated in a very western, cowboy kind of way.
Combat - Clunky, but very satisfying. The huge blood splats whenever you kill someone are qwuerky, but quite nice and add a sense of achievement whenever you blow one of these ♥♥♥♥s apart. Some of the guns are a lot more fun to fire than other, but that might have been personal experience.
Boss fights - I've done a few boss fights so far, they were both relatively easy (compared to other games) but they were the first few and only on normal difficulty, so I'm sure they will get much harder.
Duels - The duels feature in this game are really fun. Despite this, it's super easy to win a duel. I win honourably every time, with maybe a mistake hear or there. But it's a nice little feature.
Sounds - Really nice sound additions to the game. The music is pretty authentic, I feel like i'm there, and the gun shots are horrendously loud, like they would of been back then. The really over exaggerated accents of the people make me laugh, but in a good way.
General gameplay - Really fun game, fair amount of playability, shame the multiplayer is dead.

Factorio is a game about designing a game you don't have to play. Automation is the key here, and you design a factory on a desolate planet to leave the game you're currently playing which at some point, if developed correctly, plays itself. It rewards ingenuity through sheer laziness, the hallmark of industrial civilization. Mining by hand takes too long, so you build a driller, which needs fuel, so you develop a system of automated feeding belt. You need other materials to make these, and the next thing you know it's 2 AM.
I have actually no idea if this game is any good. It's compelling and addictive, but I don't know if I would call it "good" or "fun". You have to be a very specific type of person to "get" this, and I'm definitely that person, but I'm not sure if I have it in me to go the distance with this one. I garnered an unhealthy obsession with this title for more than 50 hours, and I left it mainly because I felt like I was playing but not progressing very far. It will draw you in like few other titles, and hours will melt away, for better or worse. You can spend hours chasing a problem to its source and then forget what you were originally trying to do.
What the gameplay loop boils down to here is to solve a continually escalating series of problems you create with innovative solutions you design. This is a puzzle game at its core: how do you go from coal miner with a pickaxe to developing a rocket engine; the industrial revolution in microcosm. It's infuriating, challenging, time-consuming, and kind of brilliant.
PROS:
- Fair escalation of difficulty based on your own pace
- Mentally challenging puzzles
- Fascinating exploration of automation mechanics
- Sandbox world allows experimentation
- Extremely moddable (and recommended)
Cons:
- Needs a better tutorial, especially for rails, circuits, and blueprints.
- Once you figure out an optimal solution you like, gameplay can become a tech tree grind
- Fiddly, annoying interface at times
- Overly complicated tech trees that don't show progression very well.
- Difficult to correct crtical errors early in game
- Defense from enemy mobs is a chore
- Large maps are annoying to navigate on foot

TLDR: This is a story-based MMO that has had a rocky start, but in the end is better for it.
Having watched this game while it was still 1.0 status and having just finished my time in Vana'Diel, I was rather hurt by the 1.0 iteration the team had put out considering they had experience in the MMO market. I staved off my urge to hop in to the 1.0 version of the game (which was a blessing and a curse). Deciding not to saved money in the long haul, but new comers to the game might be somewhat lost as a large deal of the story from 1.0 was washed away by the 2.0 offering of the game and is very briefly touched upon at the start of the game.
Now, compairing the two as a game side by side; 2.0 wins by a landslide. This offering of the game was a playable game. While my only gripe is that not enough of the 1.0 story was transfered into the new version of the game, it can not be overstated that the 2.0 version of the game was vastly improved from the 1.0 version (see the original review by Gametrailers to see what 1.0 was like).
The game moved to 2.0, a new direction with the story, the game play, and that direction was ushered in by the now lead developer Yoshi P. He literally set the old world on fire with the new story and set the stage for what was to come at the new end-game for 2.0. It would not be until patch 2.2 (and a steam sale) came out that I'd finally make the (rocky) delve into the game.
Over time, more story was tacked onto the game. Deepening the story of Garlean Empire, and the beastmen races that sought the destruction of the alliances of Eorzea. We saw a game burn down for the mistakes of the past, only to rise from the ashes of it's former self that in time would go on to have it's first expansion released: Heavensward. The last time we saw something similar in the entertainment industry was Firefly and it's movie, Serenity.
If you are looking for an MMO with a great story and familiar elements from your childhood, you need not look any further than XIV. We the community look forward to fighting at your side. :3

At its core its a simple game. You run. Or rather the game runs, and you jump. You collect a few orbs, and try not to fall into a bottomless pit. That's it. So simple. And yet it's one of the most satisfying things you'll do in a game. It will test your reflexes, depth perception and distance perception. Yes, those are different. There are branching paths, though usually not left right but up and down, hazards you have to identify in the background and obstacles in the foreground that will force your brain to choose the best path with your current momentum as you’re running towards them at 180mph.
The art style is a kind of retro-hyperfuturistic feel, a geometrical art noir. Though by the images shown here it looks to be simple VR polygons, it is not. It feels like a game that would exist in the movie Gattaca if that makes any sense.

I'm going to be blunt in this review.
It's a good MMO, if you are looking for one. It does have insteresting features and isn't your typical one and it's a good thing. Gameplay is good (for a MMO again) not amazing but just good. Zenimax is quite greedy in the crown store but you are not obligated to pay a dollar if you don't want to BUT there are in-game DLC so beware, things like Dark Brotherhood and Thieves Guild are like 15-20$ each I believe in the store if you don't buy the gold edition on Steam (which have 4 DLC in it) but it's not the complete collection of DLCs, so get your wallet ready if you want to access everything. Also if it's nothing you pay for, don't really expect devs to put in much effort into it and I'm talking about events and holiday stuff and the updates aren't really crazy fast, just alright.
Now the part that made me stop: they seem to twist the lore at many places to make things easier for themselves, which is very annoying since it's a really big part of TES franchise. I tried to ignore it but I just can't do it anymore, they are not really following the lore but making their own lore for many things.
My conclusion is that if you want another elder scrolls game or like me look for some lore and interesting stories, don't play this. However if you are expecting a different kind of MMO set in a TES-ish universe, you'll probably have a good bit of fun. The content is there, you get at least 40 quests (which are all voice acted, some are bad, most are alright, rarely really good) per region and a lot of random world bosses, dungeons and other kinds of anomalies laying around Tamriel.
I'll go for "No" based on my liking but it's fairly balanced, I just can't stand the lore issue (some are pretty major),
but obviously just for a game it would be "Yes" as it's not a bad game on its own.

Total war games are something of an odditity in the strategy genre, having survived through the post-Age of Empires Slump that seemed to trail off somewhere in the early noughties, Rome II is one of the first of a new generation of Total War games that manages to support it's original concept; the focus on realistic pitched battles, and the development of it's expanded empire-management, that is more typical in the last few years.
This new generation was marked with both adherance to it's customer community, with a whole host of quality-of-life HUD updates, focus on slick and simple concepts, and defiance, with Much of the game's full content locked behind paywalls and DLC packages that were very poorly recieved, and tarnished much of the company's support throughout the following years.
Rome Total war, was one of Total War's more popular games, encouraging RTS fans and history hobbyists alike, the BBC even made a television show around playing the game, 'Time Commanders' which was not too long ago renewed for a new series, ran with Rome II. Watching this original series got me very interested in tactical leadership, and lead me to a great number of games, and perhaps even the RTS series of games originally.
Rome II is a revisitation of both Rome total war as a concept, but also total war mechanics. With a decent attempt to addorn with culture and art from the times, it is only sometimes lacking in full historical acurracy, but is perhaps the best game to roleplay the expansion of the Roman Empire.
Featuring more in-depth policial options, the game very neatly presents itself as a game you can run as a commander, an administrator, or both at any given time. You do not need to focus too heavily on province management if you are a skilled commander, and likewise you do not need to focus too heavily on micromanaging battles if you are an adept administrator.
With exciting new Sea and coastal battles, Rome II offers a new perspective on tactics, but the execution of this new concept is perhaps what leads the game into my next subject, and one fatal flaw in all Total War games; the ability of the AI.
While the AI can certainly provide competative and effective executions early on in the game, any kind of familiarity with the computer, finds you learning how best to trick the computer into making mistakes that a perceptive human is simply not capable of making. Whilst some tricks do have merit, such as drawing out an army into an ambush, the AI responds as a palpable switch, flicking the exact second you take an action from across the battlefield.
In coastal battles, you need only pick the right boats to funnel the AI into sticking points, strange formations and ultimately absolute victories, and while any human would make very concious decisions that could change the outcome of these battles (Correctly placed siege, bowmen etc) The AI does not learn at all.
Partly this is the limitations of technology. In a game with so many potential placement options, and to a skilled commander, diverse range of tactical tricks, it is only natural that the current generation of AI would fall behind. The alternative would be the AI being capable of always landing perfect manouvers, and the "switch" mechanism I spoke about would only become more obvious.
In the grand campaign, the starting to middle stages of the game find you using whatever diplomatic, resources and savvy you have to survive, but the late game is just sweeping across the board, purchasing the top units and throwing them at any problem. That said, the campaign is a long juicy endevour, that you will still enjoy building for the most trying parts.
Overall, Rome II was the best of total war, at the time, and offers a great deal of unique gameplay for its's price. I reccommend buying this game and killing some time playing it.

I'm infamous for my inability to stick to MMO's of any genre. I may spend a week or two then deem a game repetitive or frivolous. Even games I've spent months on I find myself bored with mid or end game content (or just combat or character systems in general). But even I’m surprised at my own devotion for SMITE, and have logged 325 hours using the Steam client since January (though I’ve been playing the game for two full years now). The reason SMITE has stuck with me is primarily its replay value. Even though I’ve invested many hours in DOTA, LoL, and other match based MMO’s and MOBAs, I find that SMITE brings the freshest and highest quality to the genre of MOBA and MMO.
I could go on and on about how much I admire the game mechanics and content, but I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a fun RPG challenge. SMITE takes a unique perspective (literally) on MOBA systems, and every patch seems to add to the challenge’s depth. Seasons are marked with mechanical alterations to refresh gameplay, regular updates reveal interesting new gods, revisions, and fixes for this final high quality product from Hi-Rez Studios.
I personally appreciate the attention to detail SMITE grants to its effects, environment, and especially its playable characters. Appearance of the many Gods and Goddesses in SMITE are rooted in their respective mythologies, and as you grow acquainted with their various playstyles and abilities, you find yourself interested in their lore and origins. Though it may sound like an argument catering to wary parents, SMITE offers a crash course on the popular mythologies in a way its players will not forget. SMITE fosters an appreciation of mythology as it continues to depict new characters in accurate ways.
I find this game is best played with friends- communicate and coordinate for a successful conquest, experiment with different team compositions, try out bold new strategies to secure a victory. The simple objective of bringing down the Titan is analogous to a chess match. It may sound easy to take out the king, but other pieces on the board tell a more difficult tale. From the minions to the camps, the towers to the phoenixes, the Gods to the Titan, it is a grand and intricate game of strategy and foresight.  And with such a diverse cast of pieces, the game can be played over and over while still retaining the excitement of starting a new match. SMITE sets a shining example for the MOBA community, and will surely see the coming years as a continuation of its groundbreaking success.

Smite is one of those games.
It sucks you in, shows you a great time, but sometimes it wakes up on the wrong side of the bed and ruins your life.
Smite is a unique spin on the classic MOBA genre where instead of the typical 'top-down' view, it is oriented from 3rd person. This difference in Smite is the number one reason why I play it over other MOBA's. It gives the game a new essence of positioning, flanking, and skill when it comes to using your abilities. The theme of the game is also another major factor into why this game is so fun. Playing as some of the most recognizable gods in mythology, as well as discovering new and intriguing figures, is what makes Smite a blast to play. Paired with the teams skin and character developers, they come up with some really intriguing backstory and design to base the game around.
However sometimes Smite wakes up on the wrong side of the bed and ♥♥♥♥♥ on you.
My first recommendation would be to find some friends to play this game with. Its pretty easy to do in game if you don't have any friends. The biggest issue with smite is when you solo que, you can get qued with teammates who may not be inherently toxic, but have no idea what they are doing, making it fairly hard to win and enjoy the game when you solo.
My second grievance is Smite has some pretty terrible servers. My internet is perfectly fine, I run other games amazingly, however during peak hours, Smite servers can be pretty terrible if you ask me. Im not sure if they are dedicated or not, but im pretty sure Hi-Rez has a 3rd party that hosts their servers. Other than that this game is pretty fun.

BALANCING:
Hi-Rez (the game developers) historically don't know how to balance a game - meaning that anything new is overpowered, everything that is overpowered stays powerful and everything that is not powerful stays not powerful.
GAMEPLAY:
While, at the beginning, the gameplay is unique and refreshing - it soon becomes very hollow and boring. A good thing about the games combat system is that, since it's not like the usual MOBA - and is not click based - team fights and 1v1's are a lot more fair, since theres no lock on or autoattacks following people. There are situations where even a 1hp person can escape if they manage to dodge skills well enough.
The sad thing is, the combat is almost entirely based on CC (crowd control - keeping someone in place, keeping someone from attacking, using their abilities etc.) - to the point where every god in the game as a CC ability on some level. This means that whichever team can stack the most CC is the one that will usually win the team fights - which gets incredibly aggrivating and feels very unfair most of the time.
Please do not expect to play this game as a MOBA, because it fails at that - conquest (the standard MOBA setout and gameplay) is not very well done;  jungling isnt really a thing, the matches are, in my opinion atleast, very boring, and games can be lost in 10 minutes, but end in 40.
MICRO TRANSACTIONS:
SMITE has come to a point where I feel like it's bordering between a game, and a virtual representation of the emptiness of someones bank account - I have quit the game because I no longer find it very fun, while my friends "Play it" - or rather show off eachothers skins to eachother in the form of gameplay - the game, if you get too invested in the skins and events that allow you to get skins, becomes less of a game and more of a way to show off how much money you waste.
COMMUNITY:
While not toxic at all - for the most part - don't expect any sort of team communication or co-ordination aside from the key bind callouts.
OVERRALL:
If you're looking for a MOBA that will last you for a long time, this isn't the one for you. If you're looking for a more arcade-type MOBA where the games are a lot shorter and the overrall experience of the game lasts for a lot shorter a time, enjoy.

So, I was gifted this game by someone I don't particularly well, as they had a spare key, so I wasn't exactly expecting a 10/10 game, but I can safely say I was pleasently surprised. I'll go through all the important things one by one.
Graphics - They have a sort of borderlands feel to them, but are quite clunky. On max settings the game is really beautiful scenery and setting wise, and most poeple should be able to run this on high settings, as it doesn't require a huge amount of power (which is another a good thing).
Storyline/Dialogue - This is one thing I wasn't hugely impressed with. It was kind of like; do this, do that, not one big linked story. Despite this, I did find it fairly amusing how it was kind of like obviously made up/over exaggerated in a very western, cowboy kind of way.
Combat - Clunky, but very satisfying. The huge blood splats whenever you kill someone are qwuerky, but quite nice and add a sense of achievement whenever you blow one of these ♥♥♥♥s apart. Some of the guns are a lot more fun to fire than other, but that might have been personal experience.
Boss fights - I've done a few boss fights so far, they were both relatively easy (compared to other games) but they were the first few and only on normal difficulty, so I'm sure they will get much harder.
Duels - The duels feature in this game are really fun. Despite this, it's super easy to win a duel. I win honourably every time, with maybe a mistake hear or there. But it's a nice little feature.
Sounds - Really nice sound additions to the game. The music is pretty authentic, I feel like i'm there, and the gun shots are horrendously loud, like they would of been back then. The really over exaggerated accents of the people make me laugh, but in a good way.
General gameplay - Really fun game, fair amount of playability, shame the multiplayer is dead.

After that the game just repeated itself; sitting in the closet/cabinet, dying because of trial and error and totally shi**y A.I.
Some people praise the A.I., but it's just basically alien knowing exactly where you are and circling that area. It does nothing but follow you everywhere, no matter how silent you are. It decides to check the room you are in 10 times without checking the other rooms on the other end of the corridor. After it leaves the room, it runs to the end of some corridor, turns 180 degrees and runs back to the area you're at. The A.I. literally has no sense of logic, and thus I call it shi**y. Some people claim that the alien movement is randomized, so it's great; sure, it is randomized, but it totally makes it illogical and terrible.
Gun fights are cancer. No enjoyment there. Killing androids is dull.
After the part, where people think "okay this is it, the game finally ends" (after overloading some stuff), the game continues with the same crap it's been for the last 6 hours. Bushnell's Law is an aphorism which describes how the best video games should be or often are "easy to learn and difficult to master." Fotonica nails this law. What you have is one of the most simple games I've ever seen, with a challenging but rewarding learning curve. Essentially, you hold down a button to run forward, release it to jump, and hold it down again to land and continue onward. The game's objective is to reach the end of a level by jumping across platforms as fast as possible without missing and falling into the void below. On easier difficulties, a slower running pace means that even a complete novice could ace any of the games levels within a few attempts. Ramping up the difficulty to the harder levels sees the player's avatar running at breakneck speeds where even a slight mistake or flaw in the player's execution means a restart.
Fotonica is a game that will challenge and reward regardless of the time put into it. Buy it on sale for a dollar or two and have you've got a great casual game to play while waiting for downloads or updates. Or, go nuts and spend hours on hours perfecting the game and learning its intricacies. At the end of the day, Fotonica is addicting and satisfying, with solid mechanics, outstanding visuals and a grooving minimal soundtrack to boot. You can't go wrong here.

A Machine for Pigs is not a particularly scary game. I'm a relative newcomer to the horror genre, and I was certainly jumpy for the first part of the game. It was a couple of hours until that went away, but when it does, there's no getting it back, and Amnesia can't really ramp it up in any meaningful way. That said, my friends and I kept playing for a completely different reason.
Taking a look into the perverse, twisted mind of the villain of this game is throroughly intriguing. We were fascinated as we uncovered the workings and purpose of the massive Machine built underneath London, and the story is plenty good enough to keep you interested, even when you aren't scared anymore. The voice acting and writing are both pretty excellent -- the Engineer especially.
So if you're looking for the scariest thing you can play... well, don't look here. I didn't play Dark Descent, but I don't imagine this was as scary, especially since I'm such a wuss. Still, A Machine for Pigs is an excellent story-based game, and I would recommend it solely on those merits.

Transistor really is a brilliant spark of genius from Supergiant Games (an independent company, mind you) in which they have painted a breathtaking RPG experience that transcends the conventional frameworks of meaningless grinding, cliché professions, and 'skills' that rely on spamming keys whenever possible. The gameplay is heavily dependent on tactics and strategies, but the game itself guides the players to easily grasp the concepts to really shine through by utilizing a dash of planning skills.
On a different note (pardon the pun), the music is sublime from each scene-to-scene, and aurally stimulating as the play styles switch back and forth. The electronica genre of the soundscape in its entirety really befits the aesthetically vivid and stark future-esque art of the game without being "done too much" or juxtaposed in any way. The female vocal line that weaves in and out of the songs really brings-out Red's story and personality even when she... has nothing to say. The soundtracks are truly captivating - and as a music major, I don't say this lightly!
The art, too, is very stunning. The cutscenes are rich in vibrant colors and are drawn (painted) to seem as they were done with a dry-brush. They are highly stylized, chic, and tell a lot more than an average 3D CGI HD 60FPS over-the-top animation can. Seriously, you don't need a lot of motions and actions to make a scene seem interesting. Ever read a beautifully-drawn comic book before? That's pretty much how it feels to watch these cutscenes.
Finally, what would the music and art be without a great story to support? Well, they'll still be good music and art... but the story is ALSO good, I assure you! It has a pungent aroma of a modern-noir. To list a few, it has a femme fatale protagonist, an organized group of criminals as your antagonists, dangerous alleyways, cityscapes, and it's even topped with the quintessential "I have to gather more clues to figure out what's really going on" theme that exists in almost all noir fictions. However, in the midst of all these elements, the creators have planted a painfully obvious yet mild romance that continues to blossom between the star-crossed protagonists. Well, what would a good noir fiction BE without a little bit of romance, huh?
Overall, I believe Transistor will be a great addition to anyone who enjoys games with highly aesthetic qualities (BOTH in music and in art), a well-written story, and a rather unique playing style.  If ANYTHING, this game is like an interactive comic book that's definitely "worth reading" even as a casual reader. ...You know what I mean.
All in all, I give thumbs-up to Supergiant Games for concocting this gorgeous game and I hope to see more creations from them soon!

Much of the negativity here is people who are expecting a more aggressive timeline, or who are upset because the development was delayed for a project needed for funds.  I can understand those opinion, but that shouldn't be the only thing people see.
This game is definitely still early access.  Don't buy it expecting a complete game.  With that said, the game has a lot of potential and isn't NMS (as some people have compared, NMS showed footage in an outright lie... if a game isn't doing that then the comparisons should just stop!)
I'd highly recommend looking at the game with the same critical eye as to all early access products.  That aside, however, the game has some interesting ideas.
In essense, the game is built upon the premise of a persistent 3d world version of something similar to Mount and Blade, but with heavier focuses on things like economics and politics.  Of course, that's just what it aims at.  The game isn't bad, it just isn't complete.  There's still some fun to be had in the current version, but it's pretty short.  If you aren't looking at possibilities and wanting to support such a game in the early stages, that's great!  Give it a few months for them to add in some of the newer updates... which should put in a lot more gameplay according to what's supposed to come.  Consider it when it is ready enough to meet what you want.
That's it.  The game offers something different from anything else as it is meant to be... but it isn't there yet.  It's an early access title.  People are negative because they needed some time away from developing (although they at least communicated about it after some requests.)  Status quo is met, continue on!
Personally, I hope they keep working and improving.  The game has a strong potential as something different and interesting, rather than following the exact same formula of so many other games.  So I recommend with the cautions above... if you don't like early access, don't jump in yet.  If you are scared of the potential not being realized, then just keep an eye on it for later.  Don't rush in, but don't decide it is a dead project that will never move on when there's still work and communication being shown related to in-dev builds!  :)

I am still a bad shot with the bow. I do believe this is user error and impatience more than it is a fault of the game. I saw a horse in game today. Couldn't shoot him either. I can tell you though, my poor character must have the digestive tract of a champion eating all those berries with no ill effects.
The mouse is still a little touchy on anything but the lowest sensitivity so this might still need a little tweaking. However, I found it MUCH MUCH more enjoyable to play.
As to my high player hours. NO, I did not ACTUALLY play that many hours. I'd say at least 90 percent of that was spent with either me having walked away from the computer and forgetting to shut it down or being on a menu screen trying to get my character from giving me vertigo.
Over all, at this stage of development I can change my thumbs down to a thumbs up.
Keep these things in mind though:
1. This is not a game for everyone, and that is ok. There is no storyline, no plot, no mystery. It is surviving and building and being a productive member of your little society in the game.  I love the open ended, completely free to do whatever I want and go where I will.
2. This is not a game for the impatient. Everything you want to do is going to take time. It isn't fast, it isn't furious (unless you meet a bear). I'd say it's a very, almost zen, planning and deciding how to get from point a to point b in the least amount of steps kind of game.
3. It is still in development. I'm not sad that my money went to this game to help it become greater. This is how we get awesome games. They all had to start somewhere.
Thanks for recommending that I give it another go. Like I said, not for everyone, but I like it.

Setting the look sensitivity all the way down does: absolutely nothing. Setting the look sensitivity all the way to the other side does: absolutely nothing.

FONTONICA is a pretty interesting game, in a good way for me.
FONTONICA is essentially a runner type game where there is only one control to use, the run/release button. You hold down a button to run and you jump when you release that button. There are three gamemodes for this game: arcade, endless, and  multiplayer. I didn't really play multiplayer so I can't speak to that, but arcade and endless are actually quite refreshing.
First with arcade. Arcade mode features ending levels, in which you have to run and jump to the end. Each level often has different layers/platforms, as in depending on how you ran and jump, you could be on an upper layer/platform. The benefit to being on an upper layer/platform is that even if you ♥♥♥♥ up, theres a chance you'll land on a lower layer/platform. The goal of arcade mode is to beat every level and get to the end of each in the fastest time possible while collecting these orb like things if you can. Once you pass a certain speed, the lines turn yellow.
For endless mode, it is exactly what it says it is. You just keep running and try to get faster and faster till you mess up and fall into nothingness. Endless mode is quite interesting to test your reactions and ability to make fast judgements, especially at later stages when you are running super fast.
Now with the game modes aside, the actual gameplay is quite fun and refreshing with this kind of minimalistic style of gameplay. Couple this with quite a unique, but good style of art (or linework if you would call it), and the game really has an appealing point to it. It actually gave off quite a trippy feel to it, and I can just imagine playing this game if I am in a trippy mindset. Overall, all the movements, graphics, sound effects, and other things are all well designed and fleshed out. The only qualm I had with this game was that I couldn't really understand some of the names of the levels and menus. Although I think that was intentional, I got slightly confused at times by that stuff.
Overall, great runner type game that I would recommend to all runner type game fans.
Rating: 8.7/10

FOTONICA is a decent runner game at the end of the day. With little to almost no change to the typical platforming/running formula something unique can be created only by giving its levels a minimalistic gridwire look and fitting electronica soundtrack to create a specific theme for each stage.
Running at humanly impossible speeds feels just amazing, while you need to adjust running speed, time your jumps and dives right to survive to the next platform. The learning curve may be a bit steep, but as with all those games, they feel rewarding ever so much when you finally get it right.
Santa Ragione has created something unique for them and I can applaud them for their job well done. You cannot make a wrong decision with buying this game, even if you just want to take it a bit more casually. Give it a try!
Minimalistic art for a minimalistic game. While playing, visuals never feel overloaded but always sufficient for the established gameplay mechanics of FOTONICA. I would not call a wireframe look particularly innovative or interesting though. Luckily a possibility to change the overall appearance of the game exists.
The levels of FOTONICA are distinctly unique and surprisingly well themed. Each of them lets you take a plethora of possible routes leading to the end. Finding the way that is manageable plus rewarding enough at the same time is up to the player.
The mostly electronica soundtrack was composed by three individual composers and fits to a T. Each of the tracks lends a theme to their respective level and creates a sense of uniqueness. Visuals and audio go hand in hand here in my opinion and fit each other perfectly.
Unfortunately, some notes are really high pitched and shrill and disrupt the otherwise marvelous soundtrack. Not only that, in some cases during my playthrough, sounds were not played when they were needed to which ended in some confusion. Apart from these minor bugs, an excellent combination of soundtrack, visual appearance and gameplay in my opinion.
FOTONICA focuses, more than other typical runner games, on correct timing and appropriate running speed. You control your runner through one key only, which, while on the ground accelerates the player and on release makes him jump. In the air, the button initiates a dive through the air, making it easier to land correctly.
Completing levels simply will not cut it, you need to find the best route through each of them and survive in order to break the approriate highscore. Testing your tenacity in three extra endless levels against other players or against up to four players directly in local splitscreen will leave you with much content to play around.
Each level also has four difficulty levels that do not increase the difficulty by altering the level, but by increasing the game speed and making reaction time windows tighter instead. A really interesting approach.

Once, while playing Fotonica, I jumped over a chasm and found myself darting through a forest at the speed of a plane, jaw dropped. I could only looked ahead, because an instant's distraction would mean dropping forever into an eternal void, but the impression of the neon trees rushing by won't leave my memory any time soon.
This game is the trippiest, most adrenaline-filled one I have ever enjoyed. As your avatar starts running, always on a straight line through rising and falling obstacles, you hear their panting and your own heartbeat accelerates, trying to keep up. Then the simple-line world around the track unfolds at the corner of your eyes, and you have somehow bent the laws of physics with your body. Fotonica is way more than a running simulator or a platformer: its absolutely immersive levels stand out as a beautiful aesthetic experience. Simple, futuristic, liberating.

2/5 -- good effort, just not what I was expecting. I played this for a couple hours on the basis of nostalgia.
I will say, there are many RO-esque features to this game; however, it lacks the community that the original RO had.
Similar graphics to RO being 2.5D in a 2D environment. You follow a main storyline to do your levelling through quests, which is much more efficient than grinding mobs. There are ample people on each server to help you with questions -- not to mention all the guides and skill trees available online.
I wanted to get into a new MMO with friends, but unfortunately due to the lack of true content, many friends stopped playing as soon as they experienced it. There's nothing much to do other than your main quest and grinding dungeons with people. Levelling is a lot less boring with someone else.
Perhaps if you're looking for a game similar to RO's style, quest/dungeon heavy, with a typical cash shop, and a smaller community, this is something for you to try. If you grew up on MMOs and wanted to see a revival of the RO scene, don't try this. It's just as bad, in terms of innovative content, as RO2. Not quite sure how I feel about this game. I mean, it's scary and all, but I don't think it's as scary as TDD. And I believe the problem lays in the fact that it was not developed by Frictional Games, but was made instead by the Chinese Room. A company that's only well known title is "Dear Esther" and very lack luster 'Adventure' game.

It's not exactly like The Dark Descent, for sure. But too many people evaluate A Machine for Pigs on the standard of how similar it is to its predecessor, too afraid to look at it on its own merits. Indeed, there are fewer gameplay elements, such as an infinite lamp duration, easier/fewer puzzles, and an overall lower danger level. But what AMFP has, it does spectacularly. The Chinese Room took a more story-heavy approach and crafted the world around how it's told, and it's a tale well worth hearing. The environments are beautifully constructed, the voicework fits the characters perfectly, and Jessica Curry's music is spectacular. It's like a roller coaster: just because you're not pushing the carts yourself doesn't mean it's not a enjoyable, thrilling ride.
People looking for a game that will leave them petrified with fear will be more at home with The Dark Descent. But if you enjoyed the story of The Dark Descent and want to lose yourself in a tale just as gripping and harrowing, definitely give A Machine for Pigs a shot!

Rather than trying to repeat the success of "Amnesia," Frictional hired The Chinese Room to make “A Machine for Pigs;" a weird, little, "Halloween 3" style game that tells a complete story all its own, yet has nothing to do with the original.  To their credit, this was probably smart.  "Amnesia" was a brilliant game, but its scares were already wearing thin toward the end, so serving up a sequel that is nothing but more of the same wouldn't have gone over well.
Unfortunately, "A Machine for Pigs" isn't even a fraction of the game that "Amnesia" was.  It doesn’t really bother trying to be a horror game, for starters.  The monsters are always well lit and kind of silly looking (I kept thinking of the pig sidekick from "Beyond Good and Evil" every time I saw them), and what's more, are barely in the game at all.  The lack of horror would be fine if it succeeded in some other area, but unfortunately it doesn't.  There are some puzzles, but it's not really an adventure game either.  "Amnesia" had very few puzzles, but made great use of its physics engine in the puzzles that it did have.  In contrast, the majority of AMfP's puzzles are of the "find 3 different switches to progress" variety, with next to no use of the game’s excellent physics engine.
Given the limited scares, gameplay, and interactivity, AMfP ultimately plays more like a sequel to the Chinese Room's earlier game, "Dear Esther," rather than "Amnesia."  The ending deals with some interesting ideas about the horrors of the 20th century, but much like "Dear Esther," the developers never find a compelling means of expressing those ideas via gameplay.  So you are left with an odd tech demo type experience that is part adventure game, part horror game, and part interactive movie, but that never commits fully enough to any of these elements to do them properly.  The result, much like “Dear Esther,” reaches far, but ultimately collapses under the weight of its own pretensions, ending up playing a bit like an amateurish “Amnesia” mod awkwardly mashed up with a freshman creative writing project.
A huge disappointment.

I probably should've written a review for this game when I first played it, but I think the positive-to-negative ratio speaks for itself, and I just want to add to that. Now, with that said, I'm going to say something slightly heretical and that many may disagree with:
I liked this game better than Bastion.
Don't get me wrong, Bastion was still amazing, but this one got to me more. Let me explain why:
The Story- It's slower to grab you than Bastion, but since it's a five hour game, it's not one of those games where it only gets good after six hours or so, it usually only takes ten minutes or so before you're sold. It's a lot more vague than Bastion was, forcing the player to draw their own conclusions. Also, be warned, this is a linear story. Red is her own character, and will sometimes do thing within the story of her own accord, even though she is a silent protagonist.
The Gameplay - Definitely better than Bastion, which was a bit hack-and-slash (a genre I'm not overly fond of). How it works is like this. You can equip four abilities to use in real time, which is fine for small battles, but you'll often find yourself using the second combat system, which is the ability to pause time and set up a number of actions (within a limit) to execute once you've unpaused. Along with the abilities are two slots each on those abilities to add different effects, as well as four passive slots for more abilities. Given the number of abilities you run into, it's a very clever system for getting you to try new things, especially since getting killed doesn't set you back anywhere, but temporarily relieves you of your most favored ability. Each ability is taken from a person and stored in the Transistor, giving you the story of that person (which usually ties into the story at large) if you use that ability in a variety of ways. It's an intriquing blend of mixing up gameplay to get more story that I really like.
Aesthetic - Can't say enough here, this really is a work of art. The soundtrack is incredible, for the most part a very haunting electronic tracklist with vocals by Ashley Barret that range from forlorn to occasionally upbeat. For the most part, though, they echo the game perfectly: lonely and sad. Much like Bastion, the voical songs tie into whatever's going on at the moment, including a favorite of mine where the first boss starts singing her own version of one of Red's songs. Art-wise, Cloudbank is a very vibrant world and extremely beautiful. You can check the pictures out up there to see how gorgeous the world is.
The only negative I would give the game is that it's short and only has so much replayability. But if it's on sale and you don't have it already, you're doing youself a disservice if you don't get it. I ewould also recommend you get the soundtrack, as it's well worth it. Supergiant was even nice enough to give everyone who bought it the extended soundtrack for free.

This review may change in a decade if it turns out my $10 investment turned into gold.  While I make worse choices buying fast food every now and then, I still cannot give an A for effort here (or even a D minus).
This game is years underway, and a decade from complete.  Many Early Access games stand on their own two feet, and are worth the time.  I've only put a handful of hours into this, and I won't be able to put more until there is more to put that time into.
There are 2 major Positives to this game, in my opinion:
1) It helped me decide not to purchase No Man's Sky (because I learned not to make purchases based on "possibilities" rather than evidence)
2) The sales will probably be an indication of the market desire at this type of game (a niche spot that I myself would one day want to dig into for development)
It's lacking in many areas though (won't try to number):
-It's an empty terrain generator with menial tasks to accomplish
-The play is laggy
-The tasks are buggy
-There isn't much to actually do
It's like a first person version of Banished - but only in theory.  It's nowhere near executing on that theme.  The game removes any sense of reward or accomplishment by throwing end-game population at you from the start.  A few minutes in, and you'll go from a handful of random "settlers" to an entire village worth, with nothing to do.  There is no reward in constructing villages or doing things, because there isn't a lot of rewarding functionality in the game.  There's no personality, no interaction.  No real use of the buildings.  There is nothing happening outside of the buildings you make.
It's just bland.  And it hasn't changed in a year.  And with the small team working on it, it cannot possibly change any time soon. It's just that simple.  The hope this game wants to deliver on requires years worth of time - and it has to be a labor of love.  But instead of doing that labor, this team put it out for sale.  They're selling an idea, and it's and idea that's already delivered on in more complete fashion, via other games that are available.
If you want first person Banaished with better graphics, better mechanics, better functionality, and just smoother gameplay - get "Life is Feudal - Forest Village" instead.
This game will never do half of what is listed as its future goals.  It will die and become something else before too long.  Hate to sound negative, but this game shouldn't be for sale at such an early state.

so on and so forth, and whether or not you are an effective player is scales to the same ratio in time taken

This has been the only MMO to hold my attention for more than a month ever since the closing of City of Heroes. I never played the original FF14, but I heard the horrible reviews, and even remember seeing gameplay and feeling disgust towards it. To be honest? The only reason I even touched it was because of the free beta on PS4, and at that time I didn't know the game had undergone an overhaul. Since then I'm moving in on my 3rd month of subscription, and I regret nothing.
The game is quite a grind at times. This is what I warn everyone. Professions are a grind, quests can be a grind, and the game has a lot of areas to explore which can seem like a grind... but despite all these boring aspects, something keeps drawing me back and makes me want more. I even find the monotony of crafting really fun for some reason!
The combat is an interesting blend of auto-attack mixed with button clicking. Each class is different, and sometimes they even have a specific trick to them. This makes the game really interesting to me, because you're not always just playing a clone of another class... pressing the same buttons and using the same attacks. Each class has a designated role and are unique (And in addition, more classes are being added).
The character creation is my favorite thing about the game. Despite not having any sliders (With the exception of height and muscle tone and stuff like that), or whatever you'd call ESO's system... FF14 uses, for the most part, a selection system, where you select different facial features and stuff. Despite sounding primitive and boring, there's great potential in it, and you can generally make what you're aiming for. This, in addition to the beautiful full color palette for hair and stuff as well as the cool features like hair hightlights and "odd-eyes", really made me feel like I was creating a character -I- wanted to make, and not a character the Devs wanted me to make *COUGH*ESO*COUGH*.
The story is really interesting, and actually doesn't feel like it singles you out as the only person in the entire world (Like most MMOs have begun to do these days). While you -are- labeled as an important figure, they acknowledge you're not the only one. This makes Roleplaying a lot easier if you're into that kind of thing. You don't run into a TOR mindset of "I -AM- THE TROOPER" and stuff like that. You're just an adventurer, and they even give you a blank slate to start off with so you can really think of your character as whatever you want. Your character doesn't feel written for you.
Also, the game is just beautiful to look at. Everything about it is really pretty, and I found that my favorite place is the desert as ironic as it is. Usually deserts are really ugly and plain, but the developers take great care and consideration into every zone to make it look unique and interesting. It's not just a plain desert, but more like prairie land and canyons. The forest isn't just a big forest, but also includes things like dark, mystical woods hidden away. Things like this make the game really appealing to play. And best of all? The game is completely open. Traveling becomes easier later, but from level 1 it's possible to travel to any location you really want to (given the time and luck to pass by so many enemies!). I was able to meet up with my friend in a whole different area, even though I didn't have the airships unlocked yet (This was Ul'Dah to Gridania though, not sure if you're able to get off Limsa without unlocking the airships or the boat to Thanalan).
The community is pretty great, and really active. I play on Balmung, and I constantly see people everywhere. I see recruitment for raids, dungeons, Free Companies (guilds), and all that. There are actually sites to help you figure out the population of a server, but you'd have to google it.
The most interesting thing to me is actually the cross-platform play. People who are playing on the PS3 version, the PS4 version, and the PC version all play together. There's no console barriers, because Square uses their own servers. I myself play FF14 with my sisters, one on our PS3, one on our PS4, and me on the PC. The only downside is that if you want to switch you have to buy a whole new copy. *CAUTION* MAKE SURE YOU KNOW YOUR PC CAN HANDLE THE GAME BEFORE PURCHASING. My sister's computer couldn't so she ended up re-buying the game for PS3 and then upgrading (For free) to PS4.
Overall, great game. I love it.

A concept that is basically running immigration for an eastern-bloc country during the cold war. Sounds boring as hell, right? So deceitful it is then, because few things are more addicting. While playing, I kept finding myself thinking "Just one more day, one more then off to bed". Five hours later, it's 5AM and I'm due at work in three hours. No regrets here, either. The gameplay is simple but deep, and the story branches like a visual novel. Plus it's the only game I've ever played to truly make me actually feel -BAD- for doing what the game tells me to. Video game history teaches us that morality is black and white. Papers reveals how evoke it with more gray area than I ever thought a game could, and it's crazy how easily it does so.
There's a reason this game was voted GoTY by so many publications, and touted as simply amazing by gamers far and wide. Quirky, fun, addictive - you owe it to yourself to play this gem. GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA!

Very original Game. Yes you need it, simply because it's such a unique thing, but not for 10 bucks. I've spent approximately 20 hours with it - and that includes time spent replaying the game. I may get back at it one day.
Now that we got that out of the way - the Review.
STORY:
So you are an immigration inspector at the border of an exagerated communistic nation. Maybe it isn't even THAT exagerated, but the situations posed and the narration make for a deeply comical - but critical - atmosphere. There is a lot of Orwell's "1984" in this game (yea like EVERYBODY talking about that nowadays... OBEY!... but it really fits! *ducks*).
GRAPHICS:
The graphics are retro-simplistic but good. I like the graphics, they get the job done.
GAMEPLAY:
Now this is where Papers Please defines itself - well apart from the bizarre scenario it imposes upon you. You have to grant people access to your country - or deny them - based on the correctness of the formulae and documents they present to you. You need to check if their Birthdate, Gender and Photograph match and make sense - and the further you progress - the more things need checking. For example after a certain day all immigrating workers also need a working permit, and the game expands upon this more and more the further you go.
If you make a correct decision, you earn money. If you make too many incorrect decisions - you have to pay a fine. Simple as that.
Paper checking is done by dragging and dropping the documents on your tiny desk (you well need to do A LOT of paperwork readjustments on your tiny wooden table in the late game) and comparing the given documents to the "Rules and Regulations". If there are inconsistencies, you need to highlight a the incorrect thing in the passport (or any given document) and the corresponding rule that states that it is incorrect. Simple as that, but it sounds utterly confusing in text. After you have done this - the passport needs to be stamped with either "Access Granted" or "Denied".
Basically it's like a paperwork simulator!
Based on your successes at the job, you then need to make sure you can pay for your family's nourishment and the heat in your apartment. So if you have a bad day - they might just starve to death and you are game over. And just to screw you up, occasionally it turns out you need to feed your sick uncle and mother or whathaveyou.
STORY2:
Now i know, i have already talked about the story, but this game's gameplay is like its story that's why i pick it up again. It's an odd interweaving of events that make your decisions of letting people through - or not - matter. Basically every immigrant has something unique to say (the writing is excellent btw), but some of them are even more unique and the plot is dictated by whether or not you let them through. But there is no indication that this is the case, which is what makes this game so awesome in the first playthrough. You have this really weird feeling sometimes that the games got you by the balls, and you have this strange fear of screwing up. It must be the weirdest thing i have played and there is nothing i can really compare it to - but it has this really deep atmosphere, like in Gothic 1 - the first time you played it 15 years ago. That's as accurate as i can get, and i know comparing it to a 3D open world RPG from 200X must seem ridiculous, but that might just prove how crazy this game is.
AUDIO:
Super crisp paper sounds. I mean seriously. Stamping a document in this game is as satisfying as firing a gun in an immersive fps! So odd...
Now i know this review might not manage to sum up the game in it's entirety - but due to the fact that it is very story reliant, i would probably start spoiling the fun if i wrote more. Just get it and be surprised by it.
GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA!

I have to say after all that waiting, the expectations of this game have risen a little bit.This game failed spectacularly.

Graphics: The artstyle is bland, desaturated and the whole environment simply feels lifeless. Your character runs like a drunk wooden dummy walking on water. Coming from a game like Guild Wars 2 this game simply do not hold up.
Gameplay: The quests are very boring with everything I've encountered so far as a fetch quest. Combat is unresponsive and feels laggy. And the doors.... wth? You have to wait for your character animation to end and then wait another second to enter another area. Trust the few seconds you wait adds up.
Story: I didn't play long enough to actually become immersed in the story, which says a lot about this game actually. Usually I am a story-driven gamer. I can forgive a lot of shortcomings if the story is good. But this game from the beginning did not grip me in any way. Sure, ok, I'm a survivor in an tormented space, I escape, then WHAT? Explore the bland world? Accumulate skill points to invest in skills that look and feel EH? Run around saving NPCs you don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about? The combination of bad gameplay and uninteresting beginning really stopped me from enjoying this game at all.
I also told my mate to get this game so we can delve into another mmo. Sadly, this is not it. Now I am ashamed for telling him to actually spend money on this.
Conclusion: STAY AWAY. Go play something else.

This game is fun at first but it quickly grows old. Once I stopped fangirling over the Roman setting, it became obvious that this is a total step backwards in almost every way. After about 15 hours of playtime and conquering Carthage as Rome, I don't enjoy this game any more. It seems like you are punished for expanding. Here's what I mean, You are only able to have a certain number of generals/admirals, and you can't raise any units without a general/admiral. That effectively limits the number of armies you can have. In my last play session I counted 10 cities under my control, and that gave me enough "Imperium" to have 6 generals in my empire. I couldn't even have 1 ♥♥♥♥ing army per city.
You can build defences which provide meagre units for a town's defense, but any serious army will plow through them without even a dent. Also consider the fact that 1-2 of your armies will probably be on campaign, trying to take new land, so that means that the vast majority of your empire will be sitting pretty waiting for any faction to steam roll it. Building a fleet to transport an army over seas is no longer needed, you simply click on the sea and your army will instantly craft a fleet of transport ships to carry your thousands of me across. I never actually saw the need to build and maintain a navy untill it was too late.
I went into the game knowing that food shortages were severe and crucial to keep under wraps, so I spent the first 20-30 turns building the italian peninsula into a giant farm to produce food and money. After taking a few more cities my empire was literally starving each turn. Apparently a Sicilian farm or fish market is far too complex for Romans to learn to use, becuase you'll be espected to dismantle and rebuild nearly every building in every city you sack, ensuring that your delicate Roman workers are at home. Public order is also a nightmare if you let it get out of hand. It all adds up to this feeling that the game doesn't want you to expand and grow your empire. I got this feeling almost immediately that I was spreading myself way too thin almost as soon as I started doing anything offensive. The limit on armies and ridiculous food shortages, coupled with the morale problems of every city you take makes you feel extremely stressed out all the time. This game just doesn't have the feel of past total war games for me. I think it all comes down to that feeling like you're punished for growing your empire.
Maybe there's a way to ensure your empire will be fine and have enough of everything to expand, and I'm just an idiot. But at this point, I'm so tired of this♥♥♥♥♥♥game, I'm uninstalling it now. I'm sticking to Rome 1 and I recomend you do too. Once you get past the graphics, Rome 1 is better in almost every way (and maybe even the graphics, I get 30 fps avg on the campaign map and it looks like pixellated♥♥♥♥♥ while the battle map looks like shiny plastic from afar and a pixellated mess up close, but here at least I get 60 fps)

Most people say that you need around 6 hours to beat this once.
If you explore every bit and wait for every dialogue, play around with the different functions, crank up the difficulty to max whenever possible and only have reasonable luck with the random based challenges 8-10h is more appropriate (listening to the awesome music included).
So with actually playing the game it's 10 hours worth of amazing content for the first playthrough. And the second seems to offer some more things to keep you entertained.
I didn't find anything that this game does not do really good except for some user interface issues (mostly when installing functions, though you can drag&drop and stuff, it's just a bit strange when you change a whole lot).
---------
Please be aware though, there is one minor design flaw. In fact this may wipe your progress if you are not careful so please read on IF you want to play on maxed difficulty and change around your playstyle a lot:
After reaching the top of the tower DO NOT LEAVE unless you have a foolproof ability kit or turned off all/some limiters. The game saves after a cut-scene and you will have to fight a high tier dog and some minions. YOU DO NOT GET THE OPTION TO CHANGE YOUR BUILD EVEN IF YOU LOAD. You can pretty much always beat anything before even with a sub-par build and a few deaths but this encounter can be devastating with the wrong build. It took me several minutes of optimizing a test build that was not working as intended.
---------
Probably the only game where I used Tab for other things than minimizing the window. And I used it a lot. Definitely the only game where I didn't do anything else except holding the Tab key at times...
Buy this if you have a working Tab key. If not, wait for a discount. Or don't, because it's incredible. Seriously, the only problem people are having with this game is that it is too short. Great games are always too short, or we wouldn't play the bad games anyway...
Edit: 2nd playthrough
The design flaw as explained above is here more apparent and it happens more often, though you should have a good setup at this point anyway. being able to have multiples of the same function also makes stuff very interesting. Most encounters are very easy (with the correct kit) but some encounters seem to be randomized so you can have pretty challenging fights, even though I nearly instantly killed anything, I still only had about 20-30% life after most fights. The challenge rooms you get access to are okay (fighting against a last boss kind of type is forgettable though), the randomized fights can be a nightmare and the repeating "only fighting against an increasing number of men" is dumb and very unfair with the wrong abilities. This changes in the later rooms though and I had some pretty fun times going through the last 16 waves, losing my good abilities right at the start and only reaching my standard setup right at the last wave.
So far a recursion seems unnecessary, the real meat (plot, style, music) is already inside your bellies, so the only thing left is to play around with the game mechanics. Those are excellent but you should know when to stop before you ruin your experience. See that mode as optional and not as required and you will be fine :)
