This is a very fun game to play. It feels rough and messy, but not in the bad sense. I get the impression that the developers tried to go for that feeling. The game has been streamlined. (It's also not buggy.) The gameplay consists of puzzle solving, physics stuff and other great game styles (the gameplay style varies a lot actually, it never gets boring!). There's always an element of randomness (which is what makes the game feel slightly "messy"). The randomness can get annoying sometimes, but it also adds to that special atmosphere. It took me about 4 hours to complete World of Goo. Those 4 hours were great. Every level contains a non-mandatory "OCD" special tasks, e.g. solve the level in less than X moves, which will take probably another 6-8 hours to complete. Additionally, there are editors and fanmade levels / level packs out there if you still can't get enough of the game. There certainly is enough content available, even if it doesn't look like it at first.

I bought this game about a year ago, and it didn't work.  I would have expected a game released in any form, even early access/beta, to be in a playable state.  I only recently was able to get the game working properly.  The graphics are almost Skyrim quality, but the gameplay (from what I've been able to get done when the game isn't crashing) is more like Minecraft.  The reasonable alternative is to get either Skyrim or Minecraft (or both) and play those instead.  Character building in the beginning is slow, and the "tutorials" don't provide enough useful information to get the game into full swing.
To back up the above statement, check out
.
•You can't really succeed in this game unless you pick the traits that let you hit things with a sword, start settlements, and build complex objects.
•It shouldn't be too much to ask to render the inside of the tree trunk.  Or at least create a flat part at the end of the cylinder of tree so I don't see the awfulness that is the tree that doesn't exist within itself.
•The interface for using tools is confusing.  There is a reason that other games (developed by professional studios who make money by not being s♥♥♥holes to their customers and who actually deliver finished products) have a few simple systems that are replicated across many games.
•Is there really no fast way to eat things?  Do I really have to go into my inventory every time I want to eat a whateverberry and drag it onto my face?
•I want a savegame with a save file.  None of this "save the world" stuff where I can't go back and undo all the mistakes I made (owing to the fact that only a few of the skills are actually useful).
•How do I join an NPC settlement?  They seem to be doing better than I am at this, and all they do is kinda derp around.
•Give us a regular f♥♥♥ing dialog box, none of this weird conversation tree/bush/kudzu madness.
•Actually, the bug where you can keep chopping at the stumps of tress that have been cut down earlier to get infinite wood is kind of nice.  Keep that one around.
•What exactly is the value of a "wood"?  Building recipes and scaffolds seem to think of it as a log (about half or a whole tree), but the crafting menu where you turn one wood into a plank says otherwise.
•Using nothing but a plank of wood and your teeth, you can create a fully functional arrow.  A few planks and no string makes a bow that you can shoot them with.  This also raises questions about the value of one wood.
•Why is it that I can just walk on water with no repurcussions?  How is it that I can't drown?  Can you at least slow down the time it takes to cross water so it feels like a legitimate obstacle?

•I can climb steep slopes by jumping up them.  In real life (this is technically some sort of sandboxy rpg simulator thing, right?) you either don't go up these slopes or you climb with your hands (instead of holding swords and axes).

I get why people might be turned off by this game. Monthly subscriptions have long fallen from grace, not everybody enjoys the Japanese aesthetic, it doesn't really bring anything new to the table, etc. Final Fantasy XIV is very traditional MMO with clearly defined character roles, familiar combat and loot systems, dungeons and everything else you expect from a title like that. However, it does all of those things exceptionally well.
There is a lot of content to enjoy with substantial updates that have so far been free. The focus is clearly on group content and righteously so as the dungeons an large scale boss fights are easily the highlights of the game. In recent years, many MMOs have walked away from the holy trinity of Tank - Healer - Damage Dealer but Final Fantasy XIV embraces it which I for one greatly appreciate. You always get the feeling that you were relevant for the success of a dungeon run as all roles are equally important. This feeling is something that I missed sorely in other recent MMO titles that are either built so that "everyone can do everything" or hide away the group content that actually requires you to work together until the end-game. Final Fantasy XIV on the other hand eases you into all of its group content so even if you've never played an MMO before you'll quickly find your way around. The game allows you to level all classes on one character. The class you are currently playing as is determined by the weapon you have equipped. So you can experiment around until you find what suits your playstyle best. Combat plays out as you'd expect with global cooldowns, hotbars for skills and items, etc. Later int he game enemies and especially bosses require a fair bit of movement and positioning so there is a very dynamic feel to every fight.
Presentation-wise both sound and graphics are good but not great. There are better looking MMOs out there but spell effects still look cool and character models are well done for the most part. There are some low-res textures here and there but certainly not bad enough to hurt the experience. Plus graphics are not all that important in a game like this anyway.
A few awkward voice actors really stand out among the other which are decent enough. Sadly just about everything except main story cut-scenes isn't voice which is a shame but let's be honest, nobody reads what quest NPCs have to say anyway. ;)
Final Fantasy XIV is a great game that has a lot to offer for fans of traditional MMOs and can also serve as a great introduction for the uninitiated. Those looking for a more action-oriented take on online RPGs might not get what they are look for but if you like strategic battles and want a fresh take on tried and tested gameplay mechanics definitely give this one a try.

Please be aware though, there is one minor design flaw. In fact this may wipe your progress if you are not careful so please read on IF you want to play on maxed difficulty and change around your playstyle a lot:
After reaching the top of the tower DO NOT LEAVE unless you have a foolproof ability kit or turned off all/some limiters. The game saves after a cut-scene and you will have to fight a high tier dog and some minions. YOU DO NOT GET THE OPTION TO CHANGE YOUR BUILD EVEN IF YOU LOAD. You can pretty much always beat anything before even with a sub-par build and a few deaths but this encounter can be devastating with the wrong build. It took me several minutes of optimizing a test build that was not working as intended.
---------
Probably the only game where I used Tab for other things than minimizing the window. And I used it a lot. Definitely the only game where I didn't do anything else except holding the Tab key at times...
Buy this if you have a working Tab key. If not, wait for a discount. Or don't, because it's incredible. Seriously, the only problem people are having with this game is that it is too short. Great games are always too short, or we wouldn't play the bad games anyway...
Edit: 2nd playthrough
The design flaw as explained above is here more apparent and it happens more often, though you should have a good setup at this point anyway. being able to have multiples of the same function also makes stuff very interesting. Most encounters are very easy (with the correct kit) but some encounters seem to be randomized so you can have pretty challenging fights, even though I nearly instantly killed anything, I still only had about 20-30% life after most fights. The challenge rooms you get access to are okay (fighting against a last boss kind of type is forgettable though), the randomized fights can be a nightmare and the repeating "only fighting against an increasing number of men" is dumb and very unfair with the wrong abilities. This changes in the later rooms though and I had some pretty fun times going through the last 16 waves, losing my good abilities right at the start and only reaching my standard setup right at the last wave.
So far a recursion seems unnecessary, the real meat (plot, style, music) is already inside your bellies, so the only thing left is to play around with the game mechanics. Those are excellent but you should know when to stop before you ruin your experience. See that mode as optional and not as required and you will be fine :)

Why people like this game, I'm not sure.  The ship and graphics are good as any game, and made me look forward to playing it.  But the gameplay and AI, "uugghh".
I have really enjoyed spy and sneaking around games, but much of this game is 'hide and seek' with Ai.  The maps themselves are poorly imagnined.  The vent ducts you can use only follow dev logic. It's a #* spaceship or port!  Air ducts you can crawl in should be as diverse as the corridors and rooms, but no, they are nothing but shot links from one room to another linking only one or two room per map area,  and follow no logical use, are too few,  just placed where devs want you to hide.
Scary? not a chance.  Everything is done as a animation you have no control over.  So if the alien catches you sneaking around or hiding, the animation kicks in and you watch yourself get killed.  IT's not scary.  What would be scary is if you got caught or found and you could still run or control you charaters, and would be killed no matter what.   Instead, the animation pulls you out of the moment and is like  a big annoucement, "I've caught you watch yourself die."   And because it is the same animation, you know exactly what to expect.  Caught facing it, push you down and jump on you.   catch from behind, poke through your chest.
I can't believe I'm about to say this next bit, because I love animations, but there are too many animations.  Sometimes you can have an animation, thirty seconds of walking, then another animation.  I would have rather had interactive gameplay instead of constantly pullling me out of the moment with a movie.
The damage logic doesn't make sense at all.  You have a revolver (looks like a .38).  And a jack/wrench.  Now you can kill a person with one shot, or hit them three or four times with a wrech.  Androids, on the other hand, can take 16 headshots with the pistol and it does nothing, but you can kill and android with 3-4 strikes of the wrench.  What?  How did they come up with a wrench that gets more powerful while the gun becomes useless.
The game controls just make me sad.  It's dev interactive ideology gone awry.  I believe in general you should have the "use" key do what you need to make something work.  For some reason, they felt creative key commands make it more real or interactive.  So to use a jack on a door, instead of the use key, you first his use key, then press both left and right mouse buttons at the same time, then press 'a'.  Does that feel more real to you?  The worst part it it is so complicated and non-sensical, they have to display all the commands on the screen so you know what to do.  Again, their idea of immersion pulls you out of the game.  Some hatches requre you to press 'use' then right mouse then 's'.  Why?  who knows.  Just let me press the use key, which I won't need isntructions for, and open the hatch.  If the alien sniffs at the locker you hide in, text comes up telling you to hold down right mouse button to hold your breath.  What?  it is suppose to make me feel more in the moment, but again telling me by text what I"m suppose to do pulls me more out of the moment that keeps me in it.
How about the actual hiding.  This is where they were the laziest.  You can hide in lockers, cabinet, or under tables,  The same game assests everywhere.  Nothing creative or site specific.  When I was in a room filled with body bags, I should be able to hide in a body bag.  No, you got to find one of those lockers or cabinets.  And you can't jump or climb, (not part of your controls) so the entire gameplay experience is horizontal.    How about locking or disabling a door?  Nope.  Aparently, you can hack doors open, unlock hatches, and remove door jacks, but you can't do the reverse.  I would have loved if I could lock the alein in a room after tricking him to enter, even if only for a short time.  I could have come up with all kinds of strategy and gameplay options to get through.  they have so limited your options as a player, you aren't trying to figure out ways to hide or trick the alien, you are trying to figure out the path and tactics the dev want you use exactly use which consists of crawl, hide in locker/cabinet, let the ai passs, crawl, hide in locker/cabinet.
Finally, the last fail is the fear factor.  It's not hard for a game to make me jump.  I'm walking, a door flies off in front of me unexpectedly, i jump.  Here. you can predict where the alien will appear, and when.  They drop out of open ceiling holes which can be seen a mile away and the player cannot use.  Once they drop down, they partol the halls like any AI guard or security, doing rounds, coming if they hear a sound,  and sometimes stopping in odd places staring at nothing.  They don't use the vents you crawl in for some reason, and they follow you from one map location to another just because you are there even if they don't detect you.  It's all predictable.  It would have been so much scarier if they didn't alway just appear, or sometiems where there before you.  Or didn't crawl back up into the same vent they appeared from.  They were all constant reminders you weren't running from an alien, you were playing with an AI.
I think the initals of the actual  game say it all.  You are playing Alien Isolation, or AI.  Not scary, very redundant, always predictable.

Submitted for your approval; Our Planet Earth
A garden of flesh to feed the flesh of the more crafty and capable who then fall conscience victim to their realized cannabalism; such hurt then leading the survivors to questioning the inner workings of life itself.
Answers offer some salvation in respect that machines can be rebuilt; therefor are eternal and serve superhuman to the otherwise needy and fearful flesh.
The author for Amesia's 2nd tale (or 3rd if you count the earlier Penumbra Trilogy) takes some pretty deep meta-philosophy and completely removes all idealism and hyperboyle from more happy-go-lucky past philosophers.
Obviously I don't agree with the protagonist's (possessed) actions in this story but will say that without all of the fluff; "A Machine for Pigs" sums up, succinctly, the way that I too see life most days.
A good story, pleasing graphics, sounds and ambience. The only thing I can scold AMFP for is that it is too long. I'm seven hours in and only now getting close to the very end. I would say it feels like I've sat through, at least, an hour and half of drag-on filler; perhaps to prevent critics from complaining it a short game.
In instances of art like AMFP the "Less is more" suggestion should always be strongly considered; and so I take my own advice and end this review. ;)

I enjoyed the experience but A Machine for Pigs is barely a game.
The gameplay basically consist of finding item A and bring it to place B while avoiding the occasional monsters. There is no sanity meter, there are no more matchsticks, no lamp oil or even an inventory screen. This effectively removes any tension from having to survive on limited resources and if you find a broken machine you'll just have to explore the surroundings for suitable parts. Whats left is a game almost on rails.
Were I think the game succeeds is in its atmosphere. Most of the game isn't necessarily scary but always creepy. There is a persistent feeling that something is wrong and I really like that, despite the gameplay being very simplistic. The screams from the pig-men and creepy feeling from exploring a seemingly empty Victorian factory makes the experience enjoyable. The story isn't top notch but works and is mostly delivered through scattered notes, audio logs and phone calls.
Tl:dr
This basically a story driven game on rails. Do not expect Amnesia The Dark Descent.

This game is a absolute fun masterpiece that'll have you laughing and really get you caught into the game for many hours to come, so I'm going to do some Pros and Cons on why you should buy this game, but like everything else it does still have some issues
- Great Campaign - this is an extremely fun campaign with a great amount of hours to play, its mostly a cartoonish first person shooter that goes through the stories/tall tales of Silas Grieves as you take out some of the baddest guys of the west, now one of the funniest parts about this is that during the game it'll be narrated by yourself(or Silas Grieves) and sometimes as he speaks he'll say oh wait I wasn't fighting Apache Indians, bandits were fighting me Apache style and then the enemies change during gameplay, it's really funny
- Level Design - each level in the game is extremely unique and fun to explore, it's also well balanced with enemies and interactable objects, though I have gotten lost a few times in some places but its usually pretty easy to find out where your suppose to go
- Gameplay - the gameplay for this game is great as it is with most first person shooters, with numerous weapons to use and a great skill tree that allows you to upgrade your character and skills with weapons and other things and if you upgrade almost everything in a specific tree then you get a special golden gun the corresponds with the tree that you leveled up
- Runs Smoothly - During my entire play time in this game I've never had a single crash, lag, or FPS drop, the game runs absolutely perfectly
- Standoffs - this is one of my overall favorite parts of the game is standoffs, when ever you get to a bad guy or main villain in the story you'll have a standoff of or some type of gunner battle, and a few unique ones, but standoffs are like they are in the movies two people staring each other down and then making a quick draw to shoot him down honorably, it can be hard at times but it really makes you feel like your in the west especially the huge one at the end
- NO UPLAY - for once and only once Ubisoft actually made a game that doesn't require you to login in with your Uplay account before you play, and I really do like that though I would still like to get the Uplay points from the game I'd rather get steam achievements
- Not Enough Replay Value - though the campaign does have some replay value with the golden nuggets and such, and there is a timed game mode to get the best score there's just not enough to really give you more that 15 hours so it ends up being a short play
- No Multiplayer - for a game that could so easily have it but yet its not there, I would really have loved to see this game with a multiplayer feature, and the fact that its not in here feels kinda lazy
- More Features Or Modes - even though this is a great game it needs a lot more to keep you in the moment and offer a lot more replay value
I'd definitely make sure to buy this game but especially if it's on sale for like $2 which is what I payed and as I can see a complete steal, but as a overall score I'd have to give this game a 6/10 purely because of the fact that even though it's great it comes off a quick play and needs a lot more replay value and could have used more features to give the game uniqueness, any that's all for my review so if you haven't already go make sure to go get this game for a quick play and the laughs!!!

In most respects JC3 is very similar to other games of the genre; the missions follow the general pattern of "go to X and kill everything". What really sets this game apart is the tether mechanic. I was skeptical at first that such a mechanic would be reliable or even useful, but it turns out to be the game's redeeming value and is useful in pretty much any situation. Most of the world is destructable environment, which makes it enormously satisfying to watch the trees obliterated as your tank charges through the forest for no reason other than you just can. Only key environmental structures (rocks, some buildings) are static, while just about anything else can be tethered and ripped out of place. Particularly powerful tank-class enemies are a real problem, at least until you tether them to the cliff face 50 feet in the air. Enemies don't fight so well while falling from the top of the 10 story watch tower you just dragged them to the top of. Snipers causing you issues? Just rip apart the entire goddamn sniper's nest and let them die under the collapsed steel. Attack helicopter turning you into swiss cheese? Just quickly tether yourself to it and hijack it, or tether it to the ground and watch the pilot try to not die. Being chased by a swarm of enemy jeeps and tanks? Just tether them to the side of the road one by one and watch them whip around with G forces that probably should have killed them. Can't get close enough to the heavy assault vehicle to plant a bomb? Just tether it to a nearby building to flip it.
And I havent even mentioned the wingsuit or parachute systems.
Overall an amazing game. Definitely worth it.
Note: I had MAJOR performance issues (10-15fps) when I first started, but eventually found it was a problem with my RAM overclock. If anyone else has this issue, ease off your overclocks. After backing that down a bit, I'm running reliably at 140+ fps

Papers, Please is one of those games where you go in expecting to not like it. The graphics are retro (terrible compared to most other games available today), the controls overly simplistic, the music very repetitive. There are no voice actors; every conversation is shown by moving text bubbles. Finally, there is only one setting and you are completely stationary.
Put all of the above together and you would think that this is one of the most terrible games of the decade. But you would be wrong. Despite its simplicity, despite its repetitiveness, this is one of the most in depth, thought provoking games I've played in years. And with 20 different endings, there is plenty of replayability.
If you haven't played this game, you're missing out.

A "Paperwork simulator" sounds like a hard sell, but it's encouraging to see that word-of-mouth is getting people to try this wonderful little game out. It's refreshing to have something different for a change rather than another FPS, platformer or suchlike.
Your job is to give or refuse permission to enter your country to various people who come to your customs booth...... it is a hard sell, isn't it?
Okay then, your job is made more difficult in several ways. First of all, your bureaucratic government implements more and more rules as time goes on which means you have to be quicker and quicker at processing, without letting accuracy fall. Secondly, you have certain moral choices to make - you have to feed and warm your own family and that can only be done by processing people as quickly as possible. Well, unless they bribe you to let them in, or the guards bribe you to detain them or... and of course, there's always the risk of forged documentation [which you are punished for if you miss] or terrorist attack [which curtails the day].
This game is deeply engrossing. It's straightforward to begin with, but the difficulty curve is just right, adding complexity day by day - just as you master the rules something else comes along which you have to keep an eye out for. Added to the fact that there are MANY, MANY different possible endings will lead you to replay this several times in order to see what happens.
Well worth a try!

You know what? Just don't play it. It will save you a lot of trouble. Get some single player Final Fantasy and you'll have more fun.

Modern Warfare 2 is by far the least traditional of the series, with the core package broken up into three main pillars of gameplay. Single-player fans have their main campaign, if you're down for more co-op gameplay either locally or via online connection you've got the new Spec Ops mode, and Modern Warfare's groundbreaking multiplayer is back, and truly better than ever. There's an overwhelming amount of content to experience, but with each mode being 100% standalone in nature, you're getting three completely different experiences all in one. That, however, also plays a huge factor into how your final opinion of Modern Warfare 2 as a whole turns out.
First and foremost is the single-player experience. As the anchor of the Call of Duty world, campaign mode is back, and it's intense. You'll instantly get a sense of just how far the improved engine has come when you're thrown into the bustling streets of Rio de Janeiro's favela, the ice-capped mountains of Kazakhstan, the dusty roads of Afghanistan, and other unexpected locales. On the visual side of things, Modern Warfare 2 is an obvious step up over Call of Duty 4 and World at War, with a stronger emphasis on complex terrain in the environments, weather effects, destructible objects, and the overall sense of action and chaos that comes with so many visual improvements. This is only complemented further by the increased attention to sound design, with the effects of many returning weapons being re-recorded,even more in-level chatter amongst your allies, and a truly captivating score by Hans Zimmer which builds based on specific in-game moments. Modern Warfare 2 feels like an action movie through and through, with the production values alone dating Infinity Ward's last game, Call of Duty 4, quite a bit.
At the same time, the single-player campaign has its issues. For starters, it's short. I've been playing Call of Duty 4 steadily since its release, and my first completion of the Modern Warfare 2 campaign came in at just under five hours on regular difficulty. Playing through on hardened will add another hour and a half onto that. Modern Warfare 2 is definitely more chaotic this time around – partially due to the new visual effects and upped production values – and with the improved enemy AI and tough scenario design you'll be fighting for every checkpoint. One of the larger visual changes to the game's heads-up display this time around is the blood splatter system. In previous Call of Duty offerings you'd get damaged, the screen would start to shade red, and you'd be required to seek cover before your vision returned to normal. Modern Warfare 2 employs a new system, actually having a thicker blood layer added to up the realism. There's been some discussion on whether the splatter is too distracting, and in my experience with the game it's far from an issue. You'll be able to take more hits on easier difficulty settings, so while a few well-placed shots will drop players on hardened or veteran modes the added splatter is an acceptable trade-off for more overall health

Tree of Savior or ''ToS'' is a highly art graphics and rich story line MMORPG. The style of game is truely inspiring and enough reason to play the game itself. It reminds me of the Harvest Moon games, but with a play style like Maplestory or Spiral knights. The graphics already spoken for numerous times as fantastic is true and the audio soundtrack is pretty good too. There is atmospheric beats and some blood pumping ones as well for the boss fights. SO, in RPG fashion you do have Swordsman, Archer and Magician to start out with. The custimization is very limited though to start with character looking wise. The world is in chaos by monsters and demons with various names and titles, with various abilities and minnions, that have various waves of evil and destruction like all RPG games do and with some really cool art. Typical, you are the ''chosen '' one RPG style and you have to defeat all evil with the help of goddess and your uniqueness. Its straight forward, but if you read the quests and follow along while beating the baddies its a pretty intricate peice.  Goddesses are really big here and worshiping them.  While traversing and doing quests and missions you level and upgrade and equip your character as usual in MMORPGS. BUT the real neat thing for this game is that you can decide what kinda class you want and switch whenever able if it suits you. It's not just a liniear progressions or cookie cutter characters. For each of the 3 classes there is ''I'm guessing, because they keep coming up with more'' 20+ subclasses to upgrade or define what or how you want to play. It's really cool and with helpers and the usual NPC class trainers you get ahold of how to make your class really shine with the right moves and augments, to how you want to fight. The game seems pretty well done and plenty of the guilds and pvp and raids social stuff for the person who loves to party before dungeon diving. Weither its the artstyle that gets you or the class advancement or the Goddesses rule story line, try it out.

Been playing Machine for pigs for a couple of hours now, and the more you play the more disgusted I am with what Dan has done and of what he has created. The story can be abit slow at the beginning, but as you descend deep into the darkness you will see what horrors this game has.

There are some goods parts to A Machine for Pigs, like the art style, the voice-acting and ambiance, and a couple of scenes. But they are not worth going through the dull and predictable story, the really boring gameplay, the pacing that is all over the place and the cheap "trying-too-hard-to-be-the-previous-game-but-not-quite-getting-there" horror.
In short, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs is a mess, and that's a bummer.

Overall I liked the game. I think it was less scary than the first one, mainly because I think the stakes are raised more slowly (by which I mean there isn't much danger until quite a ways into the game). I for one am glad they got rid of the "sanity" mechanic - mainly because the effect they used in the first game made my eyes hurt (and I don't mean that as a metaphor - my eyes would physically water up and get sore during the sanity scenes in Amnesia).
I do think the inventory management (lamp oil, etc) is missed.

Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs maintains the core mechanics and gameplay from Amnesia: The Dark Descent so prepare to experience an intense and scary game. The game starts off very strong, but then does fall off in terms of horror mid-way through the game. The game is also shorter than the original and a lot of the "danger" elements have been removed so you are not constantly dying but experiencing the story. Recommended if you enjoyed The Dark Descent and want another pass for a horror game.

In most respects JC3 is very similar to other games of the genre; the missions follow the general pattern of "go to X and kill everything". What really sets this game apart is the tether mechanic. I was skeptical at first that such a mechanic would be reliable or even useful, but it turns out to be the game's redeeming value and is useful in pretty much any situation. Most of the world is destructable environment, which makes it enormously satisfying to watch the trees obliterated as your tank charges through the forest for no reason other than you just can. Only key environmental structures (rocks, some buildings) are static, while just about anything else can be tethered and ripped out of place. Particularly powerful tank-class enemies are a real problem, at least until you tether them to the cliff face 50 feet in the air. Enemies don't fight so well while falling from the top of the 10 story watch tower you just dragged them to the top of. Snipers causing you issues? Just rip apart the entire goddamn sniper's nest and let them die under the collapsed steel. Attack helicopter turning you into swiss cheese? Just quickly tether yourself to it and hijack it, or tether it to the ground and watch the pilot try to not die. Being chased by a swarm of enemy jeeps and tanks? Just tether them to the side of the road one by one and watch them whip around with G forces that probably should have killed them. Can't get close enough to the heavy assault vehicle to plant a bomb? Just tether it to a nearby building to flip it.

The bad: Pretty much everything else. None of the Just Cause 2 team worked on this installment, and it shows. The minimap is inexplicably gone. Vehicle handling for motorcycles and planes is absolute garbage, for other vehicles it's fine but not great. The challenges you have to do to upgrade gear range from dull to frustrating, and are made even worse by the upgrade system's completely linear path, even though it looks like a tree in the menu. Story tries to be serious instead of the tongue-in-cheek of previous games. This falls flat on its face because a) Any seriousness of the cutscene I just watched is immediately dispelled by Rico slingshotting flaming soldiers through a helicopter's blades as he makes quippy one-liners, and b) It's not a very good story. The plot is contrived and predictable. The characters are clichéd, annoying, and just plain stupid in how they act. The final battle in the campaign is also really disappointing. Oh, and those story missions are all you get--JC2's side missions are gone.
I could overlook all of this if it wasn't for the map. It's so
compared to JC2's map, which is the same size. But even though there are much fewer bases, they're not any more differentiated than the bases in JC2. The map itself is also less varied; gone are the jungle and desert biomes of JC2, as are the unique terrain features of 2. JC3 has a winter/mountain biome, but it's only got one base in it. Also, despite Medici being this big tourist destination, unlike Panau, it DOESN'T HAVE A CIVILIAN AIRPORT. Arguably the single most entertaining location in JC2, with airliners to play around with, and it's not in the new game. This more than anything else makes JC3 look rushed and unfinished.

A "Paperwork simulator" sounds like a hard sell, but it's encouraging to see that word-of-mouth is getting people to try this wonderful little game out. It's refreshing to have something different for a change rather than another FPS, platformer or suchlike.
Your job is to give or refuse permission to enter your country to various people who come to your customs booth...... it is a hard sell, isn't it?
Okay then, your job is made more difficult in several ways. First of all, your bureaucratic government implements more and more rules as time goes on which means you have to be quicker and quicker at processing, without letting accuracy fall. Secondly, you have certain moral choices to make - you have to feed and warm your own family and that can only be done by processing people as quickly as possible. Well, unless they bribe you to let them in, or the guards bribe you to detain them or... and of course, there's always the risk of forged documentation [which you are punished for if you miss] or terrorist attack [which curtails the day].
This game is deeply engrossing. It's straightforward to begin with, but the difficulty curve is just right, adding complexity day by day - just as you master the rules something else comes along which you have to keep an eye out for. Added to the fact that there are MANY, MANY different possible endings will lead you to replay this several times in order to see what happens.
Well worth a try!

Tried this game at a friend's behest.  First impressions were nice.  The game is true to its Final Fantasy heritage, and provides the atmosphere you would expect from any FF title.  Graphics were great by MMO standards, but not really up to what you would expect from a current single player Square Enix game.  It sets up a nice story, tho the cutscenes all use in-game models and feel poorly acted/animated.  Overall the mood the game creates is a good one, and one I would enjoy playing in.
That is, if the gameplay itself were at all enjoyable.
As soon as I got into the combat, I immediately groaned.  It's WoW.  The game sticks to the most basic overdone combat system possible.  Target a thing.  Press your skill keys in rotation to damage it.  It starts autoattacking you.  You take damage from that.  You step outside the AoE markers to avoid taking any extra.  Eventually, one of you dies.  Repeat ad infinitum.  Dungeons follow the same formula too.  Tank soaks aggro because autoattacks are unavoidable, healer mitigates that incoming damage, everyone else kills the stuff that's focusing the tank.  Pull a wave, do that.  Pull another, do that.  Reach the boss, do that with a few extra distractions you need to run and deal with in between hitting it.
I wanted to love this game, but sticking in the most samey, widely cloned MMO combat system just leaves it lumped right in the same group as 90% of other MMOs out there.  Why?  They're capable of being innovative.  They could have just as easily made it into a XII-style open-world exploration into menu-based RPG encounters smooth transition, with options to allow nearby players to join in on the players' side and assist.  They could have done a lot of things.  They did not.  Instead, they stuck to the most basic formula possible.
Oh, and keep in mind it IS subscription based, tho they DO offer a discount if you limit yourself to 1 character (and since you can freely change between all the classes I see no reason for needing alts).
So my final score:
Atmosphere: 9/10
Graphics: 7/10
Sound: 7/10
Gameplay: WoW/10
Substitute in your own number for that based on how much you personally enjoy WoW-style combat.  For me it's a 1/10 on that, and since combat makes up a majority of the gameplay, whether hunting for levels, killing for quests, running a dungeon or raid, if you can't love the combat you can't love the game. I would maybe return to this for the sake of just hanging out with my friends if it were free to play, but I refuse to spend another penny on a game that cannot keep me entertained during the majority of its gameplay.
If you enjoy WoW and all of its clones, I do highly recommend this game to you.  If you're like me and are bored to tears of the same system being duplicated over and over for over a decade, stay away.

Gameplay:  Slow paced, immersive, and realistic.  The most realisticc hunting game I have ever played.  I have been hunting Whitetail for over 20 years of my life and this game has plenty of "game" to choose from.  With the ability to play with up to 7 others in multiplayer, it adds a whole new style of play with the ability to corner, trap, and ambush your prey.  They even bring up ethical hunting by limiting what caliber ammo you can use for each and every animal; this is a good practice and teaching tool for young ones or beginner hunters. Props for that.
Pros:
+Open World.
+Weapons and ammo coefficients are realistic
+Animals can see you, hear you, and smell you.
+Multiple play styles (Tracking, Stalking, Tree Stand, Tripods, Box Stand, Pop-up Blinds, Baiting).
+Everything from big game like Bison, all the way down to Rabbits and Pheasant.
+Shot placement matters.
+Multiple hunting areas designed around real habbitats from around the world.
Cons:
-When calling some animals they walk in a straight line to you and it makes it hard to get a broad side shot.
-Render distance on animals is ~220 meters.  (This is engine related, I don't think EW has control over it).
-So realistic that you even have pay for certain supplies with real money lol, they really need to reduce the cost for microtransactions (***See note at bottom of review***)

Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs is a major Step back from its predecessor: Amnesia The Dark Decent.
Sanity, Inventory, And Health are no longer present. In Amnesia:TDD, looking at a monster, hanging out in dark places or witnessing a disturbing event would lower your sanity. Completing objectives would raise your sanity. In the sequel that's no longer the case now. Health regenerates like in most first person shooters. Blood covers the screen, than slowly disappears as you recover. making the game unchallenging and easy to play.
The level design is stunning, But offers little in exploration. The game feels very confined and linear. Hidden notes are typically set right along the main path, making them almost impossible to miss. The monsters are scary, But encounters with them are rare, and very easy to avoid. Monsters typiccly patrol an area in a set pattern that is easily manuvered. The game is simply too easy and does not present any sort of challenge.
The Game also suffers from Performance issues on certain systems. I had my frame rate tank to horrendous values in some areas. Turning the settings as low as possible did not affect performance in anyway. The game is optimized very poorly.
Overall, Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs Is a big disappointment compared to the original Amnesia. I would not recommend this game.

A masterpiece that is definately worth playing. If you have followed the alien story line, you will not be dissapointed. I have to give credit to the visual effects department and the art directors, because the game looks amazing, but more importantly, it feels like you are playing inside the Alien timeline. The interiors and environments you play in feels just perfect. Think Stanley Kubrick's "2001: A Space Odyssee", but still staying true to the Alien look and feel.
The game itself is pretty decent. It's not a first person shooter by definition, so let's just get that out of the way. The game has a first person perspective, however, focuses more on non combat manouvers such as stealth gameplay, tools and crafting to make the game more interesting. The game has a thoughtful and interesting storyline and has a lot of dialogue and audio recordings to fill in the missing pieces. You also interact with the environment in somewhat interesting ways in order to complete missions. You will use "weapons" but only when you really have to. They have done a great job in keeping the game challenging. There is only so much you can do inside a spaceship and within the setting which the game takes place, and I think they have done a pretty good job in creating an immersive environment for players to explore, especially if you explore a little further. And let's be honest, it's an Alien game, it's suppose to follow the plot and setting of what we would expect from the Alien timeframe.
If people complain and say the game is boring or not challenging enough, they have obviously not played the game on the most difficult level (nightmare). It is incredably challenging and really difficult at times. There were times that I got frustrated because it was somewhat impossible to complete some of the missions on the most difficult setting, but it's not called nightmare mode for no reason.
If you are a fan of the Alien anthology, just play the game, it's awesome.

Pros so far:
-The game is pretty.
-The interface is fairly intuitve.
-Actually the map is bigger than I thought.  Much more so.
Cons so far:
-The interface is clunky.  It's not been optimized to be ergonomic.
-The tab interface takes up the whole screen.  I don't like this.
-When crafting, you cannot leave the full screen crafting UI.  I can see this being deadly if you're out in the wild.
-Switching out tools and weapons is somewhat tedious.
-There's not much to do.
-It's not overly obvious what to do to get started.  Just jump in and fiddle with it.
The cons are mainly because it is VERY early access.  I expect a lot of these things will improve.  Feedback is probably welcome by the devs as to how to optimize the game so the UI is friendly.  I got in cheap.  If I spend about another hour in it, I'll have got my money's worth.  Either way, it was only  $5.99 USD.
It has potential, but as with all potential, it can be wasted.
Funny thing:  I took a few pot shots at a deer.  I never saw it fall over dead, and I never got close enough to "use" it with the E key, but somehow I had a piece of stag meat in my pack.

It's a very fun game. It takes monotony and finds away to make it fun and you feel invested in what you're doing. You're scanning people's passports for errors using various tools as an immigration officer for a fictional Russian-like country.
For the most part it's pretty stright forward but as time goes on the things you have to look for become more numerous and more subtle raising the difficulty as time goes on. For every day you complete you get money. And with that money you decide which necessities your family can afford. Maybe today they get to eat. Tomarrow they may get some heat in your apartment so they don't freeze to death. Maybe your son needs medication or he won't make it through the night. Rarley will have enough to do everything and if you don't manage your funds it's very likley that some or all of your family will die.
But it's not all just checking passes and hoping your family doesn't die from having their basic needs go unforfilled. There is a bigger story happening and while you're never outright told if you fulfill certain requirements the story will turn down one of a handful of paths.
It's a very interesting game and I highly recommend it.

Tried this game at a friend's behest.  First impressions were nice.  The game is true to its Final Fantasy heritage, and provides the atmosphere you would expect from any FF title.  Graphics were great by MMO standards, but not really up to what you would expect from a current single player Square Enix game.  It sets up a nice story, tho the cutscenes all use in-game models and feel poorly acted/animated.  Overall the mood the game creates is a good one, and one I would enjoy playing in.
That is, if the gameplay itself were at all enjoyable.
As soon as I got into the combat, I immediately groaned.  It's WoW.  The game sticks to the most basic overdone combat system possible.  Target a thing.  Press your skill keys in rotation to damage it.  It starts autoattacking you.  You take damage from that.  You step outside the AoE markers to avoid taking any extra.  Eventually, one of you dies.  Repeat ad infinitum.  Dungeons follow the same formula too.  Tank soaks aggro because autoattacks are unavoidable, healer mitigates that incoming damage, everyone else kills the stuff that's focusing the tank.  Pull a wave, do that.  Pull another, do that.  Reach the boss, do that with a few extra distractions you need to run and deal with in between hitting it.
I wanted to love this game, but sticking in the most samey, widely cloned MMO combat system just leaves it lumped right in the same group as 90% of other MMOs out there.  Why?  They're capable of being innovative.  They could have just as easily made it into a XII-style open-world exploration into menu-based RPG encounters smooth transition, with options to allow nearby players to join in on the players' side and assist.  They could have done a lot of things.  They did not.  Instead, they stuck to the most basic formula possible.
Oh, and keep in mind it IS subscription based, tho they DO offer a discount if you limit yourself to 1 character (and since you can freely change between all the classes I see no reason for needing alts).
So my final score:
Atmosphere: 9/10
Graphics: 7/10
Sound: 7/10
Gameplay: WoW/10
Substitute in your own number for that based on how much you personally enjoy WoW-style combat.  For me it's a 1/10 on that, and since combat makes up a majority of the gameplay, whether hunting for levels, killing for quests, running a dungeon or raid, if you can't love the combat you can't love the game. I would maybe return to this for the sake of just hanging out with my friends if it were free to play, but I refuse to spend another penny on a game that cannot keep me entertained during the majority of its gameplay.
If you enjoy WoW and all of its clones, I do highly recommend this game to you.  If you're like me and are bored to tears of the same system being duplicated over and over for over a decade, stay away.

Ignore my gametime, I recently got the steam version of the game through Humble Bundle, I've been playing using the official launcher since January 2014 (Beta).
This is by far the best MMO on the market, as someone who's spent six to seven years playing the likes of WoW, SWTOR and every other mainstream MMO out there, none of them come close to the freedom and enjoyment I've gotten from ESO.
For Elder Scrolls fans the first thing you need to acknowledge is that this is an MMORPG, not a single player RPG. Whilst, yes, you can play the entire game alone if you so wish (It's what I mostly do), this isn't Elder Scrolls VI and it isn't trying to be.
That said I find the lore and story of ESO to be presented far better than in previous Elder Scrolls games where it was more of a side thing, ESPECIALLY IN THE DLC! (At least get Orsinium, it's about the same size as the Morrowind expansion and much cheaper). Ignore people who rip on it for a few minor errors with books, with every province in Tamriel to explore at least in part, this is the biggest chunk of lore we've gotten so far.
Speaking of provinces, you can't go everywhere, there's still a lot of the map left undiscovered. Indeed the only province that is 'complete' is Valenwood (Though the Summerset isles might be joining them if the rumors about the next expansion are true). And many of the places you can go are separated by loading screens, so it's not completely open world (This is due to technological limitations).
The endgame can be quite hard to get into due to the massive skill-gap between players but there's plenty of stuff to do as a casual, with over 300 hours+ worth of story content alone before DLC and the criminal system. You'll probably end up sinking more time into a single character than an entire playthrough of Skyrim.
On a minor note this game is huge and will take up a lot of storage on your hardrive.
Overall I heartily recommend this Elder Scrolls Online, it's come a long way since launch and definitely deserves another look if you didn't like it back then.

Best game based on a movie franchise ever. Not only it is a terrific survival horror, it also serves as a canon full-fledged sequel to the original movie, and surprisingly it works very well at that. Forget Prometheus, play this game instead.

Also have this game on PS3, and I gotta say this is an Alien game done right! It's dripping with atmosphere and the whole thing is a love letter to fans (which I am a huge fan) unlike Aliens Colonial Marines. This is a very heavy stealth oriented game, you do have weapons but you use them at your own perile as any noise will attract very unwanted attention, so it's best to have an escape plan before you act. The AI is the best I've ever seen (as far as the Alien), completely unpredictable and no patterns that you can use to your advantage whatsoever unless you're dealing with other humans or working joes. Alien deals one hit kills and you can't outrun it so don't even try, the only way you can fend it off is with a flame thrower or molotove cocktails. The story is the best one ever iterated in an Aliens game, following after the events of the first movie and before the second and ties into it without ruining the cannon unlike a certain someone *cough.. colonial marines cough..* and plays into the universe very well. The Alien also learns from your actions, use a tactic too much and it will pick up on it and act accordingly. Love how it doesn't rely on jumpscares and utilizes the tension in every good possible way, especially with the save system which can feel very rewarding to reach, also can cause some understandable frustration, there are no autosaves so that causes a lot of back tracking through sometimes legnthy sections, and with an unkillable and unpredictable enemy this will happen a lot. This game has a stunning attention to detail and if you're a fan of the franchise you will absolutely appreciate it. Some issuses are with lip syncing, they can be bad at times. I appreciate the filler sections that are there for mainly atmosphere and fans, legthening the amount of playtime but I can see it being a slight annoyance to others but I'm certainly not complaining, you get your money's worth here. Note that this game is stressful and you must have patience when you play, this is the furthest thing from running and gunning and breezing through sections, but with proper timing and skill you can make it past sections without taking too much time. Over all I reccomend this game to everyone who is a fan of the franchise and anyone who loves stealth based horror games, also I personally love that they got the original cast from the movies to take part in this game along with the DLC's it just adds to the overall experience. Also... NEVER RUN!!

Finally an Alien game that does the 1979 movie justice. It really feels like you're there.
I rewatched the movie after finishing the game and was very pleasantly surprised after seeing how accurately the game replicates the aesthetic from the movie. Environments, objects and characters are very clearly modeled after those from the movie.
With that said, the graphics are stunning and sound design is well done as well. Story is okay, not bad by any means, but nothing special either. Ending could've been better.
The gameplay is good and, like I said, really brings the atmosphere from the movie to the first person. However, the game is quite lengthy and it feels like it overstays its welcome. Instead of making it 18-20 hours, they should've cut out the filler parts and made it 10-12 hours.  I think it would work better that way because the longer the game, the more familiar you become with the alien. It stops being scary and becomes more of a nuisance, an annoying hurdle that needs to be passed. This is especially true when you get the flamethrower, it basically removes any remaining scare factor that alien used to have.
DLC is short and really nothing special, you won't miss anything if you skip it.
Bonus points for Linux support.

As a person who has always enjoyed a good western i have to say i had alot of fun with this game i cannot say i am familiar with the Call of Juarez series as a whole but i decided to buy this one and have found it to be very refreshing and enjoyable its not that often that you see many western games around so for a start i would recommend this game for a change of pace from the norm of games. Call of Jaurez Gunslinger has you take up the Bounty Hunting life of Silas Greaves who is equally skilled at Gunslinger and telling a good story in the local Saloon while downing a shot of Whisky.
Right away what i liked was the unique story telling approach that this game took with Silas telling his listeners what was happening and you then doing what he was saying and there were times when he would say he did something or fought someone and then the next he explains it differently and it takes you back to do it the next way he explains it. To me this was very different from how most games tell a story of there campaign and i found it very refreshing and interesting and just in general alot of fun.
In terms of actual gameplay its very straightfoward and uses the typical control style of most fps games so it was easy to jump into and start gunning down your foes. There were some really awesome features like dodging bullets and have a quickeye mode allowing you to shoot multiple targets quickly to some there features might seem abit gimicky but i can assure you that it does add some very fun elements to the game and you have to make use of them correctly to get your way through the tough spots.
Another nice feature is the upgrade system instead of just starting of the game and blazing your way through like alot of shooters you are offered to upgrade your character in certain areas like duel wielding pistols or taking a route down the rifle upgrade tree or shotgun this system allows you to develop your character to specilize in a specific are or you can disperse upgrades evenly its entirely up to you so you can go through each playthrough using a different setup for your character. There is also a unique system the game has when you have a classic western gunslinger duel and although the control system isnt perfect and at first is abit hard to get use to the duels are alot of fun in duel mode once you learn how to do them.
To bring up some negatives i was rather disapointed in the limited selection of weapons there are only about 3 pistols a rifle and a shotgun and although you can get upgraded versions of there weapons that have different visuals and amounts power and accuracy they are in essence the same weapons and as a result there isnt alot of variety there. Also even though the story is good to my mind its abit to short i was able to finish it on the standard difficulty in about 5 and a hald hours which is a little to short to my tastes but you could play on higher difficulties to make it more challenging and you could go around gathering all the collectables to increase that game length.
In terms of graphics and visuals its very beautiful with lots of great locations that help drive the story and immerse you in the gameplay ranging from old towns to forests and canyons to fighting in saloons and on trains so its very diverse which is fantastic. Another great feature i like was the addition of historical figures like Billy the Kid Butch Cassidy Sundance Kid and Jesse James and Silas's take on what he says really happens with these characters and his encounters and battles with them.
The Plot does possess a really nice twist to it which was nice when you got to the end and were able to enjoy it to sum up i do recommend this game as it is alot of fun and it does feel like a really great shooter even if it is abit short but i still think its worth it i give it a solid 6.5/10

Good:
(1) Fantastic aesthetics, looks beautiful throughout. Great use of music. Very immersive, enough so that I played the game straight through without pausing.
(2) The relationship between the main character and the dude in the sword is very well communicated. Plus, they don't neatly fit the usual guy / girl lead character tropes, so the story isn't as predictable as you'd expect. Yay!
(3) Some cool gameplay mechanics, especially the combat planning mode. Lots of ways to combine skills, especially when you go for new game plus and keep leveling your character. The last boss was completely unlike any other enemy in the game and actually required some deep thought to figure out a reliable solution to.
Some observations:
(1) It's obvious how OP Cull combined with the Void and Crash debuffs are. If you use the hiding skill beforehand, you can use Cull to one-shot each of the last boss's forms...
(2) You're practically forced to use combat planning attacks at every opportunity if you don't want to die over and over. It reminds me too much of how much of a crutch VATS was in the Fallout games...
(3) Unlocking parts of the story by having to use each ability in a different way didn't feel quite right, either. They could've tied some other non-story element to that mechanic, like bonus artwork or something...
Bad:
(1) Way too short, even for a game I bought on sale. Took me five hours. A good fifteen or so minutes of that was spent messing around with different skill combinations on the last boss.
(2) Losing your combat abilities when you "died" felt like an arbitrary punishment. If that's going to be a thing, then at least let us have our abilities back when the battle ends, and not two access terminals later. Going into the next fight without your best ability is basically death, anyways.
(3) There are a bunch of side characters in this game that don't get fleshed out enough.... and by that, I mean everyone that isn't Red or the dude in the sword.
Even worse:
The ending was a let down. She has the power of creation in her hands, and she does THAT with it? You've gotta be kidding me. If you can use the sword to command the robots to rebuild the city, you can command them to do other... favors... I won't say anything else due to spoilers but that was a really unsatisfying finish.
I'll recommend Transistor, but just barely: Only pull out your wallet if this game is on sale.

Now I mean no discredit to what this game does well. From the start, I felt motivated to explore and discover, and the entry puzzles of where are the switches were enjoyable and kept me intrigued. With this, I felt as though it was a complete and up to par game, unlike the original.
In the end, I don't recommend this game, unless you strictly enjoy sprinting carefree through a mysterious mansion flashing your lantern on and off, singing "Lights" by Ellie Goulding.

When I pressed "play" for the first time I really wanted to like this game. After all the reviews that I've read I was ready for everything and I wanted to approach the game with a free mind, enjoying what the game had to give me.
But even so, this game has a huge flaw. It's boring.
The mechanics of this game are quite non-existant. There's nothing you must do, no ability whatsoever, no thinking games or else. All the "puzzles" are senseless to the story, which is narrated ONLY by reading deluded notes and texts around the world. To understand what you have to do in a puzzle you have to read a text where the main character explains what to do and why... This to me is the hugest of the failures of the narration in this game.
On the technical aspect, the architecture of the places is redundant and boring. It's the same room repeated on and on, with some sporadical steampunk machine in the way. There rooms make no sense, it's not like you could actually feel that the place is living, you can't identify a kitchen, a salon, a living room... there are a few, key rooms, and the rest of them is kilometers of "what is this room for? why is there a chair here? what was the purpose of this place?". This was exactly the same flaw I've seen in the previous Amnesia and Penumbra games, with the difference that the atmosphere that the other games created was so much superior that you literally had no time to think about the flawed architecture of the places. But here... you don't have much to do than run from corridor to corridor trying to understand what you have to do next or what is the path the programmers have thought for you.
One last thing: complete darkness is not scary. It's fatiguing. If I have a torchlight in my hands I want to see where I'm going. Otherwise I'll just get motion sickness and eye strain. In this game all the lights are dead, they make no light at all, and even pumping up the gamma makes no difference whatsoever except painting a white coat all over the screen.
Conclusion: catch it if it's in a bundle, otherwise there are better games to play out there.

Bastion was a lovely surprise in the summer of 2011, easily weedling it's way to the very top of my list of favorite games. Supergiant Games was instantly put on my radar after their first game, so I was delighted to find out that they were making another game. However, I fell into this idea that it would just be impossible for them to make a game as memorable and creative as Bastion. I was very wrong. Transistor is simply a masterpiece.
Pros-
- Beautiful art direction and fluid animation
- Memorable characters and excellent voice work by Logan Cunningham
- Interesting combat with varied skills and combinations
- Satisfying progression
- Twists on gameplay via "Limiters"
- Quirky interactions between the main cast
- New Game Plus
- Great Developers
- Divine OST
Cons-
- Camera can (very rarely) be cumbersome due to architecture
- Story can be somewhat difficult to follow early on (didn't detract from my experience, though others may find it jarring)
- I wish there was more of it; completed my initial playthrough in roughly 6 1/2 hours.
In short: If you played Bastion and loved it, play Transistor. If you're looking for a game with great design and all around excellent craftsmanship, play Transistor. If you're looking for something different, play Transistor. And so, with all things said and done- play Transistor.

Play for the story and the creepy atmosphere. No horror game excels Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs in those regards.
IMPORTANT NOTE to anyone who has played Amnesia: The Dark Descent:
Please do not take this game as a sequel to Amnesia: The Dark Descent. What many people do wrong with this game is that they go with the mindset of the previous Amnesia - going for the horror.
Now, I'm not saying it's wrong to play horror games for the horror in them, and it definitely is not a surprise why people think of this as a sequel, what with the blaring "Amnesia" in the name. However, while the game does make an occasional reference to the original, it's significantly better to think of this as a stand-alone game.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent was made by Frictional Games. They have made a name for themselves by bringing back the horror in the horror genre. Their games have that creeping atmosphere that you can never be rid of. From Penumbra: Black Plague onwards, they took a theme of defenselessness, which definitely has been a big asset.
Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs was made by The Chinese Room. When Frictional Games thought about making a sequel to the Amnesia series, they decided to have an other company make it instead. Being impressed by Dear Esther, they approached The Chinese Room for sharing similar mindsets in their game development. Frictional Games did not want The Chinese Room to make a game that is similar to the original, they wanted them to make a game in their own way.
Two different companies make a game of the same world, with the same theme. It's obvious there'll be differences.
From Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, you'll get to experience a creepy, gross, horrifying story of a mad man trying to redeem himself.
From Amnesia: The Dark Descent, you'll get a full-blown horror blast in your face. Scrreeeaaaam.

I got this game in a bundle of others and for the longest time thought that it was a bit of a joke.
Checking passport numbers? pictures? stamping card? oh, what incredible fun </sarcasm>
Then, I played it...
Sure, memorising the countries, major towns, districts and keeping an eye on the date was a pain... but when sabotage, espionage, complicated underlying struggles of day-to-day life and the strange memory of my time doing similar things as an actual job... I am actually enjoying this game!
hang on, need to scan someone for a bomb because their weight does not add up to their ID card. Their city matches, but I saw them earlier with a fake passport! I need to make sure I don't let a terrorist through or it might be me they blow up next!
ACK! I didn't check the name on that last worker permit! After stuffing up the forged stamp on the other two, i'm getting my pay docked!
Thank goodness i'm in with a guard who'se cutting me a slice of his bonus for my arresting folks with illegal info or I wouldn't be able to feed my family, pay for my sick mother-in-law's medicine or keep the house warm... I'm trying to save up for a bigger apartment too, but I doubt i'm going to get enough money after that incident with the secret sect I turned in...
It's not for everyone, but if you have a halfway decent memory (or a handy note-book like me) you will do well from the get-go. Work fast, focus hard and provide for your family...
Stay sly, work on the side and crack the code given to you
be smart, keep yourself under the radar and don't get arrested.
Day by day, you will face discrete small-world problems... but other days, you may find you help make the news!
This is not your standard game. This is a bit of a work-sim! I think this should be played in schools to teach kids to spot-check info quickly. There's a strange beauty to this game!

Having put myself through DS1, I was expecting DS2 to be a complete pushover. I was wrong. Very wrong in fact, as I learned within the first ~10 hours of playing. Your character seems much more vulnerable and enemies far more aggressive, which actually makes the experience more enjoyable, once you get used to it...
The premise of the game is not dissimilar to DS1, or indeed any "Souls" game; free exploration of the game world with little initial explanation of the plot, and arguably the most flexible class/level-up system in all of gaming to allow the player to (attempt to) survive said world as they see fit. This game isn't really about its plot however, more about the challenge of surviving and exploring the game world; if plot is what you're after, play Witcher!
Some minor changes to gameplay have been made, but nothing too special or that hasn't been seen before from its predecessors (DeS, DS1).
+ Expansive game world with more aggressive AI than DS1; makes surviving areas/exploring/getting to places much more satisfying, world is more realised than DS1, more varied (particularly with DLC).
+ Character is more realistically vulnerable in this game.
+ Good level design linking areas together in unexpected ways, but sadly negated by "warp" system at bonfires.
+ Free choice of skillsets/weapons means great flexibility in how encounters can be tackled. No "right" way to play the game.
+ Some minor puzzle elements (particularly DLC), which were not expanded greatly upon.
- Game is not that different from predecessors; not particularly original plot, borrows heavily from other games in series (enemies and their animations, some bosses).
- Gameplay becomes predictable (yes, there is an enemy waiting around this corner too!); insults player's intelligence by overusing the same kind of tricks repeatedly.
- There are some elements of gameplay which are intended to be "innovative" but are actually just plain cheap (e.g. invisible enemies in a particular section).
- Bosses are much easier in this game compared to DS1, and as such do not really feel like "bosses" in the same sense; not memorable as in DS1 (for instance who could forget O&S?!). Indeed, some of the DS2 bosses are either direct copies or rip-offs. Additionally, more varied bosses would have been welcome, rather than mostly giant "blokes with swords".
If you own Demon Souls, or Dark Souls 1, there is no need to play this game really, with DeS being the best of the series. There is nothing truly new or original here in comparison; it is really just more of the same.

I have never found an MMO I enjoyed, but I love the Elder Scrolls games so I gave this one a shot.  What a waste of time and money.  It doesn't feel like an Elder Scrolls game at all.  In previous Elder Scrolls games, you are the main character in the story and your choices effect the world around you and the story that is being told.  When you complete a quest, it's unique; only you are able to rescue the missing girl, or return the stolen goods, or assassinate the political rival, etc.
In ESO, you're just one of many people all doing the same quests.  You see them doing the exact same quest you are doing.  They slay the mighty beast, and you have to wait for it to respawn so you can slay the mighty beast and finish the quest.  Watch out for the impatient players who will cut in line and make you wait again for the beast to respawn.  And watch out for players who will wait for the treasure to appear after you slay the mighty beast and they loot the chests before you get there.
You'll see dozens of players talking to inivisible NPC's, making them look like lunatics (or a game bug).  Then, once you finish the quest, it's your turn to look like the crazy person talking to nobody as you watch crowds of other players marching into the dungeon you just fought your way out of. The choices you make don't seem to have any noticable impact on the world.   There's just  no sense of immersion.
So in short, if you like MMO's, maybe you'll like ESO.  If you're looking for an immersive story where you get to be the hero (or villain) and your choices have consequences, skip this one.
Wanna live in a fantasy, but you don't like to be alone? This is for you.

I'm comparing this game to Rome total war 1.  Campaign wise, the game feels worse.  Generals are required to recruit units, and you can't recruit armies far away from your cities.  Other than that multiplayer is much better than Rome 1.  Rome 1 was much more imbalanced, with Urban cohort and praetorian cavalry spam, and with Rome and Egypt being the strongest factions.  Rome 2 has much better balance,  better graphics, and better historical authenticity (No more a historical ancient egyptian style graphics).  Initially there were problems with Rome 2's launch, but currently it feels much better now.  Just based on graphics and the historical setting alone, this ranks among the top total war games, probalby just behind shogun 2/Napoleon.
Big balance changes compared to Rome 1 mostly deals with changes with Cavalry.  In Rome 1, cavalry was really cheap, and did enormous damage.  In Rome 2, cav has been split into shock and melee cavalry.  Shock has large charge bonuis, while having weak melee combat, while melee cavalry have weak charge but are good in melee.  Cavalry costs have in generally been increased relatively 50% for heavy armored cavalry.  Changes are pretty fair though.

No More Room in Hell is a F2P survival horror game that seperates itself from your basic zombie massacre game as it mainly focuses on survival not killing. A few attacks from an enemy can take you out of the game as quick as it starts. This will resuslt in your former self coming back as an A.I controlled zombie which will attack fellow players. The game has "Objective" maps and "Survival" maps, Objective maps put the player in a situation where they must get from A to B, they will have to find keys, explosions, and shortcuts to get to their objective. Survival maps see the player protected different sites that are represented by letters. These sites have a set amount of health and can be compromised if too many zombies are in it. This is your basic defence mode. The game has a wide variety of maps and weapons, guns are hard to find and ammo is even harder. You'll mainly be using melee weapons in the game which means close combat with the undead. This game is a fantastic survival game and even does better than that of paid survival games. This game is definitely better with friends as it is intended to be a cooperative experience. I highly recommend this game for anyone who is looking for a good free survival horror game.

Hiding in a locker, I spy the alien got out of the room and dart to the right. So I emerge and move left.. moving slowly and watching my 6...looking behind myself as i move backwards.. In conclusion, after you reach your crew and have to find a medical kit to save one of them, this game takes a HUGE left turn into the abyss. Original review with 6hrs game time:
A VERY NICELY DONE Sci-Fi thriller with survival crazed humans taking pot shots at you,  spooky androids with glowing eyes looking to snap your neck, while telling you to calm down, and oh yeah,  a big alien hell bent on giving you a full frontal labotomy! The characters are both creepy and a bit scary.  The atmosphere is just about near perfect! Not too dark, but just enough to give you the willies, and not too bright to make stealth movement feel like stealth.  The graphics on ultra look very nice and fluid from the sweat on the realistic character skins to the steam venting from various pipes. From the jet like fire from the damaged space station structures to the water gushing from coolant lines.. the atmosphere and ambience is nice and works very well!  There are save points along the way that are spaced out enough to require a bit of effort to make it to a save point, but not too far apart to make hard parts cumbersome and too repetative. The story and voice acting are well done and make me want to learn more from the personal data terminals and tape recorders past the "need to know" info. I find that I am genuinely interested in how things progressed to the point that you find yourself trapped in it. You WILL jump.. if not from being spotted and shot to death by humans, or being apprehended and throttled by androids, or being dragged out of your hiding spot by the alien, then it will be for sheer joy at making a checkpoint unscathed.. Now you can unclentch your pooper and take a deep breath... You're just getting started!
There are light puzzles. The main part is figuring out what to do for them.  The text tips between checkpoints  flashes pretty fast, so unless you're a speed reader,  you probably wont catch it all. For each puzzle there are control instructions that gives a bit of a hint on how to solve them.   So far, they're not hard at all. After a fail or two, the sequence of events becomes more clear. I like that some of the puzzles I got right off while others I had to think about a little bit before having that "AHA!" moment.
You pick up things and craft bigger things from them with recipes/blueprints that you find along the way.. like a med kit..WHICH YOU WILL NEED, a flash bang and a few other goodies that I havent used yet. The crafting is pretty straight forward. You pull up your crafting guide where you assign needed elements for the object and then craft it.  You have a limited inventory so crafting things early, when you have the blueprint, is key to picking up more stuff along the way.
Combat so far has consisted of only beating the brains out of a few trigger happy humans with a very large wrench called a "maintenance jack".  They drop some pretty hefty revolvers in death but you can't pick them up.  You have to find a revolver just for you that you can carry. Although I'm not sure what good it is.. The alien is oblivious to it and two androids on two occassions took a full cylinder to the head and neck, pumped out a white substance and proceded to twist the head of my character around backwards...bone cracks and all..LOL.. it was awesome!
I thought I would check this title out and take a quick look at it.. LOL... That "quick look" turned into a 6hrs stretch of some really fun and engaging game play that I can hardly wait to get back to!
Fully Recommended!
